en: 1. Chapter on Dependent Origination, Part One: Chapter One of the First Division, translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang under Imperial Decree.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavat was staying at Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha.

He was accompanied by a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus, all of whom were arhats whose outflows were exhausted and who were free from further afflictions; they had attained true mastery, with minds well-liberated and wisdom well-liberated, like well-trained thoroughbred horses or great dragons; they had done what was to be done and accomplished what was to be accomplished; having laid down the heavy burden and attained their own benefit, they had exhausted the fetters of existence and were liberated through right knowledge, reaching the sovereign heart of the supreme ultimate.
With the exception of Ānanda alone, who remained on the stage of training and attained the fruit of stream-entry, Mahākāśyapa was the foremost.
Furthermore, there was a community of five hundred bhikṣuṇīs, all of whom were arhats, with Mahāprajāpatī as their leader.
Furthermore, there were immeasurable *upāsakas* and *upāsikās*, all of whom had seen the Noble Truths.

There were also immeasurable and incalculable assemblies of *bodhisattva-mahāsattvas*, all of whom had attained the gates of *dhāraṇī* and the gates of *samādhi*. They dwelt in emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*); they had already attained the patience regarding the equality of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-samatā-kṣānti*) and were fully accomplished in the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*). Their eloquence in exposition was inexhaustible, and they sported with mastery in the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).

The wisdom and abandonment they had realized were forever beyond regression; their speech and conduct were majestic and solemn, such that all who heard them received it with reverence. They were courageous and diligent, free from all laziness; able to renounce kin and wealth while disregarding their own bodies and lives; free from hypocrisy and deceit, untainted and without seeking; they impartially proclaimed the True Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.

They have entered deeply into the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*) and exhausted the most ultimate realms; having attained fearlessness, their minds are serene. They transcend the domains of all Māras and emerge from all karmic obstructions; they crush and destroy all enemies that are the afflictions (*kleśa*), raise the banner of the True Dharma, and subdue all heterodox arguments. Neither Śrāvakas nor Pratyekabuddhas can fathom them. They have attained mastery over the mind and mastery over the Dharma;

they are already liberated from the obstructions of karma, afflictions, and views. They are skillful and unerring in the analytical selection and exposition of phenomena. Having entered the profound gateway of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) regarding the dharma of arising and ceasing, they are free from views and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), have abandoned all fetters (*paryavasthāna*), and their wisdom penetrates the principles of the Noble Truths.

Throughout countless kalpas, he has made vast and solemn vows; his countenance is serene and joyful, and he is the first to speak in greeting others. He is far removed from frowning or scowling, and his speech is pure and harmonious. His eulogies are skillful and his eloquence is unimpeded; amidst boundless assemblies, his majestic virtue is solemn and awe-inspiring. He commands mastery in exalting and suppressing others, remaining entirely fearless, and for many koṭis of kalpas, he preaches with inexhaustible artistry.

Regarding all dharma-gates, he observes them with profound understanding: they are like illusions, like mirages, like dreams, like the moon reflected in water, like echoes, like flowers in the sky, like images, like shadows and light, like magical transformations, and like a city of Gandharvas—though none possess any reality, they appear as if they do.

Free from inferior states of mind, they preach the Dharma with fearlessness; they are able to realize and enter immeasurable Dharma-gates and skillfully know the mental activities and inclinations of sentient beings, delivering them through subtle wisdom.

Their minds are unimpeded toward all sentient beings, and they have accomplished the supreme *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena). They skillfully enter the wisdom of the equality of all dharmas and can know the profound nature of phenomena as it truly is. According to what is appropriate for each, they skillfully cause others to awaken and enter [the truth], and they are able to excellently expound the Dharma-gate of dependent origination.

They embrace the great vows for boundless Buddha-lands; throughout the worlds of the ten directions, the right mindfulness of countless Buddhas is ever-present before them. They are able to attend upon all Buddhas appearing in the world, and they also exhort them to turn the wheel of the true Dharma, never entering *parinirvāṇa* while delivering immeasurable multitudes.

He is skillfully able to subdue and extinguish the flames of the various afflictions and the entanglements of views of all sentient beings; in a mere moment, he sports in hundreds of thousands of samādhis, manifesting boundless and preeminent merits.
These bodhisattvas possess such an ocean of sublime merits that even if one were to praise them for immeasurable koṭis of great kalpas, one could never exhaust them.
Their names are:
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhadrapāla, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Ratnagotra, and the Bodhisattva Ratnagarbha.
the Mahāsattva, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Ratnadatta, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Nāyaka, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sūradatta,
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Jyotirdatta, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Devadatta,
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Viśālamati, and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vipulamati;
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Jñānavijaya, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Uttamajñāna,
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vardhamānajñāna, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Anantajñāna, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Amoghadarśin,
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Anāvaraṇajñāna, and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Suprasthita.
...the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Suvīra, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Ati-vīrya,
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Nitya-vīrya, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Nitya-prayoga, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Anikṣiptadhura,
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sūryagarbha, and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Candragarbha...
[Sarva-]buddha, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Anupamaprajña, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara,
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī,
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Ratnamudrāhasta, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mārabalapramardin, the Bodhisattva Vajraprajña...
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sāgaramati, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajragarbha, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Nityotkṣiptahasta,
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahākaruṇācitta, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāvyūha,
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vyūharāja, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Śikhara, and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Ratnaśikhara.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Guṇarāja, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya, and so forth—
immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, all of whom were Dharma-princes capable of succeeding to the rank of Buddha, acting as their leaders.

At that time, the World-Honored One, upon the lion throne, spread out his own sitting mat (niṣīdana) and sat cross-legged. With body upright and resolve firm, he dwelt in mindfulness directed toward the object before him and entered the sublime samādhi known as the King of Samādhis. All other samādhis were subsumed within this samādhi, for they are its outflow.

At that time, the World-Honored One, with perfect knowledge and mindfulness, arose calmly from the Samādhirāja-samādhi. With his pure divine eye, he surveyed the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; his entire body was filled with joy, and from the thousand-spoked wheel marks on the soles of both feet, he emitted sixty hundred thousand koṭi-nayuta rays of light each.

From his ten toes, both insteps, both heels, four ankles, two shins, two calves, two knees, two thighs, two hips, waist and ribs, abdomen and back, the center of the navel, the heart region, the *guṇa* letter on the chest, both breasts, both armpits, both shoulders, both scapulae, both elbows, both upper arms, both wrists, both hands, ten fingers, neck and throat, chin and jaw, cheeks and forehead, crown of the head, both eyebrows, both eyes, both ears, both nostrils, the four teeth of the mouth, forty teeth, and the *ūrṇā-kośa* between the brows—from each of these individual parts of the body, sixty hundred thousand *koṭi-nayuta* rays of light were emitted.

Each of these rays of light individually illuminates a trichiliocosm, and from there they spread successively to illuminate as many Buddha-worlds in the ten directions as there are sands in the Ganges; any sentient being who encounters this light will surely attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

At that time, every pore of the World-Honored One’s body was filled with a joyful radiance, and from each emerged sixty hundred thousand koṭi-nayuta rays of light. Each of these individual rays illuminated a trichiliocosm, and from there they spread successively until they pervaded Buddha-worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions. Any sentient being who encountered this light would certainly attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

At that time, the World-Honored One emanated from his body a constant radiance that illuminated this trichiliocosm; from there, it spread successively until it pervaded the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Any sentient beings who encountered this light were certain to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
At that time, the World-Honored One extended his broad and long tongue from his mouth, completely covering the trichiliocosm, and smiled with a serene joy.

Furthermore, from his tongue-mark, there flowed forth immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of light rays of various colors. From each of these multicolored light rays appeared precious lotus flowers; each flower had a thousand petals, was the color of pure gold, and was adorned with various jewels. They were exquisitely decorated, radiant, and most delightful to behold. Their fragrance was intense, wafting and pervading everywhere. Their texture was fine, smooth, light, and soft, producing sublime bliss upon contact. Within the calyx of every flower sat an emanation Buddha in the full lotus posture, proclaiming the sounds of the wondrous Dharma. Each of these Dharma sounds expounded teachings corresponding to the Prajñāpāramitā; any sentient being who hears them will surely attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
From this point on, the teaching spread successively throughout the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, benefiting beings in the same manner.

At that time, the World-Honored One, without rising from his seat, again entered the *siṃhavikrīḍita* (Lion’s Play) samādhi and manifested supernormal powers, causing this trichiliocosm to undergo six kinds of movement:

namely, shaking, intense shaking, and extreme shaking; surging, intense surging, and extreme surging; quaking, intense quaking, and extreme quaking; crashing, intense crashing, and extreme crashing; roaring, intense roaring, and extreme roaring; and bursting, intense bursting, and extreme bursting.

Furthermore, he caused this world-system to surge up in the east and subside in the west, surge up in the west and subside in the east, surge up in the south and subside in the north, surge up in the north and subside in the south, surge up in the center and subside at the edges, and surge up at the edges and subside in the center.
The ground was pure, radiant, fine, and soft, bringing benefit and happiness to all sentient beings.

At that time, all sentient beings within this trichiliocosm—including those in the realms of hell, animals, hungry ghosts, and other perilous, unfavorable states—were entirely freed from suffering and hardship. Having passed away from those states, they were reborn among humans and the six heavens of the desire realm; all of them remembered their past lives and, leaping for joy, went together to the Buddha’s dwelling, where with deep and pure hearts they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet.

From there, it spread successively throughout the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, with six kinds of miraculous transformations through the Buddha’s spiritual power.

At that time, all sentient beings in the evil realms and elsewhere within those worlds were freed from suffering and hardship; they passed away from those states and were reborn among humans and in the six heavens of the desire realm. All of them remembered their past lives and, leaping for joy, traveled together from their respective realms to the presence of the Buddha, where they prostrated at his feet.

At that time, throughout this trichiliocosm and other worlds in the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, sentient beings were transformed: the blind could see, the deaf could hear, the mute could speak, the insane regained their mindfulness, the distracted attained concentration, the poor obtained wealth, the naked obtained clothing, the hungry obtained food, the thirsty obtained drink, the sick were healed, the ugly became handsome, the deformed became whole, those with impaired faculties became complete, the bewildered and fainting regained consciousness, and the exhausted found rest and comfort.

At that time, all sentient beings turned their minds toward one another, regarding each other as fathers and mothers, elder and younger brothers, elder and younger sisters, friends, and kin. They abandoned wrong speech, action, and livelihood, and cultivated right speech, action, and livelihood; they abandoned the ten paths of unwholesome action and cultivated the ten paths of wholesome action; they abandoned evil thoughts and cultivated wholesome thoughts; they abandoned non-celibate conduct and cultivated pure celibacy. Delighting in purity and discarding filth, finding joy in stillness and abandoning clamor, their bodies and minds became serene, and a wondrous bliss suddenly arose within them, like that of a practitioner entering the third dhyāna.
Furthermore, a superior wisdom suddenly manifested before them, and they all thought:

"Generosity, self-discipline, patience, diligence, tranquility, and discernment; being free from negligence and practicing the holy life; and maintaining loving-kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity toward all sentient beings without mutual disturbance—how excellent this is!"

At that time, the World-Honored One sat upon the lion throne, his radiance extraordinary and his majestic virtue towering high. He eclipsed the trichiliocosm as well as the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; Mount Sumeru, the Cakravāḍa mountains, and all other palaces of nāgas, devas, and even those of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens were entirely obscured and no longer visible.

He was like the full autumn moon outshining the host of stars, like the summer sun’s orb whose brilliance overwhelms all colors, and like the Great King of Mountains, the four-jeweled Sumeru, whose majestic light towers far above all other peaks as it shines down upon them.
By means of his supernatural power, the Buddha manifested his original physical body so that all sentient beings throughout this trichiliocosm could behold it.
At that time, the immeasurable and innumerable devas of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens,
down to the Cāturmahārājika heaven of the desire realm, as well as all others— both humans and non-humans— saw him.
The Tathāgata sat upon the lion throne, his majestic radiance shining like a great mountain of gold;
filled with joy and leaping for gladness, they marveled at this unprecedented event, each holding various and immeasurable celestial flowers,
fragrant garlands, ointments, incense, powdered incense, robes, necklaces, precious banners, flags, canopies, and musical instruments.
Various treasures, as well as immeasurable kinds of celestial blue lotuses,
celestial red lotuses, celestial white lotuses, celestial fragrant lotuses, celestial yellow lotuses, celestial red lotuses,
celestial *dīnāra* tree flowers, and celestial fragrant leaves, along with other immeasurable flowers born of water and land, he took and went to the Buddha.
They scattered these offerings over the Buddha.

By the Buddha’s supernatural power, the various flower garlands and other items whirled upward and merged to form a flower pedestal, equal in size to the trichiliocosm. Heavenly flower canopies, jeweled bells, and pearl banners hung down from it, their exquisite decorations swirling in profusion, most delightful to behold.
At that time, this buddha-field was exquisitely adorned, just like the Western World of Ultimate Bliss.

The radiance of the Buddha’s light illuminated the myriad things of the trichiliocosm, and the entirety of space became the color of gold; it was likewise so in all the buddha-worlds of the ten directions, each as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River.

At that time, throughout this trichiliocosm—namely Jambudvīpa in the south, Pūrvavideha in the east, Aparagoyānī in the west, and Uttarakuru in the north—all the people therein, through the Buddha’s spiritual power, each saw the Buddha sitting directly before them, and everyone thought, "The Tathāgata is teaching the Dharma to me alone."

In this manner, the gods of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, the Paranirmitavaśavartin Heaven, the Brahmakāyika Heaven, the Brahmapurohita Heaven, the Mahābrahma Heaven, the Parīttābha Heaven, the Apramāṇābha Heaven, the Ābhāsvara Heaven, the Parīttaśubha Heaven, the Apramāṇaśubha Heaven, the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven, the Bṛhatphala Heaven, the Avṛha Heaven, the Atapa Heaven, the Sudṛśa Heaven, the Sudarśana Heaven, and the Akaniṣṭha Heaven—by the supernatural power of the World-Honored One, each saw the Buddha sitting directly before them, and all thought that the Tathāgata was preaching the Dharma to them alone.

At that time, the World-Honored One did not rise from his seat; with a serene smile, he emitted a great radiance from the gate of his face, which shone throughout the trichiliocosm and all other Buddha-worlds in the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

At that time, all sentient beings within this trichiliocosm Buddha-field, following the Buddha’s light, universally beheld in the ten directions all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas—equal in number to the sands of the Ganges River—surrounded by assemblies of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas, as well as all other distinct categories of sentient and insentient beings.

At that time, all sentient beings in the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, following the Buddha’s light, also beheld this land and Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, surrounded by an assembly of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas, as well as all other categories of sentient and insentient beings.

At that time, in the eastern direction, throughout as many worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, there was a final world named Ratnāvatī. There dwelt the Buddha named Ratnagotra Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed Worthy One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, Bhagavān. At that time, he was currently residing there in peace and stability, teaching the Great Prajñāpāramitā to the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.

In that world there was a bodhisattva named Samantaprabha. Seeing this great light, the trembling of the great earth, and the marks of the Buddha’s body, his mind was filled with uncertainty; he went before the Buddha, prostrated at his feet, and said:
“World-Honored One!
"By what cause and by what condition has this auspicious omen appeared?
At that time, the Buddha Ratnagotra addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantaprabha, saying:
"O son of good family!"

From here, to the west, across as many worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, there is a final world named Sahā. There resides the Buddha Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed Leader, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, Bhagavān. He currently dwells there in peace and security, and for the sake of the assembly of Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas, he is about to preach the Great Prajñāpāramitā; it is by the spiritual power of that Buddha that this auspicious sign has appeared.
Having heard this, Samantaprabha was filled with joy and leaped for gladness; he addressed the Buddha again, saying:
“World-Honored One!

I now request to go to the Sahā world to behold, pay homage to, and make offerings to the Tathāgata Śākyamuni and the assembly of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who have attained the *dhāraṇī* gates and *samādhi* gates of unimpeded understanding, as well as those who possess mastery over supernormal powers and dwell in their final bodies as heirs to the sovereign position.”
“I only pray that you will, out of compassion and pity, grant me your permission!
At that time, the Buddha Ratnagotra addressed the Bodhisattva Samantaprabha, saying: “Excellent!
"Excellent!
Now is precisely the right time; go as you intend.
He then took a thousand golden lotus flowers, each with a thousand petals and adorned with various jewels, and bestowed them upon Samantaprabha Bodhisattva, instructing him thus:
"Take these flowers to the place where Śākyamuni Buddha resides and speak these words on my behalf:
'The Tathāgata Ratnagotra sends his greetings to you in measureless abundance:
Are you free from illness and affliction? Is your daily life light and easy? Are your physical strength and vitality harmonious? Do you dwell in peace and happiness?'"
"Are the affairs of the world endurable?
Are sentient beings easy to deliver?
I hold this lotus flower to entrust it to the World-Honored One as a Buddhist service."

"When you arrive in that realm, you should abide in right mindfulness and clearly comprehend it; observe that buddha-field and the great assembly, and do not harbor thoughts of contempt or self-deprecation. Why is this so?"
"The majestic power of those bodhisattvas is difficult to equal; with compassion and vows perfuming their hearts, they have been born in that land for great causes and conditions.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Samantaprabha accepted the flowers and received the command. Together with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of monastic and lay bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, as well as countless hundreds of thousands of boys and girls, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him to the right, and took his leave. Each carrying immeasurable varieties of flowers, incense, precious banners, pennants, canopies, robes, jeweled ornaments, and other offerings, they set out. As they passed through the Buddha-worlds of the eastern direction, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, they made offerings, paid homage, showed respect, and offered praise at each and every Buddha’s abode, never passing by without doing so.
Arriving at the presence of the Buddha, they prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him hundreds of thousands of times, and then withdrew to stand to one side.
The Bodhisattva Samantaprabha came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

From here, to the east, across as many worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, there is a final world named Prabhūta-ratna. There dwells a Buddha named Ratnākara Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed Worthy One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, Bhagavān.

He sends his greetings to the Blessed One, inquiring whether you have little illness and little affliction, whether your daily life is light and easy, whether your physical strength is harmonious, and whether you dwell in peace and happiness.
"Are the affairs of the world endurable?
Are sentient beings easy to deliver?
I offer these thousand-stalked golden lotuses to the World-Honored One as a Buddhist service."
Then, Śākyamuni Buddha accepted these lotuses and scattered them back toward the eastern buddha-worlds, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

Through the Buddha’s spiritual power, these lotuses pervaded all those buddha-fields; within each lotus calyx, there appeared a transformation Buddha seated in the full-lotus posture, preaching the Dharma associated with the Great Prajñāpāramitā to the bodhisattvas. Any sentient beings who heard it would certainly attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

At that time, when Samantaprabha and his retinue saw this event, they were filled with joy and leaped for gladness, exclaiming that it was unprecedented. Each, according to their own roots of goodness and the extent of their offerings, made offerings, paid homage, showed respect, and praised the Buddha and the bodhisattvas; having done so, they withdrew and sat to one side.
In this manner, prior to the final world, in each and every buddha-field to the east, there was a Tathāgata manifesting before a great assembly to proclaim the sublime Dharma.

In each of those buddha-fields, there was likewise a preeminent bodhisattva who, seeing this great radiance, the trembling of the earth, and the marks of the Buddha’s body, approached the Buddha and said:
“World-Honored One!
"By what cause and by what condition has this auspicious omen appeared?

At that time, each of those Buddhas replied individually, "In the western direction there is a world called Sahā, where the Buddha is named Śākyamuni. He is about to preach the Great Prajñāpāramitā to the bodhisattvas; it is through the spiritual power of that Buddha that this auspicious omen has been manifested."
Upon hearing this, the leading bodhisattvas were filled with joy and each requested to go to the Sahā world to behold, pay homage to, and make offerings to the Buddha and the bodhisattvas there.
Those Tathāgatas praised them for their readiness to go and, each offering a thousand-jeweled golden lotus flower, addressed them, saying:
"Take these and go to the presence of that Buddha; speak my words to him in full detail:"
"I send you my greetings and inquire after your well-being:
Are you free from illness and affliction? Is your daily life light and easy? Are your physical strength and vitality harmonious? Do you dwell in peace and happiness?
Can you endure the affairs of the world?"
"Are the sentient beings there easy to deliver?
Take these lotus flowers to entrust to the World-Honored One as a Buddha-activity.

"When you arrive in that realm, you should abide in right mindfulness, observing that Buddha-land and its bodhisattvas; do not harbor thoughts of contempt or disparagement, lest you bring harm upon yourself."
Why is this? Because those bodhisattvas possess a majestic virtue difficult to equal; with compassion and vows perfuming their minds, they have been born in that land due to great causal conditions.

One by one, the leaders accepted the flowers and received the command, each accompanied by immeasurable and innumerable bodhisattvas, boys, and girls. They took leave of the Buddha, carrying offerings and setting forth, making offerings to every Buddha and bodhisattva in each successive buddha-field they passed through, without missing a single one.
Arriving at the place where the Buddha was, they prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him hundreds of thousands of times, and offered flowers while presenting their business.

Having accepted the flowers, the Buddha scattered them back toward the eastern direction; through the Buddha’s supernormal power, they pervaded all buddha-fields. Within each flower pedestal there appeared a transformation Buddha, who preached the Great *Prajñāpāramitā* for the bodhisattvas, so that all who heard it would surely attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

The leading bodhisattvas and their retinues, having seen this, were filled with joy and marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence. Each, according to the extent of their own roots of goodness and the number of offerings they possessed, made offerings, paid homage, showed respect, and offered praise to the Buddhas and bodhisattvas; having done so, they withdrew and sat to one side.

At that time, to the south, beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there was a final world named Free from All Sorrow (*Sarva-śoka-vigata*). There, the Buddha known as Aśoka-guṇa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed Worthy, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, Bhagavān, currently dwelt in peace and stability, teaching the Great Prajñāpāramitā to a multitude of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.

In that place there was a bodhisattva named Vigatāśoka. Seeing this great radiance, the trembling of the earth, and the marks of the Buddha’s body, his mind was filled with uncertainty; he approached the Buddha, prostrated at his feet, and said:
“World-Honored One!
"For what cause and for what reason has this auspicious omen appeared?
At that time, the Buddha Aśokaguṇa addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vigatāśoka, saying: "Good son!"

From here to the north, extending through worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there is a final world named Sahā. There dwells the Buddha Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed Leader of Men, Tamer of Beings, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, Bhagavān. He currently resides there in peace and security, and for the sake of the assembly of Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas, he is expounding the Great Prajñāpāramitā; it is by the supernatural power of that Buddha that this auspicious omen has appeared.
Having heard this, Vigataśoka was filled with joy and leaped for gladness; he addressed the Buddha once more, saying:
"World-Honored One!

Chapter Two: Training in Contemplation, Part One.

At that time, the Blessed One, knowing that all those in the various worlds—whether gods, Māras, or Brahmās; whether śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas; whether gandharvas or asuras; whether nāgas, yakṣas, or other spirits; whether the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas dwelling in their final bodies who have succeeded to the rank of the Honored One; or all others, human or non-human, who had a karmic connection with the Dharma—had gathered together, addressed the Venerable Śāriputra, saying:
"If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva wishes to perfectly awaken to all phenomena in all their aspects, he should train in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā)."

At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, Śāriputra was filled with joy and exultation; he immediately rose from his seat, approached the Buddha, prostrated at his feet, bared his right shoulder while covering his left, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined in reverence, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
“How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to fully awaken to all phenomena in all their aspects study the perfection of wisdom?
The Buddha addressed the venerable Śāriputra, saying: “Śāriputra!”

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should, by means of non-abiding as their skillful method, dwell in the perfection of wisdom, because neither that which is dwelled upon nor that which dwells can be apprehended.
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should fulfill the perfection of generosity by means of non-renunciation, because the giver, the recipient, and the gift cannot be apprehended.

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should fulfill the perfection of ethical discipline by means of non-protection, because neither the characteristics of transgression nor those of non-transgression can be apprehended.

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should fulfill the perfection of patience by means of non-appropriation, because neither the characteristic of movement nor the characteristic of immovability can be apprehended.
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should fulfill the perfection of diligence by employing non-exertion as their skillful means, because physical and mental exertion or indolence are unapprehendable.

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should fulfill the perfection of meditative concentration by means of non-conceptualization, because neither the presence of flavor nor the absence of flavor can be apprehended.
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should fulfill the perfection of wisdom by means of non-attachment, because the intrinsic nature and characteristics of all phenomena cannot be apprehended.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, bodhisattva mahāsattvas dwelling in the perfection of wisdom,

by means of non-apprehension as their expedient, should fulfill the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path, because these thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are unapprehendable."

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, dwelling securely in the perfection of wisdom, should, by means of non-apprehension as their expedient, fulfill the gate of liberation of emptiness, the gate of liberation of signlessness, and the gate of liberation of wishlessness, because these three gates of liberation cannot be apprehended.

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, dwelling securely in the perfection of wisdom, should, by means of non-apprehension as their skillful method, fulfill the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments, because these dhyānas, immeasurables, and formless attainments are unapprehendable.

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, dwelling in the perfection of wisdom, should, by means of non-apprehension as their skillful method, fulfill the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten totalities; for liberation, the bases of mastery, the meditative attainments, and the totalities are unapprehendable.

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, dwelling securely in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), by means of the expedient of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), should fulfill the nine perceptions (*navasaṃjñā*). These are: the perception of bloatedness (*vyādhmātaka-saṃjñā*), the perception of festering pus (*vipūyaka-saṃjñā*), the perception of bloody disfigurement (*vilohitaka-saṃjñā*), the perception of bluish discoloration (*vinīlaka-saṃjñā*), the perception of being devoured (*vikhādita-saṃjñā*), the perception of dismemberment (*vikṣiptaka-saṃjñā*), the perception of skeletons (*asthi-saṃjñā*), the perception of burning (*vidagdhaka-saṃjñā*), and the perception that all worlds are unreliable (*sarvalokānāśvāsika-saṃjñā*); for such perceptions are ultimately unapprehendable.

“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, dwelling in the perfection of wisdom, by means of non-apprehension as their skillful method, should fulfill the ten recollections: namely, the recollection of the Buddha, the recollection of the Dharma, the recollection of the Saṅgha, the recollection of ethical discipline, the recollection of relinquishment, the recollection of the devas, the recollection of inhalation and exhalation, the recollection of disenchantment, the recollection of death, and the recollection of the body; for these recollections are unapprehendable.”

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, dwelling securely in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), should fulfill the ten perceptions by means of non-apprehension as their skillful method. These are: the perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering, the perception of non-self, the perception of impurity, the perception of death, the perception that all worlds are not to be delighted in, the perception of revulsion toward food, the perception of abandonment, the perception of detachment, and the perception of cessation; for such perceptions are themselves unapprehendable.

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, dwelling in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), by means of the expedient of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), should fulfill eleven knowledges: namely, the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*), the knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*), the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*), the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*), the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*), the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*), the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), and the knowledge of how things are spoken of (*yathā-vāda-jñāna*). This is because such knowledges are unapprehendable.

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, dwelling in the perfection of wisdom, by means of non-apprehension as their expedient, should fulfill the samādhi with vitarka and vicāra, the samādhi without vitarka and with only vicāra, and the samādhi without vitarka or vicāra, because these three types of concentration are unapprehendable.

“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, dwelling in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), by means of non-apprehension as their skillful method, should fulfill the faculty of ‘I shall come to know the unknown,’ the faculty of ‘knowing,’ and the faculty of ‘one who has known,’ because such faculties are unapprehendable.”

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, dwelling securely in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), by means of the expedient of non-apprehension, should fulfill the contemplation of the impure, the contemplation of pervasive filling, all-knowledge (sarvajñajñāna), as well as śamatha and vipaśyanā; for these five kinds [of phenomena] are unapprehendable.

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, dwelling securely in the perfection of wisdom, should, by means of non-apprehension as their skillful method, fulfill the four means of attraction, the four sublime abodes, the three types of clear knowledge, the five eyes, the six supernormal powers, and the six perfections; for these six kinds of things are unapprehendable.

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, dwelling securely in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), by means of the method of non-apprehension, should fulfill the seven noble riches, the eight great personages' awakenings, the knowledge of the nine abodes of sentient beings, the doors of dhāraṇī, and the doors of samādhi; for these five kinds [of phenomena] are unapprehendable.

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, dwelling securely in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), should fulfill the ten stages (bhūmi), the ten practices (caryā), the ten patiences (kṣānti), and the twenty superior intentions (adhyāśaya) by means of non-apprehension; for these four types are unapprehendable.

“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, abiding in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), by means of the expedient of non-apprehension, should fulfill the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, the thirty-two marks of a great man, and the eighty secondary signs; for these six types of things are unapprehendable.”

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, dwelling securely in the perfection of wisdom, by means of the expedient of non-apprehension, should fulfill the quality of non-forgetfulness, the state of constant equanimity, all-knowledge, the knowledge of the aspects of the path, the knowledge of all aspects, and the subtle knowledge of all aspects; for these six dharmas are unapprehendable.

All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, dwelling securely in the perfection of wisdom, should, by means of non-apprehension as their skillful method, fulfill great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity, as well as other immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas; for such dharmas are unapprehendable.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), they should train in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā)."

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to swiftly fulfill all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), they should study the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to swiftly perfect the knowledge of the mental activities of all sentient beings and the subtle knowledge of all aspects, they should study the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to uproot all habitual tendencies of the afflictions, they should study the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to enter the bodhisattva’s state of right determination and departure from birth (samyaktvaniyāma), they should study the perfection of wisdom.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to transcend the stages of the śrāvaka and the pratyekabuddha, they should train in the perfection of wisdom.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to abide in the stage of non-retrogression of a bodhisattva, they should train in the perfection of wisdom.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain the six kinds of swift supernatural powers, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to know the distinctions in the mental activities and inclinations of all sentient beings, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to surpass the wisdom and activity of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, they should train in the perfection of wisdom.”
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain all the gates of dhāraṇī and the gates of samādhi, they should study the perfection of wisdom.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to surpass, with a single thought-moment accompanied by sympathetic joy, all the generosity of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, they should study the perfection of wisdom.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes, with a single moment of mind accompanied by sympathetic joy, to surpass all the pure ethical discipline of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, they should train in the perfection of wisdom.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes, with a single thought-moment accompanied by sympathetic joy, to surpass all the concentration, wisdom, liberation, and knowledge and vision of liberation of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, they should train in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes, with a single moment of mind accompanied by sympathetic joy, to surpass all the meditative concentrations, liberations, samādhis, and meditative attainments of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, as well as all other wholesome dharmas, they should train in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes, by means of the wholesome dharmas cultivated in a single thought-moment, to surpass all the wholesome dharmas of ordinary beings, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas, they should study the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to practice even a small portion of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, and through skillful means dedicates these for the sake of all sentient beings toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, they shall obtain immeasurable and boundless merit; such a one should study the perfection of wisdom.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,

if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to cause the practice of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom to be free from all obstacles and swiftly reach fulfillment, they should study the perfection of wisdom."

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to see the Buddhas in every lifetime, to constantly hear the true Dharma and attain the awakening of a Buddha, and to receive the Buddhas' mindfulness, instructions, and guidance, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain the body of a Buddha, complete with the thirty-two marks of a great man and fully adorned with the eighty secondary characteristics, they should study the perfection of wisdom.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to constantly remember their past lives in every lifetime, never forget the mind of great enlightenment (*mahābodhicitta*), stay far removed from evil friends and draw near to virtuous friends, and perpetually cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, they should study the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to possess great majesty and virtue in every lifetime, to crush the hosts of Māras and enemies, and to subdue all non-Buddhists, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to remain far removed from all afflictions and karmic obstructions in every lifetime, and to penetrate all phenomena with a mind free of hindrance, they should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain the continuity of a virtuous mind, virtuous aspirations, and virtuous conduct in every lifetime, always without slackening or abandonment, they should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.”

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to be born into the family of the Buddhas and enter the stage of the youthful truth (kumārabhūmi), and desires never to be separated from the Buddhas and bodhisattvas, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to be endowed with all the primary and secondary marks in every lifetime, to be as dignified and majestic as a Buddha so that all sentient beings who see him rejoice, to give rise to the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and to be able to swiftly accomplish the merits of all Buddhas, they should study the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes, by means of the power of various superior roots of goodness, to be able to produce supreme and exquisite offerings at will to honor, revere, respect, and praise all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and desires to cause those roots of goodness to be swiftly perfected, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to fulfill all the needs of sentient beings for food and drink, clothing, beds, bedding, medicinal requisites for sickness, various flowers and incense, lamps, vehicles, gardens, houses, wealth and grain, rare treasures, ornaments, music, and other such various superior and exquisite articles of enjoyment, they should study the perfection of wisdom.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,

if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to skillfully establish all sentient beings throughout the entirety of space, the dharma-realm, and all worlds, causing them all to abide in the perfection of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, they should study the perfection of wisdom."

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to obtain the merit generated by a single thought of virtue, such that it remains inexhaustible until they sit upon the sublime seat of awakening and realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should train in the perfection of wisdom.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to be praised by all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and the assemblies of bodhisattva mahāsattvas throughout the worlds of the ten directions, they should study the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to be able, with a single arousal of the mind, to reach everywhere throughout the worlds of the ten directions—each as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—to make offerings to the Buddhas and to bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings, they should study the perfection of wisdom.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to be able, with a single utterance, to pervade as many worlds in each of the ten directions as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, praising the Buddhas and instructing sentient beings, they should study the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes, in a single moment of thought, to establish all sentient beings in as many Buddha-worlds of the ten directions as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, causing them all to practice and study the path of the ten virtuous actions, to receive the three refuges, and to uphold the prohibitive precepts, they should train in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes, in a single moment of thought, to establish all sentient beings in as many Buddha-worlds in the ten directions as there are sands in the Ganges River, causing them all to practice and study the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless absorptions, and to attain the five supernormal powers, they should study the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes, in a single moment of thought, to establish all sentient beings in as many Buddha-worlds of the ten directions as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, causing them to abide in the Mahāyāna, practice the conduct of a bodhisattva, and not disparage other vehicles, they should study the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to succeed to the lineage of the Buddhas so that it remains unbroken, to protect the family of bodhisattvas so that they do not regress, and to adorn and purify the buddha-fields so that they are swiftly accomplished, they should study the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to penetrate inner emptiness,

outer emptiness, inner-and-outer emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common-characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, they should train in the perfection of wisdom."

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to penetrate the suchness of all phenomena, the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, the non-erroneous nature, the unchanging nature, the state of equality, the nature of freedom from birth, the fixedness of dharmas, the stability of dharmas, the limit of reality, the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm, they should study the perfection of wisdom.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to penetrate the exhaustiveness of all phenomena (yāvadbhāvikatā) and their suchness (yathāvadbhāvikatā), they should study the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to penetrate the nature of all phenomena as the causal condition, the immediately preceding condition, the object-condition, and the dominant condition, they should train in the perfection of wisdom.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to penetrate the fact that all phenomena are like illusions, like dreams, like echoes, like images, like reflections, like mirages, like flowers in the sky, like cities of Gandharvas, and like magical transformations—all of which are manifestations of mind alone, empty in both nature and characteristics—they should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to know the most minute particles within the trichiliocosm—the empty space, the great earth, the various mountains, the great oceans, rivers, ponds, mountain torrents, valleys, marshes, lakes, and the elements of earth, water, fire, and wind—they should study the Prajñāpāramitā."

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to split a single hair into a hundred parts and, taking one such part, lift all the waters of the great oceans, rivers, ponds, streams, valleys, marshes, and lakes of the trichiliocosm and cast them away into other boundless worlds, yet do so without distressing or harming the aquatic creatures, they should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva sees the kalpa-fire burning throughout the trichiliocosm, with heaven and earth ablaze, and wishes to extinguish it all at once by blowing upon it with a single breath, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva sees the wind-circle upon which the trichiliocosm rests surging upward with violent force, about to blow the Sumeru Mountain, Mahāsumeru, the Cakravāḍa Mountains, Mahācakravāḍa, as well as other minor mountains, the great earth, and all such things in the trichiliocosm until they are shattered like chaff, and wishes to block that wind-force with a single finger so that it ceases and does not arise, he should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to fill the entirety of space within a trichiliocosm by sitting cross-legged in a single spot, they should study the perfection of wisdom."

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to take up with a single hair-tether all things within the trichiliocosm—the Sumeru Mountains, the Great Sumeru Mountains, the Cakravāḍa Mountains, the Great Cakravāḍa Mountains, as well as other minor mountains, the great earth, and so forth—and cast them beyond immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless worlds in another direction, yet without causing any harm or disturbance to any sentient beings, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to fully satisfy, through a single offering of food, a flower, incense, a banner, a parasol, a pennant, a canopy, a lamp, a robe, or a musical performance, all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, along with their assemblies of disciples, throughout as many worlds in each of the ten directions as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, and to thereby honor, revere, respect, and praise them, they should train in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to securely establish all sentient beings in each of the worlds of the ten directions—each as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River—causing them to abide in the aggregate of ethical discipline, or the aggregate of concentration, or the aggregate of wisdom, or the aggregate of liberation, or the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation; or causing them to abide in the fruit of stream-entry, or the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning, or the fruit of arhatship; or causing them to abide in pratyekabuddha enlightenment, or even causing them to enter the realm of nirvana without remainder, they should train in the perfection of wisdom.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they are able to know, as it truly is, that such giving results in a great reward."
That is to say, knowing things as they truly are:
"By such giving one is born into a great kṣatriya clan; by such giving one is born into a great brāhmaṇa clan;
by such giving one is born into a great householder clan; by such giving one obtains..."
Born into a great clan of householders, one who practices such generosity will be reborn among the gods of the Four Great Kings,
or among the Thirty-three Gods, or among the Yāma gods, or among the Tuṣita gods, or among the gods who Delight in Emanation,
or among the gods who Wield Power over Others' Emanations; by means of this generosity, one attains the first dhyāna.
They may contemplate the second dhyāna, the third dhyāna, or the fourth dhyāna;

through this giving, they may attain the concentration of the sphere of infinite space, the concentration of the sphere of infinite consciousness, the concentration of the sphere of nothingness, or the concentration of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; through this giving, they may attain the thirty-seven [factors of enlightenment].
Regarding the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣikadharma*): by means of this giving, one attains the three gates of liberation;
by means of this giving, one attains the eight liberations, or the eight bases of mastery, or the nine successive attainments, or the ten totalities;
by means of this giving, one attains the gates of dhāraṇī or the gates of samādhi; by means of this giving, one attains...
Entering the bodhisattva’s state of right determination and transcendence (*samyaktva-niyāma*), through this giving, one attains the Stage of Utmost Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*),

or the Stage of Purity (*vimalā-bhūmi*), or the Stage of Radiance (*prabhākari-bhūmi*), or the Stage of Blazing Wisdom (*arciṣmatī-bhūmi*), or the Stage of Difficult Victory (*sudurjayā-bhūmi*), or the Stage of Presence (*abhimukhi-bhūmi*),
or the Stage of Far-Going (*dūraṅgamā-bhūmi*), or the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*), or the Stage of Good Intelligence (*sādhumatī-bhūmi*), or the Stage of Dharma...
Cloud Ground: By means of this giving, one attains the five eyes or the six supernormal powers of a Buddha;

by means of this giving, one attains the ten powers of a Buddha, or the four fearlessnesses, or the four analytical knowledges, or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, or great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity. By means of this...
Through giving, one attains the thirty-two marks of a great man or the eighty secondary signs;
by means of this giving, one attains the quality of non-forgetfulness or the state of constant equanimity;

by means of this giving, one attains all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), or the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), or the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*); and by means of this giving, one attains the fruit of a stream-enterer (*srotāpattiphala*).
Some attain the fruit of once-returning, some the fruit of non-returning, some the fruit of arhatship, some the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha,
and some the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
To know these—pure ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom—as they truly are, and to likewise obtain their great fruits and rewards, is also thus.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom can know as it truly is:

'Such skillful means in giving can fulfill the perfection of giving; such skillful means in giving can fulfill the perfection of ethical discipline; such skillful means in giving can fulfill the perfection of patience; such skillful means in giving can fulfill the perfection of diligence; such skillful means in giving can fulfill the perfection of meditative concentration; and such skillful means in giving can fulfill the perfection of wisdom.'"

“He knows it as it truly is: that such skillful means regarding pure ethical discipline can fulfill the perfection of ethical discipline; that such skillful means regarding pure ethical discipline can fulfill the perfection of patience; that such skillful means regarding pure ethical discipline can fulfill the perfection of diligence; that such skillful means regarding pure ethical discipline can fulfill the perfection of meditative concentration; that such skillful means regarding pure ethical discipline can fulfill the perfection of wisdom; and that such skillful means regarding pure ethical discipline can fulfill the perfection of generosity.”

"One is able to know it as it truly is: such skillful means of patience can fulfill the perfection of patience; such skillful means of patience can fulfill the perfection of diligence; such skillful means of patience can fulfill the perfection of meditative concentration; such skillful means of patience can fulfill the perfection of wisdom; such skillful means of patience can fulfill the perfection of generosity; and such skillful means of patience can fulfill the perfection of ethical discipline."

"He knows according to reality: 'Such skillful means of diligence can fulfill the perfection of diligence; such skillful means of diligence can fulfill the perfection of meditative concentration; such skillful means of diligence can fulfill the perfection of wisdom; such skillful means of diligence can fulfill the perfection of generosity; such skillful means of diligence can fulfill the perfection of ethical discipline; and such skillful means of diligence can fulfill the perfection of patience.'"

"One is able to know as it truly is: such skillful means in meditative concentration can fulfill the perfection of meditative concentration; such skillful means in meditative concentration can fulfill the perfection of wisdom; such skillful means in meditative concentration can fulfill the perfection of generosity; such skillful means in meditative concentration can fulfill the perfection of ethical discipline; such skillful means in meditative concentration can fulfill the perfection of patience; and such skillful means in meditative concentration can fulfill the perfection of diligence."

"One is able to know it as it truly is: such skillful means of wisdom can fulfill the perfection of wisdom; such skillful means of wisdom can fulfill the perfection of generosity; such skillful means of wisdom can fulfill the perfection of ethical discipline; such skillful means of wisdom can fulfill the perfection of patience; such skillful means of wisdom can fulfill the perfection of diligence; and such skillful means of wisdom can fulfill the perfection of meditative concentration."
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) know, as they truly are, these [perfections of] generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; and by means of skillful means (upāyakauśalya), how is he able to fulfill the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom?”
The Buddha addressed the Venerable Śāriputra, saying:

“All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practicing the perfection of wisdom are able to know things as they truly are. If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, employing the skillful means of non-apprehension, practices the perfection of generosity, they thoroughly understand that the giver, the recipient, and the gift are all unapprehendable. Through such skillful means in generosity, they are able to fulfill the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.”

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, employing the skillful means of non-apprehension, practices the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*), they thoroughly comprehend that all characteristics of transgression and non-transgression are unapprehendable; through such skillful means in ethical discipline, they are able to fulfill the perfections of ethical discipline, patience (*kṣānti*), diligence (*vīrya*), meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), wisdom (*prajñā*), and generosity (*dāna*).

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, employing the skillful means of non-apprehension, practices the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), thoroughly realizes that all signs of movement and non-movement are unapprehendable; through such skillful means of patience, they are able to fulfill the perfections of patience, diligence, meditative concentration, wisdom, generosity, and ethical discipline.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, taking non-apprehension as the means, practices the perfection of diligence and thoroughly realizes that all physical and mental exertion and indolence are unapprehendable, then through such skillful means of diligence, they are able to fulfill the perfections of diligence, meditative concentration, wisdom, generosity, ethical discipline, and patience.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, employing the skillful means of non-apprehension, practices the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*), thoroughly realizes that all things—whether possessing flavor or lacking flavor—are unapprehendable; through such skillful means in meditative concentration, they are able to fulfill the perfections of meditative concentration, wisdom (*prajñā*), generosity (*dāna*), ethical discipline (*śīla*), patience (*kṣānti*), and diligence (*vīrya*).

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, employing the skillful means of non-apprehension, practices the perfection of wisdom and thoroughly realizes that the intrinsic nature or characteristics of all phenomena are unapprehendable, then through such skillful means of wisdom, they are able to fulfill the perfections of wisdom, generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain all the qualities of the past, future, and present Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, they should train in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā)."
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to be able to reach the further shore of all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena, they should study the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to exhaustively fathom the suchness (tathatā), the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), non-arising (anutpāda), and the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) of all phenomena of the past, future, and present, they should study the perfection of wisdom.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to be a leader among all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, they should study the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to be a personal attendant to the Buddhas, they should study the perfection of wisdom.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to become an inner retinue to all buddhas, they should study the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to possess a great retinue in every lifetime, they should study the perfection of wisdom.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to always have other bodhisattvas as their companions, they should study the perfection of wisdom.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to purify the vessel of the body so as to be worthy of receiving the offerings and respect of the world, they should study the perfection of wisdom.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to forever subdue all stingy and greedy minds, they should study the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes that all minds of transgressing the precepts never arise again, they should study the perfection of wisdom.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to forever eliminate all thoughts of anger and resentment, they should study the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to forever abandon all thoughts of indolence, they should study the perfection of wisdom.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to forever stifle all distracted minds, they should study the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to forever distance themselves from all minds of unwholesome wisdom, they should study the perfection of wisdom.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to universally establish all sentient beings in the meritorious action consisting of giving, the meritorious action consisting of ethical discipline, the meritorious action consisting of cultivation, the meritorious action consisting of service, and the meritorious action consisting of material support, they should train in the perfection of wisdom.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain the five eyes—namely, the fleshly eye, the divine eye, the wisdom eye, the dharma eye, and the buddha eye—they should study the perfection of wisdom.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,

if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to see with the divine eye all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas in Buddha-worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions, they should train in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā)."

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to hear with the divine ear the true Dharma taught by all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas in as many Buddha-worlds in the ten directions as there are sands in the Ganges River, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to know, as they truly are, the minds and mental factors of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas throughout as many world-systems in each of the ten directions as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, they should train in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to hear the true Dharma at the presence of each and every Buddha in as many worlds in the ten directions as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, never becoming weary or negligent, and wishes to never forget the Dharma they have heard until reaching unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should train in the perfection of wisdom.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to see the various buddha-fields of the ten directions throughout the past, future, and present, they should study the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to thoroughly penetrate the profound meaning and intent of all the sūtras, geyas, vyākaraṇas, gāthās, udānas, nidānas, avadānas, jātaka-s, vaipulyas, adbhuta-dharmas, upadeśas, and saṃsaya-parihārakas spoken by the Buddhas of the ten directions in the past, future, and present—whether these have been heard or not heard by the śrāvakas and others—they should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to personally receive, uphold, read, recite, master, and skillfully understand the meaning and intent of the Dharma-gates taught by all the Buddhas of the past, future, and present throughout the ten directions, and to explain them extensively for others, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to personally practice, in accordance with reality and as it was taught, the Dharma-gates spoken by all Buddhas of the past, future, and present throughout the ten directions, and also wishes to skillfully encourage others to practice in accordance with reality and as it was taught, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to provide illumination for the dark worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions, and for those places between each world that are not reached by the light of the sun, moon, and other luminaries, they should train in the perfection of wisdom.”
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to [act] within the worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the ten directions— worlds that are shrouded in ignorance and darkness,
where sentient beings abound in wrong views, do not believe in evil conduct, do not believe in sublime conduct,
do not believe in the maturation of the results of evil or sublime conduct, do not believe in past lives, do not believe in future lives, and do not believe in suffering—
They do not believe in the truth of suffering, they do not believe in the truth of its origin, they do not believe in the truth of its cessation, nor do they believe in the truth of the path.
They do not believe that practices such as generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom can yield mundane and supramundane fruits.
Furthermore, they have not heard the names of the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Sangha. At that time,...

They shall then be transformed and inspired to give rise to right view; hearing the names of the Triple Gem, they will joyfully believe and accept them, abandon all unwholesome conduct, and cultivate all sublime practices, thereby training in the Prajñāpāramitā.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes, by means of their own power, to cause the sentient beings in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions to be able to see if they are blind, to hear if they are deaf, to speak if they are mute, to regain mindfulness if they are insane, to attain concentration if they are distracted, to obtain wealth if they are poor, to obtain clothing if they are naked, to obtain food if they are hungry, to obtain drink if they are thirsty, to be cured of illness if they are sick, to become handsome and dignified if they are ugly, to have complete limbs if they are physically deformed, to have their sense faculties perfected if they are deficient, to awaken from confusion if they are dazed, and to find peace and stability if they are exhausted, they should train in the *prajñāpāramitā*.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes, by means of their own power, to cause the sentient beings in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions to face one another with a mind of loving-kindness—regarding each other as father or mother, elder or younger brother, elder or younger sister, friend or relative—and to dwell without mutual harm, instead bringing one another benefit and happiness, they should study the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes, by means of their own power, to cause all sentient beings in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the ten directions who are in the evil realms to be liberated from those evil realms and be reborn in the happy realms, and to cause those who are already in the happy realms to dwell forever in the happy realms without falling back into the evil realms, they should train in the perfection of wisdom.”

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes, by means of their own majestic power, to cause all sentient beings in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions who practice unwholesome deeds to cultivate wholesome deeds without ever becoming weary, they should study the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes, by means of their own power, to cause all sentient beings in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the ten directions to abide in the aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*), those who are distracted to abide in the aggregate of meditative concentration (*samādhiskandha*), those who are deluded to abide in the aggregate of wisdom (*prajñāskandha*), those who have not attained liberation to abide in the aggregate of liberation (*vimuktiskandha*), and those who have not attained the knowledge and vision of liberation to abide in the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimuktijñānadarśanaskandha*), they should train in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes, by means of their own power, to cause sentient beings in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions who have not yet seen the truths to see the truths—whether to establish them in the fruit of a stream-enterer, a once-returner, or a non-returner; or to cause them to realize the fruit of an arhat; or to cause them to realize the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; or to cause them to realize even up to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment—they should train in the perfection of wisdom.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to train in the sublime deportment of all Buddhas—so that sentient beings never tire of beholding it, and so as to cause all evil to cease and all goodness to arise—they should train in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects thus:
'When shall I gaze like an elephant king and preach the Dharma to the assembly with a solemn and dignified bearing?'"
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to accomplish these matters, they should study the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects thus:
‘When shall my actions of body, speech, and mind all become completely pure and proceed in accordance with wisdom?’”
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to accomplish these matters, they should study the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects thus:
‘When shall I walk at will with my feet not touching the ground by a distance of four finger-breadths?’”
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to accomplish these matters, they should study the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects thus:
'When shall I obtain immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of the Four Great Kings' assemblies...'"
The gods of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, the Heaven of the Thirty-three, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven,
the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, the Brahmakāyika Heaven, the Brahmapurohita Heaven,
the Brahmapārṣadya Heaven, the Mahābrahmā Heaven, the Ābhāsvara Heaven, the Parīttābhā Heaven, the Apramāṇābhā Heaven, and the Ābhāsvara Heaven.
The Śuddhāvāsa, Parīttaśuddha, Apramāṇaśuddha, Śubhakṛtsna, Vṛhatphala, Parīttābha, Apramāṇābha, Ābhāsvara,
Puṇyaprasava, Anabhraka, Abṛha, Sudṛśa, Sudarśana, Akaniṣṭha heavens,
as well as the various nāgas and devas, made offerings and paid homage.
"How shall they be honored, revered, praised, and followed by a retinue as they proceed to the Bodhi tree?
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to accomplish these matters should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects thus:

'At what time shall I obtain immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of gods of the Four Great Kings, up to the gods of the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, as well as nāgas and spirits, who shall provide me with a seat of precious cloth beneath the Bodhi tree?'"
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to accomplish these matters, they should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects thus:

'When shall I sit cross-legged beneath the Bodhi tree and, with my hands adorned with various wondrous marks, touch the great earth, causing the earth goddess and her retinue to appear simultaneously to serve as witnesses?'"
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to accomplish these matters, they should study the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects thus:
'When shall I sit beneath the Bodhi tree, subdue the hosts of Māras, and realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?'"
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to accomplish this matter, they should train in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects thus:
‘When shall I realize unexcelled, perfect enlightenment such that, in whatever place I walk, stand, sit, or lie down, it shall all become diamond (vajra)?’”
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to accomplish these matters, they should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects thus:
