‘At what time shall I renounce my royal status, such that on the very day I go forth from home I shall attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening; and on that same day I shall turn the sublime wheel of Dharma, immediately causing immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings to distance themselves from dust and leave behind defilement, giving rise to the pure Dharma-eye;’”
Furthermore, you cause immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings to forever exhaust all outflows, attaining liberation through both mind and wisdom;
and you also cause immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings to attain non-retrogression in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to accomplish this matter, they should train in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects thus:

‘At what time shall I attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, having immeasurable and innumerable śrāvakas and bodhisattvas as my assembly of disciples; and at one time of preaching the Dharma, immeasurable and innumerable classes of sentient beings, without rising from their seats, simultaneously realize the fruit of arhatship?’”
"How can immeasurable and innumerable classes of sentient beings, without rising from their seats, simultaneously attain non-retrogression in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to accomplish this matter should study the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects thus: 'When shall my lifespan become inexhaustible;

when shall my body possess immeasurable and boundless radiance, adorned with the primary and secondary marks such that those who behold it never tire; when shall lotus flowers with a thousand petals naturally emerge whenever I walk to support my feet, causing a thousand-spoked wheel to appear upon the ground; when shall the great earth tremble as I take each step and move along, yet without disturbing the sentient beings dwelling on the ground; and when shall my entire body turn as I look back, and wherever my feet tread upon the vajra-limit, the earth itself revolve accordingly, like the circumference of a chariot wheel? "
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to accomplish this matter, they should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects thus:

'When shall I emit immeasurable and innumerable rays of light from every limb and joint of my body, illuminating the boundless worlds of the ten directions, and wherever they shine, bring great benefit to all sentient beings?'"
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to accomplish these matters, they should study the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects thus:

'When shall I attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, such that in my buddha-field there is not even the name of any greed, hatred, or delusion, nor shall one ever hear of the evil destinies of the hells, the animal realm, or the realm of hungry ghosts?'"
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to accomplish this matter, they should train in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects thus:

‘At what time shall I attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, such that the sentient beings in my buddha-field will possess sublime wisdom like those in other buddha-fields,’ and constantly thinks:”

Practicing generosity, self-discipline, patience, diligence, tranquility, and discernment; cultivating the holy life with freedom from negligence; and maintaining loving-kindness, compassion, empathetic joy, and equanimity toward all sentient beings without causing them harm—would this not be excellent?
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to accomplish these matters, they should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects thus:

'When shall I attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, such that the sentient beings in my buddha-field will have accomplished various kinds of sublime merits, and all the Buddhas and bodhisattvas in other buddha-fields will join in praising them?'"
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to accomplish these matters, they should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects thus:

'When shall I attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening? Once my work of transformation is finished and I have entered parinirvāṇa, may the True Dharma never come to an end, so that I may constantly perform deeds for the benefit of sentient beings?'"
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to accomplish this matter, they should train in the *prajñāpāramitā*.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva reflects thus:

‘At what time shall I attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, such that all sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, who hear my name, will surely attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?’”
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to accomplish these matters, they should study the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). Śāriputra!
Bodhisattva mahāsattvas who wish to attain such immeasurable, innumerable, inconceivable, and marvelous merits should study the perfection of wisdom.”
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Scroll Three.
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Scroll Four.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang under Imperial Decree.
The Second Part of the Second Chapter on Training in Contemplation from the First Division.
The Buddha addressed Śāriputra:
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they are already able to accomplish such merits as these.”
At that time, the Four Great Heavenly Kings of the trichiliocosm were all filled with great joy and thought to themselves:
"We should now present four alms bowls to this Bodhisattva, just as the heavenly kings of old presented their bowls to the previous Buddhas."
At that time, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa, Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, and Paranirmitavaśavartin heavens within this trichiliocosm were all filled with great joy and thought to themselves:
"We shall all provide offerings, pay homage, show respect, and offer praise to such a bodhisattva, so that the fierce hosts of the asuras may diminish and the retinues of the devas may increase."

At that time, the Brahmakāyika, Brahmapurohita, Brahmakāyika-parṣadya, Mahābrahmā, Ābhāsvara, Parīttābhā, Apramāṇābhā, Ābhāsvarāśubha, Śubha, Parīttaśubha, Apramāṇaśubha, Śubhakṛtsna, Bṛhatphala, Avṛha, Atapa, Sudṛśa, Sudarśana, and Akaniṣṭha devas of the three-thousandfold world system were filled with joy and delight, and all thought to themselves:
"We shall entreat such a bodhisattva to quickly realize unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment and turn the sublime wheel of Dharma for the benefit of all."

"Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom and increases the six perfections, all the sons and daughters of good family in that world—whether they see him or hear of him—will all rejoice greatly and think:

'May we become such bodhisattvas; may we become their parents, brothers, sisters, wives, children, retinues, acquaintances, and friends. By this means, may we cultivate all wholesome deeds and likewise realize unsurpassed enlightenment.'"
At that time, from the gods of the Four Great Kings up to those of the Akaniṣṭha Heaven in that world, all who saw or heard of this were filled with great joy and thought to themselves:

"We shall employ various skillful means to cause this bodhisattva to abandon unchaste conduct, so that from the first generation of the mind until the attainment of Buddhahood, he may constantly practice the holy life."
Why is this? If even the desire for the colored realm of existence acts as an obstacle to birth in the Brahma Heaven, how much more so for attaining unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment!

Therefore, it is the Bodhisattva who severs desire, leaves the household life, and practices pure conduct that can attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, not one who does not sever it.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Must bodhisattva-mahāsattvas necessarily have parents, wives, children, and various kinsmen and friends?”
The Buddha addressed the Venerable Śāriputra, saying:
“There are some bodhisattvas who possess parents, wives, children, and kinsmen as they cultivate the practice of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva;

there are also some bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have no wives or children, and from their first generation of the mind of awakening until they attain buddhahood, they constantly cultivate the pure conduct (brahmacarya), remaining inviolate in their youthful innocence.”

There may be bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, through skillful means, manifest the enjoyment of the five desires, only then renouncing them with weary detachment to leave the household life and practice the holy life, thereby attaining unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"Śāriputra!

Suppose, for example, there were a magician or his apprentice skilled in the arts of illusion who conjured up various objects endowed with the five kinds of exquisite sensual pleasures, and within them they indulged at will and enjoyed themselves together. What do you think?"
"Does that which is produced by illusion have any reality?
Śāriputra replied, "No!"
"No, World-Honored One!
No, Sugata!"
The Buddha said, "Śāriputra!

It is the same for the bodhisattva mahāsattva: desiring to bring sentient beings to maturity, he employs skillful means to manifest as one who experiences the five desires, yet in reality, no such thing exists."

Nevertheless, this bodhisattva-mahāsattva develops a profound sense of weary revulsion toward the five desires and is not defiled by the faults of the five desires. By means of immeasurable methods, he censures and disparages all desires: because desire is a blazing fire that burns body and mind; because desire is filth and evil that defiles oneself and others;

because desire is like an executioner who constantly inflicts harm in the past, future, and present; because desire is like an enemy who watches for an opportunity throughout the long night to cause ruin and loss; because desire is like a grass torch, like a bitter fruit, like a sharp sword, like a mass of fire, like a vessel of poison, like a deceptive illusion, like a dark well, and like a deceitful friend or a caṇḍāla.

Śāriputra! By means of such immeasurable doors of censure, the bodhisattva mahāsattvas rebuke and condemn all sensual desires; having thoroughly understood these faults of desire, how could they ever truly indulge in the experience of sensual pleasures?
"It is only for the benefit of those sentient beings to be converted that he employs skillful means to manifest the experience of various desires.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the perfection of wisdom?
The Buddha addressed the venerable Śāriputra, saying: "Śāriputra!..."
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they should contemplate in this way:

"In reality, there is no bodhisattva, nor do they perceive a bodhisattva; they do not perceive the name 'bodhisattva,' nor do they perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor do they perceive the name 'perfection of wisdom'; they do not perceive practice, nor do they perceive non-practice."
Why is this? Śāriputra, the intrinsic nature of a bodhisattva is empty; the designation "bodhisattva" is empty.
Why is this? Form is empty of intrinsic nature; it is not by means of emptiness that form is empty.
Emptiness is not form, yet form is not separate from emptiness, and emptiness is not separate from form. Form is itself emptiness, and emptiness is itself form.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty of intrinsic nature; this is not by means of emptiness.

The emptiness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is not feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not separate from emptiness, and emptiness is not separate from feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are themselves emptiness, and emptiness itself is feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Why is this? Śāriputra!

This is merely a name called "bodhi"; this is merely a name called "sattva"; this is merely a name called "bodhisattva"; this is merely a name called "emptiness"; and these are merely names called "form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness."

Thus, this intrinsic nature is without arising, without cessation, without defilement, and without purification; when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom in this way, they do not perceive arising, do not perceive cessation, do not perceive defilement, and do not perceive purification.
Why is this? It is because one merely establishes adventitious names and gives rise to conceptual discrimination regarding various phenomena;
having established these adventitious names, one engages in conventional discourse accordingly, and as one speaks in such a manner, one gives rise to corresponding attachments.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not perceive any of these things; because they do not perceive them, they do not give rise to attachment.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they should contemplate in this way:

'Bodhisattva' is merely a name; 'Buddha' is merely a name; 'perfection of wisdom' is merely a name; 'form' (rūpa) is merely a name; and 'feeling,' 'perception,' 'volitional formations,' and 'consciousness' (vedanā, saṃjñā, saṃskārāḥ, vijñāna) are merely names."
The sense-base of the eye is merely a name; the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are merely names.
The sense-base of forms is merely a name; the sense-bases of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena are merely names.
The eye-element is merely a name; the elements of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are merely names.
The realm of form exists as a mere name; the realms of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena exist as mere names.
The realm of eye-consciousness exists as a mere name; the realms of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness exist as mere names.
Eye-contact exists as a mere name; ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact exist as mere names.

The various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition exist merely as names; the various feelings produced with ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact as conditions exist merely as names.
The earth element exists merely as a name; the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements exist merely as names.

The causal condition exists merely as a name; the immediately preceding condition, the object condition, and the dominant condition exist merely as names; and all phenomena produced from conditions exist merely as names.

Ignorance is merely a name; volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are merely names;
the perfection of generosity is merely a name; and the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom are merely names.

Inner emptiness is merely a name; outer emptiness, inner-and-outer emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate truth, the emptiness of conditioned phenomena, the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersal emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature are merely names.

The four foundations of mindfulness are merely names; the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path are merely names.
The gate of liberation of emptiness is merely a name; the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness are merely names.
The noble truth of suffering exists as a mere name; the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path exist as mere names.
The four dhyānas exist as mere names; the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and the eight liberations exist as mere names;
the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities exist as mere names.
The gates of dhāraṇī are merely names; the gates of samādhi are merely names. The Ground of Utmost Joy is merely a name;

the Ground of Freedom from Defilement, the Ground of Radiant Light, the Ground of Blazing Wisdom, the Ground of Supreme Difficulty to Conquer, the Ground of Presence, the Ground of Far-Going, the Ground of Immovability, the Ground of Excellent Intelligence, and the Ground of the Cloud of Dharma are merely names.

The Ground of Right Contemplation is merely a name; the Ground of the Seed-Nature, the Eighth Ground, the Ground of Vision, the Ground of Thinness, the Ground of Freedom from Desire, the Ground of Completion, the Ground of the Pratyekabuddha, the Ground of the Bodhisattva, and the Ground of the Tathāgata are merely names.
The five eyes are merely names; the six supernormal powers are merely names;

the ten powers of a Tathāgata are merely names; the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are merely names;
the thirty-two marks of a Great Man are merely names; and the eighty minor marks are merely names.
The quality of non-forgetfulness exists as a mere name; the state of constant abiding in equanimity exists as a mere name;
all-knowledge exists as a mere name; the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects exist as mere names;
the knowledge of all modes of knowledge exists as a mere name; and the permanent eradication of the continuity of afflictive habitual tendencies exists as a mere name.

The fruit of stream-entry is merely a name; the fruits of once-returning, non-returning, and arhatship are merely names; solitary-buddha enlightenment is merely a name; all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are merely names; the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas is merely a name;
worldly dharmas are merely names; supramundane dharmas are merely names;
contaminated dharmas are merely names; uncontaminated dharmas are merely names.
"Conditioned phenomena are merely names; unconditioned phenomena are merely names. "Śāriputra!
Just as 'self' is merely a name, designated as 'self,' yet in reality it cannot be found."

In this way, sentient beings, life-principles, born beings, nourishers, persons, individuals, mind-born ones, youths, agents, instigators of action, originators, instigators of origination, experiencers, instigators of experience, knowers, and seers are also merely names.
That is to say, from "sentient beings" up to "seers," because they are empty of being unobtainable, one merely applies adventitious names in accordance with worldly convention;
all phenomena are likewise, and one should not cling to them.

Therefore, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not perceive a self, nor even a perceiver; furthermore, they do not perceive the intrinsic nature of any phenomena.

“Śāriputra! When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in this manner, they cannot be surpassed by the wisdom of any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, with the sole exception of the wisdom of the Buddhas, because of the emptiness of non-apprehension (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*).”
Why is this? It is because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas find nothing to be apprehended in either the name or that which is named, for they do not perceive them and have no attachment to them.
Śāriputra! If bodhisattva mahāsattvas can practice the perfection of wisdom in this manner, it is called practicing the profound perfection of wisdom well.

Śāriputra! Suppose you and Mahāmaudgalyāyana were to fill the entire continent of Jambudvīpa with as much wisdom as there is in forests of rice, sesame, bamboo, reeds, and sugarcane; compared to the wisdom of a single bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of prajñāpāramitā, that wisdom would not equal even one hundredth part, nor one thousandth part, nor one hundred-thousandth part, nor one koṭi-th part, nor one hundred-koṭi-th part, nor one thousand-koṭi-th part, nor one hundred-thousand-koṭi-th part. It would not equal even a numerical fraction, a calculable fraction, a reckonable fraction, a figurative fraction, or even a fraction of an upaniṣad.
Why is this? Śāriputra!
This wisdom of the bodhisattva mahāsattva can cause all sentient beings to incline toward parinirvāṇa; the wisdom of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas is not like this.
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
the wisdom cultivated in a single day by a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of prajñāpāramitā cannot be equaled by the wisdom of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
“Śāriputra! Let alone Jambudvīpa.

Suppose you and Mahāmaudgalyāyana were to fill the four great continents, and all the wisdom possessed by as many rice, hemp, bamboo, reeds, and sugarcane groves as there are—compared to the wisdom of a single bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, it would not equal even a hundredth part, nor a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth part, nor a *koṭi*-th part, nor a hundred-*koṭi*-th part, nor a thousand-*koṭi*-th part, nor a hundred-thousand-*koṭi*-th part; it would not even bear comparison by way of number, calculation, reckoning, analogy, or even by way of the infinitesimal (*upaniṣad*).”
Why is this? Śāriputra,
it is because the wisdom of these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas can cause all sentient beings to attain parinirvāṇa, whereas the wisdom of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas is not like this.
Furthermore, Śāriputra,

because the wisdom cultivated by a single bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) in a single day cannot be equaled by the wisdom of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

“Śāriputra! Setting aside the four great continents, suppose you and Mahāmaudgalyāyana were to fill an entire trichiliocosm, such that your combined wisdom was like a forest of rice, sesame, bamboo, reeds, or sugarcane. Compared to the wisdom of a single bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*, your wisdom would not equal even one hundredth part, nor one thousandth part, nor one hundred-thousandth part, nor one *koṭi*-th part, nor one hundred-*koṭi*-th part, nor one thousand-*koṭi*-th part, nor one hundred-thousand-*koṭi*-th part; it would not equal even a numerical fraction, a calculable fraction, a reckonable fraction, a metaphorical fraction, or even a *upaniṣad* fraction.”
Why is this? Śāriputra,
it is because the wisdom of these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas can cause all sentient beings to incline toward parinirvāṇa, whereas the wisdom of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas is not like this.
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
the wisdom cultivated in a single day by a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of prajñāpāramitā cannot be equaled by the wisdom of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
“Śāriputra! Set aside one trichiliocosm. Suppose you and Mahāmaudgalyāyana were to fill as many Buddha-worlds in the ten directions as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River;

even the combined wisdom of all those beings, which is like a forest of rice, sesame, bamboo, reeds, or sugarcane, compared to the wisdom of a single bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), would not equal a hundredth part, nor a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth part, nor a *koṭi*-th part, nor a hundred-*koṭi*-th part, nor a thousand-*koṭi*-th part, nor a hundred-thousand-*koṭi*-th part. It would not equal any numerical fraction, any calculable fraction, any estimable fraction, any illustrative fraction, nor even a fraction of the infinitesimal (*upaniṣad*).”
Why is this? Śāriputra!
This wisdom of the bodhisattva mahāsattva can cause all sentient beings to incline toward parinirvāṇa; the wisdom of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas is not like this.
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
the wisdom cultivated in a single day by a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) cannot be equaled by the wisdom of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Whether it be the wisdom of the stream-enterer, once-returner, non-returner, or arhat of the śrāvaka vehicle; the wisdom of the pratyekabuddha vehicle; the wisdom of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva; or the wisdom of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas—all these wisdoms are without distinction, do not contradict one another, are without arising or ceasing, and are empty by their very nature.”

If phenomena are without distinction, non-contradictory, without arising or ceasing, and empty of intrinsic nature—such that no distinction among these phenomena can be apprehended—how is it, World-Honored One, that you say the wisdom cultivated by a single bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom in a single day cannot be equaled by the wisdom of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas?
The Buddha addressed the Venerable Śāriputra, saying: “Śāriputra,
what do you think?”

Regarding the wisdom cultivated and the superior accomplishments achieved by a single bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of prajñāpāramitā in a single day—do all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas possess such things?
Śāriputra said:
“No, World-Honored One!”
"No, Sugata! "Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
What do you think?
If a single bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom were to cultivate wisdom for a single day, thinking to himself:

"I shall practice the subtle wisdom of all aspects, the knowledge of all, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects, in order to benefit and bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings."

"Having awakened to all aspects of all phenomena, he employs skillful means to establish all sentient beings in the realm of nirvana without remainder. Do all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas possess such wisdom?"
Śāriputra said:
"No, World-Honored One!"
"No, Sugata! "Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
What do you think?
Could any of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas ever form such a thought as this:
"I shall realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and through skillful means establish all sentient beings in the realm of nirvana without remainder"?
"No," Śāriputra replied. "No!"
"No, World-Honored One!
No, Sugata!"
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
What do you think?
Could any of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas ever form such a thought as this:..."
"I shall practice the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom;
I shall practice the sublime applications of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the branches of the noble path;
I shall practice the sublime four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless absorptions."
I shall practice the eight sublime liberations, the eight spheres of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten spheres of totality;
I shall practice the sublime gateways to liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;

I shall abide in internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate truth, the emptiness of conditioned phenomena, the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersal emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature.

I shall abide in suchness, the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, non-falsity, immutability, equality, the state beyond birth, the fixedness of dharma, the stability of dharma, the limit of reality, the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm;
I shall abide in the sublime noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path;
and I shall practice all doors of dhāraṇī and all doors of samādhi.

I shall practice the Ground of Utmost Joy, the Ground of Purity, the Ground of Radiant Light, the Ground of Blazing Wisdom, the Ground of Supreme Difficulty to Conquer, the Ground of Manifestation, the Ground of Far-Reaching Progress, the Ground of Immovability, the Ground of Excellent Intelligence, and the Ground of the Dharma Cloud;
I shall perfect the supernormal powers of a bodhisattva, bring sentient beings to maturity, and purify the buddha-fields;
I shall perfect the five eyes and the six supernormal powers.

I shall fulfill the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
I shall fulfill the thirty-two marks of a Great Being and the eighty minor marks;
I shall fulfill the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant dwelling in equanimity.

I shall fulfill all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*); I shall forever uproot all afflictions along with their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) and realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), skillfully establishing immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings in the realm of nirvana without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇadhātu*).
"No," Śāriputra replied. "No!"
"No, World-Honored One!
No, Sugata!"
The Buddha said,
“Śāriputra! All bodhisattva mahāsattvas who practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) form this thought:”

"I shall practice the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; even unto the point that I shall forever uproot all afflictions and habitual tendencies, realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and through skillful means establish immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings in the realm of nirvana without remainder."
"Śāriputra! For example, a firefly does not have such a thought as:
'My light can illuminate the entire Jambudvīpa and cause it all to be brightly lit.'"
"In this way, all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas do not have such a thought:

'I shall practice the perfection of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; and even until I have forever uprooted all afflictions along with their habitual tendencies and realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, I shall through skillful means establish immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless sentient beings in the realm of nirvana without remainder.'"

"Śāriputra! For example, just as the radiance of the solar orb blazes intensely, illuminating Jambudvīpa so that there is nowhere it does not pervade, so too do all bodhisattva mahāsattvas practicing the perfection of wisdom constantly form this thought:

'I shall practice the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; furthermore, I shall forever uproot all afflictions and habitual tendencies, realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, and through skillful means establish immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings in the realm of nirvana without remainder.'"

"For this reason, Śāriputra, you should know that all the wisdom possessed by all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, compared to the wisdom cultivated in a single day by a single bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), does not equal even one hundredth part; it does not equal one thousandth part; it does not equal one hundred-thousandth part; it does not equal one koṭi-th part; it does not equal one hundred-koṭi-th part; it does not equal one thousand-koṭi-th part; it does not equal one hundred-thousand-koṭi-th part; nor does it equal any part reached by calculation, enumeration, reckoning, analogy, or even by the fraction of upaniṣad."
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

How is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to transcend the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, attain the stage of non-retrogression of a bodhisattva, and purify the path to unsurpassed buddha-enlightenment?”
The Buddha addressed the Venerable Śāriputra, saying: “Śāriputra!

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, from their first generation of the mind of awakening, practice the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, wisdom, skillful means, sublime aspiration, power, and knowledge; and when they abide in the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—they are then able to transcend all stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, attain the bodhisattva stage of non-retrogression, and purify the path to unsurpassed buddha-enlightenment.”
Then, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Abiding in what stage can the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas serve as a true field of merit for all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas?”
The Buddha addressed the Venerable Śāriputra, saying: “Śāriputra!

From the first generation of the mind of awakening, bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, wisdom, skillful means, sublime aspiration, power, and knowledge. Abiding in the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, until they sit upon the seat of sublime awakening, they always serve as true fields of merit for all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.”

Why is this? Śāriputra, it is because of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva that all wholesome dharmas appear in the world; that is to say, because of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, there appear in the world the ten paths of wholesome action, the five precepts for lay devotees, the eight precepts of the upavāsa fast, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and the meritorious actions consisting of giving, morality, and cultivation.

Furthermore, it is by depending upon the bodhisattva mahāsattvas that the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of miraculous power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold noble path, the gateways to liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, and the noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path appear in the world; furthermore,
it is by depending upon the bodhisattva mahāsattvas that the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence,
meditative concentration, and wisdom appear in the world, as well as internal emptiness.
External emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate truth, the emptiness of conditioned phenomena,
the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, the emptiness of dispersion, the emptiness of non-alteration,
the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the emptiness of self-characteristics, the emptiness of common characteristics, the emptiness of all phenomena, the unapprehendable...
When emptiness, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence appear in the world,
there exist the suchness of all phenomena, the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, the non-illusory nature, the unchanging nature, equanimity,
the state beyond birth, the fixedness of phenomena, the stability of phenomena, and the limit of reality.
The realm of space and the inconceivable realm appear in the world;
the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten universal bases appear in the world;
all doors of dhāraṇī and doors of samādhi, as well as the ten stages of the bodhisattva, appear in the world; and the five... [are present].
The eye and the six supernormal powers appear in the world;

the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha appear in the world;
and the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant dwelling in equanimity appear.
In the world, there appears omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*);
there appear immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless wholesome dharmas, such as the maturing of sentient beings and the purification of buddha-fields.
"Because of the existence of such wholesome dharmas, there come to be in the world great clans of kṣatriyas, great clans of brahmins, great clans of householders, and great clans of lay merchants;

because of the existence of such wholesome dharmas, there come to be in the world the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, the Heaven of the Thirty-three, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven."

Because these various wholesome dharmas exist, there come to be in the world the gods of the Brahma-realm assembly (Brahmapārisadya), the gods of the Brahma-ministers (Brahmapurohita), the gods of the Great Brahma (Mahābrahmā), the gods of light (Ābhāsvara), the gods of limited light (Parīttābha), the gods of immeasurable light (Apramāṇābha), the gods of pervasive light-purity (Ābhāsvarābha), the pure gods (Śubha), the gods of limited purity (Parīttaśubha), the gods of immeasurable purity (Apramāṇaśubha), the gods of pervasive purity (Śubhakṛtsna), the vast gods (Vṛhatphala), the gods of limited vastness (Parīttavastu), the gods of immeasurable vastness (Apramāṇavastu), the gods of vast fruit (Bṛhatphala), the gods of non-percipient beings (Asañjñisattva), the gods of no-affliction (Avṛha), the gods of no-heat (Atapa), the gods of good-appearance (Sudṛśa), the gods of good-vision (Sudarśana), and the gods of the ultimate form (Akaniṣṭha).

Because these various wholesome dharmas exist, there likewise come to be in the world the gods of the sphere of infinite space (Ākāśānantyāyatana), the gods of the sphere of infinite consciousness (Vijñānānantyāyatana), the gods of the sphere of nothingness (Ākiñcanyāyatana), and the gods of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (Naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana).
Because there are such wholesome dharmas, there are in the world those who have entered the stream, once-returners, non-returners, arhats, and pratyekabuddhas;
because there are such wholesome dharmas, there are in the world bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Must the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas further requite the kindness of their donors?”
The Buddha addressed the Venerable Śāriputra, saying: "Śāriputra!
The bodhisattva mahāsattvas no longer need to requite the kindness of their donors."
For what reason?
Because they have already received much retribution. Why is this so?
Śāriputra! All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas act as great donors, bestowing immeasurable wholesome dharmas upon all sentient beings;
that is to say, they bestow upon sentient beings the ten paths of wholesome action, the five lay precepts, the eight fast-day precepts, and the four dhyānas.
[He] contemplates the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and the three types of meritorious action consisting of giving, morality, and cultivation; furthermore,
he bestows upon sentient beings the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers,
the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold noble path, emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
The doors of liberation, the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path;

furthermore, bestowing upon sentient beings the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, wisdom, skillful means, sublime aspiration, power, and knowledge;
and furthermore, bestowing upon sentient beings inner emptiness and outer emptiness.

...emptiness of the internal and external (*adhyātma-bahirdhā-śūnyatā*), emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*), great emptiness (*mahā-śūnyatā*), emptiness of the ultimate (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), emptiness of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-śūnyatā*),

emptiness of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*), absolute emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*), emptiness of the limitless (*anavara-agra-śūnyatā*), emptiness of dispersion (*anavakāra-śūnyatā*), emptiness of non-alteration (*anavakāra-śūnyatā*),

emptiness of essential nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*), emptiness of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*), emptiness of common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*), emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*), and emptiness of the unapprehendable (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*).
...emptiness of non-existence, emptiness of intrinsic nature, and emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence; furthermore,
[he teaches] to sentient beings the suchness of all phenomena, the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, the non-falsity,
the non-alteration, the equality, the state beyond birth, the fixedness of phenomena, the stability of phenomena, the limit of reality, and space.

The realms and the inconceivable realm; furthermore, bestowing upon sentient beings the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten totalities;
furthermore, bestowing upon sentient beings the gates of dhāraṇī, the gates of samādhi, and the ten stages of the bodhisattva;
furthermore, bestowing upon sentient beings the five eyes and the six supernormal powers; furthermore, bestowing...

To sentient beings, they bestow the Tathāgata’s ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;

furthermore, they bestow upon sentient beings the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant abiding in equanimity; and they further bestow upon sentient beings all-knowledge and the knowledge of the aspects of the path.
Wisdom and the knowledge of all aspects; furthermore, bestowing upon sentient beings the four means of attraction— generosity, pleasant speech, beneficial conduct, and cooperation—
to bring sentient beings to maturity, to purify Buddha-fields through skillful means,
and to bestow upon sentient beings the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, arhatship, and the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha.
Furthermore, they bestow upon sentient beings all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and the unsurpassed, perfect,
and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas. "Śāriputra!..."
Because Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas bestow upon all sentient beings such immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless categories of wholesome dharmas, they are called great donors.
"By this, one has already repaid the kindness of all donors; this is the true field of merit for the growth of supreme blessings.
3. Chapter on Correspondence, Part One: The First Section of the Chapter on Correspondence, Number Three. At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
With what phenomena is a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom associated, such that they may be said to be associated with the perfection of wisdom?
The Buddha addressed the Venerable Śāriputra, saying: "Śāriputra!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) is said to be practicing the perfection of wisdom because they are in accord with the emptiness of form (rūpa)."
Because it is associated with the emptiness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, it should be said to be associated with the perfection of wisdom.
"Śāriputra!..."
A bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, because they are in accord with the emptiness of the sense base of the eye, should be said to be in accord with the perfection of wisdom;
because they are in accord with the emptiness of the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, they should be said to be in accord with the perfection of wisdom.

“Śāriputra! A bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, because they are in accord with the emptiness of the sense base of form, should be said to be in accord with the perfection of wisdom;
because they are in accord with the emptiness of the sense bases of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena, they should be said to be in accord with the perfection of wisdom.”

“Śāriputra! A bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, because they are in accord with the emptiness of the eye-element, should be said to be in accord with the perfection of wisdom;
because they are in accord with the emptiness of the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-elements, they should be said to be in accord with the perfection of wisdom.”

“Śāriputra! A bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), because they are in accord with the emptiness of the realm of form (rūpadhātu), should be said to be in accord with the perfection of wisdom;
because they are in accord with the emptiness of the realms of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena (dharmadhātu), they should be said to be in accord with the perfection of wisdom.”

“Śāriputra! A bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, because of being in accord with the emptiness of the visual consciousness element, should be said to be in accord with the perfection of wisdom;
because of being in accord with the emptiness of the auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, and mental consciousness elements, they should be said to be in accord with the perfection of wisdom.”
“Śāriputra! A bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, because they are in accord with the emptiness of eye-contact, should be said to be in accord with the perfection of wisdom;
because they are in accord with the emptiness of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact, they should be said to be in accord with the perfection of wisdom.”

“Śāriputra! A bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) is said to be engaged with the perfection of wisdom because they are in accord with the emptiness of all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition;
they are said to be engaged with the perfection of wisdom because they are in accord with the emptiness of all feelings produced with ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact as conditions.”

“Śāriputra! A bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, because they are in accord with the emptiness of the earth element, should be said to be in accord with the perfection of wisdom;
because they are in accord with the emptiness of the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements, they should be said to be in accord with the perfection of wisdom.”

"Śāriputra! A bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) should be said to be in accord with the perfection of wisdom because they are in accord with the emptiness of causes and conditions (hetu-pratyaya).

They should be said to be in accord with the perfection of wisdom because they are in accord with the emptiness of the immediately preceding condition (samanantara-pratyaya), the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya), the dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya), and all phenomena produced from these various conditions."

“Śāriputra! A bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), because they are in accord with the emptiness of ignorance (avidyā), should be said to be in accord with the perfection of wisdom;

because they are in accord with the emptiness of volitional formations (saṃskāra), consciousness (vijñāna), name-and-form (nāmarūpa), the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana), contact (sparśa), feeling (vedanā), craving (tṛṣṇā), grasping (upādāna), becoming (bhava), birth (jāti), and old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair (jarāmaraṇa-śoka-parideva-duḥkha-daurmanasyopāyāsa), they should be said to be in accord with the perfection of wisdom.”

“Śāriputra! A bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, because they are in accord with the emptiness of the perfection of generosity, should be said to be in accord with the perfection of wisdom;

because they are in accord with the emptiness of the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, they should be said to be in accord with the perfection of wisdom.”
“Śāriputra! A bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, because they are in accord with internal emptiness, should be said to be in accord with the perfection of wisdom;

because they are in accord with external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, endless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, they should be said to be in accord with the perfection of wisdom.”

“Śāriputra! A bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) is said to be ‘conjoined with the perfection of wisdom’ because they are conjoined with the emptiness of suchness (tathatā).

They are said to be ‘conjoined with the perfection of wisdom’ because they are conjoined with the emptiness of the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), the non-erroneous nature, the unchanging nature, equality, the state beyond birth, the fixed nature of phenomena (dharmaniyāmatā), the stability of phenomena (dharmaniyāmatā), the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), the realm of space (ākāśadhātu), and the inconceivable realm.”

“Śāriputra! A bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, because they are in accord with the emptiness of the four foundations of mindfulness, should be said to be in accord with the perfection of wisdom;

because they are in accord with the emptiness of the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path, they should be said to be in accord with the perfection of wisdom.”

“Śāriputra! A bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, because they are in accord with the emptiness of the noble truth of suffering, should be said to be in accord with the perfection of wisdom;
because they are in accord with the emptiness of the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path, they should be said to be in accord with the perfection of wisdom.”

“Śāriputra! A bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, because they are in accord with the emptiness of the ten paths of wholesome action, should be said to be in accord with the perfection of wisdom;
because they are in accord with the emptiness of the five lay precepts and the eight precepts of the upavāsa fast, they should be said to be in accord with the perfection of wisdom.”

“Śāriputra! A bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, because they are in accord with the emptiness of meritorious actions consisting of giving, should be said to be in accord with the perfection of wisdom;
because they are in accord with the emptiness of meritorious actions consisting of morality and cultivation, they should be said to be in accord with the perfection of wisdom.”

“Śāriputra! A bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, because they are in accord with the emptiness of the four dhyānas, should be said to be in accord with the perfection of wisdom;
because they are in accord with the emptiness of the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions, they should be said to be in accord with the perfection of wisdom.”

“Śāriputra! A bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), because they are in accord with the emptiness of the eight liberations (aṣṭavimokṣa), should be said to be in accord with the perfection of wisdom;

because they are in accord with the emptiness of the eight bases of mastery (abhibhvāyatana), the nine successive attainments (navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti), and the ten totalities (daśakṛtsnāyatana), they should be said to be in accord with the perfection of wisdom.”

“Śāriputra! A bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, because they are in accord with the emptiness of the gate of liberation of emptiness, should be said to be in accord with the perfection of wisdom;
because they are in accord with the emptiness of the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness, they should be said to be in accord with the perfection of wisdom.”

“Śāriputra! A bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), because they are in accord with the emptiness of all doors of dhāraṇī, should be said to be in accord with the perfection of wisdom;
because they are in accord with the emptiness of all doors of samādhi, they should be said to be in accord with the perfection of wisdom.”

“Śāriputra! A bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, because they are in accord with the emptiness of the Stage of Extreme Joy, should be said to be in accord with the perfection of wisdom;

because they are in accord with the emptiness of the Stages of the Stainless, the Radiant, the Blazing Wisdom, the Extremely Difficult to Conquer, the Manifest, the Far-Reaching, the Immovable, the Excellent Intelligence, and the Cloud of Dharma, they should be said to be in accord with the perfection of wisdom.”

“Śāriputra! A bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) is said to be in accord with the perfection of wisdom because they are in accord with the emptiness of the five eyes;
they are said to be in accord with the perfection of wisdom because they are in accord with the emptiness of the six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā).”

“Śāriputra! A bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, because they are in accord with the emptiness of the ten powers of a Buddha, should be said to be in accord with the perfection of wisdom;

because they are in accord with the emptiness of the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, they should be said to be in accord with the perfection of wisdom.”

“Śāriputra! A bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, because they are in accord with the emptiness of the thirty-two marks of a great man, should be said to be in accord with the perfection of wisdom;
because they are in accord with the emptiness of the eighty minor marks, they should be said to be in accord with the perfection of wisdom.”

“Śāriputra! A bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, because they are in accord with the emptiness of the quality of non-forgetfulness, should be said to be in accord with the perfection of wisdom;
because they are in accord with the emptiness of the nature of constant equanimity, they should be said to be in accord with the perfection of wisdom.”

“Śāriputra! Because a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom is in accord with the emptiness of all-knowledge (sarvajñatā), they should be said to be in accord with the perfection of wisdom;

because they are in accord with the emptiness of the knowledge of the paths (mārgajñatā) and the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā), they should be said to be in accord with the perfection of wisdom.”

“Śāriputra! Because a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom is in accord with the emptiness of all-knowledge (sarvajñajñāna), they should be said to be in accord with the perfection of wisdom;
because they are in accord with the emptiness of having forever uprooted the habitual tendencies of all afflictions, they should be said to be in accord with the perfection of wisdom.”

“Śāriputra! A bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, because they are in accord with the emptiness of the fruit of stream-entry, should be said to be in accord with the perfection of wisdom;

because they are in accord with the emptiness of the fruits of once-returner, non-returner, arhatship, and the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, they should be said to be in accord with the perfection of wisdom.”

“Śāriputra! A bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, because they are in accord with the emptiness of the practices of all bodhisattva mahāsattvas, should be said to be in accord with the perfection of wisdom;
because they are in accord with the emptiness of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas, they should be said to be in accord with the perfection of wisdom.”

“Śāriputra! A bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) is said to be engaged with the perfection of wisdom because they are in accord with the emptiness of self (*ātma-śūnyatā*).

They are said to be engaged with the perfection of wisdom because they are in accord with the emptiness of sentient beings (*sattva*), life-principle (*jīva*), living being (*jantu*), nourisher (*poṣa*), person (*puruṣa*), individual (*pudgala*), mind-born (*manuja*), youth (*mānava*), agent (*kāraka*), instigator of action (*kārāpaka*), originator (*utthāpaka*), instigator of origination (*utthāpaka*), experiencer (*vedaka*), instigator of experience (*vedayitṛ*), knower (*jñātṛ*), and seer (*paśyaka*)."
“Śāriputra! Because a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom is thus in accord with emptiness, it should be said that they are in accord with the perfection of wisdom.”

“Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom is in accord with such emptiness as this, they do not perceive form as being either conjoined or unconjoined; they do not perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as being either conjoined or unconjoined.”

Why is this? Śāriputra, it is because this bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive form as being a phenomenon that arises or a phenomenon that ceases; nor does he perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as being phenomena that arise or phenomena that cease.

One does not perceive form as being either a defiled dharma or a pure dharma; one does not perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as being either a defiled dharma or a pure dharma.

Śāriputra! This bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive form as conjoined with feeling; he does not perceive feeling as conjoined with perception; he does not perceive perception as conjoined with formations; and he does not perceive formations as conjoined with consciousness.
Why is this? Śāriputra,
there is not even the slightest dharma that joins with another dharma, because their intrinsic nature is empty.
Why is that? Śāriputra, all forms are empty; they are not form.
All feelings, perceptions, mental formations, and consciousnesses are empty; they are not [identical to] feelings, perceptions, mental formations, or consciousness.
Why is this? Śāriputra!
All forms are empty; they do not possess the characteristic of being subject to transformation and obstruction.
All sensations are empty; they do not possess the characteristic of experiencing and receiving.
All perceptions are empty; they do not possess the characteristic of grasping at mental images.
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are empty; they do not possess the characteristic of being produced.
All consciousnesses (*vijñāna*) are empty; they do not possess the characteristic of discernment. Why is this?
Śāriputra! Form is not different from emptiness; emptiness is not different from form. Form is itself emptiness; emptiness is itself form.

Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not different from emptiness; emptiness is not different from feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are themselves emptiness; emptiness is itself feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Why is this? Śāriputra!
This mark of emptiness of all phenomena is neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing; it is not of the past, not of the future, and not of the present.
“Śāriputra! Thus, in emptiness there is no form; there is no feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;
there is no earth element, and no water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements.”
There is no eye-base, nor ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-base;
there is no form-base, nor sound, odor, taste, tangible-object, or mental-phenomena base;
there is no eye-element, nor ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-element.
In the formless realm, there are no realms of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental objects;
there is no realm of eye-consciousness, nor realms of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-consciousness;
there is no eye-contact, nor contact of ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind.
There are no feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, nor any feelings produced with ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-contact as condition;

there is no arising of ignorance and no cessation of ignorance; there is no arising of volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, or aging, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; there is no cessation of volitional formations up to the cessation of aging, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair;
there is no noble truth of suffering, nor the noble truths of origin, cessation, or the path.
There is no attainment, no clear realization;
there is no stream-enterer, no fruit of stream-entry;
there is no once-returner, no fruit of once-returning.
There is no non-returner, no fruit of non-returning; there is no arhat, no fruit of arhatship;
there is no pratyekabuddha, no pratyekabuddha-enlightenment.
There is no bodhisattva, and there is no bodhisattva practice;
there is no Buddha, and there is no Buddha-enlightenment. Śāriputra!
Because a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom is associated with such dharmas as these, it should be said that they are associated with the perfection of wisdom.
The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra,
Scroll Four (and Five) Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang under Imperial Decree.
Part One, Chapter Three on Correspondence, Part Two:

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they do not perceive form as either corresponding or non-corresponding; they do not perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as either corresponding or non-corresponding."
One does not perceive the eye-base as either associated or dissociated; one does not perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-base as either associated or dissociated.
One does not perceive the form-base as either associated or dissociated; one does not perceive the sound, odor, taste, tangible-object, or mental-object-base as either associated or dissociated.
One does not perceive the eye-element as either associated or dissociated; one does not perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-element as either associated or dissociated.

One does not perceive the realm of form as either associated or dissociated; one does not perceive the realms of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental phenomena as either associated or dissociated.

One does not perceive the realm of eye-consciousness as either associated or dissociated; one does not perceive the realms of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-consciousness as either associated or dissociated.
One does not perceive eye-contact as either associated or dissociated; one does not perceive ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact as either associated or dissociated.

He does not perceive the various feelings arising with eye-contact as a condition, whether they are associated or dissociated; he does not perceive the various feelings arising with ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact as conditions, whether they are associated or dissociated.

He does not perceive the earth element, whether it is associated or dissociated; he does not perceive the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements, whether they are associated or dissociated.

He does not perceive causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), whether they are associated or dissociated; he does not perceive the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), or the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), whether they are associated or dissociated; he does not perceive the various phenomena arising from conditions, whether they are associated or dissociated.

One does not perceive ignorance as either associated or dissociated; one does not perceive volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or aging, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair as either associated or dissociated.
One does not perceive the desire realm as either associated or dissociated; one does not perceive the form or formless realms as either associated or dissociated.

One does not perceive the perfection of generosity as either associated or dissociated; one does not perceive the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, or wisdom as either associated or dissociated.

One does not perceive inner emptiness as either associated or dissociated; nor does one perceive outer emptiness, inner-and-outer emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersion emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, or the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature as either associated or dissociated.

One does not perceive whether suchness is associated or dissociated; one does not perceive whether the dharma-realm, the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), non-falsity, immutability, equality, the state beyond birth, the fixed nature of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*), the stability of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the realm of space, or the inconceivable realm are associated or dissociated.

One does not perceive whether the four foundations of mindfulness are associated or dissociated; one does not perceive whether the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the eightfold noble path are associated or dissociated.

One does not perceive whether the noble truth of suffering is associated or dissociated; one does not perceive whether the noble truths of origin, cessation, or the path are associated or dissociated.

They do not perceive the ten paths of wholesome action as either associated or dissociated; they do not perceive the five precepts of a lay follower (*upāsaka*) or the eight precepts of the one-day fast (*upoṣadha*) as either associated or dissociated;

they do not perceive meritorious actions consisting of giving as either associated or dissociated, nor do they perceive meritorious actions consisting of morality or cultivation as either associated or dissociated;
they do not perceive the four dhyānas as either associated or dissociated, nor do they perceive the four immeasurables or the four formless attainments as either associated or dissociated.

He does not perceive the eight liberations as either associated or dissociated; he does not perceive the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, or the ten totalities as either associated or dissociated.

He does not perceive the door of emptiness liberation as either associated or dissociated; he does not perceive the doors of signlessness and wishlessness liberations as either associated or dissociated.
He does not perceive any of the doors of dhāraṇī as either associated or dissociated; he does not perceive any of the doors of samādhi as either associated or dissociated.

One does not perceive the Ground of Great Joy as either associated or dissociated; one does not perceive the Ground of Purity, the Ground of Radiance, the Ground of Blazing Wisdom, the Ground of Difficult Victory, the Ground of Presence, the Ground of Far-Going, the Ground of Immovability, the Ground of Excellent Intelligence, or the Ground of the Dharma Cloud as either associated or dissociated.
One does not perceive the five eyes as either associated or dissociated; one does not perceive the six supernormal powers as either associated or dissociated.

One does not perceive the ten powers of a Buddha as either associated or dissociated; one does not perceive the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great joy, great equanimity, or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha as either associated or dissociated.

One does not perceive the thirty-two marks of a great man as being either associated or dissociated; one does not perceive the eighty secondary characteristics as being either associated or dissociated.
One does not perceive the quality of non-forgetfulness as being either associated or dissociated; one does not perceive the nature of constant equanimity as being either associated or dissociated.

One does not perceive omniscience as being either associated or dissociated; one does not perceive the knowledge of the paths, the knowledge of all aspects, or the subtle knowledge of all aspects as being either associated or dissociated.

He does not perceive the omniscience of all-knowledge as either associated or dissociated; he does not perceive the permanent uprooting of all afflictions and habitual tendencies as either associated or dissociated.

He does not perceive the fruit of stream-entry as either associated or dissociated; he does not perceive the fruits of once-returner, non-returner, or arhatship as either associated or dissociated. He does not perceive the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha as either associated or dissociated; he does not perceive any of the practices of a bodhisattva mahāsattva as either associated or dissociated; and he does not perceive the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas as either associated or dissociated.

One does not perceive a self as either associated or dissociated; nor does one perceive a sentient being, a life-principle, a creature, a nourisher, a person, an individual, a mind-born, a youth, an agent, an instigator of action, an originator, an instigator of origination, an experiencer, an instigator of experience, a knower, or a seer as either associated or dissociated.
Śāriputra! For these reasons, you should know that when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they are said to be in accord with the perfection of wisdom.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they do not observe emptiness as being associated with or dissociated from emptiness; they do not observe signlessness as being associated with or dissociated from signlessness; they do not observe wishlessness as being associated with or dissociated from wishlessness."
Why is this? Śāriputra, it is because emptiness,
signlessness, and wishlessness are neither associated nor dissociated.
Śāriputra! Because bodhisattva mahāsattvas practicing the perfection of wisdom are associated with such dharmas, it should be said that they are associated with the perfection of wisdom.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, having entered into the emptiness of the intrinsic characteristics of all phenomena, they do not perceive form as either associated or dissociated; they do not perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as either associated or dissociated."
This bodhisattva mahāsattva does not contemplate whether form is associated or dissociated with the prior limit.
Why is this? Because he does not perceive a prior limit.
One does not contemplate whether feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness are associated or dissociated with the past limit.
Why? Because one does not perceive a past limit.
One does not contemplate whether form is associated or dissociated with the future limit.
Why? Because one does not perceive a future limit.
One does not contemplate whether feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness are associated or dissociated with the future limit.
Why is this? Because one does not perceive a future limit.
One does not contemplate whether form is associated or dissociated with the present.
Why? Because one does not perceive the present.
One does not contemplate whether feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness are associated or dissociated with the present.
Why? Because one does not perceive the present.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā),
they do not observe whether the past limit (pūrvānta) is associated or dissociated with the future limit (aparānta), nor do they observe whether the past limit is associated with the present."
If they are not associated, one does not contemplate whether the later limit is associated or dissociated with the earlier limit;
one does not contemplate whether the later limit is associated or dissociated with the present;
one does not contemplate whether the present is associated or dissociated with the earlier limit; nor does one contemplate whether the present is associated with the later limit.
If they are not associated, one does not contemplate the past with the future or the present—whether associated or dissociated;
one does not contemplate the future with the past or the present—whether associated or dissociated;
one does not contemplate the present with the past or the future—whether associated or dissociated. One does not...
One contemplates the past, the future, and the present, whether they are associated or dissociated.
Why is this? Śāriputra!
Śāriputra, because the three periods of time are empty,
when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) and correspond with such dharmas, they should be said to correspond with the perfection of wisdom.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they do not observe all-knowledge as being either associated or dissociated with the past."
Why is this? Since one does not even perceive the existence of the past, how much less could one observe whether omniscience is associated with or dissociated from the past!
One does not observe whether omniscience is associated with or dissociated from the future.
Why is this? Since one does not even perceive the existence of the future, how much less could one observe whether all-knowledge is associated or dissociated with the future!
One does not observe whether all-knowledge is associated or dissociated with the present.
Why is this? One does not even perceive the existence of the present, much less observe whether omniscience is associated with or dissociated from the present! Śāriputra!
Because all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom and are associated with such dharmas, it should be said that they are associated with the perfection of wisdom.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they do not perceive all-knowledge as being either associated with or dissociated from form."
Why is this? Since one does not even perceive the existence of form, how much less could one observe all-knowledge as being either associated or dissociated with form!
One does not observe all-knowledge as being either associated or dissociated with feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.

Why is this? Because one does not even perceive the existence of feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness, much less observe whether all-knowledge is associated or dissociated with feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness!
Śāriputra! Because bodhisattva mahāsattvas practicing the perfection of wisdom are associated with such dharmas as these, they should be said to be associated with the perfection of wisdom.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they do not observe whether all-knowledge is associated or dissociated with the sense base of the eye."

Why is this? Since one does not even perceive the existence of the sense-base of the eye, how much less could one observe whether omniscience is associated or dissociated with the sense-base of the eye!
One does not observe whether omniscience is associated or dissociated with the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind.

Why is this? Since one does not even perceive the existence of the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind, how much less could one observe omniscience as being either associated or dissociated with the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind!
Śāriputra! Because bodhisattva mahāsattvas practicing the perfection of wisdom are associated with such dharmas, they should be said to be associated with the perfection of wisdom.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
