He does not cling to the nature of the supernormal power of the realization of the recollection of past lives; he does not cling to the phenomena of the supernormal power of the realization of the recollection of past lives; he does not cling to the one who attains the supernormal power of the realization of the recollection of past lives. Regarding both clinging and non-clinging, he clings to nothing at all.”
Why is this? Śāriputra,

it is because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have realized that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty, that their intrinsic nature is detached, and that their intrinsic nature is fundamentally unapprehendable.
Śāriputra! This bodhisattva mahāsattva does not form such a thought as:
"I now evoke the supernormal power of knowledge of past lives for my own amusement or for the amusement of others," except solely for the sake of attaining the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).

"Śāriputra! This is the perfection of the supernormal power of the realization of the recollection of past lives, which is brought forth by a bodhisattva mahāsattva when practicing the perfection of wisdom."
At that time, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

What is the perfection of the superknowledge of the realization of the divine eye-wisdom (divyacakṣur-abhijñā) brought forth by a bodhisattva mahāsattva when practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā)?”
The Buddha addressed the Venerable Śāriputra, saying: “Śāriputra!

There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who possess the supernormal power of the realization of the divine eye-knowledge, which is most excellent, pure, and surpasses that of the human or celestial eyes. They are able to see, as it truly is, the various forms and appearances of sentient and non-sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions, each as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. That is to say, they universally perceive all classes of sentient beings at the time of death and at the time of birth—their beautiful forms and coarse forms, their superior and inferior states, and their rebirths in happy or miserable realms—seeing all such various forms and appearances.”

Therefore, one further understands that sentient beings undergo various distinctions in rebirth according to the power and function of their karma: those who accomplish virtuous conduct of body, virtuous conduct of speech, and virtuous conduct of mind, and who praise the noble ones and the causes and conditions of right view, shall upon the dissolution of the body after death ascend to a happy destination—either being born among the devas or born among humans to experience various sublime pleasures;

whereas those who accomplish unwholesome conduct of body, unwholesome conduct of speech, and unwholesome conduct of mind, and who revile the noble ones and the causes and conditions of wrong view, shall upon the dissolution of the body after death fall into an evil destination—either being born in hell, or born as an animal, or born in the realm of hungry ghosts, or born in a borderland among base, lowly, and defiled classes of beings to experience various intense sufferings.
In this way, he knows as they truly are the various classes of karma of sentient beings and the distinctions in the fruits they receive.

"Śāriputra, although this bodhisattva mahāsattva possesses such functions of the divine eye, he does not exalt himself therein; he does not cling to the nature of the supernormal power of the realization of the knowledge of the divine eye, nor does he cling to the matter of the supernormal power of the realization of the knowledge of the divine eye, nor does he cling to those who can attain such a supernormal power of the realization of the knowledge of the divine eye. He is without attachment to either clinging or non-clinging."
Why is this? Śāriputra,

it is because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have realized that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty, that their intrinsic nature is detached, and that their intrinsic nature is fundamentally unapprehendable.
Śāriputra! This bodhisattva mahāsattva does not form such a thought as:

"I shall now bring forth the supernormal power of the divine eye for my own amusement or for the amusement of others," except solely for the sake of attaining the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).

"Śāriputra! This is the perfection of the supernormal power of realization through the knowledge of the divine eye, which is brought forth by a bodhisattva mahāsattva when practicing the perfection of wisdom."
At that time, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One,

how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), bring forth the perfection of the supernormal power of the realization of the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣayajñānasākṣātkriyābhijñāpāramitā)?”
The Buddha addressed the Venerable Śāriputra, saying: “Śāriputra!

There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who possess the supernormal knowledge of the realization of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣayajñānasākṣātkriyābhijñā*), and who are able to know, as it truly is, whether the outflows of all sentient beings—whether themselves or others—in all worlds throughout the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, have been exhausted or not.”

This supernormal power relies upon the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*); it is only when all obstructions and their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are severed that it becomes perfected. At the time of attaining the irreversible Bodhisattva stage, it is also termed the "exhaustion of all outflows" (*āsrava-kṣaya*), because they never again arise or manifest.

Although a bodhisattva attains this supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows, they do not fall to the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha; rather, they proceed solely toward unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, as they no longer seek any other benefit or purpose.

“Śāriputra! Although this bodhisattva mahāsattva possesses such application of the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣayajñāna*), he does not exalt himself therein; he does not cling to the nature of the supernormal power of realizing the exhaustion of outflows, nor to the matter of realizing the exhaustion of outflows, nor to the one who is able to attain such a supernormal power of realizing the exhaustion of outflows. He is without attachment in both attachment and non-attachment.”
Why is this? Śāriputra,

it is because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have realized that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty, that their intrinsic nature is detached, and that their intrinsic nature is fundamentally unapprehendable.
Śāriputra! This bodhisattva mahāsattva does not form such a thought as:

"I shall now manifest the supernormal power of the realization of the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows for my own amusement or for the amusement of others," except solely for the sake of attaining the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).

"Śāriputra! This is the perfection of the superknowledge of the realization of the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣayajñānasākṣātkriyābhijñā) that is brought forth by a bodhisattva mahāsattva when practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā)."

“In this way, Śāriputra, when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they are able to fulfill and purify the perfection of the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*). Because these six supernormal powers are fulfilled and purified, they attain the fulfillment of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), namely, all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).”
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,

when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they abide in the perfection of generosity and purify the path of all-knowledge and the knowledge of all aspects, because through ultimate emptiness they do not give rise to a mind of stinginess regarding giving."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,

when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they abide in the perfection of ethical discipline and purify the path of all-knowledge and the knowledge of all aspects, because through ultimate emptiness they do not give rise to thoughts of either maintaining or violating ethical discipline."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,

when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they abide in the perfection of patience and purify the path of all-knowledge and the knowledge of all aspects, because through ultimate emptiness, they do not give rise to thoughts of compassion, anger, or resentment."

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they abide in the perfection of diligence, purifying the path of all-knowledge and the knowledge of all aspects, because by means of ultimate emptiness, they do not give rise to thoughts of either exertion or indolence."

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they abide in the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*), purifying the path of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), because through ultimate emptiness (*atyantaśūnyatā*), they do not give rise to a mind that is either tranquil or distracted."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,

when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they abide within the perfection of wisdom and purify the path of all-knowledge and the knowledge of all aspects, because through ultimate emptiness they do not give rise to a mind of either wisdom or delusion."

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they abide in the perfections of generosity and ethical discipline, purifying the path to all-knowledge and the knowledge of all aspects; for, by means of ultimate emptiness, they do not give rise to thoughts of stinginess regarding giving or of transgression regarding ethical discipline."

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they abide in the perfections of generosity and patience, purifying the path to all-knowledge and the knowledge of all aspects; for, by means of ultimate emptiness, they do not give rise to thoughts of stinginess regarding giving, nor thoughts of malice toward compassion and loving-kindness."

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they abide in the perfections of generosity and diligence, purifying the path of all-knowledge and the knowledge of all aspects; for, by means of ultimate emptiness, they do not give rise to thoughts of stinginess regarding giving or laziness regarding diligence."

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they abide in the perfections of generosity and meditative concentration, purifying the path of all-knowledge and the knowledge of all aspects; for, by means of ultimate emptiness, they do not give rise to the stinginess of giving or to a distracted mind."

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they abide in the perfection of generosity and the perfection of wisdom, purifying the path of all-knowledge and the knowledge of all aspects. This is because, through ultimate emptiness, they do not give rise to thoughts of stinginess regarding giving or delusion regarding wisdom."

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they abide in the perfections of ethical discipline and patience, purifying the path of all-knowledge and the knowledge of all aspects. This is because, through ultimate emptiness, they do not give rise to thoughts of upholding or violating the precepts, nor thoughts of loving-kindness, compassion, anger, or resentment."

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they abide in the perfections of ethical discipline and diligence, purifying the path of all-knowledge and the knowledge of all aspects; for, by means of ultimate emptiness, they do not give rise to thoughts of upholding or violating ethical discipline, nor of vigor or indolence."

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they abide in the perfections of ethical discipline and meditative concentration, purifying the path to all-knowledge and the knowledge of all aspects; for, by means of ultimate emptiness, they do not give rise to thoughts of upholding or violating ethical discipline, nor of tranquility or distraction."

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they abide in the perfection of ethical discipline and the perfection of wisdom, purifying the path of all-knowledge and the knowledge of all aspects. This is because, through ultimate emptiness, they do not give rise to thoughts of either upholding or violating ethical discipline, nor of wisdom or folly."

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they abide in the perfections of patience and diligence, purifying the path of all-knowledge and the knowledge of all aspects; for, by means of ultimate emptiness, they do not give rise to thoughts of compassion or anger, nor of vigor or indolence."

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they abide in the perfections of patience and meditative concentration, purifying the path of all-knowledge and the knowledge of all aspects. This is because, through ultimate emptiness, they do not give rise to compassion or anger, nor to a mind of either tranquility or distraction."

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they abide in the perfections of patience and wisdom, purifying the path to all-knowledge and the knowledge of all aspects; for, by means of ultimate emptiness, they do not give rise to thoughts of compassion or anger, nor of wisdom or delusion."

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they abide in the perfections of diligence and meditative concentration, purifying the path of all-knowledge and the knowledge of all aspects; this is because, through ultimate emptiness, they give rise neither to exertion nor laziness, and neither to a mind of tranquility nor distraction."

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they abide in the perfection of diligence and the perfection of wisdom, purifying the path of all-knowledge and the knowledge of all aspects. This is because, through ultimate emptiness, they do not give rise to thoughts of exertion or indolence, nor of wisdom or delusion."

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they abide in the perfections of meditative concentration and wisdom, purifying the path of all-knowledge and the knowledge of all aspects; this is because, through ultimate emptiness, they do not give rise to thoughts of either tranquility-and-distraction or wisdom-and-delusion."

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they abide in the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, and patience, purifying the path of all-knowledge and the knowledge of all aspects. By means of ultimate emptiness, they do not give rise to thoughts of stinginess regarding giving, nor of transgression regarding ethical discipline, nor of malice regarding loving-kindness and compassion."

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they abide in the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, and diligence, purifying the path of all-knowledge and the knowledge of all aspects. This is because, through ultimate emptiness, they do not give rise to thoughts of stinginess regarding giving, nor of transgression regarding ethical discipline, nor of laziness regarding diligent vigor."

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they abide in the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, and meditative concentration, purifying the path of all-knowledge and the knowledge of all aspects. This is because, through ultimate emptiness, they do not give rise to stinginess regarding giving, nor to transgression regarding ethical discipline, nor to distraction regarding the mind of tranquility."

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they abide in the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, and wisdom, purifying the path to all-knowledge and the knowledge of all aspects. This is because, through ultimate emptiness, they do not give rise to thoughts of stinginess regarding giving, transgression regarding ethical discipline, or delusion regarding wisdom."

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they abide in the perfections of generosity, patience, and diligence, purifying the path of all-knowledge and the knowledge of all aspects. This is because, through ultimate emptiness, they do not give rise to thoughts of stinginess regarding giving, malice toward loving-kindness and compassion, or indolence toward vigor."

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they abide in the perfections of generosity, patience, and meditative concentration, purifying the path of all-knowledge and the knowledge of all aspects. This is because, through ultimate emptiness, they do not give rise to thoughts of stinginess regarding giving, nor thoughts of malice regarding loving-kindness and compassion, nor thoughts of distraction regarding tranquility."

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they abide in the perfections of generosity, patience, and wisdom, purifying the path of all-knowledge and the knowledge of all aspects. This is because, through ultimate emptiness, they do not give rise to thoughts of stinginess regarding giving, malice regarding loving-kindness and compassion, or delusion regarding wisdom."

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they abide in the perfections of generosity, diligence, and meditative concentration, purifying the path of all-knowledge and the knowledge of all aspects. This is because, through ultimate emptiness, they do not give rise to stinginess regarding giving, nor to laziness regarding diligence, nor to distraction regarding the mind of tranquility."

“In this way, Śāriputra, when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they abide in the six perfections and purify the path of all-knowledge and the knowledge of all aspects. Because ultimate emptiness has neither coming nor going, there is no giving and no stinginess, for these are merely conventional designations;
there is no pure ethical discipline and no violation of ethical discipline, for these are merely conventional designations.”
There is no patience and no anger, because they are merely conventional designations;
there is no diligence and no indolence, because they are merely conventional designations;
there is no meditative concentration and no distraction, because they are merely conventional designations.
There is no wisdom and no delusion, for these are merely conventional designations. Thus, this bodhisattva mahāsattva does not cling to entering [the path], nor does he cling to not entering;

he does not cling to having crossed over, nor does he cling to not having crossed over; he does not cling to generosity, nor does he cling to stinginess; he does not cling to pure ethical discipline, nor does he cling to violating ethical discipline; he does not cling to patience, nor does he cling to anger; he does not cling to diligence, nor does he cling to laziness; he does not cling to meditative concentration, nor does he cling to distraction; he does not cling to wisdom, nor does he cling to delusion.

“Śāriputra! At that time, this bodhisattva mahāsattva likewise does not cling to the giver, nor does he cling to the miserly; he does not cling to the one who maintains pure precepts, nor does he cling to the one who violates the precepts; he does not cling to the one who practices patience, nor does he cling to the one who is angry; he does not cling to the one who exerts diligence, nor does he cling to the one who is indolent; he does not cling to the one who practices meditative concentration, nor does he cling to the one who is distracted; he does not cling to the one who possesses wisdom, nor does he cling to the one who is deluded.”
Śāriputra! At that time, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will have no attachment even toward attachment or non-attachment. Why is this?
Śāriputra! This is because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have realized that all phenomena are ultimately empty. Śāriputra!
At that time, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will not be attached to revilement or praise, not be attached to harm or benefit, and not be attached to contempt or reverence.

Why is this? Śāriputra, because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas realize that all phenomena are ultimately unarisen; within the dharma of non-arising, there is no dharma of reviling or praising, no dharma of harming or benefiting, and no dharma of contempt or reverence.

Śāriputra! At that time, this bodhisattva mahāsattva does not become attached to those who revile him, nor to those who praise him; he does not become attached to those who harm him, nor to those who benefit him; he does not become attached to those who treat him with contempt, nor to those who show him respect.

Why is this? Śāriputra, it is because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas realize that all phenomena are empty by their very nature. Within this emptiness of intrinsic nature, there is no one who reviles or praises, no one who harms or benefits, and no one who treats them with contempt or respect.
Śāriputra! At that time, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will have no attachment even toward attachment or non-attachment. Why is this?
Śāriputra! This bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, forever severs all attachment and non-attachment.
Thus it is, Śāriputra!
When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, the merit they obtain is supreme, most sublime, and inconceivable; it is not possessed by any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.

Śāriputra! Once this bodhisattva mahāsattva has thus perfected these merits, he further matures sentient beings through superior generosity, pleasant speech, beneficial conduct, and cooperation. Furthermore, by means of various firm great vows and courageous diligence, he purifies buddha-fields. Through these, he swiftly realizes the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment that he seeks.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,

when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they give rise to a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings, whether they are inferior or superior, beautiful or ugly."
Once this bodhisattva mahāsattva has given rise to a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings, he further gives rise to a mind of benefit and happiness.
Once this bodhisattva mahāsattva has given rise to a mind of benefit and happiness toward all sentient beings, he attains equality regarding the nature of all phenomena.

Having attained equanimity regarding the nature of all phenomena, this bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to universally establish all sentient beings within the equanimity of all phenomena, thereby performing great benefit for them.

Śāriputra! By virtue of these causes and conditions, this bodhisattva mahāsattva, in the present life, receives the protective mindfulness of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas throughout the worlds of the ten directions; he also receives the collective praise of the assembly of all bodhisattva mahāsattvas throughout the ten directions; he also receives the mutual respect and affection of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas who practice the holy life; and he is likewise honored, revered, respected, and praised by all the world’s devas, humans, asuras, and others.

Śāriputra! By virtue of these causes and conditions, wherever this bodhisattva-mahāsattva is born, his eyes shall never see unlovely forms; his ears shall never hear unlovely sounds; his nose shall never smell unlovely odors; his tongue shall never taste unlovely flavors; his body shall never feel unlovely tangibles; and his mind shall never grasp unlovely dharmas.

Śāriputra! By virtue of these causes and conditions, the merit attained by this bodhisattva mahāsattva increases and becomes ever more sublime, remaining forever non-retrogressive until the attainment of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

When the Buddha had spoken these words on the supreme merits of this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, immeasurable great bhikṣus in the assembly rose from their seats and each offered various kinds of new, pure, and superior robes to the World-Honored One. Having made these offerings, they all resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the World-Honored One smiled, and from his face issued rays of light of various colors.
Then Ānanda rose from his seat, bared his left shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined in reverence, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“For what cause and for what reason do you manifest this smile?
The smiles of the Buddhas never occur without cause or condition; we only pray that the World-Honored One will compassionately explain it to us!
At that time, the Buddha addressed Ānanda, saying:

"These immeasurable bhikṣus who have risen from their seats shall, after this, during the sixty-first kalpa known as the Star-like Kalpa, all attain Buddhahood under a single name: Mahādhvajaketu Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed Worthy One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, Bhagavān."
"After these bhikṣus pass away from here, they shall be reborn in the eastern land of Akṣobhya Buddha, where they will diligently cultivate the holy life in the presence of that Buddha.

At that time, there were again sixty hundred thousand sons of gods who, upon hearing the merits and benefits of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* as taught by the Buddha, all resolved to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

The World-Honored One prophesied that he would, within the Dharma of the Tathāgata Maitreya, leave the household life with pure faith and diligently practice the holy life; the Tathāgata Maitreya will grant him the prophecy that he shall attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, turn the wheel of the true Dharma, and deliver immeasurable multitudes, causing them all to realize the eternal bliss of nirvāṇa.

At that time, by the Buddha’s spiritual power, the entire assembly here beheld the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and their respective assemblies in each of the thousand Buddha-lands throughout the ten directions.
The meritorious adornments of those buddha-fields are so subtle, exquisite, and supreme that at that time, the meritorious adornments of this Sahā world-system could not compare to them.
At that time, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings in this assembly each made a vow, saying:
"By means of all the purely virtuous deeds we have cultivated, may we be reborn in those various Buddha-lands."
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the aspiration in his mind, again smiled, and from his face issued forth rays of light of various colors.
Then Ānanda rose from his seat once more and respectfully asked the Buddha about the cause and conditions for his smile.
At that time, the Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Do you now see these immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings who have risen from their seats?
Ānanda replied:
"Yes, indeed!
I have seen it.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"When these sentient beings exhaust their lifespan here, they shall each be reborn in various Buddha-fields according to the power of their vows;
there, in the presence of those Buddhas, they shall cultivate the bodhisattva practices until they attain unsurpassed,

perfect, and complete enlightenment, never being separated from the Buddhas in whatever place they are born, and constantly making offerings, paying homage, showing respect, and praising them with diligent effort."
They practice the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; they abide in internal emptiness,
external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness,
the emptiness of the ultimate, the emptiness of conditioned phenomena, the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, absolute emptiness, and the emptiness of that which has no limit.
Emptiness, the emptiness of dispersion, the emptiness of non-alteration, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the emptiness of self-characteristics, the emptiness of common characteristics,
the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature,
and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence; abiding in suchness, the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, and non-falsity.
The nature, immutability, equanimity, the state beyond birth, the fixed order of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the stability of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*),
the realm of space (*ākāśadhātu*), and the inconceivable realm; [the cultivation of] the four foundations of mindfulness,
the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path.
The factors of the path consist of abiding securely in the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path;
practicing the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments;

practicing the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative concentrations, and the ten totalities; and practicing the liberations of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
...the gates; practicing all *dhāraṇī* gates and *samādhi* gates;
practicing the stages of a bodhisattva mahāsattva; practicing the five eyes and the six supernormal powers;
practicing the ten powers of a buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great...
Having abandoned [the other perfections] and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and having fully perfected the practice of the quality of non-forgetfulness,
the nature of constant equanimity, as well as the practice of all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*),

and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), along with all other bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices, they shall simultaneously attain Buddhahood, all bearing the same name: namely, Zhuang (Adorned).
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World,
Unsurpassed Worthy One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, Bhagavān— [the Tathāgata] Śrīrāja.

one is able to realize the unequaled sublime Dharma, namely, unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.

Those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice the perfection of wisdom are most honored, most supreme, most excellent, and most wondrous, possessing great power. They are able to realize the peerless and wondrous Dharma, namely, unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

One is able to attain an unequaled self-nature, namely, a body exquisitely adorned with boundless and preeminent marks and signs;
one is able to realize the unequaled sublime Dharma, namely, unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

and they are able to attain the unequaled self-body, namely, a body exquisitely adorned with boundless and preeminent marks and signs.”

One is able to attain an unequaled self-nature, namely, a body exquisitely adorned with boundless and supreme marks and signs;
one is able to realize the unequaled sublime Dharma, namely, unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.
“World-Honored One!

Those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice the perfection of wisdom are most honored and supreme, most excellent and sublime, and possess great power; they are able to practice the peerless eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities; they are able to fulfill the peerless eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities; they are able to perfect the peerless eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities;
and they are able to attain a peerless self-nature, namely, a body exquisitely adorned with boundless and preeminent marks and signs.”

One is able to attain an unequaled self-nature, namely, a body exquisitely adorned with boundless, supreme marks and signs;
one is able to realize the unequaled sublime Dharma, namely, unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

they are able to attain an unequaled self-nature, namely, a body wonderfully adorned with boundless and preeminent marks and signs.”
They are able to realize the peerless and sublime Dharma, namely, unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

One is able to attain an unequaled self-nature, namely, a body exquisitely adorned with boundless and preeminent marks and signs;
one is able to realize the unequaled sublime Dharma, namely, unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.

they are able to attain a peerless self-body, namely, a body exquisitely adorned with boundless and preeminent marks and signs.”
They are able to realize the peerless, sublime Dharma, namely, unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

One is able to attain an unequaled self-nature, namely, a body exquisitely adorned with boundless and preeminent marks and signs;

One is able to attain an unequaled self-nature, namely, a body exquisitely adorned with boundless and supreme marks and signs;
one is able to realize the unequaled sublime Dharma, namely, unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.
“World-Honored One!

It is because the Tathāgata also practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), and by practicing and abiding in it, he has fully perfected and endowed himself with all manner of merits; thus he attains form that is unequaled and peerless, attains feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness that are unequaled and peerless, realizes enlightenment that is unequaled and peerless, and turns the wheel of Dharma that is unequaled and peerless, delivering immeasurable sentient beings and causing them to obtain supreme benefit and peace.”

The Buddhas of the past, future, and present have also diligently practiced and studied this Prajñāpāramitā; they have all fully perfected various merits, have realized unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, will realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and are currently realizing unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment. They turn the sublime wheel of Dharma to deliver immeasurable multitudes, causing them to obtain supreme benefit and peace.
Therefore, World-Honored One,
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to cross over to the further shore of all dharmas, they should study the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
“World-Honored One!

All those in the world—whether devas, humans, or asuras—who practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), should be offered worship, reverence, respect, praise, and protection by all beings, so that they may practice the perfection of wisdom with diligence, free from obstacles and hindrances.”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the śrāvakas and the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, saying: "So it is! So it is!"

As you have said, all those in the world—whether devas, humans, or asuras—who practice the perfection of wisdom, should be honored, revered, respected, praised, and protected by all beings, so that they may practice the perfection of wisdom with diligence, free from hindrance and obstruction.
Why is this? It is because of these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas that there appear in the world humans and devas, namely:
great clans of kṣatriyas, great clans of brahmins, great clans of householders, and great clans of lay merchants.

Great clans, such as those of a wheel-turning monarch; or the gods of the Realm of the Four Great Kings, the Heaven of the Thirty-three, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven;
or the gods of the Brahmakāyika, Brahmapurohita, Brahmakāyika-pariṣad, and Mahābrahmā heavens; or the Ābhāsvara Heaven.
...the Heaven of Limited Light, the Heaven of Immeasurable Light, and the Heaven of Pervasive Purity;
or the Heaven of Purity, the Heaven of Limited Purity, the Heaven of Immeasurable Purity, and the Heaven of Universal Purity;
or the Vast Heaven, the Heaven of Limited Vastness, the Heaven of Immeasurable Vastness, and the Heaven of Vast Fruit; or the Heaven of Non-percipient Beings, or the Heaven Without Affliction.
the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, the Abṛha Heaven, the Atapa Heaven,
the Sudṛśa Heaven, the Sudarśana Heaven, and the Akaniṣṭha Heaven; as well as the gods of the Sphere of Infinite Space, the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness, the Sphere of Nothingness,
and the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception appear in the world.

It is because of these bodhisattva mahāsattvas that there appear in the world the stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arhats, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattva mahāsattvas, and all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.
It is because of these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas that the Three Jewels appear in the world, bringing great benefit to all sentient beings.

It is because of these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas that various means of livelihood and articles of comfort appear in the world; that is to say, food and drink, clothing, bedding, dwellings, lamps, and precious gems such as mani-jewels, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, jade, coral, gold, and silver appear in the world.
"To state it briefly: all the happiness of humans, devas, and others in the world, as well as the bliss of nirvāṇa, does not exist without such bodhisattva-mahāsattvas."

Why is this? It is because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas themselves correctly practice the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, and they also teach others to practice them;

they themselves correctly abide in internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common-characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, and they also teach others to abide therein.

They themselves abide in suchness, the dharma-realm, the nature of phenomena, non-illusoriness, immutability, equality, the state beyond birth, the fixed nature of phenomena, the stability of phenomena, the limit of reality, the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm; they also teach others to so abide.

They themselves correctly practice the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path; they also teach others to so practice.
They themselves correctly abide in the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path; they also teach others to so abide.
They themselves correctly practice the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments, and they also teach others to practice them;
they themselves correctly practice the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten totalities, and they also teach others to practice them;
they themselves correctly practice the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—and they also teach others to practice them.
They themselves correctly practice the gateways of dhāraṇīs and samādhis, and also teach others to practice them;
they themselves correctly practice the various bodhisattva stages, and also teach others to practice them;
they themselves correctly practice the five eyes and the six supernormal powers, and also teach others to practice them.

They themselves correctly practice the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and they also teach others to practice them;
they themselves correctly practice the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant equanimity, and they also teach others to practice them;
they themselves correctly practice all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects, and they also teach others to practice them.
Therefore, by means of this practice of the perfection of wisdom, all sentient beings obtain supreme benefit and peace.

Furthermore, from this mark of the tongue, he emitted immeasurable and innumerable rays of light of various colors, universally illuminating Buddha-worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions.

At that time, in each of the Buddha-fields of the eastern direction, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there were immeasurable and incalculable bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, having beheld this light, each went to their respective Buddha, prostrated themselves in reverence, and said:
“World-Honored One!...”
"By whose spiritual power is this?

"Now is the very time; go as you intend.

Chapter Seven: Instruction and Admonition, Part One.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Venerable Subhūti:

"By means of your eloquence, you should proclaim for the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas the Dharma associated with the *prajñāpāramitā*, instructing and admonishing those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas so that they may reach the ultimate consummation in the study and practice of the *prajñāpāramitā*."
At that time, the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, along with the great śrāvakas, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, humans, non-humans, and others, all had this thought:

"Now, will the Venerable Subhūti, by the power of his own wisdom and eloquence, proclaim for the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas the Dharma associated with the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), instructing and exhorting the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas so that they may reach the ultimate realization in the study of the perfection of wisdom? Or will he do so by relying on the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power?"

The Venerable Subhūti, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the assembly of bodhisattva mahāsattvas, as well as the great śrāvakas, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, humans, non-humans, and others, addressed the Venerable Śāriputra:
"One should know that all the teachings spoken by the disciples of the Buddhas are sustained by the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha."

Why is this? Śāriputra, when the Buddhas proclaim the essential teachings of the Dharma for others, those who receive the Buddha’s instruction and practice with diligent application are able to realize the true nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*). Consequently, whatever they proclaim for others will never be in contradiction with that true nature; therefore, the words of the Buddha are like a lamp that transmits its light.

Śāriputra! Relying upon the majestic power and sustaining grace of the Buddha, I shall proclaim for the assembly of bodhisattva mahāsattvas the Dharma associated with the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), instructing and guiding these bodhisattva mahāsattvas so that they may reach the ultimate consummation in the study of the perfection of wisdom; this is not by the power of my own wisdom or eloquence.
"Why is this? Because the dharmas associated with the profound perfection of wisdom are not the domain of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has commanded:

‘By means of your eloquence, you should proclaim for the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas the Dharma associated with the *prajñāpāramitā*, instructing and exhorting the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas so that they may reach the ultimate consummation in the study and practice of the *prajñāpāramitā*.’”
“World-Honored One!
In this context, what dharma is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
Furthermore, what dharma is called the prajñāpāramitā?”
“World-Honored One!

I do not perceive any dharma that can be called a bodhisattva mahāsattva, nor do I perceive any dharma that can be called the prajñāpāramitā; since I do not even perceive these two names, how am I to proclaim for the assembly of bodhisattva mahāsattvas the dharmas corresponding to the prajñāpāramitā, and how am I to instruct and admonish those bodhisattva mahāsattvas so that they may reach the ultimate perfection in the cultivation and study of the prajñāpāramitā?”
The Buddha said, “Subhūti!

A bodhisattva mahāsattva is merely a name, called ‘bodhisattva mahāsattva’; the perfection of wisdom is also merely a name, called ‘perfection of wisdom’; and these two names are likewise merely names.”
"Subhūti!

These three names are neither arising nor ceasing; they are merely conceptualizations and designations, established through verbal expression. Such provisional names do not exist internally, nor externally, nor in between the two, for they cannot be apprehended."
“Subhūti, you should know this:

for example, ‘self’ is merely a provisional designation; such a designation is neither born nor extinguished. It is only through perception and conceptualization, and by means of conventional expression and discourse, that we refer to it as ‘self.’”

In this way, sentient beings, life-principles, those who are born, those who are nourished, persons, individuals, mind-born ones, young scholars, agents, instigators of action, originators, instigators of origination, experiencers, instigators of experience, knowers, and seers are also merely conventional designations. Thus, these names are conventionally designated as neither arising nor ceasing; they exist only as perceptions and conceptualizations, established through verbal expression as "sentient beings" up to "seers."
All these things exist merely as provisional designations; these provisional designations do not exist internally, nor externally, nor in between the two, because they cannot be apprehended.
Thus it is, Subhūti!

Whether it be a bodhisattva mahāsattva, or the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), or these two names—all are merely conventional dharmas (*prajñapti-dharma*). Such conventional dharmas are neither born nor extinguished; they exist only as conceptualization (*saṃjñā*) and designation (*prajñapti*), established through verbal expression as "bodhisattva mahāsattva," "perfection of wisdom," and these two names.

These three kinds [of dharmas] exist only as provisional designations; these provisional designations do not exist internally, nor do they exist externally, nor do they exist in between the two, for they are unattainable.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!..."

For example, form (*rūpa*) is merely a conventional phenomenon; likewise, these conventional phenomena are neither born nor extinguished. There is only perception and conceptualization, which, through designation and verbal expression, are called "form.

In the same way, feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are also merely conventional phenomena; likewise, these conventional phenomena are neither born nor extinguished. There is only perception and conceptualization, which, through designation and verbal expression, are called feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness.
All these are merely provisional designations; these provisional designations do not exist internally, nor externally, nor in between the two, because they cannot be apprehended.
Thus it is, Subhūti!

Whether it be a bodhisattva mahāsattva, or the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), or these two names—all are merely conventional dharmas. Such conventional dharmas are neither born nor extinguished; they exist only as conceptualization and designation, established through speech and expression, which we call "bodhisattva mahāsattva," "perfection of wisdom," and these two names.

These three kinds [of dharmas] exist only as provisional designations; these provisional designations do not abide internally, nor do they abide externally, nor do they abide in between the two, for they cannot be apprehended.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

For example, the sense-base of the eye is merely a conventional dharma; such a conventional dharma is neither born nor extinguished, yet through conceptualization and designation, it is spoken of by means of verbal expression as the "sense-base of the eye.

Likewise, the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are also merely conventional dharmas; such conventional dharmas are neither born nor extinguished, yet through conceptualization and designation, they are spoken of by means of verbal expression as the "sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind."

All these things exist only as provisional designations; these provisional designations do not abide within, nor do they abide without, nor do they abide in between the two, because they cannot be apprehended.
Thus it is, Subhūti!

Whether it be a bodhisattva mahāsattva, or the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), or these two names—all are merely conventional dharmas (*prajñaptidharma*). Such conventional dharmas are neither born nor extinguished; they exist only as conceptualization (*saṃjñā*) and designation (*prajñapti*), established through verbal expression as "bodhisattva mahāsattva," "perfection of wisdom," and these two names.
These three kinds [of things] exist only as provisional designations; these designations do not exist internally, nor externally, nor in between the two, for they are unapprehendable.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!"

For example, the sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*) is merely a conventional dharma; such a conventional dharma is neither born nor extinguished, yet through perception and conceptualization, it is designated by speech and expression as "the sense-base of form.

Likewise, the sense-bases of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) are also merely conventional dharmas; such conventional dharmas are neither born nor extinguished, yet through perception and conceptualization, they are designated by speech and expression as "the sense-bases of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena."
All these things exist merely as provisional designations; these provisional designations do not exist internally, nor externally, nor in between the two, because they cannot be apprehended.
Thus it is, Subhūti!

Whether it be the bodhisattva-mahāsattva, or the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), or these two names—these are all conventional dharmas. Such conventional dharmas are neither born nor extinguished; they exist only as conceptualization and designation, established through verbal expression as "bodhisattva-mahāsattva," as "perfection of wisdom," and as these two names.

These three kinds [of things] exist only as provisional designations; these provisional designations do not exist internally, nor externally, nor in between the two, because they cannot be apprehended.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!..."

For example, the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*) is merely a conventional phenomenon (*prajñapti-dharma*); such a conventional phenomenon is neither born nor extinguished, yet through conceptualization (*saṃjñā*) and subsequent conceptualization (*anu-saṃjñā*), it is designated by verbal expression as the "eye-element.

Likewise, the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-elements (*śrotra-, ghrāṇa-, jihvā-, kāya-, manodhātu*) are also merely conventional phenomena; such conventional phenomena are neither born nor extinguished, yet through conceptualization and subsequent conceptualization, they are designated by verbal expression as the "ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-elements."

One should not contemplate the practices of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as belonging to either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa; one should not contemplate the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas as belonging to either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa.

One should not contemplate the practices of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as being internal, external, or in between; one should not contemplate the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas as being internal, external, or in between.

One should not contemplate the practices of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as being obtainable or unobtainable; one should not contemplate the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas as being obtainable or unobtainable.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, whether it be the bodhisattva-mahāsattva, or the perfection of wisdom, or the names of these two, none of them are seen to exist within the realm of the conditioned (*saṃskṛtadhātu*), nor are they seen to exist within the realm of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛtadhātu*)."
Why is this? Subhūti!
When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they do not give rise to conceptualization or discursive differentiation regarding any phenomena.

Subhūti! When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he dwells in non-conceptualization regarding all phenomena; he is able to practice the perfection of giving, and is also able to practice the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.

He is able to dwell in internal emptiness, and is also able to dwell in external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, endless emptiness, dispersion emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of non-apprehensibility, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature.

They are able to abide in suchness, and likewise able to abide in the dharma-realm, the nature of phenomena, non-falsity, immutability, equality, the state beyond birth, the fixed nature of phenomena, the stability of phenomena, the limit of reality, the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm;

they are able to cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness, and likewise able to cultivate the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path;
they are able to abide in the noble truth of suffering, and likewise able to abide in the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path.
They are able to cultivate the four dhyānas, and are also able to cultivate the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments;
they are able to cultivate the eight liberations, and are also able to cultivate the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities;
they are able to cultivate the gate of liberation of emptiness, and are also able to cultivate the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness.
They are able to cultivate all dharani-doors and also able to cultivate all samadhi-doors;

they are able to cultivate the Ground of Extreme Joy, as well as the Ground of Purity, the Ground of Radiance, the Ground of Blazing Wisdom, the Ground of Difficult Victory, the Ground of Presence, the Ground of Far-Going, the Ground of Immovability, the Ground of Excellent Intelligence, and the Ground of Dharma Clouds;
they are able to cultivate the five eyes and also able to cultivate the six supernormal powers.

They are able to cultivate the ten powers of a Buddha, as well as the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
they are able to cultivate the quality of non-forgetfulness, as well as the nature of constant dwelling in equanimity;
they are able to cultivate all-knowledge, as well as the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects.

“Subhūti! At such a time, this bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive a bodhisattva mahāsattva, nor does he perceive the name ‘bodhisattva mahāsattva’; he does not perceive the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), nor does he perceive the name ‘perfection of wisdom. He strives only with right diligence for the sake of the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñatājñāna).”
Why is this? Subhūti!

It is because this bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, has thoroughly realized the true nature of all phenomena and understands that within them there is neither defilement nor purity.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they should realize, as it truly is, the conventional designation of names and the conventional designation of phenomena."
"Subhūti!
When these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have awakened to names and dharmas as they truly are, they do not cling to form; they do not cling to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;
they do not cling to the eye base, nor do they cling to the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind bases."
They do not cling to the sphere of forms, nor to the spheres of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena;
they do not cling to the eye-element, nor to the elements of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind;
they do not cling to the element of forms, nor to the elements of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena.
He does not cling to the element of eye-consciousness, nor does he cling to the elements of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-consciousness;
he does not cling to eye-contact, nor does he cling to ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact;

he does not cling to any feelings—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that arise conditioned by eye-contact, nor does he cling to any feelings—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that arise conditioned by ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact.
They do not cling to the earth element, nor to the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements;
they do not cling to causes and conditions, nor to the immediate condition, the object condition, the dominant condition, or the phenomena produced from these conditions;

they do not cling to ignorance, nor to volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
They do not cling to the realm of the conditioned, nor do they cling to the realm of the unconditioned;
they do not cling to the realm of outflows, nor do they cling to the realm without outflows;

they do not cling to the perfection of generosity, nor do they cling to the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, wisdom, skillful means, sublime aspiration, power, and knowledge.

He does not cling to internal emptiness; he does not cling to external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate truth, the emptiness of conditioned phenomena, the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, absolute emptiness, the emptiness of the limitless, the emptiness of dispersion, the emptiness of non-alteration, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the emptiness of self-characteristics, the emptiness of common characteristics, the emptiness of all dharmas, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, or the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature.

He does not cling to suchness; he does not cling to the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, non-falsity, non-alteration, equality, the nature of transcendence from birth, the fixedness of dharma, the stability of dharma, the limit of reality, the realm of space, or the inconceivable realm.

They do not cling to the four foundations of mindfulness; they do not cling to the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, or the eightfold noble path;
they do not cling to the noble truth of suffering, nor do they cling to the noble truths of the origin, cessation, or the path;
they do not cling to the four dhyānas, nor do they cling to the four immeasurables or the four formless attainments.
They do not cling to the eight liberations; they do not cling to the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive concentrations, or the ten totalities;
they do not cling to the gate of liberation of emptiness, nor to the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness;
they do not cling to the gates of dhāraṇī, nor to the gates of samādhi.

He does not cling to the Ground of Great Joy, nor to the Ground of Purity, the Ground of Radiance, the Ground of Blazing Wisdom, the Ground of Extreme Difficulty to Conquer, the Ground of Presence, the Ground of Far-Going, the Ground of Immovability, the Ground of Excellent Intelligence, or the Ground of the Cloud of Dharma;
he does not cling to the five eyes, nor to the six supernormal powers;
he does not cling to the ten powers of a Buddha, nor to the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
They do not cling to great loving-kindness, nor do they cling to great compassion, great joy, or great equanimity;
they do not cling to the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, nor do they cling to the eighty secondary characteristics;
they do not cling to the quality of non-forgetfulness, nor do they cling to the nature of constant abiding in equanimity.
They do not cling to all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*); they do not cling to the knowledge of the paths (*mārgākārajñatā*) or the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*);
they do not cling to the fruit of stream-entry, nor to the fruits of once-returning, non-returning, or arhatship, nor to the enlightenment of a solitary buddha (*pratyekabuddhabodhi*);
they do not cling to any of the practices of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, nor to the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).

He does not cling to a self; he does not cling to a sentient being, a life-principle, a soul, a nourisher, a spirit, a person, an individual, a mind-born, a youth, an agent, an experiencer, a knower, or a seer;
he does not cling to ordinary beings, he does not cling to noble ones, he does not cling to bodhisattvas, and he does not cling to Tathāgatas;
he does not cling to names, and he does not cling to signs.
One does not cling to the adornment and purification of Buddha-fields, one does not cling to the maturation of sentient beings, and one does not cling to skillful means. Why is this?
Because all phenomena are non-existent; for the one who clings, that which is clung to, the locus of clinging, and the time of clinging are all unattainable.
“In this way, Subhūti!
Because bodhisattva mahāsattvas practicing the perfection of wisdom have no attachment to any phenomena,
they are able to increase generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, [meditative concentration, and wisdom].”
The perfections of meditative concentration, wisdom, skillful means, sublime aspiration, power,
and knowledge can likewise abide in internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness,
great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, and boundless emptiness.
Emptiness, the emptiness of dispersion, the emptiness of non-alteration, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the emptiness of self-characteristics, the emptiness of common characteristics,
the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature,
and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence; they are also able to abide in suchness, the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, and the...
It also increases the nature of falsity, the nature of immutability, equality, the nature of being free from birth, the fixed nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*),
the stability of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the realm of space (*ākāśadhātu*), and the inconceivable realm;
it also increases the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four immeasurables, the four formless absorptions, and the eight [liberations].
They can also augment the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; they can enter the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth;
they can abide on the bodhisattva’s stage of non-retrogression; and they can perfect all *dhāraṇīs*.
They can also fulfill the dharma-gates of dhāraṇī and the dharma-gates of samādhi;

they can also fulfill the Ground of Extreme Joy, the Ground of Purity, the Ground of Radiant Light, the Ground of Blazing Wisdom, the Ground of Utmost Difficulty to Conquer, the Ground of Manifestation, the Ground of Far-Going, the Ground of Immovability, the Ground of Excellent Intelligence, and the Ground of the Dharma Cloud; they can also fulfill the five eyes.
...the six supernormal powers; they can also fulfill the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
they can also fulfill great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity;
and they can also fulfill the thirty-two marks of a Great Being and the eighty minor marks.
Excellent; they will also be able to fulfill the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant equanimity, and they will also be able to fulfill all-knowledge,
the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects, as well as attain the most supreme supernormal powers of a bodhisattva.

Having attained supernormal powers, they travel from one buddha-field to another for the sake of maturing sentient beings, for the sake of purifying their own buddha-fields, and to behold the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas; and having beheld them, they make offerings, pay homage, revere, and praise them, so that all their roots of virtue may grow.
Once these roots have grown well, they are able to hear and receive all the true Dharma of the Buddhas according to what they wish to hear.

Having heard and received it, until they sit upon the sublime seat of awakening (bodhimanda), they are able to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening without ever forgetting it, attaining mastery over all dhāraṇī-doors and samādhi-doors.

At that time, the Buddha addressed the Venerable Subhūti:
“Based on what meaning do you say this?”
Form itself is not the bodhisattva mahāsattva; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness themselves are not the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Apart from form there is no bodhisattva mahāsattva; apart from feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness there is no bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Within form there is no bodhisattva mahāsattva; within feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness there is no bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Is it that within a bodhisattva mahāsattva there is no form, and within a bodhisattva mahāsattva there is no feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;
and is it that apart from form there is no bodhisattva mahāsattva, and apart from feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness there is no bodhisattva mahāsattva?
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If awakening, or a sentient being (*sattva*), or form (*rūpa*), or feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are ultimately unapprehendable because their nature does not exist, how much less could there be a bodhisattva mahāsattva?”

Since this does not exist, how can it be said that "form itself is the bodhisattva mahāsattva," or "feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness themselves are the bodhisattva mahāsattva";
or that "the bodhisattva mahāsattva is other than form," or "the bodhisattva mahāsattva is other than feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness"?
Is there a bodhisattva mahāsattva within form? Is there a bodhisattva mahāsattva within feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness?
Is there form within a bodhisattva mahāsattva? Are there feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness within a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
Is there a bodhisattva mahāsattva apart from form? Is there a bodhisattva mahāsattva apart from feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness?

“World-Honored One!

Since bodhi, sattva, and dharmas such as form (*rūpa*) are all unobtainable, it is impossible to say that the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is identical to form and the other dharmas, or that the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is distinct from form and the other dharmas, or that the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva exists within form and the other dharmas, or that form and the other dharmas exist within the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, or that there is a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva apart from form and the other dharmas.”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
So it is! So it is! It is just as you have said.

Subhūti! Because dharmas such as form are unapprehendable, the bodhisattva mahāsattva is also unapprehendable; because the bodhisattva mahāsattva is unapprehendable, the practice of the perfection of wisdom is also unapprehendable.
"Subhūti!
When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they should train in this way.
Furthermore, Subhūti!"

Is there the suchness of all-knowledge within the bodhisattva mahāsattva, and is there the suchness of the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects within the bodhisattva mahāsattva?

Is there a bodhisattva mahāsattva apart from the suchness of all-knowledge, and is there a bodhisattva mahāsattva apart from the suchness of the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects?
“World-Honored One!

Since dharmas such as form and suchness are both unapprehendable, it is impossible to say that the suchness of dharmas such as form is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva; or that a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is other than the suchness of dharmas such as form; or that there is a bodhisattva-mahāsattva within the suchness of dharmas such as form; or that the suchness of dharmas such as form exists within the bodhisattva-mahāsattva; or that there is a bodhisattva-mahāsattva apart from the suchness of dharmas such as form.”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
So it is! So it is! It is just as you have said.

Subhūti! Because dharmas such as form are unapprehendable, the true nature (*tathatā*) of dharmas such as form is also unapprehendable. Because both dharmas and their true nature are unapprehendable, the bodhisattva mahāsattva is also unapprehendable; and because the bodhisattva mahāsattva is unapprehendable, the *prajñāpāramitā* he practices is also unapprehendable.
"Subhūti!
When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they should train in this way.
Furthermore, Subhūti!"
