...the samādhi of severing the object of focus, the samādhi of non-alteration, the samādhi of non-genus,
the samādhi of entering names and signs, the samādhi of non-action, the samādhi of entering definitive names, the samādhi of practicing signlessness,
the samādhi of being free from cataracts and darkness, and the samādhi of possessing practice...
The samādhi of equanimity, the samādhi of immovability, the samādhi of transcending the spheres,
the samādhi of gathering all merits, the samādhi of dwelling without mind, the samādhi of dwelling with certainty, the samādhi of pure and wondrous flowers,
the samādhi of possessing the factors of enlightenment, and the samādhi of boundless eloquence.
The earth [samādhi], the boundless lamp samādhi, the unequaled samādhi, the samādhi that transcends all dharmas,
the samādhi that definitively discerns all dharmas, the samādhi that disperses doubt, the samādhi of non-abiding,
the samādhi of the adornment of the single characteristic, and the samādhi that brings forth the modes of activity.
The samādhi of a single mode of activity, the samādhi of being free from all modes of activity, the samādhi of sublime activity,
the samādhi of distancing oneself from the depths of all existence, the samādhi of entering all conventional designations and linguistic expressions,
the samādhi of the firm jewel, and the samādhi of non-attachment to any phenomena.
The earth-samādhi, the samādhi adorned with lightning-flames, the samādhi of dispelling,
the unsurpassed samādhi, the dharma-torch samādhi, the wisdom-lamp samādhi, the samādhi of approaching non-retrogressive supernormal powers,
the samādhi of liberation from sounds and syllables, and the blazing torch samādhi.
The Samādhi of the Ground, the Samādhi of the Mark of Adornment and Purity, the Samādhi of Signlessness, the Samādhi of the Mark of Untroubled Patience,
the Samādhi Endowed with All Sublime Marks, the Samādhi Endowed with Dhāraṇī,
the Samādhi of Indifference Toward All Suffering and Pleasure, the Samādhi of the Mark of Inexhaustible Conduct, and the Samādhi of Subduing the One.
The samādhi of discerning the nature of all that is correct and deviant; the samādhi of severing hatred and attachment; the samādhi of departing from opposition and compliance;
the samādhi of stainless luminosity; the samādhi of extreme firmness; the samādhi of the pure light of the full moon;
the samādhi of great adornment; the samādhi of the heatless lightning-flash; and the [samādhi] capable of...
The samādhi that illuminates all worlds, the samādhi that can rescue all worlds,
the samādhi of the equality of meditative concentration, the samādhi of the principle of equality between the dustless and the dusty,
the samādhi of the principle of equality between the non-contentious and the contentious, and the samādhi without nesting place, without signs, and without attachment.
The samādhi of equanimity, the samādhi of definitive abiding in suchness, the samādhi of emerging from the vessel,
the samādhi that incinerates all afflictions, the samādhi of the great torch of wisdom,
the samādhi that gives birth to the ten powers, the samādhi of opening and revealing, and the samādhi that destroys bodily misconduct.
The samādhi of destroying verbal misconduct, the samādhi of destroying mental misconduct,
the samādhi of thorough investigation, the samādhi like space, and the samādhi of non-attachment like space.
“Śāriputra! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva constantly dwells in and does not abandon such samādhis as these, they will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.”

Furthermore, there are other immeasurable and innumerable gateways of samādhi and gateways of dhāraṇī; if a bodhisattva mahāsattva can skillfully train in them, they will also cause them to quickly realize unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, addressed Śāriputra, saying:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in such samādhis as these, you should know that they have already received the prophecy from the Buddhas of the past, and they shall also receive the prophecy from the Buddhas of the present throughout the ten directions."

Śāriputra! Although this bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in such samādhis, he does not perceive these samādhis, nor does he become attached to them. Furthermore, he does not think: "I have entered these samādhis;
I am now entering these samādhis; I shall enter these samādhis; it is only I who can enter them, and not others."
"By means of this power of meditative concentration, all such discursive thoughts and conceptualizations do not manifest.
Then, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"Is there a distinct, truly existent bodhisattva mahāsattva who dwells in these various samādhis and has already received a prophecy from the Buddhas of the past and present?"
Subhūti replied, “No, Śāriputra!”
Why is this? Śāriputra,
the perfection of wisdom is not different from the various samādhis, and the various samādhis are not different from the perfection of wisdom.
The bodhisattva mahāsattva is not different from the perfection of wisdom and samādhi, and the perfection of wisdom and samādhi are not different from the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
The perfection of wisdom is itself all samādhis, and all samādhis are themselves the perfection of wisdom.
The bodhisattva mahāsattva is himself the perfection of wisdom and the samādhis, and the perfection of wisdom and the samādhis are themselves the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
"Why is this? It is because the nature of all phenomena is equal.
Śāriputra said:
"If the nature of all phenomena is equal, can this samādhi be manifested?
Subhūti replied, "It cannot be manifested."
Śāriputra asked,
"Does this bodhisattva mahāsattva have any conceptualization or understanding regarding this samādhi?
Subhūti replied:
"He has no conceptual understanding.
Śāriputra asked,
"For what reason does he have no conceptual understanding?"
Subhūti replied,
"Because they are without conceptual discrimination. Śāriputra said:
"Why is he without conceptual discrimination? Subhūti replied,
"Because the nature of all phenomena is entirely non-existent, he does not give rise to conceptual discrimination within meditative concentration."
For this reason, this bodhisattva mahāsattva has no conceptual understanding whatsoever regarding all phenomena and samādhis.
Why is this? Because all phenomena and samādhis are utterly non-existent; and within that which is non-existent, there is no basis for the arising of conceptual distinctions or understandings.
At that time, the Bhagavat praised Subhūti, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
It is as you have said.

Therefore, I declare that among the assembly of śrāvakas who dwell in the concentration of non-contention (*araṇā-samādhi*), you are the foremost; for this reason, my statement is consistent with the truth.
Subhūti!

A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to train in the perfection of wisdom should train in this way; one who wishes to train in the perfections of meditative concentration, diligence, patience, ethical discipline, and generosity should train in this way.
"Subhūti!

A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to train in the four dhyānas should train in this way; one who wishes to train in the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions should train in this way."
"Subhūti!

A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to train in the four foundations of mindfulness should train in this way; one who wishes to train in the four right endeavors, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold noble path should train in this way."
"Subhūti!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to train in the five eyes should train in this way; one who wishes to train in the six supernormal powers should train in this way.
Subhūti!"

A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to train in the ten powers of a buddha should train in this way; one who wishes to train in the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects should train in this way.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One,

when a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this manner, is he training correctly in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), and so on, up to training correctly in the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā)?”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this manner, they are training correctly in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), by means of the expedient of non-apprehension.”
“...up to and including training for the sake of all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method.
At that time, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this manner, do they train in the perfection of wisdom by means of non-apprehension as their expedient, and so on, up to training in the knowledge of all aspects by means of non-apprehension as their expedient?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this manner, they train in the perfection of wisdom by means of non-apprehension as the expedient, and so on, up to training in all-aspect omniscience by means of non-apprehension as the expedient.”
Śāriputra asked:
“Regarding ‘non-attainment,’ what kind of phenomena are not to be attained?
The Buddha said:
"The self is unapprehendable because it is ultimately pure;

likewise, sentient beings, life-principles, creatures, nourishers, persons, individuals, mind-born ones, young scholars, agents, instigators of action, originators, instigators of origination, experiencers, instigators of experience, knowers, and seers are unapprehendable because they are ultimately pure."
Form is unapprehendable because it is ultimately pure;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are unapprehendable because they are ultimately pure.
The sense-base of the eye is unapprehendable because it is ultimately pure.
The sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind cannot be apprehended, because they are ultimately pure.
The sense base of form cannot be apprehended, because it is ultimately pure;
the sense bases of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena cannot be apprehended, because they are ultimately pure.

The eye element, the form element, the eye-consciousness element, as well as eye-contact and the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, are unapprehendable because they are ultimately pure;

the ear element, the sound element, the ear-consciousness element, as well as ear-contact and the various feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition, are unapprehendable because they are ultimately pure;

the nose element, the odor element, the nose-consciousness element, as well as nose-contact and the various feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition, are unapprehendable because they are ultimately pure.

The tongue element, the taste element, the tongue-consciousness element, as well as tongue-contact and the various feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition, are unapprehendable because they are ultimately pure;

the body element, the tangible object element, the body-consciousness element, as well as body-contact and the various feelings produced with body-contact as a condition, are unapprehendable because they are ultimately pure;

the mind element, the mental-object element, the mind-consciousness element, as well as mind-contact and the various feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition, are unapprehendable because they are ultimately pure.
The earth element is unapprehendable because it is ultimately pure;
the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements are unapprehendable because they are ultimately pure.
The desire realm cannot be apprehended because it is ultimately pure;
the form and formless realms cannot be apprehended because they are ultimately pure.
The noble truth of suffering cannot be apprehended because it is ultimately pure.
The noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path are unapprehendable, because they are ultimately pure.
Ignorance is unapprehendable, because it is ultimately pure;

likewise, volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, and old age, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are unapprehendable, because they are ultimately pure.
The four dhyānas are unapprehendable because they are ultimately pure;
the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments are unapprehendable because they are ultimately pure.
The four foundations of mindfulness are unapprehendable because they are ultimately pure.

The four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eight branches of the noble path cannot be apprehended, because they are ultimately pure.
The perfection of generosity is unapprehendable because it is ultimately pure;
the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom are unapprehendable because they are ultimately pure.
The five eyes are unattainable because they are ultimately pure;
the six supernormal powers are unattainable because they are ultimately pure;
the ten powers of a Buddha are unattainable because they are ultimately pure.

The four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects are unapprehendable, because they are ultimately pure.
The stream-enterer is unapprehendable because of ultimate purity;
the once-returner, the non-returner, and the arhat are unapprehendable because of ultimate purity.
The pratyekabuddha is unapprehendable because of ultimate purity.
"The Bodhisattva cannot be apprehended because he is ultimately pure;
the Tathāgata cannot be apprehended because he is ultimately pure.
Śāriputra said:
“World-Honored One!
What is the meaning of what you have called ‘ultimate purity’?
The Buddha said:

"All dharmas do not emerge and do not arise; they do not perish and are not exhausted; they are neither defiled nor pure; they are neither attained nor conditioned—this is called the meaning of ultimate purity."
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this manner, what dharma is he training in?”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this manner, they train in nothing at all regarding any phenomena. Why is this?"
"All phenomena do not exist in the manner that foolish, ordinary worldlings grasp them; one should train within this.
Śāriputra asked, "If that is so, in what manner do all phenomena exist?"
The Buddha said:
"All phenomena exist as such through being non-existent; if one cannot thoroughly comprehend these phenomena that are thus non-existent, it is called ignorance."
Śāriputra asked:
"What phenomena are non-existent, such that failing to comprehend them is called ignorance?
The Buddha said:

“Form is non-existent; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are non-existent, because of internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate truth, the emptiness of the conditioned, the emptiness of the unconditioned, absolute emptiness, the emptiness of the limitless, the emptiness of dispersion, the emptiness of non-alteration, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the emptiness of specific characteristics, the emptiness of common characteristics, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.”
“Śāriputra! The eye-base does not exist;
the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases do not exist, because of internal emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence.”

The sphere of form does not exist; the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena do not exist, because of internal emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.

“Śāriputra! The eye element, the form element, the eye-consciousness element, and eye-contact, as well as all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, do not exist, because of internal emptiness and so forth, up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.

The ear element, the sound element, the ear-consciousness element, and ear-contact, as well as all feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition, do not exist, because of internal emptiness and so forth, up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.”

The nose element, the odor element, the nose-consciousness element, as well as nose-contact and all feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition, do not exist, because of internal emptiness and so forth, up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence;

the tongue element, the taste element, the tongue-consciousness element, as well as tongue-contact and all feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition, do not exist, because of internal emptiness and so forth, up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence;

the body element, the tangible object element, the body-consciousness element, as well as body-contact and all feelings produced with body-contact as a condition, do not exist, because of internal emptiness and so forth, up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.

The mind element, the phenomena element, the mind-consciousness element, as well as mental contact and all feelings produced with mental contact as a condition, do not exist, because of internal emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.

“Śāriputra! The earth element does not exist; the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements do not exist, because of internal emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.”
“Śāriputra! The desire realm does not exist; the form and formless realms do not exist, because of internal emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.

“Śāriputra! The noble truth of suffering does not exist; the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path do not exist, because of internal emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.”
“Śāriputra! Ignorance does not exist;

formative forces, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and old age, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair do not exist, because of internal emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.”

“Śāriputra! Greed, hatred, and delusion do not exist; the various speculative views do not exist, because of internal emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.”
“Śāriputra! The four dhyānas do not exist;
the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments do not exist, because of internal emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.

“Śāriputra! The four foundations of mindfulness do not exist; the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path do not exist, because of internal emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence.”

“Śāriputra! The perfection of generosity is non-existent; the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom are non-existent, because of internal emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.”
“Śāriputra! The five eyes do not exist, and the six supernormal powers do not exist, because of internal emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.”

“Śāriputra! The ten powers of a Buddha do not exist; the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great joy, great equanimity, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) do not exist, because of internal emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence (*abhāvasvabhāvaśūnyatā*).”
“Śāriputra! If foolish ordinary beings cannot comprehend such dharmas as being non-existent, this is called ignorance (*avidyā*).

Driven by the power of that ignorance and craving, they conceptually cling to the two extremes of annihilationism and eternalism; consequently, they neither know nor see the non-existent nature of all dharmas, and thus they conceptualize those dharmas.”
Due to conceptualization, one becomes attached to form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, up to and including attachment to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Because of this attachment, one conceptually discriminates the non-existence of all phenomena; consequently, one neither knows nor sees these phenomena.
Śāriputra asked,
"Regarding what dharmas is there neither knowing nor seeing?
The Buddha said:
"To not know and not see form; to not know and not see feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; and so on, up to not knowing and not seeing the knowledge of all aspects."
"Because they neither know nor see all phenomena, they fall among the ranks of foolish worldlings and are unable to escape.
Śāriputra asked, "From what are they unable to escape?"
The Buddha said:
"They cannot transcend the realm of desire; they cannot transcend the realm of form; they cannot transcend the formless realm."

Because they are unable to achieve transcendence, they cannot accomplish the teachings of the śrāvakas, they cannot accomplish the teachings of the pratyekabuddhas, they cannot accomplish the teachings of the bodhisattvas, and they cannot accomplish the teachings of the Tathāgatas; because they do not accomplish them, they are unable to have faith and acceptance.
Śāriputra asked,
"In what dharma do they fail to have faith and acceptance?
The Buddha said:

"He cannot believe in or accept the emptiness of form; he cannot believe in or accept the emptiness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; and so on, up to the emptiness of the knowledge of all aspects. Because he does not believe in or accept it, he cannot abide [in it]."
Śāriputra asked,
"In what phenomena does he not abide?
The Buddha said:

That is to say, they are unable to abide in the four foundations of mindfulness; they are unable to abide in the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path.
They are unable to abide in the perfection of generosity, nor are they able to abide in the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
They cannot abide in the stage of non-retrogression;
they cannot abide in the five eyes; they cannot abide in the six supernormal powers.

They cannot abide in the ten powers of a Buddha, nor in the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects.
"For this reason they are called foolish ordinary beings (*bāla-pṛthagjana*), because they cling to all phenomena as having intrinsic nature.
Śāriputra asked:
"To what phenomena do they cling as having intrinsic nature?"
The Buddha said, "Śāriputra!
They have an inherent nature of attachment toward form; they have an inherent nature of attachment toward feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness."
“Śāriputra! They cling to the nature of existence in the sphere of the eye; they cling to the nature of existence in the spheres of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.”
They cling to the nature of existence in the sphere of form; they cling to the nature of existence in the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena. "Śāriputra!
They [cling] to the eye-element, the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, and to eye-contact, as well as that which arises conditioned by eye-contact..."

They give rise to various feelings and cling to their inherent existence; they cling to the inherent existence of the ear element, the sound element, the ear-consciousness element, and ear-contact, as well as to the various feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition;

they cling to the inherent existence of the nose element, the odor element, the nose-consciousness element, and nose-contact, as well as to the various feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition.

They cling to the existence of a self-nature in the tongue element, the taste element, and the tongue-consciousness element, as well as in tongue-contact and the various feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition;

they cling to the existence of a self-nature in the body element, the tangible object element, and the body-consciousness element, as well as in body-contact and the various feelings produced with body-contact as a condition; and in the mind element...
“The dharma-element, the mental-consciousness-element, and mental contact, as well as all feelings produced with mental contact as a condition,
are grasped as having an intrinsic nature. Śāriputra!”
He clings to the nature of existence in the earth element, and he clings to the nature of existence in the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements. "Śāriputra!
They cling to the nature of existence within the desire realm, and they cling to the nature of existence within the form and formless realms.
"Śāriputra! They cling to the nature of existence within the noble truth of suffering, and they cling to the nature of existence within the noble truths of origination, cessation, and the path."

“Śāriputra! They cling to the nature of substantiality in ignorance; they cling to the nature of substantiality in volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.”
“Śāriputra! They cling to the nature of existence in greed, hatred, and delusion; they cling to the nature of existence in all speculative views. Śāriputra!”
They cling to the four dhyānas as having intrinsic nature; they cling to the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments as having intrinsic nature. "Śāriputra!

They cling to the four foundations of mindfulness as having intrinsic nature; they cling to the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path as having intrinsic nature."

“Śāriputra! They cling to the perfection of generosity as having an intrinsic nature; they cling to the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom as having an intrinsic nature.”
“Śāriputra! They cling to the five eyes as having an intrinsic nature; they cling to the six supernormal powers as having an intrinsic nature. Śāriputra!”

They cling to the ten powers of a Buddha as having an intrinsic nature; they cling to the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects as having an intrinsic nature.
“Śāriputra! Because foolish ordinary beings cling to the existence of intrinsic nature in all phenomena, they are unable to believe in or accept the emptiness of all phenomena.
Due to this lack of faith, they cannot accomplish the noble dharmas of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, or tathāgatas; thus, they are unable to abide in the noble dharmas.”
Therefore, Śāriputra,

bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who wish to study the perfection of wisdom and who wish to accomplish all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), should train accordingly by means of non-apprehension as their skillful method.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One,

is it the case that there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who train in this manner, yet do not train in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), and thus are unable to accomplish the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñatājñāna)?”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in such a manner, they are not training in the perfection of wisdom and will be unable to accomplish all-knowledge.”
Śāriputra said:
“World-Honored One,
for what reason would a bodhisattva mahāsattva who trains in this manner not be training in the perfection of wisdom, and thus fail to accomplish the knowledge of all modes?”
The Buddha said, “Śāriputra!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva lacks skillful means and discriminatively clings to the perfection of wisdom, or discriminatively clings to the perfections of meditative concentration, diligence, patience, ethical discipline, and generosity— if a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this manner, they are not training in the perfection of wisdom and will be unable to accomplish the knowledge of all modes.”

“Śāriputra! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva lacks skillful means and discriminates with attachment toward form, and discriminates with attachment toward feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness—if a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this manner, he is not training in the perfection of wisdom and will be unable to accomplish the knowledge of all modes.”

“Śāriputra! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva lacks skillful means and discriminates with attachment toward the sphere of the eye, and discriminates with attachment toward the spheres of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—if a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this manner, they are not training in the perfection of wisdom and cannot accomplish the knowledge of all aspects.”

“Śāriputra! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva lacks skillful means and discriminates with attachment toward the sphere of form, and discriminates with attachment toward the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena—should a bodhisattva mahāsattva train in this manner, he is not training in the perfection of wisdom and will be unable to accomplish the knowledge of all modes.”

“Śāriputra! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva lacks skillful means and discriminates with attachment toward the eye-element, the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, as well as eye-contact and the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition—if a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this manner, they are not training in the perfection of wisdom and cannot accomplish the knowledge of all modes.”

“Śāriputra! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva lacks skillful means and discriminates with attachment toward the ear element, the sound element, the ear-consciousness element, as well as ear-contact and the various feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition—if a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this manner, they are not training in the perfection of wisdom and cannot accomplish the knowledge of all modes.”

“Śāriputra! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva lacks skillful means and discriminates, clings to, and becomes attached to the nose element, the odor element, the nose-consciousness element, as well as nose-contact and the various feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition—should a bodhisattva mahāsattva train in this manner, they are not training in the perfection of wisdom and will be unable to accomplish all-knowledge.”

“Śāriputra! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva lacks skillful means and discriminates, clings to, and becomes attached to the tongue element, the taste element, the tongue-consciousness element, as well as tongue-contact and the various feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition—such a bodhisattva mahāsattva who trains in this manner is not training in the perfection of wisdom, and cannot accomplish the knowledge of all aspects.”

“Śāriputra! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva lacks skillful means and discriminates with attachment toward the body element, the tangible object element, the body-consciousness element, as well as body-contact and the various feelings produced with body-contact as a condition—such a bodhisattva mahāsattva who trains in this manner is not training in the perfection of wisdom, and cannot accomplish the knowledge of all modes.”

“Śāriputra! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva lacks skillful means and discriminatively clings to the mind-element, the phenomena-element, the mind-consciousness-element, as well as mental contact and the various feelings produced with mental contact as a condition—should a bodhisattva mahāsattva train in this manner, they are not training in the perfection of wisdom and will be unable to accomplish all-knowledge.”

“Śāriputra! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva lacks skillful means and discriminates with attachment toward the earth element, and discriminates with attachment toward the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements—if a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this manner, they are not training in the perfection of wisdom and cannot accomplish the knowledge of all modes.”

“Śāriputra! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva lacks skillful means and discriminatively clings to the noble truth of suffering, and discriminatively clings to the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path—such a bodhisattva mahāsattva who trains in this manner is not training in the perfection of wisdom, and cannot accomplish the knowledge of all modes.”

“Śāriputra! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva lacks skillful means and conceptually discriminates and adheres to ignorance, and conceptually discriminates and adheres to volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and old age, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair—in this way, such a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in a manner that is not the training in the perfection of wisdom, and cannot accomplish the knowledge of all modes.”

“Śāriputra! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva lacks skillful means and discriminatively clings to the four dhyānas, and discriminatively clings to the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments, such a bodhisattva mahāsattva who trains in this manner is not training in the perfection of wisdom, and cannot accomplish the knowledge of all modes.”

“Śāriputra! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva lacks skillful means and discriminatively clings to the four foundations of mindfulness; if they discriminatively cling to the four right endeavors, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold noble path—if a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in such a manner, they are not training in the perfection of wisdom and cannot accomplish the knowledge of all modes.”

“Śāriputra! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva lacks skillful means and discriminatively clings to the five eyes, or discriminatively clings to the six supernormal powers, such a bodhisattva mahāsattva who trains in this manner is not training in the perfection of wisdom and cannot accomplish the knowledge of all modes.”

“Śāriputra! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva lacks skillful means and conceptually clings to the ten powers of a buddha; if they conceptually cling to the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects—then a bodhisattva mahāsattva who trains in this manner is not training in the perfection of wisdom and cannot accomplish the knowledge of all aspects.”
“Śāriputra! For this reason, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who train in such a manner; they are not training in the perfection of wisdom and cannot accomplish the knowledge of all modes.”
Śāriputra said:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this manner, does he not fail to train in the perfection of wisdom and thus fail to accomplish the knowledge of all modes?"
The Buddha said:
"It is so! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this manner, they are not training in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) and cannot accomplish the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñājñāna)."
Then, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How is it that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, by training in this perfection of wisdom, they are able to accomplish the knowledge of all modes?”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor even perceive the knowledge of all aspects, this is training in the perfection of wisdom, and thus they will be able to accomplish the knowledge of all modes.”
"Why is this? Because it takes non-apprehension as its skillful means.
Śāriputra said:
“By means of non-apprehension of what phenomena does this bodhisattva mahāsattva practice?
The Buddha said:

“This bodhisattva mahāsattva practices by means of non-apprehension of the perfection of generosity; by means of non-apprehension of the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; and so on, up to practicing by means of non-apprehension of the ten powers of a buddha; and by means of non-apprehension of the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).”
Śāriputra asked:
"When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), for what reason does he take non-apprehension as his skillful means?"
The Buddha said:

“When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he takes non-apprehension as his means by way of internal emptiness, up to and including non-apprehension as his means by way of the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.”
Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom in this manner, by training in the perfection of wisdom, they are able to accomplish the knowledge of all modes.
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Scroll 41; The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Scroll 42.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
11. Chapter on Similes, Part One: Chapter Eleven, Part One, "Similes.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
If someone were to ask:
"Can an illusory being train in the perfection of wisdom and accomplish the knowledge of all modes?
Can an illusory being train in the perfections of meditative concentration, diligence, patience, ethical discipline, and generosity and accomplish the knowledge of all modes?"
"How should I answer when I receive this question?
'World-Honored One!
If someone were to ask:'"
"Can an illusory person train in the four dhyānas and accomplish the knowledge of all modes?
Can an illusory person train in the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments and accomplish the knowledge of all modes?"
"How should I answer when I receive this question?
'World-Honored One!
If someone were to ask:'"
"Can an illusory person train in the four foundations of mindfulness and accomplish the knowledge of all modes?

Can an illusory person train in the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold noble path and accomplish the knowledge of all modes?"
"How should I answer when I receive this question?
World-Honored One!
If someone were to ask: "
"Can an illusory person train in the gate of liberation of emptiness and accomplish the knowledge of all modes?
Can an illusory person train in the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness and accomplish the knowledge of all modes?"
"How should I answer when I receive this question?
'World-Honored One!
If someone were to ask:'"
"Can an illusory person train in the five eyes and accomplish the knowledge of all modes?
Can an illusory person train in the six supernormal powers and accomplish the knowledge of all modes?"
"How should I answer when I receive such a question?
World-Honored One!
If someone were to ask: "
"Can an illusory person train in the ten powers of a Buddha and accomplish the knowledge of all modes?

Can an illusory person train in the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, the knowledge of all things, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects, and thereby accomplish the knowledge of all modes?"
“If I were to receive this question, how should I answer?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“I shall now question you; answer as you see fit.”
"Subhūti, what do you think?
Is form different from an illusion?"
“Are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness different from an illusion? Subhūti replied, “No!”
World-Honored One!

Why is this? Form is not different from illusion, and illusion is not different from form; form is itself illusion, and illusion is itself form. Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.
“Subhūti! What do you think?
Is the sense base of the eye different from an illusion?”
“Are the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind different from an illusion?
Subhūti replied, “No, they are not.”
World-Honored One!

Why is this? The sense-base of the eye is not different from illusion, and illusion is not different from the sense-base of the eye; the sense-base of the eye is itself illusion, and illusion is itself the sense-base of the eye. It is likewise for the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
“Subhūti, what do you think?
Is the sphere of form different from an illusion?”
“Are the sense bases of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena different from an illusion?
Subhūti replied, “No, they are not.”
World-Honored One!

Why is this? The sphere of form is not different from illusion, and illusion is not different from the sphere of form; the sphere of form is itself illusion, and illusion is itself the sphere of form. It is the same for the spheres of sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena.
“Subhūti! What do you think?
Is the eye-element different from an illusion?”
“Is the form realm, the eye-consciousness realm, as well as eye-contact and the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition,
different from an illusion? Subhūti replied, “No!”
World-Honored One!

Why is this? The eye-element is not different from illusion, and illusion is not different from the eye-element; the eye-element is itself illusion, and illusion is itself the eye-element. It is likewise for the form-element up to the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition.
“Suvikrāntavikrāmin! What do you think?
Is the ear-element different from an illusion?”
"Is there any difference between the sphere of sound, the sphere of ear-consciousness, ear-contact, and the various feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition,
and an illusion? Subhūti replied, "No, indeed!"
World-Honored One!

Why is this? The ear-element is not different from illusion, and illusion is not different from the ear-element; the ear-element is itself illusion, and illusion is itself the ear-element. It is the same for the sound-element, and even for all sensations produced with ear-contact as a condition.
“Suvikrāntavikrāmin! What do you think?
Is the nose-element different from an illusion?”
"Is the realm of fragrance, the realm of nose-consciousness, nose-contact, and the various sensations produced with nose-contact as a condition different from an illusion? Subhūti replied, "No!"
World-Honored One!

Why is this? The nose-element is not different from illusion, and illusion is not different from the nose-element; the nose-element is itself illusion, and illusion is itself the nose-element. It is the same for the odor-element, and even for the various sensations produced with nose-contact as a condition.
“Subhūti! What do you think?
Is the tongue-element different from an illusion?”
“Is the realm of taste, the realm of tongue-consciousness, as well as tongue-contact and the various feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition,
different from an illusion? Subhūti replied, “No!”
World-Honored One!

Why is this? The tongue-element is not different from illusion, and illusion is not different from the tongue-element; the tongue-element is itself illusion, and illusion is itself the tongue-element. It is the same for the taste-element, and even for all sensations produced with tongue-contact as a condition.
“Subhūti! What do you think?
Is the body-element different from an illusion?”
"Is the element of tangibles, the element of body-consciousness, body-contact, and the various feelings produced with body-contact as a condition different from an illusion?
Subhūti replied, "No,
[World-Honored One]."
World-Honored One!

Why is this? The body element is not different from illusion, and illusion is not different from the body element; the body element is itself illusion, and illusion is itself the body element. It is the same for the contact element, up to and including the various feelings produced with body-contact as a condition.
“Subhūti! What do you think?
Is the mind-element different from an illusion?”
“Is the dharma-element, the mind-consciousness element, and mental contact, as well as the various feelings produced with mental contact as a condition,
different from an illusion? Subhūti replied, “No!”
World-Honored One!

Why is this? The mind-element is not different from illusion, and illusion is not different from the mind-element; the mind-element is itself illusion, and illusion is itself the mind-element. It is the same for the dharma-element, and even for all feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition.
“Subhūti! What do you think?
Is the earth element different from an illusion?”
"Are the elements of water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness different from an illusion? Subhūti replied, "No!"
World-Honored One!

Why is this? The earth element is not different from illusion, and illusion is not different from the earth element; the earth element is itself illusion, and illusion is itself the earth element. It is likewise for the elements of water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness.
“Subhūti, what do you think?
Is the noble truth of suffering different from an illusion?”
"Are the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path different from an illusion?
Subhūti replied, "No, they are not."
World-Honored One!

Why is this? The Noble Truth of Suffering is not different from illusion, and illusion is not different from the Noble Truth of Suffering; the Noble Truth of Suffering is itself illusion, and illusion is itself the Noble Truth of Suffering. It is the same for the Noble Truths of Origination, Cessation, and the Path.
“Subhūti! What do you think?
Is ignorance different from an illusion?”

Are volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, becoming, birth, and old age, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair different from an illusion?
Subhūti replied,
“No, World-Honored One!”

Why is this? Ignorance is not different from illusion, and illusion is not different from ignorance; ignorance is itself illusion, and illusion is itself ignorance. This is likewise true for all factors from volitional formations up to old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair.
“Subhūti! What do you think?
Are the four dhyānas different from an illusion?”
"Are the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions different from an illusion? Subhūti replied, "No!"
World-Honored One!

Why is this? The four dhyānas are not different from illusion, and illusion is not different from the four dhyānas; the four dhyānas are themselves illusion, and illusion is itself the four dhyānas. The same is also true for the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments.
“Suvikrāntavikrāmin! What do you think?
Are the four foundations of mindfulness different from an illusion?”
"Are the four right endeavors, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eight branches of the noble path different from an illusion?
Subhūti replied, "No, they are not."
World-Honored One!

Why is this? The four foundations of mindfulness are not different from illusion, and illusion is not different from the four foundations of mindfulness; the four foundations of mindfulness are themselves illusion, and illusion is itself the four foundations of mindfulness. It is the same for the four right efforts up to the eightfold noble path.
"Subhūti, what do you think?
Is the gate of liberation that is emptiness different from an illusion?"
"Is the gate of liberation of signlessness and the gate of liberation of wishlessness different from an illusion? Subhūti replied, "No!"
World-Honored One!

Why is this? The gate of liberation of emptiness is not different from illusion, and illusion is not different from the gate of liberation of emptiness; the gate of liberation of emptiness is itself illusion, and illusion is itself the gate of liberation of emptiness. It is the same for the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness.
“Subhūti, what do you think?
Is the perfection of generosity different from an illusion?”
"Is there any difference between the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration,
and wisdom, and an illusion? Subhūti replied, "No, indeed!"
“World-Honored One!

Why is this? The perfection of generosity is not different from illusion, and illusion is not different from the perfection of generosity; the perfection of generosity is itself illusion, and illusion is itself the perfection of generosity. It is the same for the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.”
“Subhūti, what do you think?
Are the five eyes different from an illusion?”
"Are the six superknowledges different from an illusion? Subhūti replied, "No!"
"World-Honored One!

Why is this? The five eyes are not different from illusion, and illusion is not different from the five eyes; the five eyes are themselves illusion, and illusion is itself the five eyes. It is the same for the six supernormal powers."
“Suvikrāntavikrāmin! What do you think?
Is there any difference between the ten powers of a Buddha and an illusion?”

Are the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects different from an illusion?
Subhūti replied,
“No, World-Honored One!”

Why is this? The ten powers of a Buddha are not different from illusion, and illusion is not different from the ten powers of a Buddha; the ten powers of a Buddha are themselves illusion, and illusion itself is the ten powers of a Buddha. This is likewise true for the four fearlessnesses up to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
“Suvikrāntavikrāmin! What do you think?
Is unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening different from an illusion?”
Subhūti replied,
“No, World-Honored One!”

Why is this? Unsurpassed perfect enlightenment is not different from illusion, and illusion is not different from unsurpassed perfect enlightenment; unsurpassed perfect enlightenment is itself illusion, and illusion is itself unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think?
Does an illusion have affliction or purification?"
Subhūti replied,
“No, World-Honored One!”
“Subhūti! What do you think?
Does an illusion have arising or cessation?”
Subhūti replied,
“No, World-Honored One!”
"Subhūti, what do you think?
If a phenomenon is neither defiled nor purified, and neither arises nor ceases, can that phenomenon study the perfection of wisdom and accomplish the knowledge of all modes?"
Subhūti replied,
“No, World-Honored One!”
“Subhūti, what do you think? If a phenomenon is neither defiled nor purified,

and neither arises nor ceases, can that phenomenon study the perfections of meditative concentration, diligence, patience, ethical discipline, and generosity to accomplish the knowledge of all modes?”
Subhūti replied,
“No, World-Honored One!”
“Subhūti! What do you think?
If a phenomenon is without defilement and without purification, and without arising and without cessation, can that phenomenon study the four dhyānas and accomplish the knowledge of all modes?”
Subhūti replied,
“No, World-Honored One!”
“Subhūti, what do you think?

If a dharma is neither defiled nor purified, and neither arises nor ceases, can that dharma train in the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions to accomplish the knowledge of all modes?”
Subhūti replied,
“No, World-Honored One!”
“Suvikrāntavikrāmin! What do you think?
If a phenomenon is neither defiled nor purified, neither arising nor ceasing, can that phenomenon study the four foundations of mindfulness and accomplish the knowledge of all modes?”
Subhūti replied,
“No, World-Honored One!”
“Subhūti! What do you think?

If a dharma is neither defiled nor purified, neither arising nor ceasing, can that dharma train in the four right endeavors, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold noble path to accomplish the knowledge of all modes?”
Subhūti replied,
“No, World-Honored One!”
“Subhūti! What do you think?
If a phenomenon is neither defiled nor purified, neither arising nor ceasing, can that phenomenon study the gate of liberation that is emptiness and accomplish the knowledge of all modes?”
Subhūti replied,
“No, World-Honored One!”
“Subhūti! What do you think?

If a dharma is neither defiled nor purified, neither arising nor ceasing, can that dharma train in the gateways of liberation—signlessness and wishlessness—and thereby accomplish the knowledge of all modes?”
Subhūti replied,
“No, World-Honored One!”
“Subhūti! What do you think?
If a dharma is neither defiled nor purified, neither arising nor ceasing, can that dharma study the five eyes and accomplish the knowledge of all modes?”
Subhūti replied,
“No, World-Honored One!”
“Subhūti! What do you think?

If a phenomenon is without defilement and without purification, and without arising and without cessation, could that phenomenon study the six supernormal powers and accomplish the knowledge of all modes?”
Subhūti replied,
“No, World-Honored One!”
“Subhūti! What do you think?
If a dharma is neither defiled nor purified, and neither arises nor ceases, can that dharma study the ten powers of a Buddha and accomplish the knowledge of all modes?”
Subhūti replied,
“No, World-Honored One!”
“Subhūti, what do you think? If a dharma is without defilement and without purification,

without arising and without cessation, can that dharma train in the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects, and thereby accomplish the knowledge of all modes?”
Subhūti replied,
“No, World-Honored One!”
“Subhūti! What do you think?
Apart from the dharmas such as the five aggregates, the notion, the conceptualization, and the conventional designation, does there exist a bodhisattva mahāsattva?”
Subhūti replied,
“No, World-Honored One!”
“Subhūti, what do you think? Is it only by means of the conceptualization,
the designation, and the conventional expression regarding the dharmas such as the five aggregates that one refers to them as ‘bodhisattva-mahāsattva’?”
Subhūti replied, “So it is,
World-Honored One!”
“Subhūti! What do you think?
Regarding these mere conventional designations, expressions, and conceptualizations of phenomena such as the five aggregates—do they possess affliction or purification, or arising and ceasing?”
Subhūti replied,
"No, World-Honored One!"
“Subhūti, what do you think? If a phenomenon is without perception and without equivalent perception,

without designation and without verbal expression, without name and without the designation of a name, without body and without bodily action, without speech and without vocal action, without mind and without mental action, without affliction and without purification, and without arising and without cessation— could such a phenomenon study the perfection of wisdom up to the knowledge of all aspects and accomplish the knowledge of all-knowledge?”
Subhūti replied,
“No, World-Honored One!”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can, by means of this non-apprehension as a skillful method, train in the perfection of wisdom up to the knowledge of all aspects, you should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to accomplish the knowledge of all modes."
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One,

when a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening by training in the perfection of wisdom, they should train in the perfection of wisdom like an illusory person, making no conceptual distinctions regarding any phenomena.”
"Why is this? You should know that the illusory person is the five aggregates and so forth, and the five aggregates and so forth are the illusory person.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"What do you think?
Can the five aggregates and so forth, which are like an illusion, study the perfection of wisdom and accomplish the knowledge of all modes?
Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One! Why is this? Because..."
"These five aggregates, which are like an illusion, have non-existence as their intrinsic nature, because an intrinsic nature of non-existence cannot be apprehended.
"Subhūti, what do you think?"

Can one who trains in the perfection of wisdom and accomplishes the knowledge of all modes do so while [the aggregates] are like a dream, like an echo, like a reflection of light, like an image, like a flower in the sky, like a mirage, like a city of Gandharvas, or like transformed aggregates?
Subhūti replied,
“No, World-Honored One!”

Why is this? Because these five aggregates, from those like a dream up to those like a magical transformation, have non-existence as their intrinsic nature; for an intrinsic nature of non-existence cannot be apprehended.
“Subhūti! What do you think?
Are these phenomena—the five aggregates and so forth—which are like an illusion and so on, each distinct from one another?”
Subhūti replied,
“No, World-Honored One!”

Why is this? These form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness that are like illusions are precisely these form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness that are like dreams; these form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness that are like illusions are precisely these six sense bases and so forth that are like illusions; and these six sense bases and so forth that are like illusions are precisely these form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness that are like illusions. This is because all are unapprehendable due to internal emptiness, and so on, up to being unapprehendable due to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One,
when bodhisattva mahāsattvas who have newly set out in the Great Vehicle hear this profound *prajñāpāramitā* being taught, will their minds not become startled, terrified, or afraid?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has newly set out in the Great Vehicle practices the perfection of wisdom, if they lack skillful means and are not sustained by virtuous friends, their mind will be startled, terrified, and afraid upon hearing this teaching of the profound perfection of wisdom."
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, which bodhisattva mahāsattvas,

when practicing the perfection of wisdom, possess skillful means such that, upon hearing this teaching of the profound perfection of wisdom, their minds are not startled, not terrified, and not afraid?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, with a mind corresponding to the knowledge of all modes, they observe that the characteristics of permanence and impermanence in form are unapprehendable; they observe that the characteristics of permanence and impermanence in feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are unapprehendable.

With a mind corresponding to the knowledge of all modes, they observe that the characteristics of pleasure and suffering in form are unapprehendable; they observe that the characteristics of pleasure and suffering in feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are unapprehendable.”

With a mind corresponding to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), one contemplates that the characteristics of self and non-self in form (*rūpa*) are unapprehendable; one contemplates that the characteristics of self and non-self in feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are unapprehendable.

With a mind corresponding to the knowledge of all modes, one contemplates that the characteristics of purity and impurity in form are unapprehendable; one contemplates that the characteristics of purity and impurity in feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are unapprehendable.

With a mind corresponding to the knowledge of all modes, one contemplates that the characteristics of emptiness and non-emptiness in form are unapprehendable; one contemplates that the characteristics of emptiness and non-emptiness in feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are unapprehendable.

With a mind corresponding to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), one contemplates that form is signless (*animitta*) and yet possesses signs, such that no sign can be apprehended; one contemplates that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are signless and yet possess signs, such that no sign can be apprehended.

With a mind corresponding to the knowledge of all modes, one contemplates that form is wishless (*apraṇihita*) and yet possesses the sign of wishing, such that no sign of wishing can be apprehended; one contemplates that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are wishless and yet possess the sign of wishing, such that no sign of wishing can be apprehended.

With a mind corresponding to the knowledge of all modes, one contemplates that form is tranquil (*śānta*) and yet possesses the sign of non-tranquility, such that no sign of non-tranquility can be apprehended; one contemplates that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are tranquil and yet possess the sign of non-tranquility, such that no sign of non-tranquility can be apprehended.

With a mind directed toward the knowledge of all modes, one contemplates that the characteristics of form being distant or not distant cannot be apprehended; one contemplates that the characteristics of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness being distant or not distant cannot be apprehended.
"Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom in this way, because they possess skillful means, their mind is not startled, not terrified, and not afraid upon hearing this teaching of the profound perfection of wisdom."

“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, with a mind corresponding to the knowledge of all modes, they observe that the characteristics of permanence and impermanence in the sense-base of the eye are unapprehendable; they observe that the characteristics of permanence and impermanence in the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are unapprehendable.

With a mind corresponding to the knowledge of all modes, they observe that the characteristics of pleasure and suffering in the sense-base of the eye are unapprehendable; they observe that the characteristics of pleasure and suffering in the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are unapprehendable.”

With a mind corresponding to the knowledge of all modes, one contemplates that within the sense base of the eye, the characteristics of self and non-self are unapprehendable; one contemplates that within the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, the characteristics of self and non-self are unapprehendable.

With a mind corresponding to the knowledge of all modes, one contemplates that within the sense base of the eye, the characteristics of purity and impurity are unapprehendable; one contemplates that within the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, the characteristics of purity and impurity are unapprehendable.

With a mind corresponding to the knowledge of all modes, one contemplates that within the sense base of the eye, the characteristics of emptiness and non-emptiness are unapprehendable; one contemplates that within the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, the characteristics of emptiness and non-emptiness are unapprehendable.

By means of the mind directed toward the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), one contemplates that within the sense-base of the eye (*cakṣur-āyatana*), there is no characteristic of signlessness (*animitta-lakṣaṇa*) nor can any characteristic of having signs (*sanimitta-lakṣaṇa*) be apprehended; one contemplates that within the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, there is no characteristic of signlessness nor can any characteristic of having signs be apprehended.

By means of the mind directed toward the knowledge of all modes, one contemplates that within the sense-base of the eye, there is no characteristic of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-lakṣaṇa*) nor can any characteristic of having wishes (*sapranihita-lakṣaṇa*) be apprehended; one contemplates that within the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, there is no characteristic of wishlessness nor can any characteristic of having wishes be apprehended.

By means of the mind directed toward the knowledge of all modes, one contemplates that within the sense-base of the eye, there is no characteristic of tranquility (*śānta-lakṣaṇa*) nor can any characteristic of non-tranquility (*aśānta-lakṣaṇa*) be apprehended; one contemplates that within the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, there is no characteristic of tranquility nor can any characteristic of non-tranquility be apprehended.

With a mind directed toward the knowledge of all modes, one contemplates that the sense base of the eye cannot be apprehended as having the characteristic of being either detached or non-detached; one likewise contemplates that the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind cannot be apprehended as having the characteristic of being either detached or non-detached.
Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom in this way, because they possess skillful means, their mind is not startled, terrified, or frightened upon hearing this profound perfection of wisdom being taught.

“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, with a mind corresponding to the knowledge of all modes, they observe that the characteristics of permanence and impermanence in the sphere of form are unapprehendable; they observe that the characteristics of permanence and impermanence in the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena are unapprehendable.

With a mind corresponding to the knowledge of all modes, they observe that the characteristics of pleasure and suffering in the sphere of form are unapprehendable; they observe that the characteristics of pleasure and suffering in the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena are unapprehendable.”

With a mind corresponding to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), one contemplates that within the sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) the marks of self and non-self are unapprehendable; one contemplates that within the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibles, and mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) the marks of self and non-self are unapprehendable.

With a mind corresponding to the knowledge of all modes, one contemplates that within the sphere of form the marks of purity and impurity are unapprehendable; one contemplates that within the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibles, and mental objects the marks of purity and impurity are unapprehendable.

With a mind corresponding to the knowledge of all modes, one contemplates that within the sphere of form the marks of emptiness and non-emptiness are unapprehendable; one contemplates that within the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibles, and mental objects the marks of emptiness and non-emptiness are unapprehendable.

By means of the mind directed toward the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), one contemplates that in the sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*), there is neither signlessness nor the presence of signs, for such signs are unapprehendable; one contemplates that in the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), there is neither signlessness nor the presence of signs, for such signs are unapprehendable.

By means of the mind directed toward the knowledge of all modes, one contemplates that in the sphere of form, there is neither wishlessness nor the presence of wishes, for such signs are unapprehendable; one contemplates that in the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental objects, there is neither wishlessness nor the presence of wishes, for such signs are unapprehendable.

By means of the mind directed toward the knowledge of all modes, one contemplates that in the sphere of form, there is neither tranquility nor the absence of tranquility, for such signs are unapprehendable; one contemplates that in the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental objects, there is neither tranquility nor the absence of tranquility, for such signs are unapprehendable.

With a mind directed toward the knowledge of all modes, one contemplates that the characteristics of form being distant or not distant cannot be apprehended; one contemplates that the characteristics of sound, odor, taste, tangibles, and mental phenomena being distant or not distant cannot be apprehended.
Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom in this way, because they possess skillful means, their mind is not startled, alarmed, or terrified upon hearing this profound perfection of wisdom being taught.

“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, with a mind corresponding to the knowledge of all modes, they observe that the eye element, the form element, the eye-consciousness element, as well as eye-contact and the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, cannot be apprehended as having the characteristics of permanence or impermanence;

with a mind corresponding to the knowledge of all modes, they observe that the eye element, the form element, the eye-consciousness element, as well as eye-contact and the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, cannot be apprehended as having the characteristics of pleasure or suffering.”

With a mind corresponding to the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), one contemplates that within the eye-element, the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, and the eye-contact, as well as the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, the characteristics of self and non-self are unapprehendable;

with a mind corresponding to the knowledge of all modes, one contemplates that within the eye-element, the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, and the eye-contact, as well as the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, the characteristics of purity and impurity are unapprehendable;

with a mind corresponding to the knowledge of all modes, one contemplates that within the eye-element, the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, and the eye-contact, as well as the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, the characteristics of emptiness and non-emptiness are unapprehendable.
