Just as the phrases and meanings of the ultimate purity of the four foundations of mindfulness are non-existent and unobtainable, and the phrases and meanings of the ultimate purity of the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold noble path are non-existent and unobtainable, so too, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they observe that the phrases and meanings of ‘bodhisattva’ are non-existent and unobtainable.”

“Subhūti! Just as the phrases and meanings of the ultimate purity of the gate of liberation of emptiness are non-existent and unobtainable, and the phrases and meanings of the ultimate purity of the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness are non-existent and unobtainable, so too, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they contemplate that the phrases and meanings of ‘bodhisattva’ are non-existent and unobtainable.”

"Subhūti! Just as the ultimate pure characteristics and referents of the perfection of giving are non-existent and unapprehendable, and the ultimate pure characteristics and referents of the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom are non-existent and unapprehendable, so too, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they observe that the referent of 'bodhisattva' is non-existent and unapprehendable."

"Subhūti! Just as the referential meaning of the ultimate purity of the five eyes is non-existent and unattainable, and the referential meaning of the ultimate purity of the six supernormal powers is non-existent and unattainable, so too, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they observe that the referential meaning of 'bodhisattva' is non-existent and unattainable."

“Subhūti! Just as the phrases and meanings of the ultimate purity of the Buddha’s ten powers are non-existent and unapprehendable, and just as the phrases and meanings of the ultimate purity of the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects are non-existent and unapprehendable, so too, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they contemplate that the phrases and meanings of ‘bodhisattva’ are non-existent and unapprehendable.”
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
Just as the referential meaning of the term 'ultimately pure' does not exist and cannot be apprehended because a self does not exist;

so too, the referential meaning of the terms 'sentient being,' 'life-principle,' 'born being,' 'nourisher,' 'person,' 'mind-born,' 'young man,' 'agent,' 'instigator of action,' 'ariser,' 'instigator of arising,' 'experiencer,' 'instigator of experience,' 'knower,' and 'seer' do not exist and cannot be apprehended, because sentient beings up to seers do not exist."
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they contemplate that the referent of the term "bodhisattva" is non-existent and unapprehendable; it is just like this.

"Subhūti! Just as when the sun rises, the referent of the term 'darkness' does not exist and cannot be apprehended, so too, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they observe that the referent of the term 'bodhisattva' does not exist and cannot be apprehended."

"Subhūti! Just as when a kalpa is consumed by fire, the referents and meanings of all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) do not exist and cannot be apprehended, so too, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they contemplate that the referents and meanings of 'bodhisattva' do not exist and cannot be apprehended."

“Subhūti! Just as within the aggregate of ethical discipline (śīlaskandha) of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, there is no such thing as the term ‘immorality’ and it cannot be found, so too, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they observe that the term ‘bodhisattva’ does not exist and cannot be found.”

“Subhūti! Just as within the aggregate of concentration of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, the meaning of the term ‘distraction’ does not exist and cannot be apprehended, so too, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they observe that the meaning of the term ‘bodhisattva’ does not exist and cannot be apprehended.”

“Subhūti! Just as within the aggregate of wisdom of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, the referent of the term ‘delusion’ does not exist and cannot be apprehended, so too, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they observe that the referent of the term ‘bodhisattva’ does not exist and cannot be apprehended.”

“Subhūti! Just as within the aggregate of liberation of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, there is no such thing as a phrase or meaning for ‘liberation’ that can be found or apprehended, so too, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they contemplate that the phrase and meaning of ‘bodhisattva’ likewise do not exist and cannot be apprehended.”

“Subhūti! Just as within the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha’s aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation, the referent of the term ‘knowledge and vision of liberation’ does not exist and cannot be apprehended, so too, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they observe that the referent of the term ‘bodhisattva’ does not exist and cannot be apprehended.”

“Subhūti! Just as within the various luminances such as the sun and moon, the referential meaning of ‘darkness’ does not exist and cannot be apprehended, so too, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they observe that the referential meaning of ‘bodhisattva’ does not exist and cannot be apprehended.”

“Subhūti! Just as within the light of a Buddha, all expressions and referents for the radiance of the sun, moon, jewels, fire, lightning, and so forth are non-existent and unapprehendable; and just as all expressions and referents for the radiance of the gods from the Realm of the Four Great Kings up to the Heaven of Controlling Others’ Emanations, and from the Heaven of Brahma’s Retinue up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, are non-existent and unapprehendable—so too, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they observe that the expression and referent of ‘bodhisattva’ are non-existent and unapprehendable.”
"Why is this so, Subhūti?

Whether it be awakening, or a sentient being, or the meaning of the term 'bodhisattva'—all these are neither associated nor dissociated; they are formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and of a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of signlessness."
“Subhūti!
Regarding all phenomena, bodhisattva mahāsattvas should train and should know that they are entirely non-existent, unimpeded, and unattached.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What are all dharmas?
Regarding these all dharmas, what are they that are non-existent, unimpeded, and unattached, such that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should train in them and know them?”

The Buddha told Subhūti: “All phenomena refer to wholesome phenomena and unwholesome phenomena; determinate phenomena and indeterminate phenomena; mundane phenomena and supramundane phenomena; contaminated phenomena and uncontaminated phenomena; conditioned phenomena and unconditioned phenomena; shared phenomena and unshared phenomena.”
"Subhūti! These are called all dharmas.
Regarding these all dharmas, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should train and should know them as being entirely non-existent, unimpeded, and without attachment."
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what are wholesome dharmas?”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"It refers to being filial and obedient toward one's parents; making offerings to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas; honoring and serving teachers and elders;
and the meritorious deeds consisting of generosity, the meritorious deeds consisting of ethical discipline, and the meritorious deeds consisting of cultivation."
The merit of attending to the sick; the merit of skillful means;

the ten paths of wholesome action, namely: abstaining from taking life, abstaining from taking what is not given, abstaining from sexual misconduct, abstaining from false speech, abstaining from divisive speech, abstaining from harsh speech, abstaining from frivolous chatter, non-covetousness, non-ill will, and right view;

and the ten perceptions, namely: the perception of bloatedness, the perception of festering, the perception of bloody-red, the perception of livid-blue, the perception of dismemberment, the perception of being devoured, the perception of scattering, the perception of skeletons, the perception of burning, and the perception that all worlds are not worth delighting in.
The four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments;

there are ten recollections, namely: recollection of the Buddha, recollection of the Dharma, recollection of the Saṅgha, recollection of ethical discipline, recollection of relinquishment, recollection of the devas, recollection of inhalation and exhalation, recollection of peace, recollection of death, and recollection of the body.
"Subhūti! These are called wholesome dharmas.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what are unwholesome dharmas?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"They are the ten unwholesome courses of action: namely, taking life, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, frivolous speech, covetousness, ill will, and wrong view; as well as anger, enmity, concealment, resentment, guile, deceit, hypocrisy, harmfulness, envy, stinginess, and pride."
“Subhūti! These are called unwholesome dharmas.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what are the dharmas that are determinately taught?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“Namely, all wholesome dharmas and unwholesome dharmas are called ‘determined dharmas’ (vyākṛta-dharma).
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
“What are indeterminate phenomena?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“They are indeterminate bodily action, indeterminate verbal action, indeterminate mental action; indeterminate four great elements, indeterminate five faculties, indeterminate six bases, indeterminate formless phenomena; indeterminate five aggregates, indeterminate twelve bases, indeterminate eighteen constituents; and indeterminate resultant phenomena.”
"Subhūti! These are called indeterminate dharmas.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What are mundane dharmas?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"They are the five aggregates, the twelve bases, the eighteen elements, the ten paths of action, the four meditative absorptions, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and the twelvefold dependent origination."
"Subhūti! These are called worldly dharmas.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What are supramundane dharmas?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

That is to say: the supramundane four foundations of mindfulness, the four right endeavors, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eight branches of the noble path, the gate of liberation of emptiness, the gate of liberation of signlessness, the gate of liberation of wishlessness, the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of "knowing," the faculty of "one who has known," the concentration with directed thought and sustained investigation, the concentration without directed thought and with only sustained investigation, the concentration without directed thought and without sustained investigation, clarity, liberation, mindfulness, clear comprehension, and appropriate attention.
“There are eight liberations, namely:
possessing form, one perceives forms; this is the first liberation.
Having no internal perception of form, one perceives external forms; this is the second liberation.”
The liberation through the perception of purity, realized by bodily witness, is the third liberation;

transcending all perceptions of form, extinguishing perceptions of sensory impact, not attending to perceptions of diversity, one enters and dwells fully in the sphere of infinite space—this is the fourth liberation;
transcending the entire sphere of infinite space, one enters the sphere of infinite consciousness and dwells fully in the sphere of infinite consciousness—this is the fifth liberation.
Transcending the sphere of infinite consciousness, one enters and dwells in the full possession of the sphere of nothingness; this is the sixth liberation.
Transcending the sphere of nothingness, one enters and dwells in the full possession of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; this is the seventh liberation.

Transcending the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one enters and dwells in the full possession of the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling; this is the eighth liberation.
“There are nine successive attainments, namely:

being detached from sensual desires and unwholesome states, with directed thought and evaluation, born of seclusion, accompanied by rapture and pleasure, one enters and dwells in the first dhyāna; this is the first dhyāna.

With the subsiding of directed thought and evaluation, through internal clarity and mental unification, without directed thought or evaluation, born of concentration, accompanied by rapture and pleasure, one enters and dwells in the second dhyāna; this is the second dhyāna.”

Detached from joy, one dwells in equanimity, possessed of mindfulness and clear comprehension; experiencing happiness with the body, of which the Noble Ones say, "One who dwells in equanimity is mindful and abides in happiness," one enters and dwells fully in the third dhyāna—this is the third absorption.

With the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, one enters and dwells fully in the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and possesses purity of equanimity and mindfulness—this is the fourth absorption.

Transcending all perceptions of form, with the cessation of perceptions of sensory impact, and not attending to perceptions of diversity, one enters and dwells fully in the sphere of infinite space—this is the fifth absorption.
Transcending the sphere of infinite space, one enters and dwells fully in the sphere of infinite consciousness; this is the sixth absorption.
Transcending the sphere of infinite consciousness, one enters and dwells fully in the sphere of nothingness; this is the seventh absorption.
Transcending the sphere of nothingness, one enters and dwells fully in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; this is the eighth absorption.
Transcending the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one enters and dwells in the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling; this is the ninth absorption.

“Internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate truth, the emptiness of conditioned phenomena, the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, absolute emptiness, the emptiness of the limitless, the emptiness of dispersion, the emptiness of non-alteration, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the emptiness of self-characteristics, the emptiness of common characteristics, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature; the six perfections, the five eyes, the six superknowledges, the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects.”
“Subhūti! These are called supramundane dharmas.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What are the phenomena with outflows?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"The five aggregates, twelve bases, eighteen elements, four meditative concentrations, four immeasurables, four formless attainments, and all phenomena whatsoever that fall within the three realms."
"Subhūti! These are called contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*).
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What are the untainted dharmas?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

That is to say: the four supramundane dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments; the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path; the three gates of liberation, the six perfections, the five eyes, and the six superknowledges; the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity; the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects.
"Subhūti! These are called the untainted dharmas.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What are conditioned phenomena?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

That is to say: phenomena associated with the desire realm, phenomena associated with the form realm, phenomena associated with the formless realm; the five aggregates, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of miraculous power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold noble path, the three gates of liberation, the six perfections, the five eyes, the six superknowledges, the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects; and all things whatsoever that have arising, abiding, alteration, and cessation.
"Subhūti! These are called conditioned phenomena.
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is unconditioned dharma?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“If there are dharmas that can be apprehended as being without arising, without abiding, without change, and without cessation—namely, the exhaustion of greed, the exhaustion of hatred, the exhaustion of delusion; suchness, the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, the stability of dharmas, the fixedness of dharmas, non-falsity, non-alteration, the nature of transcendence from birth, equality, and the limit of reality.”
"Subhūti! These are called unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*).
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What are the shared dharmas?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"They are the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and the five supernormal powers of the world,
Subhūti! These are called common dharmas."
"Why is this? Because they are common to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What are the unique qualities?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

That is to say: the four untainted dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments; the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path; the three doors of liberation, the six perfections, the five eyes, and the six superknowledges; the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity; the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects.
"Subhūti! These are called the unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma). Why is that?"
Because they are not shared with ordinary beings, Subhūti!
When bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they should not cling to such phenomena that are empty of their own characteristics.
Why is this? Because the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena cannot be differentiated. Subhūti!
When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they should awaken to all phenomena by means of non-duality as their skillful method. Why is this?
Because all phenomena have the characteristic of being immovable, Subhūti!
That which is non-dual and immovable regarding all phenomena is the meaning of the term "bodhisattva."
"For this reason, that which is without a referent is the referent of a bodhisattva.
*The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Scroll 46; *The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Scroll 47.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Thirteen: On the Mahāsattva. Part One: The First Section of Chapter Thirteen on the Mahāsattva.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
For what reason is a bodhisattva further called a mahāsattva?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“A bodhisattva shall certainly become the foremost among the great assembly of sentient beings; for this reason, they are further called a ‘mahāsattva.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
“What is this great assembly of sentient beings among whom the bodhisattva will certainly become the leader?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“The great assembly of sentient beings refers to those abiding on the stage of the spiritual lineage, the eighth stage, the stage of stream-enterer, once-returner, non-returner, arhat, and pratyekabuddha; as well as the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas from their first generation of the mind of awakening up to the stage of non-retrogression. This is called the great assembly of sentient beings.”
“Because a bodhisattva will certainly be the foremost among such a great multitude of sentient beings, they are further called a ‘mahāsattva’ (great being).
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
“For what reasons and conditions will such a bodhisattva mahāsattva certainly become a leader among the great assembly of sentient beings?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva has generated a mind like a vajra that is resolute and cannot be destroyed; by virtue of this mind, he will certainly become a leader among the great assembly of sentient beings.”
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is called the diamond-like mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to such a thought:
‘I shall don the firm armor and, within the vast wilderness of boundless birth and death, destroy the immeasurable enemies that are the afflictions.’”
I shall dry up the boundless and profound great ocean of saṃsāra.
I shall relinquish all internal and external bodies and wealth that are dear to me.
I shall bring about great benefit for all sentient beings with an impartial mind.
I shall rescue all sentient beings by means of the Dharma of the three vehicles, causing them all to enter parinirvāṇa in the realm of nirvana without remainder.
Although I shall bring all sentient beings to extinction through the Dharma of the three vehicles, in reality, I do not perceive any sentient being who attains extinction.
I shall, in accordance with reality, fully awaken to all phenomena as being without arising and without cessation.
I shall practice the six pāramitās solely with a mind directed toward the knowledge of all modes of knowledge.
I shall practice and study so as to attain ultimate penetration and universal entry into sublime wisdom regarding all phenomena.
I shall penetrate the single gateway of principle that encompasses the characteristics of all phenomena.
I shall penetrate the gateway of the two principles of all phenomena, up to the gateways of infinite principles.
I shall cultivate and master the sublime wisdom that penetrates the single principle-gateway of all phenomena.
I shall train in and master the sublime wisdom of the two approaches to all phenomena, up to and including mastery of the sublime wisdom of infinite approaches.
I shall train in and bring forth the gateways of infinite meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), and formless attainments (*ārūpya*).
I shall train to bring forth the boundless dharmas of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the three gateways to liberation, and the dharmas of the six perfections.

I shall train to bring forth the boundless dharmas of the five eyes, the six superknowledges, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects.
"Subhūti! This is called the diamond-like mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in this mind by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method, and because he does not rely on it to give rise to arrogance or conceit, he will certainly become a leader among the great assembly of sentient beings."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to such a thought:

'Whatever sufferings and afflictions are experienced by all classes of sentient beings within the realms of hell, animals, hungry ghosts, humans, and gods, I shall take them upon myself in their stead and cause them to be at peace.'"
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva gives rise to such a thought:

"For the sake of even a single sentient being, I shall undergo all manner of intense sufferings in the various hells for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of kalpas, using countless skillful means to teach and transform them so that they realize nirvana without remainder."

In this manner, for the sake of every single sentient being, one by one, he undergoes various kinds of intense suffering in the hells for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of great kalpas; furthermore, he teaches and transforms each one through countless skillful means, causing them to realize nirvana without remainder.

Having performed these deeds, they personally plant roots of goodness; then, after further passing through immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of kalpas, they fully cultivate and accumulate the provisions for enlightenment, and only thereafter proceed to realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
“Subhūti! This is called the diamond-like mind (*vajropamacitta*) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in this mind by means of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), and because he does not rely on it to give rise to arrogance or self-exaltation, he will certainly become a leader among the great assembly of sentient beings.”
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva has generated a distinguished and vast mind that is resolute and will never regress or perish, by virtue of this mind, he shall certainly become a leader among the great assembly of sentient beings."
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is called the sublime and vast mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to such a thought:

'From my first production of the thought of awakening until I realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, throughout this interval, I vow never to give rise to thoughts of desire, thoughts of hatred, thoughts of delusion, thoughts of anger, thoughts of resentment, thoughts of concealment, thoughts of vexation, thoughts of deception, thoughts of guile, thoughts of envy, thoughts of stinginess, thoughts of arrogance, thoughts of harmfulness, or thoughts of views and pride; nor shall I give rise to thoughts directed toward the stages of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.'"
"Subhūti! This is called the sublime and vast mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in this mind by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method, and because they do not rely on it to give rise to arrogance or haughtiness, they will certainly become a leader among the great assembly of sentient beings."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva has generated a mind that is unshakeable and will certainly not regress or be destroyed, by virtue of this mind, he shall surely become a leader among the great assembly of sentient beings."
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is called the unshakable mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to such a thought:
‘I shall, with a mind directed toward the knowledge of all modes, cultivate and initiate all that is to be cultivated and all that ought to be done.’”
“Suvikrāntavikrāmin!
This is called the unshakable mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in this mind by means of the expedient of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), and because they do not rely on it to give rise to arrogance or conceit, they will certainly become a leader among the great assembly of sentient beings.”
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva has generated a mind intent on benefiting and bringing peace and happiness that is absolutely unshakable, by virtue of this mind, he will certainly become a leader among the great assembly of sentient beings."
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
what is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s mind of benefit and peace?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to such a thought:
'I shall, until the end of the future limit, act as a refuge, a bridge, a ship, and an island for all sentient beings; I shall rescue, protect, and shelter them, never abandoning them.'"
"Subhūti! This is called the mind of benefit and happiness of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in this mind by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method, and because he does not rely on it to give rise to arrogance or conceit, he will certainly become a leader among the great assembly of sentient beings."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they are always able to love the Dharma, delight in the Dharma, rejoice in the Dharma, and find joy in the Dharma. By virtue of these conditions, they will certainly become a leader among the great multitude of sentient beings."
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is this ‘dharma’?”
“How is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, always loves, delights in, and rejoices in this Dharma?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“As for what is called ‘Dharma,’ it refers to all sentient beings and all phenomena, whether material or immaterial, which are all devoid of intrinsic nature and utterly unapprehendable; their true mark is indestructible—this is what is called ‘Dharma.’”
To speak of "loving the Dharma" means to give rise to desire and aspiration for this Dharma;
to speak of "delighting in the Dharma" means to extol its merits;
to speak of "rejoicing in the Dharma" means to receive it with joy and faith.
"To speak of 'rejoicing in the Dharma' means that one yearns for this Dharma and practices it extensively. Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom in this way, by employing the method of non-apprehension, they are always able to love the Dharma, delight in the Dharma, rejoice in the Dharma, and find joy in the Dharma. Furthermore, because they do not rely on this to give rise to arrogance or haughtiness, they will certainly become a leader among the great assembly of sentient beings."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method, and because they abide in internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersal emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of non-apprehensibility, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, they will certainly become a leader among the great assembly of sentient beings."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, dwells in the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method, he will certainly become a leader among the great multitude of sentient beings."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method, they abide in the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right endeavors, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path; therefore, they will certainly become a leader among the great multitude of sentient beings."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, dwells in the gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method, they will certainly become a leader among the great multitude of sentient beings."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, dwells in the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method, they will certainly become a leader among the great multitude of sentient beings."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, dwells in the five eyes and the six supernormal powers by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method, he will certainly become a leader among the great multitude of sentient beings."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, by employing the method of non-apprehension, they abide in the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects; therefore, they will certainly become the foremost among the great assembly of sentient beings."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, dwells in the vajra-like samādhi by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method, and so on, up to dwelling in the samādhi of liberation that is unattached, unconditioned, unstained, and like space, by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method, he shall certainly become a leader among the great assembly of sentient beings."
“Subhūti! By means of such various causes and conditions as these, this bodhisattva mahāsattva will certainly become a leader among the great assembly of sentient beings.”
"Subhūti! For this reason, a bodhisattva is further called a mahāsattva.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I, too, would like to speak on how it is for this reason that a bodhisattva is further called a mahāsattva.
The Buddha said:
"Śāriputra, speak as you wish. Śāriputra said:
“World-Honored One!

Because these bodhisattvas are able to teach sentient beings—by means of non-apprehension as their expedient—to sever the view of a self, the view of a sentient being, the view of a life-principle, the view of a living being, the view of a nourisher, the view of a person, the view of a *pudgala*, the view of a mind-born being, the view of a youth, the view of an agent, the view of one who causes to act, the view of an originator, the view of one who causes to originate, the view of an experiencer, the view of one who causes to experience, the view of a knower, and the view of a seer, these bodhisattvas are further named *mahāsattvas*.”
“World-Honored One!

Because these bodhisattvas are able, for the sake of sentient beings, to teach the dharma that severs the views of permanence and annihilation by employing the skillful means of non-apprehension, these bodhisattvas are further named Mahāsattvas.”
“World-Honored One!

Because these bodhisattvas are able to teach sentient beings, by means of non-apprehension as their skillful method, the dharma that severs the views of existence and non-existence, these bodhisattvas are further named Mahāsattvas.”
“World-Honored One!

Because these bodhisattvas are able, for the sake of sentient beings, to teach the dharma that severs the views of the aggregates, the bases, the elements, the truths, and dependent origination by employing the method of non-apprehension, these bodhisattvas are further named Mahāsattvas.”
“World-Honored One!

Because these bodhisattvas are able, for the sake of sentient beings, to teach the dharma that severs views regarding the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments by employing the method of non-apprehension, these bodhisattvas are further named Mahāsattvas.”
“World-Honored One!

Because these bodhisattvas are able, for the sake of sentient beings, to teach the dharma that severs views regarding the four foundations of mindfulness, views regarding the four right efforts, views regarding the four bases of power, views regarding the five faculties, views regarding the five powers, views regarding the seven factors of enlightenment, and views regarding the eightfold noble path—by employing the method of non-apprehension—they are further called ‘mahāsattvas.’”
“World-Honored One!

Because these bodhisattvas are able, for the sake of sentient beings, to teach by means of non-apprehension the severance of views regarding the three gates of liberation and the dharmas of the six perfections, these bodhisattvas are further named Mahāsattvas.”
“World-Honored One!

Because these bodhisattvas are able, for the sake of sentient beings, to teach the dharma of severing the vision of the five eyes and the vision of the six supernormal powers by employing the method of non-apprehension, these bodhisattvas are further named mahāsattvas.”
“World-Honored One!

Because these bodhisattvas are able, for the sake of sentient beings, to use the method of non-apprehension to teach the dharma that severs views regarding the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered understandings, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, the view of all-knowledge, the view of the knowledge of the paths, and the view of the knowledge of all aspects, these bodhisattvas are further named Mahāsattvas.”
“World-Honored One!

Because these bodhisattvas are able, for the sake of sentient beings, to use the method of non-apprehension to teach the severing of the view of maturing sentient beings, the view of purifying buddha-fields, the view of bodhisattvas, the view of buddhas, and the view of turning the wheel of Dharma, these bodhisattvas are further named Mahāsattvas.”
“World-Honored One!

To speak in brief, because these bodhisattvas are able, for the sake of sentient beings, to teach the severance of all views by employing the method of non-apprehension, these bodhisattvas are further named Mahāsattvas.”
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti asked Śāriputra:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, for the sake of sentient beings, can teach the dharma that severs all views by employing the method of non-apprehension, for what reason would a bodhisattva mahāsattva themselves have anything apprehended?"
Yet, as a skillful means, they give rise to views regarding form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness;
they give rise to views regarding the sense base of the eye, and the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind;

they give rise to views regarding the sense base of forms, and the sense bases of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena; they give rise to views regarding the element of the eye, and the element of forms...
One gives rise to the view of the eye-consciousness element, eye-contact, and the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition;
one gives rise to the view of the ear-element, sound-element, ear-consciousness element, ear-contact, and the various feelings produced with ear-contact as condition;
one gives rise to the view of the nose-element, odor-element, nose-consciousness element, and nose-contact... [and so forth].

Regarding the views concerning the various feelings born of conditions, one gives rise to views regarding the tongue element, the taste element, the tongue-consciousness element, as well as tongue-contact and the various feelings born of tongue-contact as a condition;

one gives rise to views regarding the body element, the tangible-object element, the body-consciousness element, as well as body-contact and the various feelings born of body-contact as a condition; and one gives rise to views regarding the mind element.

One perceives the element of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), the element of mental consciousness (*manovijñānadhātu*), and mental contact (*manaḥsaṃsparśa*)—as well as all sensations produced with mental contact as their condition—and gives rise to views regarding the earth element, and gives rise to views regarding the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements;

one gives rise to views regarding the noble truth of suffering, and gives rise to views regarding the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path; one gives rise to views regarding ignorance (*avidyā*) and volitional formations (*saṃskāra*).
...consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, becoming, birth, and old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair;
they give rise to views regarding the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments;
they give rise to views regarding the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, and the four bases of psychic power.
They perceive the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path;
they perceive the gate of liberation of emptiness, and the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness;
they perceive the perfection of generosity, as well as the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
They frequently give rise to the vision of the five eyes and the vision of the six supernormal powers; they give rise to the vision of the Buddha’s ten powers,
the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity,
the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, all-knowledge, the knowledge of the aspects of the path, and the knowledge of all aspects.
"Do you perceive the perception of maturing sentient beings, the perception of purifying Buddha-fields, the perception of bodhisattvas,
the perception of buddhas, or the perception of turning the wheel of Dharma?
The Venerable Śāriputra replied to Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, lacks skillful means and takes 'attainment' as their means, they will give rise to views of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; and even give rise to views of a Buddha or views of turning the wheel of Dharma. Such a bodhisattva mahāsattva is unable, by taking 'non-attainment' as their means, to teach sentient beings the dharma for severing all views."

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if they possess skillful means, they are able to teach sentient beings the dharma for severing all views by employing the method of non-apprehension. Such a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not give rise to a view of form, nor of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; they do not give rise to a view of a Buddha, nor even a view of turning the wheel of Dharma.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I, too, would like to speak on how it is for this reason that a bodhisattva is further named a mahāsattva.”
The Buddha said:
"Suvikrāntavikrāmin! Speak as you wish."
Subhūti said to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, because bodhisattvas,
for the sake of the knowledge of all modes, generate the mind of awakening— the unequaled mind, the mind not shared with any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas— and yet do not even grasp at such a mind."
Why is this? World-Honored One!

That mind of the knowledge of all modes is truly untainted and does not fall within the three realms; the mind that seeks the knowledge of all modes is likewise untainted and does not fall within the three realms. Because one should not grasp at or cling to such a mind, this bodhisattva is further named a Mahāsattva.
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"In what way does the bodhisattva mahāsattva possess a mind that is unequaled and not shared with any śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha?"
Subhūti replied:

"From the first production of the thought of enlightenment, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas do not perceive any phenomena as having arising or cessation, decrease or increase, coming or going, or defilement or purification."
Śāriputra!

If one does not perceive that all phenomena have arising or ceasing, decrease or increase, coming or going, defilement or purity, nor does one perceive the mind of a śrāvaka, the mind of a pratyekabuddha, the mind of a bodhisattva, or the mind of a Tathāgata.

Śāriputra! This is called the unequaled mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, a mind not shared with any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; yet, bodhisattva mahāsattvas do not even grasp at or cling to such a mind.
Then, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"If one should not grasp at such a mind, then one should likewise not grasp at the minds of all foolish commoners, ordinary persons, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas;
nor should one grasp at the mind of form, nor should one grasp at the minds of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness."
The mind should not cling to the sense-base of the eye; nor should the mind cling to the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind.
The mind should not cling to the sense-base of forms; nor should the mind cling to the sense-bases of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena.

The mind should not cling to the eye-element; nor should the mind cling to the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, eye-contact, or the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition.

The mind should not cling to the ear element; the mind should also not cling to the sound element, the ear-consciousness element, ear-contact, or the various feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition.

The mind should not cling to the nose element; the mind should also not cling to the odor element, the nose-consciousness element, nose-contact, or the various feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition.

The mind should not cling to the tongue element; the mind should also not cling to the taste element, the tongue-consciousness element, tongue-contact, or the various feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition.

One should not take mental attachment to the body element; one should also not take mental attachment to the contact element, the body-consciousness element, body-contact, or the various feelings arising with body-contact as condition.

One should not take mental attachment to the mind element; one should also not take mental attachment to the phenomena element, the mind-consciousness element, mind-contact, or the various feelings arising with mind-contact as condition.
One should not take mental attachment to the earth element; one should also not take mental attachment to the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements.
One’s mind should not cling to the noble truth of suffering; one’s mind should likewise not cling to the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path.

One’s mind should not cling to ignorance; one’s mind should likewise not cling to volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, or aging, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
One’s mind should not cling to the four dhyānas; one’s mind should likewise not cling to the four immeasurables or the four formless attainments.

One should not take up attachment to the mind regarding the four applications of mindfulness; one should likewise not take up attachment to the mind regarding the four right endeavors, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, or the eightfold noble path.

One should not take up attachment to the mind regarding the gate of liberation of emptiness, nor should one take up attachment to the mind regarding the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness.

One should not take up attachment to the mind regarding the perfection of generosity, nor should one take up attachment to the mind regarding the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, or wisdom.
One should not take mental attachment to the five eyes; one should also not take mental attachment to the six supernormal powers;

one should not take mental attachment to the ten powers of a Buddha; nor should one take mental attachment to the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, or the knowledge of all aspects.
"Why is this? It is because all such minds lack the intrinsic nature of mind.
Subhūti replied:
"So it is! So it is! It is exactly as you have said."
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:

"If all minds should not be grasped because they lack the nature of mind, then form should not be grasped because it lacks the nature of form; feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness should likewise not be grasped because they lack the nature of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness.

The eye-base should not be grasped because it lacks the nature of the eye-base; the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases should likewise not be grasped because they lack the nature of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases."

One should not cling to the sense-base of form because it lacks the intrinsic nature of the sense-base of form; one should likewise not cling to the sense-bases of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental objects because they lack the intrinsic nature of the sense-bases of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental objects.

One should not cling to the eye-element because it lacks the intrinsic nature of the eye-element; nor should one cling to the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, eye-contact, and all feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, because they lack the intrinsic nature of the form-element up to the feelings produced with eye-contact as condition.

One should not cling to the ear-element because it lacks the intrinsic nature of the ear-element; nor should one cling to the sound-element, the ear-consciousness-element, ear-contact, and all feelings produced with ear-contact as condition, because they lack the intrinsic nature of the sound-element up to the feelings produced with ear-contact as condition.

Because the nose-element lacks the nature of a nose-element, one should not grasp it; because the odor-element, the nose-consciousness-element, nose-contact, and the various feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition lack the nature of the odor-element up to the various feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition, one should likewise not grasp them.

Because the tongue-element lacks the nature of a tongue-element, one should not grasp it; because the taste-element, the tongue-consciousness-element, tongue-contact, and the various feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition lack the nature of the taste-element up to the various feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition, one should likewise not grasp them.

Because the body-element lacks the nature of a body-element, one should not grasp at it; because the touch-element, the body-consciousness-element, body-contact, and all sensations produced with body-contact as a condition lack the nature of the touch-element up to the nature of all sensations produced with body-contact as a condition, one should likewise not grasp at them.

Because the mind-element lacks the nature of a mind-element, one should not grasp at it; because the phenomena-element, the mind-consciousness-element, mind-contact, and all sensations produced with mind-contact as a condition lack the nature of the phenomena-element up to the nature of all sensations produced with mind-contact as a condition, one should likewise not grasp at them.

Because the earth-element lacks the nature of an earth-element, one should not grasp at it; because the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness-elements lack the nature of the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness-elements, one should likewise not grasp at them.

The noble truth of suffering should not be grasped at, because it lacks the intrinsic nature of the noble truth of suffering; the noble truths of origination, cessation, and the path should likewise not be grasped at, because they lack the intrinsic nature of the noble truths of origination, cessation, and the path.

Ignorance should not be grasped at, because it lacks the intrinsic nature of ignorance; formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, and old age, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair should likewise not be grasped at, because they lack the intrinsic nature of formations through to old age, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.

The four dhyānas should not be grasped at, because they lack the intrinsic nature of the four dhyānas; the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions should likewise not be grasped at, because they lack the intrinsic nature of the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions.

Because the four foundations of mindfulness lack the intrinsic nature of the four foundations of mindfulness, one should not cling to them; because the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path lack the intrinsic nature of the four right efforts up to the eightfold noble path, one should likewise not cling to them;

because the liberation door of emptiness lacks the intrinsic nature of the liberation door of emptiness, one should not cling to it; and because the liberation doors of signlessness and wishlessness lack the intrinsic nature of the liberation doors of signlessness and wishlessness, one should likewise not cling to them.

Because the perfection of generosity lacks the intrinsic nature of the perfection of generosity, one should not cling to it; because the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom lack the intrinsic nature of ethical discipline up to wisdom, one should likewise not cling to them;

because the five eyes lack the intrinsic nature of the five eyes, one should not cling to them; and because the six supernormal powers lack the intrinsic nature of the six supernormal powers, one should likewise not cling to them.

Because the ten powers of a Buddha lack the intrinsic nature of the ten powers of a Buddha, one should not grasp at them. Because the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great joy, great equanimity, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects lack the intrinsic nature of the four fearlessnesses up to the knowledge of all aspects, one should likewise not grasp at them.
Subhūti replied, “So it is! So it is!”
"It is exactly as you have said.
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:

"If the mind of the knowledge of all modes is truly untainted and does not fall within the three realms, then the minds of all foolish commoners, ordinary beings, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas should also be truly untainted and not fall within the three realms."
Why is this? Because these various minds are likewise empty of intrinsic nature. Why is that?
"Because the dharma of the emptiness of intrinsic nature is truly without outflows and does not fall within the three realms.
Subhūti replied, "So it is!"
"So it is! It is exactly as you have said. Śāriputra said:

“Form, too, should be truly untainted and not fall within the three realms; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, too, should be truly untainted and not fall within the three realms.”
Why is this? Because form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are all empty by their very nature.
For what reason?
"Because the dharma of intrinsic emptiness is truly untainted and does not fall within the three realms.
Subhūti replied, "So it is!"
"So it is! It is exactly as you have said. Śāriputra said:

“The eye-base, too, should be truly untainted and not fall within the three realms; the ear-base, nose-base, tongue-base, body-base, and mind-base, too, should be truly untainted and not fall within the three realms.”
Why is this? Because the sense bases of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are all empty by their very nature. Why is that so?
"Because the dharma of intrinsic emptiness is truly untainted and does not fall within the three realms.
Subhūti replied, "So it is!"
"So it is! It is exactly as you have said. Śāriputra said:

"The sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) should also be truly untainted (*anāsrava*) and not fall within the three realms; the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) should likewise be truly untainted and not fall within the three realms."
Why is this? Because the sense bases of form, sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena are all empty by their very nature. Why is that so?
"Because the dharma of intrinsic emptiness is truly untainted and does not fall within the three realms.
Subhūti replied, "So it is!"
"So it is! It is exactly as you have said. Śāriputra said:

"The eye-element should also truly be untainted and not fall within the three realms; the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, as well as eye-contact and the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition should also truly be untainted and not fall within the three realms."
Why is this? Because the eye-faculty, up to and including the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, are all empty of intrinsic nature. Why is that?
"Because the dharma of intrinsic emptiness is truly untainted and does not fall within the three realms.
Subhūti replied, "So it is!"
"So it is! It is exactly as you have said. Śāriputra said:

"The ear-element (*śrotra-dhātu*) should also be truly untainted (*anāsrava*) and not included within the three realms; the sound-element (*śabda-dhātu*), the ear-consciousness-element (*śrotra-vijñāna-dhātu*), as well as ear-contact (*śrotra-saṃsparśa*) and all feelings (*vedanā*) produced with ear-contact as their condition, should also be truly untainted and not included within the three realms."
Why is this? Because the ear-element, and so forth up to the various feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition, are all empty by their very nature. Why is that?
"Because the dharma of intrinsic emptiness is truly without outflows and does not fall within the three realms.
Subhūti replied, "So it is!"
"So it is! It is exactly as you have said. Śāriputra said:

“The nose element (*ghrāṇadhātu*) should also truly be untainted (*anāsrava*) and not fall within the three realms; the odor element (*gandhadhātu*), the nose-consciousness element (*ghrāṇavijñānadhātu*), as well as nose-contact (*ghrāṇasparśa*) and all feelings (*vedanā*) produced with nose-contact as a condition, should also truly be untainted and not fall within the three realms.”
Why is this? Because the nose element, and even all feelings produced with nose-contact as condition, are all empty of intrinsic nature. Why is that?
"Because the dharma of the emptiness of intrinsic nature is truly untainted and does not fall within the three realms.
Subhūti replied, "So it is!"
"So it is! It is exactly as you have said. Śāriputra said:

"The tongue element (*jihvā-dhātu*) should also truly be untainted (*anāsrava*) and not fall within the three realms; the taste element (*rasa-dhātu*), the tongue-consciousness element (*jihvā-vijñāna-dhātu*), as well as tongue-contact (*jihvā-saṃsparśa*) and all feelings (*vedanā*) produced with tongue-contact as a condition, should also truly be untainted and not fall within the three realms."
Why is this? Because the tongue element, and even the various feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition, are all empty of intrinsic nature. Why is that so?
"Because the dharma of intrinsic emptiness is truly untainted and does not fall within the three realms.
Subhūti replied, "So it is!"
"So it is! It is exactly as you have said. Śāriputra said:

"The body element (*kāyadhātu*) should also truly be untainted (*anāsrava*) and not fall within the three realms; the touch element (*spraṣṭavyadhātu*), the body-consciousness element (*kāyavijñānadhātu*), as well as body-contact (*kāyasparśa*) and all feelings (*vedanā*) produced with body-contact as a condition, should also truly be untainted and not fall within the three realms."
Why is this? Because all sensations produced with the body-element and even body-contact as conditions are empty of intrinsic nature. Why is that?
"Because the dharma of the emptiness of intrinsic nature is truly untainted and does not fall within the three realms.
Subhūti replied, "So it is!"
"So it is! It is exactly as you have said. Śāriputra said:

“The mind-element (*manodhātu*) should also truly be untainted (*anāsrava*) and not fall within the three realms; likewise, the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*), the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*), mental contact (*manaḥsaṃsparśa*), and all feelings (*vedanā*) produced with mental contact as a condition should also truly be untainted and not fall within the three realms.”
Why is this? Because the mental faculty, up to and including the various feelings produced with mental contact as a condition, are all empty of intrinsic nature. Why is that?
"Because the dharma of intrinsic emptiness is truly untainted and does not fall within the three realms.
Subhūti replied, "So it is!"
"So it is! It is exactly as you have said. Śāriputra said:

"The earth element should also be truly untainted and not fall within the three realms; the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements should also be truly untainted and not fall within the three realms."
Why is this? Because the elements of earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness are all empty by their very nature.
For what reason?
"Because the dharma of the emptiness of intrinsic nature is truly untainted and does not fall within the three realms.
Subhūti replied, "So it is!"
"So it is! It is exactly as you have said. Śāriputra said:

"The Noble Truth of Suffering should also be truly untainted and not fall within the three realms; the Noble Truths of Origination, Cessation, and the Path should likewise be truly untainted and not fall within the three realms."
Why is this? Because the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path are all empty by their very nature. Why is that so?
"Because the dharma of intrinsic emptiness is truly without outflows and does not fall within the three realms.
Subhūti replied, "So it is!"
"So it is! It is exactly as you have said. Śāriputra said:

“Then ignorance (*avidyā*) should also truly be untainted (*anāsrava*) and not fall within the three realms; likewise, volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), feeling (*vedanā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), becoming (*bhava*), birth (*jāti*), and old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair (*jarāmaraṇa-śoka-parideva-duḥkha-daurmanasyopāyāsa*) should also truly be untainted and not fall within the three realms.”
Why is this? Because ignorance, up to and including old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair, are all empty by their very nature. Why is that so?
"Because the dharma of intrinsic emptiness is truly outflow-free and does not fall within the three realms.
Subhūti replied, "So it is!"
"So it is! It is exactly as you have said. Śāriputra said:

"The four dhyānas should also be truly untainted and not fall within the three realms; the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments should also be truly untainted and not fall within the three realms."
Why is this? Because the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments are all empty by their very nature. Why is that so?
"Because the dharma of emptiness by its very nature is truly untainted and does not fall within the three realms.
Subhūti replied, "So it is!"
"So it is! It is exactly as you have said. Śāriputra said:

“The four foundations of mindfulness should also truly be untainted and not fall within the three realms; the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path should also truly be untainted and not fall within the three realms.”
Why is this? Because the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path are all empty by their very nature. Why is that so?
"Because the dharma of intrinsic emptiness is truly untainted and does not fall within the three realms.
Subhūti replied, "So it is!"
"So it is! It is exactly as you have said. Śāriputra said:

"The liberation door of emptiness should also be truly untainted and not fall within the three realms; the liberation doors of signlessness and wishlessness should likewise be truly untainted and not fall within the three realms."
Why is this? Because the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—are all empty by their very nature. Why is that so?
"Because the dharma of emptiness by its very nature is truly without outflows and does not fall within the three realms.
Subhūti replied, "So it is!"
"So it is! It is exactly as you have said. Śāriputra said:

"The perfection of generosity should also be truly untainted and not fall within the three realms; the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom should also be truly untainted and not fall within the three realms."
Why is this? Because the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom are all empty by their very nature. For what reason?
"Because the dharma of intrinsic emptiness is truly untainted and does not fall within the three realms.
Subhūti replied, "So it is!"
"So it is! It is exactly as you have said. Śāriputra said:
“The five eyes should also be truly untainted and not fall within the three realms; the six supernormal powers should also be truly untainted and not fall within the three realms. Why is this?
This is because the five eyes and the six supernormal powers are all empty by their very nature. Why is this so?
Because dharmas that are empty by nature are truly without outflows and do not fall within the three realms.
Subhūti replied, “So it is! So it is!”
"It is exactly as you have said. Śāriputra said:

"The ten powers of a Buddha must also be truly untainted and not fall within the three realms; the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects must also be truly untainted and not fall within the three realms."
Why is this? Because the ten powers of a Buddha, up to and including all-aspect omniscience, are all empty by their very nature. Why is that so?
"Because the dharma of emptiness by its very nature is truly without outflows and does not fall within the three realms.
Subhūti replied, "So it is!"
"So it is! It is exactly as you have said.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed Subhūti, saying:
"If mind, form, and other phenomena are not to be grasped because they lack the intrinsic nature of mind, form, and so forth, then all phenomena should be entirely equal and without distinction."
Subhūti replied, “So it is! So it is!”
"It is exactly as you have said. Śāriputra asked:
"If all dharmas are definitively without distinction, why does the Tathāgata speak of various distinctions among dharmas such as mind and form?"
Subhūti replied, "This is merely that the Tathāgata, following conventional discourse, designates these various distinctions; it is not by way of ultimate reality."
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:

"If the minds and the phenomena of form, etc., of all foolish commoners, ordinary persons, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and tathāgatas are all by nature empty, and are thus truly untainted and do not fall within the three realms, then the noble ones and ordinary persons, as well as omniscience and non-omniscience, should all be equal and without distinction."
Subhūti replied, “So it is! So it is!”
"It is exactly as you have said. Śāriputra asked,
"If there is truly no distinction between ordinary beings and noble ones, why has the Tathāgata spoken of various differences among ordinary beings and noble ones?"
Subhūti replied, “This, too, is the Tathāgata’s conventional designation of these various distinctions in accordance with worldly discourse; it does not exist by way of ultimate reality.”
Śāriputra!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom in this way, by means of the expedient of non-apprehension, they neither rely upon nor cling to the bodhicitta they have generated—the mind that is unequaled and not shared with any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas—and they likewise do not grasp at or adhere to any phenomena. For this reason, they are called a mahāsattva.
At that time, the Venerable Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
I, too, would like to speak on how it is for this reason that a bodhisattva is further named a mahāsattva."
The Buddha said:
“Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
Speak as you wish.”
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra said:
“World-Honored One!

Because all bodhisattvas don the great armor of merit out of a desire to bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings, and because they set out for the Great Vehicle and ride upon the Great Vehicle, they are further called ‘mahāsattvas’ (Great Beings).”
At that time, Śāriputra asked Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra:
"In what way does a bodhisattva mahāsattva don the great armor of merit out of a desire to bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings?"
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra said: “Śāriputra!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivates the practice of awakening, it is not for the sake of benefiting a small number of sentient beings; rather, they cultivate the practice of awakening for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings.”
"Śāriputra!
This is called the great armor of merit donned by a bodhisattva mahāsattva who desires to bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the perfection of generosity and cultivates the perfection of generosity, they do not cultivate the perfection of generosity for the sake of bringing benefit and happiness to a limited number of sentient beings; rather, they cultivate the perfection of generosity for the sake of bringing benefit and happiness to all sentient beings.

“Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the perfection of ethical discipline and cultivates the perfection of ethical discipline, they do not cultivate the perfection of ethical discipline for the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to a limited number of sentient beings; rather, they cultivate the perfection of ethical discipline for the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings.”

“Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the perfection of patience and cultivates the perfection of patience, they do not cultivate the perfection of patience for the sake of bringing benefit and happiness to only a few sentient beings; rather, they cultivate the perfection of patience for the sake of bringing benefit and happiness to all sentient beings.”

“Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the perfection of diligence and cultivates the perfection of diligence, he does not do so for the sake of bringing benefit and happiness to a limited number of sentient beings; rather, he cultivates the perfection of diligence for the sake of bringing benefit and happiness to all sentient beings.”

“Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the perfection of meditative concentration and cultivates the perfection of meditative concentration, they do not cultivate the perfection of meditative concentration for the sake of bringing benefit and happiness to a limited number of sentient beings; rather, they cultivate the perfection of meditative concentration for the sake of bringing benefit and happiness to all sentient beings.”

“Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the perfection of wisdom and cultivates the perfection of wisdom, they do not cultivate the perfection of wisdom for the sake of bringing benefit and happiness to only a few sentient beings; rather, they cultivate the perfection of wisdom for the sake of bringing benefit and happiness to all sentient beings.”
“Śāriputra! This is called the great armor of merit donned by a bodhisattva mahāsattva who desires to bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!”
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas don the great armor of merit; their aim to benefit and bring happiness to sentient beings knows no limits. That is to say, they do not form such thoughts as:
"I shall cause this many sentient beings to attain nirvana without remainder, but I shall not cause that many sentient beings to attain it;
I shall cause this many sentient beings to abide in unsurpassed enlightenment, but I shall not cause that many sentient beings to abide therein."

Nevertheless, because this bodhisattva mahāsattva intends to cause all sentient beings universally to attain nirvana without remainder and to abide in unsurpassed enlightenment, he dons such armor of great merit.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva forms this thought:
'I shall personally fulfill the perfection of generosity, and I shall also teach all sentient beings to cultivate and fulfill the perfection of generosity;'"

I shall personally fulfill the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, and I shall also teach all sentient beings to cultivate and bring to fulfillment these same perfections, from ethical discipline up to wisdom.
I shall personally abide in internal emptiness and also teach all sentient beings to abide in internal emptiness;

I shall personally abide in external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-altering emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, and I shall also teach all sentient beings to abide in external emptiness up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.

I shall dwell myself in the four dhyānas and also teach all sentient beings to cultivate the four dhyānas; I shall dwell myself in the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments and also teach all sentient beings to cultivate the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments.
I shall abide myself in the four foundations of mindfulness and also teach all sentient beings to cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness;

I shall abide myself in the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path, and also teach all sentient beings to cultivate the four right efforts up to the eightfold noble path.
I shall abide myself in the gate of liberation of emptiness, and also instruct all sentient beings to cultivate the gate of liberation of emptiness;
I shall abide myself in the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness, and also instruct all sentient beings to cultivate the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness.
I shall abide myself in the five eyes and also instruct all sentient beings to cultivate the five eyes;
I shall abide myself in the six supernormal powers and also instruct all sentient beings to cultivate the six supernormal powers.
I shall abide myself in the ten powers of a Buddha, and also instruct all sentient beings to cultivate the ten powers of a Buddha;

I shall abide myself in the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, omniscience, the knowledge of the aspects of the path, and the knowledge of all aspects, and also instruct all sentient beings to cultivate the four fearlessnesses up to the knowledge of all aspects.
"Śāriputra! This is called the donning of the great armor of merit by a bodhisattva mahāsattva who desires to bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings.
The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Scroll Forty-seven."
