Just as the nature of ever-abiding equanimity is designated as being comprised solely of adventitious factors—it comes from nowhere in the ten directions or the three periods of time, goes nowhere, and abides nowhere; within the nature of ever-abiding equanimity there is no name, and within the name there is no nature of ever-abiding equanimity; it is neither joined nor separated, but is merely a conventional designation.

Why is this? Because both the nature of constant dwelling in equanimity and its name are empty of intrinsic nature; within the emptiness of intrinsic nature, neither the nature of constant dwelling in equanimity nor its name exists and cannot be apprehended.

The name "Bodhisattva-mahāsattva" is likewise thus: it is comprised solely of adventitious designations; throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time, it comes from nowhere, goes nowhere, and abides nowhere. Within the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva there is no name, and within the name there is no Bodhisattva-mahāsattva; they are neither joined nor separated, being merely conventional designations.

Why is this? Because both the bodhisattva-mahāsattva and the name are empty of intrinsic nature; within the emptiness of intrinsic nature, neither the bodhisattva-mahāsattva nor the name exists and cannot be apprehended.
Śāriputra! For this reason, I say that a bodhisattva mahāsattva exists only as a mere designation.

“Śāriputra! Just as the names of all dharanī-doors are merely comprised of adventitious designations—coming from nowhere in the ten directions and three periods of time, going nowhere, and abiding nowhere; such that within all dharanī-doors there are no names, and within names there are no dharanī-doors; they are neither conjoined nor separated, being merely provisional designations.”

Why is this? Because all dharani-doors and their names are empty of intrinsic nature; within the emptiness of intrinsic nature, neither the dharani-doors nor the names exist and cannot be apprehended.

Just as the names of all samādhi-gates are comprised merely of adventitious designations, they come from nowhere in the ten directions and three periods of time, go nowhere, and abide nowhere; within all samādhi-gates there are no names, and within names there are no samādhi-gates. They are neither joined nor separated, being merely conventional designations.

Why is this? Because all gateways of samādhi, together with their names, are empty of intrinsic nature; and within the emptiness of intrinsic nature, neither the gateways of samādhi nor their names exist or can be apprehended.

The name of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is likewise so: it is comprised solely of adventitious designations; throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time, it comes from nowhere, goes nowhere, and abides nowhere. Within the bodhisattva-mahāsattva there is no name, and within the name there is no bodhisattva-mahāsattva; they are neither joined nor separated, being merely conventional designations.

Why is this? Because both the bodhisattva-mahāsattva and the name are empty of intrinsic nature; and within the emptiness of intrinsic nature, neither the bodhisattva-mahāsattva nor the name exists or can be apprehended.
Śāriputra! For this reason, I say that a bodhisattva mahāsattva exists only as a provisional designation.

“Śāriputra! Just as the name ‘inner emptiness’ is merely a provisional designation, it comes from nowhere in the ten directions or the three periods of time, goes nowhere, and has no place of abiding. Within inner emptiness there is no name, and within the name there is no inner emptiness; they are neither joined nor separated, but are merely conventionally established.”

Why is this? Because internal emptiness and the name are both empty of intrinsic nature; and within the emptiness of intrinsic nature, neither internal emptiness nor the name exists or can be apprehended.

Names such as outer emptiness, inner-and-outer emptiness, emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-altering emptiness, essential emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common-characteristic emptiness, emptiness of all phenomena, unapprehendable emptiness, emptiness of non-existence, emptiness of intrinsic nature, and emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence are subsumed under the category of mere names. They come from nowhere in the ten directions and three periods of time, go nowhere, and abide nowhere. Within the emptinesses from outer emptiness up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, there are no names; within names, there is no emptiness from outer emptiness up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence. They are neither conjoined nor separated, being merely provisional designations.

Why is this? Because from external emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, both these and names are empty of intrinsic nature; and within the emptiness of intrinsic nature, neither external emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature nor names exist and cannot be apprehended.

The name of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is likewise thus: it is comprised solely of adventitious designations; throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time, it comes from nowhere, goes nowhere, and abides nowhere. Within the bodhisattva mahāsattva there is no name, and within the name there is no bodhisattva mahāsattva. They are neither conjoined nor separate, being merely conventional designations.

Why is this? Because both the bodhisattva-mahāsattva and the name are empty of intrinsic nature; within the emptiness of intrinsic nature, neither the bodhisattva-mahāsattva nor the name exists, and neither can be apprehended.
Śāriputra! For this reason, I say that a bodhisattva mahāsattva exists only as a provisional designation.

“Śāriputra! Just as the name ‘tathatā’ (suchness) is merely a designation applied adventitiously, it comes from nowhere in the ten directions and three periods of time, goes nowhere, and abides nowhere. Within tathatā there is no name; within the name there is no tathatā. They are neither conjoined nor separated, being merely a conventional designation.”
Why is this? Because both suchness and names are empty of intrinsic nature; and within the emptiness of intrinsic nature, neither suchness nor names exist, being unapprehendable.

The Dharma-realm, the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the non-falsehood of phenomena, the unchanging nature, the inconceivable realm, the realm of space, the realm of cessation, the realm of detachment, the realm of extinction, equality, the nature of freedom from birth, the fixed nature of phenomena, the abiding of phenomena, the realm of non-existence, the realm of signlessness, the realm of non-action, the realm of the unconditioned, the realm of peace, the realm of tranquility, primordial non-being, the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), and ultimate *nirvāṇa*—these names are merely comprised of adventitious designations. They come from nowhere in the ten directions and three periods of time, they go nowhere, nor do they abide anywhere. Within the Dharma-realm up to ultimate *nirvāṇa*, there are no names; within names, there is no Dharma-realm up to ultimate *nirvāṇa*. They are neither joined nor separated, being merely provisional designations.

Why is this? Because from the dharma-realm up to ultimate nirvāṇa, together with names, they are all empty of intrinsic nature; and within the emptiness of intrinsic nature, neither the dharma-realm up to ultimate nirvāṇa nor names exist and cannot be apprehended.

The name "Bodhisattva-mahāsattva" is likewise thus: it is comprised solely of adventitious designations; throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time, it comes from nowhere, goes nowhere, and abides nowhere. Within the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva there is no name, and within the name there is no Bodhisattva-mahāsattva. It is neither joined nor separated, but is merely a conventional designation.

Why is this? Because both the bodhisattva-mahāsattva and the name are empty of intrinsic nature; and within the emptiness of intrinsic nature, neither the bodhisattva-mahāsattva nor the name exists or can be apprehended.
Śāriputra! For this reason, I say that a bodhisattva mahāsattva exists only as a provisional designation.

“Śāriputra! Just as the Ground of Supreme Joy is designated as being comprised of mere guests—it comes from nowhere in the ten directions or the three times, goes nowhere, and abides nowhere; within the Ground of Supreme Joy there is no name, and within the name there is no Ground of Supreme Joy; it is neither joined nor separated, but is merely a conventional designation.”

Why is this? Because the Stage of Extreme Joy and its name are both empty of intrinsic nature; within the emptiness of intrinsic nature, neither the Stage of Extreme Joy nor the name exists and cannot be apprehended.

The names of the stages—Vimalā, Prabhākārī, Arciṣmatī, Sudurjayā, Abhimukhī, Dūraṃgamā, Acalā, Sādhumatī, and Dharmameghā—are comprised merely as adventitious designations. They come from nowhere in the ten directions or the three periods of time, they go nowhere, nor do they abide anywhere. Within the stages from Vimalā up to Dharmameghā there is no name; within the name there is no stage from Vimalā up to Dharmameghā. They are neither conjoined nor separated, being merely conventional designations.

Why is this? Because from the Stainless Stage (*vimalā-bhūmi*) up to the Cloud of Dharma Stage (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*), both these stages and their names are empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnya*). Within the emptiness of intrinsic nature, neither the Stages from the Stainless up to the Cloud of Dharma nor their names exist or can be apprehended.

The name of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is likewise thus: it is comprised solely of adventitious designations; throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time, it comes from nowhere, goes nowhere, and abides nowhere. Within the bodhisattva-mahāsattva there is no name, and within the name there is no bodhisattva-mahāsattva; they are neither joined nor separated, being merely conventional designations.

Why is this? Because both the bodhisattva-mahāsattva and the name are empty of intrinsic nature; within the emptiness of intrinsic nature, neither the bodhisattva-mahāsattva nor the name exists, and neither can be apprehended.
Śāriputra! For this reason, I say that a bodhisattva mahāsattva exists only as a provisional designation.

“Śāriputra! Just as the stage of an ordinary person (pṛthagjanabhūmi) is designated as being merely a guest, it comes from nowhere in the ten directions and three periods of time, goes nowhere, and has no place of abiding. Within the stage of an ordinary person there is no name, and within the name there is no stage of an ordinary person; they are neither joined nor separated, but are merely conventional designations.”

Why is this? Because the stage of an ordinary person and its designation are both empty of intrinsic nature; within the emptiness of intrinsic nature, neither the stage of an ordinary person nor its designation exists or can be apprehended.

Just as the stage of the lineage (*gotrabhūmi*), the eighth stage, the stage of possessing vision, the stage of attenuation, the stage of freedom from desire, the stage of having completed what was to be done, the stage of the solitary realizer, the stage of the bodhisattva, and the stage of the Tathāgata are designated merely as adventitious, they come from nowhere in the ten directions and three periods of time, go nowhere, and abide nowhere; within these stages from the stage of the lineage up to the stage of the Tathāgata there is no name, and within the name there is no stage from the stage of the lineage up to the stage of the Tathāgata. They are neither joined nor separated, being merely conventional designations.

Why is this? Because the stage of the spiritual lineage (*gotrabhūmi*) up to the stage of the Tathāgata, together with their names, are empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnya*); and within the emptiness of intrinsic nature, neither the stage of the spiritual lineage up to the stage of the Tathāgata nor their names exist or can be apprehended.

The name "bodhisattva-mahāsattva" is likewise thus: it is comprised solely of adventitious designations; throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time, it comes from nowhere, goes nowhere, and abides nowhere. Within the bodhisattva-mahāsattva there is no name, and within the name there is no bodhisattva-mahāsattva; they are neither joined nor separated, but are merely conventional designations.

Why is this? Because both the bodhisattva-mahāsattva and the name are empty of intrinsic nature; within the emptiness of intrinsic nature, neither the bodhisattva-mahāsattva nor the name exists and cannot be apprehended.
Śāriputra! For this reason, I say that a bodhisattva-mahāsattva exists only as a mere designation.

“Śāriputra! Just as the name ‘Hearer Vehicle’ (śrāvakayāna) is merely a designation, it comes from nowhere in the ten directions or the three times, goes nowhere, and abides nowhere; within the Hearer Vehicle there is no name, and within the name there is no Hearer Vehicle. It is neither joined nor separated, but is merely a conventional designation.”

Why is this? Because the Śrāvaka vehicle and its name are both empty of intrinsic nature; within the emptiness of intrinsic nature, neither the Śrāvaka vehicle nor its name exists and cannot be apprehended.

Just as the names "Pratyekabuddhayāna" and "Mahāyāna" are merely comprised of adventitious designations—coming from nowhere in the ten directions or the three periods of time, going nowhere, and abiding nowhere; such that within the Pratyekabuddhayāna and Mahāyāna there are no names, and within the names there is no Pratyekabuddhayāna or Mahāyāna—they are neither conjoined nor separated, being merely provisional designations.

Why is this? Because the Pratyekabuddhayāna, the Mahāyāna, and their names are all empty of intrinsic nature; and within the emptiness of intrinsic nature, neither the Pratyekabuddhayāna, nor the Mahāyāna, nor their names exist or can be apprehended.

The name "Bodhisattva-mahāsattva" is likewise thus: it is comprised solely of adventitious designations. Throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time, it comes from nowhere, goes nowhere, and abides nowhere. Within the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva there is no name, and within the name there is no Bodhisattva-mahāsattva; they are neither joined nor separated, but are merely provisional designations.

Why is this? Because both the bodhisattva-mahāsattva and the name are empty of intrinsic nature; within the emptiness of intrinsic nature, neither the bodhisattva-mahāsattva nor the name exists and cannot be apprehended.
Śāriputra! For this reason, I say that a bodhisattva mahāsattva exists only as a mere designation.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti again replied to Śāriputra:
"As the Venerable has asked: 'For what reason is it said that we, as they are described, are ultimately unarisen?'"
"Śāriputra, since I am ultimately non-existent and cannot be apprehended, how could there be birth?

Sentient beings, life-principles, born beings, nourishers, persons, individuals, mind-born ones, youths, agents, instigators of action, originators, instigators of origination, experiencers, instigators of experience, knowers, and seers are ultimately non-existent and cannot be apprehended; how could there be birth?"
“Śāriputra! Form is ultimately non-existent; since it cannot be apprehended, how could it arise?
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are ultimately non-existent; since they cannot be apprehended, how could they arise?”
“Śāriputra! The sense-base of the eye is ultimately non-existent; since it cannot be apprehended, how could it arise?
The sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are ultimately non-existent; since they cannot be apprehended, how could they arise?”
“Śāriputra! The sphere of form is ultimately non-existent; since it cannot be apprehended, how could it arise?
The spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena are ultimately non-existent; since they cannot be apprehended, how could they arise?”
"Śāriputra! The eye-element is ultimately non-existent; since it cannot be apprehended, how could it arise?

The form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, eye-contact, and the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition are ultimately non-existent; since they cannot be apprehended, how could they arise?"
“Śāriputra! The ear element is ultimately non-existent; since it cannot be apprehended, how could it arise?

The sound element, the ear-consciousness element, ear-contact, and the various feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition are ultimately non-existent; since they cannot be apprehended, how could they arise?”
“Śāriputra! The nose element (*ghrāṇadhātu*) is ultimately non-existent; since it cannot be apprehended, how could it arise?

The odor element (*gandhadhātu*), the nose-consciousness element (*ghrāṇavijñānadhātu*), as well as nose-contact (*ghrāṇasamsparśa*) and the various feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition, are ultimately non-existent; since they cannot be apprehended, how could they arise?”
“Śāriputra! The tongue element is ultimately non-existent; since it cannot be apprehended, how could it arise?

The taste element, the tongue-consciousness element, tongue-contact, and all sensations produced with tongue-contact as a condition are ultimately non-existent; since they cannot be apprehended, how could they arise?”
“Śāriputra! The body element is ultimately non-existent; since it cannot be apprehended, how could it arise?

The tangible object element, the body-consciousness element, body-contact, and all sensations produced with body-contact as a condition are ultimately non-existent; since they cannot be apprehended, how could they arise?”
“Śāriputra! The mind-element (*manodhātu*) is ultimately non-existent; since it cannot be apprehended, how could it arise?

The dharma-element, the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*), as well as mental contact (*manaḥsaṃsparśa*) and the various feelings produced with mental contact as a condition, are ultimately non-existent; since they cannot be apprehended, how could they arise?”
“Śāriputra! The earth element is ultimately non-existent; since it cannot be apprehended, how could it arise?
The water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements are ultimately non-existent; since they cannot be apprehended, how could they arise?”
“Śāriputra! Ignorance is ultimately and entirely non-existent; since it cannot be apprehended, how could there be its arising?

Formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, sensation, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are ultimately and entirely non-existent; since they cannot be apprehended, how could there be their arising?”
“Śāriputra! Internal emptiness is ultimately and entirely non-existent; since it cannot be apprehended, how could it arise?

External emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, unchanging emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence are ultimately and entirely non-existent; since they cannot be apprehended, how could they arise?”
“Śāriputra! The perfection of generosity is ultimately non-existent; since it cannot be apprehended, how could it arise?
The perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom are ultimately non-existent; since they cannot be apprehended, how could they arise?”
“Śāriputra! The four dhyānas are ultimately non-existent; since they cannot be apprehended, how could they arise?
The four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions are ultimately non-existent; since they cannot be apprehended, how could they arise?”
“Śāriputra! The eight liberations are ultimately non-existent; since they cannot be apprehended, how could they arise?
The eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities are ultimately non-existent; since they cannot be apprehended, how could they arise?”
“Śāriputra! The four foundations of mindfulness are ultimately non-existent; since they cannot be apprehended, how could they arise?

The four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path are ultimately non-existent; since they cannot be apprehended, how could they arise?”
“Śāriputra! The gate of liberation of emptiness is ultimately non-existent; since it cannot be apprehended, how could it arise?
The gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness are ultimately non-existent; since they cannot be apprehended, how could they arise?”
“Śāriputra! The five eyes are ultimately non-existent; since they cannot be apprehended, how could they arise?
The six supernormal powers are ultimately non-existent; since they cannot be apprehended, how could they arise?”
“Śāriputra! The ten powers of a Buddha are ultimately non-existent; since they cannot be apprehended, how could they arise?

The four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are ultimately non-existent; since they cannot be apprehended, how could they arise?”
“Śāriputra! Omniscience (sarvajñatā) is ultimately non-existent; since it cannot be apprehended, how could it arise?
The knowledge of the paths (mārgākārajñatā) and the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā) are ultimately non-existent; since they cannot be apprehended, how could they arise?”
“Śāriputra! The quality of non-forgetfulness is ultimately and entirely non-existent; since it cannot be apprehended, how could it arise?
The nature of constant abiding in equanimity is ultimately and entirely non-existent; since it cannot be apprehended, how could it arise?”
“Śāriputra! All dharanī-doors ultimately do not exist at all; since they cannot be apprehended, how could they arise?
All samādhi-doors ultimately do not exist at all; since they cannot be apprehended, how could they arise?”
“Śāriputra! The Ground of Utmost Joy is ultimately non-existent; since it cannot be apprehended, how could it arise?

The Ground of Purity, the Ground of Radiance, the Ground of Blazing Wisdom, the Ground of Supreme Difficulty to Conquer, the Ground of Presence, the Ground of Far-Going, the Ground of Immovability, the Ground of Excellent Intelligence, and the Ground of the Dharma Cloud are all ultimately non-existent; since they cannot be apprehended, how could they arise?”
“Śāriputra! The stage of ordinary beings (pṛthagjanabhūmi) ultimately does not exist at all; since it cannot be apprehended, how could there be its arising?

The stage of the spiritual lineage (gotrabhūmi), the eighth stage (aṣṭamabhūmi), the stage of those who have seen the truth (darśanabhūmi), the stage of refinement (tanubhūmi), the stage of freedom from desire (vītarāgabhūmi), the stage of completion (kṛtāvibhūmi), the stage of the solitary realizer (pratyekabuddhabhūmi), the stage of the bodhisattva (bodhisattvabhūmi), and the stage of the Tathāgata (tathāgatabhūmi)—these ultimately do not exist at all; since they cannot be apprehended, how could there be their arising?”
“Śāriputra! The Śrāvaka-yāna ultimately and completely does not exist; since it cannot be apprehended, how could it arise?
The Pratyekabuddha-yāna and the Mahāyāna ultimately and completely do not exist; since they cannot be apprehended, how could they arise?”
“Śāriputra! For this reason, I say:
‘Just as it is said that we are ultimately unarisen.’”
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti again replied to Śāriputra:
"Regarding what the Venerable has said—
'For what reason do you say that all phenomena are likewise entirely without intrinsic nature?'— Śāriputra!"
All phenomena are entirely devoid of an inherent nature of combination.
Why is this? Because the inherent nature of any phenomenon that exists through combination is empty.
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"What dharma is entirely devoid of the nature of combination?
Subhūti replied:
"Śāriputra! Form has no inherent nature of aggregation; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness all have no inherent nature of aggregation. Śāriputra!"
“The sphere of the eye has no inherent nature of synthesis; the spheres of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind have no inherent nature of synthesis.
Śāriputra!...”
The sense base of form has no inherent nature of combination; the sense bases of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena likewise have no inherent nature of combination. "Śāriputra!

The eye-element has no self-nature of synthesis; the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, eye-contact, and all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition have no self-nature of synthesis.

“Śāriputra! The ear element has no inherent nature of combination; the sound element, the ear-consciousness element, ear-contact, and all feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition have no inherent nature of combination.”

“Śāriputra! The nose element has no inherent nature of combination whatsoever; the odor element, the nose-consciousness element, nose-contact, and all feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition have no inherent nature of combination whatsoever.”

“Śāriputra! The tongue element has no inherent nature of conjunction; the taste element, the tongue-consciousness element, tongue-contact, and all feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition have no inherent nature of conjunction.”

“Śāriputra! The body element has no inherent nature of combination whatsoever; the tangible object element, the body-consciousness element, body-contact, and all feelings produced with body-contact as a condition have no inherent nature of combination whatsoever.”

“Śāriputra! The mind-element has no inherent nature of combination whatsoever; the dharma-element, the mental-consciousness-element, as well as mental contact and the various feelings produced with mental contact as a condition, all lack an inherent nature of combination.”
“Śāriputra! The earth element has no inherent nature of combination; the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements likewise have no inherent nature of combination.”

“Śāriputra! Ignorance has no inherent nature of combination; likewise, volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, and old age, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair all lack an inherent nature of combination.”

“Śāriputra! Internal emptiness has no inherent nature of synthesis whatsoever. External emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common-characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence—all these have no inherent nature of synthesis whatsoever.”

“Śāriputra! The perfection of generosity has no inherent nature of composite aggregation; the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom likewise have no inherent nature of composite aggregation.”
“Śāriputra! The four dhyānas all lack an inherent nature of synthesis; the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments all lack an inherent nature of synthesis.”

“Śāriputra! The eight liberations have no inherent nature of combination; the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten totalities all lack an inherent nature of combination.”

“Śāriputra! The four foundations of mindfulness have no inherent nature of combination; the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path all lack an inherent nature of combination.”

“Śāriputra! The liberation door of emptiness has no inherent nature of conjunction whatsoever; the liberation doors of signlessness and wishlessness likewise have no inherent nature of conjunction whatsoever.”
“Śāriputra! The five eyes have no inherent nature of combination; the six supernormal powers have no inherent nature of combination. Śāriputra!”

The ten powers of a Buddha are entirely devoid of a composite self-nature; likewise, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are all entirely devoid of a composite self-nature.
“Śāriputra! All-knowledge has no inherent nature of synthesis; the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects have no inherent nature of synthesis.”
“Śāriputra! The quality of non-forgetfulness has no inherent nature of synthesis whatsoever; the quality of constant abiding in equanimity has no inherent nature of synthesis whatsoever. Śāriputra!”
All dharani-doors are entirely devoid of a composite intrinsic nature; all samadhi-doors are entirely devoid of a composite intrinsic nature. "Śāriputra!

The Stage of Utmost Joy has no inherent nature of synthesis; the Stages of the Stainless, the Luminous, the Radiant Wisdom, the Extremely Difficult to Conquer, the Manifest, the Far-Reaching, the Immovable, the Excellent Intelligence, and the Cloud of Dharma all lack any inherent nature of synthesis.

“Śāriputra! The stage of ordinary beings has no inherent nature of synthesis; likewise, the stage of the spiritual lineage, the eighth stage, the stage of possessing vision, the stage of refinement, the stage of freedom from desire, the stage of having accomplished what was to be done, the stage of the solitary realizer, the stage of the bodhisattva, and the stage of the Tathāgata all lack any inherent nature of synthesis.”
“Śāriputra! The Śrāvaka vehicle has no inherent nature of synthesis whatsoever; the Pratyekabuddha vehicle and the Mahāyāna likewise have no inherent nature of synthesis whatsoever. Śāriputra!”
For this reason, I say:
all phenomena are likewise entirely devoid of intrinsic nature.
Furthermore, Śāriputra:
All phenomena are neither permanent nor subject to dispersal.
Why is this? Because if a phenomenon were not permanent, it would lack the nature of inexhaustibility.
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"What dharma is neither impermanent nor subject to dispersal?
Subhūti replied:
“Śāriputra! Form is neither permanent nor subject to dispersion; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither permanent nor subject to dispersion. Śāriputra!”
The eye-base is impermanent and yet without dispersal; the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases are impermanent and yet without dispersal. "Śāriputra!

The sphere of form is neither permanent nor subject to dispersal; the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena are likewise neither permanent nor subject to dispersal. "Śāriputra!

The eye-element is neither permanent nor subject to dispersal; the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, eye-contact, and all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition are likewise neither permanent nor subject to dispersal.

“Śāriputra! The ear element is neither permanent nor subject to dispersal; the sound element, the ear-consciousness element, ear-contact, and all feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition are neither permanent nor subject to dispersal.”

“Śāriputra! The nose element is neither permanent nor subject to dispersion; the odor element, the nose-consciousness element, nose-contact, and all feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition are neither permanent nor subject to dispersion.”

“Śāriputra! The tongue element is impermanent and yet does not perish; the taste element, the tongue-consciousness element, tongue-contact, and all feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition are impermanent and yet do not perish.”

“Śāriputra! The body element (kāyadhātu) is neither permanent nor subject to dispersal; the touch element (spraṣṭavyadhātu), the body-consciousness element (kāyavijñānadhātu), body-contact (kāyasparśa), and all feelings (vedanā) arising conditioned by body-contact are neither permanent nor subject to dispersal.”

“Śāriputra! The mind-element (manodhātu) is neither permanent nor subject to dispersal; the dharma-element, the mind-consciousness-element, and the mental contact (manaḥsaṃsparśa), as well as all feelings produced with mental contact as a condition, are neither permanent nor subject to dispersal.”
“Śāriputra! The earth element is impermanent and yet does not perish; the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements are impermanent and yet do not perish.”

“Śāriputra! The noble truth of suffering is neither permanent nor subject to dispersion; the noble truths of origination, cessation, and the path are neither permanent nor subject to dispersion. Śāriputra!”

Ignorance is neither permanent nor subject to dispersion; likewise, volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, and old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are neither permanent nor subject to dispersion.

“Śāriputra! Internal emptiness is neither permanent nor subject to dispersal. External emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate truth, the emptiness of conditioned phenomena, the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, absolute emptiness, the emptiness of the limitless, the emptiness of dispersion, the emptiness of non-alteration, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the emptiness of specific characteristics, the emptiness of common characteristics, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature are neither permanent nor subject to dispersal.”

“Śāriputra! The perfection of generosity is neither permanent nor subject to dispersal; the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom are likewise neither permanent nor subject to dispersal.”
“Śāriputra! The four dhyānas are impermanent and yet are not lost; the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions are impermanent and yet are not lost.”

“Śāriputra! The eight liberations are neither permanent nor subject to dispersal; the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities are neither permanent nor subject to dispersal.”

“Śāriputra! The four foundations of mindfulness are neither permanent nor subject to loss; the four right endeavors, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path are neither permanent nor subject to loss.”

“Śāriputra! The gate of liberation of emptiness is neither permanent nor subject to dispersal; the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness are neither permanent nor subject to dispersal.”
“Śāriputra! The five eyes are impermanent and yet there is no loss; the six supernormal powers are impermanent and yet there is no loss. Śāriputra!”

The ten powers of a Buddha are neither impermanent nor subject to dispersal; likewise, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are neither impermanent nor subject to dispersal.

“Śāriputra! All-knowledge (sarvajñatā) is neither permanent nor subject to dispersal; the knowledge of the paths (mārgajñatā) and the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā) are neither permanent nor subject to dispersal.”
“Śāriputra! The quality of non-forgetfulness is neither permanent nor subject to dispersion; the state of constant dwelling in equanimity is neither permanent nor subject to dispersion. Śāriputra!”
"All dharanī-doors are neither permanent nor subject to dispersal; all samādhi-doors are neither permanent nor subject to dispersal. Śāriputra!"

The Ground of Utmost Joy is neither permanent nor subject to loss; the Ground of Purity, the Ground of Radiance, the Ground of Blazing Wisdom, the Ground of Difficult Victory, the Ground of Presence, the Ground of Far-Going, the Ground of Immovability, the Ground of Excellent Intelligence, and the Ground of the Dharma Cloud are likewise neither permanent nor subject to loss.

“Śāriputra! The stage of the ordinary person is neither permanent nor subject to dispersion; the stage of the lineage, the eighth stage, the stage of having seen the truths, the stage of refinement, the stage of freedom from desire, the stage of completion, the stage of the solitary buddha, the stage of the bodhisattva, and the stage of the Tathāgata are likewise neither permanent nor subject to dispersion.”
"Śāriputra! The Śrāvaka vehicle is neither permanent nor subject to dispersal; the Pratyekabuddha vehicle and the Mahāyāna are likewise neither permanent nor subject to dispersal. Śāriputra!"
For this reason, I say:
all phenomena are likewise entirely devoid of intrinsic nature.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
All phenomena are neither pleasant nor subject to dispersal.
Why is this? Because if a phenomenon is not pleasant, it lacks the nature of exhaustion.

“Śāriputra! The nose element is neither pleasure nor subject to dispersal; the odor element, the nose-consciousness element, nose-contact, and all feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition are neither pleasure nor subject to dispersal.”

“Śāriputra! The tongue element is neither pleasure nor subject to dispersal; the taste element, the tongue-consciousness element, tongue-contact, and all feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition are neither pleasure nor subject to dispersal.”

“Śāriputra! The body element is neither pleasant nor subject to dispersal; the tangible object element, the body-consciousness element, as well as body-contact and the various feelings produced with body-contact as a condition, are neither pleasant nor subject to dispersal.”

“Śāriputra! The earth element is neither pleasure nor subject to dispersion; the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements are neither pleasure nor subject to dispersion.”

“Śāriputra! all phenomena are likewise entirely devoid of intrinsic nature.

At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:

“Śāriputra! The four foundations of mindfulness transcend the world and are never lost; the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path also transcend the world and are never lost.”
“Śāriputra! The gate of liberation of emptiness transcends the world and is without loss; the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness also transcend the world and are without loss.”
“Śāriputra! The five eyes that transcend the world are likewise never lost; the six supernormal powers that transcend the world are likewise never lost. Śāriputra!”

The ten powers of a Buddha transcend the world and are without dispersal; the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha transcend the world and are without dispersal.
“Śāriputra! Omniscience transcends the world and is without loss; the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects transcend the world and are likewise without loss.”
“Śāriputra! The quality of non-forgetfulness is supramundane and is never lost; the state of constant abiding in equanimity is supramundane and is never lost. Śāriputra!”
"All the gateways of dhāraṇī that transcend the world are likewise without loss or dispersal; all the gateways of samādhi that transcend the world are likewise without loss or dispersal. Śāriputra!"

The supramundane nature of the Ground of Utmost Joy is also without loss; likewise, the supramundane natures of the Ground of Purity, the Ground of Radiance, the Ground of Blazing Wisdom, the Ground of Extreme Difficulty to Conquer, the Ground of Manifestation, the Ground of Far-Going, the Ground of Immovability, the Ground of Excellent Intelligence, and the Ground of the Cloud of Dharma are also without loss.

“Śāriputra! The stage of the ordinary person transcends the world and is without loss; likewise, the stage of the lineage, the eighth stage, the stage of having seen the truths, the stage of refinement, the stage of freedom from desire, the stage of completion, the stage of the solitary realizer, the stage of the bodhisattva, and the stage of the Tathāgata transcend the world and are without loss.”
“Śāriputra! The supramundane Śrāvakayāna is likewise without loss; the Pratyekabuddhayāna and the Mahāyāna that transcend the world are also without loss.”
“Śāriputra! For this reason, I say:
all phenomena are likewise entirely devoid of intrinsic nature.”
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
all phenomena are unconditioned and do not perish. Why is this?
"If a dharma is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it is because its nature is inexhaustible.
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"What dharma is unconditioned and also without dispersal?"
Subhūti replied, “Śāriputra!
Form is unconditioned and thus without loss; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also unconditioned and without loss.”
“Śāriputra! The sphere of the eye is unconditioned and without loss; the spheres of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are also unconditioned and without loss.”
“Śāriputra! The sphere of form is unconditioned and without loss; the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena are also unconditioned and without loss.”

“Śāriputra! The eye-element is unconditioned and without loss; the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, eye-contact, and all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition are also unconditioned and without loss.”

“Śāriputra! The ear element is unconditioned and without dispersal; the sound element, the ear-consciousness element, as well as ear-contact and the various sensations produced with ear-contact as a condition, are also unconditioned and without dispersal.”

“Śāriputra! The nose element is unconditioned and without dispersal; the odor element, the nose-consciousness element, nose-contact, and all feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition are also unconditioned and without dispersal.”

“Śāriputra! The tongue element is unconditioned and without dispersal; the taste element, the tongue-consciousness element, tongue-contact, and all feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition are also unconditioned and without dispersal.”

“Śāriputra! The body element is unconditioned and without dispersal; the tangible object element, the body-consciousness element, body-contact, and all feelings produced with body-contact as a condition are unconditioned and without dispersal.”

“Śāriputra! The mind-element (manodhātu) is unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) and without loss; the dharma-element (dharmadhātu), the mind-consciousness-element (manovijñānadhātu), as well as mind-contact (manaḥsaṃsparśa) and the various feelings (vedanā) arising with mind-contact as condition, are also unconditioned and without loss.”
“Śāriputra! The element of earth is unconditioned and does not disperse; the elements of water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness are also unconditioned and do not disperse.”
“Śāriputra, the noble truth of suffering is unconditioned and does not perish; the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path are unconditioned and do not perish.
Śāriputra, [it is thus.]”

Ignorance is unconditioned and does not perish; likewise, volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, and old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are unconditioned and do not perish.

“Śāriputra! The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) of internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*) is also without dispersal; the unconditioned of external emptiness (*bahirdhā-śūnyatā*), internal-and-external emptiness (*adhyātma-bahirdhā-śūnyatā*), emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*), great emptiness (*mahā-śūnyatā*), emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), emptiness of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-śūnyatā*), emptiness of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*), absolute emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*), emptiness of the limitless (*anavara-agra-śūnyatā*), emptiness of dispersion (*anavakāra-śūnyatā*), emptiness of non-alteration (*anavakāra-śūnyatā*), emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*), emptiness of self-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*), emptiness of common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*), emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*), emptiness of the unapprehendable (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*), emptiness of non-existence (*abhāva-śūnyatā*), emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*), and emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence (*abhāvasvabhāva-śūnyatā*) is also without dispersal.”

“Śāriputra! The perfection of generosity is unconditioned and without loss; the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom are also unconditioned and without loss.”
“Śāriputra! The unconditioned nature of the four dhyānas is also without loss; the unconditioned nature of the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions is also without loss.”

“Śāriputra! The eight liberations are unconditioned and without loss; the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten universal bases are unconditioned and without loss.”

“Śāriputra! The four foundations of mindfulness are unconditioned and do not perish; the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold noble path are also unconditioned and do not perish.”
“Śāriputra! The gate of liberation of emptiness is unconditioned and without loss; the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness are also unconditioned and without loss.”
“Śāriputra! The five eyes are unconditioned and without loss; the six supernormal powers are unconditioned and without loss. Śāriputra!”

The ten powers of a Buddha are unconditioned and without loss; the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are unconditioned and without loss.

“Śāriputra! All-knowledge (sarvajñatā) is unconditioned and does not perish; the knowledge of the aspects of the path (mārgākārajñatā) and the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā) are also unconditioned and do not perish.”
“Śāriputra! The quality of non-forgetfulness is unconditioned and without loss; the state of constant abiding in equanimity is unconditioned and without loss. Śāriputra!”
"All dhāraṇī-doors are unconditioned and without loss; all samādhi-doors are unconditioned and without loss. Śāriputra!"

The unconditioned nature of the Ground of Utmost Joy is also without loss; likewise, the unconditioned nature of the Ground of Purity, the Ground of Radiant Light, the Ground of Blazing Wisdom, the Ground of Extreme Difficulty to Conquer, the Ground of Manifestation, the Ground of Far-Going, the Ground of Immovability, the Ground of Excellent Intelligence, and the Ground of the Cloud of Dharma is also without loss.

“Śāriputra! The unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) of the stage of ordinary beings is also without loss; the unconditioned of the stage of the spiritual lineage, the eighth stage, the stage of possessing vision, the stage of refinement, the stage of freedom from desire, the stage of having completed what was to be done, the stage of the pratyekabuddha, the stage of the bodhisattva, and the stage of the Tathāgata are also without loss.”
“Śāriputra! The unconditioned of the Śrāvaka vehicle is also without loss; the unconditioned of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle and the Great Vehicle is likewise without loss. Śāriputra!”
For this reason, I say:
all phenomena are likewise entirely devoid of intrinsic nature.
Furthermore, Śāriputra:
"All phenomena are neither permanent nor subject to destruction.
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"In what way are all phenomena neither permanent nor subject to destruction?"
Subhūti replied:
"Śāriputra, form is neither permanent nor subject to destruction."
Why is this? Because such is their intrinsic nature.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither permanent nor subject to destruction.
Why is this? Because such is their intrinsic nature. "Śāriputra!
The eye-base is neither permanent nor subject to destruction. Why is this?
Because such is its intrinsic nature.
The spheres of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are neither permanent nor subject to destruction.
Why is this? Because such is their intrinsic nature.
“Śāriputra, the sphere of form is neither permanent nor subject to destruction. Why is this?
Because it is its very nature:
the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena are neither permanent nor subject to destruction. Why is this?
Because such is its intrinsic nature.
"Śāriputra, the eye-element is neither permanent nor subject to destruction."
Why is this? Because such is their intrinsic nature.
The form element, the eye-consciousness element, eye-contact, and all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition are neither permanent nor subject to destruction.
Why is this? Because such is their intrinsic nature. "Śāriputra!
The ear-element is neither permanent nor subject to destruction. Why?
Because such is its intrinsic nature.
The sphere of sound, the sphere of auditory consciousness, and ear-contact, as well as all feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition, are neither permanent nor subject to destruction.
Why is this? Because such is their intrinsic nature.
“Śāriputra, the nose-element is neither permanent nor subject to destruction. Why is this?
Because such is their intrinsic nature.

The fragrance element, the nose-consciousness element, and nose-contact, as well as all feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition, are neither permanent nor subject to destruction. Why is this?
Because such is its intrinsic nature.
"Śāriputra, the tongue element is neither permanent nor subject to destruction."
Why is this? Because such is their intrinsic nature.
The taste element, the tongue-consciousness element, and tongue-contact, as well as all sensations produced with tongue-contact as a condition, are neither permanent nor subject to destruction.
Why is this? Because such is their intrinsic nature. "Śāriputra!
The body-element is neither permanent nor subject to destruction. Why?
Because such is its intrinsic nature.
The element of tangibles, the element of body-consciousness, body-contact, and all feelings produced with body-contact as a condition are neither permanent nor subject to destruction.
Why is this? Because such is their intrinsic nature.
“Śāriputra, the mind-element (manodhātu) is neither eternal nor subject to destruction. Why is this?
Because it is its very nature.

The dharma-element, the mind-consciousness-element, and mental contact, as well as all feelings produced with mental contact as a condition, are neither permanent nor subject to destruction. Why is this?
Because such is its intrinsic nature.
"Śāriputra, the earth element is neither permanent nor subject to destruction."
Why is this? Because such is their intrinsic nature.
The elements of water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness are neither permanent nor subject to destruction.
Why is this? Because such is their intrinsic nature. "Śāriputra!
The noble truth of suffering is neither permanent nor subject to destruction. Why is this?
Because such is its intrinsic nature.
The noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path are neither permanent nor subject to destruction. Why?
Because such is their intrinsic nature.
“Śāriputra, ignorance is neither permanent nor subject to destruction. Why is this?
Because it is their very nature, volitional formations,

consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, and old age, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are neither permanent nor subject to destruction.
Why is this? Because such is their intrinsic nature. "Śāriputra!
Internal emptiness is neither permanent nor subject to destruction. Why?
Because such is its intrinsic nature.

External emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate truth, the emptiness of conditioned phenomena, the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, absolute emptiness, the emptiness of the limitless, the emptiness of dispersion, the emptiness of non-alteration, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the emptiness of specific characteristics, the emptiness of common characteristics, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence are neither permanent nor subject to destruction.
Why is this? Because such is their intrinsic nature, Śāriputra!
The perfection of generosity is neither permanent nor subject to destruction.
Why? Because its intrinsic nature is such.
The perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom are neither permanent nor subject to destruction.
Why is this? Because such is their intrinsic nature.
“Śāriputra! The four dhyānas are neither permanent nor subject to destruction. Why is this?
Because such is their intrinsic nature.
The four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions are neither permanent nor subject to destruction. Why is this?
Because such is their intrinsic nature. "Śāriputra,
the eight liberations are neither permanent nor subject to destruction."
Why is this? Because such is their intrinsic nature.
The eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten universal bases are neither permanent nor subject to destruction.
Why is this? Because such is its intrinsic nature. "Śāriputra!
The four foundations of mindfulness are neither permanent nor subject to destruction. Why?
Because such is their intrinsic nature.

The four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path are neither permanent nor subject to destruction. Why is this?
Because such is its intrinsic nature.
"Śāriputra, the gate of liberation that is emptiness is neither permanent nor subject to destruction."
Why is this? Because such is their intrinsic nature.
The gateways of liberation—signlessness and wishlessness—are neither permanent nor subject to destruction.
Why is this? Because such is their intrinsic nature. "Śāriputra!
The five eyes are neither permanent nor subject to destruction. Why is this?
Because such is their intrinsic nature.
The six supernormal powers are neither permanent nor subject to destruction. Why is this?
Because such is their intrinsic nature.
“Śāriputra! The ten powers of the Buddha are neither permanent nor subject to destruction. Why is this?
Because it is their very nature,

the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are neither permanent nor subject to destruction.
Why is this? Because such is their intrinsic nature. "Śāriputra!
All-knowledge is neither permanent nor subject to destruction. Why?
Because its intrinsic nature is such.
The knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects are neither eternal nor subject to destruction. Why is this?
Because such is their intrinsic nature.
“Śāriputra! The quality of non-forgetfulness is neither permanent nor subject to destruction. Why is this?
Because it is of such an inherent nature,
the state of constant dwelling in equanimity is neither permanent nor subject to destruction. Why is this?
Because such is their intrinsic nature. "Śāriputra,
all dhāraṇī-doors are neither permanent nor subject to destruction."
Why is this? Because such is their intrinsic nature.
All gateways of samādhi are neither permanent nor subject to destruction.
Why is this? Because such is their intrinsic nature.
"Śāriputra!..."
The Ground of Supreme Joy is neither permanent nor subject to destruction. Why?
Because its intrinsic nature is such.

The Ground of Freedom from Defilement, the Ground of Radiant Light, the Ground of Blazing Wisdom, the Ground of Utmost Difficulty to Conquer, the Ground of Manifestation, the Ground of Far-reaching Travel, the Ground of Immovability, the Ground of Excellent Intelligence, and the Ground of the Dharma-Cloud are neither permanent nor subject to destruction.
Why is this? Because such is their intrinsic nature. "Śāriputra!
The stage of the ordinary person is neither permanent nor subject to destruction. Why?
Because its intrinsic nature is such.

The stage of the spiritual lineage, the eighth stage, the stage of possessing vision, the stage of refinement, the stage of freedom from desire, the stage of having completed what was to be done, the stage of the solitary realizer, the stage of the bodhisattva, and the stage of the Tathāgata are neither permanent nor subject to destruction.
Why is this? Because such is its intrinsic nature. "Śāriputra!
The Śrāvaka vehicle is neither permanent nor subject to destruction. Why is this?
Because its intrinsic nature is such.
The Pratyekabuddhayāna and the Mahāyāna are neither permanent nor subject to destruction. Why?
Because such is their intrinsic nature.
"Śāriputra! To speak in brief, all wholesome dharmas are neither permanent nor subject to destruction. Why is this?
Because such is their intrinsic nature (*dharmatā*).
All non-virtuous phenomena are neither permanent nor subject to destruction. Why is this?
Because it is their very nature.
All dharmas that are determinate are neither eternal nor subject to destruction. Why is this?
Because it is their very nature:
all indeterminate phenomena (avyākṛta-dharma) are neither permanent nor subject to destruction. Why is this?
Because such is their intrinsic nature.
All contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*) are neither permanent nor subject to destruction. Why is this?
Because such is their intrinsic nature.
All untainted phenomena (anāsrava-dharma) are neither permanent nor subject to destruction. Why is this?
Because it is their very nature:
all conditioned phenomena are neither permanent nor subject to destruction. Why is this?
Because it is its very nature:
all unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*) are neither permanent nor subject to destruction. Why is this?
Because it is its very nature, Śāriputra!
For this reason, I have made this statement:
"All phenomena are likewise; they are entirely devoid of intrinsic nature.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti again replied to Śāriputra:
"As the Venerable One has asked, 'For what reason is it said that form and all other phenomena are ultimately unarisen?'"
"Śāriputra, the intrinsic nature of form is ultimately unarisen. Why is this? Because..."
Because they are not created.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are by their very nature ultimately unarisen. Why is this?
Because it is not something produced. Why is this?
Because an agent of form, up to and including consciousness, cannot be apprehended.
“Śāriputra! The essential nature of the eye-base is ultimately unarisen. Why is this?
Because they are not produced.
The essential nature of the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind is ultimately non-arising. Why is this?
Because they are not produced. Why is this?
Because an agent cannot be found for the sense base of the eye, up to and including the sense base of the mind.
“Śāriputra! The intrinsic nature of the sphere of form is ultimately non-arising. Why is this?
Because they are not produced.
The spheres of sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena are by their very nature ultimately unarisen. Why is this?
Because it is not something produced. Why is this?
Because within the sense bases from form (rūpāyatana) up to mental objects (dharmāyatana), an agent cannot be found.
"Śāriputra! The intrinsic nature of the eye-element is ultimately non-arising. Why is this?
Because they are not produced:
the form element, the eye-consciousness element, eye-contact, and all feelings arisen with eye-contact as a condition are by their very nature ultimately non-arising.
Why is this? Because it is not something produced. For what reason?
Because an agent cannot be found for the various feelings produced with the eye-element, up to and including those produced with eye-contact as condition.
"Śāriputra! The intrinsic nature of the ear-element is ultimately unarisen."
Why is this? Because they are not produced.
The sphere of sound, the sphere of ear-consciousness, ear-contact, and all sensations born with ear-contact as a condition are, by their very nature, ultimately non-arising.
Why is this? Because it is not something produced. For what reason?
Because an agent cannot be found for the various feelings produced with the ear-element, up to and including those produced with ear-contact as a condition.
"Śāriputra, the intrinsic nature of the nose-element is ultimately non-arising."
Why is this? Because they are not produced.
The fragrance-element, the nose-consciousness-element, nose-contact, and all sensations produced with nose-contact as a condition are, by their very nature, ultimately non-arising.
Why is this? Because it is not something produced. For what reason?
Because an agent cannot be found for the various feelings produced with the nose element, up to and including those produced with nose-contact as a condition.
"Śāriputra, the intrinsic nature of the tongue element is ultimately non-arising."
Why is this? Because they are not produced.
The taste element, the tongue-consciousness element, tongue-contact, and all sensations arising with tongue-contact as a condition are, by their very nature, ultimately non-arising.
Why is this? Because it is not something produced. Why is that so?
Because an agent cannot be found for the various feelings produced with the tongue element and even up to tongue-contact as conditions.
"Śāriputra, the intrinsic nature of the body element is ultimately unarisen."
Why is this? Because it is not something produced.
The element of tangibles, the element of body-consciousness, body-contact, and all sensations arising with body-contact as a condition are by their very nature ultimately non-arising.
Why is this? Because it is not something produced. For what reason?
Because an agent cannot be found for the various feelings produced with the body-element and even up to body-contact as conditions.
"Śāriputra! The intrinsic nature of the mind-element is ultimately unarisen."
Why is this? Because they are not produced.
The dharma-element, the mental-consciousness-element, as well as mental contact and the various feelings produced with mental contact as a condition, are by their very nature ultimately non-arising.
Why is this? Because it is not something produced. Why is that so?
Because an agent cannot be found for the various feelings produced with the mind-element and so forth, up to those produced with mind-contact as condition.
"Śāriputra, the intrinsic nature of the earth element is ultimately unarisen."
Why is this? Because they are not created.
The intrinsic natures of the elements of water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness are ultimately unarisen.
Why is this? Because it is not something produced. Why is that so?
Because an agent cannot be found within the element of earth up to the element of consciousness.
"Śāriputra, the intrinsic nature of the noble truth of suffering is ultimately non-arising."
Why is this? Because they are not produced.
The intrinsic nature of the noble truths of origination, cessation, and the path is ultimately non-arising.
Why is this? Because it is not something produced. Why is that so?
Because an agent cannot be found in the noble truth of suffering, up to and including the noble truth of the path.
"Śāriputra, the intrinsic nature of ignorance is ultimately unarisen."
Why is this? Because they are not created.

The intrinsic nature (*prakṛti*) of volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, becoming, birth, and old age, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair is ultimately non-arising.
Why is this? Because it is not something produced. For what reason?
Because an agent for [the links] from ignorance through old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair cannot be found. "Śāriputra,
the intrinsic nature of internal emptiness is ultimately unarisen."
Why is this? Because it is not something produced.

External emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, endless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-altering emptiness, essential emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common-characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence—these are by their very nature ultimately unarisen.
Why is this? Because it is not something produced. For what reason?
Because an agent cannot be apprehended within the emptiness of the internal up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature. "Śāriputra,
the essential nature of the perfection of generosity is ultimately unarisen."
Why is this? Because they are not produced.
The intrinsic nature of the perfections of pure ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom is ultimately non-arising.
Why is this? Because it is not something created. For what reason?
Because an agent cannot be found for the perfection of generosity up to and including the perfection of wisdom.
"Śāriputra, the four dhyānas are by their very nature ultimately unarisen."
Why is this? Because they are not produced.
The four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions are by their very nature ultimately unarisen.
Why is this? Because it is not something produced. Why is that so?
Because an agent cannot be found in the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments. "Śāriputra,
the intrinsic nature of the eight liberations is ultimately non-arising."
Why is this? Because they are not produced.
The eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities are by their very nature ultimately non-arising.
Why is this? Because it is not something produced. For what reason?
Because an agent cannot be found in the eight liberations up to the ten spheres of totality.
"Śāriputra, the intrinsic nature of the four foundations of mindfulness is ultimately unarisen."
Why is this? Because they are not produced.
The four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path are by their very nature ultimately unarisen.
Why is this? Because it is not something produced. For what reason?
Because an agent cannot be found within the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path.
"Śāriputra, the intrinsic nature of the gate of liberation through emptiness is ultimately non-arising."
Why is this? Because it is not something produced.
The intrinsic nature of the gates of liberation—signlessness and wishlessness—is ultimately non-arising.
Why is this? Because it is not something produced. Why is that so?
This is because an agent cannot be apprehended within the gate of liberation of emptiness, the gate of liberation of signlessness, or the gate of liberation of wishlessness. "Śāriputra,
the intrinsic nature of the five eyes is ultimately non-arising."
Why is this? Because they are not produced.
The six supernormal powers are ultimately unarisen by their very nature.
Why is this? Because it is not something produced. For what reason?
Because an agent cannot be apprehended by means of the five eyes or the six supernormal powers.
"Śāriputra, the intrinsic nature of the Buddha’s ten powers is ultimately unarisen."
Why is this? Because they are not produced.

The four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are, by their very nature, ultimately non-arising.
Why is this? Because it is not something produced. For what reason?
Because an agent cannot be apprehended in the ten powers of a Buddha, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
"Śāriputra, the intrinsic nature of all-knowledge is ultimately unarisen."
Why is this? Because it is not something produced.
The nature of the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects is ultimately non-arising.
Why is this? Because it is not something produced. For what reason?
Because an agent cannot be apprehended in omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgākārajñatā*), or the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
"Śāriputra, the nature of the quality of non-forgetfulness (*asaṃpramoṣadharma*) is ultimately unborn."
Why is this? Because it is not something produced.
The nature of constant abiding in equanimity is ultimately non-arising by its very essence.
Why is this? Because it is not something produced. For what reason?
Because an agent cannot be found in the quality of non-forgetfulness or the state of constant equanimity.
"Śāriputra, the intrinsic nature of all dhāraṇī-doors is ultimately unarisen."
Why is this? Because they are not produced.
The intrinsic nature of all gateways to samādhi is ultimately non-arising.
Why is this? Because it is not something produced. For what reason?
Because an agent for all the gateways of dhāraṇī and all the gateways of samādhi cannot be apprehended.
"Śāriputra, the fundamental nature of the Stage of Utmost Joy is ultimately non-arising."
Why is this? Because they are not produced.

The Stainless Ground, the Radiant Ground, the Ground of Blazing Wisdom, the Ground of Supreme Difficulty to Conquer, the Ground of Presence, the Ground of Far-Going, the Immovable Ground, the Ground of Excellent Intelligence, and the Ground of the Dharma Cloud are by their very nature ultimately non-arising.
Why is this? Because it is not something produced. For what reason?
Because an agent—from the Stage of Utmost Joy up to the Stage of the Cloud of Dharma—cannot be apprehended.
"Śāriputra! The fundamental nature of the stage of ordinary beings is ultimately non-arising."
Why is this? Because they are not produced.

The stage of the spiritual lineage (*gotrabhūmi*), the eighth stage, the stage of possessing vision (*darśanabhūmi*), the stage of refinement (*tanubhūmi*), the stage of freedom from desire (*vītarāgabhūmi*), the stage of completion (*kṛtāvibhūmi*), the stage of the solitary realizer (*pratyekabuddhabhūmi*), the stage of the bodhisattva (*bodhisattvabhūmi*), and the stage of the Tathāgata (*tathāgatabhūmi*)—the intrinsic nature of these is ultimately non-arising.
Why is this? Because it is not something created. For what reason?
Because an agent cannot be found from the stage of an ordinary person up to the stage of a Tathāgata.
"Śāriputra! The intrinsic nature of the Śrāvaka vehicle is ultimately non-arising."
Why is this? Because they are not produced.
The nature of the Pratyekabuddhayāna and the Mahāyāna is ultimately non-arising.
Why is this? Because it is not something produced. For what reason?
Because an agent of the Śrāvaka vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, or the Mahāyāna cannot be apprehended. "Śāriputra,
for this reason I say this:..."
"Form and all other phenomena are ultimately unarisen.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti replied again to Śāriputra:
"As the Venerable One has said, 'For what reason is it said that if something is ultimately unarisen, it is not called form and so forth?'"
"Thus it is, Śāriputra! Thus it is!"
If there is ultimate non-arising, then it is not designated as form and so forth.
Why is this? Śāriputra!
Because the intrinsic nature of form is empty, if a dharma is empty by its intrinsic nature, then it cannot be designated as arising, ceasing, abiding, or changing.
For this reason, that which is ultimately unarisen is not called "form."

Śāriputra, because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty of intrinsic nature, if a phenomenon is empty of intrinsic nature, it cannot be designated as arising, ceasing, abiding, or changing.
For this reason, if there is ultimately no arising, then it is not designated as feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. "Śāriputra,
because the sense base of the eye is empty of intrinsic nature, if a phenomenon is empty of intrinsic nature, then it cannot be designated as arising, ceasing, abiding, or changing."
For this reason, if there were ultimately no arising, it would not be designated as the "eye-base" (*cakṣur-āyatana*).

Śāriputra, because the intrinsic nature of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind bases is empty, if a phenomenon is empty of intrinsic nature, then it cannot be designated as arising, ceasing, abiding, or changing.
For this reason, if there is ultimate non-arising, they are not designated as the sense bases of ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind. Śāriputra,
because the sense base of form is empty of intrinsic nature, if a dharma is empty of intrinsic nature, it cannot be established as arising, ceasing, abiding, or changing.
For this reason, if there is ultimately no arising, it is not designated as the sense base of form (*rūpāyatana*).

Śāriputra, because the sense bases of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) are empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnya*), if a phenomenon is empty of intrinsic nature, then it cannot be designated as arising, ceasing, abiding, or changing.
For this reason, if there is ultimate non-arising, then it is not designated as the sense bases of sound, odor, taste, touch, or mental phenomena. "Śāriputra,
because the nature of the eye-faculty is empty, if a phenomenon is empty by its very nature, then it cannot be established as arising, ceasing, abiding, or changing."
For this reason, if there is ultimate non-arising, it is not designated as the "eye-element. Śāriputra, because the form-element,

the eye-consciousness-element, eye-contact, and all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition are empty of intrinsic nature, if a dharma is empty of intrinsic nature, it cannot be designated as arising, ceasing, abiding, or changing.
For this reason, if there is ultimate non-arising, it is not termed the form realm, nor even the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition. "Śāriputra!
Because the nature of the ear-element (*śrotradhātu*) is empty, if a phenomenon is empty by nature, it cannot be designated as arising, ceasing, abiding, or changing.
For this reason, that which is ultimately unarisen is not called the "ear-element."
Śāriputra!

Because the element of sound, the element of ear-consciousness, auditory contact, and all feelings produced with auditory contact as a condition are empty of intrinsic nature, if a phenomenon is empty of intrinsic nature, it cannot be designated as arising, ceasing, abiding, or changing.
For this reason, if there is ultimately no arising, it is not termed the sound element, nor the various feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition. "Śāriputra!
Because the nose element (*ghrāṇadhātu*) is empty of intrinsic nature, and because a phenomenon that is empty of intrinsic nature cannot be designated as arising, ceasing, abiding,
or changing— for this reason, that which is ultimately non-arising is not called the "nose element."

Śāriputra! Because the fragrance element, the nose-consciousness element, nose-contact, and all sensations produced with nose-contact as a condition are empty of intrinsic nature, and because if a phenomenon is empty of intrinsic nature, it cannot be designated as arising, ceasing, abiding, or changing.
For this reason, if there is ultimate non-arising, it is not called the fragrance element, nor the various feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition. "Śāriputra!
Because the tongue-element (*jihvā-dhātu*) is empty of intrinsic nature, and if a phenomenon is empty of intrinsic nature, it cannot be designated as arising, ceasing, abiding, or changing.
For this reason, that which is ultimately non-arising is not called the "tongue-element."
Śāriputra!

Because the taste element, the tongue-consciousness element, tongue-contact, and all feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition are empty of intrinsic nature, if a phenomenon is empty of intrinsic nature, it cannot be designated as arising, ceasing, abiding, or changing.
For this reason, if there is ultimately no arising, it is not designated as the taste element, nor even as the various feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition. "Śāriputra!
Because the nature of the body-element (*kāyadhātu*) is empty, if a phenomenon is empty of intrinsic nature, it cannot be designated as arising, ceasing, abiding, or changing.
For this reason, that which is ultimately unarisen is not called the "body-element."
Śāriputra!

Because the element of tangibles, the element of body-consciousness, body-contact, and all sensations produced with body-contact as a condition are empty of intrinsic nature, if a phenomenon is empty of intrinsic nature, it cannot be designated as arising, ceasing, abiding, or changing.
For this reason, if there is ultimately no arising, it is not termed the "element of contact" (spraṣṭavyadhātu), nor even the various feelings produced with body-contact as a condition.
"Śāriputra!..."
Because the nature of the mind-element (*manodhātu*) is empty, if a phenomenon is empty by nature, it cannot be designated as arising, ceasing, abiding, or changing.
