For what reason does a non-returner, for the sake of the fruit of non-returning, cultivate the path that abandons the five lower fetters?
For what reason does an arhat, for the sake of the fruit of arhatship, cultivate the path that abandons the five fetters pertaining to the higher realms?
For what reason does a pratyekabuddha, for the sake of pratyekabuddha-enlightenment, cultivate the path that realizes dependent origination?

For what reason do Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, for the sake of liberating immeasurable sentient beings, cultivate hundreds of thousands of difficult and painful practices and undergo boundless varieties of intense suffering?
"For what reason has the Tathāgata realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
For what reason do the Buddhas turn the sublime wheel of Dharma for the sake of sentient beings?
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti replied to Śāriputra:

“I do not perceive, within the dharma of non-arising, any differentiation of rebirth among the six destinies; I do not perceive, within the dharma of non-arising, anyone who enters the clear realization of the truths; I do not perceive, within the dharma of non-arising, anyone who attains the fruit of a stream-enterer, a once-returner, a non-returner, or an arhat; I do not perceive, within the dharma of non-arising, anyone who attains the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; nor do I perceive, within the dharma of non-arising, any bodhisattva mahāsattva who attains the knowledge of all aspects or the five kinds of enlightenment.”
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
it is not that within the dharma of non-arising I perceive a stream-enterer as having attained the fruit of stream-entry through the path of abandoning the three fetters;
nor is it that within the dharma of non-arising I perceive a once-returner as having attained the fruit of once-returning through the path of attenuating greed, hatred, and delusion."
It is not that, within the dharma of non-arising, I perceive a non-returner as being for the fruit of non-returning, and thus cultivate the path to sever the five lower fetters;
nor is it that, within the dharma of non-arising, I perceive an arhat as being for the fruit of arhatship, and thus cultivate the path to sever the five higher fetters.
It is not that I perceive within the dharma of non-arising any pratyekabuddha who, for the sake of pratyekabuddha-enlightenment, cultivates and realizes the path of dependent origination.

Nor is it that I perceive within the dharma of non-arising any bodhisattva mahāsattva who, for the sake of liberating immeasurable sentient beings, cultivates hundreds of thousands of difficult and painful practices and undergoes boundless varieties of intense suffering; yet these bodhisattva mahāsattvas likewise do not give rise to the thought of "difficult and painful practice."

Why is that? It is not by dwelling in the notion of difficult practices and ascetic austerities that one can perform beneficial deeds for immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless sentient beings. Śāriputra!

Nevertheless, by taking non-apprehension as their skillful means, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas give rise to great compassion for all sentient beings, dwelling with the thought that they are like their parents, like their brothers, like their wives and children, and like their own bodies; in this way, they are able to bring great benefit to immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless sentient beings.
Śāriputra! All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should form this thought:

"Just as my own self-nature cannot be found when sought through all modes, in all places, and at all times among all phenomena, so it is with all internal and external phenomena; they are entirely non-existent and unobtainable."

Why is this? Because if bodhisattva-mahāsattvas dwell in these perceptions and practice difficult and arduous austerities, they are able to benefit immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings.
Therefore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not grasp at or cling to any phenomena. Śāriputra,

it is not that I perceive any buddhas within the dharma of non-arising who have realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, turned the sublime wheel of Dharma, and delivered immeasurable multitudes.
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"Do you now intend to realize a dharma of arising by means of a dharma of arising, or do you intend to realize a dharma of non-arising by means of a dharma of non-arising?"
Subhūti replied,
“I truly do not wish to realize a dharma of arising through a dharma of arising, nor do I truly wish to realize a dharma of non-arising through a dharma of non-arising.”
Śāriputra said:
"If that is so, do you now intend to realize the dharma of non-arising by means of the dharma of arising, or do you intend to realize the dharma of arising by means of the dharma of non-arising?"
Subhūti replied,
"I do not wish to realize the dharma of non-arising by means of the dharma of arising, nor do I wish to realize the dharma of arising by means of the dharma of non-arising."
Śāriputra asked, "If this is so,
is there then absolutely no attainment and no clear realization?
Subhūti replied:
"Although there is attainment and there is clear realization, one does not realize by means of these two dharmas.

Śāriputra, it is only in accordance with worldly convention that attainment and clear realization are provisionally established; in the ultimate sense, there is neither attainment nor clear realization."

It is merely in accordance with worldly convention that one designates "stream-enterer" and "fruit of stream-entry," "once-returner" and "fruit of once-returning," "non-returner" and "fruit of non-returning," "arhat" and "fruit of arhatship," "pratyekabuddha" and "pratyekabuddha-enlightenment," "bodhisattva mahāsattva" and "unexcelled perfect enlightenment. In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), there is no stream-enterer up to and including unexcelled perfect enlightenment.
Śāriputra said:

"If it is the case that 'attainment' and 'clear realization' exist only as conventional designations according to worldly discourse and not in the ultimate sense, then would it not also be the case that the distinctions among the six realms of existence exist only as conventional designations according to worldly discourse and not in the ultimate sense?"
Subhūti replied, “So it is! So it is!”
It is exactly as you have said.
Why is this so? Śāriputra!
"In the ultimate sense, there is no karma and no maturation; there is no arising and no ceasing;
there is no defilement and no purification. Then, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"Do you now wish to cause unarisen phenomena to arise, or do you wish to cause already arisen phenomena to arise?"
Subhūti replied,
"I do not wish to cause unarisen dharmas to arise, nor do I wish to cause already arisen dharmas to arise.
Śāriputra said:
“What is this dharma that is unarisen, which you, O Venerable One, do not wish to arise?
Subhūti replied: “Śāriputra!...”
Form is a non-arising dharma; I do not wish for it to arise.
Why? Because its intrinsic nature is empty.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are dharmas that do not arise; I do not wish for them to arise.
Why is this? Because they are empty of intrinsic nature.
“Śāriputra! The sense-base of the eye is a non-arising dharma; I do not wish for it to arise. Why is this?
Because they are empty of intrinsic nature, the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are non-arising phenomena; I do not wish for them to arise. Why is this?
Because it is empty of intrinsic nature.
"Śāriputra, the sphere of form is a non-arising phenomenon; I do not wish for it to arise."
Why is this? Because they are empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*).
The spheres of sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) are non-arising dharmas; I do not wish for them to arise.
Why is this? Because their intrinsic nature is empty.
"Śāriputra!..."
The eye-element is a non-arising dharma; I do not wish to cause it to arise. Why?
Because its intrinsic nature is empty.
The form realm, the eye-consciousness realm, eye-contact, and all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition are dharmas that do not arise;
I do not wish for them to arise. Why is this?
Because it is empty of intrinsic nature.
"Śāriputra, the ear-element is a non-arising dharma; I do not wish for it to arise."
Why is this? Because they are empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*).

The sphere of sound, the sphere of auditory consciousness, and auditory contact, as well as all feelings produced with auditory contact as a condition, are non-arising phenomena; I do not wish for them to arise.
Why is this? Because their intrinsic nature is empty.
"Śāriputra!..."
The nose element is a non-arising dharma; I do not wish to cause it to arise. Why?
Because its intrinsic nature is empty.
The fragrance element, the nose-consciousness element, nose-contact, and all feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition are dharmas that do not arise;
I do not wish for them to arise. Why is this?
Because it is empty of intrinsic nature.
"Śāriputra, the tongue-element is a non-arising dharma; I do not wish for it to arise."
Why is this? Because their intrinsic nature is empty.
The taste element, the tongue-consciousness element, tongue-contact, and all sensations produced with tongue-contact as a condition are non-arising phenomena; I do not wish for them to arise.
Why is this? Because their intrinsic nature is empty.
"Śāriputra!..."
The body-element is a non-arising dharma; I do not wish to cause it to arise. Why?
Because its intrinsic nature is empty.
The element of tangibles, the element of body-consciousness, body-contact, and all feelings produced with body-contact as a condition are dharmas that do not arise;
I do not wish for them to arise. Why is this?
Because it is empty of intrinsic nature.
"Śāriputra, the mind-element is a non-arising dharma; I do not wish for it to arise."
Why is this? Because they are empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

The dharma-element, the mind-consciousness element, as well as mental contact and the various feelings produced with mental contact as a condition, are non-arising phenomena; I do not wish for them to arise.
Why is this? Because they are empty of intrinsic nature.
"Śāriputra!..."
The earth element is a non-arising phenomenon; I do not wish to cause it to arise. Why?
Because its intrinsic nature is empty.
The elements of water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness are non-arising phenomena; I do not wish for them to arise.
Why is this? Because they are empty of intrinsic nature.
“Śāriputra! The noble truth of suffering is a dharma that is unarisen; I do not wish for it to arise. Why is this?
Because they are empty of intrinsic nature, the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path are non-arising dharmas; I do not wish to cause them to arise. Why is this?
Because they are empty of intrinsic nature.
"Śāriputra, ignorance is a non-arising dharma; I do not wish for it to arise."
Why is this? Because they are empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnya*).

Form, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are dharmas that do not arise; I do not wish to cause them to arise.
Why is this? Because its intrinsic nature is empty.
"Śāriputra!..."
Internal emptiness is a non-arising dharma; I do not wish to cause it to arise. Why?
Because its intrinsic nature is empty.

Outer emptiness, inner-and-outer emptiness, emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, emptiness of dispersion, emptiness of non-alteration, emptiness of essential nature, emptiness of self-characteristic, emptiness of common characteristic, emptiness of all phenomena, emptiness of the unapprehendable, emptiness of non-existence, emptiness of intrinsic nature, and emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence are dharmas that do not arise; I do not wish to cause them to arise.
Why is this? Because their intrinsic nature is empty.
"Śāriputra!..."
The perfection of generosity is a non-arising dharma; I do not wish for it to arise.
Why? Because its intrinsic nature is empty.
The perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom are non-arising phenomena; I do not wish for them to arise. Why is this?
Because they are empty of intrinsic nature.
"Śāriputra, the four dhyānas are non-arising dharmas; I do not wish for them to arise."
Why is this? Because they are empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnya*).
The four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions are non-arising phenomena (*anutpāda-dharma*); I do not wish for them to arise.
Why is this? Because their intrinsic nature is empty.
"Śāriputra!..."
The eight liberations are non-arising dharmas; I do not wish for them to arise.
Why? Because they are empty of intrinsic nature.
The eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten totalities are dharmas that do not arise; I do not wish for them to arise.
Why is this? Because they are empty of intrinsic nature.
“Śāriputra! The four foundations of mindfulness are dharmas that do not arise; I do not wish for them to arise. Why is this?

Because they are empty of intrinsic nature, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path are non-arising phenomena; I do not wish for them to arise.
Why is this? Because their intrinsic nature is empty.
"Śāriputra!..."
The gate of liberation of emptiness is a non-arising dharma; I do not wish to cause it to arise. Why?
Because its intrinsic nature is empty.
The gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness are non-arising dharmas;
I do not wish for them to arise.
Why? Because they are empty by their very nature.
“Śāriputra! The five eyes are dharmas that are unarisen; I do not wish for them to arise. Why is this?
Because they are empty of intrinsic nature, the six supernormal powers are non-arising phenomena; I do not wish for them to arise. Why is this?
Because they are empty of intrinsic nature.
"Śāriputra, the ten powers of a Buddha are non-arising phenomena; I do not wish for them to arise."
Why is this? Because they are empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*).

The four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are non-arising phenomena; I do not wish for them to arise.
Why is this? Because their intrinsic nature is empty.
"Śāriputra!..."
All-knowledge is a non-arising dharma; I do not wish to cause it to arise. Why?
Because its intrinsic nature is empty.
The knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects are non-arising dharmas;
I do not wish for them to arise.
Why? Because they are empty of intrinsic nature.
“Śāriputra! The quality of non-forgetfulness is a dharma that is unarisen; I do not wish for it to arise. Why is this?
Because it is empty of intrinsic nature, the state of constant equanimity is a non-arising phenomenon; I do not wish for it to arise. Why is this?
Because they are empty of intrinsic nature. "Śāriputra!
All dhāraṇī-doors are non-arising phenomena; I do not wish for them to arise."
Why is this? Because their intrinsic nature is empty.
All gateways of samādhi are non-arising dharmas; I do not wish to cause them to arise.
Why is this? Because their intrinsic nature is empty.
"Śāriputra!..."
Ordinary beings are dharmas that do not arise; I do not wish for them to arise.
Why is this? Because they are empty of intrinsic nature.
The dharmas of ordinary beings are non-arising dharmas; I do not wish to cause them to arise. Why is this?
Because they are empty of intrinsic nature.
“Śāriputra! The stream-enterer is a non-arising dharma; I do not wish for them to arise. Why is this?
Because they are empty of intrinsic nature, the dharmas of a stream-enterer are non-arising dharmas; I do not wish for them to arise. Why is this?
Because it is empty of intrinsic nature.
"Śāriputra, the once-returner is a dharma that is non-arising; I do not wish for it to arise."
Why is this? Because it is empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
The dharma of once-returning is a dharma that does not arise; I do not wish to cause it to arise.
Why is this? Because their intrinsic nature is empty.
"Śāriputra!..."
The non-returner is a dharma that does not arise; I do not wish for it to arise. Why?
Because its intrinsic nature is empty.
The dharma of non-returning is a dharma that does not arise;
I do not wish for it to arise.
Why? Because its intrinsic nature is empty.
“Śāriputra! An arhat is a dharma that does not arise; I do not wish for them to arise. Why is this?
Because they are empty of intrinsic nature, the dharmas of an arhat are non-arising dharmas; I do not wish for them to arise. Why is this?
Because they are empty of intrinsic nature. "Śāriputra!
A pratyekabuddha is a non-arising dharma; I do not wish for them to arise."
Why is this? Because they are empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnya*).
The dharmas of the Pratyekabuddhas are non-arising dharmas; I do not wish to cause them to arise.
Why is this? Because they are empty of intrinsic nature.
"Śāriputra!..."
The Bodhisattva is a non-arising dharma; I do not wish to cause him to arise. Why?
Because his intrinsic nature is empty.
The Dharma of a bodhisattva is a non-arising dharma; I do not wish to cause it to arise. Why?
Because its intrinsic nature is empty.
“Śāriputra! The Tathāgata is of a nature that is unborn; I do not wish to cause him to be born. Why is this?
Because they are empty of intrinsic nature, the dharmas of the Tathāgata are non-arising dharmas; I do not wish to cause them to arise. Why is this?
"Because they are empty of intrinsic nature. Śāriputra said:
"What are these dharmas that have already arisen, which you, O Venerable One, do not wish to cause to arise?"
Subhūti replied:
"Form is a dharma that has already arisen; I do not wish to cause it to arise. Why is this?
Because they are empty of intrinsic nature.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are dharmas already arisen; I do not wish for them to arise. Why is this?
Because they are empty of intrinsic nature.
"Śāriputra, the sense-base of the eye is a dharma that has already arisen; I do not wish for it to arise."
Why is this? Because they are empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*).
The sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are dharmas already arisen; I do not wish for them to arise.
Why is this? Because their intrinsic nature is empty.
"Śāriputra!..."
The sense-base of form is a dharma that has already arisen;
I do not wish for it to arise.
Why? Because its intrinsic nature is empty.

At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"Venerable sir, do you now wish for birth to arise, or do you wish for non-birth to arise?"
Subhūti replied:
"I do not wish for that which has already arisen to arise, nor do I wish for that which has not yet arisen to arise. Why is this?"

Śāriputra! Birth and non-birth—these two dharmas are both neither associated nor dissociated, neither with form nor formless, neither visible nor invisible, and neither resistant nor non-resistant; they all share one and the same characteristic, which is called "signlessness" (animitta).
“Śāriputra!
For this reason, I do not wish for birth to arise, nor do I wish for non-birth to arise.
Then, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
“O Benevolent One!
Regarding the dharma of non-arising that you have spoken of, do you delight in eloquently explaining the characteristics of non-arising?
Subhūti replied:
"Regarding the dharma of non-arising that I have taught, I do not delight in discoursing upon the characteristics of non-arising. Why is this?

Whether it be the dharma of non-arising, the characteristics of non-arising, or the delight in discourse—all such things are neither associated nor dissociated; they are neither with form nor without form; they are neither visible nor invisible; they are neither resistant nor non-resistant; they are all of one single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of signlessness (animitta)."
Śāriputra said:
"Regarding the dharmas that are non-arising, one gives rise to the expression 'non-arising. Is this expression 'non-arising' itself also non-arising?
Subhūti replied:
"So it is! So it is! Why is this so?
“Śāriputra! Form is unarisen;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also unarisen. Why is this?
Because they are all empty of intrinsic nature.
"Śāriputra, the sense base of the eye is unarisen; the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are also unarisen."
Why is this? Because they are all empty by their very nature. "Śāriputra!..."

Why is this? Because they are all empty by their very nature.

Why is this? Because they are all empty by their very nature. "Śāriputra!..."

The ear element does not arise; the sound element, the ear-consciousness element, as well as auditory contact and the various feelings produced with auditory contact as a condition, also do not arise. Why is this?

Why is this? Because they are all empty by their very nature. "Śāriputra!..."
For this reason, although one utters the word "non-arising" regarding phenomena that do not arise,
there is no meaning of arising. Śāriputra,
it is because the dharma taught, the words by which it is taught, the speaker, and the listener are all non-arisen.
Then, Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
"Venerable sir, you are the foremost among those who preach the Dharma.
For what reason?"
"Because they are able to answer all questions and interrogations without any obstruction. Subhūti replied:

"Those disciples of the Buddhas who have no dependence or attachment toward any phenomena are, by the very nature of things, able to answer each and every question and interrogation with mastery and fearlessness."
"Why is this? Because all phenomena have nothing upon which they rely.
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:

Subhūti replied, "Śāriputra!..."
The intrinsic nature of form is empty, because it cannot be apprehended internally, externally, or in between;

the nature of the dharma of the once-returner is empty, because it cannot be apprehended internally, externally, or in between the two.”
“Śāriputra! The non-returner (*anāgāmin*) is empty of intrinsic nature, because he cannot be apprehended internally, externally, or in between the two;
the dharma of the non-returner is empty of intrinsic nature, because it cannot be apprehended internally, externally, or in between the two.”
“Śāriputra! An arhat is empty of intrinsic nature, because he cannot be apprehended internally, externally, or in between the two;
the dharmas of an arhat are empty of intrinsic nature, because they cannot be apprehended internally, externally, or in between the two.”
“Śāriputra! The intrinsic nature of a pratyekabuddha is empty, because it cannot be apprehended internally, externally, or in between the two;
the intrinsic nature of the dharmas of a pratyekabuddha is empty, because they cannot be apprehended internally, externally, or in between the two.”
“Śāriputra! The intrinsic nature of a bodhisattva is empty, because it cannot be apprehended internally, externally, or in between the two;
the intrinsic nature of the dharmas of a bodhisattva is empty, because they cannot be apprehended internally, externally, or in between the two.”
“Śāriputra! The intrinsic nature of the Tathāgata is empty, because it cannot be apprehended internally, externally, or in between the two;
the intrinsic nature of the dharmas of the Tathāgata is empty, because they cannot be apprehended internally, externally, or in between the two.”
“Śāriputra! For this reason, I say that all phenomena are entirely without support.
Chapter 21: The Path of Purification, Part One. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed Śāriputra, saying:
"When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the six perfections, they should purify form; they should purify feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
They should purify the sense base of the eye; they should purify the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
They should purify the sense base of forms; they should purify the sense bases of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena."
One should purify the eye element; one should purify the form element, the eye-consciousness element, and eye-contact, as well as all feelings produced with eye-contact as their condition.
One should purify the ear element; one should purify the sound element, the ear-consciousness element, and ear-contact, as well as all feelings produced with ear-contact as their condition.
One should purify the nose element; one should purify the odor element, the nose-consciousness element, and nose-contact, as well as all feelings produced with nose-contact as their condition.
One should purify the tongue element; one should purify the taste element, the tongue-consciousness element, tongue-contact, and all feelings produced with tongue-contact as their condition.
One should purify the body element; one should purify the tangible-object element, the body-consciousness element, body-contact, and all feelings produced with body-contact as their condition.
One should purify the mind element; one should purify the mental-object element, the mind-consciousness element, mind-contact, and all feelings produced with mind-contact as their condition.
One should purify the earth element; one should purify the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements.
One should purify the noble truth of suffering; one should purify the noble truths of origination, cessation, and the path.

One should purify ignorance; one should purify volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, and old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.

One should purify internal emptiness; one should purify external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature.
One should purify the perfection of generosity; one should purify the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
One should purify the four dhyānas; one should purify the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions.
One should purify the eight liberations; one should purify the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten totalities;

one should purify the four foundations of mindfulness; one should purify the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path;
one should purify the gate of liberation of emptiness; and one should purify the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness.
One should purify the five eyes; one should purify the six supernormal powers;

one should purify the ten powers of a Buddha; one should purify the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
one should purify the quality of non-forgetfulness; and one should purify the nature of constant abiding in equanimity.
One should purify all doors of dhāraṇī; one should purify all doors of samādhi;
one should purify all-knowledge, the knowledge of the aspects of the path, and the knowledge of all aspects;
one should purify the path to enlightenment.
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
“How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva purify the path to enlightenment while practicing the six perfections?”
Subhūti replied, "Śāriputra, each of the six pāramitās has two kinds: first, the mundane; second, the supramundane."
Śāriputra asked,
"What is the worldly perfection of generosity?
Subhūti replied:

"If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva acts as a great donor, they are able to give to all śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, the poor, the sick, the orphaned, the destitute, travelers on the road, and beggars: food to those who need food, drink to those who need drink, vehicles to those who need vehicles, clothing to those who need clothing, incense to those who need incense, flowers to those who need flowers, ornaments to those who need ornaments, houses to those who need houses, medicine to those who need medicine, light to those who need light, and bedding to those who need bedding; in this way, they give away all such necessities of life and utensils according to whatever each requires."

Furthermore, if there should come those who beg for a son, he gives a son; those who beg for a daughter, he gives a daughter; those who beg for a wife or concubine, he gives a wife or concubine; those who beg for official rank, he gives official rank; those who beg for a kingdom, he gives a kingdom; those who beg for a royal throne, he gives a royal throne; those who beg for his head or eyes, he gives his head or eyes; those who beg for his hands or feet, he gives his hands or feet; those who beg for his limbs and joints, he gives his limbs and joints; those who beg for his flesh or blood, he gives his flesh or blood; those who beg for his marrow or bones, he gives his marrow or bones; those who beg for his ears or nose, he gives his ears or nose; those who beg for servants, he gives servants; those who beg for precious wealth, he gives precious wealth; and those who beg for living beings, he gives living beings. In all such cases, he bestows upon them every internal and external thing according to their requests.
Although one performs such giving, there is still a basis upon which it rests; that is to say, one forms this thought: "I am the giver and he is the recipient;
I am the donor; I am not stingy or greedy; I am able to relinquish everything in accordance with the Buddha's teaching; I am practicing the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā)."
When he practices giving, he employs the skillful means of "having something to be attained," dedicating it together with all sentient beings toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Again, he forms this thought:
"I dedicate this merit to all sentient beings, so that they may attain peace and happiness in this life and future lives, even unto the realization of nirvana without remainder."
"He practices giving while attached to the three spheres: first, the notion of self; second, the notion of another; and third, the notion of giving.
Because he practices giving while attached to these three spheres, it is called the mundane perfection of giving."
For what reason is this giving called "worldly"?
Because it proceeds in common with the world and does not transcend or move beyond worldly phenomena, it is thus termed the "worldly perfection of giving" (dānapāramitā).
Śāriputra asked,
"What is the supramundane perfection of giving?
Subhūti replied:

"If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices giving with the three spheres purified—first, not grasping at oneself as the giver; second, not grasping at another as the recipient; and third, not being attached to the gift or the fruit of the gift—this is what is meant by a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practicing giving with the three spheres purified."
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, with great compassion as their foremost guide, bestows the merit of the practice of giving universally upon all sentient beings, they apprehend nothing at all regarding those sentient beings. Although they dedicate it together with all sentient beings toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they do not perceive even the slightest mark therein.
Because one practices giving without any attachment whatsoever, it is called the supramundane perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*).
For what reason is this giving termed "supramundane"?
Because it does not act in common with the world and is able to transcend and rise above worldly phenomena, this is called the supramundane perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*).
Śāriputra asked:
"What is the worldly perfection of ethical discipline?
Subhūti replied:
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, although upholding the precepts, has a basis for doing so—meaning they think:

‘I uphold pure morality for the benefit of all sentient beings; I am able to remain unoffending regarding pure śīla in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching; I am practicing the perfection of morality (śīlapāramitā).’”
When he maintains the precepts, he employs the method of "having something to be attained" to dedicate them together with all sentient beings toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Again, he forms this thought:
"I dedicate this merit to all sentient beings, so that they may attain peace and happiness in this life and future lives, even unto the realization of nirvana without remainder."
He observes and upholds the precepts while clinging to the three wheels: first, the notion of self; second, the notion of others; and third, the notion of the precepts.
Because he observes and upholds the precepts while clinging to these three wheels, it is called the mundane perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*).
For what reason is this pure ethical discipline called "mundane"?
Because it functions in common with the world and does not transcend or move beyond mundane phenomena, it is thus termed the mundane perfection of pure ethical discipline (*laukika-śīla-pāramitā*).
Śāriputra asked:
"What is the supramundane perfection of pure ethical discipline?
Subhūti replied:

"If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva maintains the precepts with the three spheres purified—first, not grasping at the notion 'I can maintain the precepts'; second, not grasping at the sentient beings who are protected; and third, not being attached to the precepts or the fruits of the precepts—this is what is meant by a bodhisattva-mahāsattva maintaining the precepts with the three spheres purified."

Furthermore, Śāriputra, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, with great compassion as his foremost guide, bestows the merit of the precepts he maintains universally upon all sentient beings; yet, regarding these sentient beings, he apprehends nothing at all. Although he dedicates this together with all sentient beings toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, he perceives not even the slightest mark therein.
Because one upholds the precepts without any attachment whatsoever, it is called the supramundane perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*).
For what reason is this ethical discipline termed "supramundane"?

Because it does not act in common with the world and because it is able to transcend and emerge from worldly phenomena, this is called the supramundane perfection of pure ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*).
Śāriputra asked,
"What is the worldly perfection of patience?
Subhūti replied:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing patience, has a basis for doing so—meaning they form this thought:
'I practice patience for the benefit of all sentient beings; I am correctly cultivating supreme patience in accordance with the Buddha's teaching; I am practicing the perfection of patience. "
When he cultivates patience, he employs the method of "attaining something" to dedicate [the merit] together with all sentient beings toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Again, he forms this thought:
"I dedicate this merit to all sentient beings, so that they may attain peace and happiness in this life and future lives, even unto the realization of nirvana without remainder."
He practices patience while being attached to the three spheres: first, the notion of self; second, the notion of another; and third, the notion of patience.
Because he practices patience by being attached to these three spheres, it is called the mundane perfection of patience.
For what reason is this patience called "mundane"?
Because it functions in common with the world and does not transcend or move beyond mundane phenomena, it is thus termed the mundane perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).
Śāriputra asked,
“What is the supramundane perfection of patience?
Subhūti replied:

“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices patience, there is purity of the three spheres: first, not grasping at a self that can practice patience; second, not grasping at the sentient beings toward whom one practices patience; third, not being attached to the patience itself or its fruit. This is what is meant by the purity of the three spheres when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices patience.”

Furthermore, Śāriputra, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, taking great compassion as the foremost, bestows upon all sentient beings the merit of the patience he has cultivated; yet, regarding all sentient beings, he apprehends nothing at all. Although he dedicates this together with all sentient beings toward Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, within that dedication he does not perceive even the slightest mark.
Because one cultivates patience by being entirely without grasping, it is called the supramundane perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).
For what reason is this patience called supramundane?
Because it does not act in common with the world and because it can transcend and emerge from worldly dharmas, this is called the supramundane perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).
Śāriputra asked,
"What is the worldly perfection of diligence?
Subhūti replied:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, despite being diligent and energetic, relies upon something—namely, thinking:

'I am diligent and energetic for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings; I exhort my body and mind following the Buddha's teaching without ever succumbing to indolence; I am practicing the perfection of diligence.'"
When he practices with diligence, he employs the skillful means of "having something to be attained" to dedicate [the merit] together with all sentient beings toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Again, he forms this thought:
"I dedicate this merit to all sentient beings, so that they may attain peace and happiness in this life and future lives, even unto the realization of nirvana without remainder."
He exerts diligent effort while being attached to three wheels: first, the notion of self; second, the notion of others; and third, the notion of diligence itself.
Because he cultivates diligence while being attached to these three wheels, it is called the mundane perfection of diligence (vīrya-pāramitā).
For what reason is this diligence called "mundane"?
Because it proceeds in common with the world and does not transcend or move beyond mundane phenomena, it is thus termed the mundane perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*).
Śāriputra asked,
“What is the supramundane perfection of diligence?
Subhūti replied:

"If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices with diligent vigor while maintaining the purity of the three spheres: first, not grasping at a self that can practice vigor; second, not grasping at the sentient beings for whose sake one acts; and third, not being attached to the vigor or its fruit—this is what is meant by a bodhisattva-mahāsattva maintaining the purity of the three spheres when practicing with diligent vigor."
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

A bodhisattva mahāsattva takes great compassion as the foremost guide and cultivates the merit of diligence to bestow universally upon all sentient beings. Regarding these sentient beings, they apprehend nothing at all; and although they dedicate this together with all sentient beings toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they do not perceive even the slightest mark therein.
Because one exerts diligent effort while being entirely without grasping, it is called the supramundane perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*).
For what reason is this diligence termed supramundane?
Because it does not act in common with the world and is able to transcend and emerge from worldly phenomena, it is called the supramundane perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*).
Śāriputra asked,
"What is the worldly perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā)?
Subhūti replied:
"If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, while practicing meditative concentration, nevertheless has a basis for doing so—namely, thinking:

'I practice meditative concentration for the benefit of all sentient beings; I correctly cultivate supreme samādhi in accordance with the Buddha's teaching; I am practicing the perfection of meditative concentration.'"
When he practices meditative concentration, he employs the method of "having something to be attained" to dedicate [the merit] together with all sentient beings toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
He further reflects:
"I dedicate this merit to all sentient beings, so that they may attain peace and happiness in this life and future lives, even unto the realization of nirvana without remainder."
He practices meditative concentration while clinging to three wheels: first, the notion of self; second, the notion of another; and third, the notion of meditative concentration.
Because he practices meditative concentration by clinging to these three wheels, it is called mundane meditative concentration pāramitā.
For what reason is this meditative absorption called "mundane"?

Because it functions in common with the mundane world and does not transcend or move beyond mundane phenomena, it is thus termed the mundane perfection of meditative absorption (*laukika-dhyāna-pāramitā*).
Śāriputra asked:
"What is the supramundane perfection of meditative concentration?
Subhūti replied:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices meditative concentration with the three spheres purified—first, not grasping at a self that can practice concentration; second, not grasping at sentient beings for whose sake one acts; and third, not being attached to the meditative concentration or its fruit—this is what is meant by a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing meditative concentration with the three spheres purified."

Furthermore, Śāriputra, the bodhisattva mahāsattva, taking great compassion as the foremost, cultivates the merit of meditative concentration and bestows it universally upon all sentient beings. Regarding these sentient beings, he perceives nothing at all; and although he dedicates this together with all sentient beings toward anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi, within that dedication he does not perceive even the slightest mark.
Because one cultivates meditative concentration (dhyāna) by being entirely without grasping, it is called the supramundane perfection of meditative concentration (lokottara-dhyāna-pāramitā).
For what reason is this meditative concentration termed "supramundane"?
Because it does not act in common with the world and is able to transcend and emerge from worldly phenomena, it is called the supramundane dhyāna-pāramitā.
Śāriputra asked,
"What is the worldly perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā)?
Subhūti replied:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing *prajñā*, nevertheless relies on something, thinking:

'I practice *prajñā* for the benefit of all sentient beings; I am practicing the supreme *prajñā* correctly according to the Buddha's teaching; I can repent and eliminate my own misdeeds; seeing the faults of others, I never revile or despise them; I can rejoice in the merit cultivated by others; I can entreat the Buddhas to turn the sublime wheel of Dharma; I can correctly discern and resolve matters as I have heard them; I am practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*.'"
When he cultivates wisdom, he employs the method of "attaining something" to dedicate it together with all sentient beings toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Again, he forms this thought:
"I dedicate this merit to all sentient beings, so that they may attain peace and happiness in this life and future lives, even unto the realization of nirvana without remainder."
He practices prajñā while clinging to the three wheels: first, the notion of self; second, the notion of others; and third, the notion of prajñā.
Because he practices prajñā by clinging to these three wheels, it is called mundane prajñāpāramitā.
For what reason is this prajñā called "mundane"?
Because it functions in common with the world and does not transcend or move beyond mundane phenomena, it is thus called the mundane *prajñāpāramitā*.
Śāriputra asked:
"What is supramundane prajñāpāramitā? Subhūti replied:

"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivates prajñā, the three spheres are pure: first, not grasping at a self that can cultivate wisdom; second, not grasping at the sentient beings for whom it is done; third, not being attached to prajñā or its fruit. This is what is meant by the purity of the three spheres when a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivates prajñā."

Furthermore, Śāriputra, the bodhisattva mahāsattva, taking great compassion as the foremost, cultivates the merit of prajñā and bestows it universally upon all sentient beings; yet regarding these sentient beings, they apprehend nothing at all. Although they dedicate this together with all sentient beings toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, within that dedication they do not perceive even the slightest mark.
Because one cultivates prajñā by being entirely without attachment, it is called the supramundane Prajñāpāramitā.
For what reason is this prajñā termed "supramundane"?
Because it does not act in common with the world and is able to transcend and emerge from worldly phenomena, it is called the supramundane *prajñāpāramitā*.
“Śāriputra! In this way, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the six perfections, they purify the path to enlightenment.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed Subhūti, saying:
“What is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s path to awakening?
Subhūti replied, “Śāriputra!...”

Internal emptiness is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s path to enlightenment; external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-altering emptiness, essential emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common-characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature are called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s path to enlightenment.

“Śāriputra! Suchness (tathatā) is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s path to awakening; the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), non-falsity, immutability, equality, the state beyond birth, the fixedness of phenomena, the stability of phenomena, the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm are called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s path to awakening.”

“Śāriputra! The noble truth of suffering is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s path to enlightenment; the noble truths of origination, cessation, and the path are called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s path to enlightenment.”

“Śāriputra! The perfection of generosity is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s path to awakening; the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom are called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s path to awakening.”

“Śāriputra! The four dhyānas are called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s path to awakening; the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions are called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s path to awakening.”

“Śāriputra! The eight liberations are called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s path to enlightenment; the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten totalities are called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s path to enlightenment.”

“Śāriputra! The four foundations of mindfulness are called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s path to awakening; the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold noble path are called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s path to awakening.”

“Śāriputra! The gate of liberation of emptiness is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s path to awakening; the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness are called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s path to awakening.”
“Śāriputra! The five eyes are called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s path to awakening; the six supernormal powers are called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s path to awakening.”

“Śāriputra! The ten powers of a Buddha are called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s path to enlightenment; the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s path to enlightenment.”

“Śāriputra! The quality of non-forgetfulness is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s path to awakening; the state of constant abiding in equanimity is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s path to awakening.”
“Śāriputra! All gateways of dhāraṇī are called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s path to awakening; all gateways of samādhi are called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s path to awakening.”

“Śāriputra! All-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s path to enlightenment; the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) are called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s path to enlightenment.”
“Śāriputra! Such an immeasurable and boundless mass of great merit is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s path to enlightenment.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed Subhūti, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!
It is truly as you have said."
"By the power of which perfection (pāramitā) are such qualities brought about?
Subhūti replied, "Śāriputra!..."
All such merits are brought about by the power of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Why is this? Śāriputra!
In this way, the perfection of wisdom serves as the mother of all wholesome dharmas, for all wholesome dharmas of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and tathāgatas arise from it.

Śāriputra! Thus, this perfection of wisdom universally encompasses all wholesome dharmas, for all the wholesome dharmas of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and tathāgatas abide by means of it.

Śāriputra! Because the Buddhas of the past fully perfected their cultivation of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they have already realized unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, turned the sublime wheel of Dharma, and delivered immeasurable multitudes.

Because the Buddhas of the future will fully perfect their cultivation of the perfection of wisdom, they shall realize unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, turn the sublime wheel of Dharma, and deliver immeasurable multitudes.

Because the Buddhas of the worlds of the ten directions have now fully perfected their cultivation of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), they have realized unexcelled, perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*) and turned the sublime wheel of Dharma to deliver immeasurable multitudes.
The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle Seventy-Five;
The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle Seventy-Six.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
The First Part of the Chapter on the Path of Purification, Twenty-one, Part Two: "Śāriputra!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon hearing the teaching of the *prajñāpāramitā*, has no doubt or confusion in mind, you should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in such an abiding, never departing from mental attention (*manasikāra*). That is to say, they desire to rescue and protect all sentient beings, and they never abandon the mental attention of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) for all sentient beings."
At that time, Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in such an abiding without being separated from mental attention, then all sentient beings should also become bodhisattva mahāsattvas."
Why is this? Because all sentient beings also never depart from this mental attention; thus, there would be no distinction between a bodhisattva mahāsattva and all sentient beings.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti praised Śāriputra, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
It is exactly as you have said; you are able to grasp the meaning of what I have taught according to reality.
Why is this so? Śāriputra!
Because sentient beings do not exist, one should know that mental attention (*manasikāra*) also does not exist;

because the self, the life-principle, the being, the nourisher, the person, the individual, the mind-born, the youth, the agent, the experiencer, the knower, and the seer do not exist, one should know that mental attention also does not exist.
Because sentient beings lack substantial reality, one should know that mental attention also lacks substantial reality;
because the self up to the viewer lack substantial reality, one should know that mental attention also lacks substantial reality.
Because sentient beings lack intrinsic nature, one should know that mental attention also lacks intrinsic nature;

At that time, the World-Honored One praised Subhūti, saying:

All those who wish to proclaim the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) to bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should do so exactly as you have proclaimed it.
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who wish to study the perfection of wisdom should study it in accordance with what you have taught.

When the Venerable Subhūti was teaching this Prajñāpāramitā for the sake of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, this trichiliocosm underwent six kinds of transformations: namely, it shook, shook violently, and shook intensely; it surged, surged violently, and surged intensely; it quaked, quaked violently, and quaked intensely; it crashed, crashed violently, and crashed intensely; it roared, roared violently, and roared intensely; it thundered, thundered violently, and thundered intensely. It rose in the east and sank in the west; it rose in the west and sank in the east;
it rose in the south and sank in the north; it rose in the north and sank in the south; it rose in the center and sank at the periphery; it rose at the periphery and sank in the center.
At that time, the Tathāgata smiled. The Venerable Subhūti addressed him, saying:
"World-Honored One, for what cause and for what reason do you manifest this smile?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Just as I here, in this trichiliocosm Sahā world, proclaim the perfection of wisdom for the sake of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas, so too do the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, in immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless worlds throughout the ten directions, proclaim the perfection of wisdom for the sake of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas."

Now, in this Sahā world-system of three thousandfold great thousands, there are twelve nayutas of devas and humans who, having heard the teaching of the Prajñāpāramitā, have attained the patience of non-arising regarding all phenomena.

Now, in each of the immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless worlds throughout the ten directions, there are likewise immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings who, having heard the Prajñāpāramitā taught by those Buddhas, have also resolved their minds upon Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Chapter 22: The Chapter on the Heavenly Kings, Part One. Section 22-1.

At that time, all the Four Great Heavenly Kings throughout this trichiliocosm, each accompanied by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of the four great heavenly hosts, came to the assembly and took their seats.

all the Santuṣita kings throughout this trichiliocosm, each accompanied by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of Santuṣita deva hosts, came and sat together in the assembly;

all the Mahābrahmā-devānām-indras of this trichiliocosm, each accompanied by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of gods of the first dhyāna heaven, came and sat together in the assembly;

The exquisite bodily radiance produced by the superior karma of these various hosts of devas is like the light constantly manifested from the body of the Tathāgata; it does not equal even a hundredth part, nor a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth part, nor even a hundred-thousand-koṭi-nayuta-th part. In terms of numerical proportion, calculation, reckoning, analogy, or even the *upaniṣad* (ultimate) fraction, it does not approach even a single part.

Why is this? Because the light constantly manifested from the body of the Tathāgata is blazing and radiant; among all lights, it is the most honored, the most supreme, the most ultimate, the most exquisite, peerless, unequalled, unsurpassed, and foremost. It eclipses the lights of all devas so that they do not appear, just as black iron is outshone by Jambūnada gold.
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed Subhūti, saying:

listen attentively! Listen attentively!

He contemplates the impurity of the mind-element (*manodhātu*), and he contemplates the impurity of the phenomena-element (*dharmadhātu*), the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*), as well as mental contact (*manaḥsaṃsparśa*) and the various feelings produced with mental contact as condition;

he contemplates the emptiness of the mind-element, and he contemplates the emptiness of the phenomena-element, the mind-consciousness-element, as well as mental contact and the various feelings produced with mental contact as condition;

he contemplates the signlessness of the mind-element, and he contemplates the signlessness of the phenomena-element, the mind-consciousness-element, as well as mental contact and the various feelings produced with mental contact as condition.

One contemplates the wishless nature of the mind-element; one contemplates the wishless nature of the dharma-element, the mind-consciousness-element, and mental contact, as well as all feelings produced with mental contact as their condition.

One contemplates the tranquility of the mind-element; one contemplates the tranquility of the dharma-element, the mind-consciousness-element, and mental contact, as well as all feelings produced with mental contact as their condition.

One contemplates the detachment of the mind-element; one contemplates the detachment of the dharma-element, the mind-consciousness-element, and mental contact, as well as all feelings produced with mental contact as their condition.

One contemplates the mind-element as a disease; one contemplates the dharma-element, the mind-consciousness-element, mental contact, and the various feelings born with mental contact as conditions as a disease.

One contemplates the mind-element as an abscess; one contemplates the dharma-element, the mind-consciousness-element, mental contact, and the various feelings born with mental contact as conditions as an abscess.

One contemplates the mind-element as an arrow; one contemplates the dharma-element, the mind-consciousness-element, mental contact, and the various feelings born with mental contact as conditions as an arrow.
One contemplates the mind-element as a sore; one contemplates the dharma-element, the mind-consciousness-element, mental contact, and all feelings arising with mental contact as condition as sores.

One contemplates the mind-element as feverish affliction; one contemplates the dharma-element, the mind-consciousness-element, mental contact, and all feelings arising with mental contact as condition as feverish afflictions.

One contemplates the mind-element as oppression; one contemplates the dharma-element, the mind-consciousness-element, mental contact, and all feelings arising with mental contact as condition as oppressions.

He contemplates the disintegration of the mind-element (*manodhātu*), and he contemplates the disintegration of the mental-object-element (*dharmadhātu*), the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*), and the mind-contact (*manaḥsaṃsparśa*) as well as all feelings (*vedanā*) produced with mind-contact as condition;

he contemplates the decay of the mind-element, and he contemplates the decay of the mental-object-element, the mind-consciousness-element, and the mind-contact as well as all feelings produced with mind-contact as condition;

he contemplates the fluctuation of the mind-element, and he contemplates the fluctuation of the mental-object-element, the mind-consciousness-element, and the mind-contact as well as all feelings produced with mind-contact as condition.

He contemplates that the mind-element quickly perishes; he contemplates that the dharma-element, the mental-consciousness-element, and the mental contact, as well as all feelings produced with mental contact as their condition, quickly perish.

He contemplates that the mind-element is fearful; he contemplates that the dharma-element, the mental-consciousness-element, and the mental contact, as well as all feelings produced with mental contact as their condition, are fearful.

He contemplates that the mind-element is loathsome; he contemplates that the dharma-element, the mental-consciousness-element, and the mental contact, as well as all feelings produced with mental contact as their condition, are loathsome.

One contemplates that the mind-element (manodhātu) is beset by calamity; one contemplates that the mental-object-element (dharmadhātu), the mind-consciousness-element (manovijñānadhātu), and the mental contact (manaḥsaṃsparśa), as well as all feelings produced with mental contact as condition, are beset by calamity.

One contemplates that the mind-element is beset by misfortune; one contemplates that the mental-object-element, the mind-consciousness-element, and the mental contact, as well as all feelings produced with mental contact as condition, are beset by misfortune.

One contemplates that the mind-element is beset by pestilence; one contemplates that the mental-object-element, the mind-consciousness-element, and the mental contact, as well as all feelings produced with mental contact as condition, are beset by pestilence.

One contemplates that the mind-element (*manodhātu*) is afflicted; one contemplates that the mental-object-element (*dharmadhātu*), the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*), and the mental contact (*manaḥsaṃsparśa*), as well as all feelings (*vedanā*) produced with mental contact as a condition, are afflicted.

One contemplates that the nature of the mind-element is insecure; one contemplates that the nature of the mental-object-element, the mind-consciousness-element, and the mental contact, as well as all feelings produced with mental contact as a condition, is insecure.

One contemplates that the mind-element is not to be relied upon; one contemplates that the mental-object-element, the mind-consciousness-element, and the mental contact, as well as all feelings produced with mental contact as a condition, are not to be relied upon.

He contemplates that the mind-element is without arising and without cessation; he contemplates that the dharma-element, the mind-consciousness-element, and mental contact, as well as all feelings produced with mental contact as condition, are without arising and without cessation.

He contemplates that the mind-element is without defilement and without purification; he contemplates that the dharma-element, the mind-consciousness-element, and mental contact, as well as all feelings produced with mental contact as condition, are without defilement and without purification.

He contemplates that the mind-element is unconditioned and unconstructed; he contemplates that the dharma-element, the mind-consciousness-element, and mental contact, as well as all feelings produced with mental contact as condition, are unconditioned and unconstructed.
Kauśika! This is the Prajñāpāramitā of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.

contemplates the earth element as suffering, and contemplates the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements as suffering;”
One contemplates the earth element as selfless; one contemplates the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements as selfless.
One contemplates the earth element as impure; one contemplates the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements as impure.
One contemplates the earth element as empty; one contemplates the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements as empty.
One contemplates the earth element as signless; one contemplates the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements as signless.
One contemplates the earth element as wishless; one contemplates the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements as wishless.
One contemplates the earth element as peaceful; one contemplates the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements as peaceful.
One contemplates the earth element as secluded; one contemplates the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements as secluded.
One contemplates the earth element as like a disease; one contemplates the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements as like a disease.
One contemplates the earth element as like an abscess; one contemplates the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements as like an abscess.
One contemplates the earth element as an arrow, and one contemplates the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements as arrows;
one contemplates the earth element as a wound, and one contemplates the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements as wounds;
one contemplates the earth element as a feverish affliction, and one contemplates the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements as feverish afflictions.
He contemplates the oppression of the earth element, and contemplates the oppression of the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements;
he contemplates the disintegration of the earth element, and contemplates the disintegration of the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements;
he contemplates the decay of the earth element, and contemplates the decay of the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements.
He contemplates the instability of the earth element; he contemplates the instability of the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements.

He contemplates the dreadfulness of the earth element; he contemplates the dreadfulness of the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements.
One contemplates the earth element as repulsive; one contemplates the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements as repulsive.
One contemplates the earth element as subject to calamity; one contemplates the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements as subject to calamity.
One contemplates the earth element as subject to misfortune; one contemplates the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements as subject to misfortune.
He contemplates that there is pestilence in the earth element; he contemplates that there is pestilence in the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements.
He contemplates that there is plague in the earth element; he contemplates that there is plague in the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements.
He contemplates that the nature of the earth element is not peaceful or secure; he contemplates that the nature of the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements is not peaceful or secure.
One contemplates that the earth element is not to be relied upon; one contemplates that the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements are not to be relied upon.

One contemplates that the earth element is without arising and without cessation; one contemplates that the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements are without arising and without cessation.

One contemplates that the earth element is without defilement and without purity; one contemplates that the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements are without defilement and without purity.
One contemplates the earth element as unconditioned and uncreated; one contemplates the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements as unconditioned and uncreated. Kausika!
This is the perfection of wisdom of the bodhisattva mahāsattva. "Kauśika!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with a mind directed toward the knowledge of all modes, employing the method of non-apprehension, contemplates the impermanence of ignorance; and contemplates the impermanence of volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; [this is the perfection of wisdom]."
One contemplates ignorance as suffering, and one contemplates volitional formations up to old age, death, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair as suffering;
one contemplates ignorance as non-self, and one contemplates volitional formations up to old age, death, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair as non-self;
one contemplates ignorance as impure, and one contemplates volitional formations up to old age, death, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair as impure.
One contemplates that ignorance is empty; one contemplates that volitional formations, up to and including old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair, are empty.
One contemplates that ignorance is signless; one contemplates that volitional formations, up to and including old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair, are signless.
One contemplates that ignorance is wishless; one contemplates that volitional formations, up to and including old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair, are wishless.
One contemplates the stillness of ignorance; one contemplates the stillness of volitional formations up to old age, death, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair.
One contemplates the detachment from ignorance; one contemplates the detachment from volitional formations up to old age, death, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair.
One contemplates ignorance as a disease; one contemplates volitional formations up to old age, death, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair as diseases.
One contemplates ignorance as a boil; one contemplates volitional formations up to old age, death, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair as boils.
One contemplates ignorance as an arrow; one contemplates volitional formations up to old age, death, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair as arrows.
One contemplates ignorance as a wound; one contemplates volitional formations up to old age, death, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair as wounds.
One contemplates the feverish affliction of ignorance, and contemplates the feverish affliction of volitional formations up to old age, death, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair;
one contemplates the urgent oppression of ignorance, and contemplates the urgent oppression of volitional formations up to old age, death, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair;
one contemplates the ruinous decay of ignorance, and contemplates the ruinous decay of volitional formations up to old age, death, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair.
One contemplates the decay of ignorance, and contemplates the decay of volitional formations up to old age, death, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair;
one contemplates the instability of ignorance, and contemplates the instability of volitional formations up to old age, death, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair;
one contemplates the rapid cessation of ignorance, and contemplates the rapid cessation of volitional formations up to old age, death, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair.
One contemplates that ignorance is fearsome; one contemplates that volitional formations, up to and including aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair, are fearsome.
One contemplates that ignorance is loathsome; one contemplates that volitional formations, up to and including aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair, are loathsome.

One contemplates that ignorance is fraught with calamity; one contemplates that volitional formations, up to and including aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair, are fraught with calamity.
One contemplates that ignorance has calamities, and one contemplates that volitional formations through to old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair have calamities;
one contemplates that ignorance has epidemics, and one contemplates that volitional formations through to old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair have epidemics;
one contemplates that ignorance has pestilences, and one contemplates that volitional formations through to old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair have pestilences.

One contemplates that the nature of ignorance is unstable and insecure; one contemplates that the nature of volitional formations, up to and including old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair, is unstable and insecure.
One contemplates that ignorance is untrustworthy; one contemplates that volitional formations, up to and including old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair, are untrustworthy.

One contemplates that ignorance is without arising and without cessation; one contemplates that volitional formations, up to and including old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair, are without arising and without cessation.

One contemplates that ignorance is neither defiled nor pure; one contemplates that volitional formations, up to and including old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair, are neither defiled nor pure.

One contemplates that ignorance is unconditioned and uncreated; one contemplates that volitional formations, up to and including old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair, are unconditioned and uncreated.
Kauśika! This is the prajñāpāramitā of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Kauśika!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with a mind directed toward the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), employing the method of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), contemplates internal emptiness as being without self or what belongs to self; and contemplates external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersion emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential emptiness, emptiness of own-marks, emptiness of common marks, emptiness of all dharmas, emptiness of the unapprehendable, emptiness of non-existence, emptiness of own-nature, and emptiness of the own-nature of non-existence as being without self or what belongs to self;
and contemplates internal emptiness as signless (*animitta*), and contemplates external emptiness up to the emptiness of the own-nature of non-existence as signless.
He contemplates inner emptiness as wishless, and contemplates outer emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature as wishless;
he contemplates inner emptiness as tranquil, and contemplates outer emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature as tranquil;
he contemplates inner emptiness as secluded, and contemplates outer emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature as secluded.

One contemplates inner emptiness as being unconditioned and uncreated; one contemplates outer emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature, as being unconditioned and uncreated.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with a mind directed toward the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), employing the method of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), observes that suchness (*tathatā*) is without self or what belongs to a self; observes that the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), non-illusory nature, unchanging nature, equality, the state beyond birth, the fixed nature of phenomena, the stability of phenomena, the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the realm of space (*ākāśadhātu*), and the inconceivable realm are without self or what belongs to a self;
observes that suchness is signless (*animitta*), observes that the realm of phenomena up to the inconceivable realm are signless;
and observes that suchness is wishless (*apraṇihita*), observes that the realm of phenomena up to the inconceivable realm are wishless.
He contemplates the tranquility of suchness; he contemplates the tranquility of the dharma-realm, up to and including the inconceivable realm;
he contemplates the detachment of suchness; he contemplates the detachment of the dharma-realm, up to and including the inconceivable realm;
he contemplates the non-arising and non-ceasing of suchness; he contemplates the non-arising and non-ceasing of the dharma-realm, up to and including the inconceivable realm.

One contemplates that suchness is unconditioned and uncreated; one contemplates that the dharma-realm, up to and including the inconceivable realm, is unconditioned and uncreated.

if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with a mind corresponding to the knowledge of all modes, practices the perfection of meditative concentration by means of non-apprehension as the expedient;
and if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with a mind corresponding to the knowledge of all modes, practices the perfection of wisdom by means of non-apprehension as the expedient.
Kauśika! This is the prajñāpāramitā of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Kauśika!

if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with a mind corresponding to the knowledge of all modes, practices the four immeasurables by means of non-apprehension as the expedient;

if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with a mind corresponding to the knowledge of all modes, practices the five faculties by means of non-apprehension as the expedient;
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with a mind corresponding to the knowledge of all modes, practices the five powers by means of non-apprehension as the expedient;

if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with a mind corresponding to the knowledge of all modes, practices the eight branches of the noble path by means of non-apprehension as the expedient.

if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with a mind corresponding to the knowledge of all modes, practices the gate of liberation of signlessness by means of non-apprehension as the expedient;

if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with a mind corresponding to the knowledge of all modes, employs the method of non-apprehension to cultivate the six supernormal powers.”
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with a mind corresponding to the knowledge of all modes, practices the ten powers of a buddha by means of the expedient of non-apprehension;

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with a mind corresponding to the knowledge of all modes, practices great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity by means of non-apprehension as the expedient;
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with a mind corresponding to the knowledge of all modes, practices the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha by means of non-apprehension as the expedient.
