“Subhūti! The mind of the Tathāgata does not abide in the perfection of generosity; it does not abide in the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, or wisdom.”
Why is this? Because the perfection of generosity and so forth cannot be apprehended.
"Suvikrāntavikrāmin!..."
The Tathāgata’s mind does not abide in the four dhyānas, nor does it abide in the four immeasurables or the four formless absorptions.
Why is this? Because the four dhyānas and so forth are unapprehendable.

“Subhūti! The mind of the Tathāgata does not abide in the eight liberations, nor does it abide in the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, or the ten totalities. Why is this?
Because the eight liberations and so forth are unapprehendable. "Subhūti!

The Tathāgata’s mind does not abide in the four foundations of mindfulness; it does not abide in the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the eightfold noble path."
Why is this? Because the four foundations of mindfulness and so forth are unapprehendable. "Subhūti!..."
The mind of the Tathāgata does not abide in the liberation door of emptiness, nor does it abide in the liberation doors of signlessness and wishlessness.
Why is this? Because the liberation door of emptiness and the others are unapprehendable.
“Subhūti! The Tathāgata’s mind does not abide in the five eyes, nor does it abide in the six supernormal powers. Why is this?
Because the five eyes and so forth are unattainable. "Subhūti!

The mind of the Tathāgata does not abide in the ten powers of a Buddha; it does not abide in the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha."
Why is this? Because the ten powers of a Buddha and so forth are unapprehendable.
"Suvikrāntavikrāmin!
The Tathāgata’s mind does not abide in the quality of non-forgetfulness, nor does it abide in the nature of constant equanimity.
Why is this? Because qualities such as non-forgetfulness are ultimately unapprehendable.
“Subhūti! The mind of the Tathāgata does not abide in any of the dhāraṇī-doors, nor does it abide in any of the samādhi-doors. Why is this?
Because all dharani-doors and so forth are unapprehendable. "Subhūti!
The Tathāgata’s mind does not abide in omniscience; it does not abide in the knowledge of the aspects of the path, nor in the knowledge of all aspects."
Why is this? Because all-knowledge and so forth are unapprehendable.
"Suvikrāntavikrāmin! "
The mind of the Tathāgata does not abide in the Śrāvaka vehicle, nor does it abide in the Pratyekabuddha vehicle or the Unsurpassed Vehicle. Why is this?
Because the Śrāvaka vehicle and the others are unattainable.

“Subhūti! The mind of the Tathāgata does not abide in the fruit of a stream-enterer nor in the path leading toward the fruit of a stream-enterer; it does not abide in the fruits of a once-returner, a non-returner, or an arhat, nor in the paths leading toward the fruits of a once-returner, a non-returner, or an arhat.”
Why is this? Because the stream-enterers and so forth cannot be apprehended.
"Subhūti!..."

The mind of the Tathāgata does not abide in the Pratyekabuddha nor in the enlightenment of a Pratyekabuddha; it does not abide in the Bodhisattva, the Tathāgata, or the dharmas of the Bodhisattva and the Tathāgata. Why is this?
Because Pratyekabuddhas and so forth cannot be apprehended. "Subhūti!

The mind of the Tathāgata does not abide in the Ground of Extreme Joy nor in its phenomena; it does not abide in the Ground of Purity, the Ground of Radiance, the Ground of Blazing Wisdom, the Ground of Difficult Victory, the Ground of Presence, the Ground of Far-Going, the Ground of Immovability, the Ground of Good Intelligence, or the Ground of Dharma Clouds, nor in their phenomena."
Why is this? Because the Stage of Utmost Joy and the others cannot be apprehended.
"Subhūti!..."

The mind of the Tathāgata does not abide in the stage of ordinary beings or in dharmas; it does not abide in the stage of the spiritual lineage, the eighth stage, the stage of possessing vision, the stage of refinement, the stage of freedom from desire, the stage of having completed what was to be done, the stage of the solitary realizer, the stage of the bodhisattva, nor in the stage of the Tathāgata or in dharmas.
Why is this? Because the stage of ordinary beings and so forth cannot be apprehended.
"Thus it is, Subhūti!"
“The mind of the Tathāgata abides nowhere at all among all phenomena, yet it is not that it does not abide.
Then, the Venerable Subhūti said to Śāriputra:

“In this way, although a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the perfection of wisdom, they are just like the Tathāgata, who abides nowhere at all among all phenomena, yet it is not that he does not abide.”
Why is this? "Śāriputra!

Although a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), he neither dwells nor does not dwell in form (rūpa); likewise, he neither dwells nor does not dwell in feeling (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), formations (saṃskāra), or consciousness (vijñāna)."
Why is this? Because the aggregate of form and the others are characterized by non-duality.
"Śāriputra!..."

Although a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the perfection of wisdom, they neither dwell nor do not dwell in the sense-base of the eye; likewise, they neither dwell nor do not dwell in the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
Why is this? Because the sense base of the eye and so forth are characterized by non-duality.
"Śāriputra!..."

Although a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the perfection of wisdom, he neither dwells nor does not dwell in the sphere of form; likewise, he neither dwells nor does not dwell in the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental phenomena.
Why is this? Because the sense base of form and so forth are without dual characteristics.
"Śāriputra!..."

Although a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the perfection of wisdom, they neither dwell nor do not dwell in the eye-element; likewise, they neither dwell nor do not dwell in the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, eye-contact, or the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition.
Why is this? Because the eye-element and so forth have no dual characteristics.
"Śāriputra!..."

Although a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the perfection of wisdom, they neither dwell nor do not dwell in the element of the ear; likewise, they neither dwell nor do not dwell in the element of sound, the element of ear-consciousness, auditory contact, or the various feelings produced with auditory contact as a condition.
Why is this? Because the ear-element and so forth possess no dual characteristics. "Śāriputra!

Although a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the perfection of wisdom, they neither dwell nor do not dwell in the nose element; they likewise neither dwell nor do not dwell in the odor element, the nose-consciousness element, nose-contact, or the various feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition.
Why is this? Because the nose element and so forth possess no dual characteristics.
"Śāriputra!..."

Although a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the perfection of wisdom, they neither dwell nor do not dwell in the tongue element; they likewise neither dwell nor do not dwell in the taste element, the tongue-consciousness element, tongue-contact, or the various feelings arising with tongue-contact as a condition.
Why is this? Because the tongue-element and so forth possess no dual characteristics.
"Śāriputra!..."

Although a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the perfection of wisdom, they neither dwell nor do not dwell in the body-element; nor do they dwell nor do they not dwell in the touch-element, the body-consciousness-element, body-contact, or the various feelings produced with body-contact as a condition.
Why is this? Because the body-element and so forth are characterized by non-duality.
"Śāriputra!..."

Although a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they neither dwell nor do not dwell in the sphere of mind (manodhātu); likewise, they neither dwell nor do not dwell in the sphere of phenomena (dharmadhātu), the sphere of mental consciousness (manovijñānadhātu), mental contact (manaḥsaṃsparśa), or the various feelings (vedanā) produced with mental contact as a condition.
Why is this? Because the mental faculty (*manodhātu*) and so forth possess no dual characteristics.
"Śāriputra!..."

Although a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the perfection of wisdom, they neither dwell nor do not dwell in the earth element; likewise, they neither dwell nor do not dwell in the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements.
Why is this? Because the earth element and so forth possess no dualistic characteristics.
"Śāriputra!..."

Although a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the perfection of wisdom, they neither dwell nor do not dwell in the noble truth of suffering; likewise, they neither dwell nor do not dwell in the noble truths of origination, cessation, and the path.
Why is this? Because the Noble Truth of Suffering and so forth are characterized by non-duality.
"Śāriputra!..."

Although a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the perfection of wisdom, they neither dwell nor do not dwell in ignorance; likewise, they neither dwell nor do not dwell in volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
Why is this? It is because ignorance and the others lack the characteristic of duality. "Śāriputra!

Although a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), they neither dwell nor do not dwell in internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*); nor do they dwell, nor do they not dwell, in external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, endless emptiness, dispersal emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, emptiness of all phenomena, unapprehendable emptiness, emptiness of non-existence, emptiness of intrinsic nature, or emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature.
Why is this? Because internal emptiness and so forth possess no dual characteristics.
"Śāriputra!..."

Although a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the perfection of wisdom, they neither dwell nor do not dwell in suchness; likewise, they neither dwell nor do not dwell in the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, the non-illusory nature, the unchanging nature, equality, the nature free from birth, the fixed nature of dharmas, the stability of dharmas, the limit of reality, the realm of space, or the inconceivable realm.
Why is this? Because suchness and so forth are characterized by non-duality.
"Śāriputra!..."

Although a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the perfection of wisdom, they neither dwell nor do not dwell in the perfection of generosity; likewise, they neither dwell nor do not dwell in the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
Why is this? Because the perfection of generosity and the others are characterized by non-duality.
"Śāriputra!..."

Although a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they neither dwell nor do not dwell in the four dhyānas; likewise, they neither dwell nor do not dwell in the four immeasurables (apramāṇa) or the four formless absorptions (ārūpyasamāpatti).
Why is this? Because the four dhyānas and so forth are characterized by non-duality.
"Śāriputra!..."

Although a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the perfection of wisdom, they neither dwell nor do not dwell in the eight liberations; likewise, they neither dwell nor do not dwell in the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, or the ten totalities.
Why is this? Because the eight liberations and so forth are characterized by non-duality. "Śāriputra!

Although a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the perfection of wisdom, they neither dwell nor do not dwell in the four foundations of mindfulness; likewise, they neither dwell nor do not dwell in the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the eightfold noble path.
Why is this? Because the four foundations of mindfulness and so forth are characterized by non-duality.
"Śāriputra!..."

Although a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the perfection of wisdom, they neither dwell nor do not dwell in the gate of liberation of emptiness; likewise, they neither dwell nor do not dwell in the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness.
Why is this? Because the gate of liberation of emptiness and so forth are non-dual in their characteristics.
"Śāriputra!..."

Although a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the perfection of wisdom, they neither dwell nor do not dwell in the five eyes; likewise, they neither dwell nor do not dwell in the six supernormal powers.
Why is this? Because the five eyes and so forth are without dual characteristics.
"Śāriputra!..."

Although a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they neither dwell nor do not dwell in the ten powers (daśabala) of a Buddha; likewise, they neither dwell nor do not dwell in the four fearlessnesses (vaiśāradya), the four analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid), great loving-kindness (maitrī), great compassion (karuṇā), great sympathetic joy (muditā), great equanimity (upekṣā), and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (āveṇika-buddhadharma).
Why is this? Because the ten powers of the Buddha and so forth are characterized by non-duality.
"Śāriputra!..."

Although a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the perfection of wisdom, they neither dwell nor do not dwell in the quality of non-forgetfulness; likewise, they neither dwell nor do not dwell in the state of constant equanimity.
Why is this? Because the quality of non-forgetfulness and so forth are characterized by non-duality.
"Śāriputra!..."

Although a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they neither dwell nor do not dwell in any of the doors of dhāraṇī; likewise, they neither dwell nor do not dwell in any of the doors of samādhi.
Why is this? Because all dharanī-doors, etc., are characterized by non-duality.
"Śāriputra!..."

Although a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the perfection of wisdom, they neither dwell nor do not dwell in all-knowledge; likewise, they neither dwell nor do not dwell in the knowledge of the paths or the knowledge of all aspects.
Why is this? Because all-knowledge and so forth are characterized by non-duality.
"Śāriputra!..."

Although a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the perfection of wisdom, they neither dwell nor do not dwell in the vehicle of the śrāvakas; likewise, they neither dwell nor do not dwell in the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas or the unsurpassed vehicle.
Why is this? Because the Śrāvaka vehicle and so forth are without dual characteristics.
"Śāriputra!..."

Although a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the perfection of wisdom, they neither dwell nor do not dwell in the fruit of stream-entry or the path leading toward it; likewise, they neither dwell nor do not dwell in the fruits of once-returner, non-returner, or arhat, nor in the paths leading toward those fruits.
Why is this? Because the stream-enterer and the others are without dualistic characteristics. "Śāriputra!..."

Although a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the perfection of wisdom, they neither dwell nor do not dwell in the pratyekabuddha or the awakening of a pratyekabuddha; nor do they dwell or not dwell in the bodhisattvas, the Tathāgatas, or the dharmas of the bodhisattvas and Tathāgatas.
Why is this? Because Pratyekabuddhas and others are devoid of dualistic characteristics. "Śāriputra!..."

Although a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the perfection of wisdom, they neither dwell nor do not dwell in the Ground of Extreme Joy, nor in the Dharma; they neither dwell nor do not dwell in the Ground of Purity, the Ground of Radiance, the Ground of Blazing Wisdom, the Ground of Difficult Victory, the Ground of Presence, the Ground of Far-Going, the Ground of Immovability, the Ground of Good Intelligence, or the Ground of the Cloud of Dharma, nor in the Dharma.
Why is this? Because the Joyous Ground (pramuditā-bhūmi) and so forth are characterized by non-duality.
"Śāriputra!..."

Although a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the perfection of wisdom, they neither dwell nor do not dwell in the stage of ordinary beings or in phenomena; they neither dwell nor do not dwell in the stage of the spiritual lineage, the eighth stage, the stage of possessing vision, the stage of refinement, the stage of freedom from desire, the stage of completion, the stage of the solitary buddha, the stage of the bodhisattva, or the stage of the Tathāgata, nor in phenomena.
Why is this? Because the stage of ordinary beings and so forth lack the characteristic of duality.
"Śāriputra!..."
A bodhisattva mahāsattva, with respect to the perfection of wisdom, should train in this way by means of non-apprehension: neither abiding nor not abiding.
Chapter 23: The Chapter on the Sons of the Gods (Devaputraparivarta), Part One, Section 23-1. At that time, there were certain sons of the gods in the assembly who thought to themselves:

"The words and incantations of the yakṣas and others, though they may be obscure, can still be understood; yet although the Venerable Subhūti has displayed this Prajñāpāramitā through various modes of expression, we have been unable to comprehend it at all."
Subhūti, knowing what was in their minds, addressed them, saying:
"Do you, sons of the gods, not understand what I have said?
The sons of the gods replied:
"So it is! So it is! The Venerable Subhūti spoke again to him, saying:
"I have not uttered a single word here, nor have you heard anything; what, then, is there to be understood? Why is this?
Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is utterly devoid of letters and verbal expression, within it neither speaker, listener, nor one who understands can be found."
The characteristics of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment realized by all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are likewise profound in this way.
"O Devaputra, you should know this!"

Just as a transformation body of the Buddha might manifest immeasurable bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās who gather together, and further manifest a single person capable of expounding the Dharma to proclaim the sublime teaching within that assembly.
"What do you think?
Is there therein anyone who can truly speak, listen, or understand?
The devaputras replied:
"No, Venerable One! Subhūti replied.
"In this way, O Devaputra!
Because all dharmas are like transformations, within the Prajñā, neither the speaker, the listener, nor the one who understands can be apprehended."
“Son of Heaven, you should know this!
Suppose one were in a dream and saw the Buddha instructing and exhorting bodhisattvas and śrāvakas. What do you think?
Is there therein anyone who truly speaks, listens, or understands?”
The devaputras said:
"No, Venerable One!"
Subhūti replied: “It is so, O Devaputra!
Since all phenomena are like dreams, within the Prajñāpāramitā, neither a speaker, nor a listener, nor one who understands can be apprehended.”
“O Son of Heaven, you should know this!

Suppose there were two people in a single mountain valley, each staying on one side praising the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, and they both produced sounds at the same time. What do you think?”
"Can these two echoes hear each other or understand each other?
The sons of the gods replied, "No!"
"Venerable One!
Subhūti replied, "So it is, O Devaputra!"
Because all phenomena are like echoes, within *prajñā* neither speaker, listener, nor one who understands can be apprehended.
"O Son of Heaven, you should know this!
Suppose a skilled illusionist or his apprentice were at a crossroads to conjure the fourfold assembly and a single Buddha-body standing in their midst preaching the Dharma. What do you think?
"In this, is there anyone who truly exists who can speak, who can listen, or who can understand?
The sons of the gods replied, "No!"
"Venerable One!
Subhūti replied, "So it is, O Devaputra!"
"Because all phenomena are like illusions, within this Prajñāpāramitā, neither the speaker, the listener, nor the one who understands can be apprehended.
At that time, the sons of the gods again had this thought:

"Although the Venerable Subhūti uses various skillful means to explain this Prajñāpāramitā so as to make it easy to understand, its underlying intent is exceedingly profound, even more profound, subtle, and even more subtle, such that it is difficult to fathom."
Subhūti, knowing what was in the mind of that deity, addressed him, saying:
"O Devaputra, you should know this!
Form is neither profound nor subtle; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise neither profound nor subtle."

Why is this? Because the profound and subtle nature of form cannot be apprehended, and the profound and subtle natures of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness likewise cannot be apprehended.
"O Son of Heaven, you should know this!"
The eye-base is neither profound nor subtle; the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases are likewise neither profound nor subtle. Why is this?

Because the profound and subtle nature of the eye-base cannot be apprehended, and because the profound and subtle natures of the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-bases likewise cannot be apprehended.
"O Son of Heaven, you should know this!"
The sphere of form is neither profound nor subtle; the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena are likewise neither profound nor subtle. Why is this so?

Because the subtle nature of the sense-base of form cannot be apprehended, and because the subtle natures of the sense-bases of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena likewise cannot be apprehended.
"O Devaputra, you should know this!"

The eye-element is neither profound nor subtle; the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, as well as eye-contact and the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, are also neither profound nor subtle.

Why is this? Because the subtle nature of the eye-element cannot be apprehended, and because the subtle nature of the form-element, up to and including the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, likewise cannot be apprehended.
"O Son of Heaven, you should know this!

The ear-element is neither profound nor subtle; the sound-element, the ear-consciousness-element, as well as ear-contact and all feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition, are likewise neither profound nor subtle."

Why is this? Because the subtle and profound nature of the ear-element (*śrotra-dhātu*) cannot be apprehended; likewise, the subtle and profound nature of the sound-element (*śabda-dhātu*) and even all sensations produced with ear-contact as a condition (*śrotra-saṃsparśa-pratyaya-ja-vedanā*) cannot be apprehended.
“O Son of Heaven, you should know this!

The nose element is neither profound nor subtle; the odor element, the nose-consciousness element, as well as nose-contact and the various sensations produced with nose-contact as a condition, are likewise neither profound nor subtle.”

Why is this? Because the subtle and profound nature of the nose-element (*ghrāṇadhātu*) cannot be apprehended, and because the subtle and profound nature of everything from the odor-element (*gandhadhātu*) up to the various sensations produced with nose-contact as a condition (*ghrāṇasparśapratyayaja-vedanā*) also cannot be apprehended.
“Son of Heaven, you should know!

The tongue-element is neither profound nor subtle; the taste-element, the tongue-consciousness-element, as well as tongue-contact and all sensations produced with tongue-contact as a condition, are likewise neither profound nor subtle.”

Why is this? Because the subtle nature of the tongue element cannot be apprehended, and because the subtle nature of everything from the taste element up to the various sensations produced with tongue-contact as a condition also cannot be apprehended.
“O Son of Heaven, you should know this!

The body element is neither profound nor subtle; the tangible element, the body-consciousness element, as well as body-contact and the various feelings produced with body-contact as a condition, are likewise neither profound nor subtle.”

Why is this? Because the subtle nature of the body element (*kāyadhātu*) cannot be apprehended, and because the subtle nature of the tangible object element (*spraṣṭavyadhātu*) up to the various feelings (*vedanā*) produced with body-contact as a condition also cannot be apprehended.
“O Son of Heaven, you should know this!

The mind-element is neither profound nor subtle; the dharma-element, the mind-consciousness-element, as well as mind-contact and the various feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition, are likewise neither profound nor subtle.”

Why is this? Because the profound subtlety of the mind-element (*manodhātu*) cannot be apprehended, and because the profound subtlety of everything from the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*) up to the various sensations produced with mind-contact as a condition (*manas-saṃsparśapratyaya-ja-vedanā*) likewise cannot be apprehended.
“O Son of Heaven, you should know that the earth element is neither profound nor subtle; likewise, the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements are neither profound nor subtle.”

Why is this? Because the subtle and profound nature of the earth element cannot be apprehended, and the subtle and profound natures of the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements likewise cannot be apprehended.
“O Son of Heaven, you should know this!
The Noble Truth of Suffering is neither profound nor subtle; the Noble Truths of Origination, Cessation, and the Path are likewise neither profound nor subtle.”

Why is this? Because the profound and subtle nature of the Noble Truth of Suffering cannot be apprehended, and the profound and subtle natures of the Noble Truths of Origination, Cessation, and the Path likewise cannot be apprehended.
“O Son of Heaven, you should know this!

Ignorance is neither profound nor subtle; volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, and old age, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are likewise neither profound nor subtle.”

Why is this? Because the subtle and profound nature of ignorance cannot be apprehended, and because the subtle and profound nature of everything from volitional formations up to old age, death, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair likewise cannot be apprehended.
“Son of Heaven, you should know this!

Internal emptiness is neither profound nor subtle; external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-altering emptiness, essential emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common-characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence are likewise neither profound nor subtle.”

Why is this? Because the profound and subtle nature of internal emptiness cannot be apprehended, and likewise, the profound and subtle nature of external emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of non-existence and intrinsic nature, cannot be apprehended.
“O Son of Heaven, you should know this!

Suchness is neither profound nor subtle; the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), the non-illusory nature, the unchanging nature, the nature of equality, the nature free from arising, the fixedness of phenomena, the stability of phenomena, the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm are likewise neither profound nor subtle.”

Why is this? Because the profound and subtle nature of true thusness (tathatā) cannot be apprehended, and because the profound and subtle natures of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), up to and including the inconceivable realm (acintyadhātu), likewise cannot be apprehended.
“O Son of Heaven, you should know this!

The perfection of generosity is neither profound nor subtle; the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom are likewise neither profound nor subtle.”

Why is this? Because the profound and subtle nature of the perfection of generosity cannot be apprehended, and likewise, the profound and subtle nature of the perfections from ethical discipline up to wisdom cannot be apprehended.
“O Son of Heaven, you should know this!
The four dhyānas are neither profound nor subtle; the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments are likewise neither profound nor subtle.”

Why is this? Because the subtle and profound nature of the four dhyānas cannot be apprehended, and the subtle and profound nature of the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions likewise cannot be apprehended.
“Son of Heaven, you should know!
The eight liberations are neither profound nor subtle; the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities are likewise neither profound nor subtle.”

Why is this? Because the subtle and profound nature of the eight liberations cannot be apprehended, and because the subtle and profound nature of the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten totalities likewise cannot be apprehended.
“O Son of Heaven, you should know this!

The four foundations of mindfulness are neither profound nor subtle; the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path are likewise neither profound nor subtle.”

Why is this? Because the profound subtlety of the four foundations of mindfulness cannot be apprehended, and the profound subtlety of the four right efforts up to the eightfold noble path likewise cannot be apprehended.
“Son of Heaven, you should know this!
The five eyes are neither profound nor subtle; the six supernormal powers are likewise neither profound nor subtle. Why is this so?
Because the profound and subtle nature of the five eyes cannot be apprehended, and because the profound and subtle nature of the six supernormal powers also cannot be apprehended.
"O Son of Heaven, you should know!

The ten powers of a Buddha are neither profound nor subtle; the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are likewise neither profound nor subtle."

Why is this? Because the profound and subtle nature of the Buddha’s ten powers cannot be apprehended, and because the profound and subtle nature of the four fearlessnesses, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, likewise cannot be apprehended.
“Son of Heaven, you should know!
The quality of non-forgetfulness is neither profound nor subtle; the state of constant abiding in equanimity is likewise neither profound nor subtle. Why is this so?
Because the profound subtlety of the quality of non-forgetfulness cannot be apprehended, and because the profound subtlety of the state of constant equanimity also cannot be apprehended.
"O Son of Heaven, you should know this!
All dharani-doors are neither profound nor subtle; all samadhi-doors as well are neither profound nor subtle. Why is this?
Because the profound and subtle nature of all dharanī-gates cannot be apprehended, and because the profound and subtle nature of all samādhi-gates likewise cannot be apprehended.
"O Son of Heaven, you should know this!"

All-knowledge (sarvajñatā) is neither profound nor subtle; the knowledge of the aspects of the path (mārgākārajñatā) and the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā) are likewise neither profound nor subtle. Why is this?

Because the subtle nature of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) cannot be apprehended, and because the subtle natures of the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) likewise cannot be apprehended.
"O Son of Heaven, you should know this!"
The Śrāvaka vehicle is neither profound nor subtle; the Pratyekabuddha vehicle and the Unsurpassed Vehicle (Anuttarayāna) are likewise neither profound nor subtle. Why is this?
Because the profound and subtle nature of the Śrāvaka vehicle cannot be apprehended, and the profound and subtle nature of the Pratyekabuddha and Unsurpassed vehicles likewise cannot be apprehended.
“Son of Heaven, you should know this!
The stream-enterer is neither profound nor subtle; the once-returner, the non-returner, and the arhat are likewise neither profound nor subtle.”

Why is this? Because the subtle and profound nature of the stream-enterer cannot be apprehended, and the subtle and profound natures of the once-returner, the non-returner, and the arhat likewise cannot be apprehended.
“Son of Heaven, you should know this!

The stage of entering the stream and the fruit of stream-entry are neither profound nor subtle; likewise, the stages of entering once-returning and the fruit of once-returning, the stages of entering non-returning and the fruit of non-returning, and the stages of entering arhatship and the fruit of arhatship are also neither profound nor subtle.”

Why is this? Because the profound and subtle nature of the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry and the fruit of stream-entry cannot be apprehended; likewise, the profound and subtle nature of the candidate for the fruit of once-returning and the fruit of once-returning, up to the candidate for arhatship and the fruit of arhatship, also cannot be apprehended.
“Son of Heaven, you should know this!
The Pratyekabuddha is neither profound nor subtle; the path leading toward the fruit of a Pratyekabuddha is likewise neither profound nor subtle. Why is this?
Because the profound and subtle nature of the pratyekabuddha cannot be apprehended, and because the profound and subtle nature of the pratyekabuddha’s path and its fruit also cannot be apprehended.
"O Son of Heaven, you should know this!"
The bodhisattva mahāsattva is neither profound nor subtle, and the samyaksaṃbuddha is likewise neither profound nor subtle. Why is this?
Because the profound and subtle nature of the bodhisattva mahāsattva cannot be apprehended, and the profound and subtle nature of the samyaksaṃbuddha likewise cannot be apprehended.
“Son of Heaven, you should know this!
The Dharma of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is neither profound nor subtle; unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment is likewise neither profound nor subtle.”

Why is this? Because the profound and subtle nature of the dharmas of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot be apprehended, and the profound and subtle nature of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment likewise cannot be apprehended.
“Son of Heaven, you should know this!

The Ground of Utmost Joy is neither profound nor subtle; the Ground of Freedom from Defilement, the Ground of Radiant Light, the Ground of Blazing Wisdom, the Ground of Extreme Difficulty to Conquer, the Ground of Manifestation, the Ground of Far-Going, the Ground of Immovability, the Ground of Excellent Wisdom, and the Ground of the Dharma Cloud are likewise neither profound nor subtle.”

Why is this? Because the profound and subtle nature of the Stage of Utmost Joy cannot be apprehended, and likewise, the profound and subtle natures of the Stages from the Stainless up to the Cloud of Dharma cannot be apprehended.
“O Son of Heaven, you should know this!

The dharmas of the Stage of Utmost Joy are neither profound nor subtle; the dharmas of the Stage Free from Defilement, the Stage of Radiant Light, the Stage of Blazing Wisdom, the Stage Difficult to Conquer, the Stage of Presence, the Stage of Far-Going, the Stage of Immovability, the Stage of Excellent Intelligence, and the Stage of the Cloud of Dharma are likewise neither profound nor subtle.”

Why is this? Because the subtle and profound nature of the dharmas of the Stage of Utmost Joy cannot be apprehended, and likewise, the subtle and profound nature of the dharmas from the Stage Free from Defilement up to the Stage of the Cloud of Dharma cannot be apprehended.
“Son of Heaven, you should know this!

The stage of ordinary beings is neither profound nor subtle; likewise, the stage of the spiritual lineage, the eighth stage, the stage of possessing vision, the stage of refinement, the stage of freedom from desire, the stage of completion, the stage of the solitary realizer, the stage of the bodhisattva, and the stage of the Tathāgata are also neither profound nor subtle.”

Why is this? Because the profound and subtle nature of the stage of ordinary beings cannot be apprehended, and because the profound and subtle natures of the stages from the lineage stage up to the stage of the Tathāgata likewise cannot be apprehended.
“O Son of Heaven, you should know!

The dharmas of the stage of ordinary beings are neither profound nor subtle; likewise, the dharmas of the stage of the spiritual lineage, the eighth stage, the stage of possessing vision, the stage of refinement, the stage of freedom from desire, the stage of completion, the stage of the solitary realizer, the stage of the bodhisattva, and the stage of the Tathāgata are also neither profound nor subtle.”

Why is this? Because the subtle and profound nature of the dharmas of the stage of ordinary beings cannot be apprehended, and because the subtle and profound nature of the dharmas of the stages from the lineage stage up to the Tathāgata stage likewise cannot be apprehended.
Then, those sons of the gods again had this thought:
"In the Dharma taught by the Venerable Subhūti, form is not established, nor are feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness established."
Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of the aggregate of form cannot be expressed.
"In the Dharma taught by the Venerable Subhūti, the sense base of the eye is not established, nor are the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind established."
Why is this? Because the nature of the sense base of the eye, and so forth, is ineffable.
"In the Dharma taught by the Venerable Subhūti, he does not designate the sense base of form, nor does he designate the sense bases of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental phenomena."
Why is this? Because the nature of the sphere of form and so forth is ineffable.

Within the Dharma taught by the Venerable Subhūti, there is no designation of the eye-element, nor the designation of the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, or eye-contact, nor the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition.
Why is this? Because the nature of the eye-element and so forth is ineffable.

Within the Dharma taught by the Venerable Subhūti, there is no designation of the ear-element, no designation of the sound-element, the ear-consciousness-element, nor of ear-contact, nor of the various feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition.
Why is this? Because the nature of the ear-element is itself ineffable.

Within the Dharma taught by the Venerable Subhūti, there is no designation of a nose-element, nor a fragrance-element, nor a nose-consciousness-element, nor nose-contact, nor any feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition.
Why is this? Because the nature of the nose-element (*ghrāṇadhātu*) is itself inexpressible.

Within the Dharma taught by the Venerable Subhūti, there is no designation of the tongue-element (*jihvādhātu*), no designation of the taste-element (*rasadhātu*), the tongue-consciousness-element (*jihvāvijñānadhātu*), tongue-contact (*jihvāsaṃsparśa*), nor any feelings (*vedanā*) produced with tongue-contact as a condition.
Why is this? Because the nature of the tongue-element (*jihvā-dhātu*) is ineffable.

"In the Dharma taught by the Venerable Subhūti, there is no establishment of the body-element (*kāya-dhātu*), nor the establishment of the touch-element (*spraṣṭavya-dhātu*), the body-consciousness-element (*kāya-vijñāna-dhātu*), body-contact (*kāya-saṃsparśa*), or the various feelings (*vedanā*) produced with body-contact as a condition."
Why is this? Because the nature of the body-element and so forth is ineffable.

"In the Dharma taught by the Venerable Subhūti, the mind-element is not established; the dharma-element, the mind-consciousness-element, as well as mind-contact and the various feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition, are not established."
Why is this? Because the nature of the mental element (*manodhātu*) is ineffable.
"In the Dharma taught by the Venerable Subhūti, the earth element is not established, nor are the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements established."
Why is this? Because the nature of the earth element is ineffable.
"Within the Dharma taught by the Venerable Subhūti, the Noble Truth of Suffering is not established, nor are the Noble Truths of Origination, Cessation, and the Path established."
Why is this? Because the nature of the Noble Truth of Suffering is ultimately ineffable.

Within the Dharma taught by the Venerable Subhūti, there is no designation of ignorance; nor is there any designation of volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
Why is this? Because the nature of ignorance and so forth is ineffable.

"In the Dharma taught by the Venerable Subhūti, he does not designate internal emptiness; he does not designate external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersion emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common-characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all dharmas, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, or the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature."
Why is this? Because the nature of internal emptiness and so forth is ineffable.

Within the Dharma taught by the Venerable Subhūti, he does not designate *tathatā* (suchness), nor does he designate the *dharmadhātu* (dharma-realm), the *dharmatā* (dharma-nature), the non-falsity, the immutability, the equality, the state of being free from birth, the fixedness of dharma, the stability of dharma, the limit of reality, the realm of space, or the inconceivable realm.
Why is this? Because the nature of true suchness (tathatā) and so forth is ineffable.

"In the Dharma taught by the Venerable Subhūti, there is no designation of the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā), nor is there any designation of the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, or wisdom."
Why is this? Because the nature of the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā) and so forth is ineffable.
"In the Dharma taught by the Venerable Subhūti, the four dhyānas are not established, nor are the four immeasurables (apramāṇa) or the four formless attainments (ārūpyasamāpatti) established."
Why is this? Because the nature of the four dhyānas is ineffable.

Within the Dharma taught by the Venerable Subhūti, he does not designate the eight liberations, nor does he designate the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, or the ten totalities.
Why is this? Because the nature of the eight liberations is itself ineffable.

Within the Dharma taught by the Venerable Subhūti, there is no establishment of the four foundations of mindfulness, nor the establishment of the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the eightfold noble path.
Why is this? Because the nature of the four foundations of mindfulness is itself ineffable.
Within the Dharma taught by the Venerable Subhūti, he does not posit the gate of liberation of emptiness, nor does he posit the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness.
Why is this? Because the nature of the liberation door of emptiness is ineffable.
Within the Dharma taught by the Venerable Subhūti, the five eyes are not established, nor are the six supernormal powers established.
Why is this? Because the nature of the five eyes is ineffable.

Within the Dharma taught by the Venerable Subhūti, one does not designate the ten powers of a Buddha, nor does one designate the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
Why is this? Because the nature of the ten powers of a Buddha is ineffable.
Within the Dharma taught by the Venerable Subhūti, there is no establishment of the quality of non-forgetfulness, nor is there any establishment of the nature of constant equanimity.
Why is this? Because the nature of the dharma of non-forgetfulness is itself ineffable.
Within the Dharma taught by the Venerable Subhūti, no gateways of dhāraṇī are established, nor are any gateways of samādhi established.
Why is this? Because the nature of all dhāraṇī-doors is ineffable.

Within the Dharma taught by the Venerable Subhūti, there is no designation of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), nor is there any designation of the knowledge of the paths (*mārgākārajñatā*) or the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Why is this? Because the nature of all-knowledge (sarvajñatā) is itself ineffable.
"In the Dharma taught by the Venerable Subhūti, there is no establishment of the Śrāvaka vehicle, no establishment of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, nor of the Unsurpassed Vehicle."
Why is this? Because the nature of the Śrāvaka vehicle cannot be described.
"In the Dharma taught by the Venerable Subhūti, there is no designation of stream-enterers, no designation of once-returners, no designation of non-returners, and no designation of arhats."
Why is this? Because the nature of stream-entry and so forth is inexpressible.

"In the Dharma taught by the Venerable Subhūti, there is no designation of the candidate for stream-entry or the fruit of stream-entry; there is no designation of the candidate for once-returning or the fruit of once-returning, the candidate for non-returning or the fruit of non-returning, or the candidate for arhatship or the fruit of arhatship."
Why is this? Because the nature of one who has entered the stream, the fruit of stream-entry, and so forth, cannot be described.

"In the Dharma taught by the Venerable Subhūti, there is no designation of a pratyekabuddha, nor is there any designation of one who is a candidate for pratyekabuddhahood or the fruit of pratyekabuddhahood."
Why is this? Because the nature of a pratyekabuddha cannot be described.
"In the Dharma taught by the Venerable Subhūti, no bodhisattva-mahāsattva is established, nor is a samyaksaṃbuddha established."
Why is this? Because the nature of the bodhisattva mahāsattva is itself inexpressible.
Within the Dharma taught by the Venerable Subhūti, one does not designate the dharma of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, nor does one designate unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Why is this? Because the dharma-nature of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is inherently ineffable.

Within the Dharma taught by the Venerable Subhūti, there is no designation of the Ground of Extreme Joy, nor is there any designation of the Ground of Purity, the Ground of Radiance, the Ground of Blazing Wisdom, the Ground of Supreme Difficulty to Conquer, the Ground of Presence, the Ground of Far-Going, the Ground of Immovability, the Ground of Excellent Intelligence, or the Ground of the Dharma Cloud.
Why is this? Because the nature of the Ground of Supreme Joy (pramuditā-bhūmi) and so forth is ineffable.

Within the Dharma taught by the Venerable Subhūti, he does not designate the dharmas of the Ground of Supreme Joy; nor does he designate the dharmas of the Ground of Purity (vimalā-bhūmi), the Ground of Radiance (prabhākari-bhūmi), the Ground of Blazing Wisdom (arciṣmatī-bhūmi), the Ground Difficult to Conquer (sudurjayā-bhūmi), the Ground of Presence (abhimukhī-bhūmi), the Ground of Far-Going (dūraṅgamā-bhūmi), the Ground of Immovability (acalā-bhūmi), the Ground of Good Intelligence (sādhumatī-bhūmi), or the Ground of the Cloud of Dharma (dharmameghā-bhūmi).
Why is this? Because the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) in the Stage of Utmost Joy is ultimately ineffable.

Within the Dharma taught by the Venerable Subhūti, there is no designation of the stage of ordinary beings, nor the designation of the stage of the spiritual lineage, the eighth stage, the stage of those with vision, the stage of refinement, the stage of freedom from desire, the stage of completion, the stage of the solitary realizer, the stage of the bodhisattva, or the stage of the Tathāgata.
Why is this? Because the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanabhūmi*) and so forth cannot be described.

"In the Dharma taught by the Venerable Subhūti, there is no establishment of the dharmas of the stage of an ordinary person; there is no establishment of the dharmas of the stage of the lineage (*gotrabhūmi*), the stage of the eighth person (*aṣṭamaka-bhūmi*), the stage of possessing vision (*darśana-bhūmi*), the stage of refinement (*tanu-bhūmi*), the stage of freedom from desire (*vītarāga-bhūmi*), the stage of having completed what was to be done (*kṛtāvī-bhūmi*), the stage of a solitary buddha (*pratyekabuddha-bhūmi*), the stage of a bodhisattva (*bodhisattva-bhūmi*), or the stage of a Tathāgata (*tathāgata-bhūmi*)."
Why is this? Because the dharma-nature and so forth of the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana-bhūmi*) are ineffable.
Furthermore, within the Dharma taught by the Venerable Subhūti, there is no establishment of written characters or verbal expressions.
"Why is this? It is because the nature of letters and language is inherently ineffable.
At that time, Subhūti, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the devaputras, addressed them, saying:
"So it is! So it is! It is just as you have reflected."

All phenomena, up to and including unsurpassed enlightenment, cannot be reached by words or language; therefore, within the Prajñāpāramitā there is nothing spoken, nothing heard, and no one who understands. For this reason, among all phenomena, you should cultivate firm patience in accordance with what has been taught.
All those who wish to abide in or realize the fruit of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, or arhatship, also attain their ultimate goal by relying on this patience;
all those who wish to abide in or realize the enlightenment attained by a pratyekabuddha, also attain their ultimate goal by relying on this patience;
and all those who wish to abide in or realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, must rely on this patience to attain their ultimate goal.
Thus it is, O sons of the gods!

From the first generation of the mind of awakening until the ultimate goal, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should abide in this profound *prajñāpāramitā*—which is without speaking, without listening, and without understanding—and should constantly and diligently practice it without ever abandoning it.
At that time, the sons of the gods again thought to themselves:
"For what kind of sentient beings does the Venerable Subhūti now wish to preach what Dharma?
Subhūti, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the sons of the gods, then addressed them, saying:
“Son of Heaven, you should know!
I now wish to preach the Dharma that is like an illusion, like a transformation, and like a dream, for those sentient beings who are like illusions, like transformations, and like dreams.”
"Why is this? Because such listeners have neither heard, nor understood, nor realized anything within what has been spoken.
At that time, the sons of the gods again asked:
"Are the one who speaks, the one who listens, and the Dharma that is taught all like an illusion, like a magical transformation,
and like a dream? Subhūti replied, "So it is!"
So it is! It is as you have said.

Just as illusory beings speak the illusory Dharma for illusory beings, as conjured beings speak the conjured Dharma for conjured beings, and as dream-beings speak the dream-like Dharma for dream-beings.
"O Son of Heaven, you should know this!

I am like an illusion, like a transformation, like a dream. The sentient beings, life-principles, born beings, nourished beings, persons (*puruṣa*), individuals (*pudgala*), mind-born beings (*manuja*), young scholars (*māṇava*), agents, experiencers, knowers, and seers that I perceive are like illusions, like transformations, like things seen in a dream."
Why is this? Because our own intrinsic nature is empty.
"O Son of Heaven, you should know this!

Form is like an illusion, like a transformation, like what is seen in a dream; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are like an illusion, like a transformation, like what is seen in a dream.
Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) and the others is empty.
"O Son of Heaven, you should know this!

The sense base of the eye is like an illusion, like a transformation, like what is seen in a dream; the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are like an illusion, like a transformation, like what is seen in a dream.
Why is this? Because the sense bases, such as the eye, are empty of intrinsic nature.
"O Devaputra, you should know this!"

The sphere of form is like an illusion, like a transformation, like what is seen in a dream; the spheres of sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena are like an illusion, like a transformation, like what is seen in a dream.
Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of the sense-base of form and so forth is empty.
"O Son of Heaven, you should know this!"

The eye-element is like an illusion, like a transformation, like what is seen in a dream; the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, eye-contact, and all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition are like an illusion, like a transformation, like what is seen in a dream.
Why is this? Because the nature of the eye-sphere and so forth is empty.
"O Son of Heaven, you should know this!

The ear element is like an illusion, like a transformation, like what is seen in a dream; the sound element, the ear-consciousness element, as well as ear-contact and all sensations produced with ear-contact as a condition, are like an illusion, like a transformation, like what is seen in a dream.
Why is this? Because the nature of the auditory element (*śrotradhātu*) and so forth is empty.
"O Son of Heaven, you should know this!

The nose element is like an illusion, like a transformation, like what is seen in a dream; the fragrance element, the nose-consciousness element, as well as nose-contact and the various feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition, are like an illusion, like a transformation, like what is seen in a dream.
Why is this? Because the nature of the nose-element and so forth is empty.
"O Son of Heaven, you should know this!"

The tongue element is like an illusion, like a transformation, like what is seen in a dream; the taste element, the tongue-consciousness element, and tongue-contact, as well as all feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition, are like an illusion, like a transformation, like what is seen in a dream.
Why is this? Because the tongue-element and so forth are empty of intrinsic nature.
"O Son of Heaven, you should know this!

The body element is like an illusion, like a transformation, like what is seen in a dream; the tangible object element, the body-consciousness element, as well as body-contact and the various feelings produced with body-contact as a condition, are like an illusion, like a transformation, like what is seen in a dream.
Why is this? Because the nature of the body-element (*kāyadhātu*) and so forth is empty of intrinsic nature.
"O Devaputra, you should know this!"

The mind-element is like an illusion, like a transformation, like what is seen in a dream; the dharma-element, the mind-consciousness-element, as well as mind-contact and the various feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition, are like an illusion, like a transformation, like what is seen in a dream.
Why is this? Because the nature of the mental realm (*manodhātu*) and so forth is empty.
"O Son of Heaven, you should know this!

The earth element is like a magical illusion, like a transformation, like what is seen in a dream; the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements are like a magical illusion, like a transformation, like what is seen in a dream.
Why is this? Because the self-nature of the earth element and so forth is empty.
"O Son of Heaven, you should know this!

The noble truth of suffering is like an illusion, like a transformation, like what is seen in a dream; the noble truths of origination, cessation, and the path are like an illusion, like a transformation, like what is seen in a dream.
Why is this? Because the noble truth of suffering and the others are empty of intrinsic nature.
"O Devaputra, you should know this!

Ignorance is like an illusion, like a transformation, like what is seen in a dream; volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, and old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair are like illusions, like transformations, like what is seen in a dream.
Why is this? Because ignorance and the other [afflictions] are empty of intrinsic nature.
"O Son of Heaven, you should know this!

Inner emptiness is like an illusion, like a transformation, like what is seen in a dream; outer emptiness, inner-and-outer emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate truth, the emptiness of conditioned phenomena, the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, the emptiness of dispersion, the emptiness of non-alteration, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the emptiness of self-characteristics, the emptiness of common characteristics, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of non-apprehensibility, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature are like an illusion, like a transformation, like what is seen in a dream.
Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of internal emptiness and so forth is itself empty.
"O Son of Heaven, you should know this!"

Suchness is like a magical illusion, like a transformation, like what is seen in a dream; the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, the non-falsity, the unchanging nature, the equality, the state beyond birth, the fixedness of dharmas, the stability of dharmas, the limit of reality, the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm are like a magical illusion, like a transformation, like what is seen in a dream.
Why is this? Because suchness and so forth are empty of intrinsic nature.
*Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Scroll 81.
The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Scroll Eighty-Two.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
Part One: Chapter Twenty-Three, "The Various Devaputras," Part Two.
“Son of Heaven, you should know!

The perfection of generosity is like an illusion, like a transformation, like a dream; the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom are like an illusion, like a transformation, like a dream.”
Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of the perfection of generosity and the others is empty.
"O Son of Heaven, you should know this!"

The four dhyānas are like an illusion, like a transformation, like what is seen in a dream; the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments are like an illusion, like a transformation, like what is seen in a dream.
Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of the four dhyānas and so forth is empty.
"O Son of Heaven, you should know this!

The eight liberations are like an illusion, like a transformation, like what is seen in a dream; the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten totalities are like an illusion, like a transformation, like what is seen in a dream.
Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of the eight liberations and so forth is empty.
"O Son of Heaven, you should know this!"

The four foundations of mindfulness are like an illusion, like a transformation, like what is seen in a dream; the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path are like an illusion, like a transformation, like what is seen in a dream.
Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of the four foundations of mindfulness and so forth is empty.
"O Son of Heaven, you should know this!"

The gate of liberation of emptiness is like an illusion, like a transformation, and like what is seen in a dream; the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness are like an illusion, like a transformation, and like what is seen in a dream.
Why is this? Because the self-nature of the gate of liberation through emptiness and so forth is itself empty.
"O Son of Heaven, you should know this!"
The five eyes are like illusions, like transformations, like what is seen in a dream; the six supernormal powers are like illusions, like transformations, like what is seen in a dream. Why is this?
Because the five eyes and so forth are empty of intrinsic nature.
"O Son of Heaven, you should know!

The ten powers of a Buddha are like an illusion, like a transformation, like what is seen in a dream; the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered understandings, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are like an illusion, like a transformation, like what is seen in a dream."
Why is this? Because the ten powers of the Buddha and so forth are empty of intrinsic nature.
"O Son of Heaven, you should know this!

The quality of non-forgetfulness is like an illusion, like a transformation, like what is seen in a dream; the state of constant dwelling in equanimity is like an illusion, like a transformation, like what is seen in a dream.
Why is this? Because the nature of the dharmas such as non-forgetfulness is empty.
"O Son of Heaven, you should know this!
All dharani-doors are like illusions, like transformations, and like what is seen in a dream; all samadhi-doors are like illusions, like transformations, and like what is seen in a dream.
Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of all dharani-gates and so forth is empty.
"O Son of Heaven, you should know this!

All-knowledge is like an illusion, like a transformation, like what is seen in a dream; the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects are like an illusion, like a transformation, like what is seen in a dream.
Why is this? Because the self-nature of all-knowledge and so forth is empty.
"O Son of Heaven, you should know this!

The Śrāvaka vehicle is like an illusion, like a transformation, like what is seen in a dream; the Pratyekabuddha vehicle and the Unsurpassed Vehicle are like an illusion, like a transformation, like what is seen in a dream.
Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the Śrāvaka vehicle and so forth is empty.
"O Son of Heaven, you should know this!

The stream-enterer is like an illusion, like a transformation, like what is seen in a dream; the once-returner, the non-returner, and the arhat are like an illusion, like a transformation, like what is seen in a dream.
Why is this? Because the nature of those such as the stream-enterers is empty.
"O Son of Heaven, you should know this!

The candidate for the fruit of stream-entry and the fruit of stream-entry are like an illusion, like a transformation, like what is seen in a dream; the candidate for the fruit of once-returning and the fruit of once-returning, the candidate for the fruit of non-returning and the fruit of non-returning, and the candidate for the fruit of arhatship and the fruit of arhatship are like an illusion, like a transformation, like what is seen in a dream.
Why is this? Because the nature of those who are stream-enterers, the fruit of stream-entry, and so forth, is empty.
"O Son of Heaven, you should know this!

The pratyekabuddha is like an illusion, like a transformation, like what is seen in a dream; the pratyekabuddha’s progress toward the fruit of a pratyekabuddha is like an illusion, like a transformation, like what is seen in a dream.
Why is this? Because the self-nature of the pratyekabuddhas and others is empty.
"O Son of Heaven, you should know this!"
A bodhisattva mahāsattva is like an illusion, like a transformation, like what is seen in a dream; a samyaksaṃbuddha is like an illusion, like a transformation, like what is seen in a dream.
Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and so forth is empty.
"O Son of Heaven, you should know this!"

The dharmas of a bodhisattva mahāsattva are like an illusion, like a transformation, like what is seen in a dream; unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment is like an illusion, like a transformation, like what is seen in a dream.
Why is this? Because the dharmas of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva are empty of intrinsic nature.
"O Son of Heaven, you should know this!"

The Ground of Utmost Joy is like an illusion, like a transformation, like a dream-vision; the Ground Free from Defilement, the Ground of Radiant Light, the Ground of Blazing Wisdom, the Ground of Supreme Difficulty to Conquer, the Ground of Manifestation, the Ground of Far-Going, the Ground of Immovability, the Ground of Excellent Intelligence, and the Ground of the Dharma-Cloud are like illusions, like transformations, like dream-visions.
Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of the Stage of Extreme Joy and the others is empty.
"O Son of Heaven, you should know this!

The dharmas of the Stage of Utmost Joy are like an illusion, like a transformation, like what is seen in a dream; the dharmas of the Stage Free from Defilement, the dharmas of the Stage of Radiant Light, the dharmas of the Stage of Blazing Wisdom, the dharmas of the Stage Difficult to Conquer, the dharmas of the Stage of Presence, the dharmas of the Stage of Far-Going, the dharmas of the Immovable Stage, the dharmas of the Stage of Excellent Intelligence, and the dharmas of the Stage of the Cloud of Dharma are like an illusion, like a transformation, like what is seen in a dream.
Why is this? Because the dharmas of the Stage of Utmost Joy (pramuditā-bhūmi) and so forth are empty of intrinsic nature (svabhāva-śūnya).
"O Devaputra, you should know this!

The stage of the ordinary person is like an illusion, like a transformation, like what is seen in a dream; the stage of the spiritual lineage, the eighth stage, the stage of having seen the truths, the stage of refinement, the stage of freedom from desire, the stage of completion, the stage of the solitary realizer, the stage of the bodhisattva, and the stage of the Tathāgata are like an illusion, like a transformation, like what is seen in a dream.
Why is this? Because the nature of the stage of ordinary beings and so forth is empty.
"O Son of Heaven, you should know this!"

The dharmas of the stage of ordinary beings are like an illusion, like a transformation, like what is seen in a dream; the dharmas of the stage of the spiritual lineage, the eighth stage, the stage of possessing vision, the stage of refinement, the stage of freedom from desire, the stage of completion, the stage of the pratyekabuddha, the stage of the bodhisattva, and the stage of the Tathāgata are like an illusion, like a transformation, like what is seen in a dream.
Why is this? Because the nature of the dharmas of the stage of ordinary beings is empty of self-nature.
"O Son of Heaven, you should know this!

The conditioned realm is like an illusion, like a transformation, like what is seen in a dream; the unconditioned realm is like an illusion, like a transformation, like what is seen in a dream. Why is this so?
Because the conditioned realm and so forth are empty of intrinsic nature.
"O Son of Heaven, you should know!
For this reason, I have made this statement:"

Just as illusory sentient beings teach illusory dharmas to illusory beings, as conjured sentient beings teach conjured dharmas to conjured beings, and as dream-like sentient beings teach dream-like dharmas to dream-like beings.
Then the sons of the gods asked Subhūti:

"Does the Venerable One now teach only that we, and everything from form up to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, are like an illusion, like a transformation, and like what is seen in a dream; or does he also teach that subtle, tranquil, and ultimate nirvāṇa is like an illusion, like a transformation, and like what is seen in a dream?"
Subhūti said: "O sons of the gods!

I do not merely say that 'self,' 'form,' and so forth, up to 'unsurpassed perfect enlightenment,' are like illusions, like transformations, and like things seen in a dream; I also proclaim that subtle, tranquil, ultimate nirvāṇa is likewise like an illusion, like a transformation, and like something seen in a dream."
"O Son of Heaven, you should know!
Even if there were another dharma superior to nirvāṇa, I would likewise declare it to be like an illusion, like a transformation, like what is seen in a dream. Why is this so? Because..."
"Because illusions, transformations, and dream-phenomena, as well as all dharmas up to and including *nirvāṇa*, are entirely non-dual and indivisible.

Chapter 24: Receiving the Teaching, Part One. Section 24.1: Receiving the Teaching. At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, the Venerable Mahākoṣṭhila, the Venerable Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, the Venerable Mahākātyāyana, and other great *śrāvakas*, together with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, simultaneously raised their voices and addressed Subhūti:

"This Prajñāpāramitā that has been taught is thus profound, difficult to see, and difficult to realize; it is beyond the sphere of discursive thought and transcends the reach of investigation. It is subtle, serene, supreme, and foremost, realized only within the inner experience of the most noble ones. Since it cannot be fathomed even by those of worldly wisdom, who could believe and accept such a Dharma?"
Subhūti replied, "There are bodhisattva mahāsattvas who,

dwelling on the stage of non-retrogression, can with deep faith accept this profound prajñāpāramitā— which is difficult to see, difficult to realize, beyond the sphere of discursive thought, transcending the realm of conceptualization, subtle, peaceful, and supreme."

Furthermore, those who have already seen the Noble Truths as well as Arhats whose outflows are exhausted, in order to fulfill their aspirations, are also able to believe in and accept this Prajñāpāramitā.

Furthermore, there are sons and daughters of good family who, in the past, have personally approached, made offerings to, and made great vows before immeasurable, countless hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of Buddhas; who have planted many roots of goodness and possess sharp faculties and wisdom; and who are sustained by spiritual friends—these individuals are also able to believe in and accept this profound Prajñāpāramitā, which is difficult to see, difficult to realize, beyond the sphere of discursive thought, transcending the realm of thought, subtle, tranquil, supreme, and foremost.
Why is this? "Such persons as these never differentiate form by means of emptiness or non-emptiness, nor do they differentiate emptiness or non-emptiness by means of form;

they do not differentiate feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness by means of emptiness or non-emptiness, nor do they differentiate emptiness or non-emptiness by means of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness."
One does not discriminate between form as having marks or being markless, nor does one discriminate between having marks or being markless by means of form;

one does not discriminate between feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as having marks or being markless, nor does one discriminate between having marks or being markless by means of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
One does not discriminate between the presence or absence of aspiration regarding form, nor does one discriminate between the presence or absence of aspiration regarding form;

one does not discriminate between the presence or absence of aspiration regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor does one discriminate between the presence or absence of aspiration regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
One does not discriminate between arising and non-arising with respect to form, nor does one discriminate between form and arising or non-arising;

one does not discriminate between arising and non-arising with respect to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor does one discriminate between feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness and arising or non-arising.
One does not discriminate between form and its cessation or non-cessation, nor does one discriminate between its cessation or non-cessation based on form;

one does not discriminate between feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness and their cessation or non-cessation, nor does one discriminate between their cessation or non-cessation based on feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
One does not discriminate between form and tranquility or non-tranquility, nor does one discriminate between tranquility or non-tranquility and form;

one does not discriminate between feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness and tranquility or non-tranquility, nor does one discriminate between tranquility or non-tranquility and feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
One does not discriminate form by means of "separation" or "non-separation," nor does one discriminate separation or non-separation by means of form;

one does not discriminate feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness by means of "separation" or "non-separation," nor does one discriminate separation or non-separation by means of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.

“Such persons as these never, at any time, discriminate between emptiness and non-emptiness with respect to the sense-base of the eye, nor do they discriminate between the sense-base of the eye and emptiness or non-emptiness;

they do not discriminate between emptiness and non-emptiness with respect to the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, nor do they discriminate between the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind and emptiness or non-emptiness.”
One does not discriminate the sense base of the eye as having marks or being markless, nor does one discriminate the sense base of the eye as having marks or being markless;

one does not discriminate the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as having marks or being markless, nor does one discriminate the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as having marks or being markless.
One does not discriminate the sphere of the eye as being with aspiration or without aspiration, nor does one discriminate the sphere of the eye as being with aspiration or without aspiration;

one does not discriminate the spheres of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as being with aspiration or without aspiration, nor does one discriminate the spheres of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as being with aspiration or without aspiration.
One does not discriminate the eye-base by way of arising or non-arising, nor does one discriminate arising or non-arising by way of the eye-base;

one does not discriminate the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-base by way of arising or non-arising, nor does one discriminate arising or non-arising by way of the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-base.
One does not discriminate between cessation and non-cessation regarding the sense base of the eye, nor does one discriminate between cessation and non-cessation by means of the sense base of the eye;

One does not differentiate between arising and non-arising by means of internal emptiness, nor does one differentiate internal emptiness by means of arising and non-arising;

one does not differentiate between arising and non-arising by means of external emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature, nor does one differentiate external emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature by means of arising and non-arising.
