For what reason, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this way, does he not train for the sake of the appropriation or destruction of the tongue-element; nor for the sake of the appropriation or destruction of the taste-element, the tongue-consciousness-element, tongue-contact, or the various feelings arisen with tongue-contact as a condition?”

“Subhūti! For what reason, when training in this way, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva not train for the sake of the appropriation or destruction of the body-element, nor for the sake of the appropriation or destruction of the touch-element, the body-consciousness-element, body-contact, or the various feelings produced with body-contact as a condition?”

“Subhūti! For what reason does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when training in this way, not train for the sake of the appropriation or destruction of the mind-element; nor for the sake of the appropriation or destruction of the dharma-element, the mind-consciousness-element, mind-contact, or the various feelings produced with mind-contact as condition?”

“Subhūti! For what reason, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this way, does he not train for the sake of being grasped by or destroyed by the earth element, nor for the sake of being grasped by or destroyed by the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements?”

“Subhūti! For what reason does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when training in this way, not train for the sake of grasping or destroying the noble truth of suffering, nor for the sake of grasping or destroying the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path?”

“Subhūti! For what reason does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when training in this way, not train for the sake of being grasped by or destroyed by ignorance; nor for the sake of being grasped by or destroyed by volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, or aging, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair?”

“Subhūti! For what reason does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when training in this way, not train for the sake of being grasped or destroyed by inner emptiness; nor for the sake of being grasped or destroyed by outer emptiness, inner-and-outer emptiness, emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, endless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, unchanging emptiness, essential emptiness, emptiness of self-characteristic, emptiness of common characteristic, emptiness of all phenomena, emptiness of non-apprehensibility, emptiness of non-existence, emptiness of intrinsic nature, or emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence?”

“Subhūti! For what reason does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when training in this way, not train for the sake of being grasped by or destroyed by suchness; nor for the sake of being grasped by or destroyed by the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), the non-illusory nature, the unchanging nature, equality, the nature free from birth, the fixed nature of phenomena (dharmaniyāmatā), the stability of phenomena (dharmasthititā), the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), the realm of space (ākāśadhātu), or the inconceivable realm?”

“Subhūti! For what reason does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when training in this way, not train for the sake of being grasped or destroyed by the perfection of generosity; nor does he train for the sake of being grasped or destroyed by the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, or wisdom?”

“Subhūti! For what reason does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when training in this way, not train for the sake of being appropriated or destroyed by the four dhyānas, nor for the sake of being appropriated or destroyed by the four immeasurables or the four formless attainments?”

"Subhūti! For what reason does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when training in this way, not train for the sake of being grasped by or destroyed by the eight liberations; nor does he train for the sake of being grasped by or destroyed by the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, or the ten pervasive bases?"

“Subhūti, for what reason does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when training in this way, not train for the sake of the appropriation or destruction of the four foundations of mindfulness; nor for the sake of the appropriation or destruction of the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the eightfold noble path?”

“Subhūti! For what reason does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when training in this way, not train for the sake of being grasped or destroyed by the gate of liberation of emptiness, nor for the sake of being grasped or destroyed by the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness?”

“Subhūti! For what reason does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when training in this way, not train for the sake of the five eyes being grasped or destroyed, nor for the sake of the six supernormal powers being grasped or destroyed?”

“Subhūti! For what reason does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when training in this way, not train for the sake of being sustained by or destroyed by the ten powers of a buddha? Nor does he train for the sake of being sustained by or destroyed by the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, or the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha?”

“Subhūti! For what reason does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when training in this way, not train for the sake of being grasped by or destroyed by the quality of non-forgetfulness, nor for the sake of being grasped by or destroyed by the state of constant equanimity?”

“Subhūti, for what reason does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when training in this way, not train for the sake of being grasped or destroyed by all-knowledge (sarvajñatā), nor for the sake of being grasped or destroyed by the knowledge of the aspects of the path (mārgākārajñatā) or the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā)?”

“Subhūti! For what reason, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this way, does he not train for the sake of being grasped and destroyed by any of the dhāraṇī-doors, nor does he train for the sake of being grasped and destroyed by any of the samādhi-doors?”

"Subhūti! For what reason does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when training in this way, not train for the sake of the acquisition and destruction of the state of a stream-enterer, nor for the sake of the acquisition and destruction of the states of a once-returner, a non-returner, or an arhat?"

“Subhūti! For what reason, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this way, does he not train for the sake of being grasped by or destroyed by the stage of entering the stream or the fruit of stream-entry; nor for the sake of the stage of entering once-returning or the fruit of once-returning, the stage of entering non-returning or the fruit of non-returning, or the stage of entering arhatship or the fruit of arhatship?”

“Subhūti! For what reason does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when training in this way, not train for the sake of being grasped or destroyed by the state of a pratyekabuddha, nor for the sake of being grasped or destroyed by the path of a pratyekabuddha or the fruit of a pratyekabuddha?”

“Subhūti, for what reason does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when training in this manner, not train for the sake of the destruction of being grasped by a bodhisattva mahāsattva, nor for the sake of the destruction of being grasped by a samyaksaṃbuddha?”

"Subhūti! For what reason does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when training in this way, not train for the sake of the appropriation or destruction of the bodhisattva mahāsattva dharmas, nor for the sake of the appropriation or destruction of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening?"

“Subhūti! For what reason does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when training in this way, not train for the sake of being subsumed or destroyed by the Śrāvaka vehicle, nor for the sake of being subsumed or destroyed by the Pratyekabuddha vehicle or the Unsurpassed Vehicle?”
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti replied to Śāriputra:
"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this way, he does not perceive any form that is to be grasped or destroyed, nor does he perceive anyone who can grasp or destroy form;

he does not perceive any feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness that is to be grasped or destroyed, nor does he perceive anyone who can grasp or destroy feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness."
Why is this? Because the aggregate of form and so forth—whether as subject or object, internal or external—are all empty and cannot be apprehended.
"Śāriputra!..."

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this way, they do not perceive that the sense-base of the eye is something to be grasped or something to be destroyed, nor do they perceive anyone who can grasp or destroy the sense-base of the eye.

They do not perceive that the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind are things to be grasped or things to be destroyed, nor do they perceive anyone who can grasp or destroy the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind.
Why is this? Because the sense bases, such as the eye, whether as subject or object, are both internally and externally empty and cannot be apprehended.
"Śāriputra!..."

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this way, they do not perceive any form-base (*rūpāyatana*) that is to be grasped or destroyed, nor do they perceive anyone who can grasp or destroy the form-base.

They do not perceive any sound, odor, taste, tangible object, or mental-object base (*dharmāyatana*) that is to be grasped or destroyed, nor do they perceive anyone who can grasp or destroy the sound, odor, taste, tangible object, or mental-object base.
Why is this? Because the sense base of form and so forth—whether as subject or object, internal or external—are all empty and cannot be apprehended.
"Śāriputra!..."

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this way, they do not perceive that the eye-element is something to be grasped or destroyed, nor do they perceive anyone who can grasp or destroy the eye-element.

They do not perceive that the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, eye-contact, or the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition are things to be grasped or destroyed, nor do they perceive anyone who can grasp or destroy the form-element, up to and including the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition.
Why is this? Because the eye-element and so forth—whether as subject or object, internal or external—are all empty and cannot be apprehended.
"Śāriputra!..."

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this manner, they do not perceive the ear-element as something that can be grasped or destroyed, nor do they perceive anyone who can grasp or destroy the ear-element.

They do not perceive the sound-element, the ear-consciousness-element, ear-contact, or the various feelings produced with ear-contact as conditions as things that can be grasped or destroyed, nor do they perceive anyone who can grasp or destroy these, from the sound-element up to the various feelings produced with ear-contact as conditions.
Why is this? Because the ear-element and so forth—whether as subject or object, internal or external—are all empty and cannot be apprehended.
"Śāriputra!..."

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this way, they do not perceive the nose element as something that can be grasped or destroyed, nor do they perceive anyone who can grasp or destroy the nose element.

They do not perceive the odor element, the nose-consciousness element, nose-contact, or the various feelings produced with nose-contact as conditions as being graspable or subject to destruction, nor do they perceive anyone who can grasp or destroy these, from the odor element up to the various feelings produced with nose-contact as conditions.
Why is this? Because the nose element and so forth—whether as subject or object, internal or external—are all empty and cannot be apprehended.
"Śāriputra!..."

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this manner, they do not perceive the tongue-element as something that can be grasped or destroyed, nor do they perceive anyone who can grasp or destroy the tongue-element.

They do not perceive the taste-element, the tongue-consciousness-element, tongue-contact, or the various feelings produced with tongue-contact as conditions as being graspable or destructible, nor do they perceive anyone who can grasp or destroy these, from the taste-element up to the various feelings produced with tongue-contact as conditions.
Why is this? Because the tongue-element and so forth—whether as subject or object, internal or external—are all empty and cannot be apprehended.
"Śāriputra!..."

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this manner, they do not perceive the body-element (*kāyadhātu*) as something that can be grasped or destroyed, nor do they perceive anyone who can grasp or destroy the body-element.

They do not perceive the touch-element (*spraṣṭavyadhātu*), the body-consciousness-element (*kāyavijñānadhātu*), body-contact (*kāyasparśa*), or the various feelings (*vedanā*) produced with body-contact as conditions as things that can be grasped or destroyed, nor do they perceive anyone who can grasp or destroy the touch-element up to the various feelings produced with body-contact as conditions.
Why is this? Because the body-element and so forth—whether as subject or object—are both internally and externally empty and cannot be apprehended.
"Śāriputra!..."

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this way, they do not perceive that the mind-element (*manodhātu*) is something to be grasped or destroyed, nor do they perceive anyone who can grasp or destroy the mind-element.

They do not perceive that the dharma-element, the mind-consciousness-element, mental contact, or the various feelings produced with mental contact as condition are things to be grasped or destroyed, nor do they perceive anyone who can grasp or destroy anything from the dharma-element up to the various feelings produced with mental contact as condition.
Why is this? Because the mental faculty (*manodhātu*) and so forth—whether as subject or object, internal or external—are all empty and cannot be apprehended.
"Śāriputra!..."

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this manner, they do not perceive that the earth element is something to be grasped or destroyed, nor do they perceive anyone who can grasp or destroy the earth element;

they do not perceive that the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements are things to be grasped or destroyed, nor do they perceive anyone who can grasp or destroy the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements.
Why is this? Because the earth element and so forth—whether as subject or object, internal or external—are all empty and cannot be apprehended.
"Śāriputra!..."

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this manner, they do not perceive the noble truth of suffering as something to be grasped or something to be destroyed, nor do they perceive anyone who can grasp or destroy the noble truth of suffering.

They do not perceive the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path as things to be grasped or things to be destroyed, nor do they perceive anyone who can grasp or destroy the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path.
Why is this? Because the Noble Truth of Suffering and so forth—whether as subject or object, internally or externally—are both empty and unapprehendable.
"Śāriputra!..."

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this way, they do not perceive that ignorance is something to be grasped or something to be destroyed, nor do they perceive anyone who can grasp or destroy ignorance.

They do not perceive that volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, or old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are things to be grasped or things to be destroyed, nor do they perceive anyone who can grasp or destroy anything from volitional formations up to old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
Why is this? Because ignorance and the rest—whether as subject or object—are empty both internally and externally, and thus cannot be apprehended.
"Śāriputra!..."

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this way, they do not perceive that internal emptiness is something to be grasped or destroyed, nor do they perceive anyone who could grasp or destroy internal emptiness.

They do not perceive that external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, or the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence is something to be grasped or destroyed, nor do they perceive anyone who could grasp or destroy anything from external emptiness up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.
Why is this? Because internal emptiness and so forth—whether as the agent or the object—are both internally and externally empty and thus unapprehendable.
"Śāriputra!..."
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this manner, they do not perceive any suchness that can be grasped or destroyed, nor do they perceive anyone who can grasp or destroy suchness.

They do not perceive any dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), non-erroneous nature, unchanging nature, equality, nature free from birth, fixedness of dharma, stability of dharma, reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*), space-element (*ākāśadhātu*), or inconceivable realm (*acintyadhātu*) that can be grasped or destroyed, nor do they perceive anyone who can grasp or destroy anything from the dharma-realm up to the inconceivable realm.
Why is this? Because suchness and so forth—whether as subject or object—are empty both internally and externally, and thus cannot be apprehended.
"Śāriputra!..."

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this way, they do not perceive the perfection of generosity as something that can be grasped or destroyed, nor do they perceive anyone who can grasp or destroy the perfection of generosity;

they do not perceive the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, or wisdom as things that can be grasped or destroyed, nor do they perceive anyone who can grasp or destroy the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, or wisdom.
Why is this? Because the perfection of generosity and the others—whether as agent or object—are both internally and externally empty and thus unapprehendable.
"Śāriputra!..."
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this way, they do not perceive the four dhyānas as something to be grasped or destroyed, nor do they perceive anyone who can grasp or destroy the four dhyānas;

they do not perceive the four immeasurables or the four formless attainments as something to be grasped or destroyed, nor do they perceive anyone who can grasp or destroy the four immeasurables or the four formless attainments.
Why is this? Because the four dhyānas and so forth—whether as subject or object, internally or externally—are all empty and cannot be apprehended.
"Śāriputra!..."
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this way, they do not perceive the eight liberations as something that can be grasped or destroyed, nor do they perceive anyone who can grasp or destroy them.

They do not perceive the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, or the ten totalities as something that can be grasped or destroyed, nor do they perceive anyone who can grasp or destroy the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, or the ten totalities.
Why is this? Because the eight liberations and so forth—whether as subject or object, internal or external—are both empty and unapprehendable.
"Śāriputra!..."

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this way, they do not perceive the four foundations of mindfulness as something to be grasped or destroyed, nor do they perceive anyone who can grasp or destroy them. They do not perceive the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the eightfold noble path as something to be grasped or destroyed, nor do they perceive anyone who can grasp or destroy the four right efforts up to the eightfold noble path.
Why is this? Because the four foundations of mindfulness and so forth—whether as the agent or the object—are unapprehendable, being empty both internally and externally.
"Śāriputra!..."

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this way, they do not perceive the liberation door of emptiness as something that can be grasped or destroyed, nor do they perceive anyone who can grasp or destroy the liberation door of emptiness;

they do not perceive the liberation doors of signlessness and wishlessness as things that can be grasped or destroyed, nor do they perceive anyone who can grasp or destroy the liberation doors of signlessness and wishlessness.
Why is this? Because the gate of liberation of emptiness and so forth—whether as subject or object, internally or externally—are both empty and cannot be apprehended.
"Śāriputra!..."
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this manner, they do not perceive that the five eyes are anything to be grasped or destroyed, nor do they perceive anyone who can grasp or destroy them;
they do not perceive that the six supernormal powers are anything to be grasped or destroyed, nor do they perceive anyone who can grasp or destroy them.
Why is this? Because the five eyes, whether as subject or object, are both internally and externally empty and cannot be apprehended.
"Śāriputra!..."

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this way, they do not perceive the ten powers of a buddha as something that can be grasped or destroyed, nor do they perceive anyone who can grasp or destroy the ten powers of a buddha.

They do not perceive the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, or the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha as things that can be grasped or destroyed, nor do they perceive anyone who can grasp or destroy these qualities from the four fearlessnesses up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha.
Why is this? Because the ten powers of the Buddha, whether as subject or object, are both internally and externally empty and thus unapprehendable.
"Śāriputra!..."

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this manner, they do not perceive that the quality of non-forgetfulness is something to be grasped or something to be destroyed, nor do they perceive anyone who can grasp or destroy the quality of non-forgetfulness;

they do not perceive that the nature of constant equanimity is something to be grasped or something to be destroyed, nor do they perceive anyone who can grasp or destroy the nature of constant equanimity.
Why is this? Because dharmas such as non-forgetfulness—whether as subject or object, internal or external—are both empty and unapprehendable.
"Śāriputra!..."

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this way, they do not perceive any all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) that can be grasped or destroyed, nor do they perceive anyone who can grasp or destroy all-knowledge;

they do not perceive any knowledge of the paths (*mārgākārajñatā*) or all-aspect knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) that can be grasped or destroyed, nor do they perceive anyone who can grasp or destroy the knowledge of the paths or all-aspect knowledge.
Why is this? Because all-knowledge and so forth—whether as subject or object, internal or external—are both empty and unapprehendable.
"Śāriputra!..."

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this way, they do not perceive any dhāraṇī doors as being graspable or subject to destruction, nor do they perceive anyone who can grasp or destroy all dhāraṇī doors;
they do not perceive any samādhi doors as being graspable or subject to destruction, nor do they perceive anyone who can grasp or destroy all samādhi doors.
Why is this? Because all dharani-doors, whether as subject or object, are both internally and externally empty and cannot be apprehended.
"Śāriputra!..."

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this manner, they do not perceive a stream-enterer as something to be grasped or something to be destroyed, nor do they perceive anyone who can grasp or destroy a stream-enterer;

they do not perceive a once-returner, a non-returner, or an arhat as something to be grasped or something to be destroyed, nor do they perceive anyone who can grasp or destroy a once-returner, a non-returner, or an arhat.
Why is this? Because the stream-enterers and so forth—whether as subject or object—are unapprehendable, being empty both internally and externally.
"Śāriputra!..."

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this manner, they do not perceive the state of stream-entry or the fruit of stream-entry as something to be grasped or destroyed, nor do they perceive anyone who can grasp or destroy the state of stream-entry or the fruit of stream-entry.

They do not perceive the state of once-returning or its fruit, the state of non-returning or its fruit, or the state of arhatship or its fruit as something to be grasped or destroyed, nor do they perceive anyone who can grasp or destroy the state of once-returning or its fruit, the state of non-returning or its fruit, or the state of arhatship or its fruit.
Why is this? Because the stream-enterer’s path and the fruit of stream-entry, whether as subject or object, are both empty internally and externally and are thus unapprehendable.
"Śāriputra!..."

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this manner, they do not perceive a pratyekabuddha as something to be grasped or destroyed, nor do they perceive anyone who could grasp or destroy a pratyekabuddha;

they do not perceive the path toward the fruit of a pratyekabuddha as something to be grasped or destroyed, nor do they perceive anyone who could grasp or destroy that path toward the fruit of a pratyekabuddha.
Why is this? Because the Pratyekabuddhas and so forth—whether as subject or object—are unapprehendable, being empty both internally and externally.
"Śāriputra!..."

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this way, they do not perceive a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is to be grasped or destroyed, nor do they perceive one who can grasp or destroy a bodhisattva mahāsattva;
they do not perceive a samyaksaṃbuddha who is to be grasped or destroyed, nor do they perceive one who can grasp or destroy a samyaksaṃbuddha.
Why is this? Because for Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas and others, both the subject and the object—both internally and externally—are empty and cannot be apprehended.
"Śāriputra!..."

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this way, they do not perceive any dharma of a bodhisattva mahāsattva that can be grasped or destroyed, nor do they perceive anyone who can grasp or destroy the dharmas of a bodhisattva mahāsattva;

they do not perceive unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment as something that can be grasped or destroyed, nor do they perceive anyone who can grasp or destroy unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Why is this? Because for a bodhisattva mahāsattva, the dharmas—whether as subject or object—are equally empty both internally and externally, and thus cannot be apprehended.
"Śāriputra!..."

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this manner, they do not perceive the Śrāvaka vehicle as something to be grasped or destroyed, nor do they perceive anyone who can grasp or destroy the Śrāvaka vehicle;

they do not perceive the Pratyekabuddha vehicle or the Unsurpassed Vehicle (Anuttarayāna) as something to be grasped or destroyed, nor do they perceive anyone who can grasp or destroy the Pratyekabuddha vehicle or the Unsurpassed Vehicle.
Why is this? Because the Śrāvaka vehicle and so forth—whether as subject or object, internally or externally—are both empty and cannot be apprehended.
"Śāriputra!..."
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with respect to form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness;

with respect to the sense base of the eye, and the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; with respect to the sense base of forms, and the sense bases of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and phenomena;
and with respect to the eye element, the form element, the eye-consciousness element, and eye-contact—

...the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition; regarding the ear-element, the sound-element, the ear-consciousness-element, and ear-contact, as well as the various feelings produced with ear-contact as condition;

regarding the nose-element, the odor-element, the nose-consciousness-element, and nose-contact, as well as the various feelings produced with nose-contact as condition; regarding the tongue-element...
The taste-element, the tongue-consciousness-element, and tongue-contact, as well as all feelings produced with tongue-contact as their condition;
the body-element, the touch-element, the body-consciousness-element, and body-contact, as well as all feelings produced with body-contact as their condition;
and the mind-element, the mental-object-element, the mind-consciousness-element, and mind-contact, as well as [all feelings produced with mind-contact as their condition].
Whatever feelings arise, whether in the earth element, or in the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements;
in the noble truth of suffering, or in the noble truths of the origin, cessation, and the path;
or in ignorance, or in volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, and aging.
Death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair are empty of internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness,
the emptiness of the ultimate truth, the emptiness of conditioned phenomena, the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness,
the emptiness of dispersion, the emptiness of non-alteration, the emptiness of essential nature, and the emptiness of specific characteristics.
The emptiness of common characteristics, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature,
and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence; with respect to suchness, the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature,
the non-illusory nature, the unchanging nature, equality, the nature of freedom from birth, the fixed nature of dharmas, and the dharma.
The station, the limit of reality, the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm;
regarding the perfection of generosity, the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom;
regarding the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and the eight liberations.
The eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities;
the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path;
the gate of liberation of emptiness, the gate of liberation of signlessness, and the gate of liberation of wishlessness; and the five eyes.

Regarding the six supernormal powers; regarding the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
regarding the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant equanimity; regarding all-knowledge, the knowledge of the aspects of the path, and the [knowledge of all modes].
The wisdom of all characteristics, regarding all dharani-doors and all samadhi-doors,
regarding the stream-enterer, the once-returner, the non-returner, and the arhat; regarding the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry and the fruit of stream-entry,

the candidate for the fruit of once-returning and the fruit of once-returning, the candidate for the fruit of non-returning and the fruit of non-returning, and the candidate for the fruit of arhatship and the [fruit of arhatship]...
Regarding the fruit of arhatship, regarding the stage of the candidate for pratyekabuddhahood and the fruit of pratyekabuddhahood,
regarding the bodhisattva mahāsattva and the samyaksaṃbuddha, regarding the dharma of the bodhisattva mahāsattva and unexcelled perfect enlightenment,
and regarding the śrāvaka vehicle, the pratyekabuddha vehicle, and the unexcelled vehicle, one does not perceive anything therein that can be grasped or...
When there is neither that which is destroyed nor even any perceiver who destroys, yet one trains in the perfection of wisdom,
this bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to accomplish the knowledge of all modes.
At that time, Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"Does a bodhisattva mahāsattva who trains in the perfection of wisdom in this manner succeed in accomplishing the knowledge of all modes?"
Subhūti replied:

“A bodhisattva mahāsattva who trains in the perfection of wisdom in this manner is able to accomplish the knowledge of all modes, because they train through skillful means without grasping at or destroying any phenomena.”
Śāriputra said:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices skillful means without grasping at or destroying any phenomena, how can they accomplish the knowledge of all modes?"
Subhūti said: "Śāriputra!

When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive form as arising or ceasing; he does not perceive feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness as arising or ceasing."
One does not perceive form as being either grasped or rejected; one does not perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as being either grasped or rejected.
One does not perceive form as being either defiled or pure; one does not perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as being either defiled or pure.
One does not perceive form as being either accumulated or dispersed; one does not perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as being either accumulated or dispersed.
One does not perceive form as increasing or decreasing, nor does one perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as increasing or decreasing.
Why is this? Because the nature of the aggregate of form is empty, non-existent, and unattainable.

Śāriputra! It is by training in the perfection of wisdom in this manner that a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes the knowledge of all modes, because they employ the skillful means of neither training nor accomplishing anything.

“Śāriputra! When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive the arising or the ceasing of the sense base of the eye; he does not perceive the arising or the ceasing of the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind.

He does not perceive the grasping or the relinquishing of the sense base of the eye; he does not perceive the grasping or the relinquishing of the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind.”
One does not perceive the sense base of the eye as either defiled or pure; one does not perceive the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as either defiled or pure.

One does not perceive the sense base of the eye as either accumulating or dispersing; one does not perceive the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as either accumulating or dispersing.
One does not perceive the sense base of the eye as either increasing or decreasing; one does not perceive the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as either increasing or decreasing.
Why is this? Because the nature of the sense-base of the eye is empty, non-existent, and unapprehendable. Śāriputra!

When these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas train in this manner in the perfection of wisdom, they are able to accomplish all-knowledge, by means of the skillful method of having nothing to learn and nothing to accomplish.

“Śāriputra! When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive the arising or the ceasing of the sphere of form; he does not perceive the arising or the ceasing of the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental phenomena.

He does not perceive the grasping or the relinquishing of the sphere of form; he does not perceive the grasping or the relinquishing of the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental phenomena.”
One does not perceive the sphere of forms as defiled or pure; one does not perceive the spheres of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena as defiled or pure.
One does not perceive the sphere of forms as accumulating or dispersing; one does not perceive the spheres of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena as accumulating or dispersing.
One does not perceive the sphere of forms as increasing or decreasing; one does not perceive the spheres of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena as increasing or decreasing.
Why is this? Because the sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) and its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) are empty, non-existent, and unapprehendable. Śāriputra!

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, training in this manner in the perfection of wisdom, is able to accomplish all-knowledge, by means of the skillful method of having nothing to learn and nothing to accomplish.

“Śāriputra! When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive the eye-element as arising or ceasing; he does not perceive the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, eye-contact, or the various feelings produced with eye-contact as conditions as arising or ceasing.

He does not perceive the eye-element as being grasped or relinquished; he does not perceive the form-element, up to and including the various feelings produced with eye-contact as conditions, as being grasped or relinquished.”
One does not perceive the eye-element as defiled or pure; one does not perceive the form-element, up to and including the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, as defiled or pure.

One does not perceive the eye-element as accumulating or dispersing; one does not perceive the form-element, up to and including the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, as accumulating or dispersing.

One does not perceive the eye-element as increasing or decreasing; one does not perceive the form-element, up to and including the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, as increasing or decreasing.
Why is this? Because the nature of the eye-element is empty, non-existent, and unattainable. Śāriputra!
This bodhisattva mahāsattva, by training thus in the perfection of wisdom, is able to accomplish all-knowledge, because they employ the skillful means of neither training nor accomplishing anything.

“Śāriputra! When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not perceive the ear-element as arising or ceasing; they do not perceive the sound-element, the ear-consciousness-element, ear-contact, or the various feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition as arising or ceasing.

They do not perceive the ear-element as being grasped or abandoned; they do not perceive the sound-element, up to and including the various feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition, as being grasped or abandoned.”
One does not perceive the ear-element as defiled or pure; one does not perceive the sound-element, nor even the various feelings produced with ear-contact as condition, as defiled or pure.

One does not perceive the ear-element as accumulating or dispersing; one does not perceive the sound-element, nor even the various feelings produced with ear-contact as condition, as accumulating or dispersing.

One does not perceive the ear-element as increasing or decreasing; one does not perceive the sound-element, nor even the various feelings produced with ear-contact as condition, as increasing or decreasing.
Why is this? Because the nature of the ear-element is empty, non-existent, and unobtainable. Śāriputra!

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, by training thus in the perfection of wisdom, is able to accomplish the knowledge of all modes, because they employ as their skillful means the state of having nothing to learn and nothing to accomplish.

Chapter on Training in Prajñāpāramitā, Part One, Twenty-sixth, Section Five: “Śāriputra!

When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive the arising or the cessation of the nose element; he does not perceive the arising or the cessation of the odor element, the nose-consciousness element, nose-contact, or the various feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition.”

One does not perceive the nose element as either grasping or rejecting; one does not perceive the odor element, nor even the various feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition, as either grasping or rejecting.

One does not perceive the nose element as either defiled or pure; one does not perceive the odor element, nor even the various feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition, as either defiled or pure.

One does not perceive the nose element as either accumulating or dispersing; one does not perceive the odor element, nor even the various feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition, as either accumulating or dispersing.

One does not perceive the increase or decrease of the nose element; one does not perceive the increase or decrease of the odor element, nor even the various feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition. Why is this?
Because the nature of the nose-element (*ghrāṇadhātu*) is empty, non-existent,
and unapprehendable. Śāriputra,

when a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) in this manner, they are able to accomplish all-knowledge (*sarvajñājñāna*), by means of the skillful method of having nothing to learn and nothing to accomplish.

“Śāriputra! When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive the arising or the ceasing of the tongue element; he does not perceive the arising or the ceasing of the taste element, the tongue-consciousness element, tongue-contact, or the various sensations produced with tongue-contact as condition.

He does not perceive the grasping or the relinquishing of the tongue element; he does not perceive the grasping or the relinquishing of the taste element, up to and including the various sensations produced with tongue-contact as condition.”
One does not perceive the tongue element as defiled or pure; one does not perceive the taste element, nor even the various feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition, as defiled or pure.

One does not perceive the tongue element as accumulating or dispersing; one does not perceive the taste element, nor even the various feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition, as accumulating or dispersing.

One does not perceive the tongue element as increasing or decreasing; one does not perceive the taste element, nor even the various feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition, as increasing or decreasing.
Why is this? Because the nature of the tongue-element is empty, non-existent, and unapprehendable. Śāriputra!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in the perfection of wisdom in this manner, they are able to accomplish all-knowledge, by means of the skillful method of neither training nor accomplishing anything.

“Śāriputra! When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive the body element as arising or ceasing; he does not perceive the contact element, the body-consciousness element, body-contact, or the various feelings produced with body-contact as conditions as arising or ceasing.

He does not perceive the body element as being grasped or abandoned; he does not perceive the contact element, up to and including the various feelings produced with body-contact as conditions, as being grasped or abandoned.”

One does not perceive the body element as either defiled or pure; one does not perceive the contact element, nor even the various feelings produced with body-contact as a condition, as either defiled or pure.

One does not perceive the body element as either accumulating or dispersing; one does not perceive the contact element, nor even the various feelings produced with body-contact as a condition, as either accumulating or dispersing.

One does not perceive the body element as either increasing or decreasing; one does not perceive the contact element, nor even the various feelings produced with body-contact as a condition, as either increasing or decreasing.
Why is this? Because the nature of the body element is equal to emptiness, being non-existent and unapprehendable. Śāriputra!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in the perfection of wisdom in this manner, they are able to accomplish all-knowledge, by means of the skillful method of neither training nor accomplishing anything.

“Śāriputra! When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive the arising or the ceasing of the mind-element; he does not perceive the arising or the ceasing of the phenomena-element, the mind-consciousness-element, or mental contact, nor the various feelings produced with mental contact as condition.

He does not perceive the grasping or the relinquishing of the mind-element; he does not perceive the grasping or the relinquishing of the phenomena-element, up to and including the various feelings produced with mental contact as condition.”

One does not perceive the mind-element as either defiled or pure; one does not perceive the dharma-element, nor even the various feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition, as either defiled or pure.

One does not perceive the mind-element as either accumulating or dispersing; one does not perceive the dharma-element, nor even the various feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition, as either accumulating or dispersing.

One does not perceive the mind-element as either increasing or decreasing; one does not perceive the dharma-element, nor even the various feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition, as either increasing or decreasing.
Why is this? Because the nature of the mental element (*manodhātu*) is empty, non-existent, and unapprehendable. Śāriputra!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in the perfection of wisdom in this manner, they are able to accomplish all-knowledge, because they employ the skillful means of neither training nor accomplishing anything.

“Śāriputra! When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive the earth element as arising or ceasing; he does not perceive the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements as arising or ceasing.
He does not perceive the earth element as being grasped or abandoned; he does not perceive the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements as being grasped or abandoned.”
One does not perceive the earth element as defiled or pure; one does not perceive the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements as defiled or pure.
One does not perceive the earth element as accumulating or dispersing; one does not perceive the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements as accumulating or dispersing.
One does not perceive the earth element as increasing or decreasing; one does not perceive the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements as increasing or decreasing.
Why is this? Because the nature of the earth element is empty, non-existent, and unattainable. Śāriputra!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in the perfection of wisdom in this manner, they are able to accomplish all-knowledge, by means of the skillful method of having nothing to learn and nothing to accomplish.

“Śāriputra! When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive the noble truth of suffering as arising or ceasing; he does not perceive the noble truths of origin, cessation, or the path as arising or ceasing.

He does not perceive the noble truth of suffering as something to be grasped or abandoned; he does not perceive the noble truths of origin, cessation, or the path as something to be grasped or abandoned.”
One does not perceive the noble truth of suffering as either defiled or pure; one does not perceive the noble truths of origin, cessation, or the path as either defiled or pure.
One does not perceive the noble truth of suffering as either accumulating or dispersing; one does not perceive the noble truths of origin, cessation, or the path as either accumulating or dispersing.
One does not perceive the noble truth of suffering as either increasing or decreasing; one does not perceive the noble truths of origin, cessation, or the path as either increasing or decreasing.
Why is this? Because the nature of the noble truth of suffering is empty, non-existent, and unattainable. Śāriputra!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in the perfection of wisdom in this manner, they are able to accomplish all-knowledge, by means of the skillful method of neither training nor accomplishing anything.

“Śāriputra! When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive ignorance as arising or ceasing; he does not perceive volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair as arising or ceasing.

He does not perceive ignorance as being taken up or relinquished; he does not perceive volitional formations, and so on, up to old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair as being taken up or relinquished.”
One does not perceive ignorance as either defiled or pure; one does not perceive formations, up to and including old age, death, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair, as either defiled or pure.

One does not perceive ignorance as either accumulating or dispersing; one does not perceive formations, up to and including old age, death, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair, as either accumulating or dispersing.

One does not perceive ignorance as either increasing or decreasing; one does not perceive formations, up to and including old age, death, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair, as either increasing or decreasing.
Why is this? Because the nature of ignorance is empty, non-existent, and unapprehendable. Śāriputra!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in the perfection of wisdom in this manner, they are able to accomplish all-knowledge, by means of the skillful method of having nothing to learn and nothing to accomplish.

“Śāriputra! When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive the arising or ceasing of internal emptiness; he does not perceive the arising or ceasing of external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, endless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common-characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all dharmas, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, or the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature.

He does not perceive the grasping or abandoning of internal emptiness; he does not perceive the grasping or abandoning of external emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature.”
One does not perceive inner emptiness as defiled or pure; one does not perceive outer emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, as defiled or pure.

One does not perceive inner emptiness as accumulating or dispersing; one does not perceive outer emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, as accumulating or dispersing.

One does not perceive inner emptiness as increasing or decreasing; one does not perceive outer emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, as increasing or decreasing.
Why is this? Because the nature of internal emptiness is itself empty, non-existent, and unapprehendable. Śāriputra!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in the perfection of wisdom in this manner, they are able to accomplish all-knowledge, because they employ the skillful means of neither training nor accomplishing anything.

“Śāriputra! When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive the arising or the ceasing of suchness; he does not perceive the arising or the ceasing of the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, the non-illusory nature, the unchanging nature, equality, the nature of being free from birth, the fixed nature of dharmas, the stability of dharmas, the limit of reality, the realm of space, or the inconceivable realm.
He does not perceive the grasping or the relinquishing of suchness; he does not perceive the grasping or the relinquishing of the dharma-realm, up to and including the inconceivable realm.”
One does not perceive true thusness as defiled or pure; one does not perceive the dharma-realm, up to and including the inconceivable realm, as defiled or pure.
One does not perceive true thusness as accumulating or dispersing; one does not perceive the dharma-realm, up to and including the inconceivable realm, as accumulating or dispersing.
One does not perceive true thusness as increasing or decreasing; one does not perceive the dharma-realm, up to and including the inconceivable realm, as increasing or decreasing.
Why is this? Because the nature of true suchness (tathatā) is equal to emptiness, being non-existent and unapprehendable. Śāriputra!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in the perfection of wisdom in this manner, they are able to accomplish all-knowledge, by means of the skillful method of neither training nor accomplishing anything.

“Śāriputra! When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive the arising or the ceasing of the perfection of generosity; he does not perceive the arising or the ceasing of the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, or wisdom.

He does not perceive the grasping or the relinquishing of the perfection of generosity; he does not perceive the grasping or the relinquishing of the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, or wisdom.”

One does not perceive the perfection of generosity as either defiled or pure; one does not perceive the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, or wisdom as either defiled or pure.

One does not perceive the perfection of generosity as either accumulating or dispersing; one does not perceive the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, or wisdom as either accumulating or dispersing.

One does not perceive the perfection of generosity as either increasing or decreasing; one does not perceive the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, or wisdom as either increasing or decreasing.
Why is this? Because the nature of the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) is empty, non-existent, and unapprehendable. Śāriputra!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in the perfection of wisdom in this manner, they are able to accomplish all-knowledge, by means of the skillful method of having nothing to learn and nothing to accomplish.

“Śāriputra! When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive the arising or the cessation of the four dhyānas; he does not perceive the arising or the cessation of the four immeasurables or the four formless attainments.
He does not perceive the grasping or the relinquishing of the four dhyānas; he does not perceive the grasping or the relinquishing of the four immeasurables or the four formless attainments.”
One does not perceive the four dhyānas as either defiled or pure; one does not perceive the four immeasurables or the four formless attainments as either defiled or pure.
One does not perceive the four dhyānas as either accumulating or dispersing; one does not perceive the four immeasurables or the four formless attainments as either accumulating or dispersing.
One does not perceive the four dhyānas as either increasing or decreasing; one does not perceive the four immeasurables or the four formless attainments as either increasing or decreasing.
Why is this? Because the nature of the four dhyānas is empty, non-existent, and unattainable. Śāriputra!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in the perfection of wisdom in this manner, they are able to accomplish all-knowledge, by means of the skillful method of neither training nor accomplishing anything.

“Śāriputra! When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive the arising or the ceasing of the eight liberations; he does not perceive the arising or the ceasing of the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, or the ten totalities.

He does not perceive the grasping or the relinquishing of the eight liberations; he does not perceive the grasping or the relinquishing of the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, or the ten totalities.”
One does not perceive the eight liberations as defiled or pure; one does not perceive the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, or the ten totalities as defiled or pure.

One does not perceive the eight liberations as accumulating or dispersing; one does not perceive the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, or the ten totalities as accumulating or dispersing.

One does not perceive the eight liberations as increasing or decreasing; one does not perceive the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, or the ten totalities as increasing or decreasing.
Why is this? Because the nature of the eight liberations is empty, non-existent, and unattainable. Śāriputra!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in the perfection of wisdom in this manner, they are able to accomplish all-knowledge, by means of the skillful method of neither training nor accomplishing anything.

“Śāriputra! When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive the four foundations of mindfulness as arising or ceasing; he does not perceive the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, or the eightfold noble path as arising or ceasing.

He does not perceive the four foundations of mindfulness as being grasped or relinquished; he does not perceive the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, or the eightfold noble path as being grasped or relinquished.”

One does not perceive the four foundations of mindfulness as either defiled or pure; one does not perceive the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the eightfold noble path as either defiled or pure.

One does not perceive the four foundations of mindfulness as either accumulating or dispersing; one does not perceive the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the eightfold noble path as either accumulating or dispersing.

One does not perceive the four foundations of mindfulness as either increasing or decreasing; one does not perceive the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the eightfold noble path as either increasing or decreasing.
Why is this? Because the nature of the four foundations of mindfulness is empty, non-existent, and unapprehendable. Śāriputra!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in the perfection of wisdom in this manner, they are able to accomplish all-knowledge, by means of the skillful method of having nothing to learn and nothing to accomplish.

“Śāriputra! When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive the arising or the cessation of the gate of liberation that is emptiness; he does not perceive the arising or the cessation of the gates of liberation that are signlessness and wishlessness.

He does not perceive the grasping or the relinquishing of the gate of liberation that is emptiness; he does not perceive the grasping or the relinquishing of the gates of liberation that are signlessness and wishlessness.”
One does not perceive the gate of liberation of emptiness as either defiled or pure; one does not perceive the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness as either defiled or pure.

One does not perceive the gate of liberation of emptiness as either accumulating or dispersing; one does not perceive the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness as either accumulating or dispersing.

One does not perceive the gate of liberation of emptiness as either increasing or decreasing; one does not perceive the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness as either increasing or decreasing.
Why is this? Because the nature of the gate of liberation of emptiness is itself empty, non-existent, and unapprehendable. Śāriputra!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in the perfection of wisdom in this way, they are able to accomplish all-knowledge, by means of the skillful method of neither training nor accomplishing anything.

“Śāriputra! When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive the five eyes as arising or ceasing, nor does he perceive the six supernormal powers as arising or ceasing;
he does not perceive the five eyes as being grasped or relinquished, nor does he perceive the six supernormal powers as being grasped or relinquished.”
One does not perceive the five eyes as defiled or pure; one does not perceive the six supernormal powers as defiled or pure.
One does not perceive the five eyes as accumulating or dispersing; one does not perceive the six supernormal powers as accumulating or dispersing.
One does not perceive the five eyes as increasing or decreasing; one does not perceive the six supernormal powers as increasing or decreasing.
Why is this? Because the nature of the five eyes is empty, non-existent, and unattainable. Śāriputra!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in the perfection of wisdom in this manner, they are able to accomplish all-knowledge, by means of the skillful method of having nothing to learn and nothing to accomplish.

“Śāriputra! When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not perceive the ten powers of a buddha as arising or ceasing; they do not perceive the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, or the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha as arising or ceasing.

They do not perceive the ten powers of a buddha as being grasped or abandoned; they do not perceive the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, or the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha as being grasped or abandoned.”

He does not perceive the ten powers of a Buddha as defiled or pure; he does not perceive the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha as defiled or pure.

He does not perceive the ten powers of a Buddha as accumulating or dispersing; he does not perceive the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha as accumulating or dispersing.

He does not perceive the ten powers of a Buddha as increasing or decreasing; he does not perceive the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha as increasing or decreasing.
Why is this? Because the nature of the Buddha’s ten powers is equal to emptiness, being non-existent and unattainable. Śāriputra!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in the perfection of wisdom in this manner, they are able to accomplish all-knowledge, by means of the skillful method of neither training nor accomplishing anything.

“Śāriputra! When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive the dharma of non-forgetfulness as either arising or ceasing; he does not perceive the nature of constant equanimity as either arising or ceasing.
He does not perceive the dharma of non-forgetfulness as either grasping or relinquishing; he does not perceive the nature of constant equanimity as either grasping or relinquishing.”
One does not perceive the quality of non-forgetfulness as either defiled or pure, nor does one perceive the nature of constant equanimity as either defiled or pure;
one does not perceive the quality of non-forgetfulness as either accumulating or dispersing, nor does one perceive the nature of constant equanimity as either accumulating or dispersing;
one does not perceive the quality of non-forgetfulness as either increasing or decreasing, nor does one perceive the nature of constant equanimity as either increasing or decreasing.
Why is this? Because the nature of the quality of non-forgetfulness is empty, non-existent, and unattainable. Śāriputra!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in the perfection of wisdom in this manner, they are able to accomplish all-knowledge, by means of the skillful method of neither training nor accomplishing anything.

“Śāriputra! When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive the arising or the cessation of all-knowledge; he does not perceive the arising or the cessation of the knowledge of the paths or the knowledge of all aspects.
He does not perceive the grasping or the relinquishing of all-knowledge; he does not perceive the grasping or the relinquishing of the knowledge of the paths or the knowledge of all aspects.”

The Tathāgata is neither associated nor dissociated from the suchness (tathatā) apart from the Śrāvaka vehicle; he is likewise neither associated nor dissociated from the suchness apart from the Pratyekabuddha vehicle or the Unsurpassed Vehicle.”

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Scroll 93 [and] Scroll 94,
