The First Division, Chapter Twenty-seven on Seeking Prajñā, Part Six.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti again addressed Śakra, the Lord of Devas, saying: “Kauśika!
Regarding your previous question as to where one should seek the *prajñāpāramitā* practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva, Kauśika:

the *prajñāpāramitā* practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not be sought within form (*rūpa*), nor should it be sought within feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), or consciousness (*vijñāna*);
nor should it be sought apart from form, nor apart from feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.

Why is this so? Whether it be form, or feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; whether it be apart from form, or apart from feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; whether it be the bodhisattva-mahāsattva, or the prajñāpāramitā—seeking them in such a manner, all these are neither associated nor dissociated, neither with form nor without form, neither visible nor invisible, neither resistant nor non-resistant; they are all of one single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of signlessness (animitta).
Why is this? Kauśika!
The perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva is not form, nor is it feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
It is not apart from form, nor apart from feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
Why is this? Because all such things are of a nature that is non-existent and cannot be apprehended.
Because they are non-existent and unapprehendable, the perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva is not form, nor is it feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;
yet it is not apart from form, nor is it apart from feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
Therefore, the perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not be sought within form, nor should it be sought within feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;
nor should it be sought apart from form, nor should it be sought apart from feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.

“Kauśika! The perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not be sought within the sense base of the eye, nor should it be sought within the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind;
nor should it be sought apart from the sense base of the eye, nor apart from the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind.”

Why is this so? Whether it be the sense base of the eye, or the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; whether one is apart from the sense base of the eye, or apart from the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; whether it be a bodhisattva mahāsattva, or the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), or the seeking of such things—all these are neither associated nor dissociated, neither with form nor formless, neither visible nor invisible, neither resistant nor non-resistant; they all share a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of signlessness (animitta).
Why is this? Kauśika!
The perfection of wisdom practiced by bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is not the sense-base of the eye, nor is it the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind.
It is not apart from the sense base of the eye, nor apart from the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind.
Why is this? Because all such things are of a nature that is non-existent and cannot be apprehended.

Because they are non-existent and unapprehendable, the perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva is not the sense-base of the eye, nor the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind;
yet it is not apart from the sense-base of the eye, nor apart from the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind.

Therefore, the *prajñāpāramitā* practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not be sought within the sense base of the eye, nor should it be sought within the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind;
nor should it be sought apart from the sense base of the eye, nor apart from the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind.

“Kauśika! The perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not be sought within the sphere of form, nor should it be sought within the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental phenomena;
nor should it be sought apart from the sphere of form, nor apart from the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental phenomena.”

Why is this so? Whether it be the sense-base of form, or the sense-bases of sound, odor, taste, touch, or mental phenomena; whether one is apart from the sense-base of form, or apart from the sense-bases of sound, odor, taste, touch, or mental phenomena; whether it be the bodhisattva-mahāsattva, or the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), or the seeking of such things—all these are neither associated nor dissociated, neither with form nor formless, neither visible nor invisible, neither resistant nor non-resistant. They all share a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of signlessness (animitta).
Why is this? Kauśika!
The perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva is not the sphere of form, nor is it the sphere of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental phenomena.
It is not apart from the sphere of form, nor apart from the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental phenomena. Why is this?
Because all such things are of a nature that is non-existent and cannot be apprehended.

Because nothing exists and nothing can be apprehended, the perfection of wisdom practiced by the bodhisattva mahāsattva is not the sphere of form, nor is it the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental phenomena;
yet it is not apart from the sphere of form, nor is it apart from the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental phenomena.

Therefore, the Prajñāpāramitā practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not be sought within the sphere of form, nor should it be sought within the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental phenomena;
nor should it be sought apart from the sphere of form, nor apart from the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental phenomena.

“Kauśika! The *prajñāpāramitā* practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not be sought within the eye-element; it should not be sought within the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, eye-contact, or the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition.
Nor should it be sought apart from the eye-element; nor should it be sought apart from the form-element, up to and including the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition.”

Why is this so? Whether it be the eye-element, the form-element, or even the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition; whether one is apart from the eye-element, apart from the form-element, or even apart from the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition; whether it be the bodhisattva-mahāsattva, or the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), or the seeking of such things—all these are neither associated nor dissociated, neither material nor immaterial, neither visible nor invisible, neither resistant nor non-resistant. They all share a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of signlessness (animitta).
Why is this? Kauśika!

The perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva is not the eye-element, nor the form-element, nor the eye-consciousness-element, nor eye-contact, nor the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition; it is not these.
It is not apart from the eye-element, nor apart from the form-element, up to and including the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition. Why is this?
Because all such things are of a nature that is non-existent and cannot be apprehended.

Because they are non-existent and unapprehendable, the Prajñāpāramitā practiced by Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is not the eye-element, nor the form-element, nor even the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition;
yet it is not apart from the eye-element, nor apart from the form-element, nor apart from the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition.

Therefore, the *prajñāpāramitā* practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not be sought within the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*), nor should it be sought within the form-element (*rūpadhātu*) up to the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition;
nor should it be sought apart from the eye-element, nor apart from the form-element up to the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition.

“Kauśika! The *prajñāpāramitā* practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not be sought within the sphere of the ear (*śrotradhātu*), nor should it be sought within the sphere of sounds (*śabdadhātu*), the sphere of auditory consciousness (*śrotravijñānadhātu*), auditory contact (*śrotrasaṃsparśa*), or the various feelings (*vedanā*) produced with auditory contact as a condition;
nor should it be sought apart from the sphere of the ear, nor apart from the sphere of sounds, up to and including the various feelings produced with auditory contact as a condition.”

Why is this so? Whether it be the ear-element, the sound-element, or even the various sensations produced with ear-contact as a condition; whether one is apart from the ear-element, apart from the sound-element, or apart from the various sensations produced with ear-contact as a condition; or whether it be a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, or the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), or the seeking of such things—all these are neither associated nor dissociated, neither with form nor without form, neither visible nor invisible, neither resistant nor non-resistant. They all share a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of signlessness (animitta).
Why is this? Kausika!

The perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva is not the ear element, nor the sound element, nor the ear-consciousness element, nor ear-contact, nor the various sensations produced with ear-contact as a condition.
It is not apart from the ear-element, nor apart from the sound-element, up to and including the various feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition.
Why is this? Because all such things are of a nature that is non-existent and cannot be apprehended.

Because they are non-existent and unapprehendable, the *prajñāpāramitā* practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva is not the ear-element, nor the sound-element, nor even the various feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition;
yet it is not apart from the ear-element, nor apart from the sound-element, nor apart from the various feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition.

Therefore, the perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not be sought within the ear-element, nor should it be sought within the sound-element, up to and including the various sensations produced with ear-contact as a condition;
nor should it be sought apart from the ear-element, nor should it be sought apart from the sound-element, up to and including the various sensations produced with ear-contact as a condition.

“Kauśika! The *prajñāpāramitā* practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not be sought within the sphere of the nose (*ghrāṇadhātu*), nor within the sphere of odors (*gandhadhātu*), the sphere of nose-consciousness (*ghrāṇavijñānadhātu*), nose-contact (*ghrāṇasamsparśa*), or the various feelings (*vedanā*) produced with nose-contact as a condition;
nor should it be sought apart from the sphere of the nose, nor apart from the sphere of odors, up to and including the various feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition.”

Why is this so? Whether it be the nose element (*ghrāṇadhātu*), the odor element (*gandhadhātu*), or even the various feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition; whether one is separated from the nose element, separated from the odor element, or even separated from the various feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition—whether it be the bodhisattva mahāsattva, or the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), or the pursuit of such things—all are neither associated nor dissociated, neither material nor immaterial, neither visible nor invisible, neither resistant nor non-resistant. They all share a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of signlessness (*animitta*).
Why is this? Kauśika!

The perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva is not the nose element, nor the odor element, nor the nose-consciousness element, nor nose-contact, nor the various feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition.
It is not apart from the nose element, nor apart from the fragrance element, nor even the various feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition.
Why is this? Because all such things are of a nature that is non-existent and cannot be apprehended.

Because they are non-existent and unapprehendable, the *prajñāpāramitā* practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva is not the nose element (*ghrāṇadhātu*), nor the odor element (*gandhadhātu*), nor even the various sensations produced with nose-contact as a condition;
it is not apart from the nose element, nor apart from the odor element, nor even apart from the various sensations produced with nose-contact as a condition.

Therefore, the *prajñāpāramitā* practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not be sought within the nose-element (*ghrāṇadhātu*), nor should it be sought within the odor-element (*gandhadhātu*) up to and including the various feelings (*vedanā*) produced with nose-contact (*ghrāṇasparśa*) as a condition;
nor should it be sought apart from the nose-element, nor apart from the odor-element up to and including the various feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition.

“Kauśika! The perfection of wisdom practiced by bodhisattva mahāsattvas should not be sought within the tongue element; it should not be sought within the taste element, the tongue-consciousness element, tongue-contact, or the various feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition.
It should not be sought apart from the tongue element; nor should it be sought apart from the taste element, up to and including the various feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition.”

Why is this so? Whether it be the tongue element, the taste element, or even the various feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition; whether one is apart from the tongue element, apart from the taste element, or apart from the various feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition; or whether it be a bodhisattva mahāsattva, or the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), or the seeking of such things—all these are neither associated nor dissociated, neither material nor immaterial, neither visible nor invisible, neither resistant nor non-resistant. They are all of a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of signlessness (animitta).
Why is this? Kausika!

The perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahasattva is not the tongue-element, nor the taste-element, nor the tongue-consciousness-element, nor tongue-contact, nor the various sensations produced with tongue-contact as a condition.
It is not apart from the tongue-element, nor apart from the taste-element, up to and including the various feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition.
Why is this? Because all such things are of a nature that is non-existent and cannot be apprehended.

Because they are non-existent and unattainable, the *prajñāpāramitā* practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva is not the tongue element (*jihvādhātu*), nor the taste element (*rasadhātu*), nor even the various sensations (*vedanā*) produced with tongue-contact (*jihvāsaṃsparśa*) as a condition;
yet it is not apart from the tongue element, nor apart from the taste element, nor apart from the various sensations produced with tongue-contact as a condition.

Therefore, the perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not be sought within the tongue element, nor should it be sought within the taste element, up to and including the various feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition;
nor should it be sought apart from the tongue element, nor should it be sought apart from the taste element, up to and including the various feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition.

“Kauśika! The perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not be sought within the body-element (*kāya-dhātu*), nor should it be sought within the touch-element (*spraṣṭavya-dhātu*), the body-consciousness-element (*kāya-vijñāna-dhātu*), body-contact (*kāya-saṃsparśa*), or the various feelings (*vedanā*) produced with body-contact as their condition;
nor should it be sought apart from the body-element, nor apart from the touch-element, up to and including the various feelings produced with body-contact as their condition.”

Why is this so? Whether it be the body element (*kāyadhātu*), the tangible object element (*spraṣṭavyadhātu*), or even the various feelings produced with body-contact as a condition; whether one is separated from the body element, separated from the tangible object element, or even separated from the various feelings produced with body-contact as a condition; or whether it be a bodhisattva mahāsattva, or the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), or the seeking of such things—all these are neither associated nor dissociated, neither with form nor formless, neither visible nor invisible, neither resistant nor non-resistant. They are all of a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of signlessness (*animitta*).
Why is this? Kausika!

The perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva is not the body-element, nor the touch-element, nor the body-consciousness-element, nor body-contact, nor the various sensations produced with body-contact as a condition.
It is not apart from the body element, nor apart from the contact element, nor even apart from the various feelings produced with body-contact as a condition.
Why is this? Because all such things are of a nature that is non-existent and cannot be apprehended.

Because they are non-existent and unapprehendable, the perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva is not the body element, nor the touch element, nor the various feelings produced with body-touch as a condition;
yet it is not apart from the body element, nor apart from the touch element, nor apart from the various feelings produced with body-touch as a condition.

Therefore, the *prajñāpāramitā* practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not be sought within the body-element (*kāyadhātu*), nor should it be sought within the contact-element (*spraṣṭavyadhātu*) or even within the various feelings (*vedanā*) produced with body-contact as a condition;
nor should it be sought apart from the body-element, nor should it be sought apart from the contact-element or even apart from the various feelings produced with body-contact as a condition.

“Kauśika! The *prajñāpāramitā* practiced by bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should not be sought within the mental faculty (*manodhātu*), nor should it be sought within the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), the mental-consciousness realm (*manovijñānadhātu*), mental contact (*manaḥsaṃsparśa*), or the various sensations (*vedanā*) produced with mental contact as a condition;
nor should it be sought apart from the mental faculty, nor apart from the dharma-realm up to the various sensations produced with mental contact as a condition.”

Why is this? Whether it be the mind-element (*manodhātu*), the phenomena-element (*dharmadhātu*), or even the various feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition—if one is separated from the mind-element, or separated from the phenomena-element, or even the various feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition; or whether it be a bodhisattva mahāsattva, or the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), or the seeking of such things—all these are neither associated nor dissociated, neither material nor immaterial, neither visible nor invisible, neither resistant nor non-resistant. They all share a single characteristic, which is called "signlessness" (*animitta*).
Why is this? Kauśika!

The prajñāpāramitā practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva is not the mind-element, nor the dharma-element, nor the mental-consciousness-element, nor mental contact, nor the various sensations produced with mental contact as a condition.
It is not apart from the mind-element, nor apart from the phenomena-element, up to and including the various feelings produced with mind-contact as condition. Why is this so?
Because all these things are of a nature that is non-existent and cannot be apprehended.

Because they are non-existent and unapprehendable, the *prajñāpāramitā* practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva is not the mind-element (*manodhātu*), nor the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*), nor even the various sensations produced with mind-contact as a condition;
yet it is not apart from the mind-element, nor apart from the dharma-element, nor even apart from the various sensations produced with mind-contact as a condition.

Therefore, the Prajñāpāramitā practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not be sought within the sphere of mind (*manodhātu*), nor should it be sought within the sphere of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) or even within the various sensations produced with mental contact as their condition;
nor should it be sought apart from the sphere of mind, nor apart from the sphere of phenomena or even the various sensations produced with mental contact as their condition.

“Kauśika! The perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not be sought within the earth element, nor should it be sought within the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements;
nor should it be sought apart from the earth element, nor apart from the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements.”

Why is this so? Whether it be the earth element, or the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements; whether one is apart from the earth element, or apart from the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements; whether it be a bodhisattva mahāsattva, or the *prajñāpāramitā*, or the seeking of such things—all these are neither associated nor dissociated, neither with form nor formless, neither visible nor invisible, neither resistant nor non-resistant. They all share a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of signlessness (*animitta*).
Why is this? Kausika!
The perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva is not the earth element, nor is it the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements.
It is not apart from the earth element, nor apart from the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements.
Why is this so? Because all these are of a nature that is non-existent and cannot be apprehended.
Because they are non-existent and unapprehendable, the perfection of wisdom practiced by bodhisattva mahāsattvas is not the earth element, nor the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements;
it is not apart from the earth element, nor apart from the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements.

Therefore, the perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not be sought within the earth element, nor should it be sought within the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements;
nor should it be sought apart from the earth element, nor apart from the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements.

“Kauśika! The perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not be sought within the noble truth of suffering, nor should it be sought within the noble truths of origination, cessation, or the path;
nor should it be sought apart from the noble truth of suffering, nor apart from the noble truths of origination, cessation, or the path.”

Why is this so? Whether it be the noble truth of suffering, or the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path; or whether it be the departure from the noble truth of suffering, or the departure from the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path; or whether it be a bodhisattva mahāsattva, or the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā)—if one seeks them in such a manner, all of these are neither associated nor dissociated, neither with form nor formless, neither visible nor invisible, neither resistant nor non-resistant; they are all of a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of signlessness (animitta).
Why is this? Kauśika!
The perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva is not the noble truth of suffering, nor is it the noble truths of origination, cessation, or the path.
It is not apart from the noble truth of suffering, nor apart from the noble truths of origination, cessation, and the path. Why is this?
Because all these things are of a nature that is non-existent and cannot be apprehended.

Because all things are non-existent and unattainable, the perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva is not the noble truth of suffering, nor is it the noble truths of origination, cessation, or the path;
it is not separate from the noble truth of suffering, nor is it separate from the noble truths of origination, cessation, or the path.

Therefore, the practice of the perfection of wisdom by a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not be sought within the noble truth of suffering, nor should it be sought within the noble truths of origination, cessation, or the path;
nor should it be sought apart from the noble truth of suffering, nor apart from the noble truths of origination, cessation, or the path.

“Kauśika! The *prajñāpāramitā* practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not be sought within ignorance (*avidyā*), nor should it be sought within volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), feeling (*vedanā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), becoming (*bhava*), birth (*jāti*), or old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair (*jarāmaraṇa-śokaparidevaduḥkhadaurmanasyopāyāsa*).
Nor should it be sought apart from ignorance, nor apart from volitional formations, up to and including old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.”

Why is this so? Whether it be ignorance (*avidyā*), or volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), up to old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair; whether it be the departure from ignorance, or the departure from volitional formations, up to the departure from old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair; whether it be the bodhisattva mahāsattva, or the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), or the seeking of such things—all these are neither associated nor dissociated, neither with form nor formless, neither visible nor invisible, neither resistant nor non-resistant; they all share one single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of signlessness (*animitta*).
Why is this? Kauśika!

The perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva is not ignorance, nor is it volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
It is not apart from ignorance, nor apart from formations, up to and including old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair. Why is this?
Because all these things are non-existent by nature and cannot be apprehended.

Because nothing exists and nothing can be apprehended, the *prajñāpāramitā* practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva is neither ignorance nor the formative forces, up to and including old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair;
nor is it apart from ignorance, nor apart from the formative forces, up to and including old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair.

Therefore, the perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not be sought within ignorance, nor should it be sought within volitional formations, up to and including old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair;
nor should it be sought apart from ignorance, nor should it be sought apart from volitional formations, up to and including old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair.

“Kauśika! The *prajñāpāramitā* practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not be sought within internal emptiness; it should not be sought within external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-altering emptiness, essential emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common-characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, or the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature.
Nor should it be sought apart from internal emptiness, nor apart from external emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature.”

Why is this? Whether it be internal emptiness, external emptiness, up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature; whether it be the departure from internal emptiness, the departure from external emptiness, up to the departure from the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature; whether it be the bodhisattva-mahāsattva, or the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), or the seeking of such things—all these are neither associated nor dissociated, neither with form nor formless, neither visible nor invisible, neither resistant nor non-resistant; they all share one single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of signlessness (animitta).
Why is this? Kausika!

The perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva is not internal emptiness, nor external emptiness, nor internal-and-external emptiness, nor emptiness of emptiness, nor great emptiness, nor emptiness of the ultimate truth, nor emptiness of conditioned phenomena, nor emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, nor absolute emptiness, nor emptiness of the limitless, nor emptiness of dispersion, nor emptiness of non-alteration, nor emptiness of intrinsic nature, nor emptiness of self-characteristics, nor emptiness of common characteristics, nor emptiness of all phenomena, nor emptiness of the unapprehendable, nor emptiness of non-existence, nor emptiness of intrinsic nature, nor emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature.
It is not apart from internal emptiness, nor apart from external emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature. Why is this?
Because all such things are of a nature that is non-existent and cannot be apprehended.

Because all things are non-existent and unapprehendable, the perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva is not the emptiness of the internal, nor the emptiness of the external, up to and including the emptiness of the essential nature of non-entities;
it is not apart from the emptiness of the internal, nor apart from the emptiness of the external, up to and including the emptiness of the essential nature of non-entities.

Therefore, the *prajñāpāramitā* practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not be sought within internal emptiness, nor should it be sought within external emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence;
nor should it be sought apart from internal emptiness, nor apart from external emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.

“Kauśika! The *prajñāpāramitā* practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not be sought within *tathatā*, nor should it be sought within the *dharmadhātu*, the *dharmatā*, the non-illusory nature, the unchanging nature, the state of equality, the nature of freedom from birth, the fixedness of phenomena, the stability of phenomena, the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the realm of space, or the inconceivable realm;
nor should it be sought apart from *tathatā*, nor apart from the *dharmadhātu* up to the inconceivable realm.”

Why is this so? Whether it be suchness, the dharma-realm, or even the inconceivable realm; whether it be apart from suchness, apart from the dharma-realm, or even apart from the inconceivable realm; whether it be a bodhisattva mahāsattva, or the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), or the seeking of these things—all are neither associated nor dissociated, neither with form nor formless, neither visible nor invisible, neither resistant nor non-resistant; they all share one single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of signlessness (animitta).
Why is this so? Kauśika!

The perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva is not suchness, nor is it the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, the non-illusory nature, the unchanging nature, equality, the nature of being free from birth, the fixedness of dharmas, the stability of dharmas, the limit of reality, the realm of space, or the inconceivable realm.
It is not apart from suchness, nor apart from the dharma-realm, up to and including the inconceivable realm. Why is this so?
Because all such things are of a nature that is non-existent and cannot be apprehended.

Because they are non-existent and unapprehendable, the perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva is not suchness, nor is it the dharma-realm, up to and including the inconceivable realm;
yet it is not apart from suchness, nor is it apart from the dharma-realm, up to and including the inconceivable realm.
Therefore, the *prajñāpāramitā* practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not be sought within *tathatā*, nor should it be sought within the *dharmadhātu* up to the *acintyadhātu*;
nor should it be sought apart from *tathatā*, nor should it be sought apart from the *dharmadhātu* up to the *acintyadhātu*.

“Kauśika! The practice of the *prajñāpāramitā* of a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not be sought within the *dānapāramitā*, nor should it be sought within the *śīla*, *kṣānti*, *vīrya*, *dhyāna*, or *prajñāpāramitā*.
Nor should it be sought apart from the *dānapāramitā*, nor should it be sought apart from the *śīla*, *kṣānti*, *vīrya*, *dhyāna*, or *prajñāpāramitā*.”

Why is this so? Whether it be the perfection of generosity, or the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; whether it be apart from the perfection of generosity, or apart from the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; whether it be the bodhisattva mahāsattva, or the perfection of wisdom—seeking them in such a manner, all of these are neither conjoined nor disjoined, neither with form nor formless, neither visible nor invisible, neither resistant nor non-resistant; they are all of one single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of signlessness (*animitta*).
Why is this? Kauśika!

The perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva is not the perfection of giving, nor is it the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, or wisdom.
It is not apart from the perfection of generosity, nor apart from the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
Why is this? Because all these things are of a nature that is non-existent and unattainable.

Since they are non-existent and unattainable, the *prajñāpāramitā* practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva is not the *dānapāramitā*, nor is it the *śīla*, *kṣānti*, *vīrya*, *dhyāna*, or *prajñāpāramitā*.
It is not apart from the perfection of generosity, nor apart from the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.

Therefore, the perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not be sought within the perfection of generosity, nor should it be sought within the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, or wisdom;
nor should it be sought apart from the perfection of generosity, nor should it be sought apart from the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, or wisdom.

“Kauśika! The practice of the perfection of wisdom by a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not be sought within the four dhyānas, nor should it be sought within the four immeasurables or the four formless attainments;
nor should it be sought apart from the four dhyānas, nor should it be sought apart from the four immeasurables or the four formless attainments.”

Why is this? Whether it be the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, or the four formless attainments; whether one is apart from the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, or the four formless attainments; whether it be the bodhisattva mahāsattva, or the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), or the seeking of such things—all these are neither associated nor dissociated, neither with form nor formless, neither visible nor invisible, neither resistant nor non-resistant; they all share a single characteristic, namely, signlessness (animitta).
Why is this? Kausika!
The perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva is not the four dhyānas, nor the four immeasurables, nor the four formless attainments.
It is not apart from the four dhyānas, nor apart from the four immeasurables or the four formless attainments. Why is this?
Because all such things are of a nature that is non-existent and cannot be apprehended.

Because they are non-existent and unapprehendable, the perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva is not the four dhyānas, nor the four immeasurables, nor the four formless attainments;
yet it is not apart from the four dhyānas, nor apart from the four immeasurables, nor apart from the four formless attainments.

Therefore, the perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not be sought within the four dhyānas, nor should it be sought within the four immeasurables or the four formless attainments;
it should not be sought apart from the four dhyānas, nor should it be sought apart from the four immeasurables or the four formless attainments.

“Kauśika! The perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not be sought within the eight liberations, nor should it be sought within the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, or the ten totalities;
nor should it be sought apart from the eight liberations, nor apart from the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, or the ten totalities.”

Why is this so? Whether it be the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, or the ten universal bases; whether apart from the eight liberations, or apart from the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, or the ten universal bases; whether it be the bodhisattva mahāsattva, or the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), or the seeking of such things—all are neither associated nor dissociated, neither with form nor formless, neither visible nor invisible, neither resistant nor non-resistant. They all share one single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of signlessness (animitta).
Why is this? Kauśika!
The perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva is not the eight liberations, nor the eight bases of mastery, nor the nine successive attainments, nor the ten totalities.
It is not apart from the eight liberations, nor apart from the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, or the ten totalities. Why is this?
Because all these things are of a nature that is non-existent and cannot be apprehended.

Because they are non-existent and unapprehendable, the perfection of wisdom practiced by bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is not the eight liberations, nor the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive absorptions, or the ten totalities;
yet it is not apart from the eight liberations, nor apart from the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive absorptions, or the ten totalities.

Therefore, the perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not be sought within the eight liberations, nor should it be sought within the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, or the ten totalities;
nor should it be sought apart from the eight liberations, nor apart from the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, or the ten totalities.

“Kauśika! The *prajñāpāramitā* practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not be sought within the four foundations of mindfulness; it should not be sought within the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, or the eightfold noble path.
Nor should it be sought apart from the four foundations of mindfulness, nor apart from the four right efforts, up to and including the eightfold noble path.”

Why is this? Whether it be the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, up to and including the eight branches of the noble path; whether one is apart from the four foundations of mindfulness, apart from the four right efforts, up to and including the eight branches of the noble path; whether it be the bodhisattva mahāsattva, or the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), or the seeking of such things—all these are neither associated nor dissociated, neither material nor immaterial, neither visible nor invisible, neither resistant nor non-resistant; they all share a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of signlessness (animitta).
Why is this? Kauśika!

The perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva is not the four foundations of mindfulness; it is not the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the eightfold noble path.
It is not apart from the four foundations of mindfulness, nor apart from the four right efforts, up to and including the eight branches of the noble path. Why is this?
Because all these things are of a nature that is non-existent and cannot be apprehended.

Because they are non-existent and unapprehendable, the perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva is not the four foundations of mindfulness, nor the four right efforts, up to and including the eight branches of the noble path;
yet it is not apart from the four foundations of mindfulness, nor apart from the four right efforts, up to and including the eight branches of the noble path.

Therefore, the perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not be sought within the four applications of mindfulness, nor should it be sought within the four right efforts, up to and including the eightfold noble path;
nor should it be sought apart from the four applications of mindfulness, nor should it be sought apart from the four right efforts, up to and including the eightfold noble path.

“Kauśika! The perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not be sought within the gate of liberation of emptiness, nor should it be sought within the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness;
nor should it be sought apart from the gate of liberation of emptiness, nor should it be sought apart from the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness.”

Why is this so? Whether it be the gate of liberation of emptiness, or the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness; whether one is apart from the gate of liberation of emptiness, or apart from the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness; whether it be the bodhisattva mahāsattva, or the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), or such seeking—all these are neither associated nor dissociated, neither with form nor formless, neither visible nor invisible, neither resistant nor non-resistant; they are all of one single mark, namely, the markless.
Why is this? Kauśika!
The perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva is not the gate of liberation of emptiness, nor is it the gate of liberation of signlessness or wishlessness.
It is not apart from the gate of liberation of emptiness, nor apart from the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness. Why is this?
Because all such things are of a nature that is non-existent and cannot be apprehended.

Because nothing exists and nothing can be apprehended, the perfection of wisdom practiced by bodhisattva mahāsattvas is neither the liberation door of emptiness, nor the liberation doors of signlessness and wishlessness;
yet it is not apart from the liberation door of emptiness, nor is it apart from the liberation doors of signlessness and wishlessness.

Therefore, the *prajñāpāramitā* practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not be sought within the gate of liberation of emptiness, nor should it be sought within the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness;
nor should it be sought apart from the gate of liberation of emptiness, nor should it be sought apart from the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness.
“Kauśika! The *prajñāpāramitā* practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not be sought within the five eyes, nor should it be sought within the six supernormal powers;
it should not be sought apart from the five eyes, nor should it be sought apart from the six supernormal powers.”

Why is this? Whether it be the five eyes or the six supernormal powers, whether it be the absence of the five eyes or the absence of the six supernormal powers, whether it be the bodhisattva-mahāsattva, or the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), or the seeking of such things—all these are neither associated nor dissociated; they are neither with form nor without form; neither visible nor invisible; neither resistant nor non-resistant. They all share one and the same characteristic, which is to say: the characteristic of signlessness (animitta).
Why is this? Kauśika!
The perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva is neither the five eyes nor the six supernormal powers;
It is not apart from the five eyes, nor is it apart from the six supernormal powers. Why is this?
Because all such things are of a nature that is non-existent and cannot be apprehended.
Because nothing exists and nothing can be apprehended, the *prajñāpāramitā* practiced by the bodhisattva mahāsattva is neither the five eyes nor the six superknowledges;
yet it is not apart from the five eyes, nor is it apart from the six superknowledges.
Therefore, the practice of the perfection of wisdom by a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not be sought within the five eyes, nor should it be sought within the six supernormal powers;
it should not be sought apart from the five eyes, nor should it be sought apart from the six supernormal powers.

“Kauśika! The perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not be sought within the ten powers of a Buddha; it should not be sought within the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
Nor should it be sought apart from the ten powers of a Buddha; nor should it be sought apart from the four fearlessnesses up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.”

Why is this so? Whether it be the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, or even the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; whether one is apart from the ten powers, apart from the four fearlessnesses, or even apart from the eighteen unique qualities; whether it be a bodhisattva mahāsattva, or the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), or the seeking of such things—all are neither associated nor dissociated, neither with form nor formless, neither visible nor invisible, neither resistant nor non-resistant. They all share a single characteristic, which is called "signlessness" (animitta).
Why is this? Kauśika!

The perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva is not the ten powers of a Buddha, nor the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
It is not apart from the ten powers of a Buddha, nor apart from the four fearlessnesses, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. Why is this?
Because all such things are of a nature that is non-existent and unapprehendable.

Because they are non-existent and unapprehendable, the perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva is not the ten powers of a Buddha, nor the four fearlessnesses, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
yet it is not apart from the ten powers of a Buddha, nor apart from the four fearlessnesses, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.

Therefore, the *prajñāpāramitā* practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not be sought within the ten powers of a Buddha, nor should it be sought within the four fearlessnesses up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
nor should it be sought apart from the ten powers of a Buddha, nor apart from the four fearlessnesses up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.

“Kauśika! The *prajñāpāramitā* practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not be sought within the quality of non-forgetfulness (*asaṃpramoṣadharma*), nor should it be sought within the state of constant equanimity (*upekṣā-vihāra*).
Nor should it be sought apart from the quality of non-forgetfulness, nor should it be sought apart from the state of constant equanimity.”

Why is this so? Whether it be the quality of non-forgetfulness, or the state of constant abiding in equanimity, or the absence of the quality of non-forgetfulness, or the absence of the state of constant abiding in equanimity, or the bodhisattva mahāsattva, or the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā)—if one seeks them in such a manner, all of these are neither associated nor dissociated; they are neither with form nor without form; neither visible nor invisible; neither resistant nor non-resistant. They all share a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of signlessness (animitta).
Why is this? Kauśika!
The perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva is neither the quality of non-forgetfulness nor the state of constant abiding in equanimity.
It is not apart from the quality of non-forgetfulness, nor is it apart from the nature of constant abiding in equanimity. Why is this?
Because all such things are of a nature that is non-existent and cannot be apprehended.
Because non-existence is unapprehendable, the perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva is neither the quality of non-forgetfulness nor the state of constant equanimity;
yet it is not apart from the quality of non-forgetfulness, nor is it apart from the state of constant equanimity.

Therefore, the perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not be sought within the quality of non-forgetfulness, nor should it be sought within the state of constant equanimity;
nor should it be sought apart from the quality of non-forgetfulness, nor should it be sought apart from the state of constant equanimity.

“Kauśika! The perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not be sought within omniscience, nor should it be sought within the knowledge of the aspects of the path or the knowledge of all aspects;
nor should it be sought apart from omniscience, nor apart from the knowledge of the aspects of the path or the knowledge of all aspects.”

Why is this so? Whether it be all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), or the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*); whether it be the absence of all-knowledge, the absence of the knowledge of the aspects of the path, or the absence of the knowledge of all aspects; whether it be the bodhisattva mahāsattva, or the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), or the seeking of such things—all these are neither associated nor dissociated, neither with form nor formless, neither visible nor invisible, neither resistant (*sapratigha*) nor non-resistant. They are all of one single mark, namely, the markless (*animitta*).
Why is this? Kauśika!

The perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva is not omniscience (sarvajñatā), nor is it the knowledge of the aspects of the path (mārgākārajñatā) or the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā).
It is not apart from all-knowledge, nor apart from the knowledge of the paths, nor apart from the knowledge of all aspects. Why is this?
Because all such things are of a nature that is non-existent and cannot be apprehended.

Because nothing exists and nothing can be apprehended, the perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva is not omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), nor is it the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) or the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*);
yet it is not apart from omniscience, nor is it apart from the knowledge of the aspects of the path or the knowledge of all aspects.

Therefore, the perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not be sought within omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), nor should it be sought within the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) or the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*);
nor should it be sought apart from omniscience, nor apart from the knowledge of the aspects of the path or the knowledge of all aspects.
The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Scroll Ninety-four [and] Scroll Ninety-five.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang under Imperial Decree.
Chapter One: The Search for Prajñāpāramitā, Part Twenty-seven, Section Seven. "Kauśika!
The prajñāpāramitā practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not be sought among all the dhāraṇī-doors, nor should it be sought among all the samādhi-doors;..."
One should not seek it apart from all dharani-doors, nor should one seek it apart from all samadhi-doors. Why is this?

Whether it be all dharani-doors, or all samadhi-doors, or being apart from all dharani-doors, or being apart from all samadhi-doors, or the bodhisattva-mahasattva, or the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), or such seeking—all these are neither associated nor dissociated; they are neither with form nor without form; neither visible nor invisible; neither resistant nor non-resistant. They are all of a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of signlessness (animitta).
Why is this? Kauśika!
The perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva is not all the doors of dhāraṇī, nor is it all the doors of samādhi.
It is not apart from all dhāraṇī-doors, nor is it apart from all samādhi-doors.
Why is this? Because all such things are of a nature that is non-existent and unapprehendable.
Because they are non-existent and unapprehendable, the perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva is neither all the doors of dhāraṇī nor all the doors of samādhi;
it is neither apart from all the doors of dhāraṇī nor apart from all the doors of samādhi.
Therefore, the perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not be sought within all the gateways of dhāraṇī, nor should it be sought within all the gateways of samādhi;
it should not be sought apart from all the gateways of dhāraṇī, nor should it be sought apart from all the gateways of samādhi.
“Kauśika! The practice of the perfection of wisdom by a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not be sought among stream-enterers, nor should it be sought among once-returners, non-returners, or arhats;
nor should it be sought apart from stream-enterers, nor apart from once-returners, non-returners, or arhats.”

Why is this so? Whether it be a stream-enterer, a once-returner, a non-returner, or an arhat; whether apart from the stream-enterer, the once-returner, the non-returner, or the arhat; whether it be a bodhisattva mahāsattva, or the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), or the seeking of such things—all these are neither associated nor dissociated, neither with form nor formless, neither visible nor invisible, neither resistant nor non-resistant. They all share a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of signlessness (animitta).
Why is this? Kauśika!
The perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva is not the stage of a stream-enterer, nor that of a once-returner, a non-returner, or an arhat.
It is not apart from the stream-enterer, nor apart from the once-returner, the non-returner, or the arhat.
Why is this? Because all these things are of a nature that is non-existent and cannot be apprehended.

Because nothing exists and nothing can be apprehended, the perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva is not the state of a stream-enterer, nor that of a once-returner, a non-returner, or an arhat;
yet it is not apart from the state of a stream-enterer, nor apart from that of a once-returner, a non-returner, or an arhat.

Therefore, the *prajñāpāramitā* practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not be sought among stream-enterers (*srotāpanna*), nor should it be sought among once-returners (*sakṛdāgāmin*), non-returners (*anāgāmin*), or arhats;
nor should it be sought apart from stream-enterers, nor apart from once-returners, non-returners, or arhats.

“Kauśika! The *prajñāpāramitā* practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not be sought within the stage of entering the stream (*srotāpatti-pratipannaka*) or the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*); it should not be sought within the stage of entering once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmi-pratipannaka*), the fruit of once-returning, the stage of entering non-returning (*anāgāmi-pratipannaka*), the fruit of non-returning, the stage of entering arhatship (*arhattva-pratipannaka*), or the fruit of arhatship.

Nor should it be sought apart from the stage of entering the stream or the fruit of stream-entry; nor should it be sought apart from the stage of entering once-returning, up to and including the fruit of arhatship.”

Why is this so? Whether it be those entering the stream and those who have attained the fruit of stream-entry; those entering the stage of once-returner up to those who have attained the fruit of arhatship; whether one is apart from entering the stream and the fruit of stream-entry, or apart from entering the stage of once-returner up to the fruit of arhatship; whether it be a bodhisattva mahāsattva, or the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), or the seeking of such things—all these are neither associated nor dissociated, neither with form nor formless, neither visible nor invisible, neither resistant nor non-resistant; they all share a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of signlessness (animitta).
Why is this? Kausika!

The perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva is not the stream-entry path nor the fruit of stream-entry; it is not the once-returner path nor the fruit of once-returning, nor the non-returner path nor the fruit of non-returning, nor the arhat path nor the fruit of arhatship.
It is not apart from the stage of entering the stream and the fruit of stream-entry, nor apart from the stage of entering the once-returner up to the fruit of arhatship. Why is this?
Because all these things are of a nature that is non-existent and cannot be apprehended.

Because nothing exists and nothing can be apprehended, the *prajñāpāramitā* practiced by the bodhisattva mahāsattva is neither the stream-enterer’s path nor the fruit of stream-entry, nor the path of the once-returner up to the fruit of arhatship;
it is neither apart from the stream-enterer’s path and fruit, nor apart from the path of the once-returner up to the fruit of arhatship.

Therefore, the perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not be sought in the stage of entering the stream or in the fruit of stream-entry; it should not be sought in the stage of entering once-returning up to the fruit of arhatship.
Nor should it be sought apart from the stage of entering the stream or the fruit of stream-entry; nor should it be sought apart from the stage of entering once-returning up to the fruit of arhatship.

“Kauśika! The perfection of wisdom practiced by bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should not be sought from pratyekabuddhas, nor should it be sought from those who have entered the path toward the fruit of a pratyekabuddha;
it should not be sought apart from pratyekabuddhas, nor should it be sought apart from those who have entered the path toward the fruit of a pratyekabuddha.”

Why is this so? Whether it be a Pratyekabuddha, one who is progressing toward the fruit of a Pratyekabuddha, one who is apart from a Pratyekabuddha, or one who is apart from the progress toward the fruit of a Pratyekabuddha; whether it be a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, or the Prajñāpāramitā, or the seeking after such things—all these are neither associated nor dissociated, neither with form nor without form, neither visible nor invisible, neither resistant nor non-resistant. They all share one single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being signless (animitta).
Why is this? Kauśika!
The perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva is neither for the sake of a pratyekabuddha, nor for one who is heading toward the fruit of a pratyekabuddha.
It is not apart from the pratyekabuddha, nor is it apart from the one proceeding toward the fruit of a pratyekabuddha. Why is this?
Because all such things are of a nature that is non-existent and cannot be apprehended.

Because nothing exists and nothing can be apprehended, the perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva is neither the solitary buddha nor the path leading toward the fruit of solitary buddhahood;
it is neither separate from the solitary buddha nor separate from the path leading toward the fruit of solitary buddhahood.

Therefore, the perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not be sought from the pratyekabuddha, nor should it be sought from one who is training for the fruit of a pratyekabuddha;
it should not be sought apart from the pratyekabuddha, nor should it be sought apart from one who is training for the fruit of a pratyekabuddha.
“Kauśika! The prajñāpāramitā practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not be sought within the bodhisattva mahāsattva, nor should it be sought within the samyaksaṃbuddha;
it should not be sought apart from the bodhisattva mahāsattva, nor should it be sought apart from the samyaksaṃbuddha.”

Why is this so? Whether it be a bodhisattva-mahāsattva or a samyaksaṃbuddha, whether apart from a bodhisattva-mahāsattva or apart from a samyaksaṃbuddha, whether it be a bodhisattva-mahāsattva or the prajñāpāramitā—if one seeks them in such a manner, all of these are neither associated nor dissociated; they are neither with form nor without form; neither visible nor invisible; neither resistant nor non-resistant. They are all of a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of signlessness (animitta).
Why is this? Kauśika!
The perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva is neither the bodhisattva mahāsattva nor the samyaksaṃbuddha.
It is not apart from the bodhisattva-mahāsattva, nor is it apart from the samyaksaṃbuddha. Why is this?
Because all such things are of a nature that is non-existent and cannot be apprehended.
Because of the non-existence and unattainability [of all things], the *prajñāpāramitā* practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva is neither the bodhisattva mahāsattva nor the *samyaksaṃbuddha*;
yet it is not apart from the bodhisattva mahāsattva, nor is it apart from the *samyaksaṃbuddha*.
Therefore, the prajñāpāramitā practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not be sought within the bodhisattva mahāsattva, nor should it be sought within the samyaksaṃbuddha;
it should not be sought apart from the bodhisattva mahāsattva, nor should it be sought apart from the samyaksaṃbuddha.

“Kauśika! The perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not be sought within the dharmas of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, nor should it be sought within unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
it should not be sought apart from the dharmas of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, nor should it be sought apart from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”

Why is this? Whether it be the dharmas of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, or unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, or the dharmas apart from a bodhisattva mahāsattva, or apart from unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, or the bodhisattva mahāsattva himself, or the perfection of wisdom—if one seeks them in this way, all of these are neither associated nor dissociated; they are neither with form nor without form; neither visible nor invisible; neither resistant nor non-resistant. They are all of a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of signlessness (*animitta*).
Why is this? Kauśika!
The perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva is neither the dharma of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, nor is it unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
It is not apart from the dharmas of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, nor is it apart from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Why is this?
Because all such things are of a nature that is non-existent and unobtainable.

Because all things are non-existent and unapprehendable, the perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva is neither the dharma of a bodhisattva mahāsattva nor is it unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
yet it is not apart from the dharma of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, nor is it apart from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Therefore, the perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not be sought within the dharmas of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, nor should it be sought within unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
nor should it be sought apart from the dharmas of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, nor should it be sought apart from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

“Kauśika! The *prajñāpāramitā* practiced by bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should not be sought within the Śrāvaka vehicle, nor should it be sought within the Pratyekabuddha vehicle or the Unsurpassed Vehicle;
yet it should not be sought apart from the Śrāvaka vehicle, nor apart from the Pratyekabuddha vehicle or the Unsurpassed Vehicle.”

Why is this? Whether it be the Śrāvaka vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, or the Unsurpassed Vehicle; whether apart from the Śrāvaka vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, or the Unsurpassed Vehicle; whether it be the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, or the Prajñāpāramitā, or the seeking of such things—all these are neither associated nor dissociated, neither with form nor formless, neither visible nor invisible, neither resistant nor non-resistant; they all share one single characteristic, which is the so-called "signlessness" (animitta).
Why is this? Kauśika!

The perfection of wisdom practiced by bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is not the vehicle of the śrāvakas, nor the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, nor the unsurpassed vehicle; it is the perfection of wisdom itself.
It is not apart from the Śrāvaka vehicle, nor apart from the Pratyekabuddha vehicle or the Unsurpassed Vehicle. Why is this?
Because all such things are of a nature that is non-existent and cannot be apprehended.

Because nothing exists and nothing can be apprehended, the perfection of wisdom practiced by bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is neither the vehicle of the śrāvakas, nor the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, nor the unsurpassed vehicle;
yet it is not apart from the vehicle of the śrāvakas, nor apart from the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, nor apart from the unsurpassed vehicle.

Therefore, the practice of the perfection of wisdom by a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not be sought within the vehicle of the śrāvakas, nor should it be sought within the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas or the unsurpassed vehicle;
yet it should not be sought apart from the vehicle of the śrāvakas, nor should it be sought apart from the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas or the unsurpassed vehicle.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

The perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not be sought within the suchness of form, nor should it be sought within the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;
nor should it be sought apart from the suchness of form, nor apart from the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness."

Whether it be the suchness of form, or the suchness of feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness; whether it be the suchness apart from form, or the suchness apart from feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness; whether it be the bodhisattva mahāsattva, or the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), or the seeking of these—none of them are associated nor dissociated, neither material nor immaterial, neither visible nor invisible, neither resistant nor non-resistant; they are all of one single mark, namely, the markless.
Why is this? Kauśika!
The perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva is not the suchness of form, nor is it the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
It is not apart from the suchness of form, nor apart from the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. Why is this?
Because all these things are of a nature that is non-existent and cannot be apprehended.

Because nothing exists and nothing can be apprehended, the perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva is not the suchness of form, nor is it the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;
yet it is not apart from the suchness of form, nor is it apart from the suchness of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.

Therefore, the *prajñāpāramitā* practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not be sought within the *tathatā* (suchness) of form, nor should it be sought within the *tathatā* of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;
nor should it be sought apart from the *tathatā* of form, nor apart from the *tathatā* of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.

“Kauśika! The perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not be sought in the suchness of the eye-base; it should not be sought in the suchness of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-base.
It should not be sought apart from the suchness of the eye-base; it should not be sought apart from the suchness of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-base.”

Why is this so? Why is this? Kauśika!
The perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva is not the suchness of the sense-base of the eye, nor is it the suchness of the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind.
It is not apart from the suchness of the sense-base of the eye, nor apart from the suchness of the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. Why is this?
Because all these are of a nature that is non-existent and cannot be apprehended.

Because they are non-existent and unapprehendable, the perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva is not the suchness of the sense-base of the eye, nor is it the suchness of the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind;
nor is it apart from the suchness of the sense-base of the eye, nor is it apart from the suchness of the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind.

Therefore, the *prajñāpāramitā* practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not be sought in the suchness (*tathatā*) of the sense base of the eye, nor should it be sought in the suchness of the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind;
nor should it be sought apart from the suchness of the sense base of the eye, nor apart from the suchness of the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind.

“Kauśika! The perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not be sought within the suchness of form; it should not be sought within the suchness of sound, odor, taste, tangibles, or mental phenomena.
Nor should it be sought apart from the suchness of form; nor should it be sought apart from the suchness of sound, odor, taste, tangibles, or mental phenomena.”

Why is this so? Whether it be the suchness of the sphere of form, or the suchness of the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena; whether it be the suchness apart from the sphere of form, or the suchness apart from the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena; whether it be the bodhisattva mahāsattva, or the perfection of wisdom—when seeking them in this way, all are neither associated nor dissociated, neither with form nor formless, neither visible nor invisible, neither resistant nor non-resistant. Because all these things are non-existent by nature and cannot be apprehended.

Because all things are non-existent and unapprehendable, the perfection of wisdom practiced by the bodhisattva mahāsattva is not the suchness of the sphere of form, nor is it the suchness of the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental phenomena;
nor is it apart from the suchness of the sphere of form, nor apart from the suchness of the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental phenomena.

Therefore, the practice of the Prajñāpāramitā by a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not be sought within the suchness of form, nor should it be sought within the suchness of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental phenomena;
nor should it be sought apart from the suchness of form, nor should it be sought apart from the suchness of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental phenomena.

The *prajñāpāramitā* practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not be sought within the suchness (*tathatā*) of the eye-element; it should not be sought within the suchness of the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, eye-contact, or the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition.

Nor should it be sought apart from the suchness of the eye-element, nor apart from the suchness of the form-element, up to and including the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition.”

Why is this so? Whether it be the suchness of the eye-element, or the suchness of the form-element up to the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition; whether it be the suchness apart from the eye-element, or the suchness apart from the form-element up to the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition; whether it be the bodhisattva-mahāsattva, or the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), or the seeking of these things—all are neither associated nor dissociated, neither material nor immaterial, neither visible nor invisible, neither resistant nor non-resistant. The perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva is not the suchness of the eye-element, nor is it the suchness of the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, eye-contact, or the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition; nor is it the suchness of any other element.

It is not apart from the suchness of the eye-element, nor apart from the suchness of the form-element, up to and including the suchness of all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition. Why is this?
Because all these are of a nature that is non-existent and cannot be apprehended.

nor is it apart from the suchness of the eye-element, nor apart from the suchness of the form-element, up to and including the suchness of the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition.

Therefore, the perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not be sought within the suchness of the eye-element, nor should it be sought within the suchness of the form-element, up to and including the suchness of all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition;

nor should it be sought apart from the suchness of the eye-element, nor should it be sought apart from the suchness of the form-element, up to and including the suchness of all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition.

Nor should it be sought apart from the suchness of the ear-element, nor apart from the suchness of the sound-element, up to and including the various feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition.”

Why is this so? Whether it be the suchness of the ear-element, or the suchness of the sound-element up to the various feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition; whether it be the suchness apart from the ear-element, or the suchness apart from the sound-element up to the various feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition; whether it be the bodhisattva-mahāsattva, or the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), or the seeking of these things—all are neither associated nor dissociated, neither with form nor formless, neither visible nor invisible, neither resistant nor non-resistant; they all share one single characteristic, which is called "signlessness" (animitta).
Why is this? Kauśika!

The perfection of wisdom practiced by a bodhisattva mahāsattva is not the suchness of the ear-element, nor is it the suchness of the sound-element, the ear-consciousness-element, ear-contact, or the various feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition; it is not their suchness.

It is not apart from the suchness of the ear-element, nor apart from the suchness of the sound-element, up to and including the suchness of the various feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition. Why is this?
