When these sons and daughters of good family study this great king of spells, the Prajñāpāramitā, they do not apprehend a self, they do not apprehend a sentient being, they do not apprehend a life-principle, they do not apprehend a living being, they do not apprehend a nourisher, they do not apprehend a person, they do not apprehend a pudgala, they do not apprehend a mind-born being, they do not apprehend a man-made being, they do not apprehend an agent, they do not apprehend an experiencer, they do not apprehend a knower, and they do not apprehend a seer.”
Because we have nothing to attain, we do not harm ourselves, we do not harm others, and we do not harm both. "Kauśika!

When these sons and daughters of good family study this Great King of Mantras, the Prajñāpāramitā, they do not apprehend form; they do not apprehend feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness."
Because they do not apprehend the aggregate of form and so forth, they do not harm themselves, they do not harm others, and they do not harm both. "Kauśika!

When these sons and daughters of good family study this great king of spells, the Prajñāpāramitā, they do not apprehend the sense-base of the eye; they do not apprehend the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind."
Because they do not apprehend the sense base of the eye and so forth, they do not harm themselves, they do not harm others, and they do not harm both. "Kauśika!

When these sons of good family and daughters of good family study this Great King of Spells, the Prajñāpāramitā, they do not apprehend the sense base of form, nor do they apprehend the sense bases of sound, odor, taste, touch, or mental phenomena."
Because they do not apprehend the sphere of form and so forth, they do not harm themselves, they do not harm others, and they do not harm both. "Kauśika!

When these sons and daughters of good family study this great king of mantras, the Prajñāpāramitā, they do not apprehend the eye-element, nor the form-element, nor the eye-consciousness-element, nor eye-contact, nor the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition."
Because they do not apprehend the eye-element and so forth, they do no harm to themselves, do no harm to others, and do no harm to both. "Kauśika!

When these sons and daughters of good family study this great king of spells, the Prajñāpāramitā, they do not apprehend the ear-element; they do not apprehend the sound-element, the ear-consciousness-element, nor ear-contact, nor the various sensations produced with ear-contact as a condition."
Because they do not apprehend the ear element and so forth, they do not harm themselves, do not harm others, and do not harm both. "Kauśika!

When these sons and daughters of good family study this great king of mantras, the Prajñāpāramitā, they do not apprehend the nose element, nor the odor element, nor the nose-consciousness element, nor nose-contact, nor the various sensations produced with nose-contact as a condition."
Because they do not apprehend the nose element and so forth, they do not harm themselves, they do not harm others, and they do not harm both. "Kauśika!

When these sons and daughters of good family study this great king of spells, the Prajñāpāramitā, they do not apprehend the tongue element; they do not apprehend the taste element, the tongue-consciousness element, nor tongue-contact, nor the various sensations produced with tongue-contact as a condition."
Because they do not apprehend the tongue element and so forth, they do not harm themselves, do not harm others, and do not harm both. "Kauśika!

When these sons and daughters of good family study this Great King of Mantras, the Prajñāpāramitā, they do not apprehend the body element; they do not apprehend the touch element, the body-consciousness element, nor body-contact, nor the various feelings produced with body-contact as a condition."
Because they do not apprehend the body-element and so forth, they do not harm themselves, they do not harm others, and they do not harm both. "Kauśika!

When these sons and daughters of good family study this great king of spells, the Prajñāpāramitā, they do not apprehend the mind-element, nor the dharma-element, nor the mind-consciousness-element, nor mental contact, nor the various sensations produced with mental contact as a condition."
Because they do not apprehend the mind-element and so forth, they do no harm to themselves, do no harm to others, and do no harm to both. "Kauśika!

When these sons and daughters of good family study this great king of spells, the Prajñāpāramitā, they do not apprehend the earth element; they do not apprehend the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements."
Because they do not apprehend the earth element and so forth, they do not harm themselves, do not harm others, and do not harm both. "Kauśika!

When these sons and daughters of good family study this great king of spells, the Prajñāpāramitā, they do not apprehend the Noble Truth of Suffering, nor do they apprehend the Noble Truths of Origination, Cessation, or the Path."
Because one finds nothing to be apprehended in the Noble Truth of Suffering and the others, one does not harm oneself, does not harm others, and does not harm both. "Kauśika!

When these sons and daughters of good family study this great king of spells, the Prajñāpāramitā, they do not apprehend ignorance; they do not apprehend volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, sensation, craving, clinging, existence, birth, or old age, death, grief, lamentation, suffering, distress, and despair.
Because they do not apprehend ignorance and the other [links of dependent origination], they do no harm to themselves, do no harm to others, and do no harm to both. "Kauśika!

When these sons of good family and daughters of good family study this Great King of Mantras, the Prajñāpāramitā, they do not apprehend internal emptiness; they do not apprehend external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate truth, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, the emptiness of the limitless, the emptiness of dispersion, the emptiness of non-alteration, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the emptiness of self-characteristic, the emptiness of common characteristic, the emptiness of all dharmas, the emptiness of non-apprehensibility, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, or the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature."
Because nothing is apprehended within the emptinesses and so forth, they do not harm themselves, do not harm others, and do not harm both. "Kauśika!

When these sons and daughters of good family study this Great King of Mantras, the Prajñāpāramitā, they do not apprehend suchness; they do not apprehend the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, the non-erroneous nature, the unchanging nature, equality, the nature of being free from birth, the fixed nature of dharmas, the stability of dharmas, the limit of reality, the realm of space, or the inconceivable realm."
Because one finds nothing to be apprehended in suchness and so forth, one does not bring harm to oneself, nor harm to others, nor harm to both.
*The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Scroll 102; *The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Scroll 103.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang under Imperial Order.
Part One, Chapter Twenty-nine on “Inclusion,” Section Five: “Kauśika!

When these sons and daughters of good family study this great king of mantras, the Prajñāpāramitā, they do not apprehend the perfection of generosity, nor do they apprehend the perfections of pure ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, or wisdom.
Because one does not apprehend anything in the perfection of generosity and the other perfections, one does not harm oneself, does not harm others, and does not harm both. "Kauśika!

When these sons and daughters of good family study this great king of mantras, the Prajñāpāramitā, they do not attain the four dhyānas, nor do they attain the four immeasurables or the four formless absorptions.
Because one finds nothing to be apprehended in the four dhyānas and so forth, one does not harm oneself, does not harm others, and does not harm both. "Kauśika!..."

When these sons and daughters of good family study this great king of spells, the Prajñāpāramitā, they do not attain the eight liberations, nor do they attain the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative absorptions, or the ten totalities.
Because one does not apprehend anything in the eight liberations and so forth, one does no harm to oneself, no harm to others, and no harm to both. "Kauśika!..."

When these sons and daughters of good family study this Great King of Spells, the Prajñāpāramitā, they do not apprehend the four foundations of mindfulness; they do not apprehend the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the eightfold noble path.
Because one does not apprehend the four foundations of mindfulness and so forth, one does not harm oneself, does not harm others, and does not harm both. "Kauśika!..."

When these sons and daughters of good family study this Great King of Mantras, the Prajñāpāramitā, they do not attain the gate of liberation of emptiness, nor do they attain the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness.
Because they do not apprehend anything in the gate of liberation of emptiness and so forth, they do not harm themselves, they do not harm others, and they do not harm both. "Kauśika!..."
When these sons and daughters of good family study this great king of spells, the Prajñāpāramitā, they do not attain the five eyes, nor do they attain the six supernormal powers.
Because they do not apprehend the five eyes and so forth, they do not harm themselves, do not harm others, and do not harm both. "Kauśika!

When these sons and daughters of good family study this Great King of Mantras, the Prajñāpāramitā, they do not apprehend the ten powers of a Buddha, nor do they apprehend the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha."
Because one finds nothing to be apprehended regarding the ten powers of a Buddha and so forth, one does not bring harm upon oneself, nor harm others, nor harm both.
"Kauśika!..."

When these sons and daughters of good family study this great king of spells, the Prajñāpāramitā, they do not attain the quality of non-forgetfulness, nor do they attain the state of constant abiding in equanimity.
Because one does not apprehend anything, such as the quality of non-forgetfulness, one does not harm oneself, does not harm others, and does not harm both.
"Kauśika!..."

When these sons and daughters of good family study this great king of spells, the Prajñāpāramitā, they do not attain all-knowledge, nor do they attain the knowledge of the aspects of the path, nor the knowledge of all aspects.
Because one finds nothing to be apprehended in omniscience and the like, one does not harm oneself, nor harm others, nor harm both.
"Kauśika!..."
When these sons and daughters of good family study this great king of mantras, the Prajñāpāramitā, they do not attain any of the gates of dhāraṇī, nor do they attain any of the gates of samādhi.
Because one does not apprehend anything in all the gateways of dhāraṇī and so forth, one does not harm oneself, does not harm others, and does not harm both. "Kauśika!

When these sons and daughters of good family study this great king of spells, the Prajñāpāramitā, they do not attain the stage of stream-enterer; they do not attain once-returner, non-returner, or arhatship.
Because they do not apprehend the state of a stream-enterer and so forth, they do not harm themselves, they do not harm others, and they do not harm both. "Kauśika!

When these sons and daughters of good family study this great king of spells, the Prajñāpāramitā, they do not attain the stage of entering the stream or the fruit of a stream-enterer; they do not attain the stage of entering once-returning or the fruit of a once-returner, nor the stage of entering non-returning or the fruit of a non-returner, nor the stage of entering arhatship or the fruit of an arhat."

Because one does not apprehend the state of being a candidate for the fruit of stream-entry, nor the fruit of stream-entry itself, one does no harm to oneself, no harm to others, and no harm to both. "Kauśika!..."

When these sons and daughters of good family study this great king of mantras, the Prajñāpāramitā, they do not attain the state of a pratyekabuddha, nor do they approach the fruit of a pratyekabuddha.
Because they do not apprehend anything in the case of the Pratyekabuddhas and so forth, they do not harm themselves, they do not harm others, and they do not harm both. "Kauśika!

When these sons of good family and daughters of good family study this Great King of Spells, the Prajñāpāramitā, they do not apprehend a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, nor do they apprehend a Samyaksaṃbuddha."
Because Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas have nothing to be apprehended, they do not harm themselves, they do not harm others, and they do not harm both. “Kauśika!

When these sons and daughters of good family study this great king of mantras, the Prajñāpāramitā, they do not apprehend the dharmas of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, nor do they apprehend unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Because they find nothing to be apprehended in the dharmas of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, they do not harm themselves, they do not harm others, and they do not harm both.
"Kauśika!..."

When these sons and daughters of good family study this great king of spells, the Prajñāpāramitā, they do not attain the vehicle of the śrāvaka, nor the vehicle of the pratyekabuddha, nor the unsurpassed vehicle.
Because nothing is apprehended within the Śrāvaka vehicle and so forth, one does not bring harm to oneself, nor harm to others, nor harm to both. "Kauśika!..."

When these sons and daughters of good family study this great king of mantras, the Prajñāpāramitā, although they apprehend neither me nor the Dharma, they realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. They observe the differences in the mental activities of all sentient beings and, according to what is appropriate for them, turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma, causing all who practice as instructed to obtain benefit.

Why is this? Because in the past, the multitudes of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas diligently practiced and studied this Great Divine Mantra King of the Prajñāpāramitā; they have already realized unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, turned the wondrous wheel of Dharma, and delivered immeasurable multitudes.

In the future, the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who diligently practice and study this great king of dhāraṇīs, the Prajñāpāramitā, shall realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and turn the sublime wheel of Dharma to deliver immeasurable multitudes.

At present, in the boundless worlds of the ten directions, there are assemblies of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who diligently study and practice this Great Divine Mantra King of the Prajñāpāramitā; they have realized unexcelled, perfect enlightenment in the present, and turn the wondrous wheel of Dharma to deliver immeasurable multitudes.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters wholeheartedly hear, receive, uphold, read, recite, diligently practice, reflect upon according to principle, transcribe, explain, and widely disseminate this Prajñāpāramitā, then in whatever lands, cities, towns, or villages these good sons and good daughters may dwell—whether among humans or non-humans—they shall not be harmed by any calamities, misfortunes, or epidemics."
Why is this? Because wherever these sons and daughters of good family dwell, for the sake of this trichiliocosm and all the other immeasurable,
incalculable, and boundless worlds throughout the ten directions, [they act as] the Cāturmahārājakāyika devas...
The gods of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, the Heaven of the Thirty-three, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven,
the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, the Brahmakāyika Heaven, the Brahmapurohita Heaven,
the Brahmakāyika-sabhāgata Heaven, the Mahābrahmā Heaven, the Ābhāsvara Heaven, the Parīttābha Heaven, the Apramāṇābha Heaven, and the Ābhāsvara Heaven.
The Śuddhāvāsa Heaven, the Parīttābha Heaven, the Apramāṇābha Heaven, the Ābhāsvara Heaven, the Bṛhatphala Heaven,
the Parīttaśubha Heaven, the Apramāṇaśubha Heaven, the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven, the Avṛha Heaven, the Atapa Heaven,
the Sudṛśa Heaven, the Sudarśana Heaven, and the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, together with the nāgas, yakṣas, and asuras.
They shall constantly come to protect, respectfully make offerings to, revere, and praise [this],
so that no obstacles may arise for this Great Divine Mantra King, the Prajñāpāramitā.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family writes down this Great Divine Mantra King of the Prajñāpāramitā and places it in a pure location, honoring, making offerings to, respecting, and praising it—even if they do not hear it, uphold it, read it, recite it, diligently practice it, contemplate it according to the principle, nor explain or analyze it for others—nevertheless, all calamities, misfortunes, and epidemics shall not harm the people, non-humans, and others in that dwelling place, kingdom, city, or royal capital."

Why is this so? Because wherever this Great Divine Mantra King, the Prajñāpāramitā, resides, all the gods from the Cāturmahārājika Heaven up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, as well as the nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, and others throughout this trichiliocosm and the infinite, countless, and boundless worlds of the ten directions, will constantly come to protect, revere, make offerings to, honor, and praise it, so that no obstacles may arise for this Great Divine Mantra King, the Prajñāpāramitā.

“Kauśika! If these sons and daughters of good family merely write down this Great King of Mantras, the Prajñāpāramitā, and place it in a pure location, honoring, making offerings to, respecting, and praising it, they still obtain such benefits in this present life; how much more so if they can hear it, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, diligently practice and study it, reflect upon it according to the principle, and extensively explain and analyze it for others!”
You should know that such individuals possess boundless merit; they will swiftly realize *bodhi* and bring benefit and happiness to all. Kausika!

If good men or good women fear enemies, wild beasts, calamities, malevolent incantations, epidemics, poisons, spells, and the like, they should write down this Great Divine Spell King, the *Prajñāpāramitā*, and place it in a small sachet of incense according to their means, storing it within a precious casket and constantly carrying it with them while making respectful offerings. All matters of fear will naturally be eliminated, for devas, nāgas, and spirits will constantly guard them.

“Kauśika! For example, if a person or even an animal of the animal realm enters the precincts of the Bodhi tree, or merely reaches its vicinity, neither humans nor non-humans will be able to harm them.”

Why is this? Because all Buddhas of the past, future, and present have sat upon this very spot to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Having attained enlightenment, they bestow freedom from fear and dread, and physical and mental peace and happiness, upon all sentient beings; they establish immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings, causing them to abide in the sublime conduct of humans and devas;
they establish immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings, causing them to abide in the sublime conduct of the bliss of the Three Vehicles.

He establishes immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings, causing them to realize for themselves either the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, or the fruit of arhatship;
he establishes immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings, causing them to realize pratyekabuddha-enlightenment or unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

All such supreme matters arise from the majestic power of the Prajñāpāramitā; therefore, all devas, nāgas, asuras, and others alike protect this place, making offerings, showing reverence, honoring, and praising it.

One should know that it is likewise with wherever the *prajñāpāramitā* resides: all devas, nāgas, asuras, and others constantly come to protect it, making offerings, honoring, respecting, and praising it, so that no obstacles may arise for the *prajñāpāramitā*.

One should know that this place is a true caitya; all sentient beings should pay homage to it and offer worship with various kinds of exquisite flower garlands, powdered and scattered incenses, robes, necklaces, precious banners, flags and canopies, diverse wonders, rare treasures, music, and lamps.
Chapter 30: Comparing Merits, Part One. At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If sons or daughters of good family were to write down this profound sūtra of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, and having done so, were to adorn it with various ornaments and offer it worship, respect, reverence, and praise; and furthermore, were to make offerings with various exquisite flower garlands, powdered and scattered incenses, robes, necklaces, precious banners, pennants, canopies, diverse wonders, rare curiosities, music, and lamps.

Furthermore, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there may be sons or daughters of good family who erect stūpas adorned with the seven precious jewels, place the Buddha’s śarīra within a casket made of those jewels, and install it therein; they then offer worship, reverence, respect, and praise, further honoring it with various kinds of exquisite flower garlands, powdered and incense perfumes, robes, necklaces, jeweled banners, flags, canopies, myriad wonderful and rare objects, music, and lamps.
"Between these two accumulations of merit,
which is greater? The Buddha said, "Kauśika!"
I shall ask you further; answer as you see fit.
What do you think?
Regarding the omniscient wisdom (*sarvajñajñāna*) and the body adorned with the marks and signs obtained by the Tathāgata—by training and studying in which dharmas were these attained?
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said:
“World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata’s attainment of the knowledge of all modes and his body adorned with the marks and signs are acquired through training in this Prajñāpāramitā.”
The Buddha told Kauśika: "So it is! So it is!"
It is as you have said.
Because I have trained in the *prajñāpāramitā*, I have attained the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñājñāna*) and the body endowed with the marks and signs. Why is this?
Kauśika! It is impossible that one could realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment without training in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Thus it is, Kauśika!

One is not called a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha by virtue of attaining a body endowed with the marks and signs; rather, one is called a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha solely by virtue of realizing the knowledge of all modes of knowing.

Kauśika! The Tathāgata’s attainment of the knowledge of all modes arises because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* serves as its cause; the Buddha’s body endowed with the marks and signs merely serves as its basis. If one does not rely upon the Buddha’s body endowed with the marks and signs, the knowledge of all modes has no means by which it could manifest.

Therefore, the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) serves as the direct cause for the arising of the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna); and in order to bring this knowledge into manifestation and maintain its continuity, one further cultivates and accumulates the marks and signs of a Buddha’s body.

If this body of marks and signs were not the locus of omniscience, all devas, nāgas, asuras, and others would not offer it sincere worship, honor, respect, and praise; because this body of marks and signs serves as the basis for the Buddha’s omniscience, the devas, nāgas, asuras, and others pay it homage and make offerings.
For this reason, after my parinirvāṇa, the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, humans, non-humans, and others will reverently make offerings to my śarīras. Kausika!

If sons or daughters of good family merely offer worship, respect, honor, and praise to the *prajñāpāramitā*, these sons and daughters of good family thereby make offerings to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), as well as to the Buddha’s body endowed with the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇavyañjana*) upon which that knowledge relies, and to the Buddha’s *śarīra* relics after his parinirvāṇa.
Why is this? Kausika!
It is because the knowledge of all-knowledge, as well as the body endowed with the marks and signs of excellence and the śarīra relics, all have the perfection of wisdom as their root.

Kauśika! If good sons and good daughters merely offer worship, respect, reverence, and praise to the body of the Buddha and to his śarīra relics, these good sons and good daughters are not truly making offerings to the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) and to this Prajñāpāramitā.
Why is this? Kausika!
The physical remains of the Buddha’s body are not the root of this *prajñāpāramitā*, the knowledge of all modes.

Kauśika! For this reason, when sons and daughters of good family wish to make offerings to the Buddha—whether with their minds or their bodies—they should first hear, receive, uphold, read, recite, diligently practice, reflect upon according to the truth, transcribe, and explain the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. Thereafter, they should make offerings with various kinds of exquisite flower garlands, powdered and scattered incenses, robes, necklaces, jeweled banners, pennants, canopies, wonderful and rare treasures, music, and lamps.
"For this reason, Kauśika,

if good sons and good daughters write down this profound sūtra of the Prajñāpāramitā and honor, revere, respect, and praise it with various adornments, and further offer to it various exquisite flower garlands, powdered and scattered incenses, robes, necklaces, precious banners, pennants, canopies, myriad wonderful and rare objects, music, and lamps."

Alternatively, if good sons or good daughters, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, erect a stūpa adorned with the seven precious gems, place the Buddha’s śarīra within a jeweled casket set therein, and offer worship, reverence, respect, and praise; furthermore, they provide offerings of various kinds of exquisite flower garlands, powdered and scattered incenses, robes, necklaces, jeweled banners, pennants, canopies, myriad wonderful and rare objects, music, and lamps.
Of these two accumulations of merit, the former is greater.
Why is this? "Kauśika!..."
The perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom are all born from this very profound perfection of wisdom.

“Kauśika! Inner emptiness, outer emptiness, inner-and-outer emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence—all these appear because they emerge from this very profound *prajñāpāramitā*.”

“Kauśika! It is because True Suchness (tathatā), the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), non-falsity, immutability, equality, the state of being free from birth, the fixed nature of phenomena (dharmaniyāmatā), the stability of phenomena (dharmasthititā), the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), the realm of space (ākāśadhātu), and the inconceivable realm all emerge from this very profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).”
“Kauśika! The noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin, the noble truth of cessation, and the noble truth of the path all emerge from this very profound perfection of wisdom.”
“Kauśika! The four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless absorptions all arise from this very profound perfection of wisdom.”
“Kauśika! The eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten totalities all arise from this very profound perfection of wisdom.”

“Kauśika! This is because the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right endeavors, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path are all born from this profound perfection of wisdom.”
“Kauśika! The gate of liberation of emptiness, the gate of liberation of signlessness, and the gate of liberation of wishlessness all arise from this very profound *prajñāpāramitā*.”
“Kauśika! The five eyes and the six supernormal powers are all born from this very profound perfection of wisdom. Kauśika!”

The ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha—all these arise from this very profound perfection of wisdom.
“Kauśika! The quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant abiding in equanimity both arise from this very profound perfection of wisdom.”

“Kauśika! All-knowledge (sarvajñā), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (mārgākārajñatā), and the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā) are all produced from this very profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).”
“Kauśika! All dharanī-doors and all samādhi-doors are born from this very profound prajñāpāramitā.”
“Kauśika! All the ripening of sentient beings and the purification of Buddha-fields by Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas arise from this very profound perfection of wisdom.”

“Kauśika! All that the bodhisattva mahāsattvas possess—the perfection of lineage, the perfection of physical strength, the perfection of wealth and treasures, and the perfection of retinue—arises from this very profound prajñāpāramitā.”

“Kauśika! All the ten paths of wholesome action in the world, the honoring of śramaṇas, parents, and teachers, and the immeasurable wholesome dharmas such as generosity, ethical discipline, and cultivation—all these arise from this very profound *prajñāpāramitā*.

“Kauśika! All the great clans of kṣatriyas, the great clans of brāhmaṇas, the great clans of householders, and the great clans of lay merchants in the world are born from this very profound prajñāpāramitā.”

“Kauśika! All the gods of the World of the Four Great Kings, the Heaven of the Thirty-three, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven are born from this very profound Prajñāpāramitā.”

“Kauśika! All the gods of the world—the Brahmakāyikas, the Brahmapurohitas, the Brahmakāyikas, the Mahābrahmās, the Ābhāsvaras, the Parīttābhās, the Apramāṇābhās, the Ābhāsvaras, the Śubhakṛtsnas, the Parīttaśubhas, the Apramāṇaśubhas, the Śubhakṛtsnas, the Vṛhatphalas, the Avṛhas, the Atapas, the Sudṛśas, the Sudarśanas, and the Akaniṣṭhas—all arise from this very profound Prajñāpāramitā.”

“Kauśika! All the gods of the world who dwell in the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, are all born from this very profound perfection of wisdom.”

“Kauśika! All stream-enterers and the fruit of stream-entry, once-returners and the fruit of once-returning, non-returners and the fruit of non-returning, arhats and the fruit of arhatship—all these arise from this very profound perfection of wisdom.”
“Kauśika! All pratyekabuddhas and the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha arise from this very profound perfection of wisdom.”
“Kauśika! All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and all the dharmas of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are born from this very profound perfection of wisdom.”
“Kauśika! All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are born from such profound Prajñāpāramitā.”
“Kauśika! The omniscient wisdom—incalculable, ineffable, unsurpassed, unsurpassable, unequaled, and peerless—all arises from this profound perfection of wisdom.”
At that time, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

As for the people of Jambudvīpa who do not offer worship, reverence, respect, and praise to the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, do they perhaps not know that by offering worship, reverence, respect, and praise to the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, one obtains such great merit and benefit?”
The Buddha said, "Kauśika!
I shall now question you; answer as you see fit."
What do you think?
How many people within Jambudvīpa have attained pure confidence in the Buddha, attained pure confidence in the Dharma, and attained pure confidence in the Saṅgha?
How many people have no doubt regarding the Buddha, no doubt regarding the Dharma, and no doubt regarding the Saṅgha?
How many people have reached the ultimate certainty regarding the Buddha, the ultimate certainty regarding the Dharma, and the ultimate certainty regarding the Saṅgha?
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said:
“World-Honored One!

Within Jambudvīpa, there are some people who have attained pure confidence in the Buddha, attained pure confidence in the Dharma, and attained pure confidence in the Saṃgha; there are some people who have no doubt regarding the Buddha, no doubt regarding the Dharma, and no doubt regarding the Saṃgha; and there are some people who have reached the ultimate certainty regarding the Buddha, the ultimate certainty regarding the Dharma, and the ultimate certainty regarding the Saṃgha.”
The Buddha said:
“Kauśika! I shall ask you further; answer as you see fit.”
Kauśika! What do you think?
How many people within Jambudvīpa have attained the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment?
How many people have attained the three gates of liberation?
How many people have attained the eight liberations?
How many people have attained the nine successive meditative absorptions?
How many people have attained the four analytical knowledges?
How many people have attained the six supernormal powers?
How many people have permanently severed the three fetters and attained the fruit of stream-entry?
How many people are there who, having attenuated greed, hatred, and delusion, attain the fruit of a once-returner?
How many people are there who, having severed the five lower fetters, attain the fruit of a non-returner?
How many people have severed the five fetters of the higher realms and attained the fruit of arhatship?
How many people have resolved their minds and are certain to attain the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha?
How many people have resolved their minds and are certain to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said:
“World-Honored One!
Within Jambudvīpa, there are a small number of people who have attained the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; there are a few...”
Some people attain the three gates of liberation; some few attain the eight liberations;
some few attain the nine successive concentrations; some few attain the four analytical knowledges;
some few attain the six supernormal powers; and some few permanently sever the three fetters and attain the fruit of stream-entry. Some...
Some people, having thinned out greed, hatred, and delusion, attain the fruit of once-returner;
a few people, having severed the five lower fetters, attain the fruit of non-returner; a few people, having severed the five higher fetters, attain the fruit of arhatship;
a few people resolve their minds and are certain to proceed toward the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; and a few...
"When a person resolves their mind, they are certain to proceed toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the Buddha said to Śakra, Lord of the Devas:
"It is so! It is thus!"
"So it is! It is just as you have said, Kauśika!"

Within Jambudvīpa, there are extremely few people who achieve verified clarity regarding the Buddha, verified clarity regarding the Dharma, and verified clarity regarding the Saṅgha; even fewer have no doubt regarding the Buddha, no doubt regarding the Dharma, and no doubt regarding the Saṅgha; even fewer reach the ultimate realization regarding the Buddha, the ultimate realization regarding the Dharma, and the ultimate realization regarding the Saṅgha; even fewer attain the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; even fewer attain the three doors of liberation; even fewer attain the eight liberations; even fewer attain the nine successive meditative absorptions; even fewer attain the four analytical knowledges; and even fewer attain the six supernormal powers.

Kauśika! Within Jambudvīpa, there are very few people who have permanently severed the three fetters and attained the fruit of stream-entry; even fewer have thinned out greed, hatred, and delusion and attained the fruit of once-returning; even fewer have severed the five lower fetters and attained the fruit of non-returning; even fewer have severed the five higher fetters and attained the fruit of arhatship; even fewer have resolved their minds and are certain to proceed toward pratyekabuddha enlightenment; even fewer have resolved their minds and are certain to proceed toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; and even fewer, having already resolved their minds, practice with diligent effort to progress toward the conduct of enlightenment.
Why is this? "Kauśika!

Among the classes of sentient beings wandering through birth and death, for immeasurable lifetimes they have mostly not seen the Buddha, have not heard the True Dharma, and have not drawn near to the Saṃgha."
They do not practice generosity, do not guard pure ethical discipline, do not cultivate patience, do not arouse diligence, do not practice meditative concentration, and do not study wisdom;

they do not hear of the perfection of generosity and do not cultivate the perfection of generosity, they do not hear of the perfection of ethical discipline and do not cultivate the perfection of ethical discipline, they do not hear of the perfection of patience and do not cultivate the perfection of patience, they do not hear of the perfection of diligence and do not cultivate the perfection of diligence, they do not hear of the perfection of meditative concentration and do not cultivate the perfection of meditative concentration, and they do not hear of the perfection of wisdom and do not cultivate the perfection of wisdom.

They do not hear of internal emptiness, nor do they cultivate internal emptiness; they do not hear of external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate truth, the emptiness of conditioned phenomena, the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, the emptiness of dispersion, the emptiness of non-alteration, the emptiness of essential nature, the emptiness of self-characteristics, the emptiness of common characteristics, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of non-apprehensibility, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, or the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence; nor do they cultivate external emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.

They do not hear of suchness, nor do they cultivate suchness; they do not hear of the dharma-realm, the nature of phenomena, non-illusory nature, unchanging nature, equality, the nature of transcendence from birth, the fixed nature of phenomena, the abiding of phenomena, the reality-limit, the realm of space, or the inconceivable realm, nor do they cultivate the dharma-realm up to the inconceivable realm;

they do not hear of the noble truth of suffering, nor do they cultivate the noble truth of suffering; they do not hear of the noble truths of the origin, cessation, and the path, nor do they cultivate the noble truths of the origin, cessation, and the path;

they do not hear of the four meditative concentrations, nor do they cultivate the four meditative concentrations; they do not hear of the four immeasurables or the four formless attainments, nor do they cultivate the four immeasurables or the four formless attainments.

They do not hear of the eight liberations, nor do they cultivate the eight liberations; they do not hear of the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, or the ten totalities, nor do they cultivate the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, or the ten totalities;

they do not hear of the four foundations of mindfulness, nor do they cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness; they do not hear of the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the eightfold noble path, nor do they cultivate the four right efforts up to the eightfold noble path;

they do not hear of the gate of liberation of emptiness, nor do they cultivate the gate of liberation of emptiness; they do not hear of the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness, nor do they cultivate the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness.
They do not hear of the five eyes and do not cultivate the five eyes; they do not hear of the six supernormal powers and do not cultivate the six supernormal powers;

they do not hear of the ten powers of a Buddha and do not cultivate the ten powers of a Buddha; they do not hear of the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, nor do they cultivate these from the four fearlessnesses up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;

they do not hear of the quality of non-forgetfulness and do not cultivate the quality of non-forgetfulness; they do not hear of the nature of constant abiding in equanimity and do not cultivate the nature of constant abiding in equanimity.
They do not hear of all the gateways of dhāraṇī, nor do they cultivate all the gateways of dhāraṇī; they do not hear of all the gateways of samādhi, nor do they cultivate all the gateways of samādhi;

they do not hear of all-knowledge, nor do they cultivate all-knowledge; they do not hear of the knowledge of the aspects of the path or the knowledge of all aspects, nor do they cultivate the knowledge of the aspects of the path or the knowledge of all aspects.

“Kauśika! For this reason, you should know that within this Jambudvīpa, there are extremely few people who have attained pure confidence in the Buddha, pure confidence in the Dharma, and pure confidence in the Saṅgha; fewer still have no doubt regarding the Buddha, no doubt regarding the Dharma, and no doubt regarding the Saṅgha; even fewer still have reached the ultimate certainty regarding the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha; even fewer still attain the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; even fewer still attain the three gates of liberation; even fewer still attain the eight liberations; even fewer still attain the nine successive meditative absorptions; even fewer still attain the four analytical knowledges; and even fewer still attain the six supernormal powers.”

Kauśika! You should know that among the people in this Jambudvīpa, there are very few who have permanently severed the three fetters and attained the fruit of stream-entry; even fewer who have attenuated greed, hatred, and delusion and attained the fruit of once-returning; even fewer who have severed the five lower fetters and attained the fruit of non-returning; even fewer who have severed the five higher fetters and attained the fruit of arhatship; even fewer who have resolved their minds and are certain to proceed toward the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; even fewer who have resolved their minds and are certain to proceed toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; and even fewer who, having already resolved their minds, practice with diligent effort to progress toward the conduct of enlightenment.
At that time, the Buddha said to Śakra, the Lord of the Devas:
“I shall now question you; answer as you see fit. Kauśika!”
What do you think?
Setting aside all the human beings in Jambudvīpa,
how many sentient beings in this trichiliocosm provide offerings and show reverence to their parents and teachers?
How many sentient beings honor and revere śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas?
How many sentient beings practice giving, observe the upavāsa fast, and maintain the precepts?
How many sentient beings cultivate the ten paths of wholesome action?

How many sentient beings dwell amidst various desires with the perception of weariness, the perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering, the perception of non-self, the perception of impurity, the perception of revulsion toward food, and the perception that all worlds are not worth delighting in?
How many sentient beings cultivate the four dhyānas?
How many sentient beings cultivate the four immeasurables?
How many sentient beings cultivate the four formless attainments?
How many sentient beings have faith in the Buddha, faith in the Dharma, and faith in the Saṅgha?
How many sentient beings have no doubt regarding the Buddha, no doubt regarding the Dharma, and no doubt regarding the Saṅgha?
How many sentient beings have reached the ultimate realization of the Buddha, the ultimate realization of the Dharma, and the ultimate realization of the Saṅgha?
How many sentient beings cultivate the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment?
How many sentient beings cultivate the three gates of liberation?
How many sentient beings cultivate the eight liberations?
How many sentient beings cultivate the nine successive attainments?
How many sentient beings cultivate the four analytical knowledges?
How many sentient beings cultivate the six supernormal powers?
How many sentient beings permanently sever the three fetters and attain the fruit of stream-entry?
How many sentient beings, having thinned out greed, hatred, and delusion, attain the fruit of once-returning?
How many sentient beings, having severed the five lower fetters, attain the fruit of non-returning?
How many sentient beings have severed the five higher fetters and attained the fruit of arhatship?
How many sentient beings have resolved their minds and are certain to attain the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha?
How many sentient beings have resolved their minds and are certain to attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
How many sentient beings, having already resolved their minds, diligently practice and advance toward the conduct of enlightenment?
How many sentient beings refine and nurture the mind directed toward enlightenment?
How many sentient beings skillfully practice the perfection of wisdom through expedient means?
How many sentient beings abide in the stage of non-retrogression of a bodhisattva?
"How many sentient beings will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, replied:
"World-Honored One!"
In this trichiliocosm, there are few sentient beings who honor and respect their parents and teachers;
there are few sentient beings who honor and respect śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas;
there are few sentient beings who practice generosity, observe the uposatha, and maintain the precepts; and there are few sentient beings who cultivate the path of the ten wholesome actions.
There are some sentient beings who, amidst various desires, dwell in the perception of weariness, the perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering,
the perception of non-self, the perception of impurity, the perception of revulsion toward food, and the perception that all worlds are not to be delighted in;
there are some sentient beings who cultivate the four dhyānas, and there are some sentient beings who cultivate the four immeasurables.
There are few sentient beings who cultivate the four formless absorptions; there are few sentient beings who have faith in the Buddha, faith in the Dharma, and faith in the Saṅgha;
there are few sentient beings who are free from doubt regarding the Buddha, free from doubt regarding the Dharma, and free from doubt regarding the Saṅgha;
and there are few sentient beings who have reached ultimate certainty regarding the Buddha, ultimate certainty regarding the Dharma, and ultimate certainty regarding the Saṅgha.
There are few sentient beings who cultivate the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; there are few sentient beings who cultivate the three gates of liberation;
there are few sentient beings who cultivate the eight liberations; there are few sentient beings who cultivate the nine successive attainments;
there are few sentient beings who cultivate the four unhindered understandings; and there are few sentient beings who cultivate the six supernormal powers.
Generally speaking, there are some sentient beings who permanently sever the three fetters and attain the fruit of stream-entry;
some sentient beings who attenuate greed, hatred, and delusion and attain the fruit of once-returning; some sentient beings who sever the five lower fetters and attain the fruit of non-returning;
and some sentient beings who sever the five higher fetters and attain the fruit of arhatship.
There are some sentient beings who resolve their minds and are certain to attain the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha;
there are some sentient beings who resolve their minds and are certain to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;

there are some sentient beings who, having already resolved their minds, diligently practice and progress toward the conduct of enlightenment; and there are some sentient beings who refine and nurture themselves as they progress toward enlightenment.
In my mind, there are few sentient beings who practice the perfection of wisdom through skillful means;
there are few sentient beings who abide in the stage of non-retrogression of a bodhisattva; and there are few sentient beings who swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śakra, Lord of the Devas, saying: "So it is! So it is!"
"It is as you have said,
Kauśika! In this trichiliocosm, there are very few sentient beings who offer worship and respect to their parents."
Venerable Sir, fewer and fewer sentient beings offer worship and respect to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas;
fewer and fewer sentient beings practice giving, observe the fast, and maintain the precepts; fewer and fewer sentient beings cultivate the ten paths of wholesome action;
and fewer and fewer sentient beings dwell amidst the various desires with perceptions of disenchantment, impermanence, and suffering.
...the perception of non-self, the perception of impurity, the perception of revulsion toward food, and the perception that all worlds are not worth delighting in;
fewer sentient beings cultivate the four dhyānas, fewer sentient beings cultivate the four immeasurables,
fewer sentient beings cultivate the four formless attainments, and fewer sentient beings have faith in the Buddha and faith in the Dharma.
Fewer beings have faith in the Saṅgha; fewer beings are free from doubt regarding the Buddha, free from doubt regarding the Dharma, and free from doubt regarding the Saṅgha;
fewer beings have reached the ultimate realization of the Buddha, the ultimate realization of the Dharma, and the ultimate realization of the Saṅgha;
fewer beings cultivate the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; and fewer beings cultivate the three [vehicles].
Regarding the gates of liberation: fewer sentient beings cultivate the eight liberations; fewer sentient beings cultivate the nine successive attainments;
fewer sentient beings cultivate the four unhindered understandings; and fewer sentient beings cultivate the six supernormal powers.
Kauśika! In this trichiliocosm, there are very few sentient beings who have forever severed the three fetters and attained the fruit of stream-entry;
even fewer sentient beings have thinned out greed, hatred, and delusion and attained the fruit of once-returning; and even fewer still—
He causes more beings to sever the five lower fetters and attain the fruit of non-returning; he causes even fewer beings to sever the five higher fetters and attain the fruit of arhatship;
he causes even fewer beings to resolve their minds and be certain of attaining the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha;
and he causes even fewer beings to resolve their minds and be certain of attaining anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Furthermore—
Even fewer sentient beings, having already resolved their minds, diligently cultivate the practices leading to enlightenment;
even fewer sentient beings refine and nurture the mind set on enlightenment; even fewer sentient beings skillfully practice the *prajñāpāramitā*;
and even fewer sentient beings attain the stage of a Bodhisattva from which there is no regression. Even fewer...
"Few sentient beings quickly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Furthermore, Kausika!

With my pure, unobstructed Buddha-eye, I observe the worlds in each of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Although there are immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless sentient beings who have resolved their minds to definitely proceed toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and diligently practice the conduct leading to enlightenment, because they are far removed from the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), only one, two, or three sentient beings may reach the stage of a bodhisattva’s non-retrogression; for the most part, they fall back into the inferior stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas."
Why is this? Kauśika!
Anuttarasamyaksambodhi is extremely difficult to attain; for those of evil wisdom, indolence, inferior diligence, inferior resolve, and inferior sentient beings are unable to realize it.

Kauśika! For this reason, if any sons or daughters of good family resolve their minds to be certain of attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, diligently practice the conduct leading to enlightenment, and desire to abide on the stage of a bodhisattva’s non-retrogression, swiftly realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment without hindrance, they should repeatedly hear, receive, uphold, read, recite, diligently practice, reflect upon according to the principle, inquire of their teachers, and delight in explaining it to others—this very profound *prajñāpāramitā*.

Having performed these deeds, one should further transcribe [the text], adorning it with various precious objects, and offer worship, respect, honor, and praise; furthermore, one should make offerings with various exquisite flower garlands, powdered and incense perfumes, robes, necklaces, jeweled banners, pennants and canopies, and a multitude of wonderful, rare, musical instruments, and lamps.

“Kauśika! These sons and daughters of good family should also hear, receive, uphold, read, recite, diligently practice, reflect upon according to the principle, respectfully inquire of their teachers, and joyfully explain to others those other excellent and wholesome dharmas that are subsumed within this profound *prajñāpāramitā*.”
"What are the other sublime and virtuous dharmas that are subsumed within the profound *prajñāpāramitā*?
They are: the *dānapāramitā*, as well as the *śīla*, *kṣānti*, *vīrya*, and *dhyānapāramitās*; furthermore, they are:

internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*), external emptiness (*bahirdhā-śūnyatā*), internal-and-external emptiness (*adhyātma-bahirdhā-śūnyatā*), emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*), great emptiness (*mahā-śūnyatā*), ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), conditioned emptiness (*saṃskṛta-śūnyatā*), unconditioned emptiness (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*), absolute emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*), boundless emptiness (*anavara-agra-śūnyatā*), dispersed emptiness (*anavakāra-śūnyatā*), non-alteration emptiness (*anavakāra-śūnyatā*), essential nature emptiness (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*), self-characteristic emptiness (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*), common characteristic emptiness (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*), emptiness of all dharmas (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*), emptiness of the unapprehendable (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*), emptiness of non-existence (*abhāva-śūnyatā*), emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*), and emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence (*abhāvasvabhāva-śūnyatā*).”

Whether it be suchness, the dharma-realm, the nature of phenomena, non-falsity, immutability, equality, the state beyond birth, the fixed nature of phenomena, the stability of phenomena, the limit of reality, the realm of space, or the inconceivable realm;
whether it be the noble truth of suffering, or the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path;
or whether it be the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, or the four formless attainments.
Whether it be the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, or the ten totalities;

whether it be the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the eight branches of the noble path;
whether it be the gate of liberation of emptiness, or the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness.
Whether it be the five eyes or the six supernormal powers;

whether it be the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
whether it be the quality of non-forgetfulness or the nature of constant dwelling in equanimity.
Whether it be all the gateways of dhāraṇī, or all the gateways of samādhi;
whether it be all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, or the knowledge of all aspects;
or any other immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas—these are said to be the other sublime and wholesome dharmas that are subsumed within the profound perfection of wisdom.

Kauśika! These sons and daughters of good family should also hear, receive, uphold, recite, and reflect upon with correct reasoning upon other immeasurable Dharma-gates that accord with the profound perfection of wisdom, such as the aggregates, bases, and elements; they should not disparage them so as to create obstacles for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 103 [and] Fascicle 104.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
First Division, Chapter Thirty-Two: "The Measurement of Merit.
"For what reason, Kausika? [Because...]"
These sons and daughters of good family should form this thought:

"Because the Tathāgata, while formerly dwelling in the stage of a bodhisattva, constantly and diligently practiced the perfection of wisdom, as well as the perfections of meditative concentration, diligence, patience, ethical discipline, and generosity, he realized unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

When the Tathāgata formerly dwelt in the stage of a bodhisattva, he constantly and diligently abided in internal emptiness and external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of non-apprehensibility, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence; it was by means of these that he realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

When the Tathāgata formerly dwelt in the stage of a bodhisattva, he constantly and diligently abided in suchness, the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, non-illusory nature, unchanging nature, equality, the nature of transcendence from birth, the fixedness of phenomena, the stability of phenomena, the limit of reality, the realm of empty space, and the inconceivable realm; therefore, he realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

In the past, when the Tathāgata dwelt in the stage of a bodhisattva, he constantly and diligently abided in the noble truth of suffering, as well as the noble truths of its origin, its cessation, and the path; therefore, he realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

In the past, when the Tathāgata dwelt in the stage of a bodhisattva, he constantly and diligently cultivated the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless absorptions; therefore, he realized unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

In the past, when the Tathāgata dwelt in the stage of a bodhisattva, he constantly and diligently practiced and studied the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten totalities; therefore, he realized unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

In the past, when the Tathāgata dwelt in the stage of a bodhisattva, he constantly and diligently cultivated and studied the four applications of mindfulness, the four right endeavors, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path; therefore, he realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

In the past, when the Tathāgata dwelt in the stage of a bodhisattva, he constantly and diligently cultivated the gate of liberation of emptiness, as well as the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness; therefore, he realized unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

In the past, when the Tathāgata dwelt in the stage of a bodhisattva, he constantly and diligently cultivated the five eyes and the six supernormal powers; therefore, he realized unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

In the past, when the Tathāgata dwelt in the stage of a bodhisattva, he constantly and diligently cultivated and studied the ten powers of a buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha; therefore, he realized unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

In the past, when the Tathāgata dwelt in the stage of a bodhisattva, because he constantly and diligently cultivated the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant equanimity, he realized unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

In the past, when the Tathāgata dwelt in the stage of a bodhisattva, he constantly and diligently cultivated all dharanī-doors and all samādhi-doors; therefore, he realized unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

In the past, when the Tathāgata dwelt in the stage of a bodhisattva, he constantly and diligently cultivated and studied all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*); therefore, he realized unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).

In the past, when the Tathāgata dwelt in the stage of a bodhisattva, he constantly and diligently practiced and studied all other immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas; therefore, he realized unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

In the past, when the Tathāgata dwelt in the stage of a bodhisattva, he constantly and diligently abided in all other immeasurable dharma-gates that accord with the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, such as the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*); therefore, he realized *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

"We who now seek unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment should likewise constantly and diligently practice, train in, and abide within these dharmas, such as this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, following the Buddha."
Such profound dharmas as this Prajñāpāramitā are certainly our true Great Teacher; by constantly and diligently training in accordance with them, all our aspirations shall be fulfilled.

Such profound dharmas as this perfection of wisdom are the true Dharma-seal of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas; they are also the true Dharma-seal of all Pratyekabuddhas, Arhats, Anāgāmins, Sakṛdāgāmins, and Srotāpannas.

All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, because they have constantly and diligently studied such dharmas as this profound Prajñāpāramitā, have realized, will realize, and are currently realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

All Pratyekabuddhas, Arhats, Non-returners, Once-returners, Stream-enterers, and others, by constantly and diligently studying such dharmas as this profound Prajñāpāramitā, have reached the other shore, will reach the other shore, and are currently reaching the other shore.
"For this reason, Kauśika!

Whether the Buddha remains in the world or has entered parinirvāṇa, all sons and daughters of good family should constantly and diligently train in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), and they should constantly and diligently train in the perfections of meditative concentration (dhyāna), diligence (vīrya), patience (kṣānti), ethical discipline (śīla), and generosity (dāna)."

Why is this? Because such things as the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) are the basis for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, as well as devas, humans, asuras, and others.

“Kauśika! Whether the Buddha remains in the world or has entered parinirvāṇa, sons and daughters of good family should constantly and diligently train in reliance upon internal emptiness; they should constantly and diligently train in reliance upon external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature.”

Why is this? Because these [realities], such as internal emptiness and so forth, are the basis for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, as well as devas, humans, asuras, and others.

“Kauśika! Whether the Buddha remains in the world or has entered parinirvāṇa, sons and daughters of good family should constantly and diligently train in reliance upon suchness (tathatā); they should constantly and diligently train in reliance upon the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), the non-falsity of phenomena (avitathatā), the immutability of phenomena (ananyathābhāva), equality (samatā), the state beyond birth (anirodhatā), the fixedness of phenomena (dharmaniyāmatā), the stability of phenomena (dharmasthititā), the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), the realm of space (ākāśadhātu), and the inconceivable realm (acintyadhātu).”

Why is this? Because suchness and the like are the basis for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, as well as devas, humans, asuras, and so forth.

“Kauśika! Whether the Buddha remains in the world or has entered parinirvāṇa, sons and daughters of good family should constantly and diligently train in reliance upon the Noble Truth of Suffering; they should constantly and diligently train in reliance upon the Noble Truths of Origination, Cessation, and the Path.”

Why is this? Because these noble truths of suffering and so forth are the basis for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, as well as gods, humans, asuras, and others.

“Kauśika! Whether the Buddha remains in the world or has entered parinirvāṇa, sons and daughters of good family should constantly and diligently train in reliance upon the four dhyānas; they should constantly and diligently train in reliance upon the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments.”

Why is this? Because these four dhyānas and so forth are the basis for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, as well as devas, humans, asuras, and others.

“Kauśika! Whether the Buddha remains in the world or has entered parinirvāṇa, all sons and daughters of good family should constantly and diligently train in reliance upon the eight liberations; they should constantly and diligently train in reliance upon the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten spheres of totality.”

Why is this? Because these eight liberations and so forth are the basis for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, as well as devas, humans, asuras, and others.

“Kauśika! Whether the Buddha remains in the world or has entered parinirvāṇa, sons and daughters of good family should constantly and diligently train in reliance upon the four foundations of mindfulness; they should constantly and diligently train in reliance upon the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path.”

Why is this? Because these four foundations of mindfulness and so forth are the basis for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, as well as devas, humans, asuras, and others.

“Kauśika! Whether the Buddha remains in the world or has entered parinirvāṇa, all sons and daughters of good family should constantly and diligently train in reliance upon the gate of liberation of emptiness; they should constantly and diligently train in reliance upon the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness.”

Why is this? Because these gates of liberation, such as emptiness and the rest, are the basis for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, as well as devas, humans, asuras, and others.

“Kauśika! Whether the Buddha remains in the world or has entered parinirvāṇa, all sons and daughters of good family should constantly and diligently train in reliance upon the five eyes, and they should constantly and diligently train in reliance upon the six supernormal powers.”

Why is this? Because these five eyes and so forth are the basis for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, as well as devas, humans, asuras, and others.

“Kauśika! Whether the Buddha remains in the world or has entered parinirvāṇa, all sons and daughters of good family should constantly and diligently train themselves by relying upon the ten powers of a Buddha; they should constantly and diligently train themselves by relying upon the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.”

Why is this? Because these ten powers of a Buddha and so forth are the basis for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, as well as devas, humans, asuras, and others.

“Kauśika! Whether the Buddha remains in the world or has entered parinirvāṇa, all sons and daughters of good family should constantly and diligently train in reliance upon the quality of non-forgetfulness, and they should constantly and diligently train in reliance upon the nature of constant equanimity.”

Why is this? Because such qualities as the absence of forgetfulness are the basis for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, as well as devas, humans, asuras, and so forth.

“Kauśika! Whether the Buddha remains in the world or has entered parinirvāṇa, all sons and daughters of good family should constantly and diligently train in reliance upon all dharanī-doors and should constantly and diligently train in reliance upon all samādhi-doors.”

Why is this? Because all such dharani-doors and the like are the basis for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, as well as devas, humans, asuras, and others.

“Kauśika! Whether the Buddha remains in the world or has entered parinirvāṇa, all sons and daughters of good family should constantly and diligently train themselves in reliance upon omniscience (sarvajñatā); they should constantly and diligently train themselves in reliance upon the knowledge of the paths (mārgajñatā) and the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā).”

Why is this? Because all such things as omniscience are the basis for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, as well as devas, humans, asuras, and others.

“Kauśika! Whether the Buddha remains in the world or has entered parinirvāṇa, all sons and daughters of good family should constantly and diligently train in the remaining immeasurable and boundless teachings of the Buddha.”

Why is this? Because these remaining immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas are the basis for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, as well as devas, humans, asuras, and others.

“Kauśika! Whether the Buddha remains in the world or has entered parinirvāṇa, all sons and daughters of good family should, in accordance with the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, constantly and diligently train in the immeasurable dharma-gates such as the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*).”

Why is this? Because these immeasurable dharma-gates, such as the aggregates, bases, and elements, which accord with the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, are the basis for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, as well as devas, humans, asuras, and others.
At that time, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

If good sons and good daughters do not depart from the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*), and by means of the practice of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), listen to, receive, uphold, read, recite, diligently study, and reflect upon this *prajñāpāramitā* according to the truth; and if they extensively proclaim and disseminate it for the sake of sentient beings; or if they write it down, adorn it in various ways, and offer it with reverence, respect, honor, and praise; and furthermore, if they make offerings with various exquisite flower garlands, powdered and scattered incenses, robes, necklaces, jeweled banners, pennants, canopies, many wonderful and rare items, music, and lamps—[what would be their merit?]"
“By this causal condition, how much merit will these sons and daughters of good family obtain?
The Buddha said, “Kauśika!
I ask you again; answer as you see fit.

Suppose there are sons or daughters of good family who, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgatas, erect stūpas for the relics of the Buddhas out of various exquisite seven precious gems, adorned with a variety of rare and wonderful ornaments. These are one yojana in height and half that in width. Furthermore, throughout their entire lives, they offer worship, respect, honor, and praise by means of various celestial and exquisite flower garlands, powdered and incense perfumes, robes, necklaces, jeweled banners, flags, canopies, many kinds of rare and wonderful things, music, and lamps.
"What do you think?
Is the mass of merit produced by these sons and daughters of good family on account of this cause and condition great or not?
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, replied:
“Very many,
World-Honored One!
Very many!”
“Excellent, Sugata!
The Buddha said, “Kauśika!

If sons or daughters of good family do not depart from the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*), employing the method of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), they listen to, receive, uphold, read, recite, diligently practice, and reflect upon this *prajñāpāramitā* according to the principle; they widely proclaim and disseminate it for the sake of sentient beings; or they transcribe it, adorning it with various ornaments, and offer it with reverence, respect, honor, and praise; furthermore, they make offerings with various exquisite flower garlands, powdered and scattered incenses, robes, necklaces, precious banners, flags and canopies, many wonderful and rare items, music, and lamps.
"The mass of merit produced by these sons and daughters of good family through this cause and condition is far greater than that, immeasurable and boundless.
The Buddha told Kauśika:
"Set aside this one matter."

Furthermore, suppose there are sons or daughters of good family who, after the parinirvāṇa of various Tathāgatas, erect stūpas made of the seven exquisite precious substances for the purpose of making offerings to the Buddha’s relics. These are adorned with various rare and wonderful treasures; they are one yojana in height and half that in width, filling the entire continent of Jambudvīpa without any gaps. Moreover, throughout their entire lives, they offer worship, respect, honor, and praise with various celestial and exquisite flower garlands, powdered and scattered incenses, robes, necklaces, jeweled banners, flags, canopies, myriad wonderful and rare objects, music, and lamps.
"What do you think?
Is the mass of merit produced by these sons and daughters of good family on account of this cause and condition not great?
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, replied:
“Very many,
World-Honored One!
Very many!”
“Excellent, Sugata!
The Buddha said, “Kauśika!

If sons or daughters of good family, not departing from the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*), employ the method of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) toward this *prajñāpāramitā*, and with a sincere heart listen to it, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, diligently practice and study it, and reflect upon it according to the principle; and if they extensively proclaim and disseminate it for the sake of sentient beings; or if they transcribe it, adorning it in various ways and making offerings, paying homage, respecting, and praising it; and furthermore, if they make offerings with various exquisite flower garlands, powdered and scattered incenses, robes, necklaces, jeweled banners, pennants and canopies, many kinds of wonderful and rare objects, music, and lamps— [This is the passage to be translated.]
"The mass of merit produced by these sons and daughters of good family from this cause and condition is far greater than that, immeasurable and boundless.
The Buddha told Kauśika:
"Set aside Jambudvīpa."

Furthermore, suppose there are sons or daughters of good family who, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgatas, erect stūpas made of the seven precious jewels to honor the Buddha’s *śarīra*.
