By the great majestic power of this *prajñāpāramitā*, these sons and daughters of good family obtain such various merits and benefits in the present life as follows: those among the devas who have already resolved upon unsurpassed bodhicitta, or those who, relying on the Buddha-dharma, have obtained extraordinary benefit and happiness, will constantly come here out of reverence for the Dharma; they will follow, protect, and increase their strength."

Why is this so? Because these sons and daughters of good family have already resolved their minds upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment; they constantly act to rescue and deliver all sentient beings, constantly act to bring all sentient beings to maturity, never abandon any sentient beings, and constantly act for the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings. The various devas and others do likewise; for these reasons, they constantly follow, protect, and guard them.

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Scroll 126. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Part One: Chapter on the Measurement of Merit, Number Thirty, Section Twenty-five. At that time, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How do these sons and daughters of good family perceive all the Cāturmahārājakāyika,
Trāyastriṃśa, Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, and Paranirmitavaśavartin devas within this trichiliocosm as well as in the infinite worlds of the ten directions?
Īśvara-deva, Brahmakāyika-deva, Brahmapurohita-deva, Mahābrahmā-deva, Parīttābha-deva,
Apramāṇābha-deva, Ābhāsvara-deva, Parīttaśubha-deva, Apramāṇaśubha-deva, Śubhakṛtsna-deva, Bṛhatphala-deva, and Parīttaśubha-deva.
The Akaniṣṭha Heaven, the Sudarśana Heaven, the Sudṛśa Heaven, the Atapa Heaven, the Bṛhatphala Heaven, the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven,
the Apramāṇaśubha Heaven, and the Vast Heaven; as well as other immeasurable beings of great majesty and power,
such as nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and so forth.
Why do the mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others come to that place to behold and pay homage to,
read and recite, and make offerings with reverence, respect, honor, and praise to the profound *prajñāpāramitā* they have written down;
and why do they join their palms, circumambulate it to the right, and joyfully protect and keep it in mind?
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śakra, the Lord of the Devas, saying: “Kauśika!

If these sons and daughters of good family see a sublime radiance at the place where such profound *prajñāpāramitā* has been established, or if they smell a rare and fragrant incense or hear the sound of celestial music there, you should know that at that time, devas, nāgas, and others of great supernormal power and blazing majesty have come to that place. They observe and pay homage to, read and recite, and make offerings to, revere, respect, and praise the written profound *prajñāpāramitā*; with palms joined, they circumambulate it to the right, and with joy, they protect and keep it in mind.”
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

When these sons and daughters of good family cultivate pure and sublime conduct to adorn and purify their dwelling, and with a sincere heart make offerings to this Prajñāpāramitā, you should know that at that time, devas, nāgas, and others of great supernormal power and blazing majesty will come to that place. They will observe and pay homage to it, read and recite the profound Prajñāpāramitā written there, and having made offerings, shown respect, honored, and praised it, they will join their palms, circumambulate it to the right, and joyfully protect and keep it in mind."

Kauśika! As those gods, nāgas, and others who possess such great supernormal powers and blazing majesty arrive at that place, all the malevolent spirits and evil ghosts therein will be struck with alarm and flee in retreat; none will dare to remain.

By virtue of these causes and conditions, the minds of these sons and daughters of good family become vast; the wholesome karma they cultivate increases manifold, and there are no obstacles whatsoever in all their endeavors.
"For this reason, Kauśika!

Wherever this Prajñāpāramitā may be, one should clear away all impure things from the surrounding area, sweep and scrub it clean, apply fragrant water, and scatter perfumes. One should arrange a precious seat and install [the scripture] there, burning incense, scattering flowers, and spreading canopies and awnings. Adorn the interior with precious banners, pennants, and bells, as well as clothing, necklaces, gold, silver, precious vessels, various wonderful and rare items, music, and lamps. Thus, the place should be decorated with immeasurable varieties of colorful ornaments."

If one can make such offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā, then immeasurable devas, nāgas, and others—possessing great supernormal powers and blazing with majestic virtue—will come to that place. They will observe and pay homage to, read and recite, and offer worship, reverence, respect, and praise to the profound Prajñāpāramitā written there; they will join their palms, circumambulate it to the right, and joyfully protect and mindfully attend to it.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If these sons and daughters of good family can thus make offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā, their bodies and minds will be free from weariness; they will experience physical and mental joy, physical and mental lightness, physical and mental pliancy, and physical and mental tranquility. With their minds fixed upon the Prajñāpāramitā, when they sleep at night, they will have no evil dreams, but only auspicious ones."

"It means seeing the body of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, as the color of pure gold, endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man and fully adorned with the eighty secondary signs; emitting great radiance that universally illuminates all things, surrounded before and behind by śrāvakas and bodhisattvas, and standing in the midst of the assembly."
I heard the Buddha teach the dharmas associated with the perfection of generosity, the perfection of ethical discipline,
the perfection of patience, the perfection of diligence, the perfection of meditative concentration,
and the perfection of wisdom; I heard the Buddha teach inner emptiness, outer emptiness, and—
Internal and external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate truth, the emptiness of conditioned phenomena,
the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, the emptiness of dispersion, the emptiness of non-alteration,
the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the emptiness of specific characteristics, the emptiness of common characteristics, the emptiness of all phenomena, and the emptiness of the unapprehendable.
The dharmas associated with the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of both non-existence and intrinsic nature;

hearing the Buddha teach them as suchness (*tathatā*), the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the state of non-falsity, the state of non-alteration, equality, the state of freedom from birth,
the fixedness of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*), the stability of phenomena (*dharmasthititā*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), and space (*ākāśa*).

Regarding the elements and the dharmas associated with the inconceivable realm, they hear the Buddha teach the dharmas associated with the Noble Truth of Suffering, the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering, the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering, and the Noble Truth of the Path;
they hear the Buddha teach the dharmas associated with the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless absorptions; they hear the Buddha teach...
Having heard the Dharma associated with the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities as taught by the Buddha;
and having heard the Dharma associated with the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power,
the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path as taught by the Buddha...
He taught the dharmas associated with the gateways to liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
he heard the Buddha teach the dharmas associated with the five eyes and the six supernormal powers;
and he heard the Buddha teach the Buddha’s ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, and great compassion.
...the dharmas associated with great joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
hearing the Buddha teach the dharmas associated with the quality of non-forgetfulness and the constant abiding in equanimity;

hearing the Buddha teach the dharmas associated with all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*); hearing the Buddha teach...
He taught the dharmas associated with all dharani-doors and all samadhi-doors;
he heard the Buddha teach the dharmas associated with the practices of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas;
and he heard the Buddha teach the dharmas associated with the unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas.
Furthermore, he heard the analytical exposition of the teachings associated with the perfection of generosity,
the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of diligence,
the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom; and furthermore, he heard the analytical exposition of internal emptiness and external emptiness.
...internal and external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness,
absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, emptiness of dispersion, unchanging emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness,
common characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, and the emptiness of non-apprehensibility...
...the teachings corresponding to the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence;
furthermore, he heard the detailed analysis of suchness (*tathatā*), the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the state of non-falsity,

the state of non-alteration, equality, the state of being free from birth, the fixed nature of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*), the stability of phenomena (*dharmasthititā*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), and emptiness...
He further hears the analysis of the meaning of the dharmas associated with the element of space and the inconceivable element;
he further hears the analysis of the meaning of the dharmas associated with the noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin, the noble truth of cessation, and the noble truth of the path;
he further hears the analysis of the meaning of the dharmas associated with the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments; he further hears the analysis...

He further heard the teachings concerning the distinct dharmas associated with the eight liberations (*aṣṭau vimokṣāḥ*), the eight bases of mastery (*aṣṭāv abhibhvāyatanāni*), the nine successive attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpattayaḥ*), and the ten totalities (*daśa kṛtsnāyatanāni*);

he further heard the teachings concerning the analysis of the dharmas associated with the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*), the four right efforts (*catvāri samyakprahāṇāni*), the four bases of psychic power (*catvāra ṛddhipādāḥ*), the five faculties (*pañcendriyāṇi*), the five powers (*pañca balāni*), the seven factors of enlightenment (*sapta bodhyaṅgāni*), and the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*). Furthermore, he heard...
He heard the analysis of the meanings of the dharmas associated with the gateways to liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
furthermore, he heard the analysis of the meanings of the dharmas associated with the five eyes and the six supernormal powers;
and furthermore, he heard the analysis of the meanings of the Buddha’s ten powers, four fearlessnesses, four analytical knowledges, great compassion, and great...
The meaning of the dharmas associated with compassion, great joy, and great equanimity, as well as the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
furthermore, hearing the analytical exposition of the meaning of the dharmas associated with the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant equanimity;

furthermore, hearing the analytical exposition of the meaning of the dharmas associated with all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*); furthermore, hearing...
He discerns the meanings of the dharmas associated with all dharani-doors and all samadhi-doors;
furthermore, he hears the discernment of the meanings of the dharmas associated with all the practices of bodhisattva-mahasattvas;
and furthermore, he hears the discernment of the meanings of the dharmas associated with the unexcelled, perfect enlightenment of all buddhas.
"Or, within a dream, one may see a Bodhi tree, vast in height and breadth, adorned with various jewels.

One sees a great Bodhisattva approaching the Bodhi tree, sitting cross-legged, subduing the hosts of Māra, realizing unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and turning the wondrous wheel of Dharma to deliver immeasurable multitudes."

Furthermore, he saw immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas gathered together to discuss various meanings of the Dharma, namely: how sentient beings should be brought to maturity; how buddha-fields should be purified; how the armies of Māra should be subdued; how the practices of a bodhisattva should be cultivated; and how the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) should be fully grasped.

"Furthermore, they may dream of seeing immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of Buddhas in the eastern direction, and they also hear their voices, saying: 'In such-and-such a world, there is a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named so-and-so, who is respectfully surrounded by several hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas and several hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of Śrāvaka disciples as he teaches the Dharma.'"
The same is true for the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir.

Furthermore, one may dream that immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of Buddhas in the eastern direction enter parinirvāṇa. Having seen each Buddha pass into parinirvāṇa, there are donors who, for the sake of making offerings to the Buddha’s *śarīra*, erect immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of *stūpas* made of the seven wonderful precious substances. Moreover, at each and every *stūpa*, they offer worship, respect, reverence, and praise for immeasurable eons with immeasurable, supreme, and exquisite flower garlands, powdered and scattered incenses, robes, necklaces, jeweled banners, pennants, canopies, various wondrous and rare objects, music, and lamps.
It is likewise in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below. "Kauśika!

When these sons and daughters of good family see such auspicious signs in their dreams, whether asleep or awake, their bodies and minds are peaceful and joyful. The various devas augment their vital energy (*ojas*), causing them to feel their own bodies to be light and agile. By reason of this, they do not become excessively attached to food, drink, medicine, clothing, or bedding; their minds remain detached toward these four types of offerings. It is just as when a yoga practitioner enters a sublime meditative concentration (*samādhi*): nourished by the power of that concentration, once they have emerged from it, their mind remains detached even toward exquisite delicacies; so too is it with these."
Why is this so, Kauśika?

It is because these sons and daughters of good family are protected by the compassionate mindfulness of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, as well as Śrāvakas, Bodhisattvas, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans— those endowed with great supernormal powers and supreme majesty— who secretly infuse their bodies and minds with wondrous vital energy, thereby causing their resolve to be courageous and their physical strength to flourish.

“Kauśika! If good sons or good daughters wish to attain such merits in the present life, they should give rise to the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna-citta*), employing the method of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), and with sincere hearts listen to, receive and uphold, read and recite, diligently practice and study, reflect upon according to principle, explain, transcribe, and widely disseminate this Prajñāpāramitā.”

“Kauśika! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, although unable to hear, receive, uphold, read, recite, diligently study, or reflect upon the *prajñāpāramitā* as it truly is, nor able to widely proclaim and disseminate it for the sake of sentient beings, nevertheless writes it down, adorns it with various jewels, and further offers all that they possess—such as diverse exquisite flower garlands, powdered and scattered incenses, robes, necklaces, jeweled banners, pennants, canopies, various wonderful and rare objects, music, and lamps—to honor, revere, respect, and praise it, they shall likewise obtain the merits previously described.”
Why is this? Kauśika!
It is because these sons and daughters of good family are able to extensively benefit, bring peace, and provide happiness to immeasurable sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If sons and daughters of good family, with a mind directed toward the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) and employing the method of non-apprehension, should with sincere hearts hear, receive, uphold, read, recite, diligently practice, and reflect upon this Prajñāpāramitā according to the truth; and should widely proclaim and disseminate it for the sake of sentient beings; or should write it down, adorning it with various jewels; and furthermore, with all kinds of exquisite flower garlands, powdered and scattered incenses, robes, necklaces, jeweled banners, pennants, canopies, various wonderful and rare objects, music, and lamps—offering all that they possess as worship, respect, honor, and praise."

By this cause and condition, these sons and daughters of good family shall obtain immeasurable merit; throughout their entire lives, they will provide offerings of immeasurable kinds of superior and exquisite food, drink, clothing, bedding, medicine, and other necessities to serve, revere, honor, and praise all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, along with their assemblies of disciples, throughout the worlds of the ten directions.

Furthermore, it would be superior to the case where, after the parinirvāṇa of the Buddhas of the ten directions and their disciples, one constructs stūpas made of the seven exquisite jewels—high, wide, and magnificent—to enshrine their relics (śarīra), and then, for the remainder of one's life, makes offerings, honors, respects, reveres, and praises them with immeasurable celestial flower garlands, powdered and scattered incenses, robes, necklaces, jeweled banners, pennants, canopies, various wonderful and rare objects, music, and lamps.
Why is this so? Kauśika!
It is because all the Buddhas of the ten directions and their assemblies of disciples are born from such profound Prajñāpāramitā.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śakra, the Lord of the Devas, saying: “Kauśika!
Suppose one portion were the relics of the Buddha filling this entire Jambudvīpa, and another portion were this profound Prajñāpāramitā written down—of these two portions, which would you take?”
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Suppose one portion were filled with the *śarīra* relics of the Buddha throughout this Jambudvīpa, and another portion were this profound *prajñāpāramitā* written down; between these two portions, my mind would rather take this *prajñāpāramitā*.

Why is this? It is not that I lack faith and acceptance toward the *śarīras* (relics) of the Buddhas, nor that I do not delight in making offerings to them, honoring, respecting, revering, and praising them. However, it is because all *śarīras* are born from the *prajñāpāramitā*, and because they are all permeated and cultivated by the power of the merit of the *prajñāpāramitā*, that they are honored, respected, revered, and praised by all the world—including devas, humans, and asuras—with every kind of supreme and exquisite flower garlands, powdered and scattered incenses, robes, necklaces, precious banners, pennants, canopies, various wondrous and rare objects, music, and lamps, exhausting all that exists.
At that time, Śāriputra said to Śakra, the Lord of Devas:

"Kauśika! Since this Prajñāpāramitā cannot be grasped, being formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and of a single characteristic—namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics—how can you grasp it?"

Why is this so? Because this Prajñāpāramitā is without grasping and without relinquishing, without increase and without decrease, without accumulation and without dispersal, without benefit and without harm, and without defilement and without purity.
Thus, this perfection of wisdom does not bestow the qualities of a Buddha, nor does it abandon the qualities of an ordinary being;
it does not bestow the qualities of a bodhisattva, nor does it abandon the qualities of an ordinary being;
it does not bestow the qualities of a pratyekabuddha, nor does it abandon the qualities of an ordinary being.
It does not bestow the dharmas of the śrāvakas, nor does it abandon the dharmas of ordinary beings;
it does not bestow the unconditioned realm (*asaṃskṛtadhātu*), nor does it abandon the conditioned realm (*saṃskṛtadhātu*).

In this same way, this perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) does not bestow the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*), nor does it bestow the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, or wisdom.

In this way, the perfection of wisdom is not conjoined with internal emptiness, nor with external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate truth, the emptiness of conditioned phenomena, the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, absolute emptiness, the emptiness of the limitless, the emptiness of dispersion, the emptiness of non-alteration, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the emptiness of self-characteristics, the emptiness of common characteristics, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, or the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature.

In this way, the perfection of wisdom does not bestow upon suchness, nor upon the dharma-realm, the nature of phenomena, non-illusory nature, unchanging nature, equality, the state of being free from birth, the fixed nature of phenomena, the stability of phenomena, the limit of reality, the realm of empty space, or the inconceivable realm.
In this way, the perfection of wisdom does not bestow the noble truth of suffering, nor does it bestow the noble truths of origin, cessation, or the path.
In this way, the perfection of wisdom does not bestow the four dhyānas, nor does it bestow the four immeasurables or the four formless attainments.
In this way, the perfection of wisdom does not bestow the eight liberations, nor does it bestow the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, or the ten totalities.

In this way, the perfection of wisdom does not bestow the four applications of mindfulness, nor does it bestow the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the eightfold noble path.
In this way, the perfection of wisdom does not bestow the gate of liberation of emptiness, nor the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness.
In this way, the perfection of wisdom does not bestow the five eyes, nor the six supernormal powers.

In this way, the perfection of wisdom does not bestow the ten powers of a Buddha, nor does it bestow the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
In this way, the perfection of wisdom does not bestow the quality of non-forgetfulness, nor does it bestow the nature of constant equanimity.
In this way, the perfection of wisdom does not bestow all-knowledge, nor does it bestow the knowledge of the paths, nor does it bestow the knowledge of all aspects.
In this way, the perfection of wisdom does not bestow any of the doors of dhāraṇī, nor does it bestow any of the doors of samādhi.
In this way, the perfection of wisdom does not bestow the fruit of a stream-enterer, nor the fruit of a once-returner, a non-returner, or an arhat.
In this way, the perfection of wisdom does not bestow the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha.
In this way, the perfection of wisdom does not bestow the practice of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
"In this way, the perfection of wisdom does not [attain] unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, replied to Śāriputra:
"It is so! It is so!"
"So it is! It is exactly as you have said.
'Venerable One!'"
Thus, this perfection of wisdom is truly ungraspable; it is formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and of a single characteristic—namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics.
"Venerable One!

This Prajñāpāramitā is without grasping and without relinquishing; without increase and without decrease; without accumulation and without dispersion; without benefit and without harm; without defilement and without purity."
“Venerable sir!
This Prajñāpāramitā does not bestow the qualities of a Buddha, nor does it abandon the qualities of an ordinary person;
it does not bestow the qualities of a Bodhisattva, nor does it abandon the qualities of an ordinary person.”
He does not associate with the dharmas of pratyekabuddhas, nor does he abandon the dharmas of ordinary beings;
he does not associate with the dharmas of śrāvakas, nor does he abandon the dharmas of ordinary beings;
he does not associate with the unconditioned realm, nor does he abandon the conditioned realm.
"Venerable One!
This Prajñāpāramitā is not conjoined with the Dānapāramitā, nor is it conjoined with the Śīla-, Kṣānti-, Vīrya-, Dhyāna-, or Prajñāpāramitā."
"Venerable One!

This perfection of wisdom is not conjoined with internal emptiness, nor is it conjoined with external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate, the emptiness of the conditioned, the emptiness of the unconditioned, absolute emptiness, the emptiness of the limitless, the emptiness of dispersion, the emptiness of non-alteration, the emptiness of essential nature, the emptiness of self-characteristic, the emptiness of common characteristic, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, or the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature."
"Venerable One!

This perfection of wisdom does not associate with suchness; it does not associate with the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, the non-erroneous nature, the unchanging nature, equality, the nature of freedom from birth, the fixed nature of dharmas, the stability of dharmas, the limit of reality, the realm of empty space, or the inconceivable realm."
“Venerable sir!
This perfection of wisdom does not bestow the noble truth of suffering, nor does it bestow the noble truths of origin, cessation, or the path.
Venerable sir!”
"In this way, the perfection of wisdom is not associated with the four dhyānas, nor with the four immeasurables, nor with the four formless attainments.
O Venerable One!"
In this way, the perfection of wisdom does not bestow the eight liberations, nor the eight bases of mastery, nor the nine successive attainments, nor the ten totalities.
“Venerable One!

This Prajñāpāramitā does not bestow the four foundations of mindfulness; it does not bestow the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the eightfold noble path.”
“Venerable One!
This Prajñāpāramitā does not bestow the gate of liberation of emptiness, nor does it bestow the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness.”
“Venerable sir!
This Prajñāpāramitā does not bestow the five eyes, nor does it bestow the six supernormal powers.
Venerable sir!”

In this way, the perfection of wisdom does not bestow upon the Buddha the ten powers, nor the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
"Venerable sir!
This perfection of wisdom does not bestow the quality of non-forgetfulness, nor does it bestow the nature of constant equanimity.
Venerable sir!"
"In this way, the perfection of wisdom does not bestow omniscience, nor does it bestow the knowledge of the aspects of the path, nor the knowledge of all aspects.
O Venerable One!"
"In this way, the perfection of wisdom does not bestow any of the gateways of dhāraṇī, nor does it bestow any of the gateways of samādhi.
O Virtuous One!"
"In this way, the perfection of wisdom does not bestow the fruit of a stream-enterer, nor the fruit of a once-returner, a non-returner, or an arhat.
Venerable sir!"
In this way, the perfection of wisdom does not bestow the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha.
"Venerable One!
In this way, the perfection of wisdom does not bestow the practice of a bodhisattva mahāsattva."
“Venerable sir!
This perfection of wisdom does not [conjoin] with unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Venerable sir!”

If one can understand the perfection of wisdom in this way, this constitutes the true grasping of the profound perfection of wisdom, and it is also the true practice of the profound perfection of wisdom.

Why is this? Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* does not follow dualistic activity, as it is devoid of dualistic characteristics; likewise, the *dhyāna*, *vīrya*, *kṣānti*, *śīla*, and *dāna* *pāramitās* also do not follow dualistic activity, as they are devoid of dualistic characteristics.
At that time, the Buddha praised Śakra, the Lord of Devas, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
It is as you have said:
the profound perfection of wisdom does not follow dualistic courses. Why is this?
Because the profound perfection of wisdom has no dualistic characteristics,
likewise the perfections of meditative concentration, diligence, patience, ethical discipline, and generosity do not follow a dualistic course.
Why is this? It is because these perfections of meditative concentration, diligence, patience, ethical discipline, and generosity likewise lack the characteristic of duality.
“Kauśika! Those who wish to attribute two characteristics to the profound Prajñāpāramitā would likewise wish to attribute two characteristics to True Suchness (tathatā).”
Why is this? Kauśika!
Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and true suchness (*tathatā*) are non-dual and cannot be divided into two.

“Kauśika! Those who wish to attribute two distinct characteristics to the perfections of dhyāna, vīrya, kṣānti, śīla, and dāna, would likewise wish to attribute two distinct characteristics to suchness (tathatā).”
Why is this? Kauśika,
it is because the perfections of dhyāna, vīrya, kṣānti, śīla, and dāna are non-dual with and indivisible from suchness (tathatā).
“Kauśika! Those who wish to attribute two characteristics to the profound *prajñāpāramitā* would likewise wish to attribute two characteristics to the *dharmadhātu*.
Why is this? Kauśika,
it is because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and the *dharmadhātu* are non-dual and cannot be divided into two.

“Kauśika! Those who wish to establish a duality in the perfections of meditative concentration, diligence, patience, ethical discipline, and generosity, would likewise wish to establish a duality in the dharmadhātu.”
Why is this? Kauśika!
Because the perfections of meditative concentration, diligence, patience, ethical discipline, and generosity are non-dual with and indivisible from the dharma-realm.
“Kauśika! Those who wish to attribute two characteristics to the profound *prajñāpāramitā* would likewise wish to attribute two characteristics to the *dharmatā*.
Why is this? Kauśika,
it is because the profound perfection of wisdom and the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) are non-dual and cannot be divided into two.

“Kauśika! Those who wish to attribute two characteristics to the perfections of dhyāna, vīrya, kṣānti, śīla, and dāna, would likewise wish to attribute two characteristics to the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).”
Why is this? Kauśika!
Because the perfections of dhyāna, vīrya, kṣānti, śīla, and dāna are non-dual with and indivisible from the dharmatā.
“Kauśika! Those who wish to attribute two characteristics to the profound *prajñāpāramitā* would likewise wish to attribute two characteristics to the nature of non-falsity (*avisaṃvāditva*).”
Why is this? Kauśika,
it is because the profound perfection of wisdom and the nature of non-falsity are non-dual and cannot be divided into two.

“Kauśika! Those who would wish for the perfections of dhyāna, vīrya, kṣānti, śīla, and dāna to have two distinct characteristics, would likewise wish for the nature of non-falsity to have two distinct characteristics.”
Why is this? Kauśika!
Because the perfections of dhyāna, vīrya, kṣānti, śīla, and dāna are non-dual with and indivisible from the nature of non-falsity.
“Kauśika! Those who wish to attribute two characteristics to the profound *prajñāpāramitā* would likewise wish to attribute two characteristics to the nature of non-alteration.”
Why is this? Kausika!
This profound prajñāpāramitā and the nature of non-alteration are non-dual and cannot be divided into two.
“Kauśika! Those who wish to attribute two characteristics to the perfections of dhyāna, vīrya, kṣānti, śīla, and dāna, would likewise wish to attribute two characteristics to non-alteration itself.”
Why is this? Kauśika!
Because the perfections of dhyāna, vīrya, kṣānti, śīla, and dāna are non-dual and indivisible from the nature of non-alteration.

“Kauśika! Those who wish to attribute two characteristics to the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) are, in effect, wishing to attribute two characteristics to the nature of equality (samatā) as well.”
Why is this? Kauśika!
Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and the state of equality are non-dual and cannot be divided into two.

“Kauśika! Those who would wish for the perfections of dhyāna, vīrya, kṣānti, śīla, and dāna to have two distinct characteristics would likewise wish for samatā (the state of equality) to have two distinct characteristics.”
Why is this? Kausika,
because the perfections of meditative concentration, diligence, patience, ethical discipline, and generosity are non-dual with and indivisible from the nature of equality.
“Kauśika! Those who would wish for this profound prajñāpāramitā to have two characteristics are likewise wishing for that which is free from the nature of arising to also have two characteristics.”
Why is this? Kauśika,
it is because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and the nature of detachment are non-dual and indivisible.

“Kauśika! Those who wish to attribute two distinct characteristics to the perfections of dhyāna, vīrya, kṣānti, śīla, and dāna, would likewise wish to attribute two distinct characteristics to the nature of detachment.”
Why is this? Kauśika!
Because the perfections of dhyāna, vīrya, kṣānti, śīla, and dāna are non-dual with and indivisible from the nature of detachment from birth.
“Kauśika! Those who wish to attribute two characteristics to the profound *prajñāpāramitā* are, in effect, wishing to attribute two characteristics to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) itself.”
Why is this? Kauśika!
Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and all phenomena (*dharma*) are non-dual and cannot be divided into two.

“Kauśika! Those who wish to attribute two distinct characteristics to the perfections of dhyāna, vīrya, kṣānti, śīla, and dāna, would likewise wish to attribute two distinct characteristics to the dharmas themselves.”
Why is this? Kauśika!
Because the perfections of dhyāna, vīrya, kṣānti, śīla, and dāna are non-dual with the dharmadhātu and cannot be divided into two.
“Kauśika! Those who wish to attribute two characteristics to the profound *prajñāpāramitā* are likewise wishing to attribute two characteristics to the abiding of dharmas.”
Why is this? Kauśika!
This profound prajñāpāramitā and the abiding of phenomena (dharmasthiti) are non-dual and cannot be divided into two.

“Kauśika! Those who wish to attribute two distinct characteristics to the perfections of dhyāna, vīrya, kṣānti, śīla, and dāna, would likewise wish to attribute two distinct characteristics to the abiding of the Dharma.”
Why is this? Kauśika,
because the perfections of dhyāna, vīrya, kṣānti, śīla, and dāna are non-dual with and indivisible from the abiding of the Dharma.
“Kauśika! Those who wish for the profound Prajñāpāramitā to have two characteristics are, in effect, wishing for the *bhūtakoṭi* (the limit of reality) to also have two characteristics.”
Why is this? Kauśika!
Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) are non-dual and cannot be divided into two.

“Kauśika! Those who wish to attribute two distinct characteristics to the perfections of dhyāna, vīrya, kṣānti, śīla, and dāna, would likewise wish to attribute two distinct characteristics to the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi).”
Why is this? Kauśika,
it is because the perfections of meditative concentration, diligence, patience, ethical discipline, and generosity are non-dual with and indivisible from the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi).
“Kauśika! Those who wish to attribute two characteristics to the profound *prajñāpāramitā* would likewise wish to attribute two characteristics to the realm of empty space (*ākāśadhātu*).”
Why is this? Kauśika,
it is because the profound perfection of wisdom and the realm of empty space are non-dual and cannot be divided into two.

“Kauśika! Those who wish to attribute two distinct characteristics to the perfections of dhyāna, vīrya, kṣānti, śīla, and dāna, would likewise wish to attribute two distinct characteristics to the realm of space.”
Why is that? Kauśika!
Because the perfections of meditative concentration, diligence, patience, ethical discipline, and generosity are non-dual with and indivisible from the realm of space.
“Kauśika! Those who wish for the profound *prajñāpāramitā* to have two characteristics would likewise wish for the inconceivable realm (*acintyadhātu*) to have two characteristics.”
Why is this so? Kausika,
it is because the profound perfection of wisdom and the inconceivable realm are non-dual and cannot be divided into two.

“Kauśika! Those who would wish for the perfections of dhyāna, vīrya, kṣānti, śīla, and dāna to have two distinct characteristics would likewise wish for the inconceivable realm to have two distinct characteristics.”
Why is this? Kauśika!
Because the perfections of meditative concentration, diligence, patience, ethical discipline, and generosity are non-dual with and indivisible from the inconceivable realm.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā should be wholeheartedly prostrated to, circumambulated to the right, and honored, revered, respected, and praised by all the devas, humans, asuras, and others in the world."

Why is this? Because all the assembly of Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas, by diligently training in this very profound Prajñāpāramitā, have attained, shall attain, and are currently attaining unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"Bhagavān!

Just as when I am seated upon the throne of Śakra in the Sudharma Hall of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, preaching the True Dharma for the assembly of devas, at that time immeasurable sons of gods come to my presence to listen to what I say; they make offerings, pay respect, revere, and praise me, circumambulate me to the right, prostrate, join their palms, and depart."
"When I am not present, the sons of the gods also come to this place; though they do not see me, they pay homage and make offerings just as they did when I was here, all saying:

'This is the seat where Śakra, Lord of the Devas, preached the Dharma for the gods; we should all act as if the Lord of the Gods were present, making offerings, circumambulating to the right, and prostrating before departing.'"
“World-Honored One!

If this *prajñāpāramitā* is written down, received, upheld, read, recited, and extensively expounded and circulated for the sake of sentient beings, one should know that this place will always be visited by the assembly of the gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans of this land and the infinite worlds of the ten directions—immeasurable and innumerable in number. Even if there is no one to preach it, out of reverence for the Dharma, they will likewise offer worship, pay homage, show respect, and praise it in that place before departing.”

Why is this? It is because all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are born from this very profound Prajñāpāramitā; because all the assemblies of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, Śrāvakas, and all sentient beings obtain their sublime and wondrous requisites for happiness by relying upon this very profound Prajñāpāramitā; and because even the *śarīra* relics of the Buddha are worthy of veneration due to being permeated by the merit of this very profound Prajñāpāramitā.
"Bhagavān!

This Prajñāpāramitā serves as the cause, the condition, the support, and the means of elicitation for the practices of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and for all-knowledge (sarvajñajñāna) which they realize."
“World-Honored One!
For this reason, I say this:

suppose one portion were filled with the *śarīra* relics of the Buddha throughout this Jambudvīpa, and another portion were the transcription of this profound *prajñāpāramitā*; between these two portions, my intention would rather be to take this *prajñāpāramitā*.
“World-Honored One!

If I were to receive, uphold, read, recite, and correctly contemplate this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, because my mind would be in accord with the Dharma, I would not perceive any signs of fear whatsoever.”
Why is this so? World-Honored One!
The profound *prajñāpāramitā* is without marks, without characteristics, without words, and without speech.
“World-Honored One!

Because this perfection of wisdom is signless, markless, ineffable, and inexpressible, the perfections of meditative concentration, diligence, patience, ethical discipline, and generosity are likewise signless, markless, ineffable, and inexpressible.”

“Bhagavān, because this *prajñāpāramitā* is signless, markless, ineffable, and inexpressible, therefore inner emptiness, outer emptiness, inner-and-outer emptiness, emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, emptiness of all phenomena, unapprehendable emptiness, emptiness of non-existence, emptiness of intrinsic nature, and emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence are likewise signless, markless, ineffable, and inexpressible.”
“World-Honored One!

Because this prajñāpāramitā is without marks, without characteristics, without words, and without speech, therefore true thusness (tathatā), the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), non-falsity, immutability, equality, the state of being free from birth, the fixed nature of phenomena (dharmaniyāmatā), the stability of phenomena (dharmasthititā), the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), the realm of space (ākāśadhātu), and the inconceivable realm are also without marks, without characteristics, without words, and without speech.”
“World-Honored One!

Because this Prajñāpāramitā is signless, markless, ineffable, and inexpressible, the Noble Truth of Suffering, the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering, the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering, and the Noble Truth of the Path are likewise signless, markless, ineffable, and inexpressible.”
“World-Honored One!

Because this prajñāpāramitā is without marks, without characteristics, without words, and without speech, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments are likewise without marks, without characteristics, without words, and without speech.”
“World-Honored One!

Because this Prajñāpāramitā is without marks, without characteristics, without words, and without speech, the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities are likewise without marks, without characteristics, without words, and without speech.”
“World-Honored One!

Because this prajñāpāramitā is signless, markless, ineffable, and inexpressible, for this reason the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path are likewise signless, markless, ineffable, and inexpressible.”
“World-Honored One!

Because this prajñāpāramitā is signless, markless, ineffable, and inexpressible, the gate of liberation of emptiness, the gate of liberation of signlessness, and the gate of liberation of wishlessness are likewise signless, markless, ineffable, and inexpressible.”
“World-Honored One!

Because this prajñāpāramitā is without marks, without characteristics, without words, and without speech, the five eyes and the six supernormal powers are likewise without marks, without characteristics, without words, and without speech.”
“World-Honored One!

Because this prajñāpāramitā is without marks, without characteristics, without words, and without speech, for this reason the Buddha’s ten powers, four fearlessnesses, four unhindered understandings, great kindness, great compassion, great joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are also without marks, without characteristics, without words, and without speech.”
“World-Honored One!

Because this Prajñāpāramitā is signless, markless, ineffable, and inexpressible, therefore the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant equanimity are likewise signless, markless, ineffable, and inexpressible.”
“World-Honored One!

Because this prajñāpāramitā is without marks, without characteristics, without words, and without speech, therefore all-knowledge (sarvajñatā), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (mārgākārajñatā), and the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā) are also without marks, without characteristics, without words, and without speech.”

“Bhagavān! Because this prajñāpāramitā is without marks, without characteristics, without words, and without speech, all dhāraṇī-doors and all samādhi-doors are likewise without marks, without characteristics, without words, and without speech.”
“World-Honored One!

Because this prajñāpāramitā is without marks, without characteristics, without words, and without speech, the practice of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva is likewise without marks, without characteristics, without words, and without speech.”
“World-Honored One!

Because this prajñāpāramitā is signless, markless, ineffable, and inexpressible, the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas is likewise signless, markless, ineffable, and inexpressible.”
“World-Honored One!
Because this prajñāpāramitā is signless, markless, ineffable, and inexpressible, all dharmas are likewise signless, markless, ineffable, and inexpressible.”
“World-Honored One!

If this Prajñāpāramitā possessed marks, possessed signs, possessed words, and possessed explanations, rather than being without marks, without signs, without words, and without explanations, then the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha would not have realized that all dharmas are without marks, without signs, without words, and without explanations, thereby attaining unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and teaching all sentient beings that all dharmas are without marks, without signs, without words, and without explanations.”
“World-Honored One!

Because this *prajñāpāramitā* is without marks, without characteristics, without words, and without speech—and is not possessed of marks, characteristics, words, or speech—the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha knows that all phenomena are without marks, without characteristics, without words, and without speech; having realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, he teaches all sentient beings that all phenomena are without marks, without characteristics, without words, and without speech.”
“World-Honored One!

For this reason, the Prajñāpāramitā should be received with offerings, reverence, respect, honor, and praise by all the world—including devas, humans, and asuras—using immeasurable varieties of exquisite flower garlands, powdered and incense perfumes, robes, necklaces, precious banners, pennants, canopies, various wonders, rare treasures, music, and lamps, exhausting all that they possess.”
“World-Honored One!

If good sons and good daughters, with sincere hearts, hear, receive, uphold, read, recite, diligently study, and reflect upon this *prajñāpāramitā* according to the truth; and if they extensively proclaim and disseminate it for the sake of sentient beings, or even transcribe it and adorn it with various jewels; and if they offer worship, reverence, respect, and praise with immeasurable kinds of exquisite flower garlands, powdered and scattered incenses, robes, necklaces, jeweled banners, pennants, canopies, various wonderful and rare objects, music, and lamps—using all that they possess—then these good sons and good daughters will certainly never again fall into the hells or the realms of animals.”
Not born among ghosts, in frontier regions, in barbarian lands, or as mlecchas;
not falling into the stages of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, but inevitably proceeding toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment; constantly seeing all Buddhas and perpetually hearing the true Dharma;
never being separated from virtuous friends; purifying buddha-fields and maturing sentient beings—from one [life to the next]...
From one Buddha-field to another Buddha-field, they shall make offerings, show reverence, respect,
and praise to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and the assemblies of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, using immeasurable and most excellent flower garlands, powdered and scattered incenses,
robes, necklaces, precious banners, pennants, canopies, and various wonderful and rare treasures.
...with music, dance, and lamps as offerings.
"World-Honored One!

Suppose one portion were filled with the *śarīra* relics of the Buddha throughout this trichiliocosm, and another portion were the transcription of this profound *prajñāpāramitā*; between these two portions, my intention would be to take this *prajñāpāramitā*."
Why is this? Because all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, as well as the Buddha-śarīras within the trichiliocosm, are all born from the Prajñāpāramitā.

Furthermore, the *śarīra* relics of the Buddhas throughout the trichiliocosm are all perfumed and cultivated by the power of the merit of the *prajñāpāramitā*; therefore, they receive offerings, respect, reverence, and praise from devas, humans, asuras, and others.

By virtue of these causes and conditions, those sons and daughters of good family who offer worship, respect, reverence, and praise to the Buddha’s śarīras will certainly never again fall into the three evil realms; they will always be born among gods or humans to experience various pleasures, possessing wealth, nobility, and sovereignty according to their wishes, and shall proceed to nirvana by means of the Dharma of the Three Vehicles.
“World-Honored One!
Whether one beholds the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, or beholds this profound Prajñāpāramitā written down, these two merits are equal and without distinction.”
Why is this? Because this perfection of wisdom is equal to all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas—non-dual and indivisible.

“Bhagavān! If there is a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha who, abiding in the three bases of miraculous power, proclaims the sublime Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings— namely, the sūtras, geyas, vyākaraṇas, gāthās, udānas, nidānas, avadānas,

jātakas, vaipulyas, adbhutadharmas, upadeśas, and upadeśas— and if a son or daughter of good family were to receive, uphold, read, recite, and extensively explain this Prajñāpāramitā to others, these two merits would be equal and without distinction.”

Why is this? Because whether it be those Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, or their three modes of miraculous manifestation, or the twelvefold teachings they have proclaimed, all are born from the Prajñāpāramitā.
“Bhagavān! If all the Tathāgatas, Arhats,

and Samyaksaṃbuddhas in the worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Gaṅgā, were to abide in the three types of miraculous displays and proclaim the sublime Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings— namely, the sūtras, geyas, vyākaraṇas, gāthās, udānas, nidānas, itivṛttakas,

jātakas, vaipulyas, adbhutadharmas, avadānas, and upadeśas— and if a son or daughter of good family were to receive, uphold, recite, and extensively explain this Prajñāpāramitā to others, these two merits would be equal and without distinction.”

Why is this? Because all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas throughout the worlds of the ten directions—as numerous as the sands of the Gaṅgā—whether by means of the three types of miraculous displays or through the twelvefold scriptures they proclaim, all arise in dependence upon the Prajñāpāramitā.

“Bhagavān! If good sons and good daughters were to offer all that they possess—immeasurable varieties of exquisite flower garlands, powdered and scattered incenses, robes, necklaces, jeweled banners, pennants, canopies, various wondrous and rare objects, music, and lamps—to all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas in the worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Gaṅgā River; and were to honor, revere, respect, and praise them;”

If there are sons or daughters of good family who write out the *prajñāpāramitā*, and likewise offer worship, respect, reverence, and praise with immeasurable, supreme, and exquisite flower garlands, powdered and scattered incenses, robes, necklaces, jeweled banners, pennants, canopies, various wonderful and rare objects, music, and lamps—utilizing everything they possess—these two merits are equal and without distinction.
Why is this? Because all those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are born from reliance upon the Prajñāpāramitā.

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Scroll One Hundred and Twenty-seven, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Part One: Chapter on Measuring Merits, Number Thirty, Section Twenty-six. “World-Honored One! ...”

If sons or daughters of good family, with sincere hearts, hear, receive, uphold, read, recite, diligently study, and reflect upon this Prajñāpāramitā according to the truth, and extensively proclaim and disseminate it for the sake of sentient beings, then these sons and daughters of good family will, in future lives, not fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts, nor among the borderlands, the barbarians, or the Mlecchas; they will always possess all their faculties, be intelligent and handsome, and will not fall into the stages of the Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha.
Why is this? Because these sons and daughters of good family will certainly abide in the stage of non-retrogression of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas.
"World-Honored One! [they said.]

If sons or daughters of good family, with sincere hearts, hear, receive, uphold, read, recite, diligently practice, and reflect upon this Prajñāpāramitā according to the truth, and extensively proclaim and disseminate it for the sake of sentient beings; or if they transcribe it, adorning it with various jewels, and offer it all they possess—such as immeasurable kinds of exquisite flower garlands, powdered and scattered incenses, robes, necklaces, precious banners, flags, canopies, various wonderful and rare objects, music, and lamps—in order to honor, revere, respect, and praise it, these sons and daughters of good family will remain far removed from all decline, affliction, and fear.
World-Honored One!
Just as a debtor who fears his creditor immediately serves and draws near to a king, relying on the king’s power to escape that fear.
"Bhagavān!
Just as when someone relies upon a king and is taken under his protection, they are honored, revered, respected, and praised by all people of the world;

so too it is with the *śarīra* of the Buddha. Because it has been permeated and cultivated by this *prajñāpāramitā*, it is honored, revered, respected, and praised by devas, humans, asuras, and others."
"Bhagavān!
The knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) is also accomplished by relying upon the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). Bhagavān!"
For this reason, I say:

suppose one portion were the relics of the Buddha filling this trichiliocosm, and another portion were this profound *prajñāpāramitā* written down; of these two portions, my intention would rather take this *prajñāpāramitā*.
Why is this so, World-Honored One?
It is because it is by means of this *prajñāpāramitā* that the Buddha’s *śarīra* relics and the body adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and the eighty secondary signs are brought forth.
“World-Honored One!
It is because of this perfection of wisdom that the perfections of giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom attain complete purity.”
“World-Honored One!

It is because by means of this *prajñāpāramitā*, inner emptiness, outer emptiness, inner-and-outer emptiness, emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, limitless emptiness, emptiness of dispersion, unchanging emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, emptiness of all phenomena, emptiness of non-apprehensibility, emptiness of non-existence, emptiness of intrinsic nature, and emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence are brought to perfect purity.”
“World-Honored One!

It is because by means of this *prajñāpāramitā*, suchness, the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, non-falsity, non-alteration, equality, the nature of freedom from birth, the fixedness of dharmas, the stability of dharmas, the limit of reality, the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm are brought to perfect purity.”
“World-Honored One!

It is because by means of this prajñāpāramitā, the noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin [of suffering], the noble truth of cessation, and the noble truth of the path are brought to complete purity.”
“World-Honored One!
It is because by means of this perfection of wisdom, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless absorptions are brought to full purity.”
“World-Honored One!
It is because by means of this *prajñāpāramitā*, the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten totalities are brought to complete purity.”
“World-Honored One!

It is because of this perfection of wisdom that the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path attain complete purity.”
“World-Honored One!

It is because of this *prajñāpāramitā* that the gate of liberation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha*), the gate of liberation of signlessness (*animitta-vimokṣamukha*), and the gate of liberation of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-vimokṣamukha*) attain complete purity.”
“World-Honored One!
It is because of this perfection of wisdom that the five eyes and the six supernormal powers are brought to complete purity.
World-Honored One!”

It is because by means of this perfection of wisdom, the Buddha’s ten powers, four fearlessnesses, four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are brought to full purity.
“World-Honored One!
By means of this *prajñāpāramitā*, the quality of non-forgetfulness (*asaṃpramoṣadharma*) and the nature of constant dwelling in equanimity (*upekṣā*) are brought to complete purity.
World-Honored One!”
"Because by means of this perfection of wisdom, all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), knowledge of the paths (*mārgākārajñā*), and knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñā*) are brought to complete purity.
World-Honored One!"
"By means of this perfection of wisdom, all doors of dhāraṇī and all doors of samādhi are brought to complete purity.
World-Honored One!"
"Because by means of this perfection of wisdom, all the practices of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas attain complete purity.
World-Honored One!
Because by means of this perfection of wisdom, the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas attains complete purity."
“World-Honored One!
By means of this Prajñāpāramitā, the bodies and minds of all Buddhas are both indestructible, for it exceeds the diamond by countless multiples.”
“World-Honored One!
It is by virtue of the majestic power of this prajñāpāramitā that the five perfections, such as giving and the rest, are also designated as ‘pāramitās.’”
Why is this? Because without the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), giving and the other perfections cannot reach the further shore.
"World-Honored One! [he said.]

Whether it be this trichiliocosm or any other world, in whatever royal capitals, cities, towns, or villages there may be, if sentient beings therein uphold, recite, copy, explain, make offerings to, revere, respect, and praise this Prajñāpāramitā, those beings will not be harmed by any humans or non-humans, except for the inevitable suffering that must be experienced as a result of fixed evil karma. They shall gradually train and study, fulfilling their aspirations until they attain the nirvāṇa of the three vehicles.
“World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā possesses such great majestic power that, wherever it may be, it brings immense benefit to all sentient beings.”
"Bhagavat, such is the great spiritual power of this Prajñāpāramitā; it performs great buddha-works within this trichiliocosm. Bhagavat!"
If this profound perfection of wisdom circulates in a world-system, you should know that a Buddha has appeared in that place in the world to bring benefit and happiness to all.
"Bhagavān!

It is like a priceless great divine jewel, possessing immeasurable kinds of supreme and wondrous majesty and virtue; wherever this divine jewel resides, humans and non-humans can never cause harm or affliction."

Should there be a man or a woman who is possessed by a spirit and suffers physical and mental distress, if someone were to show them this divine jewel, the spirit would depart immediately through the power of the jewel.

Whether there be diseases of fever, or those caused by wind, or phlegm, or a combination of wind, heat, and phlegm—if one ties this divine bead to the body, none of these various ailments will fail to be cured.

This jewel can provide illumination in the dark; it cools when it is hot and warms when it is cold. Wherever this divine jewel is located, the seasons remain harmonious, being neither too cold nor too hot.
If this divine jewel is present in any location, venomous creatures such as snakes and scorpions will not dare to remain there.

Should a man or a woman be bitten by such venom and suffer unbearable agony, if someone holds this divine jewel and causes them to see it, the poison will be instantly neutralized by the power of the jewel.

If any sentient beings suffer from leprosy, malignant sores, swellings, blisters, or eye diseases such as squinting or cataracts, as well as diseases of the ears, nose, tongue, throat, or body, all these ailments will be healed by wearing this divine jewel.

If there are ponds, pools, springs, or wells whose water is turbid and foul, or which is on the verge of drying up, if one casts this jewel into them, the water immediately becomes full, fragrant, pure, and clear, endowed with the eight meritorious qualities.

If one wraps this divine jewel in various colorful garments—blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, purple, azure, or green—and casts it into water, the water will take on all those various colors following the hues of the cloth.

Thus, the majestic power of this priceless, great jewel, the divine pearl, is boundless and cannot be fully described; even when placed within a chest or casket, it causes that vessel to become fully endowed with boundless majestic power.
"Even if an empty box or casket has once held jewels, that vessel will still be cherished and esteemed by all people.
Then, the Venerable Ānanda asked Śakra, the Lord of the Devas: "Kauśika!"
"Is such a divine jewel possessed by the gods alone, or do humans also have it?
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, replied:
"Virtuous One!"
This jewel exists both among humans and in the heavens; if it is among humans, its form is small and heavy, whereas if it is in the heavens, its form is large and light.
Furthermore, when among humans, its marks are incomplete, but when in the heavens, its marks are perfectly complete.
"Those found in the heavens possess such superior majesty and virtue that they surpass the jewels of the human realm by immeasurable multiples.
Then, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

The profound *prajñāpāramitā* is likewise: it is the source of all virtues and is capable of extinguishing immeasurable evil and unwholesome dharmas; wherever it resides, it causes all physical and mental suffering and affliction of sentient beings to be completely eliminated, such that humans and non-humans alike cannot cause them harm.
"Blessed One!

This priceless great jewel, the divine pearl you have described, is not merely a metaphor for the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, but is also a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñājñāna*)."
"Bhagavān!
Thus, this Prajñāpāramitā is endowed with immeasurable, sublime qualities, and it can also bring forth immeasurable, pure, and sublime qualities of both the mundane and supramundane realms."
“World-Honored One!
The measure of the merit of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is difficult to praise. Why is this?
Because the merit of this Prajñāpāramitā is thus profound, vast, and immeasurable,
and because the Buddha’s śarīra is produced through this Prajñāpāramitā, it is worthy of receiving the offerings, veneration, respect, and praise of all the world’s devas, humans, asuras, and others.
“Bhagavān, the measure of the merit of the perfections of profound meditative concentration, diligence, patience, ethical discipline, and generosity is difficult to praise.”
Why is this? Because the merit of these perfections—dhyāna, vīrya, kṣānti, śīla, and dāna—is so profound and vast that its measure is boundless.

Because the Buddha’s *śarīra* (relics) have arisen through these perfections of meditative concentration, diligence, patience, ethical discipline, and generosity, they are worthy of receiving the offerings, reverence, respect, and praise of all the world’s devas, humans, and asuras.
“World-Honored One!
The scope of the merits of this profound internal emptiness is difficult to praise. Why is this?
Because the merit of this internal emptiness is thus profound, vast, and of boundless measure,

and because the Buddha’s *śarīra* (relics) are produced by means of this internal emptiness, they are worthy of receiving the offerings, reverence, respect, and praise of all the world, including devas, humans, and asuras.

“Bhagavān, the limits of the merit of the profound emptinesses— external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersal emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, emptiness of all phenomena, unapprehendable emptiness, emptiness of non-existence, emptiness of intrinsic nature, and emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence— are difficult to praise fully.”
Why is this? Because the merit of these [emptinesses], from external emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, is profound, vast, and immeasurable.

It is because the Buddha’s *śarīra* (relics) are produced by means of these [emptinesses], from external emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, that they are worthy of receiving the offerings, veneration, respect, and praise of all the world, including its devas, humans, and asuras.
“World-Honored One!
It is difficult to fully praise the limits of the merit of profound suchness. Why is this?
Because the virtues of such *tathatā* (thusness) are profound, vast, and immeasurable,

and because the Buddha’s *śarīra* (relics) are produced by means of this *tathatā*, they are worthy of receiving the offerings, reverence, respect, and praise of all the world, including its devas, humans, and asuras.
“World-Honored One!

The limits of the merit of the profound realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), non-illusory nature, non-alteration, equality, the state of being free from birth, the fixedness of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*), the stability of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the realm of space (*ākāśadhātu*), and the inconceivable realm are difficult to praise fully.”
Why is this? Because the merit of the dharma-realm, up to and including the inconceivable realm, is profound, vast, and immeasurable.

It is because the Buddha’s śarīra is produced by means of this dharma-realm, up to and including the inconceivable realm, that it is worthy of receiving the offerings, veneration, respect, and praise of all the worlds, including devas, humans, and asuras.
“World-Honored One!
The scope of the merit of the profound Noble Truth of Suffering is difficult to extol. Why is this?
Because the merit of this Noble Truth of Suffering is thus profound, vast, and immeasurable,

and because the Buddha’s *śarīra* (relics) are produced through this Noble Truth of Suffering, they are worthy of receiving the offerings, veneration, respect, and praise of all the world, including its devas, humans, and asuras.
“World-Honored One!
The scope of the merits of the profound Noble Truths of Origination, Cessation, and the Path is difficult to praise. Why is this so?
Because the virtues of these Noble Truths of Origination, Cessation, and the Path are so profound, vast, and immeasurable;

and because the Buddha’s *śarīra* (relics) have arisen by virtue of these Noble Truths of Origination, Cessation, and the Path, they are worthy of receiving the offerings, reverence, respect, and praise of all the world, including its devas, humans, and asuras.
“World-Honored One!
The scope of the merits of the profound four dhyānas is difficult to praise. Why is this so?
Because the merit of these four dhyānas is so profound and vast that its measure is boundless,

and because the Buddha’s śarīra was produced by means of these four dhyānas, it is worthy of receiving the offerings, veneration, respect, and praise of all the worlds, including devas, humans, and asuras.
“World-Honored One!
The scope of the merits of the profound four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions is difficult to praise. Why is this?

Because the merit of these four immeasurables and four formless attainments is so profound, vast, and boundless, the Buddha’s *śarīra* (relics) are produced by virtue of these four immeasurables and four formless attainments; therefore, they are worthy of receiving the offerings, reverence, respect, and praise of all the world’s devas, humans, and asuras.
“World-Honored One!
The scope of the merit of the profound eight liberations is difficult to extol. Why is this?
Because the merit of these eight liberations is so profound, vast, and immeasurable,

and because the Buddha’s *śarīra* (relics) have been produced by means of these eight liberations, they are worthy of receiving the offerings, veneration, respect, and praise of all the world, including its gods, humans, and asuras.
“World-Honored One!
The scope of the merits of the profound eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten universal bases is difficult to praise. Why is this so?

Because the merits of these eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), nine successive attainments (*anupūrvavihārasamāpatti*), and ten totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*) are profound, vast, and immeasurable;

and because the Buddha’s *śarīra* (relics) have been produced by means of these eight bases of mastery, nine successive attainments, and ten totalities, they are worthy of receiving the offerings, reverence, respect, and praise of all the world, including devas, humans, and asuras.
“World-Honored One!
It is difficult to fully praise the extent of the merit of these profound foundations of mindfulness. Why is this?
Because the merit of these four foundations of mindfulness is so profound, vast, and immeasurable,

and because the Buddha’s *śarīra* (relics) are produced through these four foundations of mindfulness, they are worthy of receiving the offerings, veneration, respect, and praise of all the world, including its devas, humans, and asuras.
“World-Honored One!
The scope of the merits of the profound four right efforts, four bases of power, five faculties, five powers, seven factors of enlightenment, and eightfold noble path is difficult to praise fully.”

Why is this? Because the merit of these four right efforts, four bases of power, five faculties, five powers, seven factors of enlightenment, and eightfold noble path is profound, vast, and immeasurable.

Because the Buddha’s *śarīra* (relics) are produced through these four right efforts, four bases of power, five faculties, five powers, seven factors of enlightenment, and eight branches of the noble path, they are worthy of receiving the offerings, respect, veneration, and praise of all the world, including its devas, humans, and asuras.
“World-Honored One!
The measure of the merit of this profound gate of liberation of emptiness is difficult to praise. Why is this?
Because the merit of this gateway to liberation of emptiness is thus profound, vast, and immeasurable,

and because the Buddha’s śarīra has arisen by means of this gateway to liberation of emptiness, it is worthy of receiving the offerings, reverence, respect, and praise of all the world, including devas, humans, and asuras.
“World-Honored One!
The scope of the merits of the profound gateways of liberation—signlessness and wishlessness—is difficult to praise. Why is this so?

Because the merits of these gateways of liberation—signlessness and wishlessness—are thus profound, vast, and immeasurable, the Buddha’s *śarīra* (relics) are produced by means of these gateways of signlessness and wishlessness; therefore, they are worthy of receiving the offerings, veneration, respect, and praise of all the world, including its devas, humans, and asuras.
“World-Honored One!
The measure of the merit of these profound five eyes is difficult to praise. Why is this?
Because the merit of these five eyes is so profound, vast, and immeasurable,

and because the Buddha’s *śarīra* (relics) are produced through these five eyes, they are worthy of receiving the offerings, reverence, respect, and praise of all the world, including its devas, humans, and asuras.
“World-Honored One!
The measure of the merit of these profound six supernormal powers is difficult to praise. Why is this?
Because the merit of these six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍ-abhijñā*) is so profound, vast, and immeasurable,

and because the Buddha’s relics (*śarīra*) are produced by means of these six supernormal powers, they are worthy of receiving the offerings, veneration, respect, and praise of all the world, including its gods, humans, and asuras.
“World-Honored One!
The scope of the merits of the profound ten powers of a Buddha is difficult to praise fully. Why is this?
Because the merit of the Buddha’s ten powers is thus profound, vast, and immeasurable,

and because the Buddha’s *śarīra* (relics) are produced by virtue of these ten powers, they are worthy of receiving the offerings, respect, veneration, and praise of all the world, including its devas, humans, and asuras.
“World-Honored One!

The limits of the merits of the four kinds of fearlessness, the four kinds of unimpeded understanding, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are difficult to praise.”

Why is this? Because the merits of these four fearlessnesses, four unhindered analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are profound, vast, and immeasurable.

Because the Buddha’s *śarīra* (relics) are produced by virtue of these four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, they are worthy of receiving the offerings, respect, veneration, and praise of all the world, including its devas, humans, and asuras.
“World-Honored One!
The extent of the merit of all these profound dharani-gates is difficult to praise. Why is this?
Because the merit of all these dhāraṇī-gates is profound, vast, and immeasurable,

and because the Buddha’s śarīras are produced by means of all these dhāraṇī-gates, they are worthy of receiving the offerings, veneration, respect, and praise of all the worlds, including devas, humans, and asuras.
“World-Honored One!
The scope of the merits of all these profound samādhi-gates is difficult to praise. Why is this?
Because the merits of all these gateways of samādhi are profound, vast, and immeasurable,

and because the Buddha’s śarīra is produced by means of all these gateways of samādhi, it is worthy of receiving the offerings, veneration, respect, and praise of all the world’s devas, humans, asuras, and others.
“World-Honored One!
The extent of the merit of profound omniscience is difficult to praise. Why is this?
