Because the merit of such omniscience is profound, vast, and immeasurable,

and because the Buddha’s *śarīra* (relics) are produced through this very omniscience, they are worthy of receiving the offerings, veneration, respect, and praise of all the world, including its devas, humans, and asuras.
“World-Honored One!
It is difficult to fully praise the limits of the merit of the profound knowledge of the paths and all-aspect omniscience. Why is this?
This is because the merit of the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects is so profound, vast, and boundless in measure.

Since the Buddha’s *śarīra* (relics) are produced by means of this knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects, they are worthy of receiving the offerings, reverence, respect, and praise of all the world, including its devas, humans, and asuras.
“World-Honored One!
The limits of the merit of the profound quality of non-forgetfulness are difficult to praise. Why is this?
Because the merit of such qualities of non-forgetfulness is profound, vast, and of boundless measure,

and because the Buddha’s *śarīra* (relics) arise from this very quality of non-forgetfulness, they are worthy of receiving the offerings, reverence, respect, and praise of all the world, including its devas, humans, and asuras.
“World-Honored One!
The measure of the merit of this profound state of constant dwelling in equanimity is difficult to praise. Why is this?
Because the merit of this constant abiding in equanimity is so profound, vast, and immeasurable,

and because the Buddha’s *śarīra* (relics) are produced through this constant abiding in equanimity, they are worthy of receiving the offerings, veneration, respect, and praise of all the world, including its devas, humans, and asuras.
“World-Honored One!
The limit of the merit of this profound, eternal severance of all continuities of afflictions and habitual tendencies is difficult to praise. Why is this so?

Because such merit as this—consisting in the eternal severance of all latencies of afflictions within the continuum—is profound, vast, and immeasurable, the Buddha’s *śarīra* (relics) arise precisely through this eternal severance of all latencies of afflictions within the continuum; therefore, they are worthy of receiving the offerings, veneration, respect, and praise of all the world, including devas, humans, and asuras.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One,

because the *śarīra* of the Buddha has been perfumed and cultivated by the most perfect and profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and because it is the vessel that relies upon the most pure and profound *prajñāpāramitā*, it is worthy of receiving the offerings, veneration, respect, and praise of all the world’s devas, humans, and asuras."
“World-Honored One!

Because the *śarīra* of the Buddha has been perfumed and cultivated by the most perfect perfections (*pāramitās*) of meditative concentration, diligence, patience, ethical discipline, and generosity; and because it is the vessel that serves as the basis for these most pure perfections of meditative concentration, diligence, patience, ethical discipline, and generosity, it is worthy of receiving the offerings, reverence, respect, and praise of all the world’s devas, humans, and asuras.”
“World-Honored One!

Because the relics of the Buddha have been perfumed and cultivated by abiding in the most perfect internal emptiness, and because they are the vessel that supports abiding in the most pure internal emptiness, they are worthy of receiving the offerings, respect, veneration, and praise of all the world’s devas, humans, asuras, and others.”
“World-Honored One!

Because the *śarīra* of the Buddha has been perfumed and cultivated by the perfection of the emptiness of the external, the emptiness of the internal and external, the emptiness of emptiness, the great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate truth, the emptiness of conditioned phenomena, the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, the emptiness of the absolute limit, the emptiness of the boundless, the emptiness of dispersion, the emptiness of non-alteration, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the emptiness of self-characteristics, the emptiness of common characteristics, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of non-apprehensibility, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence; and because it is the vessel that serves as the basis for abiding in the extreme purity of the emptiness of the external up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, it is worthy of receiving the offerings, respect, veneration, and praise of all the worlds, including devas, humans, and asuras.”
“World-Honored One!

Because the relics of the Buddha have been perfumed and cultivated by the most perfectly complete and abiding *tathatā*, and because they are the vessel that supports the most pure and abiding *tathatā*, they are worthy of receiving the offerings, veneration, respect, and praise of all the world’s devas, humans, and asuras.”
“World-Honored One!

Because the *śarīra* of the Buddha has been perfumed and cultivated by the perfectly complete and stable abiding of the *dharmadhātu*, the *dharmatā*, the non-falsity, the non-alteration, the equality, the state beyond birth, the fixedness of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*), the stability of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the realm of empty space, and the inconceivable realm; and because it is the vessel that supports this perfectly pure and stable abiding from the *dharmadhātu* up to the inconceivable realm, it is worthy of receiving the offerings, reverence, respect, and praise of all the world’s devas, humans, and asuras.”
“World-Honored One!

Because the Buddha’s *śarīra* are thoroughly perfected through the cultivation of abiding in the Noble Truth of Suffering, and because they are the pure vessel for abiding in the Noble Truth of Suffering, they are worthy of receiving the offerings, veneration, respect, and praise of all the world, including its devas, humans, and asuras.”
“World-Honored One!

Because the *śarīra* of the Buddha has been perfumed and cultivated by the perfectly complete and stable abiding in the Noble Truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path; and because it is the vessel that supports the perfectly pure and stable abiding in the Noble Truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, it is worthy of receiving the offerings, veneration, respect, and praise of all the world, including its devas, humans, and asuras.”
“World-Honored One!

Because the Buddha’s *śarīra* has been perfumed and cultivated by the four dhyānas in their ultimate perfection, and because it is the vessel that supports the four dhyānas in their ultimate purity, it is worthy of receiving the offerings, veneration, respect, and praise of all the world’s devas, humans, and asuras.”
“World-Honored One!

Because the Buddha’s *śarīra* has been perfumed and cultivated by the most perfect four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) and the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), and because it is the vessel upon which the most pure four immeasurables and four formless attainments rely, it is worthy of receiving the offerings, reverence, respect, and praise of all the world’s devas, humans, and asuras.”
“World-Honored One!

Because the Buddha’s *śarīra* have been perfumed and cultivated by the most perfect eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*), and because they are the vessel that serves as the support for the most pure eight liberations, they are worthy of receiving the offerings, reverence, respect, and praise of all the worlds, including devas, humans, and asuras.”
“World-Honored One!

Because the Buddha’s *śarīra* has been perfumed and cultivated by the eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), the nine successive attainments (*anupūrvavihārasamāpatti*), and the ten totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*), and because it is the vessel that supports these most pure eight bases of mastery, nine successive attainments, and ten totalities, it is worthy of receiving the offerings, reverence, respect, and praise of all the world’s devas, humans, and asuras.”
“World-Honored One!

Because the Buddha’s *śarīra* has been thoroughly cultivated through the four foundations of mindfulness in their ultimate perfection, and because it is the vessel upon which the four foundations of mindfulness in their ultimate purity rely, it is worthy of receiving the offerings, veneration, respect, and praise of all the world’s devas, humans, and asuras.”
“World-Honored One!

Because the Buddha’s *śarīra* has been cultivated by the most perfect four right efforts, four bases of power, five faculties, five powers, seven factors of enlightenment, and eightfold noble path; and because it is the vessel that supports the most pure four right efforts, four bases of power, five faculties, five powers, seven factors of enlightenment, and eightfold noble path, it is worthy of receiving the offerings, reverence, respect, and praise of all the world, including its gods, humans, and asuras.”
“World-Honored One!

Because the relics of the Buddha have been cultivated through the gate of liberation of ultimate, perfect emptiness, and because they are the vessel that serves as the support for the gate of liberation of ultimate purity, they are worthy of receiving the offerings, reverence, respect, and praise of all the world’s devas, humans, and asuras.”
“World-Honored One!

Because the Buddha’s *śarīra* have been perfumed and cultivated by the gateways of liberation that are utterly perfect, signless, and wishless; and because they are the vessel upon which these utterly pure, signless, and wishless gateways of liberation rely, they are worthy of receiving the offerings, reverence, respect, and praise of all the world’s devas, humans, and asuras.”
“World-Honored One!

Because the Buddha’s *śarīra* have been perfumed and cultivated by the most perfect five eyes, and because they are the vessel upon which the most pure five eyes rely, they are worthy of receiving the offerings, reverence, respect, and praise of all the world’s devas, humans, and asuras.”
“World-Honored One!

Because the Buddha’s *śarīra* has been perfumed and cultivated by the most perfect six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍ-abhijñā*), and because it is the vessel that supports the most pure six supernormal powers, it is worthy of receiving the offerings, reverence, respect, and praise of all the world, including devas, humans, and asuras.”
“World-Honored One!

Because the Buddha’s relics have been perfumed and cultivated by the most perfect ten powers of a Buddha, and because they are the vessel that supports the most pure ten powers of a Buddha, they are worthy of receiving the offerings, reverence, respect, and praise of all the world’s devas, humans, asuras, and others.”
“World-Honored One!

Because the relics of the Buddha have been perfumed and cultivated by the four perfect fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; and because they are the vessel that supports these most pure four fearlessnesses, four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, they are worthy of receiving the offerings, veneration, respect, and praise of all the worlds, including devas, humans, and asuras.”
“World-Honored One!

Because the Buddha’s *śarīra* have been perfumed and cultivated by all most perfect *dhāraṇī* gates, and because they are the vessel that serves as the support for all most pure *dhāraṇī* gates, they are worthy of receiving the offerings, reverence, respect, and praise of all the world’s devas, humans, and asuras.”
“World-Honored One!

Because the Buddha’s *śarīra* has been perfumed and cultivated by all perfectly complete gateways of *samādhi*, and because it is the vessel that supports all perfectly pure gateways of *samādhi*, it is worthy of receiving the offerings, reverence, respect, and praise of all the world’s devas, humans, and asuras.”
“World-Honored One!

Because the Buddha’s *śarīra* is permeated by the cultivation of the most perfect omniscience, and because it is the vessel that supports the most pure omniscience, it is worthy of receiving the offerings, veneration, respect, and praise of all the world’s devas, humans, and asuras.”
“World-Honored One!

Because the Buddha’s *śarīra* has been perfumed and cultivated by the most perfect knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), and because it is the vessel that serves as the support for the most pure knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects, it is worthy of receiving the offerings, respect, veneration, and praise of all the world, including its gods, humans, and asuras.”
“World-Honored One!

Because the Buddha’s *śarīra* has been cultivated by the most perfect and non-forgetful Dharma, and because it is the vessel that supports the most pure and non-forgetful Dharma, it is worthy of receiving the offerings, veneration, respect, and praise of all the world, including devas, humans, and asuras.”
“World-Honored One!

Because the Buddha’s *śarīra* has been cultivated by the most perfect and constant state of equanimity (*upekṣā*), and because it is the vessel that supports this most pure and constant state of equanimity, it is worthy of receiving the offerings, reverence, respect, and praise of all the world—including its devas, humans, and asuras.”
“World-Honored One!

Because the Buddha’s *śarīra* has been cultivated through the complete perfection and eternal severance of all habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the afflictions within the continuum, and because it is the vessel that serves as the basis for the complete purity and eternal severance of all habitual tendencies of the afflictions within the continuum, it is worthy of receiving the offerings, veneration, respect, and praise of all the worlds, including devas, humans, and asuras.”
“World-Honored One!

Because the *śarīra* of the Buddha has been perfumed and cultivated by the *pāramitās* of the most perfect jewels of merit, and because it is the vessel that supports the *pāramitās* of the most pure jewels of merit, it is worthy of receiving the offerings, veneration, respect, and praise of all the worlds, including devas, humans, and asuras.”
“World-Honored One!

Because the relics of the Buddha have been perfumed and cultivated by the most perfect, unstained, and non-purifying *pāramitās*, and because they are the vessel that supports the most pure, unstained, and non-purifying *pāramitās*, they are worthy of receiving the offerings, respect, veneration, and praise of all the worlds, including devas, humans, and asuras.”
“World-Honored One!

Because the Buddha’s *śarīra* has been perfumed and cultivated by the most perfect *pāramitā* of non-arising and non-ceasing, and because it is the vessel that supports the most pure *pāramitā* of non-arising and non-ceasing, it is worthy of receiving the offerings, reverence, respect, and praise of all the worlds, including devas, humans, and asuras.”
“World-Honored One!

Because the relics of the Buddha have been perfumed and cultivated by the most perfect *pāramitā* of neither-entering-nor-exiting, and because they are the vessel that supports the most pure *pāramitā* of neither-entering-nor-exiting, they are worthy of receiving the offerings, veneration, respect, and praise of all the world’s devas, humans, asuras, and others.”
“World-Honored One!

Because the Buddha’s *śarīra* has been perfumed and cultivated by the most perfect *pāramitās*, which neither increase nor decrease; and because it is the vessel that supports the most pure *pāramitās*, which neither increase nor decrease, it is worthy of receiving the offerings, reverence, respect, and praise of all the world’s devas, humans, and asuras.”
“World-Honored One!

Because the relics of the Buddha have been perfumed and cultivated by the most perfect *pāramitā* of neither coming nor going, and because they are the vessel that supports the most pure *pāramitā* of neither coming nor going, they are worthy of receiving the offerings, reverence, respect, and praise of all the world’s devas, humans, and asuras.”
“World-Honored One!

Because the Buddha’s *śarīra* has been perfumed and cultivated by the most perfect, unshakable, and unceasing *pāramitā*, and because it is the vessel that relies upon the most pure, unshakable, and unceasing *pāramitā*, it is worthy of receiving the offerings, reverence, respect, and praise of all the world’s devas, humans, and asuras.”
“World-Honored One!

Because the *śarīra* of the Buddha has been cultivated by the most perfect *pāramitās* that are free from ‘this’ and ‘that,’ and because it is the vessel that relies upon the most pure *pāramitās* that are free from ‘this’ and ‘that,’ it is worthy of receiving the offerings, veneration, respect, and praise of all the worlds, including devas, humans, and asuras.”
“World-Honored One!

Because the Buddha’s śarīra has been perfumed and cultivated by the perfection of the ultimate reality-nature of all phenomena, and because it is the vessel that supports the perfection of the utterly pure reality-nature of all phenomena, it is worthy of receiving the offerings, veneration, respect, and praise of all the world’s devas, humans, and asuras.”
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!
Setting aside the Buddha-relics that would fill a trichiliocosm,

suppose there were one portion consisting of the Buddha-relics filling as many Buddha-worlds in each of the ten directions as there are sands in the Ganges River, and another portion consisting of this profound *prajñāpāramitā* written down— of these two portions, my intention would rather be to take this *prajñāpāramitā*.

Why is this? It is because all the *śarīras* of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are born from this very profound *prajñāpāramitā*; it is because all the *śarīras* of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are perfumed and cultivated by this very profound *prajñāpāramitā*; and it is because all the *śarīras* of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas serve as the vessel that supports this very profound *prajñāpāramitā*, such that they are worthy of receiving the offerings, veneration, respect, and praise of all devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans.
“World-Honored One!

If good men and good women make offerings to, revere, respect, and praise the *śarīra* of the Buddha, these good men and good women, by virtue of this root of goodness, will experience noble and wealthy happiness among humans and devas—namely, within the great clans of Kṣatriyas, the great clans of Brāhmaṇas, the great clans of householders, and the great clans of laymen; or within the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven. By means of such preeminent roots of goodness, they shall reach the end of suffering in their final body.”
“World-Honored One!

If good sons and good daughters wholeheartedly hear, receive and uphold, read and recite, copy, explain, and contemplate according to principle this Prajñāpāramitā, by means of this Prajñāpāramitā it shall become perfected.”
Because the perfection of wisdom is thus brought to fulfillment, it further causes the perfection of meditative concentration to be brought to fulfillment.
Because the perfection of meditative concentration is thus brought to fulfillment, it further causes the perfection of diligence to be brought to fulfillment.
Because the perfection of diligence is thus brought to fulfillment, it further causes the perfection of patience to be fulfilled.
Because the perfection of patience is thus brought to fulfillment, it further causes the perfection of ethical discipline to be fulfilled.
Because the perfection of pure ethical discipline is thus brought to fulfillment, it further causes the perfection of generosity to be brought to fulfillment.
"World-Honored One!"

By this, they are further caused to abide in and bring to fulfillment inner emptiness, outer emptiness, inner-and-outer emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-altering emptiness, essential emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common-characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature.
“World-Honored One!

By this, one further causes them to abide securely in suchness, the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, non-falsity, non-alteration, equality, the state beyond birth, the fixed nature of dharmas, the stability of dharmas, the limit of reality, the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm, thereby attaining fulfillment.”
“World-Honored One!

By means of this, one further causes [beings] to dwell securely in the Noble Truth of Suffering, the Noble Truth of the Origin, the Noble Truth of Cessation, and the Noble Truth of the Path, thereby attaining fulfillment.”
“World-Honored One!
By means of this, one further causes the cultivation of the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments to reach fulfillment.
World-Honored One!”
By means of this, they further cause the cultivation of the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities to reach fulfillment.
"World-Honored One!"

By means of this, one further causes the cultivation of the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right endeavors, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path to reach fulfillment.
“World-Honored One!
By this, one further causes the cultivation of the gate of liberation of emptiness, the gate of liberation of signlessness, and the gate of liberation of wishlessness to reach fulfillment.”
“World-Honored One!
By this, one further causes the cultivation of the five eyes and the six supernormal powers to reach fulfillment.
World-Honored One!”

By means of this, they further cause the cultivation of the Buddha's ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, so that these may be brought to perfection.
“World-Honored One!

By means of this, one further causes the cultivation of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) to reach fulfillment.
World-Honored One!”
By this, they further cause the cultivation of the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant equanimity to reach fulfillment.
"World-Honored One!
By this, they further cause the cultivation of all dharani-doors and all samadhi-doors to reach fulfillment."
“World-Honored One!
By means of this, one further transcends the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and realizes entry into the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and freedom from outflows (*samyaktva-niyāma*).

Having attained entry into the stage of the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and freedom from outflows, one further attains the bodhisattva’s supreme and wondrous supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). Riding upon these supernormal powers, one travels through various buddha-fields, going from one buddha-land to another buddha-land, making offerings, paying respect, honoring, and praising the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, while listening to the True Dharma and purifying the buddha-fields.”

In order to bring all sentient beings to maturity, they give rise to sublime thoughts and vows to assume various bodies—whether as great universal monarchs, minor universal monarchs, great kings, or minor kings; whether born into the great kṣatriya clans, the great brahmin clans, the great householder clans, or the great merchant clans; or whether becoming Śakra, Lord of Devas, Mahābrahmā, Vaiśravaṇa, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, or others. Appearing in whatever form is appropriate, they bring benefit to others, gradually proceeding until they realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"Therefore, World-Honored One!

It is not that I lack faith and acceptance toward the *śarīra* relics of the Buddhas, nor do I fail to delight in making offerings to, revering, honoring, and praising them. However, regarding the merit obtained from making offerings to, revering, honoring, and praising this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, it is far greater than that. For this reason, my mind would rather take up such *prajñāpāramitā*."
“World-Honored One!

If good sons and good daughters offer worship, respect, honor, and praise to this *prajñāpāramitā*, they thereby increase all Buddha-dharmas and also embrace all worldly and world-transcending wealth, nobility, peace, happiness, and mastery; thus, they have already offered worship, respect, honor, and praise to the *śarīra* of the Buddha.”

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 128. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Part One: Chapter on Measuring Merit, Number Thirty, Section Twenty-Seven. "Furthermore, World-Honored One!"

If good sons or good daughters wish to constantly behold all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas throughout the countless and boundless worlds of the ten directions as they currently proclaim the sublime Dharma—specifically their Dharma-body, form-body, and wisdom-body—they should offer worship, honor, respect, and praise to this profound Prajñāpāramitā; they should listen to it with a sincere mind, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, diligently practice and study it, contemplate it according to the principle, and extensively explain and disseminate it for the sake of sentient beings.
“World-Honored One!

If good sons and good daughters wish to constantly behold the dharma-body, form-body, wisdom-body, and so forth of the present Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha within this buddha-field, they should offer worship, respect, reverence, and praise to this profound Prajñāpāramitā; they should listen with a sincere mind, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, diligently practice and study it, contemplate it according to principle, and extensively proclaim and disseminate it for the sake of sentient beings.”
“World-Honored One!

If good sons and good daughters wish to constantly behold the Dharma-body, form-body, wisdom-body, and so forth of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time, they should offer worship, respect, reverence, and praise to this profound Prajñāpāramitā; they should listen with a sincere heart, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, diligently practice and study it, contemplate it according to principle, and extensively proclaim and disseminate it for the sake of sentient beings.”

“Bhagavān! If sons or daughters of good family practice the perfection of wisdom, they should cultivate the recollection of the Buddha toward all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas by means of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).”
“World-Honored One!
The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is twofold:
first, the conditioned (saṃskṛta); second, the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).”
What is called the nature of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*)?
It refers to knowing, as it truly is, the cognition of a self, the cognition of a sentient being, the cognition of a life-principle, the cognition of a living being,
the cognition of a nourisher, the cognition of a person, the cognition of an individual (*pudgala*), the cognition of a mind-born being, and the cognition of a youth.
the knowledge of the agent, the knowledge of the experiencer, the knowledge of the knower, and the knowledge of the seer;
the knowledge of form, the knowledge of feeling, the knowledge of perception, the knowledge of formations, and the knowledge of consciousness;

the knowledge of the eye-base, the knowledge of the ear-base, the knowledge of the nose-base, the knowledge of the tongue-base, the knowledge of the body-base, and the knowledge of the mind-base; or the knowledge of forms...

Knowledge of the sense-base of form, knowledge of the sense-base of sound, knowledge of the sense-base of odor, knowledge of the sense-base of taste, knowledge of the sense-base of tangibles, and knowledge of the sense-base of mental phenomena;

or knowledge of the eye-element, knowledge of the form-element, knowledge of the eye-consciousness-element, knowledge of eye-contact, and knowledge of the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition; or knowledge of the ear-element, knowledge of the sound-element...
Knowledge of the ear-consciousness element, knowledge of ear-contact, and knowledge of all feelings produced with ear-contact as condition;

or knowledge of the nose element, knowledge of the odor element, knowledge of the nose-consciousness element, knowledge of nose-contact, and knowledge of all feelings produced with nose-contact as condition;
or knowledge of the tongue element, knowledge of the taste element, and knowledge of the tongue-consciousness element.
knowledge of tongue-contact, knowledge of the various feelings produced with tongue-contact as condition;

knowledge of the body-element, knowledge of the contact-element, knowledge of the body-consciousness-element, knowledge of body-contact, and knowledge of the various feelings produced with body-contact as condition;
and knowledge of the mind-element, knowledge of the mental-object-element, knowledge of the mind-consciousness-element, and knowledge of mind-contact.
knowledge of the various feelings born with mental contact as condition;
knowledge of the earth element, water element, fire element, wind element, space element, and consciousness element;
and knowledge of ignorance, formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling.
...the knowledge of craving, the knowledge of grasping, the knowledge of existence, the knowledge of birth, and the knowledge of old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair;
as well as the knowledge of the perfection of generosity, the knowledge of the perfection of ethical discipline,
the knowledge of the perfection of patience, the knowledge of the perfection of diligence, and the knowledge of the perfection of meditative concentration.
Abundant wisdom, the wisdom of the perfection of prajñā, the wisdom of internal emptiness, the wisdom of external emptiness,
the wisdom of internal and external emptiness, the wisdom of the emptiness of emptiness, the wisdom of great emptiness, the wisdom of ultimate emptiness,
the wisdom of conditioned emptiness, the wisdom of unconditioned emptiness, the wisdom of absolute emptiness, the wisdom of boundless emptiness, and the wisdom of dispersed emptiness.

The knowledge of wisdom, the knowledge of the emptiness of non-alteration, the knowledge of the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the knowledge of the emptiness of specific characteristics, the knowledge of the emptiness of common characteristics,

the knowledge of the emptiness of all phenomena, the knowledge of the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the knowledge of the emptiness of non-existence, the knowledge of the emptiness of intrinsic nature,
the knowledge of the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, as well as the knowledge of suchness and the knowledge of the dharma-realm.
...the knowledge of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-jñāna*), the knowledge of non-falsity, the knowledge of non-alteration, the knowledge of equality,
the knowledge of being free from birth, the knowledge of the fixed nature of phenomena, the knowledge of the stability of phenomena, the knowledge of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi-jñāna*),

the knowledge of the realm of space, the knowledge of the inconceivable realm; as well as the knowledge of the noble truth of suffering and the knowledge of the noble truth of the origin [of suffering].

the knowledge of the noble truth of cessation, the knowledge of the noble truth of the path; the knowledge of the four dhyānas, the knowledge of the four immeasurables, the knowledge of the four formless attainments;
the knowledge of the eight liberations, the knowledge of the eight bases of mastery, the knowledge of the nine successive attainments, the knowledge of the ten totalities;
and the knowledge of the four foundations of mindfulness, the knowledge of the four right efforts.

the knowledge of the four bases of psychic power, the knowledge of the five faculties, the knowledge of the five powers, the knowledge of the seven factors of enlightenment, and the knowledge of the eight branches of the noble path;
the knowledge of the gate of liberation of emptiness, the knowledge of the gate of liberation of signlessness, and the knowledge of the gate of liberation of wishlessness;
the knowledge of the five eyes, the knowledge of the six supernormal powers, and the ten [powers] of a Buddha...
The knowledge of the powers; the knowledge of the four fearlessnesses; the knowledge of the four analytical knowledges; the knowledge of great loving-kindness; the knowledge of great compassion;
the knowledge of great sympathetic joy; the knowledge of great equanimity; the knowledge of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
the knowledge of the state of non-forgetfulness; the knowledge of the constant abiding in equanimity; the knowledge of all-knowledge; and the knowledge of the aspects of the path.
The knowledge of knowledge, the knowledge of all-aspect omniscience; if it be the knowledge of all dhāraṇī-doors, the knowledge of all samādhi-doors;
if it be the knowledge of stream-entry, the knowledge of once-returning, the knowledge of non-returning, the knowledge of arhatship;
or the knowledge of the path of stream-entry and the fruit of stream-entry, the knowledge of the path of once-returning and the fruit of once-returning.

...the knowledge of the candidate for the fruit of non-returning and the knowledge of the fruit of non-returning; the knowledge of the candidate for arhatship and the knowledge of the fruit of arhatship;
the knowledge of a pratyekabuddha and the knowledge of pratyekabuddha-enlightenment; the knowledge of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva and the knowledge of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s practice;
the knowledge of a samyaksaṃbuddha and the knowledge of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi)...
The wisdom of the three types of enlightenment; the wisdom of wholesome phenomena, the wisdom of unwholesome phenomena, and the wisdom of indeterminate phenomena;
the wisdom of past phenomena, the wisdom of future phenomena, and the wisdom of present phenomena;

the wisdom of phenomena associated with the desire realm, the wisdom of phenomena associated with the form realm, and the wisdom of phenomena associated with the formless realm; and the wisdom of the phenomena of those in training (*śaikṣa*).
...the knowledge of dharmas of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-dharmajñāna*), the knowledge of dharmas that are neither of training nor beyond training (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa-dharmajñāna*);

if it is the knowledge of dharmas to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya-dharmajñāna*), the knowledge of dharmas to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya-dharmajñāna*), or the knowledge of dharmas not to be abandoned (*aheya-dharmajñāna*); if it is the knowledge of dharmas with form (*rūpin-dharmajñāna*) or the knowledge of dharmas without form (*arūpin-dharmajñāna*);

if it is the knowledge of dharmas with visibility (*sanidarśana-dharmajñāna*) or the knowledge of dharmas without visibility (*anidarśana-dharmajñāna*); or the knowledge of dharmas with resistance (*sapratigha-dharmajñāna*).
...the knowledge of phenomena without counterpart; whether it be the knowledge of phenomena that is with outflows or the knowledge of phenomena that is without outflows;

whether it be the knowledge of phenomena that is conditioned or the knowledge of phenomena that is unconditioned; whether it be the knowledge of phenomena that is faulty or the knowledge of phenomena that is faultless;

whether it be the knowledge of phenomena that is mundane or the knowledge of phenomena that is supramundane; or the knowledge of phenomena that is defiled or the knowledge of phenomena that is purified.
Wisdom—such immeasurable gateways of wisdom as these—are all termed the nature of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
"What is termed the nature of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*)?"

That is to say, all phenomena are without arising and without cessation, without abiding and without change, without defilement and without purity, without increase and without decrease, and without marks, unconditioned, and devoid of intrinsic nature.
What is called the self-nature of non-existence?

It refers to the absence of a self-nature, the absence of a sentient-being nature, the absence of a life-principle nature, the absence of a living-being nature, the absence of a nourisher nature, the absence of a person nature, the absence of a *pudgala* nature, the absence of a mind-born nature, the absence of a youth nature, the absence of an agent nature, the absence of an experiencer nature, the absence of a knower nature, and the absence of a seer nature;
it is the absence of a form-nature, and the absence of a feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness-nature.
If there is no nature of the eye-base, there is no nature of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-base;
if there is no nature of the form-base, there is no nature of the sound, odor, taste, tangible-object, or mental-object-base;

if there is no nature of the eye-element, there is no nature of the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, nor the nature of eye-contact, nor the nature of the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition.

If the nature of the ear element does not exist, there will be no nature of the sound element, the ear-consciousness element, ear-contact, nor the various feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition;

if the nature of the nose element does not exist, there will be no nature of the odor element, the nose-consciousness element, nose-contact, nor the various feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition;

if the nature of the tongue element does not exist, there will be no nature of the taste element, the tongue-consciousness element, tongue-contact, nor the various feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition.
If there is no nature of the body-element, there is no nature of the touch-element, the body-consciousness-element, body-contact, or the various feelings produced with body-contact as a condition;

if there is no nature of the mind-element, there is no nature of the phenomena-element, the mind-consciousness-element, mind-contact, or the various feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition;
if there is no nature of the earth-element, there is no nature of the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness-elements.

If the nature of ignorance does not exist, there is no nature of volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair;
if the nature of the perfection of generosity does not exist, there is no nature of the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, or wisdom.

If there were no emptiness of the internal, nor emptiness of the external, emptiness of both internal and external, emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, emptiness of the ultimate, emptiness of the conditioned, emptiness of the unconditioned, absolute emptiness, emptiness of the limitless, emptiness of dispersion, emptiness of non-alteration, emptiness of essential nature, emptiness of self-characteristic, emptiness of common characteristic, emptiness of all dharmas, emptiness of the unapprehendable, emptiness of non-existence, emptiness of intrinsic nature, and emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence;

and if there were no suchness, nor the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the non-falsity, the non-alteration, the sameness, the state beyond birth, the fixedness of phenomena, the stability of phenomena, the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm; [then these would not exist].
If there were no nature of the noble truth of suffering, there would be no nature of the noble truths of origination, cessation, and the path;
if there were no nature of the four dhyānas, there would be no nature of the four immeasurables or the four formless attainments;
if there were no nature of the eight liberations, there would be no nature of the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative concentrations, or the ten totalities.

If the nature of the four foundations of mindfulness does not exist, then the nature of the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path does not exist;
if the nature of the gate of liberation of emptiness does not exist, then the nature of the gate of liberation of signlessness and the gate of liberation of wishlessness do not exist;
if the nature of the five eyes does not exist, then the nature of the six supernormal powers does not exist.

If there were no nature of the ten powers of a Buddha, no nature of the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
if there were no nature of the quality of non-forgetfulness, no nature of the quality of constant abiding in equanimity;
and if there were no nature of all-knowledge, no nature of the knowledge of the paths, and no nature of the knowledge of all aspects; [then...]
If there is no nature of all dhāraṇī-doors, there is no nature of all samādhi-doors;
if there is no nature of the stream-enterer, there is no nature of the once-returner, the non-returner, or the arhat;

if there is no nature of the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry or the fruit of stream-entry itself, there is no nature of the candidate for the fruit of once-returning or the fruit of once-returning, the candidate for the fruit of non-returning or the fruit of non-returning, or the candidate for the fruit of arhatship or the fruit of arhatship.
If there is no nature of a pratyekabuddha, there is no nature of pratyekabuddha-enlightenment;
if there is no nature of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, there is no nature of the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s practice;
if there is no nature of a samyaksaṃbuddha, there is no nature of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
If there is no nature of wholesome dharmas, there is no nature of unwholesome or indeterminate dharmas;
if there is no nature of past dharmas, there is no nature of future or present dharmas;
if there is no nature of dharmas bound to the desire realm, there is no nature of dharmas bound to the form realm or the formless realm.
If there is no nature of dharmas that are beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), there is no nature of dharmas that are either in training or beyond training (*śaikṣāśaikṣa*);
if there is no nature of dharmas to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*), there is no nature of dharmas to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*) or not to be abandoned;
if there is no nature of dharmas with form (*rūpin*), there is no nature of dharmas without form (*arūpin*).
If there is no nature of phenomena with visibility, there is no nature of phenomena without visibility;
if there is no nature of phenomena with resistance, there is no nature of phenomena without resistance;
if there is no nature of phenomena that are outflowing, there is no nature of phenomena that are non-outflowing.
If there is no nature of conditioned phenomena, there is no nature of unconditioned phenomena;
if there is no nature of blameworthy phenomena, there is no nature of blameless phenomena;
if there is no nature of mundane phenomena, there is no nature of supramundane phenomena.

If there is no nature of defiled phenomena, no nature of purified phenomena, and no such natures of immeasurable categories—being empty, non-existent, signless, featureless, ineffable, unspeakable, unawakened, and unknowable—this is called the self-nature of non-existence (*abhāva-svabhāva*).
"In this way, all these dharmas, being without intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), are all termed the unconditioned nature of phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharmatā*).
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śakra, Lord of the Devas, saying: "So it is!"
So it is! It is just as you have said, Kauśika!
All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past have realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of this very profound perfection of wisdom;
all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the future shall realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of this very profound perfection of wisdom;

and all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas currently existing in the infinite, countless, and boundless worlds of the ten directions are presently realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of this very profound perfection of wisdom.

Kauśika! The śrāvaka disciples of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past also, by means of this very profound Prajñāpāramitā, have already attained the fruit of srotāpanna, and have already attained the fruits of sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, and arhat;

the śrāvaka disciples of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the future will also, by means of this very profound Prajñāpāramitā, attain the fruit of srotāpanna, and will attain the fruits of sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, and arhat.

In the present, throughout the immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless worlds of the ten directions, all the Śrāvaka disciples of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas likewise, by means of this very profound Prajñāpāramitā, have now attained the fruit of Stream-entry, and have now attained the fruits of Once-returner, Non-returner, and Arhatship.
Kauśika! The pratyekabuddhas of the past also realized the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha by means of this very profound perfection of wisdom;
the pratyekabuddhas of the future shall also realize the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha by means of this very profound perfection of wisdom.
Present Pratyekabuddhas, too, have realized the enlightenment of a Pratyekabuddha by means of this very profound Prajñāpāramitā.
Why is that, Kauśika?
Thus, within this secret treasury of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, the teachings corresponding to the three vehicles are extensively expounded.

However, these teachings take non-apprehension as their means; they take the absence of intrinsic nature and the absence of marks as their means; they take non-arising and non-ceasing as their means; they take non-defilement and non-purity as their means; they take non-creation and non-action as their means; they take non-entry and non-exit as their means; they take non-increase and non-decrease as their means; and they take non-grasping and non-rejection as their means. Such explanations are made from the perspective of conventional truth, not from the perspective of ultimate truth.
Why is this? Because this Prajñāpāramitā is neither Prajñāpāramitā nor non-Prajñāpāramitā;
it is not this shore, not the other shore, not the middle of the stream, and not dry land.
It is not water; it is neither high nor low; it is neither equal nor unequal; it is neither with marks nor without marks;
it is neither mundane nor supramundane; it is neither with outflows nor without outflows;
it is neither conditioned nor unconditioned; it is neither blameworthy nor blameless. It is not...
It is with form, not without form; it is neither visible nor invisible; it is neither resistant nor non-resistant;
it is neither wholesome nor unwholesome; it is neither determinate nor indeterminate;
it is neither past, nor future, nor present; it is neither bound to the desire realm nor bound to the form realm.
It is not bound to the formless realm; it is neither that of training, nor that of no-more-training, nor that which is neither training nor no-more-training;
it is not to be abandoned by vision, nor to be abandoned by cultivation, nor not to be abandoned; it is neither existent nor empty;
it is neither an object nor wisdom.

Kauśika! Thus, this prajñāpāramitā does not bestow the dharmas of the Buddhas, nor the dharmas of the bodhisattvas, nor the dharmas of the pratyekabuddhas, nor the dharmas of the stream-enterers, nor the dharmas of the once-returners, nor the dharmas of the non-returners, nor the dharmas of the arhats; it does not abandon the dharmas of ordinary beings.
Then, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā is the Great Pāramitā; it is the Unsurpassed Pāramitā; it is the Peerless Pāramitā.”

“Bhagavān! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices this profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), although they know the distinctions among the mental activities and spheres of all sentient beings, they do not apprehend a self; they do not apprehend a sentient being, a life-principle, a soul, a nourisher, a person, a human being, a spirit, a youth, an agent, an experiencer, a knower, or a viewer.”
"This bodhisattva mahāsattva also does not apprehend form; he does not apprehend feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness.
This bodhisattva mahāsattva also does not apprehend the eye base; he does not apprehend the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind bases."
"This bodhisattva mahāsattva also does not apprehend the sphere of form; he does not apprehend the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental phenomena.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva also does not apprehend the eye-element; he does not apprehend the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, nor eye-contact, nor the various sensations produced with eye-contact as their condition."

"This bodhisattva mahāsattva also does not apprehend the ear element; he does not apprehend the sound element, the ear-consciousness element, nor ear-contact, nor the various feelings produced with ear-contact as their condition."

"This bodhisattva mahāsattva likewise does not apprehend the nose element, nor does he apprehend the odor element, the nose-consciousness element, nose-contact, or the various feelings produced with nose-contact as their condition."

"This bodhisattva-mahāsattva likewise does not apprehend the tongue element, nor does he apprehend the taste element, the tongue-consciousness element, tongue-contact, or the various sensations produced with tongue-contact as a condition."

"This bodhisattva mahāsattva also does not apprehend the body-element (*kāyadhātu*), nor does he apprehend the touch-element (*spraṣṭavyadhātu*), the body-consciousness-element (*kāyavijñānadhātu*), as well as body-contact (*kāyasparśa*) and all feelings (*vedanā*) produced with body-contact as their condition."

“Furthermore, this bodhisattva mahāsattva does not apprehend the mind-element, nor does he apprehend the dharma-element, the mind-consciousness-element, mental contact, or the various feelings produced with mental contact as a condition.”
“This bodhisattva mahāsattva also does not apprehend the earth element; he does not apprehend the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva also does not apprehend ignorance; he does not apprehend volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.”

"This bodhisattva mahāsattva also does not apprehend the perfection of generosity, nor does he apprehend the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, or wisdom."

“Furthermore, this bodhisattva mahāsattva does not apprehend internal emptiness; nor does he apprehend external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, infinite emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common-characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, or the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.”

This bodhisattva mahāsattva likewise does not apprehend suchness; nor does he apprehend the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, the non-illusory nature, the unchanging nature, equality, the nature of being free from birth, the fixedness of dharmas, the stability of dharmas, the limit of reality, the realm of empty space, or the inconceivable realm.
“This bodhisattva mahāsattva also does not apprehend the noble truth of suffering, nor does he apprehend the noble truths of origination, cessation, or the path.
This bodhisattva mahāsattva also does not apprehend the four dhyānas, nor does he apprehend the four immeasurables or the four formless attainments.”
"This bodhisattva mahāsattva also does not apprehend the eight liberations; he does not apprehend the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, or the ten totalities.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva also does not apprehend the four applications of mindfulness; he does not apprehend the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the eightfold noble path."
"This bodhisattva mahāsattva also does not apprehend the gate of liberation of emptiness, nor does he apprehend the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness.
This bodhisattva mahāsattva also does not apprehend the five eyes, nor does he apprehend the six supernormal powers."

"This bodhisattva mahāsattva likewise does not apprehend the ten powers of a buddha, nor does he apprehend the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, or the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha."
"This bodhisattva mahāsattva also does not apprehend the quality of non-forgetfulness, nor does he apprehend the nature of constant equanimity.
This bodhisattva mahāsattva also does not apprehend all-knowledge, nor does he apprehend the knowledge of the aspects of the path, nor the knowledge of all aspects."
"This bodhisattva mahāsattva also does not apprehend any of the doors of dhāraṇī, nor does he apprehend any of the doors of samādhi.
This bodhisattva mahāsattva also does not apprehend the stage of a stream-enterer, nor does he apprehend the stages of a once-returner, a non-returner, or an arhat."

"This bodhisattva mahāsattva also does not attain the stage of entering the stream nor the fruit of stream-entry; he does not attain the stage of entering once-returning nor the fruit of once-returning, the stage of entering non-returning nor the fruit of non-returning, or the stage of entering arhatship nor the fruit of arhatship."
"This bodhisattva mahāsattva also does not apprehend a pratyekabuddha, nor does he apprehend pratyekabuddha-enlightenment.
This bodhisattva mahāsattva also does not apprehend a bodhisattva mahāsattva, nor does he apprehend the dharmas of a bodhisattva mahāsattva."
"This bodhisattva mahāsattva also does not apprehend samyaksaṃbuddhahood, nor does he apprehend the dharmas of a samyaksaṃbuddha. Why is this?
It is not because this *prajñāpāramitā* manifests through the apprehension of something that it exists.

Why is this? Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is entirely devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and cannot be apprehended; for the nature and characteristics of the grasper, the grasped, and their two bases are all empty and unapprehendable.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śakra, the Lord of Devas, saying: "So it is! So it is!"
It is as you have said. Why is this? Kausika!

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the profound Prajñāpāramitā for a long night by means of non-apprehension as their skillful method, they do not even apprehend "enlightenment" or "a sentient being," much less a "Bodhisattva Mahāsattva."
Since this bodhisattva-mahāsattva cannot be apprehended, how could the dharmas of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva be apprehended?
Since neither the bodhisattva nor the dharmas can be apprehended, how much less can the Buddhas and the dharmas of the Buddhas be apprehended!
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, again addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One,
does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice only the perfection of wisdom, or does he also practice the other five perfections?”
The Buddha said,
“Kauśika! A bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the six perfections by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method.”
When practicing generosity, one does not apprehend the giver, the recipient, or the gift and the object given;
when practicing pure ethical discipline, one does not apprehend pure ethical discipline, unwholesome discipline, or the one who maintains pure ethical discipline;
when practicing patience, one does not apprehend patience, anger, or the one who practices patience.
When practicing diligence, one does not apprehend diligence, nor does one apprehend laziness, nor does one apprehend the one who practices diligence;
when practicing meditative concentration, one does not apprehend concentration, nor does one apprehend distraction, nor does one apprehend the one who practices concentration;
when practicing wisdom, one does not apprehend wisdom, nor does one apprehend poor wisdom, nor does one apprehend the one who practices wisdom.
"Furthermore, Kauśika,
the profound *prajñāpāramitā* of the bodhisattva mahāsattva serves as their honor and guide, causing them to cultivate all the *pāramitās* so that they may be swiftly brought to fulfillment."

"When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices giving, the profound perfection of wisdom serves as their honor and guide; thus, the perfection of giving they cultivate is free from attachment and is swiftly brought to fulfillment."

"When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices pure ethical discipline, the profound perfection of wisdom serves as its sovereign and guide; thus, the perfection of ethical discipline they cultivate becomes free from attachment and is swiftly brought to fulfillment."

"When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices patience, the profound perfection of wisdom serves as their sovereign and guide; thus, the perfection of patience they cultivate is free from attachment and is swiftly brought to fulfillment."

"When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices diligence, the profound perfection of wisdom serves as their honor and guide; thus, the perfection of diligence they cultivate is free from attachment and is swiftly brought to fulfillment."

"When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices dhyāna, the profound perfection of wisdom serves as their sovereign and guide; thus, the perfection of dhyāna they cultivate is free from attachment and is swiftly brought to fulfillment."

"When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices prajñā, the profound perfection of wisdom serves as their honor and guide; thus, the perfection of wisdom they cultivate is free from attachment and is swiftly brought to fulfillment."
"Furthermore, Kauśika,
this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom by means of non-apprehension regarding all forms;
he practices the perfection of wisdom by means of non-apprehension regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness."
By means of these causes and conditions, one is free from attachment, causing that which is cultivated to be swiftly brought to fulfillment.
"This bodhisattva mahāsattva, regarding the sense base of the eye, practices the perfection of wisdom by means of non-apprehension;
regarding the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, they practice the perfection of wisdom by means of non-apprehension."
By means of these causes and conditions, one remains without attachment, causing what has been cultivated to be swiftly brought to full completion.
"This bodhisattva mahāsattva, regarding the sphere of form, practices the perfection of wisdom by means of non-apprehension;
regarding the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena, they practice the perfection of wisdom by means of non-apprehension."
By means of these causes and conditions, one becomes free from attachment, causing what has been cultivated to be swiftly brought to fulfillment.
"This bodhisattva mahāsattva, by employing the method of non-apprehension, cultivates the perfection of wisdom with respect to the eye-element;

by employing the method of non-apprehension, they cultivate the perfection of wisdom with respect to the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, eye-contact, and all sensations produced with eye-contact as a condition."
By means of these causes and conditions, one remains free from attachment, causing that which is cultivated to be swiftly brought to fulfillment.
"This Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, regarding the sphere of the ear (*śrotradhātu*), practices the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) by way of non-apprehension;

regarding the sphere of sounds (*śabdadhātu*), the sphere of ear-consciousness (*śrotravijñānadhātu*), as well as ear-contact (*śrotrasaṃsparśa*) and the various feelings (*vedanā*) produced with ear-contact as a condition, he practices the perfection of wisdom by way of non-apprehension."
By means of these causes and conditions, one becomes free from attachment, causing that which is cultivated to be swiftly brought to fulfillment.
"This bodhisattva mahāsattva, regarding the nose element (*ghrāṇadhātu*), practices the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) by way of non-apprehension;

regarding the odor element (*gandhadhātu*), the nose-consciousness element (*ghrāṇavijñānadhātu*), as well as nose-contact (*ghrāṇasamsparśa*) and the various feelings (*vedanā*) produced with nose-contact as a condition, they practice the perfection of wisdom by way of non-apprehension."
By means of these causes and conditions, one is free from attachment, causing that which is practiced to be swiftly brought to fulfillment.
"This bodhisattva mahāsattva, regarding the tongue element (*jihvā-dhātu*), practices the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) by way of non-apprehension;

regarding the taste element (*rasa-dhātu*), the tongue-consciousness element (*jihvā-vijñāna-dhātu*), as well as tongue-contact (*jihvā-saṃsparśa*) and the various feelings (*vedanā*) arising with tongue-contact as a condition, they practice the perfection of wisdom by way of non-apprehension."
By means of these causes and conditions, one is free from attachment, causing that which is cultivated to be swiftly brought to fulfillment.
"This bodhisattva mahāsattva, regarding the body-element (*kāyadhātu*), practices the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) by means of non-apprehension;

regarding the contact-element (*spraṣṭavyadhātu*), the body-consciousness-element (*kāyavijñānadhātu*), as well as body-contact (*kāyasparśa*) and the various feelings (*vedanā*) arising with body-contact as a condition, they practice the perfection of wisdom by means of non-apprehension."
By means of these causes and conditions, one is free from attachment, causing that which is cultivated to be swiftly brought to fulfillment.
"This bodhisattva mahāsattva, regarding the mind-element (*manodhātu*), practices the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) by way of non-apprehension;

regarding the dharma-element, the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*), as well as mental contact (*manaḥsaṃsparśa*) and the various feelings (*vedanā*) arising with mental contact as a condition, they practice the perfection of wisdom by way of non-apprehension."
By means of these causes and conditions, one remains without attachment, causing that which is cultivated to be swiftly brought to fulfillment.
"This bodhisattva mahāsattva, regarding the earth element, practices the perfection of wisdom by means of non-apprehension;
regarding the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements, they practice the perfection of wisdom by means of non-apprehension."
By means of these causes and conditions, one remains without attachment, causing that which is cultivated to be swiftly brought to fulfillment.
"This bodhisattva mahāsattva, regarding ignorance, cultivates the perfection of wisdom by way of non-apprehension;

regarding volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair, they cultivate the perfection of wisdom by way of non-apprehension."
By means of these causes and conditions, one is free from attachment, causing that which is cultivated to be swiftly brought to fulfillment.
"This bodhisattva mahāsattva, regarding internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*), cultivates the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method;

regarding external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, unchanging emptiness, essential emptiness, emptiness of own-marks, common emptiness, emptiness of all phenomena, emptiness of non-apprehensibility, emptiness of non-existence, emptiness of intrinsic nature, and emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, he cultivates the perfection of wisdom by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method."
By virtue of these causes and conditions, one is free from attachment, causing what has been cultivated to be swiftly brought to fulfillment.
"This bodhisattva mahāsattva, by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method, cultivates the perfection of wisdom regarding suchness;

by means of non-apprehension as the skillful method, they cultivate the perfection of wisdom regarding the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, the non-falsity, the unchanging nature, equality, the state beyond birth, the fixedness of dharmas, the stability of dharmas, the limit of reality, the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm."
By means of these causes and conditions, one becomes free from attachment, causing that which is cultivated to be swiftly brought to fulfillment.
"This bodhisattva mahāsattva, regarding the noble truth of suffering, practices the perfection of wisdom by means of non-apprehension;
regarding the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path, they practice the perfection of wisdom by means of non-apprehension."
By means of these causes and conditions, one is free from attachment, causing that which is cultivated to be swiftly brought to fulfillment.
"This bodhisattva mahāsattva, regarding the perfection of generosity, practices the perfection of wisdom by means of non-apprehension;
regarding the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, they practice the perfection of wisdom by means of non-apprehension."
By virtue of these causes and conditions, one remains without attachment, causing what is cultivated to be swiftly brought to fulfillment.
"This bodhisattva mahāsattva, by means of non-apprehension as the expedient, cultivates the perfection of wisdom within the four dhyānas;
by means of non-apprehension as the expedient, they cultivate the perfection of wisdom within the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions."
By means of these causes and conditions, one becomes free from attachment, causing that which is cultivated to be swiftly brought to fulfillment.
"This bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivates the perfection of wisdom by means of non-apprehension regarding the eight liberations;
they cultivate the perfection of wisdom by means of non-apprehension regarding the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities."
By means of these causes and conditions, one remains without attachment, causing that which is cultivated to be swiftly brought to fulfillment.
"This bodhisattva mahāsattva, by employing the method of non-apprehension, cultivates the perfection of wisdom regarding the four foundations of mindfulness;

and by employing the method of non-apprehension, they cultivate the perfection of wisdom regarding the four right endeavors, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path."
By means of these causes and conditions, one is free from attachment, causing what has been cultivated to be swiftly brought to full completion.
"This bodhisattva mahāsattva, regarding the gate of liberation of emptiness, cultivates the perfection of wisdom by taking non-apprehension as the skillful means;
regarding the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness, he cultivates the perfection of wisdom by taking non-apprehension as the skillful means."
By means of these causes and conditions, one becomes free from attachment, causing the practice one cultivates to be swiftly brought to fulfillment.
"This bodhisattva mahāsattva, by taking non-apprehension as the skillful means, cultivates the perfection of wisdom regarding the five eyes;
by taking non-apprehension as the skillful means, they cultivate the perfection of wisdom regarding the six supernormal powers."
By means of these causes and conditions, one is free from attachment, causing that which is cultivated to be swiftly brought to fulfillment.
"This bodhisattva mahāsattva, by employing the method of non-apprehension, cultivates the perfection of wisdom regarding the ten powers of a Buddha;

by employing the method of non-apprehension, they cultivate the perfection of wisdom regarding the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha."
By means of these causes and conditions, one is free from attachment, causing that which is cultivated to be swiftly brought to fulfillment.
"This bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivates the perfection of wisdom by means of non-apprehension regarding the quality of non-forgetfulness;
he cultivates the perfection of wisdom by means of non-apprehension regarding the nature of constant equanimity."
By means of these causes and conditions, one remains free from attachment, causing that which is cultivated to be swiftly brought to fulfillment.
"This bodhisattva mahāsattva, regarding all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), cultivates the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) by means of non-apprehension as the expedient;

regarding the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), they cultivate the perfection of wisdom by means of non-apprehension as the expedient."
By means of these causes and conditions, one becomes free from attachment, causing that which is practiced to be swiftly brought to fulfillment.
"This bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom by means of non-apprehension regarding all *dhāraṇī* gates;
they practice the perfection of wisdom by means of non-apprehension regarding all *samādhi* gates."
By means of these causes and conditions, one remains without attachment, causing that which is cultivated to be swiftly brought to fulfillment.
"This bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivates the perfection of wisdom by means of non-apprehension regarding the stream-enterer;
they cultivate the perfection of wisdom by means of non-apprehension regarding the once-returner, the non-returner, and the arhat."
By virtue of these causes and conditions, one is free from attachment, causing that which is cultivated to be swiftly brought to fulfillment.
"This bodhisattva mahāsattva, regarding the stage of entering the stream and the fruit of stream-entry, practices the perfection of wisdom by means of non-apprehension;

regarding the stage of entering once-returning and the fruit of once-returning, the stage of entering non-returning and the fruit of non-returning, and the stage of entering arhatship and the fruit of arhatship, they practice the perfection of wisdom by means of non-apprehension."
By means of these causes and conditions, one is free from attachment, causing that which is practiced to be swiftly brought to fulfillment.
"This bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom with the non-apprehension of anything as the skillful means toward the pratyekabuddha;
they practice the perfection of wisdom with the non-apprehension of anything as the skillful means toward the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha."
By means of these causes and conditions, one is free from attachment, causing that which is cultivated to be swiftly brought to fulfillment.
"This bodhisattva mahāsattva, regarding other bodhisattva mahāsattvas, practices the perfection of wisdom with non-apprehension as the expedient;
regarding the conduct of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, he practices the perfection of wisdom with non-apprehension as the expedient."
By means of these causes and conditions, one is free from attachment, causing that which is practiced to be swiftly brought to fulfillment.
"This bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom with non-apprehension as the skillful means toward samyaksaṃbuddha;
they practice the perfection of wisdom with non-apprehension as the skillful means toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
By means of these causes and conditions, one becomes free from attachment, causing that which is cultivated to be swiftly brought to fulfillment. "Kauśika!
Just as all the trees in Jambudvīpa—whether their branches, stems, flowers, leaves, or fruits differ in various shapes and colors—their shadows are entirely without distinction."

Thus, although the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration each differ from one another, because they are embraced by the perfection of wisdom, dedicated toward the knowledge of all modes, and employ the method of non-apprehension, they are likewise without distinction.
At that time, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā accomplishes such vast and sublime merit; such is the Prajñā...”
If the pāramitās accomplish all supreme qualities, so too does this prajñāpāramitā accomplish immeasurable supreme qualities;
so too does this prajñāpāramitā accomplish perfect supreme qualities; so too does this prajñāpāramitā accomplish the boundless.
Exalted virtues: thus the perfection of wisdom accomplishes peerless exalted virtues;
thus the perfection of wisdom accomplishes inexhaustible exalted virtues;
thus the perfection of wisdom accomplishes limitless exalted virtues; thus the perfection of wisdom...
If the pāramitās achieve peerless and supreme merit,
so too does this prajñāpāramitā achieve inconceivable and supreme merit;
so too does this prajñāpāramitā achieve ineffable and supreme merit.

“Bhagavān! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to write down this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, adorning it with various jewels, and were to honor, revere, respect, and praise it with all their possessions—offering immeasurable kinds of exquisite flower garlands, powdered and scattered incenses, robes, necklaces, precious banners, flags, canopies, various wonderful and rare objects, music, and lamps—and were to reflect upon it according to reason as taught in this sūtra.”
There may be sons or daughters of good family who write down this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, bestow it upon others so that they may uphold it, and cause it to be widely circulated.
"Between these two accumulations of merit,
which is greater? The Buddha said, "Kauśika!"
I shall question you further; answer as you see fit.

Suppose a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to receive from another the *śarīra* relics of a Buddha, place them in a precious casket, and set them in a high and exalted location. Furthermore, they would take immeasurable, supreme, and exquisite flower garlands, powdered and scattered incenses, robes, necklaces, jeweled banners, flags, canopies, various wonderful and rare objects, music, and lamps—offering all these with every resource at their disposal to pay homage, revere, respect, and praise them.

Suppose there are sons or daughters of good family who receive from others a portion of the Buddha’s *śarīra* (relics) and distribute even as much as a mustard seed to another, causing them to receive it with reverence and install it according to the Dharma; furthermore, they offer worship, respect, honor, and praise with immeasurable, exquisite flower garlands, powdered and scattered incenses, robes, necklaces, precious banners, flags, canopies, various wonderful and rare objects, music, and lamps, giving all that they possess.
"What do you think?
Between these two accumulations of merit, the former and the latter, which is greater?
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, replied:
“World-Honored One!

As I understand the meaning of the Dharma taught by the Buddha, if a son or daughter of good family should receive from others the relics of the Buddha and place them in a precious casket at a high and exalted location, and furthermore, offer all they possess—immeasurable and most excellent flower garlands, powdered and incense perfumes, robes, necklaces, precious banners, flags, canopies, various wonderful and rare objects, music, and lamps—in order to worship, revere, respect, and praise them;”

Suppose there are sons or daughters of good family who, having received from others some of the Buddha’s *śarīra* relics, distribute even as much as a mustard seed to another, causing them to receive it with reverence and enshrine it according to the Dharma; furthermore, they offer worship, honor, respect, and praise with immeasurable, supreme, and exquisite flower garlands, powdered and incense perfumes, robes, necklaces, precious banners, flags, canopies, various wonderful and rare objects, music, and lamps, giving all that they possess.
Of these two accumulations of merit, the latter is greater. Why is this?

All Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, having originally contemplated sentient beings with great compassion, [perceive] those who should attain liberation by revering, honoring, and making offerings at the reliquaries (*śarīra*) of the Buddhas. By the power of the *vajropama-samādhi*, they crush their vajra-like bodies into pieces the size of mustard seeds.
