Because the Dharma is taught within this secret treasury of the *prajñāpāramitā*, there is the designation and attainment of the Ābhāsvara, Parīttābha, Apramāṇābha, and Ābhāsvara-śubha devas in the world;

because the Dharma is taught within this secret treasury of the *prajñāpāramitā*, there is the designation and attainment of the Śuddha, Parīttaśuddha, Apramāṇaśuddha, and Śubhakṛtsna devas in the world;

because the Dharma is taught within this secret treasury of the *prajñāpāramitā*, there is the designation and attainment of the Bṛhatphala, Parīttabṛhatphala, Apramāṇabṛhatphala, and Bṛhatphala devas in the world.

Because the Dharma is taught within this secret treasury of the *prajñāpāramitā*, there come to be the designations for the Avṛha Heaven, the Atapa Heaven, the Sudṛśa Heaven, the Sudarśana Heaven, and the Akaniṣṭha Heaven;

because the Dharma is taught within this secret treasury of the *prajñāpāramitā*, there come to be the designations for the Ākāśānantyāyatana Heaven, the Vijñānānantyāyatana Heaven, the Ākiṃcanyāyatana Heaven, and the Naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana Heaven in the world.

Because of the teaching set forth within this secret treasury of the Prajñāpāramitā, there comes to be the designation and attainment of the perfection of generosity, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of diligence, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom in the world.

Because these teachings are set forth within this secret treasury of the *prajñāpāramitā*, there comes to be the designation and availability of internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*), external emptiness (*bahirdhā-śūnyatā*), internal-and-external emptiness (*adhyātma-bahirdhā-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*), great emptiness (*mahā-śūnyatā*), ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), conditioned emptiness (*saṃskṛta-śūnyatā*), unconditioned emptiness (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*), absolute emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*), boundless emptiness (*anavara-agra-śūnyatā*), dispersed emptiness (*anavakāra-śūnyatā*), non-alteration emptiness (*anavakāra-śūnyatā*), essential nature emptiness (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*), self-characteristic emptiness (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*), common characteristic emptiness (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of the unapprehendable (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of non-existence (*abhāva-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*), and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*).

Because of the teachings set forth within this secret treasury of the *prajñāpāramitā*, there is the designation and attainment in the world of suchness (*tathatā*), the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), non-illusoriness, immutability, equality, the state beyond birth, the fixed nature of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*), the stability of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the realm of space (*ākāśadhātu*), and the inconceivable realm;

because of the teachings set forth within this secret treasury of the *prajñāpāramitā*, there is the designation and attainment in the world of the noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin, the noble truth of cessation, and the noble truth of the path;

because of the teachings set forth within this secret treasury of the *prajñāpāramitā*, there is the designation and attainment in the world of the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments.

Because of the teachings set forth within this secret treasury of the *prajñāpāramitā*, there come to be established in the world the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*), the eight bases of mastery (*aṣṭābhibhvāyatana*), the nine successive attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*), and the ten totalities (*daśakṛtsnāyatana*).

Because of the teachings set forth within this secret treasury of the *prajñāpāramitā*, there come to be established in the world the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*), the four right efforts (*catvāri samyakprahāṇāni*), the four bases of psychic power (*catvāra ṛddhipādāḥ*), the five faculties (*pañcendriyāṇi*), the five powers (*pañca balāni*), the seven factors of enlightenment (*sapta bodhyaṅgāni*), and the eight branches of the noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*).

Because of the teachings set forth within this secret treasury of the *prajñāpāramitā*, there come to be established in the world the gate of liberation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha*), the gate of liberation of signlessness (*animitta-vimokṣamukha*), and the gate of liberation of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-vimokṣamukha*).
Because of the teachings set forth within this secret treasury of the *prajñāpāramitā*, there comes to be in the world the establishment of the five eyes and the six supernormal powers;

because of the teachings set forth within this secret treasury of the *prajñāpāramitā*, there comes to be in the world the establishment of the Buddha’s ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;

because of the teachings set forth within this secret treasury of the *prajñāpāramitā*, there comes to be in the world the establishment of the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant abiding in equanimity.

Because of the teachings set forth within this secret treasury of the *prajñāpāramitā*, there is the designation and attainment of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) in the world;
because of the teachings set forth within this secret treasury of the *prajñāpāramitā*, there is the designation and attainment of all doors of dhāraṇī and all doors of samādhi in the world;

because of the teachings set forth within this secret treasury of the *prajñāpāramitā*, there is the designation and attainment in the world of stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, and arhats, as well as those proceeding toward the fruit of stream-entry, those proceeding toward the fruit of once-returning, those proceeding toward the fruit of non-returning, and those proceeding toward the fruit of arhatship.

Because of the teaching set forth within this secret treasury of the *prajñāpāramitā*, there comes to be in the world the designation and attainment of the solitary realizers (*pratyekabuddha*) and the enlightenment of the solitary realizers (*pratyekabodhi*);

because of the teaching set forth within this secret treasury of the *prajñāpāramitā*, there comes to be in the world the designation and attainment of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and the practices of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas;

and because of the teaching set forth within this secret treasury of the *prajñāpāramitā*, there comes to be in the world the designation and attainment of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
Setting aside these sentient beings in each of the worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;

suppose a son or daughter of good family were to teach and transform all sentient beings in all the worlds of the ten directions, causing them all to practice and study the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and the five supernormal powers—what do you think?"
“By this cause and condition, would those sons and daughters of good family obtain much merit?
Śakra, Lord of Devas, replied:
“Very much!”
"O Bhagavān,
it is very much so!
O Sugata!"
The Buddha said,

“Kauśika! If good sons or good daughters transcribe such profound *prajñāpāramitā* and bestow it upon others for recitation, or copy it again and cause it to circulate widely, the mass of merit obtained by these good sons and good daughters is far greater than the former.”
Why is this? Kausika!

Within this secret treasury of the Prajñāpāramitā, all untainted dharmas are extensively expounded. When individuals belonging to the śrāvaka lineage practice and study these dharmas, they swiftly enter the state of right determination beyond birth (samyaktva-niyāma), and attain the fruit of a stream-enterer, the fruit of a once-returner, the fruit of a non-returner, and the fruit of an arhat.

A person of the pratyekabuddha lineage who trains in this Dharma will swiftly enter the state of rightness and departure from birth (samyaktva-niyāma), and gradually realize the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha;

a person of the bodhisattva lineage who trains in this Dharma will swiftly enter the state of rightness and departure from birth, gradually practice all the bodhisattva deeds, and realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
“Kauśika! Within this secret treasury of the Prajñāpāramitā, all untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*) are extensively explained;
that is to say, the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*), the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*), the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*),” and so forth.
The perfection of generosity, the perfection of diligence, the perfection of meditative concentration,
and the perfection of wisdom; internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness,
the emptiness of the ultimate, the emptiness of conditioned phenomena, the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, absolute emptiness, and the emptiness of the limitless.
Emptiness, the emptiness of dispersion, the emptiness of non-alteration, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the emptiness of self-characteristics, the emptiness of common characteristics,
the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of non-apprehensibility, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature,
the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, suchness, the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, and the non-falsity of reality.
The unchanging nature, equanimity, the state of being free from birth, the fixed nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the stability of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*),

the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the realm of space, the inconceivable realm, the four untainted meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*),
the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*), the eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), the nine successive attainments (*anupūrvasamāpatti*), and the ten...

The spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*), the five faculties (*indriya*), the five powers (*bala*),

the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), the eight branches of the noble path (*āryamārgāṅga*), the gate of liberation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha*), the gate of liberation of signlessness (*animitta-vimokṣamukha*),
the gate of liberation of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-vimokṣamukha*), the five eyes (*pañca-cakṣus*), the six supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*), and the ten powers of a Buddha (*daśa-tathāgatabala*).
The fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity,
the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*),
the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), all doors of dhāraṇī, all doors of samādhi, and other immeasurable [qualities].
All the Buddha-dharmas of the limits are precisely all the untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*) explained herein. "Kauśika!

If a son or daughter of good family were to instruct a single sentient being to abide in the fruit of a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), the mass of merit obtained would be superior to that of instructing all sentient beings in all the worlds of the ten directions to practice and learn the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), and the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*)."
Why is this? Kausika!

There are those who practice the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and the five superknowledges, yet they do not escape the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts. However, if sentient beings abide in the fruit of a stream-enterer, they immediately obtain permanent liberation from the three evil destinies; how much more so for the mass of merit obtained by teaching others to abide in the fruits of a once-returner, a non-returner, or an arhat—how could that not surpass the former?

“Kauśika! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to teach and transform all sentient beings in all worlds throughout the ten directions, causing them all to dwell in the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, and arhatship, the mass of merit they would obtain would not equal that of a person who teaches a single sentient being and causes them to abide in the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha.”
Why is this? Kauśika!
Because all the merits of pratyekabuddha-enlightenment exceed those of the stream-enterers and others by a hundred-thousandfold.

“Kauśika! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to teach and transform all sentient beings in all worlds throughout the ten directions, causing them all to dwell securely in the enlightenment of a Pratyekabuddha, the mass of merit they would obtain would not equal that of someone who teaches a single sentient being to incline toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”
Why is this? Kauśika!
If one instructs sentient beings to incline toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, then one ensures that the Buddha-eye in the world will not be severed.

"Why is this? It is because there are bodhisattva mahāsattvas that there exist the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, and arhatship, as well as the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha;
it is because there are bodhisattva mahāsattvas that there are Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas who realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
Because there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, there exist the Buddha-jewel, the Dharma-jewel, and the Saṅgha-jewel, upon which all the world relies and makes offerings.
For this reason, Kauśika!

All those in the world—whether devas, māras, brahmās, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, asuras, humans, or non-humans—should, with immeasurable and most excellent flower garlands, powdered and scattered incenses, robes, necklaces, precious banners, pennants, canopies, various wonders, rare treasures, music, and lamps, offer all they possess to honor, revere, respect, and praise the bodhisattva mahāsattva.

“Kauśika! By this you should know that if a son of good family or a daughter of good family writes down such profound *prajñāpāramitā* and gives it to others to read and recite, or transcribes it and causes it to be widely disseminated, the mass of merit they obtain will be infinitely and boundlessly superior to the previous mass of merit.”
Why is this? Because within this secret treasury of the Prajñāpāramitā, all the supreme and wholesome dharmas of both the mundane and supramundane realms are extensively expounded.

"Because of the teaching set forth within this secret treasury of the Prajñāpāramitā, there comes to be the designation of the great clans of kṣatriyas, the great clans of brahmins, the great clans of householders, and the great clans of laymen in the world;

because of the teaching set forth within this secret treasury of the Prajñāpāramitā, there comes to be the designation of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven in the world;

because of the teaching set forth within this secret treasury of the Prajñāpāramitā, there comes to be the designation of the Brahmakāyika Heaven, the Brahmapurohita Heaven, the Mahābrahma Heaven, and the Brahmakāyika Heaven in the world."

Because these teachings are set forth within this secret treasury of the *prajñāpāramitā*, there is the designation and attainment of the Ābhāsvara, Parīttābha, Apramāṇābha, and Ābhāsvara-śubha devas in the world;

because these teachings are set forth within this secret treasury of the *prajñāpāramitā*, there is the designation and attainment of the Śubha, Parīttaśubha, Apramāṇaśubha, and Śubhakṛtsna devas in the world;

because these teachings are set forth within this secret treasury of the *prajñāpāramitā*, there is the designation and attainment of the Bṛhatphala, Parīttabṛhatphala, Apramāṇabṛhatphala, and Bṛhatphala devas in the world.

Because the Dharma taught within this secret treasury of the *prajñāpāramitā* exists, there is the designation and attainment of the Avṛha heaven, the Atapa heaven, the Sudṛśa heaven, the Sudarśana heaven, and the Akaniṣṭha heaven in the world;

because the Dharma taught within this secret treasury of the *prajñāpāramitā* exists, there is the designation and attainment of the Ākāśānantyāyatana heaven, the Vijñānānantyāyatana heaven, the Ākiṃcanyāyatana heaven, and the Naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana heaven in the world.

Because the Dharma is taught within this secret treasury of the *prajñāpāramitā*, there exists in the world the designation and attainment of the perfection of generosity, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of diligence, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom.

Because of the teachings set forth within this secret treasury of the *prajñāpāramitā*, there come to be established in the world the designations of internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*), external emptiness (*bahirdhā-śūnyatā*), internal-and-external emptiness (*adhyātma-bahirdhā-śūnyatā*), emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*), great emptiness (*mahā-śūnyatā*), ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), conditioned emptiness (*saṃskṛta-śūnyatā*), unconditioned emptiness (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*), absolute emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*), boundless emptiness (*anavara-agra-śūnyatā*), dispersed emptiness (*anavakāra-śūnyatā*), non-alteration emptiness (*anavakāra-śūnyatā*), essential nature emptiness (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*), self-characteristic emptiness (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*), common characteristic emptiness (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*), emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*), emptiness of the unapprehendable (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*), emptiness of non-existence (*abhāva-śūnyatā*), emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*), and emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*).

Because of the teachings set forth within this secret treasury of the *prajñāpāramitā*, there is the conceptual designation and availability in the world of suchness (*tathatā*), the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), non-falsity, non-alteration, equality, the state beyond birth, the fixed nature of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*), the stability of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the realm of space (*ākāśadhātu*), and the inconceivable realm (*acintyadhātu*).

Because of the teachings set forth within this secret treasury of the *prajñāpāramitā*, there is the conceptual designation and availability in the world of the noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin [of suffering], the noble truth of cessation, and the noble truth of the path.

Because of the teachings set forth within this secret treasury of the *prajñāpāramitā*, there is the conceptual designation and availability in the world of the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments.

Because of the teachings set forth within this secret treasury of the *prajñāpāramitā*, there come to be established in the world the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*), the eight bases of mastery (*aṣṭābhibhvāyatana*), the nine successive attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*), and the ten spheres of totality (*daśakṛtsnāyatana*).

Because of the teachings set forth within this secret treasury of the *prajñāpāramitā*, there come to be established in the world the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*), the four right efforts (*catvāri samyakprahāṇāni*), the four bases of psychic power (*catvāra ṛddhipādāḥ*), the five faculties (*pañcendriyāṇi*), the five powers (*pañca balāni*), the seven factors of enlightenment (*sapta bodhyaṅgāni*), and the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*).

Because of the teachings set forth within this secret treasury of the *prajñāpāramitā*, there come to be established in the world the gate of liberation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha*), the gate of liberation of signlessness (*animitta-vimokṣamukha*), and the gate of liberation of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-vimokṣamukha*).
Because of the teachings set forth within this secret treasury of the *prajñāpāramitā*, the world comes to have the designation of the five eyes and the six supernormal powers;

because of the teachings set forth within this secret treasury of the *prajñāpāramitā*, the world comes to have the designation of the Buddha’s ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;

because of the teachings set forth within this secret treasury of the *prajñāpāramitā*, the world comes to have the designation of the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant abiding in equanimity.

Because the Dharma is taught within this secret treasury of the *prajñāpāramitā*, the designations of "all-knowledge" (*sarvajñatā*), "knowledge of the aspects of the path" (*mārgākārajñatā*), and "knowledge of all aspects" (*sarvākārajñatā*) are established and attainable in the world.
Because the Dharma is taught within this secret treasury of the *prajñāpāramitā*, the designations of all *dhāraṇī* doors and all *samādhi* doors are established and attainable in the world.

Because the Dharma is taught within this secret treasury of the *prajñāpāramitā*, the designations of stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, and arhats—along with those entering the state of a stream-enterer and the fruit of stream-entry, those entering the state of a once-returner and the fruit of once-returning, those entering the state of a non-returner and the fruit of non-returning, and those entering the state of an arhat and the fruit of arhatship—are established and attainable in the world.
Because the Dharma is taught within this secret treasury of the *prajñāpāramitā*, there comes to be the designation and attainment of the pratyekabuddhas and the pratyekabuddha-bodhi in the world;

because the Dharma is taught within this secret treasury of the *prajñāpāramitā*, there comes to be the designation and attainment of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and the bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices in the world;

because the Dharma is taught within this secret treasury of the *prajñāpāramitā*, there comes to be the designation and attainment of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and the unexcelled, perfect enlightenment of the Buddhas in the world.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters receive, uphold, recite, and contemplate according to the principle this Prajñāpāramitā, the mass of merit obtained by these good sons and good daughters surpasses that of one who teaches all sentient beings throughout Jambudvīpa, causing them to abide in the ten paths of wholesome action, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and the five supernormal powers."

“Kauśika! The mass of merit obtained by these sons and daughters of good family is even more superior than that of one who teaches all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa and Pūrvavideha, causing them to abide in the ten paths of wholesome action, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and the five supernormal powers.”

“Kauśika! The mass of merit obtained by these sons and daughters of good family is even more superior than that of one who teaches all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa, Pūrvavideha, and Aparagodānīya, causing them all to abide in the ten paths of wholesome action, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and the five supernormal powers.”

“Kauśika! The mass of merit obtained by these sons and daughters of good family is even more excellent than that of one who teaches all sentient beings throughout the four great continents, causing them to abide in the ten paths of wholesome action, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and the five supernormal powers.”

“Kauśika! The mass of merit obtained by these sons and daughters of good family is even more excellent than that of one who teaches and establishes all sentient beings in a small thousandfold world system in the ten paths of wholesome action, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and the five supernormal powers.”

“Kauśika! The mass of merit obtained by these sons and daughters of good family also surpasses that of one who teaches all sentient beings in a medium chiliocosm, causing them to abide in the ten paths of wholesome action, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and the five supernormal powers.”

“Kauśika! The mass of merit obtained by these sons and daughters of good family is even more excellent than that of one who teaches and establishes all sentient beings throughout the trichiliocosm in the ten paths of wholesome action, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and the five supernormal powers.”

“Kauśika! The mass of merit obtained by these sons and daughters of good family is even more superior than that of one who teaches all sentient beings throughout worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in each of the ten directions, causing them all to abide in the ten paths of wholesome action, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless absorptions, and the five supernormal powers.”

“Kauśika! The mass of merit obtained by these sons and daughters of good family is even more superior than that of one who teaches all sentient beings in all worlds throughout the ten directions, causing them to abide in the ten paths of wholesome action, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and the five supernormal powers.”

“Kauśika! In this context, ‘reflecting according to reality’ means that by means of a practice that is neither dual nor non-dual, one awakens to this *prajñāpāramitā*, upholds it, recites it, and reflects upon it according to reality;

furthermore, by means of a practice that is neither dual nor non-dual, one awakens to the *dhyāna*, *vīrya*, *kṣānti*, *śīla*, and *dāna* *pāramitās*, upholding them, reciting them, and reflecting upon them according to reality.”
“Kauśika! Furthermore, by means of a practice that is neither dual nor non-dual, one awakens to and correctly contemplates internal emptiness;

furthermore, by means of a practice that is neither dual nor non-dual, one awakens to and correctly contemplates external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersion emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, correctly contemplating them as they truly are.”
“Kauśika! Furthermore, by means of a practice that is neither dual nor non-dual, one awakens to and correctly contemplates *tathatā* (suchness);

furthermore, by means of a practice that is neither dual nor non-dual, one awakens to and correctly contemplates the *dharmadhātu* (dharma-realm), the *dharmatā* (dharma-nature), the non-illusory nature, the unchanging nature, the equality, the nature free from birth, the fixedness of dharma, the stability of dharma, the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm.
“Kauśika! Furthermore, by means of a practice that is neither dual nor non-dual, one awakens to and correctly contemplates the Noble Truth of Suffering;
furthermore, by means of a practice that is neither dual nor non-dual, one awakens to and correctly contemplates the Noble Truths of Origination, Cessation, and the Path.”
“Kauśika! Furthermore, by means of a practice that is neither dual nor non-dual, one awakens to the four dhyānas through correct reflection;
furthermore, by means of a practice that is neither dual nor non-dual, one awakens to the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments through correct reflection.”
“Kauśika! Furthermore, by means of a practice that is neither dual nor non-dual, one awakens to the eight liberations through correct reflection;

furthermore, by means of a practice that is neither dual nor non-dual, one awakens to the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten totalities through correct reflection.”
“Kauśika! Furthermore, by means of a practice that is neither dual nor non-dual, one awakens to the four foundations of mindfulness through correct reflection;

furthermore, by means of a practice that is neither dual nor non-dual, one awakens to the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path through correct reflection.”
“Kauśika! Furthermore, by means of a practice that is neither dual nor non-dual, one awakens to and correctly contemplates the gate of liberation of emptiness;
furthermore, by means of a practice that is neither dual nor non-dual, one awakens to and correctly contemplates the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness.”
“Kauśika! Furthermore, by means of a practice that is neither dual nor non-dual, one awakens to and correctly contemplates the five eyes;
furthermore, by means of a practice that is neither dual nor non-dual, one awakens to and correctly contemplates the six supernormal powers.”
“Kauśika! Furthermore, by means of a practice that is neither dual nor non-dual, one awakens to and correctly contemplates the ten powers of a Buddha;

furthermore, by means of a practice that is neither dual nor non-dual, one awakens to and correctly contemplates the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.”
“Kauśika! Furthermore, by means of a practice that is neither dual nor non-dual, one awakens to and correctly contemplates the quality of non-forgetfulness;
furthermore, by means of a practice that is neither dual nor non-dual, one awakens to and correctly contemplates the nature of constant equanimity.”
“Kauśika! Furthermore, by means of a practice that is neither dual nor non-dual, one awakens to and correctly contemplates all-knowledge (sarvajñatā);

furthermore, by means of a practice that is neither dual nor non-dual, one awakens to and correctly contemplates the knowledge of the paths (mārgajñatā) and the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā).”
“Kauśika! Furthermore, by means of a practice that is neither dual nor non-dual, one awakens to and correctly contemplates all *dhāraṇī* gates;
furthermore, by means of a practice that is neither dual nor non-dual, one awakens to and correctly contemplates all *samādhi* gates.”
“Kauśika! Furthermore, by means of a practice that is neither dual nor non-dual, one awakens to the bodhisattva-mahāsattva practice through correct reflection. Kauśika!”
Furthermore, by means of a practice that is neither dual nor non-dual, one awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment through correct reflection.
"Moreover, Kausika!..."

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to extensively expound this *prajñāpāramitā* to others through immeasurable gateways—proclaiming, revealing, elucidating, explaining, and analyzing its meaning and intent so that it is easily understood—the mass of merit they would obtain would surpass the merit obtained by one who themselves upholds, reads, recites, or reflects upon this *prajñāpāramitā* according to the principle.

“Kauśika! As for the meaning and purport of what is called the *prajñāpāramitā*, it means that this *prajñāpāramitā* is neither dual nor non-dual; neither with marks nor without marks; neither entering nor exiting; neither increasing nor decreasing; neither defiled nor pure; neither arising nor ceasing; neither grasping nor relinquishing; neither clinging nor not clinging; neither abiding nor not abiding; neither real nor unreal; neither associated nor dissociated; neither conjoined nor unconjoined; neither causal conditions nor non-causal conditions; neither dharma nor non-dharma; neither suchness nor non-suchness; neither the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) nor non-limit of reality. Such a purport has immeasurable gateways.”

“Kauśika! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family can extensively teach others the profound meaning and purport of this *prajñāpāramitā* so that it is easily understood, the mass of merit they obtain will be infinitely greater than the merit obtained by one who personally upholds, reads, recites, or reflects upon this *prajñāpāramitā* according to the principle.”
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters personally uphold, recite, and contemplate the Prajñāpāramitā according to the principle of reality, and extensively explain it to others through immeasurable gateways—proclaiming, expounding, elucidating, clarifying, and interpreting it, analyzing its meaning and intent so that it may be easily understood—the mass of merit obtained by these good sons and good daughters exceeds the previous mass of merit, being immeasurable and boundless."
At that time, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
All sons and daughters of good family should proclaim and reveal this Prajñāpāramitā through various skillful words and meanings.”
The Buddha said:
"Kauśika, it is so!
It is thus!"
"So it is! It is just as you have said.
All sons and daughters of good family should proclaim and reveal this Prajñāpāramitā through various skillful words and meanings."

“Kauśika! If sons or daughters of good family can proclaim and reveal such Prajñāpāramitā through various skillful words and meanings, these sons and daughters of good family will achieve an immeasurable, innumerable, boundless, and inconceivable mass of great merit.”

“Kauśika! If good sons and good daughters, for as long as their lives last, were to offer with all their available pure articles of enjoyment—such as immeasurable kinds of exquisite flower garlands, powdered and scattered incenses, robes, necklaces, precious banners, pennants, canopies, various wonders, rare curiosities, music, and lamps—to all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas throughout the immeasurable and innumerable worlds of the ten directions, honoring, revering, respecting, and praising them;”

If there are sons or daughters of good family who themselves receive, uphold, recite, and contemplate the *prajñāpāramitā* according to reason, and furthermore, relying on various skillful words and meanings, extensively expound it for others through immeasurable approaches—proclaiming, revealing, elucidating, clarifying, explaining, and analyzing its significance to make it easy to understand—the mass of merit obtained by these sons or daughters of good family is far greater than the former.
Why is this so? Kauśika!

It is because all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past, future, and present have studied the Prajñāpāramitā; they have realized, will realize, and are now realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
If good sons and good daughters, for immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless great kalpas, practice the perfection of generosity by means of apprehending something;
and for immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless great kalpas, practice the perfection of ethical discipline by means of apprehending something;..."
For immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless great eons, they practice the perfection of patience with the attainment of something as their means;
for immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless great eons, they practice the perfection of diligence with the attainment of something as their means;
for immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless great eons, they practice the perfection of meditative concentration with the attainment of something as their means.
For immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless great kalpas, one might practice the *prajñāpāramitā* by means of the expedient of apprehending something.

Yet, if a son or daughter of good family, regarding this *prajñāpāramitā*, were to receive, uphold, recite, and reflect upon it according to the principle by means of the expedient of non-apprehension; and furthermore, were to explain, proclaim, expound, reveal, and interpret it for others with various skillful words and meanings—even for a mere moment—analyzing its significance and making it easy to understand, the mass of merit obtained would be far greater than the former.
“Kauśika! What is here called ‘attaining something’ refers to when good sons and good daughters, while practicing generosity, form such thoughts as: ‘I am the one who gives;
he is the recipient; this is the fruit of giving; this is the act of giving and the gift itself.’”

"When that person practices giving, it is called abiding in generosity, but it is not called the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā), because they employ the means of apprehending something as an object.
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, while cultivating pure ethical discipline (śīla), forms this thought:
'I am able to maintain the precepts; I do so for the sake of protecting others; this is the fruit of the precepts and the precepts themselves that are maintained.'"

When they observe the precepts, it is called abiding in pure morality, but it is not called the perfection of morality (śīlapāramitā), because they employ the method of apprehending something as an object.
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, while practicing patience, forms such a thought as:
"I am able to practice patience for the sake of protecting others; this is the fruit of patience and the intrinsic nature of patience."

When they cultivate patience, it is called abiding in patience, but it is not called the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), because they employ the method of apprehending something as an object.
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, while cultivating diligence, forms this thought:
"I am able to be diligent; for the sake of cultivating abandonment, this is the fruit of diligence and the intrinsic nature of diligence."

When he practices diligence, it is called "abiding in diligence," but it is not called the perfection of diligence (*dhyānapāramitā*), because he employs the method of apprehending something as an object.
If a son or daughter of good family, while practicing meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), forms such a thought:
"I am able to cultivate concentration; that is the objective field of concentration; this is the fruit of concentration and the intrinsic nature of concentration."
"When that person practices meditative concentration, it is called 'abiding in dhyāna,' but it is not called the 'dhyāna-pāramitā,' because they employ the attainment of something as their means.
If a son or daughter of good family, when practicing prajñā, forms such a thought:
'I am able to cultivate wisdom; that is the object of wisdom; this is the fruit of prajñā, the self-nature of prajñā.'"
"When he cultivates wisdom at that time, it is called abiding in *prajñā*, but it is not called *prajñāpāramitā*, because he employs the means of apprehending something as an object. Kausika!"

Because these sons and daughters of good family employ the method of "attaining something," they are unable to bring to perfection the pāramitās of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
At that time, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How can a bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfill the pāramitās of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom?”
The Buddha said, “Kauśika!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices generosity, if they do not apprehend the giver, the recipient, the fruit of giving, the act of giving, or the objects given— by means of this non-apprehension as their skillful method— they are able to fulfill the perfection of generosity.”

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivates pure ethical discipline (*śīla*), they do not apprehend the one who maintains it, the fruit of the protected discipline, nor the nature of the discipline maintained; because they employ non-apprehension as their skillful means, they are able to fulfill the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*).

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivates patience (*kṣānti*), they do not apprehend the one who is patient, the fruit of the protected patience, nor the intrinsic nature of patience; because they employ non-apprehension as their skillful means, they are able to fulfill the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*).

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivates diligence (*vīrya*), they do not apprehend the one who exerts effort, the fruit of that exertion, nor the intrinsic nature of diligence; because they employ non-apprehension as their skillful means, they are able to fulfill the perfection of diligence (*vīryapāramitā*).

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivates dhyāna, they do not apprehend concentration, the object of concentration, the fruit of concentration, or the intrinsic nature of dhyāna; because they employ non-apprehension as their skillful means, they are able to fulfill the perfection of dhyāna.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivates prajñā, they do not apprehend wisdom, the object of wisdom, the fruit of wisdom, or the intrinsic nature of prajñā; because they employ non-apprehension as their skillful means, they are able to fulfill the perfection of prajñā.

“Kauśika! All sons and daughters of good family should proclaim the *prajñāpāramitā* by means of such wisdom of non-apprehension and through various skillful words and meanings; they should [proclaim it] by means of such non-..."

Having attained wisdom and being able to eloquently explain the various skillful words and meanings of the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*) through such non-apprehending wisdom and various skillful words and meanings,
one should likewise eloquently explain the perfection of diligence (*vīryapāramitā*) through such non-apprehending wisdom and various skillful words and meanings.
One should likewise [explain it] through such non-apprehending wisdom and various skillful words and meanings.
One should proclaim the perfection of patience with such wisdom of non-apprehension and through various skillful words and meanings;
one should proclaim the perfection of ethical discipline with such wisdom of non-apprehension and through various skillful words and meanings;
and one should proclaim the perfection of generosity with such wisdom of non-apprehension and through various skillful words and meanings.
Why is this? "Kauśika!

In future ages, there will be sons of good family and daughters of good family who proclaim a counterfeit *prajñāpāramitā* to others. When those who have first resolved upon unsurpassed bodhicitta hear that counterfeit *prajñāpāramitā*, their minds will become confused and deluded, thereby losing the Middle Way. For this reason, one should proclaim the *prajñāpāramitā* to those who have resolved upon unsurpassed bodhicitta by means of the wisdom of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) and through various skillful words and meanings."

“Kauśika! In future ages, there will be sons of good family and daughters of good family who proclaim a counterfeit dhyānapāramitā to others. When those who have first resolved upon unsurpassed bodhicitta hear that counterfeit dhyānapāramitā they have been taught, their minds will become deluded and mistaken, thereby losing the Middle Way. For this reason, one should use the wisdom of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) and various skillful words and meanings to proclaim the dhyānapāramitā to those who have resolved upon unsurpassed bodhicitta.”

“Kauśika! In future ages, there will be sons of good family and daughters of good family who proclaim a counterfeit perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*) to others. When those who have first resolved upon unsurpassed bodhicitta hear that counterfeit perfection of diligence, their minds will become deluded and they will lose the Middle Way. Therefore, one should proclaim the perfection of diligence to those who have resolved upon unsurpassed bodhicitta by means of the wisdom of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) and through various skillful words and meanings.”

“Kauśika! In future ages, there will be sons of good family and daughters of good family who proclaim a counterfeit perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) to others. When those who have first resolved upon unsurpassed bodhicitta hear that counterfeit perfection of patience they have proclaimed, their minds will become deluded and mistaken, thereby losing the Middle Way. For this reason, one should proclaim the perfection of patience to those who have resolved upon unsurpassed bodhicitta by means of the wisdom of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) and through various skillful words and meanings.”

“Kauśika! In future ages, there will be sons of good family and daughters of good family who proclaim a counterfeit perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*) to others. When those who have first resolved upon unsurpassed bodhicitta hear that counterfeit perfection of ethical discipline, their minds will become confused and deluded, thereby losing the Middle Way. Therefore, one should, by means of the wisdom of non-apprehension (*anupalambha-prajñā*) and through various skillful words and meanings, proclaim the perfection of ethical discipline to those who have resolved upon unsurpassed bodhicitta.”

“Kauśika! In future ages, there will be sons of good family and daughters of good family who proclaim a counterfeit perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*) to others. When those who have first resolved upon unsurpassed bodhicitta hear that counterfeit perfection of generosity they have proclaimed, their minds will become deluded and mistaken, thereby losing the Middle Way. For this reason, one should proclaim the perfection of generosity to those who have resolved upon unsurpassed bodhicitta by means of the wisdom of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) and through various skillful words and meanings.”

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Scroll 135. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Part One: Chapter on the Measurement of Merit, Section 30-iii/iv. At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"What is meant by teaching counterfeit *prajñāpāramitā*, *dhyāna*, *vīrya*, *kṣānti*, *śīla*,
and *dānapāramitā*? The Buddha said, "Kauśika!..."

If sons or daughters of good family speak of the perfection of wisdom, concentration, diligence, patience, ethical discipline, and generosity as being something to be attained, such speech is called speaking of counterfeit perfection of wisdom, concentration, diligence, patience, ethical discipline, and generosity.
Then, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
why is it that certain sons and daughters of good family who speak of a prajñāpāramitā with something to be attained are said to be speaking a counterfeit prajñāpāramitā?”
The Buddha said, “Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment, speak of form as either permanent or impermanent, and speak of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as either permanent or impermanent;”
One speaks of form as either pleasant or painful; one speaks of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as either pleasant or painful.
One speaks of form as either self or non-self; one speaks of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as either self or non-self.
One speaks of form as either pure or impure; one speaks of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as either pure or impure.
If there are those who are able to practice prajñā by relying on such dharmas as these, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Furthermore, it is said:

one who practices prajñā should seek whether form (rūpa) is permanent or impermanent; one should seek whether feeling (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), mental formations (saṃskāra), and consciousness (vijñāna) are permanent or impermanent.
One should investigate whether form is pleasant or painful; one should investigate whether feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are pleasant or painful.
One should investigate whether form is self or non-self; one should investigate whether feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are self or non-self.
One should investigate whether form is pure or impure; one should investigate whether feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice prajñā, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). "Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters seek form as either permanent or impermanent, or seek feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as either permanent or impermanent; [they do not thus practice the perfection of wisdom]."
One seeks whether form is pleasant or painful; one seeks whether feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are pleasant or painful.
One seeks whether form is self or non-self; one seeks whether feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are self or non-self.
One seeks whether form is pure or impure; one seeks whether feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are pure or impure.
Kauśika, I declare that one who practices the perfection of wisdom by relying on such dharmas as these is practicing a semblance of the perfection of wisdom characterized by apprehension.
As previously stated, you should know that all these refer to a semblance of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) characterized by apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, explain whether the eye-base is permanent or impermanent; explain whether the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases are permanent or impermanent;
explain whether the eye-base is pleasant or painful; explain whether the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases are pleasant or painful;
explain whether the eye-base is self or non-self; explain whether the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases are self or non-self;
To speak of the sense-base of the eye as either pure or impure, and to speak of the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind as either pure or impure—
if one is able to practice prajñā based upon such dharmas as these, this is the practice of the perfection of prajñā (prajñāpāramitā).
Furthermore, it is said:

One who practices Prajñāpāramitā should seek whether the sense-base of the eye is permanent or impermanent; one should seek whether the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are permanent or impermanent;
one should seek whether the sense-base of the eye is pleasant or painful; one should seek whether the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are pleasant or painful.
One should investigate whether the eye-base is self or non-self; one should investigate whether the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases are self or non-self.
One should investigate whether the eye-base is pure or impure; one should investigate whether the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases are pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice prajñā, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). "Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters seek the sense-base of the eye (*cakṣur-āyatana*) as either permanent or impermanent, and seek the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind (*śrotra-, ghrāṇa-, jihvā-, kāya-, mana-āyatana*) as either permanent or impermanent;
They seek whether the eye-base is pleasant or painful; they seek whether the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases are pleasant or painful.
They seek whether the eye-base is self or non-self; they seek whether the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases are self or non-self.
They seek whether the eye-base is pure or impure; they seek whether the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases are pure or impure.
“Kauśika, I declare that one who practices the perfection of wisdom by relying on such dharmas as these is practicing a semblance of the perfection of wisdom that is characterized by apprehension.”
As previously stated, you should know that all these are descriptions of a semblance of the prajñāpāramitā that involves apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment, should speak of the sphere of form as either permanent or impermanent; speak of the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena as either permanent or impermanent;
speak of the sphere of form as either pleasant or painful; speak of the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena as either pleasant or painful;

speak of the sphere of form as either self or non-self; and speak of the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena as either self or non-self; [they would be teaching emptiness].
To speak of the sense-base of form as either pure or impure, and to speak of the sense-bases of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena as either pure or impure—
if one is able to practice prajñā in reliance upon such dharmas as these, this is the practice of the perfection of prajñā.
Furthermore, it is said:

One who practices Prajñāpāramitā should seek whether the sphere of form (rūpa-āyatana) is permanent or impermanent; one should seek whether the spheres of sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena (dharma-āyatana) are permanent or impermanent;
one should seek whether the sphere of form is pleasant or painful; one should seek whether the spheres of sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena are pleasant or painful.
One should investigate whether the sphere of form is self or non-self; one should investigate whether the spheres of sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena are self or non-self.
One should investigate whether the sphere of form is pure or impure; one should investigate whether the spheres of sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena are pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice *prajñā*, they are practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*. "Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters seek whether the sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) is permanent or impermanent, and seek whether the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) are permanent or impermanent;
One seeks whether the sphere of forms is pleasant or painful; one seeks whether the spheres of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena are pleasant or painful.
One seeks whether the sphere of forms is self or non-self; one seeks whether the spheres of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena are self or non-self.
One seeks whether the sphere of forms is pure or impure; one seeks whether the spheres of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena are pure or impure.
“Kauśika, I declare that one who practices the perfection of wisdom by relying on such dharmas as these is practicing a semblance of the perfection of wisdom characterized by apprehension.”
As previously stated, you should know that all these are descriptions of a semblance of the prajñāpāramitā characterized by apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, explain whether the eye-element is permanent or impermanent; explain whether the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, eye-contact, and all feelings produced with eye-contact as condition are permanent or impermanent;

explain whether the eye-element is pleasant or painful; explain whether the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, eye-contact, and all feelings produced with eye-contact as condition are pleasant or painful;

explain whether the eye-element is self or non-self; explain whether the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, eye-contact, and all feelings produced with eye-contact as condition are self or non-self;

One speaks of the eye-element as either pure or impure; one speaks of the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, and eye-contact, as well as all feelings produced with eye-contact as their condition, as either pure or impure.
If there are those who are able to practice prajñā by relying on such dharmas as these, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Furthermore, it is said:

one who practices prajñā should investigate whether the eye-element is permanent or impermanent; one should investigate whether the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, eye-contact, and the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition are permanent or impermanent.

One should seek whether the eye-element is pleasant or painful; one should seek whether the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, eye-contact, and the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition are pleasant or painful.

One should seek whether the eye-element is self or non-self; one should seek whether the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, eye-contact, and the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition are self or non-self.

one who practices prajñā should seek whether internal emptiness is permanent or impermanent; they should seek whether external emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of intrinsic nature in the absence of nature, is permanent or impermanent.

One should seek whether inner emptiness is pleasant or painful; one should seek whether outer emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature, is pleasant or painful.
One should seek whether inner emptiness is self or non-self; one should seek whether outer emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature, is self or non-self.
One should seek whether inner emptiness is pure or impure; one should seek whether outer emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature, is pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice *prajñā*, they are practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*. "Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters seek internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*) as either permanent or impermanent, or seek external emptiness (*bahirdhā-śūnyatā*) up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*) as either permanent or impermanent; [they are practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*]."
One seeks whether internal emptiness is pleasant or painful; one seeks whether external emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, is pleasant or painful.
One seeks whether internal emptiness is self or non-self; one seeks whether external emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, is self or non-self.
One seeks whether internal emptiness is pure or impure; one seeks whether external emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, is pure or impure.
“Kauśika, I declare that one who practices the perfection of wisdom by relying on such dharmas as these is practicing a semblance of the perfection of wisdom characterized by apprehension.”
As previously stated, you should know that all these are descriptions of a semblance of the prajñāpāramitā that involves apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment, speak of whether the *tathatā* (suchness) is permanent or impermanent; or speak of whether the *dharmadhātu* (dharma-realm), *dharmatā* (dharma-nature), non-illusory nature, unchanging nature, equality, nature free from birth, fixedness of dharma, stability of dharma, the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm are permanent or impermanent;

or speak of whether the *tathatā* is pleasant or painful; or speak of whether the *dharmadhātu*, *dharmatā*, non-illusory nature, unchanging nature, equality, nature free from birth, fixedness of dharma, stability of dharma, the limit of reality, the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm are pleasant or painful;

Whether one speaks of *tathatā* as having a self or being without a self, or speaks of the *dharmadhātu*, the *dharmatā*, the non-erroneous nature, the unchanging nature, equality, the state beyond birth, the fixedness of phenomena, the stability of phenomena, the limit of reality, the realm of space, or the inconceivable realm as having a self or being without a self;

whether one speaks of *tathatā* as pure or impure, or speaks of the *dharmadhātu*, the *dharmatā*, the non-erroneous nature, the unchanging nature, equality, the state beyond birth, the fixedness of phenomena, the stability of phenomena, the limit of reality, the realm of space, or the inconceivable realm as pure or impure.
If there are those who can practice prajñā in reliance upon such dharmas as these, they are practicing the perfection of prajñā (prajñāpāramitā).
Furthermore, it is said:

one who practices prajñā should seek whether true thusness (tathatā) is permanent or impermanent; one should seek whether the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), up to the inconceivable realm (acintyadhātu), is permanent or impermanent.
One should seek whether the reality-limit is pleasant or painful; one should seek whether the dharma-realm, up to the inconceivable realm, is pleasant or painful.
One should seek whether the reality-limit is self or non-self; one should seek whether the dharma-realm, up to the inconceivable realm, is self or non-self.
One should seek whether the reality-limit is pure or impure; one should seek whether the dharma-realm, up to the inconceivable realm, is pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice *prajñā*, they are practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*. "Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters thus seek whether true suchness is permanent or impermanent, or seek whether the dharma-realm, up to the inconceivable realm, is permanent or impermanent; [they are practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*]."
Seeking true reality as either pleasure or suffering; seeking the dharma-realm, up to the inconceivable realm, as either pleasure or suffering;
seeking true reality as either self or non-self; seeking the dharma-realm, up to the inconceivable realm, as either self or non-self;
seeking true reality as either pure or impure; seeking the dharma-realm, up to the inconceivable realm, as either pure or impure.
“Kauśika, I say that one who practices the perfection of wisdom by relying on such dharmas as these is practicing a semblance of the perfection of wisdom characterized by apprehension.”
As previously stated, you should know that all these are descriptions of a semblance of the prajñāpāramitā that involves apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved upon the unexcelled mind of enlightenment, should speak of the Noble Truth of Suffering as either permanent or impermanent, or speak of the Noble Truths of Origination, Cessation, and the Path as either permanent or impermanent;
if they should speak of the Noble Truth of Suffering as either pleasant or painful, or speak of the Noble Truths of Origination, Cessation, and the Path as either pleasant or painful;
if they should speak of the Noble Truth of Suffering as either self or non-self, or speak of the Noble Truths of Origination, Cessation, and the Path as either self or non-self;
Whether one speaks of the noble truth of suffering as pure or impure, or speaks of the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path as pure or impure—
if there is one who is able to practice prajñā based on such dharmas as these, this is the practice of the perfection of prajñā (prajñāpāramitā).
Furthermore, it is said:

One who practices prajñā should seek whether the noble truth of suffering is permanent or impermanent; one should seek whether the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path are permanent or impermanent;
one should seek whether the noble truth of suffering is pleasant or painful; one should seek whether the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path are pleasant or painful.
One should seek whether the noble truth of suffering is self or non-self; one should seek whether the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path are self or non-self;
one should seek whether the noble truth of suffering is pure or impure; one should seek whether the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path are pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice *prajñā*, they are practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*. "Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters seek the Noble Truth of Suffering as either permanent or impermanent, and seek the Noble Truths of Origination, Cessation, and the Path as either permanent or impermanent;
One seeks whether the noble truth of suffering is pleasant or painful; one seeks whether the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path are pleasant or painful.
One seeks whether the noble truth of suffering is self or non-self; one seeks whether the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path are self or non-self.
One seeks whether the noble truth of suffering is pure or impure; one seeks whether the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path are pure or impure.
Kauśika, I say that one who practices the perfection of wisdom by relying on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of wisdom characterized by apprehension.
As previously stated, you should know that all these are descriptions of a semblance of the prajñāpāramitā that involves apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment, should speak of the four dhyānas as either permanent or impermanent, or speak of the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions as either permanent or impermanent;
if they should speak of the four dhyānas as either pleasant or painful, or speak of the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions as either pleasant or painful;
if they should speak of the four dhyānas as either self or non-self, or speak of the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions as either self or non-self;
To speak of the four dhyānas as either pure or impure, and to speak of the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments as either pure or impure—
if one is able to practice prajñā by relying on such dharmas as these, this is the practice of the perfection of prajñā.
Furthermore, it is said:

One who practices prajñā should seek whether the four dhyānas are permanent or impermanent; one should seek whether the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments are permanent or impermanent;
one should seek whether the four dhyānas are pleasant or painful; one should seek whether the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments are pleasant or painful.
One should seek the four dhyānas whether they are with self or without self; one should seek the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments whether they are with self or without self;
one should seek the four dhyānas whether they are pure or impure; one should seek the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments whether they are pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice prajñā, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). "Kauśika!
If good sons and good daughters seek the four dhyānas as either permanent or impermanent, or seek the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments as either permanent or impermanent;
They seek the four dhyānas as either pleasant or painful; they seek the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments as either pleasant or painful.
They seek the four dhyānas as either self or non-self; they seek the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments as either self or non-self.
They seek the four dhyānas as either pure or impure; they seek the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments as either pure or impure.
Kauśika, I declare that one who practices the perfection of wisdom by relying on such dharmas as these is practicing a semblance of the perfection of wisdom that is characterized by apprehension.
As previously stated, it should be understood that all these refer to a semblance of the *prajñāpāramitā* characterized by apprehension (*upalambha*).

The Great *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Fascicle 136, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Part One: Chapter on the Measurement of Merit, Section 30-35. "Furthermore, Kauśika!..."

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, should speak of the eight liberations as being either permanent or impermanent; speak of the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, or the ten totalities as being either permanent or impermanent;

speak of the eight liberations as being either pleasant or painful; speak of the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, or the ten totalities as being either pleasant or painful;

or speak of the eight liberations as being either self or non-self; speak of the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, or the ten totalities as being either self or non-self;
To speak of the eight liberations as either pure or impure, and to speak of the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten totalities as either pure or impure—
if one is able to practice prajñā in reliance upon such dharmas as these, this is the practice of the perfection of prajñā.
Furthermore, it is said:

One who practices prajñā should seek whether the eight liberations (aṣṭavimokṣa) are permanent or impermanent; one should seek whether the eight bases of mastery (aṣṭābhibhvāyatana), the nine successive concentrations (navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti), and the ten totalities (daśakṛtsnāyatana) are permanent or impermanent;

one should seek whether the eight liberations are pleasant or painful; one should seek whether the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive concentrations, and the ten totalities are pleasant or painful.

One should seek the eight liberations whether they are self or non-self; one should seek the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities whether they are self or non-self;

one should seek the eight liberations whether they are pure or impure; one should seek the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities whether they are pure or impure.
If there are those who, seeking such dharmas as these, practice prajñā, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). “Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters seek the eight liberations (aṣṭavimokṣa) as either permanent or impermanent; or seek the eight bases of mastery (abhibhvāyatana), the nine successive attainments (anupūrvavihārasamāpatti), and the ten totalities (kṛtsnāyatana) as either permanent or impermanent;”

They seek whether the eight liberations are pleasant or painful; they seek whether the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten totalities are pleasant or painful.
They seek whether the eight liberations are self or non-self; they seek whether the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten totalities are self or non-self.
They seek whether the eight liberations are pure or impure; they seek whether the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten totalities are pure or impure.
Kauśika, I declare that one who practices prajñāpāramitā by relying on such dharmas as these is practicing a semblance of prajñāpāramitā characterized by apprehension.
As previously stated, you should know that all these are descriptions of a semblance of the prajñāpāramitā that involves apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, should speak of the four foundations of mindfulness as either permanent or impermanent; speak of the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path as either permanent or impermanent;

speak of the four foundations of mindfulness as either pleasant or painful; speak of the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path as either pleasant or painful;

speak of the four foundations of mindfulness as either self or non-self; [they should likewise speak of] the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path as either self or non-self.

He speaks of the four foundations of mindfulness as either pure or impure; he speaks of the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path as either pure or impure.
If there are those who can practice *prajñā* by relying on such dharmas as these, they are practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Furthermore, it is said:

one who practices *prajñā* should seek whether the four foundations of mindfulness are permanent or impermanent; they should seek whether the four right efforts, up to and including the eightfold noble path, are permanent or impermanent.

One should seek whether the four foundations of mindfulness are pleasant or painful; one should seek whether the four right efforts, up to and including the eightfold noble path, are pleasant or painful.
One should seek whether the four foundations of mindfulness are self or non-self; one should seek whether the four right efforts, up to and including the eightfold noble path, are self or non-self.
One should seek whether the four foundations of mindfulness are pure or impure; one should seek whether the four right efforts, up to and including the eightfold noble path, are pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice prajñā, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). "Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters seek the four foundations of mindfulness as either permanent or impermanent, or seek the four right efforts up to the eightfold noble path as either permanent or impermanent; [they are practicing the perfection of wisdom]."
They seek whether the four foundations of mindfulness are pleasant or painful; they seek whether the four right efforts, up to and including the eightfold noble path, are pleasant or painful.
They seek whether the four foundations of mindfulness are self or non-self; they seek whether the four right efforts, up to and including the eightfold noble path, are self or non-self.
They seek whether the four foundations of mindfulness are pure or impure; they seek whether the four right efforts, up to and including the eightfold noble path, are pure or impure.
Kauśika, I declare that one who practices the perfection of wisdom by relying on such dharmas as these is practicing a semblance of the perfection of wisdom that is characterized by apprehension.
As previously explained, you should know that all these are descriptions of a semblance of the prajñāpāramitā that involves apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment, speak of the liberation door of emptiness as either permanent or impermanent, or speak of the liberation doors of signlessness and wishlessness as either permanent or impermanent;
speak of the liberation door of emptiness as either pleasant or painful, or speak of the liberation doors of signlessness and wishlessness as either pleasant or painful;
speak of the liberation door of emptiness as either self or non-self, or speak of the liberation doors of signlessness and wishlessness as either self or non-self;
To speak of the gate of liberation of emptiness as either pure or impure, and to speak of the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness as either pure or impure—
if one is able to practice prajñā based upon such dharmas as these, this is the practice of the perfection of prajñā.
Furthermore, it is said:

One who practices prajñā should seek the gate of liberation of emptiness as either permanent or impermanent; one should seek the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness as either permanent or impermanent;
one should seek the gate of liberation of emptiness as either pleasant or painful; one should seek the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness as either pleasant or painful.
One should seek the gate of liberation of emptiness whether it be self or non-self; one should seek the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness whether they be self or non-self;
one should seek the gate of liberation of emptiness whether it be pure or impure; one should seek the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness whether they be pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice prajñā, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). "Kauśika!
