If good sons and good daughters seek the gate of liberation of emptiness (śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha) as either permanent or impermanent, or seek the gates of liberation of signlessness (animitta) and wishlessness (apraṇihita) as either permanent or impermanent; [they are practicing the perfection of wisdom]."
They seek whether the gate of liberation of emptiness is pleasant or painful; they seek whether the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness are pleasant or painful.
They seek whether the gate of liberation of emptiness is self or non-self; they seek whether the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness are self or non-self.
They seek whether the gate of liberation of emptiness is pure or impure; they seek whether the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness are pure or impure.
Kauśika, I declare that one who practices the perfection of wisdom by relying on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of wisdom characterized by apprehension.
As previously stated, you should know that all these are descriptions of a semblance of the prajñāpāramitā that involves apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, speak of the five eyes as being either permanent or impermanent, or speak of the six supernormal powers as being either permanent or impermanent;
speak of the five eyes as being either pleasant or painful, or speak of the six supernormal powers as being either pleasant or painful;
speak of the five eyes as being either self or non-self, or speak of the six supernormal powers as being either self or non-self;
One speaks of the five eyes, whether pure or impure; one speaks of the six supernormal powers, whether pure or impure.
If there is anyone who practices prajñā by relying on such dharmas as these, this is the practice of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Furthermore, it is said:
One who practices prajñā should seek whether the five eyes are permanent or impermanent, and should seek whether the six supernormal powers are permanent or impermanent;
one should seek whether the five eyes are pleasant or painful, and should seek whether the six supernormal powers are pleasant or painful.
One should seek the five eyes whether they are self or non-self; one should seek the six supernormal powers whether they are self or non-self;
one should seek the five eyes whether they are pure or impure; one should seek the six supernormal powers whether they are pure or impure.
If there are those who are able to seek such dharmas as these and practice *prajñā*, they are practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*. "Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters, and others like them, thus seek the five eyes whether as permanent or impermanent, or seek the six supernormal powers whether as permanent or impermanent; [they are practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*]."
Seeking the five eyes as either pleasant or painful; seeking the six supernormal powers as either pleasant or painful;
seeking the five eyes as either self or non-self; seeking the six supernormal powers as either self or non-self;
seeking the five eyes as either pure or impure; seeking the six supernormal powers as either pure or impure.
“Kauśika, I declare that one who practices the perfection of wisdom by relying on such dharmas as these is practicing a semblance of the perfection of wisdom that is characterized by apprehension.”
As previously stated, you should know that all these are descriptions of a semblance of the prajñāpāramitā that involves apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, should speak of the ten powers of a Buddha as being either permanent or impermanent; or speak of the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha as being either permanent or impermanent;

or speak of the ten powers of a Buddha as being either pleasant or painful; or speak of the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha as being either pleasant or painful;

They speak of the ten powers of a Buddha as being with self or without self; they speak of the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha as being with self or without self.

They speak of the ten powers of a Buddha as being pure or impure; they speak of the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha as being pure or impure.
If there are those who are able to practice *prajñā* by relying on such teachings as these, they are practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Furthermore, it is said:

one who practices *prajñā* should seek whether the ten powers of a Buddha are permanent or impermanent; one should seek whether the four fearlessnesses, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, are permanent or impermanent.

One should seek whether the ten powers of a Buddha are pleasant or painful; one should seek whether the four fearlessnesses, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, are pleasant or painful.

One should seek whether the ten powers of a Buddha are self or non-self; one should seek whether the four fearlessnesses, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, are self or non-self.

One should seek whether the ten powers of a Buddha are pure or impure; one should seek whether the four fearlessnesses, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, are pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice prajñā, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). "Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters seek the ten powers of a Buddha—whether as permanent or impermanent—and seek the four fearlessnesses, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha—whether as permanent or impermanent; [they are practicing the perfection of wisdom]."
Seeking whether the ten powers of a Buddha are pleasant or painful; seeking whether the four fearlessnesses, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, are pleasant or painful;
seeking whether the ten powers of a Buddha are self or non-self; seeking whether the four fearlessnesses, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, are self or non-self;
seeking whether the ten powers of a Buddha are pure or impure; seeking whether the four fearlessnesses, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, are pure or impure.
Kauśika, I declare that one who practices the perfection of wisdom by relying on such dharmas as these is practicing a semblance of the perfection of wisdom characterized by apprehension.
As previously stated, you should know that all these are descriptions of a semblance of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) characterized by apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, speak of the quality of non-forgetfulness as either permanent or impermanent, or speak of the nature of constant equanimity as either permanent or impermanent;
speak of the quality of non-forgetfulness as either pleasant or painful, or speak of the nature of constant equanimity as either pleasant or painful;
speak of the quality of non-forgetfulness as either self or non-self, or speak of the nature of constant equanimity as either self or non-self;
To speak of the quality of non-forgetfulness as either pure or impure, and to speak of the nature of constant equanimity as either pure or impure—
if one is able to rely upon such dharmas to practice prajñā, this is the practice of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Furthermore, it is said:
One who practices prajñāpāramitā should seek the quality of non-forgetfulness as either permanent or impermanent; one should seek the nature of constant equanimity as either permanent or impermanent;
one should seek the quality of non-forgetfulness as either pleasant or painful; and one should seek the nature of constant equanimity as either pleasant or painful.
One should seek the quality of non-forgetfulness whether it be self or selfless; one should seek the state of constant equanimity whether it be self or selfless;
one should seek the quality of non-forgetfulness whether it be pure or impure; and one should seek the state of constant equanimity whether it be pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice *prajñā*, they are practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*. "Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters seek the quality of non-forgetfulness (*asaṃpramoṣadharma*) as either permanent or impermanent, or seek the nature of constant equanimity (*upekṣā*) as either permanent or impermanent;
They seek the quality of non-forgetfulness whether it be pleasant or painful; they seek the state of constant equanimity whether it be pleasant or painful.
They seek the quality of non-forgetfulness whether it be self or non-self; they seek the state of constant equanimity whether it be self or non-self.
They seek the quality of non-forgetfulness whether it be pure or impure; they seek the state of constant equanimity whether it be pure or impure.
“Kauśika, I declare that one who practices the perfection of wisdom by relying on such dharmas as these is practicing a semblance of the perfection of wisdom that involves apprehension.”
As previously stated, you should know that all these are descriptions of a semblance of the prajñāpāramitā that involves apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, speak of all-knowledge as either permanent or impermanent; speak of the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects as either permanent or impermanent;
speak of all-knowledge as either pleasant or suffering; speak of the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects as either pleasant or suffering;
speak of all-knowledge as either self or non-self; speak of the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects as either self or non-self;
To speak of all-knowledge as either pure or impure, and to speak of the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects as either pure or impure—
if one is able to practice prajñā based on such dharmas as these, this is the practice of the perfection of prajñā.
Furthermore, it is said:

One who practices *prajñā* should seek omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) as either permanent or impermanent; one should seek the knowledge of the paths (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) as either permanent or impermanent;
one should seek omniscience as either pleasant or painful; one should seek the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects as either pleasant or painful.

One should seek omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) whether it be with self or without self; one should seek the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) whether they be with self or without self.
One should seek omniscience whether it be pure or impure; one should seek the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects whether they be pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice *prajñā*, they are practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*. "Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters seek omniscience (*sarvajñatā*)—whether it be permanent or impermanent—and seek the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), whether they be permanent or impermanent; [they are practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*]."

Seeking omniscience (sarvajñatā) as either pleasure or suffering; seeking the knowledge of the aspects of the path (mārgākārajñatā) and the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā) as either pleasure or suffering;
seeking omniscience as either self or non-self; seeking the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects as either self or non-self;
seeking omniscience as either pure or impure; seeking the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects as either pure or impure.
Kauśika, I declare that one who practices the perfection of wisdom by relying on such dharmas as these is practicing a semblance of the perfection of wisdom characterized by apprehension.
As previously stated, you should know that all these are descriptions of a semblance of the prajñāpāramitā that involves apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment, explain whether all dharani-doors are permanent or impermanent; explain whether all samadhi-doors are permanent or impermanent;
explain whether all dharani-doors are pleasant or painful; explain whether all samadhi-doors are pleasant or painful;
explain whether all dharani-doors are self or non-self; explain whether all samadhi-doors are self or non-self;
To speak of all dharani-doors as either pure or impure, and to speak of all samadhi-doors as either pure or impure—
if one is able to practice prajñā based on such dharmas as these, this is the practice of the perfection of prajñā (prajñāpāramitā).
Furthermore, it is said:
One who practices Prajñāpāramitā should seek all dhāraṇī-doors as either permanent or impermanent; one should seek all samādhi-doors as either permanent or impermanent;
one should seek all dhāraṇī-doors as either pleasant or painful; one should seek all samādhi-doors as either pleasant or painful.
One should seek all dharani-doors whether they involve a self or are without self; one should seek all samadhi-doors whether they involve a self or are without self;
one should seek all dharani-doors whether they are pure or impure; one should seek all samadhi-doors whether they are pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice prajñā, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). "Kauśika!
If good sons and good daughters seek all dharanī-doors, whether they be permanent or impermanent, and seek all samādhi-doors, whether they be permanent or impermanent;..."
They seek all dharani-gates whether as pleasure or as pain; they seek all samadhi-gates whether as pleasure or as pain.
They seek all dharani-gates whether as self or as non-self; they seek all samadhi-gates whether as self or as non-self.
They seek all dharani-gates whether as pure or as impure; they seek all samadhi-gates whether as pure or as impure.
Kauśika, I declare that one who practices the perfection of wisdom by relying on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of wisdom characterized by apprehension.
As previously stated, you should know that all these are descriptions of a semblance of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) based on apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment, were to speak of the stage of entering the stream and the fruit of stream-entry as either permanent or impermanent; speak of the stage of entering once-returning and the fruit of once-returning, the stage of entering non-returning and the fruit of non-returning, and the stage of entering arhatship and the fruit of arhatship as either permanent or impermanent;

speak of the stage of entering the stream and the fruit of stream-entry as either pleasant or painful; speak of the stage of entering once-returning and the fruit of once-returning, the stage of entering non-returning and the fruit of non-returning, and the stage of entering arhatship and the fruit of arhatship as either pleasant or painful;

speak of the stage of entering the stream and the fruit of stream-entry as either self or non-self; speak of the stage of entering once-returning and the fruit of once-returning, the stage of entering non-returning and the fruit of non-returning, and the stage of entering arhatship and the fruit of arhatship as either self or non-self;

He speaks of the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry and the fruit of stream-entry, whether pure or impure; he speaks of the candidate for the fruit of once-returning and the fruit of once-returning, the candidate for the fruit of non-returning and the fruit of non-returning, and the candidate for the fruit of arhatship and the fruit of arhatship, whether pure or impure.
If there is one who can practice *prajñā* by relying on such dharmas as these, this is the practice of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Furthermore, it is said:

One who practices *prajñā* should seek whether the stage of entering the stream (*srotāpanna-pratipannaka*) and the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna-phala*) are permanent or impermanent; one should likewise seek whether the stage of entering the once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin-pratipannaka*) up to the fruit of arhatship (*arhat-phala*) are permanent or impermanent.

One should seek the fruit of stream-entry and the path of stream-entry, whether as pleasure or as pain; one should seek the fruits up to arhatship and their respective paths, whether as pleasure or as pain.

One should seek the fruit of stream-entry and the path of stream-entry, whether as self or as non-self; one should seek the fruits up to arhatship and their respective paths, whether as self or as non-self.

One should seek the fruit of stream-entry and the path of stream-entry, whether as pure or as impure; one should seek the fruits up to arhatship and their respective paths, whether as pure or as impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice prajñā, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). "Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters, and so forth, thus seek the fruit of stream-entry or the state of being a candidate for stream-entry—whether as permanent or impermanent—and seek the fruit of once-returning up to the fruit of arhatship—whether as permanent or impermanent; [they are practicing the perfection of wisdom]."
To seek the state of entering the stream or the fruit of stream-entry as either pleasure or pain; to seek the state of entering once-returning up to the fruit of arhatship as either pleasure or pain;
to seek the state of entering the stream or the fruit of stream-entry as either self or non-self; to seek the state of entering once-returning up to the fruit of arhatship as either self or non-self;
to seek the state of entering the stream or the fruit of stream-entry as either pure or impure; to seek the state of entering once-returning up to the fruit of arhatship as either pure or impure.
Kauśika, I declare that one who practices the perfection of wisdom by relying on such dharmas as these is practicing a semblance of the perfection of wisdom that involves apprehension.
As previously stated, you should know that all these are descriptions of a semblance of the prajñāpāramitā characterized by apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons, good daughters, and others who have resolved upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment should speak of all pratyekabuddha-enlightenment as either permanent or impermanent; speak of all pratyekabuddha-enlightenment as either pleasant or painful; speak of all pratyekabuddha-enlightenment as either self or non-self; or speak of all pratyekabuddha-enlightenment as either pure or impure.
If there are those who are able to practice *prajñā* by relying on such teachings as these, they are practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Furthermore, it is said:

one who practices *prajñā* should seek all pratyekabuddha-enlightenment as either permanent or impermanent; should seek all pratyekabuddha-enlightenment as either pleasant or painful; should seek all pratyekabuddha-enlightenment as either self or non-self; and should seek all pratyekabuddha-enlightenment as either pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice *prajñā*, they are practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*.

"Kauśika! If good sons and good daughters seek all pratyekabuddha-enlightenment as either permanent or impermanent; seek all pratyekabuddha-enlightenment as either pleasant or painful; seek all pratyekabuddha-enlightenment as either self or non-self; seek all pratyekabuddha-enlightenment as either pure or impure."
Kauśika, I say that one who practices the perfection of wisdom by relying on such dharmas as these is practicing a semblance of the perfection of wisdom characterized by apprehension.
As previously stated, you should know that all these are explanations of a semblance of the prajñāpāramitā that involves apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons, good daughters, and others who have resolved upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment should explain all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as either permanent or impermanent; explain all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as either pleasant or painful; explain all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as either self or non-self; or explain all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as either pure or impure.
If there are those who are able to practice *prajñā* by relying on such teachings as these, they are practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Furthermore, it is said:

one who practices *prajñā* should seek whether all the practices of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are permanent or impermanent; one should seek whether all the practices of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are pleasant or painful; one should seek whether all the practices of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas involve a self or are without self; and one should seek whether all the practices of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice *prajñā*, they are practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*.

"Kauśika! If good sons and good daughters seek all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as either permanent or impermanent; seek all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as either pleasant or painful; seek all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as either self or non-self; seek all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as either pure or impure."
Kauśika, I declare that one who practices the perfection of wisdom by relying on such dharmas as these is practicing a semblance of the perfection of wisdom that is characterized by apprehension.
As previously stated, you should know that all these are descriptions of a semblance of the prajñāpāramitā that involves apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, speak of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas as being either permanent or impermanent; speak of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas as being either pleasant or painful; speak of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas as being either self or non-self; or speak of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas as being either pure or impure.
If there are those who are able to practice *prajñā* by relying on such teachings as these, they are practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Furthermore, it is said:

one who practices *prajñā* should seek the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*) of the Buddhas as either permanent or impermanent; should seek the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas as either pleasant or painful; should seek the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas as either self or non-self; and should seek the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas as either pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice prajñā, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). "Kauśika!

If sons of good family or daughters of good family seek the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas as either permanent or impermanent; seek the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas as either pleasant or painful; seek the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas as either self or non-self; or seek the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas as either pure or impure."

Kauśika, I declare that one who practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) by relying on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of wisdom characterized by apprehension (upalambha).
"As previously stated, you should know that all these are descriptions of a semblance of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) characterized by apprehension.
Then, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
How is it that those sons and daughters of good family who speak of a dhyāna-pāramitā involving apprehension are said to be speaking of a counterfeit dhyāna-pāramitā?
The Buddha said, “Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, speak of form as either permanent or impermanent, or speak of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as either permanent or impermanent;”
One speaks of form as either pleasant or painful; one speaks of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as either pleasant or painful.
One speaks of form as either self or non-self; one speaks of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as either self or non-self.
One speaks of form as either pure or impure; one speaks of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as either pure or impure.
If there is one who is able to practice meditative concentration (dhyāna) by relying on such dharmas as these, this is the practice of the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā).
Furthermore, it is said:

One who practices meditative concentration should investigate whether form (rūpa) is permanent or impermanent; one should investigate whether feeling (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), formations (saṃskāra), and consciousness (vijñāna) are permanent or impermanent.
One should investigate whether form is pleasant or painful; one should investigate whether feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are pleasant or painful.
One should investigate whether form is self or non-self; one should investigate whether feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are self or non-self.
One should investigate whether form is pure or impure; one should investigate whether feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), they are practicing the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*). "Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters seek form (*rūpa*) as either permanent or impermanent, and seek feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) as either permanent or impermanent;
One seeks whether form is pleasant or painful; one seeks whether feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are pleasant or painful.
One seeks whether form is self or non-self; one seeks whether feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are self or non-self.
One seeks whether form is pure or impure; one seeks whether feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are pure or impure.

Kauśika, I declare that one who practices meditative concentration (dhyāna) by relying on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā) characterized by the apprehension of something to be attained.
As previously stated, you should know that all these refer to the semblance of the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyāna-pāramitā) characterized by apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, should speak of the sense base of the eye as either permanent or impermanent; speak of the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind as either permanent or impermanent;
speak of the sense base of the eye as either pleasant or painful; speak of the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind as either pleasant or painful;
speak of the sense base of the eye as either self or non-self; and speak of the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind as either self or non-self; [they would be speaking erroneously].
To speak of the sense-base of the eye as either pure or impure, and to speak of the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind as either pure or impure—
if one is able to practice meditative concentration based upon such dharmas as these, this is the practice of the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyāna-pāramitā).
Furthermore, it is said:

One who practices meditative concentration should investigate whether the sense base of the eye is permanent or impermanent; one should investigate whether the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are permanent or impermanent;
one should investigate whether the sense base of the eye is pleasant or painful; one should investigate whether the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are pleasant or painful.
One should seek whether the eye-base is self or non-self; one should seek whether the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases are self or non-self.
One should seek whether the eye-base is pure or impure; one should seek whether the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases are pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), this is the practice of the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*). "Kauśika!

If sons of good family or daughters of good family seek in this manner whether the sense base of the eye (*cakṣurāyatana*) is permanent or impermanent, and seek whether the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind (*śrotra-ghrāṇa-jihvā-kāya-manas-āyatana*) are permanent or impermanent;
They seek whether the eye-base is pleasant or painful; they seek whether the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases are pleasant or painful.
They seek whether the eye-base is self or non-self; they seek whether the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases are self or non-self.
They seek whether the eye-base is pure or impure; they seek whether the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases are pure or impure.

Kauśika, I say that for one who practices meditative concentration based on such dharmas, it is called the practice of a semblance perfection of meditative concentration characterized by apprehension.
As previously stated, one should know that all these refer to the semblance of the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*) characterized by apprehension (*upalambha*).
"Furthermore, Kauśika!..."

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, explain whether the sphere of form is permanent or impermanent; explain whether the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena are permanent or impermanent;
explain whether the sphere of form is pleasant or painful; explain whether the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena are pleasant or painful;
explain whether the sphere of form is self or non-self; explain whether the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena are self or non-self;
One speaks of the sense-field of form as either pure or impure, and speaks of the sense-fields of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena as either pure or impure.
If there is one who is able to practice meditative concentration based upon such phenomena as these, this is the practice of the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā).
Furthermore, it is said:

One who practices dhyāna should investigate whether the sphere of form (rūpāyatana) is permanent or impermanent; one should investigate whether the spheres of sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental objects (dharmāyatana) are permanent or impermanent;
one should investigate whether the sphere of form is pleasant or painful; one should investigate whether the spheres of sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental objects are pleasant or painful.
One should investigate whether the sphere of form is self or non-self; one should investigate whether the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena are self or non-self.
One should investigate whether the sphere of form is pure or impure; one should investigate whether the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena are pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), they are practicing the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*). "Kauśika!

If sons or daughters of good family seek whether the sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) is permanent or impermanent, and seek whether the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) are permanent or impermanent;
They seek whether the sphere of form is pleasant or painful; they seek whether the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental objects are pleasant or painful.
They seek whether the sphere of form is self or non-self; they seek whether the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental objects are self or non-self.
They seek whether the sphere of form is pure or impure; they seek whether the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental objects are pure or impure.

Kauśika, I declare that one who practices meditative concentration by relying on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of meditative concentration characterized by the apprehension of something to be attained.
As previously stated, you should know that all these refer to the semblance of the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*) characterized by apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment, explain whether the eye-element is permanent or impermanent; explain whether the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, eye-contact, and all sensations produced with eye-contact as condition are permanent or impermanent;

explain whether the eye-element is pleasant or painful; explain whether the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, eye-contact, and all sensations produced with eye-contact as condition are pleasant or painful;

explain whether the eye-element is self or non-self; explain whether the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, eye-contact, and all sensations produced with eye-contact as condition are self or non-self;

One speaks of the eye-element as either pure or impure; one speaks of the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, eye-contact, and all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition as either pure or impure.
If there is one who is able to practice meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) by relying on such dharmas as these, this is the practice of the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*).
Furthermore, it is said:

One who practices meditative concentration should investigate whether the eye-element is permanent or impermanent; one should investigate whether the form-element, and so forth, up to the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, are permanent or impermanent.

One should seek whether the eye-element is pleasant or painful; one should seek whether the form-element, and so forth, up to the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, are pleasant or painful.

One should seek whether the eye-element is self or non-self; one should seek whether the form-element, and so forth, up to the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, are self or non-self.

One should seek whether the eye-element is pure or impure; one should seek whether the form-element, and so forth, up to the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, are pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), they are practicing the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*). "Kauśika!

If sons of good family or daughters of good family seek in this way whether the eye-element is permanent or impermanent, or seek whether the form-element, up to the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, are permanent or impermanent;
They seek whether the eye-element is pleasant or painful; they seek whether the form-element, and so on up to the feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, are pleasant or painful.
They seek whether the eye-element is self or non-self; they seek whether the form-element, and so on up to the feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, are self or non-self.
They seek whether the eye-element is pure or impure; they seek whether the form-element, and so on up to the feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, are pure or impure.

Kauśika, I declare that one who practices meditative concentration based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of meditative concentration characterized by the apprehension of objects.
As previously explained, you should know that all of these describe a semblance of the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyāna-pāramitā) characterized by apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, explain whether the ear-element is permanent or impermanent; explain whether the sound-element, the ear-consciousness-element, ear-contact, and the various feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition are permanent or impermanent;

explain whether the ear-element is pleasant or painful; explain whether the sound-element, the ear-consciousness-element, ear-contact, and the various feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition are pleasant or painful;

explain whether the ear-element is self or non-self; and explain whether the sound-element, the ear-consciousness-element, ear-contact, and the various feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition are self or non-self.

One speaks of the ear element as either pure or impure; one speaks of the sound element, the ear-consciousness element, ear-contact, and the various feelings arisen with ear-contact as condition as either pure or impure.
If there is one who is able to practice meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) by relying on such dharmas as these, this is the practice of the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*).
Furthermore, it is said:

One who practices meditative concentration should investigate whether the ear element is permanent or impermanent; one should investigate whether the sound element, and even the various feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition, are permanent or impermanent.

One should seek whether the ear-element is pleasant or painful; one should seek whether the sound-element, and so forth, up to the various feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition, are pleasant or painful.

One should seek whether the ear-element is self or non-self; one should seek whether the sound-element, and so forth, up to the various feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition, are self or non-self.

One should seek whether the ear-element is pure or impure; one should seek whether the sound-element, and so forth, up to the various feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition, are pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), they are practicing the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*). "Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters seek the ear-element (*śrotradhātu*) as either permanent or impermanent, and seek the sound-element (*śabdadhātu*) up to the various feelings (*vedanā*) produced with ear-contact as a condition as either permanent or impermanent;
They seek whether the ear-element is pleasant or painful; they seek whether the sound-element, and so on up to the various feelings produced with ear-contact as condition, are pleasant or painful.
They seek whether the ear-element is self or non-self; they seek whether the sound-element, and so on up to the various feelings produced with ear-contact as condition, are self or non-self.
They seek whether the ear-element is pure or impure; they seek whether the sound-element, and so on up to the various feelings produced with ear-contact as condition, are pure or impure.
Kauśika, I declare that one who practices dhyāna by relying on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of dhyāna characterized by the apprehension of something to be attained.
As previously stated, one should know that all these refer to the semblance of the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*) characterized by apprehension (*upalambha*).
"Furthermore, Kauśika!..."

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, explain whether the nose-element is permanent or impermanent; explain whether the odor-element, the nose-consciousness-element, nose-contact, and the various sensations produced with nose-contact as a condition are permanent or impermanent;

explain whether the nose-element is pleasant or painful; explain whether the odor-element, the nose-consciousness-element, nose-contact, and the various sensations produced with nose-contact as a condition are pleasant or painful;

explain whether the nose-element is self or non-self; explain whether the odor-element, the nose-consciousness-element, nose-contact, and the various sensations produced with nose-contact as a condition are self or non-self.

One speaks of the nose element as either pure or impure; one speaks of the odor element, the nose-consciousness element, nose-contact, and the various feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition as either pure or impure.

If there are those who are able to practice meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) by relying on such teachings as these, this is the practice of the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*).
Furthermore, it is said:

one who practices meditative concentration should investigate whether the nose-element (*ghrāṇadhātu*) is permanent or impermanent; one should investigate whether the odor-element (*gandhadhātu*), and so forth up to the various feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition, are permanent or impermanent.

One should seek whether the nose element is pleasant or painful; one should seek whether the fragrance element, and so on up to the various feelings produced with nose-contact as condition, are pleasant or painful.

One should seek whether the nose element is self or non-self; one should seek whether the fragrance element, and so on up to the various feelings produced with nose-contact as condition, are self or non-self.

One should seek whether the nose element is pure or impure; one should seek whether the fragrance element, and so on up to the various feelings produced with nose-contact as condition, are pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), this is the practice of the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*). "Kauśika!

If sons of good family or daughters of good family seek the nose-element (*ghrāṇadhātu*) as either permanent or impermanent, and seek the odor-element (*gandhadhātu*) up to the various feelings produced with nose-contact as condition (*ghrāṇasaṃsparśapratyayaja-vedanā*) as either permanent or impermanent;..."

One seeks whether the nose element is pleasant or painful; one seeks whether the fragrance element, and so on up to the various feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition, are pleasant or painful.
One seeks whether the nose element is self or non-self; one seeks whether the fragrance element, and so on up to the various feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition, are self or non-self.
One seeks whether the nose element is pure or impure; one seeks whether the fragrance element, and so on up to the various feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition, are pure or impure.
Kauśika, I say that one who practices meditative concentration by relying on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of meditative concentration characterized by apprehension.
As previously stated, one should know that all these refer to the semblance of the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*) characterized by apprehension.

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Scroll 137, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Part One: Chapter on the Measurement of Merits, Number Thirty-six. "Furthermore, Kauśika!..."

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, should speak of the tongue-element as either permanent or impermanent; speak of the taste-element, the tongue-consciousness-element, tongue-contact, and all feelings produced with tongue-contact as condition as either permanent or impermanent;

speak of the tongue-element as either pleasant or painful; speak of the taste-element, the tongue-consciousness-element, tongue-contact, and all feelings produced with tongue-contact as condition as either pleasant or painful;

speak of the tongue-element as either self or non-self; speak of the taste-element, the tongue-consciousness-element, tongue-contact, and all feelings produced with tongue-contact as condition as either self or non-self;

One speaks of the tongue element as either pure or impure; one speaks of the taste element, the tongue-consciousness element, tongue-contact, and the various feelings arising with tongue-contact as their condition as either pure or impure.

If there are those who are able to practice meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) by relying on such teachings as these, they are practicing the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*).
Furthermore, it is said:

one who practices meditative concentration should investigate whether the tongue-element (*jihvādhātu*) is permanent or impermanent; one should investigate whether the taste-element (*rasadhātu*), and so forth, up to the various feelings (*vedanā*) produced with tongue-contact (*jihvāsaṃsparśa*) as a condition, are permanent or impermanent.

One should investigate whether the tongue element is pleasant or painful; one should investigate whether the taste element, and even those sensations produced with tongue-contact as condition, are pleasant or painful.

One should investigate whether the tongue element is self or non-self; one should investigate whether the taste element, and even those sensations produced with tongue-contact as condition, are self or non-self.

One should investigate whether the tongue element is pure or impure; one should investigate whether the taste element, and even those sensations produced with tongue-contact as condition, are pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), they are practicing the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*). "Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters seek the tongue-element (*jihvādhātu*) as either permanent or impermanent, and seek the taste-element (*rasadhātu*) up to the various feelings (*vedanā*) produced with tongue-contact (*jihvā-saṃsparśa*) as a condition as either permanent or impermanent;

One seeks whether the tongue element is pleasant or painful; one seeks whether the taste element, and so on up to the various feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition, are pleasant or painful.
One seeks whether the tongue element is self or non-self; one seeks whether the taste element, and so on up to the various feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition, are self or non-self.
One seeks whether the tongue element is pure or impure; one seeks whether the taste element, and so on up to the various feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition, are pure or impure.
Kauśika, I say that for one who practices meditative concentration based on these dharmas, it is called the semblance perfection of meditative concentration that proceeds with apprehension.
As previously stated, you should know that all these refer to a semblance of the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*) characterized by apprehension (*upalambha*).
"Furthermore, Kauśika!..."

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, explain whether the body-element is permanent or impermanent; explain whether the touch-element, the body-consciousness-element, body-contact, and all sensations produced with body-contact as a condition are permanent or impermanent;

explain whether the body-element is pleasant or painful; explain whether the touch-element, the body-consciousness-element, body-contact, and all sensations produced with body-contact as a condition are pleasant or painful;

explain whether the body-element is self or non-self; and explain whether the touch-element, the body-consciousness-element, body-contact, and all sensations produced with body-contact as a condition are self or non-self.

One speaks of the body element as either pure or impure; one speaks of the contact element, the body-consciousness element, and body-contact, as well as the various feelings arising conditioned by body-contact, as either pure or impure.
If there are those who practice meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) by relying on such dharmas as these, this is the practice of the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*).
Furthermore, it is said:

one who practices meditative concentration should investigate whether the body-element (*kāyadhātu*) is permanent or impermanent; one should investigate whether the touch-element (*spraṣṭavyadhātu*) and even the various feelings produced with body-touch as a condition are permanent or impermanent.

One should investigate whether the body element is pleasant or painful; one should investigate whether the contact element, and even the various feelings produced with body-contact as condition, are pleasant or painful.

One should investigate whether the body element is self or non-self; one should investigate whether the contact element, and even the various feelings produced with body-contact as condition, are self or non-self.

One should investigate whether the body element is pure or impure; one should investigate whether the contact element, and even the various feelings produced with body-contact as condition, are pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), this is the practice of the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*). "Kauśika!

If sons of good family or daughters of good family seek in this way whether the body-element (*kāyadhātu*) is permanent or impermanent, and seek whether the contact-element (*spraṣṭavyadhātu*)—up to the various feelings produced with body-contact as a condition—is permanent or impermanent;

One seeks whether the body element is pleasant or painful; one seeks whether the contact element, up to and including the various feelings produced with body-contact as a condition, are pleasant or painful.

One seeks whether the body element is self or non-self; one seeks whether the contact element, up to and including the various feelings produced with body-contact as a condition, are self or non-self.
One seeks whether the body element is pure or impure; one seeks whether the contact element, up to and including the various feelings produced with body-contact as a condition, are pure or impure.
Kauśika, I declare that one who practices dhyāna-pāramitā by relying on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of dhyāna-pāramitā characterized by apprehension.
As previously stated, you should know that all these refer to the semblance of the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyāna-pāramitā) characterized by apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons, good daughters, and others who have resolved upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment should be taught that the mind-element (*manodhātu*) is either permanent or impermanent; that the dharma-element, the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*), as well as mental contact (*manaḥsaṃsparśa*) and the various feelings produced with mental contact as condition are either permanent or impermanent;

that the mind-element is either pleasant or painful; that the dharma-element, the mind-consciousness-element, as well as mental contact and the various feelings produced with mental contact as condition are either pleasant or painful;

or that the mind-element is either self or non-self; that the dharma-element, the mind-consciousness-element, as well as mental contact and the various feelings produced with mental contact as condition are either self or non-self.

He speaks of the mind-element as either pure or impure; he speaks of the dharma-element, the mind-consciousness-element, and mental contact, as well as the various feelings arising with mental contact as condition, as either pure or impure.

If there is one who is able to practice meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) by relying on such teachings as these, this is the practice of the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*).
Furthermore, it is said:

One who practices meditative concentration should investigate whether the mind-element (*manodhātu*) is permanent or impermanent; one should investigate whether the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*), and even the various feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition, are permanent or impermanent.

One should seek whether the mind-element (*manodhātu*) is pleasant or painful; one should seek whether the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*), and so forth up to the feelings produced with mind-contact as condition, are pleasant or painful.

One should seek whether the mind-element is self or non-self; one should seek whether the dharma-element, and so forth up to the feelings produced with mind-contact as condition, are self or non-self.
One should seek whether the mind-element is pure or impure; one should seek whether the dharma-element, and so forth up to the feelings produced with mind-contact as condition, are pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), they are practicing the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*). "Kauśika!

If sons or daughters of good family seek in this way whether the mental faculty (*manodhātu*) is permanent or impermanent, or seek whether the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) and even the various feelings produced with mental contact as a condition are permanent or impermanent; [they are practicing the perfection of meditative concentration]."
One seeks whether the mind-element is pleasant or painful; one seeks whether the dharma-element, and so on up to the various feelings produced with mind-contact as condition, are pleasant or painful.
One seeks whether the mind-element is self or non-self; one seeks whether the dharma-element, and so on up to the various feelings produced with mind-contact as condition, are self or non-self.
One seeks whether the mind-element is pure or impure; one seeks whether the dharma-element, and so on up to the various feelings produced with mind-contact as condition, are pure or impure.
Kauśika, I declare that one who practices meditative concentration based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of meditative concentration characterized by apprehension.
As previously stated, you should know that all these refer to the semblance of the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyāna-pāramitā) characterized by apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, should speak of the earth element as either permanent or impermanent, or speak of the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements as either permanent or impermanent;
should speak of the earth element as either pleasant or painful, or speak of the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements as either pleasant or painful;
should speak of the earth element as either self or non-self, or speak of the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements as either self or non-self;
To speak of the earth element as pure or impure, and to speak of the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements as pure or impure—
if one is able to rely upon such dharmas to practice meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), this is the practice of the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*).
Furthermore, it is said:

One who practices meditative concentration (dhyāna) should investigate whether the earth element is permanent or impermanent; one should investigate whether the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements are permanent or impermanent;
one should investigate whether the earth element is pleasant or painful; and one should investigate whether the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements are pleasant or painful.
One should seek whether the earth element is self or non-self; one should seek whether the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements are self or non-self.
One should seek whether the earth element is pure or impure; one should seek whether the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements are pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), they are practicing the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*). "Kauśika!
If good sons and good daughters seek the earth element as either permanent or impermanent, and seek the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements as either permanent or impermanent;..."
One seeks whether the earth element is pleasant or painful; one seeks whether the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements are pleasant or painful.
One seeks whether the earth element is self or non-self; one seeks whether the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements are self or non-self.
One seeks whether the earth element is pure or impure; one seeks whether the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements are pure or impure.
Kauśika, I declare that one who practices meditative concentration based on these dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of meditative concentration characterized by apprehension.
As previously stated, you should know that all these refer to the semblance of the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*) characterized by apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, explain whether ignorance is permanent or impermanent; explain whether volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, and old age, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are permanent or impermanent;

and explain whether ignorance is pleasant or painful; explain whether volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, and old age, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are pleasant or painful.

One speaks of ignorance as being either self or non-self; one speaks of volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, and old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair as being either self or non-self.

One speaks of ignorance as being either pure or impure; one speaks of volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, and old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair as being either pure or impure.

If there is one who is able to practice meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) by relying on such teachings as these, this is the practice of the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*).
Furthermore, it is said:

One who practices meditative concentration should investigate whether ignorance (*avidyā*) is permanent or impermanent; they should investigate whether the formative forces (*saṃskāra*), up to old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair, are permanent or impermanent.

One should investigate whether ignorance is pleasant or painful; one should investigate whether the formative forces, up to and including old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair, are pleasant or painful.

One should investigate whether ignorance is self or non-self; one should investigate whether the formative forces, up to and including old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair, are self or non-self.

One should investigate whether ignorance is pure or impure; one should investigate whether the formative forces, up to and including old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair, are pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), this is the practice of the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*). "Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters seek whether ignorance is permanent or impermanent, and seek whether formations (*saṃskāra*) up to old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair are permanent or impermanent; [this is the practice of the perfection of meditative concentration]."

One seeks whether ignorance is pleasant or painful; one seeks whether volitional formations, up to and including old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair, are pleasant or painful.
One seeks whether ignorance is self or non-self; one seeks whether volitional formations, up to and including old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair, are self or non-self.
One seeks whether ignorance is pure or impure; one seeks whether volitional formations, up to and including old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair, are pure or impure.
Kauśika, I declare that one who practices meditative concentration based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of meditative concentration characterized by apprehension.
As previously stated, you should know that all these refer to the semblance of the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā) characterized by apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment, should speak of the perfection of generosity as either permanent or impermanent; speak of the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom as either permanent or impermanent;

speak of the perfection of generosity as either pleasant or painful; speak of the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom as either pleasant or painful;

speak of the perfection of generosity as either self or non-self; or speak of the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom as either self or non-self; [they would be teaching emptiness].

He speaks of the perfection of generosity as being either pure or impure; he speaks of the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom as being either pure or impure.
If there is one who is able to practice meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) by relying on such dharmas as these, this is the practice of the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*).
Furthermore, it is said:

One who practices meditative concentration should seek whether the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*) is permanent or impermanent; they should seek whether the perfections from ethical discipline (*śīla*) up to wisdom (*prajñā*) are permanent or impermanent.
One should seek the perfection of generosity whether it be pleasant or painful; one should seek the perfections from ethical discipline up to wisdom whether they be pleasant or painful.
One should seek the perfection of generosity whether it be self or non-self; one should seek the perfections from ethical discipline up to wisdom whether they be self or non-self.
One should seek the perfection of generosity whether it be pure or impure; one should seek the perfections from ethical discipline up to wisdom whether they be pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), they are practicing the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*). "Kauśika!

If sons of good family or daughters of good family seek the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*) as either permanent or impermanent, or seek the perfections from ethical discipline up to wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) as either permanent or impermanent;
Seeking the perfection of generosity as either pleasure or pain; seeking the perfections from ethical discipline up to wisdom as either pleasure or pain;
seeking the perfection of generosity as either self or non-self; seeking the perfections from ethical discipline up to wisdom as either self or non-self;
seeking the perfection of generosity as either pure or impure; seeking the perfections from ethical discipline up to wisdom as either pure or impure.
Kauśika, I say that one who practices dhyāna-pāramitā by relying on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of dhyāna-pāramitā characterized by the apprehension of something to be attained.
As previously stated, you should know that all these refer to the semblance of the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*) characterized by apprehension (*upalambha*).
"Furthermore, Kauśika!"

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, explain that internal emptiness is either permanent or impermanent; or explain external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersal emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature—whether as permanent or impermanent;

Whether it be pleasure or pain, one speaks of internal emptiness; one speaks of external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all dharmas, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature—whether as pleasure or as pain.

He speaks of inner emptiness—whether as self or as non-self—and he speaks of outer emptiness, inner-and-outer emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersion emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common-characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all dharmas, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence—whether as self or as non-self.

One speaks of internal emptiness as being either pure or impure; one speaks of external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersion emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of non-apprehensibility, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence—each as being either pure or impure.

If there are those who are able to practice meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) by relying on such dharmas as these, this is the practice of the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*).
Furthermore, it is said:

"One who practices meditative concentration should seek whether internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*) is permanent or impermanent; one should seek whether external emptiness (*bahirdhā-śūnyatā*), up to and including the emptiness of non-existence and intrinsic nature (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*), is permanent or impermanent."

One should seek whether inner emptiness is pleasant or painful; one should seek whether outer emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, is pleasant or painful.
One should seek whether inner emptiness is self or non-self; one should seek whether outer emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, is self or non-self.
One should seek whether inner emptiness is pure or impure; one should seek whether outer emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, is pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), they are practicing the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*). "Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters seek internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*) as either permanent or impermanent, and seek external emptiness (*bahirdhā-śūnyatā*) up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*) as either permanent or impermanent;
One seeks whether inner emptiness is pleasant or painful; one seeks whether outer emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, is pleasant or painful.
One seeks whether inner emptiness is self or non-self; one seeks whether outer emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, is self or non-self.
One seeks whether inner emptiness is pure or impure; one seeks whether outer emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, is pure or impure.
“Kauśika, I say that one who practices meditative concentration based on these dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of meditative concentration that involves apprehension.”
As previously stated, you should know that all these refer to the semblance of the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*) characterized by apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment, speak of whether the *tathatā* (suchness) is permanent or impermanent; or speak of whether the *dharmadhātu*, *dharmatā*, non-erroneous nature, unchanging nature, equality, nature free from birth, fixedness of dharma, stability of dharma, the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm are permanent or impermanent;

or speak of whether the *tathatā* is pleasant or painful; or speak of whether the *dharmadhātu*, *dharmatā*, non-erroneous nature, unchanging nature, equality, nature free from birth, fixedness of dharma, stability of dharma, the limit of reality, the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm are pleasant or painful;

One speaks of whether the *tathatā* (suchness) is with self or without self; one speaks of whether the *dharmadhātu* (dharma-realm), *dharmatā* (dharma-nature), non-illusory nature, unchanging nature, equality, the state of being free from birth, the fixedness of dharmas, the stability of dharmas, the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm are with self or without self.

One speaks of whether the *tathatā* is pure or impure; one speaks of whether the *dharmadhātu*, *dharmatā*, non-illusory nature, unchanging nature, equality, the state of being free from birth, the fixedness of dharmas, the stability of dharmas, the limit of reality, the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm are pure or impure.

If there is one who is able to practice meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) by relying on such teachings as these, this is the practice of the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*).
Furthermore, it is said:

"One who practices meditative concentration should seek whether suchness (*tathatā*) is permanent or impermanent; one should seek whether the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), up to the inconceivable realm (*acintyadhātu*), is permanent or impermanent."
One should seek whether true thusness is pleasant or painful; one should seek whether the dharma-realm, up to and including the inconceivable realm, is pleasant or painful.
One should seek whether true thusness is self or non-self; one should seek whether the dharma-realm, up to and including the inconceivable realm, is self or non-self.
One should seek whether true thusness is pure or impure; one should seek whether the dharma-realm, up to and including the inconceivable realm, is pure or impure.

If there are those who are able to seek such dharmas as these and practice meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), they are practicing the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*). "Kauśika!
If good sons and good daughters, in this way, seek whether the Tathatā is permanent or impermanent, and seek whether the dharma-dhātu, up to the inconceivable realm, is permanent or impermanent;
Seeking the reality-limit as either pleasure or suffering; seeking the dharma-realm, up to the inconceivable realm, as either pleasure or suffering;
seeking the reality-limit as either self or non-self; seeking the dharma-realm, up to the inconceivable realm, as either self or non-self;
seeking the reality-limit as either pure or impure; seeking the dharma-realm, up to the inconceivable realm, as either pure or impure.
Kauśika, I declare that one who practices meditative concentration by relying on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of meditative concentration characterized by apprehension.
As previously explained, you should know that all these refer to the semblance of the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyāna-pāramitā) characterized by apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, should speak of the Noble Truth of Suffering as either permanent or impermanent, or speak of the Noble Truths of Origination, Cessation, and the Path as either permanent or impermanent;
or speak of the Noble Truth of Suffering as either pleasant or painful, or speak of the Noble Truths of Origination, Cessation, and the Path as either pleasant or painful;

or speak of the Noble Truth of Suffering as either self or non-self, or speak of the Noble Truths of Origination, Cessation, and the Path as either self or non-self; [they would be speaking erroneously].
Whether one speaks of the noble truth of suffering as pure or impure, or speaks of the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path as pure or impure—
if there is one who is able to practice meditative concentration (dhyāna) by relying on such dharmas as these, this is the practice of the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā).
Furthermore, he spoke thus:

"One who practices dhyāna should seek whether the Noble Truth of Suffering is permanent or impermanent; one should seek whether the Noble Truths of Origination, Cessation, and the Path are permanent or impermanent;
one should seek whether the Noble Truth of Suffering is pleasant or painful; and one should seek whether the Noble Truths of Origination, Cessation, and the Path are pleasant or painful."
One should seek whether the noble truth of suffering is self or non-self; one should seek whether the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path are self or non-self;
one should seek whether the noble truth of suffering is pure or impure; one should seek whether the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path are pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), this is the practice of the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*). "Kauśika!

If sons of good family or daughters of good family seek the Noble Truth of Suffering as either permanent or impermanent, and seek the Noble Truths of Origination, Cessation, and the Path as either permanent or impermanent;..."
One seeks whether the noble truth of suffering is pleasant or painful; one seeks whether the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path are pleasant or painful.
One seeks whether the noble truth of suffering is self or non-self; one seeks whether the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path are self or non-self.
One seeks whether the noble truth of suffering is pure or impure; one seeks whether the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path are pure or impure.

Kauśika, I declare that one who practices meditative concentration by relying on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of meditative concentration characterized by the apprehension of entities.
As previously stated, you should know that all these refer to the semblance of the perfection of meditative concentration characterized by apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, should speak of the four dhyānas as either permanent or impermanent, or speak of the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions as either permanent or impermanent;
if they should speak of the four dhyānas as either pleasant or painful, or speak of the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions as either pleasant or painful;
