if they should speak of the four dhyānas as either self or non-self, or speak of the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions as either self or non-self;
To speak of the four dhyānas as either pure or impure, and to speak of the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions as either pure or impure—
if one is able to practice dhyāna by relying upon such dharmas as these, this is the practice of the perfection of dhyāna (dhyānapāramitā).
Furthermore, it is said:

One who practices dhyāna should seek whether the four dhyānas are permanent or impermanent; one should seek whether the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments are permanent or impermanent;
one should seek whether the four dhyānas are pleasant or painful; one should seek whether the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments are pleasant or painful.
One should seek the four dhyānas whether they are with self or without self; one should seek the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments whether they are with self or without self;
one should seek the four dhyānas whether they are pure or impure; one should seek the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments whether they are pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), they are practicing the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*). "Kauśika!

If sons of good family or daughters of good family seek the four dhyānas as either permanent or impermanent, or seek the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) and the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) as either permanent or impermanent;
They seek the four dhyānas as either pleasant or painful; they seek the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments as either pleasant or painful.
They seek the four dhyānas as either self or non-self; they seek the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments as either self or non-self.
They seek the four dhyānas as either pure or impure; they seek the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments as either pure or impure.

Kauśika, I declare that one who practices meditative concentration (dhyāna) by relying on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā) characterized by the apprehension of entities.
As previously stated, you should know that all these refer to a semblance of the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*) characterized by apprehension (*upalambha*).
"Furthermore, Kauśika!..."

If good sons, good daughters, and others who have resolved upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment should be told that the eight liberations are either permanent or impermanent; that the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten pervasive bases are either permanent or impermanent;
that the eight liberations are either pleasant or painful; that the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten pervasive bases are either pleasant or painful;

or that the eight liberations are either self or non-self; that the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten pervasive bases are either self or non-self; [they would be speaking erroneously].
To speak of the eight liberations as either pure or impure, and to speak of the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities as either pure or impure—
if one is able to rely upon such dharmas to practice meditative concentration, this is the practice of the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā).
Furthermore, it is said:

One who practices meditative concentration (dhyāna) should seek whether the eight liberations (aṣṭavimokṣa) are permanent or impermanent; one should seek whether the eight bases of mastery (aṣṭābhibhvāyatana), the nine successive attainments (navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti), and the ten totalities (daśakṛtsnāyatana) are permanent or impermanent;

one should seek whether the eight liberations are pleasant or painful; one should seek whether the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities are pleasant or painful.

One should seek the eight liberations whether they are self or non-self; one should seek the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities whether they are self or non-self.

One should seek the eight liberations whether they are pure or impure; one should seek the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities whether they are pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), they are practicing the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*). "Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters seek the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*) as either permanent or impermanent; if they seek the eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), the nine successive attainments (*anupūrvavihārasamāpatti*), and the ten totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*) as either permanent or impermanent;..."
They seek whether the eight liberations are pleasant or painful; they seek whether the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities are pleasant or painful.
They seek whether the eight liberations are self or non-self; they seek whether the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities are self or non-self.
They seek whether the eight liberations are pure or impure; they seek whether the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities are pure or impure.

Kauśika, I say that for one who practices meditative concentration based on such dharmas, it is called the practice of a semblance perfection of meditative concentration characterized by apprehension.
As previously explained, you should know that all of these describe a semblance of the perfection of meditative concentration characterized by apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment, should speak of the four foundations of mindfulness as either permanent or impermanent; speak of the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold noble path as either permanent or impermanent;

speak of the four foundations of mindfulness as either pleasant or painful; speak of the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold noble path as either pleasant or painful;

speak of the four foundations of mindfulness as either self or non-self; [and] speak of the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold noble path as either self or non-self;

He speaks of the four foundations of mindfulness as either pure or impure; he speaks of the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path as either pure or impure.

If there are those who are able to practice meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) by relying on such teachings as these, this is the practice of the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*).
Furthermore, it is said:

one who practices meditative concentration should seek the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) as either permanent or impermanent; one should seek the four right endeavors (*samyakprahāṇa*), up to and including the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*), as either permanent or impermanent.

One should seek whether the four foundations of mindfulness are pleasant or painful; one should seek whether the four right endeavors, up to and including the eight branches of the noble path, are pleasant or painful.

One should seek whether the four foundations of mindfulness are self or non-self; one should seek whether the four right endeavors, up to and including the eight branches of the noble path, are self or non-self.

One should seek whether the four foundations of mindfulness are pure or impure; one should seek whether the four right endeavors, up to and including the eight branches of the noble path, are pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), they are practicing the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*). "Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters seek the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) as either permanent or impermanent, or seek the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*) up to the eight branches of the noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*) as either permanent or impermanent;..."
They seek whether the four foundations of mindfulness are pleasant or painful; they seek whether the four right efforts, up to and including the eightfold noble path, are pleasant or painful.
They seek whether the four foundations of mindfulness are self or non-self; they seek whether the four right efforts, up to and including the eightfold noble path, are self or non-self.
They seek whether the four foundations of mindfulness are pure or impure; they seek whether the four right efforts, up to and including the eightfold noble path, are pure or impure.
Kauśika, I say that one who practices dhyāna-pāramitā by relying on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of dhyāna-pāramitā characterized by apprehension.
As previously stated, you should know that all these refer to the semblance of the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*) characterized by apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!"

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment, speak of the gate of liberation of emptiness as either permanent or impermanent, or speak of the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness as either permanent or impermanent;
speak of the gate of liberation of emptiness as either pleasant or painful, or speak of the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness as either pleasant or painful;
speak of the gate of liberation of emptiness as either self or non-self, or speak of the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness as either self or non-self;
To speak of the gate of liberation of emptiness as either pure or impure, and to speak of the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness as either pure or impure—
if one is able to rely upon such dharmas to practice meditative concentration, this is the practice of the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā).
Furthermore, it is said:

One who practices meditative concentration (dhyāna) should seek whether the gate of liberation of emptiness (śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha) is permanent or impermanent; one should seek whether the gates of liberation of signlessness (animitta) and wishlessness (apraṇihita) are permanent or impermanent;
one should seek whether the gate of liberation of emptiness is pleasant or painful; one should seek whether the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness are pleasant or painful.
One should seek the gate of liberation of emptiness whether it be self or non-self; one should seek the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness whether they be self or non-self;
one should seek the gate of liberation of emptiness whether it be pure or impure; one should seek the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness whether they be pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), they are practicing the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*). "Kauśika!

If sons or daughters of good family seek the liberation door of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha*)—whether it be permanent or impermanent—and seek the liberation doors of signlessness (*animitta*) and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*)—whether they be permanent or impermanent;..."
They seek whether the gate of liberation of emptiness is pleasant or painful; they seek whether the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness are pleasant or painful.
They seek whether the gate of liberation of emptiness is self or non-self; they seek whether the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness are self or non-self.
They seek whether the gate of liberation of emptiness is pure or impure; they seek whether the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness are pure or impure.
Kauśika, I say that one who practices meditative concentration based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of meditative concentration characterized by apprehension.
As previously stated, you should know that all these refer to the semblance of the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*) characterized by apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kausika!..."

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, speak of the five eyes as being either permanent or impermanent, or speak of the six supernormal powers as being either permanent or impermanent;
speak of the five eyes as being either pleasant or painful, or speak of the six supernormal powers as being either pleasant or painful;
speak of the five eyes as being either self or non-self, or speak of the six supernormal powers as being either self or non-self;
One speaks of the five eyes, whether they are pure or impure; one speaks of the six supernormal powers, whether they are pure or impure.

If there is anyone who is able to practice meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) by relying on such dharmas as these, this is the practice of the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*).
Furthermore, it is said:
One who practices meditative concentration should seek whether the five eyes are permanent or impermanent, and should seek whether the six supernormal powers are permanent or impermanent;
one should seek whether the five eyes are pleasant or painful, and should seek whether the six supernormal powers are pleasant or painful.
One should seek the five eyes whether they are self or non-self; one should seek the six supernormal powers whether they are self or non-self;
one should seek the five eyes whether they are pure or impure; one should seek the six supernormal powers whether they are pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), they are practicing the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*). "Kauśika!

If sons of good family or daughters of good family seek the five eyes, whether they are permanent or impermanent, or seek the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), whether they are permanent or impermanent;
They seek the five eyes as either pleasant or painful; they seek the six supernormal powers as either pleasant or painful.
They seek the five eyes as either self or non-self; they seek the six supernormal powers as either self or non-self.
They seek the five eyes as either pure or impure; they seek the six supernormal powers as either pure or impure.
Kauśika, I declare that one who practices meditative concentration based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of meditative concentration characterized by apprehension.
As previously stated, you should know that all these refer to the semblance of the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*) characterized by apprehension (*upalambha*).
"Furthermore, Kauśika!"

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, were to speak of the ten powers of a Buddha as being either permanent or impermanent; or speak of the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha as being either permanent or impermanent;

or speak of the ten powers of a Buddha as being either pleasant or painful; or speak of the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha as being either pleasant or painful;

He speaks of the ten powers of a Buddha as being either self or non-self; he speaks of the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha as being either self or non-self.

He speaks of the ten powers of a Buddha as being either pure or impure; he speaks of the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha as being either pure or impure.

If there are those who are able to practice meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) by relying on such dharmas as these, this is the practice of the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*).
Furthermore, it is said:

one who practices meditative concentration should seek whether the ten powers (*daśabala*) of a Buddha are permanent or impermanent; one should seek whether the four fearlessnesses (*caturvaiśāradya*), up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*), are permanent or impermanent.

One should seek whether the ten powers of a Buddha are pleasant or painful; one should seek whether the four fearlessnesses, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, are pleasant or painful.

One should seek whether the ten powers of a Buddha are self or non-self; one should seek whether the four fearlessnesses, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, are self or non-self.

One should seek whether the ten powers of a Buddha are pure or impure; one should seek whether the four fearlessnesses, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, are pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), this is the practice of the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*). "Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters seek the ten powers of a Buddha as either permanent or impermanent, or seek the four fearlessnesses up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha as either permanent or impermanent; [this is the practice of the perfection of meditative concentration]."

They seek whether the ten powers of a Buddha are pleasant or painful; they seek whether the four fearlessnesses, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, are pleasant or painful.
They seek whether the ten powers of a Buddha are self or non-self; they seek whether the four fearlessnesses, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, are self or non-self.
They seek whether the ten powers of a Buddha are pure or impure; they seek whether the four fearlessnesses, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, are pure or impure.
Kauśika, I say that one who practices dhyāna-pāramitā by relying on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of dhyāna-pāramitā characterized by the apprehension of something to be attained.
As previously stated, you should know that all these refer to a semblance of the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*) characterized by apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment, speak of the quality of non-forgetfulness as either permanent or impermanent, or speak of the nature of constant equanimity as either permanent or impermanent;
speak of the quality of non-forgetfulness as either pleasant or painful, or speak of the nature of constant equanimity as either pleasant or painful;
speak of the quality of non-forgetfulness as either self or non-self, or speak of the nature of constant equanimity as either self or non-self;
Whether the qualities of non-forgetfulness are pure or impure,

and whether the state of constant equanimity is pure or impure— if one is able to rely upon such dharmas as these to practice meditative concentration, this is the practice of the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā).
Furthermore, it is said:

One who practices dhyāna should seek whether the quality of non-forgetfulness is permanent or impermanent; one should seek whether the state of constant abiding in equanimity is permanent or impermanent;
one should seek whether the quality of non-forgetfulness is pleasant or painful; one should seek whether the state of constant abiding in equanimity is pleasant or painful.

One should seek the quality of non-forgetfulness, whether it be with a self or without a self; one should seek the state of constant abiding in equanimity, whether it be with a self or without a self.
One should seek the quality of non-forgetfulness, whether it be pure or impure; one should seek the state of constant abiding in equanimity, whether it be pure or impure.

If there are those who are able to seek such dharmas as these and practice meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), this is the practice of the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*). "Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters seek the quality of non-forgetfulness (*asaṃpramoṣadharma*) as either permanent or impermanent, or seek the nature of constant equanimity (*upekṣā*) as either permanent or impermanent;
They seek the quality of non-forgetfulness whether it be pleasant or painful; they seek the state of constant abiding in equanimity whether it be pleasant or painful.
They seek the quality of non-forgetfulness whether it be self or non-self; they seek the state of constant abiding in equanimity whether it be self or non-self.
They seek the quality of non-forgetfulness whether it be pure or impure; they seek the state of constant abiding in equanimity whether it be pure or impure.
Kauśika, I declare that one who practices meditative concentration based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of meditative concentration characterized by apprehension.
As previously explained, it should be understood that all these refer to the semblance of the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*) characterized by apprehension (*upalambha*).

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 138, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Part One: Chapter on the Measurement of Merits, Number Thirty, Section Three. "Furthermore, Kauśika!..."

If good sons, good daughters, and others, for the sake of those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, speak of omniscience as either permanent or impermanent, or speak of the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects as either permanent or impermanent;
if they speak of omniscience as either pleasant or suffering, or speak of the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects as either pleasant or suffering;
if they speak of omniscience as either self or non-self, or speak of the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects as either self or non-self;
To speak of all-knowledge as pure or impure, and to speak of the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects as pure or impure—
if one is able to practice meditative concentration by relying on such dharmas as these, this is the practice of the perfection of meditative concentration.
Furthermore, it is said:

One who practices dhyāna should seek omniscience (sarvajñatā) as either permanent or impermanent; one should seek the knowledge of the paths (mārgākārajñatā) and the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā) as either permanent or impermanent;
one should seek omniscience as either pleasant or painful; one should seek the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects as either pleasant or painful.

One should seek omniscience (sarvajñatā) whether it be with self or without self; one should seek the knowledge of the paths (mārgajñatā) and the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā) whether they be with self or without self.
One should seek omniscience whether it be pure or impure; one should seek the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects whether they be pure or impure.

If there are those who are able to seek such dharmas as these and practice meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), they are practicing the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*). "Kauśika!

If sons of good family or daughters of good family seek omniscience (*sarvajñatā*)—whether it be permanent or impermanent—and seek the knowledge of the paths (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*)—whether they be permanent or impermanent; [they are practicing the perfection of meditative concentration]."
Whether seeking all-knowledge as pleasure or suffering; whether seeking the knowledge of the aspects of the path or the knowledge of all aspects as pleasure or suffering;
whether seeking all-knowledge as self or non-self; whether seeking the knowledge of the aspects of the path or the knowledge of all aspects as self or non-self;
whether seeking all-knowledge as pure or impure; whether seeking the knowledge of the aspects of the path or the knowledge of all aspects as pure or impure.
Kauśika, I declare that one who practices meditative concentration by relying on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of meditative concentration characterized by apprehension.
As previously stated, you should know that all these refer to a semblance of the perfection of meditative concentration characterized by apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons, good daughters, and others who have resolved upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment should explain all dharani-doors as either permanent or impermanent, or explain all samadhi-doors as either permanent or impermanent;
explain all dharani-doors as either pleasant or painful, or explain all samadhi-doors as either pleasant or painful;
explain all dharani-doors as either self or non-self, or explain all samadhi-doors as either self or non-self;
He speaks of all dharanī-doors, whether pure or impure, and he speaks of all samādhi-doors, whether pure or impure.
If there is one who is able to practice meditative concentration (dhyāna) by relying on such dharmas as these, this is the practice of the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā).
Furthermore, it is said:
One who practices meditative concentration (dhyāna) should seek all doors of dhāraṇī as either permanent or impermanent; one should seek all doors of samādhi as either permanent or impermanent;
one should seek all doors of dhāraṇī as either pleasant or painful; one should seek all doors of samādhi as either pleasant or painful.
One should seek all dharani-doors whether they are with self or without self; one should seek all samadhi-doors whether they are with self or without self;
one should seek all dharani-doors whether they are pure or impure; one should seek all samadhi-doors whether they are pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), they are practicing the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*). "Kauśika!
If sons of good family or daughters of good family seek all doors of dhāraṇī, whether they be permanent or impermanent, and seek all doors of samādhi, whether they be permanent or impermanent;
They seek all dharani-gates as either pleasure or suffering; they seek all samadhi-gates as either pleasure or suffering.
They seek all dharani-gates as either self or non-self; they seek all samadhi-gates as either self or non-self.
They seek all dharani-gates as either pure or impure; they seek all samadhi-gates as either pure or impure.

Kauśika, I declare that one who practices meditative concentration (dhyāna) by relying on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā) characterized by apprehension (upalambha).
As previously stated, you should know that all these describe the semblance of the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā) characterized by apprehension (*upalambha*).
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment, were to speak of the stage of entering the stream and the fruit of the stream-enterer as either permanent or impermanent; were to speak of the stage of entering once-returning and the fruit of the once-returner, the stage of entering non-returning and the fruit of the non-returner, and the stage of entering arhatship and the fruit of the arhat as either permanent or impermanent;

were to speak of the stage of entering the stream and the fruit of the stream-enterer as either pleasant or painful; were to speak of the stage of entering once-returning and the fruit of the once-returner, the stage of entering non-returning and the fruit of the non-returner, and the stage of entering arhatship and the fruit of the arhat as either pleasant or painful;

were to speak of the stage of entering the stream and the fruit of the stream-enterer as either self or non-self; were to speak of the stage of entering once-returning and the fruit of the once-returner, the stage of entering non-returning and the fruit of the non-returner, and the stage of entering arhatship and the fruit of the arhat as either self or non-self; [they would be speaking falsely].

He speaks of the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry and the fruit of stream-entry, whether pure or impure; he speaks of the candidate for the fruit of once-returning and the fruit of once-returning, the candidate for the fruit of non-returning and the fruit of non-returning, and the candidate for the fruit of arhatship and the fruit of arhatship, whether pure or impure.
If there are those who are able to practice meditative concentration (dhyāna) by relying on such dharmas as these, this is the practice of the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā).
Furthermore, it is said:

one who practices meditative concentration should seek the fruit of the candidate for stream-entry (srotāpattipratipannaka) and the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpanna), whether they are permanent or impermanent; and one should seek the fruit of the candidate for once-returning up to the fruit of arhatship, whether they are permanent or impermanent.

One should seek whether the state of entering the stream and the fruit of stream-entry are pleasant or painful; one should seek whether the state of entering the once-returner path up to the fruit of arhatship are pleasant or painful.

One should seek whether the state of entering the stream and the fruit of stream-entry are self or non-self; one should seek whether the state of entering the once-returner path up to the fruit of arhatship are self or non-self.

One should seek whether the state of entering the stream and the fruit of stream-entry are pure or impure; one should seek whether the state of entering the once-returner path up to the fruit of arhatship are pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), they are practicing the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*). "Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters seek the stage of entering the stream (*srotāpattipratipannaka*) and the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*), whether as permanent or impermanent; or seek the stage of entering once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmipratipannaka*) up to the fruit of arhatship (*arhattvaphala*), whether as permanent or impermanent; [they are practicing the perfection of meditative concentration]."

One seeks the state of entering the stream and the fruit of stream-entry as either pleasant or painful; one seeks the state of entering the once-returner up to the fruit of arhatship as either pleasant or painful.

One seeks the state of entering the stream and the fruit of stream-entry as either self or non-self; one seeks the state of entering the once-returner up to the fruit of arhatship as either self or non-self.

One seeks the state of entering the stream and the fruit of stream-entry as either pure or impure; one seeks the state of entering the once-returner up to the fruit of arhatship as either pure or impure.
Kauśika, I say that one who practices meditative concentration based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of meditative concentration characterized by apprehension.
As previously explained, you should know that all these refer to the semblance of the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*) characterized by apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!..."

If there is one who is able to practice with diligence in accordance with such teachings as these, this is the practice of the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*).
Furthermore, it is said:

One who practices diligence should investigate whether the mind-element (*mano-dhātu*) is permanent or impermanent; one should investigate whether the dharma-element (*dharma-dhātu*), and even those sensations produced with mind-contact as a condition, are permanent or impermanent.

One should seek whether the mind-element (*manodhātu*) is pleasant or painful; one should seek whether the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*), and so on up to the various feelings produced with mind-contact as condition, are pleasant or painful.

One should seek whether the mind-element is self or non-self; one should seek whether the dharma-element, and so on up to the various feelings produced with mind-contact as condition, are self or non-self.

One should seek whether the mind-element is pure or impure; one should seek whether the dharma-element, and so on up to the various feelings produced with mind-contact as condition, are pure or impure.
If there are those who are able to seek such dharmas as these and practice with diligence, this is the practice of the perfection of diligence.

"Kauśika! If good sons and good daughters and others thus seek whether the mind-element (*manodhātu*) is permanent or impermanent; or seek whether the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*), and so on up to the various feelings produced with mind-contact as condition (*manas-saṃsparśapratyaya-utpanna-vedanā*), are permanent or impermanent; [this is the perfection of diligence]."

One seeks whether the mental faculty (*manas*) is pleasant or painful; one seeks whether the phenomena (*dharmas*), up to and including the various feelings produced with mental contact as a condition, are pleasant or painful.
One seeks whether the mental faculty is self or non-self; one seeks whether the phenomena, up to and including the various feelings produced with mental contact as a condition, are self or non-self.
One seeks whether the mental faculty is pure or impure; one seeks whether the phenomena, up to and including the various feelings produced with mental contact as a condition, are pure or impure.
Kauśika, I declare that one who practices diligence based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of diligence characterized by the apprehension of something to be attained.
As previously stated, you should know that all these are merely descriptions of a semblance of the perfection of diligence characterized by apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, were to speak of the earth element as either permanent or impermanent; speak of the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements as either permanent or impermanent;
speak of the earth element as either pleasant or painful; speak of the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements as either pleasant or painful;
speak of the earth element as either self or non-self; speak of the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements as either self or non-self;
To speak of the earth element as either pure or impure, and to speak of the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements as either pure or impure—
if one is able to rely upon such dharmas to practice with diligence, this is the practice of the perfection of diligence (vīrya-pāramitā).
Furthermore, it is said:

One who practices diligence should investigate whether the earth element is permanent or impermanent; one should investigate whether the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements are permanent or impermanent;
one should investigate whether the earth element is pleasant or painful; one should investigate whether the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements are pleasant or painful.
One should investigate whether the earth element is self or non-self; one should investigate whether the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements are self or non-self.
One should investigate whether the earth element is pure or impure; one should investigate whether the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements are pure or impure.
If there are those who are able to seek such dharmas as these and practice with diligence, this is the practice of the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*). "Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters seek the earth element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*) as either permanent or impermanent, and seek the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements (*ab-, tejo-, vāyu-, ākāśa-, vijñāna-dhātu*) as either permanent or impermanent;
One seeks whether the earth element is pleasant or painful; one seeks whether the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements are pleasant or painful.
One seeks whether the earth element is self or non-self; one seeks whether the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements are self or non-self.
One seeks whether the earth element is pure or impure; one seeks whether the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements are pure or impure.
Kauśika, I declare that one who practices diligence based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of diligence characterized by the apprehension of something to be attained.
As previously explained, you should know that all these are descriptions of a semblance of the perfection of diligence characterized by apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, explain whether ignorance is permanent or impermanent; explain whether volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and old age, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are permanent or impermanent;

and explain whether ignorance is pleasant or painful; explain whether volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and old age, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are pleasant or painful.

One speaks of ignorance as being either self or non-self; one speaks of volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, and old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair as being either self or non-self.

One speaks of ignorance as being either pure or impure; one speaks of volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, and old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair as being either pure or impure.
If there is one who is able to practice with diligence in accordance with such dharmas as these, this is the practice of the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*).
Furthermore, it is said:

One who practices diligence should investigate whether ignorance is permanent or impermanent; they should investigate whether the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) up to old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair are permanent or impermanent.

One should investigate whether ignorance is pleasant or painful; one should investigate whether the formative forces, up to and including old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair, are pleasant or painful.

One should investigate whether ignorance is self or non-self; one should investigate whether the formative forces, up to and including old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair, are self or non-self.

One should investigate whether ignorance is pure or impure; one should investigate whether the formative forces, up to and including old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair, are pure or impure.
If there are those who are able to seek such dharmas as these and practice with diligence, this is the practice of the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*). "Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters seek whether ignorance is permanent or impermanent, and seek whether formations, up to old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair, are permanent or impermanent; [this is the perfection of diligence]."
One seeks whether ignorance is pleasant or painful; one seeks whether the formative forces, up to old age, death, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair, are pleasant or painful.
One seeks whether ignorance is self or non-self; one seeks whether the formative forces, up to old age, death, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair, are self or non-self.
One seeks whether ignorance is pure or impure; one seeks whether the formative forces, up to old age, death, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair, are pure or impure.
Kauśika, I declare that one who practices diligence based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of diligence characterized by the apprehension of something to be attained.
As previously explained, one should know that all these refer to what is called the semblance perfection of vigor characterized by apprehension (*upalambha*).
*The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Scroll 139, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Part One: Chapter on the Measurement of Merits, Section 30-38. "Furthermore, Kauśika!..."

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment, should speak of the perfection of generosity as either permanent or impermanent; speak of the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom as either permanent or impermanent;

speak of the perfection of generosity as either pleasant or painful; speak of the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom as either pleasant or painful;

or speak of the perfection of generosity as either self or non-self, and speak of the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom as either self or non-self; [they would be teaching emptiness].

He speaks of the perfection of giving as being either pure or impure; he speaks of the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom as being either pure or impure.
If there are those who are able to practice with diligence in accordance with such dharmas as these, this is the practice of the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*).
Furthermore, it is said:

one who practices diligence should seek whether the perfection of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*) is permanent or impermanent; one should seek whether the perfections from ethical discipline (*śīla*) up to wisdom (*prajñā*) are permanent or impermanent.
One should seek the perfection of generosity whether it be pleasant or painful; one should seek the perfections from ethical discipline up to wisdom whether they be pleasant or painful.
One should seek the perfection of generosity whether it be self or non-self; one should seek the perfections from ethical discipline up to wisdom whether they be self or non-self.
One should seek the perfection of generosity whether it be pure or impure; one should seek the perfections from ethical discipline up to wisdom whether they be pure or impure.
If there are those who are able to seek such dharmas as these and practice with diligence, this is the practice of the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*). "Kauśika!

If sons of good family or daughters of good family seek the perfection of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*) as either permanent or impermanent, and seek the perfections from ethical discipline (*śīla*) up to wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*) as either permanent or impermanent;
One seeks the perfection of generosity whether it be pleasant or painful; one seeks the perfections from ethical discipline up to wisdom whether they be pleasant or painful.
One seeks the perfection of generosity whether it be self or selfless; one seeks the perfections from ethical discipline up to wisdom whether they be self or selfless.
One seeks the perfection of generosity whether it be pure or impure; one seeks the perfections from ethical discipline up to wisdom whether they be pure or impure.
Kauśika, I declare that one who practices diligence based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of diligence characterized by the apprehension of something to be attained.
As previously stated, you should know that all these are descriptions of what resembles the perfection of diligence characterized by apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment, explain internal emptiness as either permanent or impermanent; or explain external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-altering emptiness, essential emptiness, emptiness of self-characteristic, emptiness of common characteristic, emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature—whether as permanent or impermanent;

Whether it be pleasant or painful, one speaks of internal emptiness; whether it be pleasant or painful, one speaks of external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersion emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature.

He speaks of inner emptiness, whether as self or as non-self; he speaks of outer emptiness, inner-and-outer emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, unchanging emptiness, essential emptiness, emptiness of specific characteristics, emptiness of common characteristics, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence—whether as self or as non-self.

One speaks of internal emptiness as being either pure or impure; one speaks of external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-altering emptiness, essential emptiness, emptiness of self-characteristic, emptiness of common characteristic, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence—each of these being either pure or impure.
If there is one who is able to practice with diligence in accordance with such dharmas as these, this is the practice of the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*).
Furthermore, it is said:

"One who practices diligence should seek whether internal emptiness is permanent or impermanent; one should seek whether external emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of non-existence and intrinsic nature, is permanent or impermanent."

One should seek whether internal emptiness is pleasant or painful; one should seek whether external emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, is pleasant or painful.

One should seek whether internal emptiness is self or non-self; one should seek whether external emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, is self or non-self.

One should seek whether internal emptiness is pure or impure; one should seek whether external emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, is pure or impure.
If there are those who are able to seek such dharmas as these and practice with diligence, this is the practice of the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*). "Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters seek internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*) as either permanent or impermanent, and seek external emptiness (*bahirdhā-śūnyatā*) up to the emptiness of the nature of non-nature (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*) as either permanent or impermanent;
They seek whether internal emptiness is pleasant or painful; they seek whether external emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of non-existence and self-nature, is pleasant or painful.
They seek whether internal emptiness is self or non-self; they seek whether external emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of non-existence and self-nature, is self or non-self.
They seek whether internal emptiness is pure or impure; they seek whether external emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of non-existence and self-nature, is pure or impure.

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment, should speak of whether the *tathatā* (suchness) is permanent or impermanent; or speak of whether the *dharmadhātu* (dharma-realm), *dharmatā* (dharma-nature), non-illusory nature, unchanging nature, equality, nature free from birth, fixedness of dharma, stability of dharma, the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the realm of empty space, and the inconceivable realm are permanent or impermanent;

or speak of whether the *tathatā* is pleasant or painful; or speak of whether the *dharmadhātu*, *dharmatā*, non-illusory nature, unchanging nature, equality, nature free from birth, fixedness of dharma, stability of dharma, the limit of reality, the realm of empty space, and the inconceivable realm are pleasant or painful.

Whether one speaks of true thusness as having a self or being without a self, or whether one speaks of the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, non-falsity, immutability, equality, the state beyond birth, the fixed nature of dharmas, the stability of dharmas, the limit of reality, the realm of space, or the inconceivable realm as having a self or being without a self;

whether one speaks of true thusness as pure or impure, or whether one speaks of the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, non-falsity, immutability, equality, the state beyond birth, the fixed nature of dharmas, the stability of dharmas, the limit of reality, the realm of space, or the inconceivable realm as pure or impure.
If there are those who are able to practice with diligence in accordance with such dharmas as these, this is the practice of the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*).
Furthermore, it is said:

one who practices diligence should seek whether suchness is permanent or impermanent; one should seek whether the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), up to and including the inconceivable realm (*acintyadhātu*), is permanent or impermanent.
One should seek whether true thusness is pleasant or painful; one should seek whether the dharma-realm, up to and including the inconceivable realm, is pleasant or painful.
One should seek whether true thusness is self or non-self; one should seek whether the dharma-realm, up to and including the inconceivable realm, is self or non-self.
One should seek whether true thusness is pure or impure; one should seek whether the dharma-realm, up to and including the inconceivable realm, is pure or impure.
If there are those who are able to seek such dharmas as these and practice with diligence, this is the practice of the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*). "Kauśika!
If good sons and good daughters thus seek whether true thusness is permanent or impermanent, or seek whether the dharma-realm, up to the inconceivable realm, is permanent or impermanent;
Seeking the reality-limit as either pleasure or pain; seeking the dharma-realm, up to the inconceivable realm, as either pleasure or pain;
seeking the reality-limit as either self or non-self; seeking the dharma-realm, up to the inconceivable realm, as either self or non-self;
seeking the reality-limit as either pure or impure; seeking the dharma-realm, up to the inconceivable realm, as either pure or impure.

or speak of the Noble Truth of Suffering as either pleasant or painful, or speak of the Noble Truths of Origination, Cessation, and the Path as either pleasant or painful;

or speak of the Noble Truth of Suffering as either self or non-self, or speak of the Noble Truths of Origination, Cessation, and the Path as either self or non-self; [they would be speaking erroneously].
To speak of the Noble Truth of Suffering as either pure or impure, and to speak of the Noble Truths of Origination, Cessation, and the Path as either pure or impure—
if one is able to rely upon such dharmas to practice with diligence, this is the practice of the perfection of diligence (vīrya-pāramitā).
Furthermore, it is said:

One who practices diligence should seek whether the Noble Truth of Suffering is permanent or impermanent; one should seek whether the Noble Truths of Origination, Cessation, and the Path are permanent or impermanent;
one should seek whether the Noble Truth of Suffering is pleasant or painful; and one should seek whether the Noble Truths of Origination, Cessation, and the Path are pleasant or painful.

one should seek whether the noble truth of suffering is pure or impure; one should seek whether the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path are pure or impure.
If there are those who are able to seek such dharmas as these and practice with diligence, this is the practice of the perfection of diligence. "Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters seek the Noble Truth of Suffering as either permanent or impermanent, and seek the Noble Truths of Origination, Cessation, and the Path as either permanent or impermanent; [this is the perfection of diligence]."
One seeks whether the noble truth of suffering is pleasant or painful; one seeks whether the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path are pleasant or painful.
One seeks whether the noble truth of suffering is self or non-self; one seeks whether the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path are self or non-self.
One seeks whether the noble truth of suffering is pure or impure; one seeks whether the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path are pure or impure.

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment, were to speak of the four dhyānas as either permanent or impermanent, or speak of the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions as either permanent or impermanent;
were to speak of the four dhyānas as either pleasant or painful, or speak of the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions as either pleasant or painful;
were to speak of the four dhyānas as either self or non-self, or speak of the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions as either self or non-self;
To speak of the four dhyānas, whether pure or impure, and to speak of the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments, whether pure or impure—
if one is able to rely upon such dharmas as these and practice with diligence, this is the practice of the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*).
Furthermore, it is said:

One who practices diligence should seek the four dhyānas as either permanent or impermanent; one should seek the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments as either permanent or impermanent;
one should seek the four dhyānas as either pleasant or painful; one should seek the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments as either pleasant or painful.
One should seek the four dhyānas whether they are with self or without self; one should seek the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments whether they are with self or without self;
one should seek the four dhyānas whether they are pure or impure; one should seek the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments whether they are pure or impure.
If there are those who are able to seek such dharmas as these and practice with diligence, this is the practice of the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*). "Kauśika!
If good sons and good daughters seek the four dhyānas as either permanent or impermanent, or seek the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments as either permanent or impermanent;..."

They seek the four dhyānas as either pure or impure; they seek the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments as either pure or impure.

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, speak of the eight liberations as being either permanent or impermanent; speak of the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive absorptions, and the ten totalities as being either permanent or impermanent;
speak of the eight liberations as being either pleasant or painful; speak of the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive absorptions, and the ten totalities as being either pleasant or painful;
or speak of the eight liberations as being either self or non-self; speak of the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive absorptions, and the ten totalities as being either self or non-self;

speak of the four foundations of mindfulness as either pleasant or painful; speak of the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path as either pleasant or painful;

speak of the four foundations of mindfulness as either self or non-self; and speak of the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path as either self or non-self;

one who practices diligence should seek whether the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) are permanent or impermanent; one should seek whether the four right endeavors (*samyakprahāṇa*), up to and including the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*), are permanent or impermanent.

They seek the four foundations of mindfulness as either pleasant or painful; they seek the four right efforts, up to and including the eightfold noble path, as either pleasant or painful.
They seek the four foundations of mindfulness as either self or non-self; they seek the four right efforts, up to and including the eightfold noble path, as either self or non-self.
They seek the four foundations of mindfulness as either pure or impure; they seek the four right efforts, up to and including the eightfold noble path, as either pure or impure.
