"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment, should speak of the gate of liberation of emptiness as either permanent or impermanent, or speak of the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness as either permanent or impermanent;
if they should speak of the gate of liberation of emptiness as either pleasant or painful, or speak of the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness as either pleasant or painful;
if they should speak of the gate of liberation of emptiness as either self or non-self, or speak of the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness as either self or non-self;
To speak of the gate of liberation of emptiness as either pure or impure, and to speak of the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness as either pure or impure—
if one is able to rely upon such dharmas as these and practice with diligence, this is the practice of the perfection of diligence (vīrya-pāramitā).
Furthermore, it is said:

One who practices diligence should seek whether the gate of liberation of emptiness is permanent or impermanent; one should seek whether the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness are permanent or impermanent;
one should seek whether the gate of liberation of emptiness is pleasant or painful; one should seek whether the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness are pleasant or painful.
One should seek the gate of liberation of emptiness whether it be self or non-self; one should seek the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness whether they be self or non-self;
one should seek the gate of liberation of emptiness whether it be pure or impure; one should seek the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness whether they be pure or impure.
If there are those who are able to seek such dharmas as these and practice with diligence, this is the practice of the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*). "Kauśika!

If sons of good family or daughters of good family seek the gate of liberation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha*)—whether it be permanent or impermanent—and seek the gates of liberation of signlessness (*animitta*) and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*)—whether they be permanent or impermanent;..."
They seek whether the gate of liberation of emptiness is pleasant or painful; they seek whether the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness are pleasant or painful.
They seek whether the gate of liberation of emptiness is self or non-self; they seek whether the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness are self or non-self.
They seek whether the gate of liberation of emptiness is pure or impure; they seek whether the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness are pure or impure.
Kauśika, I declare that one who practices diligence based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of diligence characterized by the apprehension of something to be attained.
As previously stated, you should know that all these describe a semblance of the perfection of diligence characterized by apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, speak of the five eyes as either permanent or impermanent, or speak of the six supernormal powers as either permanent or impermanent;
speak of the five eyes as either pleasant or painful, or speak of the six supernormal powers as either pleasant or painful;
speak of the five eyes as either self or non-self, or speak of the six supernormal powers as either self or non-self;
One speaks of the five eyes, whether pure or impure, and one speaks of the six supernormal powers, whether pure or impure.
If there is anyone who is able to practice with diligence based upon such dharmas as these, this is the practice of the perfection of diligence (vīrya-pāramitā).
Furthermore, he spoke thus:
"One who practices diligence should seek whether the five eyes are permanent or impermanent, and should seek whether the six supernormal powers are permanent or impermanent;
one should seek whether the five eyes are pleasant or painful, and should seek whether the six supernormal powers are pleasant or painful."
One should seek the five eyes whether they are self or non-self; one should seek the six supernormal powers whether they are self or non-self;
one should seek the five eyes whether they are pure or impure; one should seek the six supernormal powers whether they are pure or impure.
If there are those who are able to seek such dharmas as these and practice with diligence, this is the practice of the perfection of diligence. "Kauśika!
If good sons and good daughters seek the five eyes as either permanent or impermanent, or seek the six supernormal powers as either permanent or impermanent;
Seeking the five eyes as either pleasant or painful; seeking the six supernormal powers as either pleasant or painful;
seeking the five eyes as either self or non-self; seeking the six supernormal powers as either self or non-self;
seeking the five eyes as either pure or impure; seeking the six supernormal powers as either pure or impure.
Kauśika, I declare that one who practices diligence based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance perfection of diligence characterized by the apprehension of something to be attained.
As previously stated, one should know that all these are merely descriptions of a semblance of the perfection of diligence characterized by apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment, were to speak of the ten powers of a Buddha as being either permanent or impermanent; or speak of the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha as being either permanent or impermanent;

or speak of the ten powers of a Buddha as being either pleasant or painful; or speak of the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha as being either pleasant or painful;

They speak of the ten powers of a Buddha as being either self or non-self; they speak of the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha as being either self or non-self.

They speak of the ten powers of a Buddha as being either pure or impure; they speak of the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha as being either pure or impure.
If there are those who are able to practice with diligence in accordance with such dharmas as these, this is the practice of the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*).
Furthermore, it is said:

One who practices diligence should seek whether the ten powers of a Buddha are permanent or impermanent; one should seek whether the four fearlessnesses, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, are permanent or impermanent.

One should seek whether the ten powers of a Buddha are pleasant or painful; one should seek whether the four fearlessnesses, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, are pleasant or painful.

One should seek whether the ten powers of a Buddha are self or non-self; one should seek whether the four fearlessnesses, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, are self or non-self.

One should seek whether the ten powers of a Buddha are pure or impure; one should seek whether the four fearlessnesses, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, are pure or impure.
If there are those who are able to seek such dharmas as these and practice with diligence, this is the practice of the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*). "Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters seek the ten powers of a Buddha—whether they are permanent or impermanent—and seek the four fearlessnesses, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha—whether they are permanent or impermanent; [this is the perfection of diligence]."
Seeking whether the ten powers of a Buddha are pleasant or painful; seeking whether the four fearlessnesses, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, are pleasant or painful;
seeking whether the ten powers of a Buddha are self or non-self; seeking whether the four fearlessnesses, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, are self or non-self;
seeking whether the ten powers of a Buddha are pure or impure; seeking whether the four fearlessnesses, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, are pure or impure.
Kauśika, I declare that one who practices diligence based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of diligence characterized by the apprehension of something to be attained.
As previously stated, it should be understood that all these refer to a semblance of the perfection of diligence characterized by apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment, speak of the quality of non-forgetfulness as either permanent or impermanent, or speak of the nature of constant equanimity as either permanent or impermanent;
if they speak of the quality of non-forgetfulness as either pleasant or painful, or speak of the nature of constant equanimity as either pleasant or painful;
if they speak of the quality of non-forgetfulness as either self or non-self, or speak of the nature of constant equanimity as either self or non-self;
To speak of the quality of non-forgetfulness as either pure or impure, and to speak of the nature of constant equanimity as either pure or impure—
if one is able to rely upon such dharmas as these and practice with diligence, this is the practice of the perfection of diligence (vīrya-pāramitā).
Furthermore, it is said:
One who practices diligence should seek the quality of non-forgetfulness as either permanent or impermanent, and should seek the nature of constant equanimity as either permanent or impermanent;
one should seek the quality of non-forgetfulness as either pleasant or painful, and should seek the nature of constant equanimity as either pleasant or painful.
One should seek the quality of non-forgetfulness whether it be self or selfless; one should seek the state of constant equanimity whether it be self or selfless;
one should seek the quality of non-forgetfulness whether it be pure or impure; and one should seek the state of constant equanimity whether it be pure or impure.
If there are those who are able to seek such dharmas as these and practice with diligence, this is the practice of the perfection of diligence. "Kauśika!

If sons of good family or daughters of good family seek in this way the qualities of non-forgetfulness, whether they are permanent or impermanent; if they seek the nature of constant equanimity, whether it is permanent or impermanent;
One seeks the quality of non-forgetfulness whether it be pleasant or painful; one seeks the state of constant equanimity whether it be pleasant or painful.
One seeks the quality of non-forgetfulness whether it be self or non-self; one seeks the state of constant equanimity whether it be self or non-self.
One seeks the quality of non-forgetfulness whether it be pure or impure; one seeks the state of constant equanimity whether it be pure or impure.
Kauśika, I declare that one who practices diligence based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of diligence characterized by the apprehension of something to be attained.
As previously stated, you should know that all these are said to be the semblance of the perfection of diligence characterized by apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, speak of omniscience as either permanent or impermanent, or speak of the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects as either permanent or impermanent;
if they speak of omniscience as either pleasant or painful, or speak of the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects as either pleasant or painful;
if they speak of omniscience as either self or non-self, or speak of the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects as either self or non-self;
To speak of all-knowledge as either pure or impure, and to speak of the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects as either pure or impure—
if there is one who is able to practice with diligence based upon such dharmas as these, this is the practice of the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*).
Furthermore, it is said:

One who practices diligence should seek omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) as either permanent or impermanent; one should seek the knowledge of the paths (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) as either permanent or impermanent;
one should seek omniscience as either pleasant or painful; one should seek the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects as either pleasant or painful.

One should seek omniscience (sarvajñatā) whether it be with self or without self; one should seek the knowledge of the paths (mārgajñatā) and the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā) whether they be with self or without self;
one should seek omniscience whether it be pure or impure; one should seek the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects whether they be pure or impure.
If there are those who are able to seek such dharmas as these and practice with diligence, this is the practice of the perfection of diligence. "Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters seek omniscience (sarvajñatā) as either permanent or impermanent, or seek the knowledge of the paths (mārgajñatā) and the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā) as either permanent or impermanent;
Whether seeking all-knowledge as pleasure or suffering; whether seeking the knowledge of the aspects of the path or the knowledge of all aspects as pleasure or suffering;
whether seeking all-knowledge as self or non-self; whether seeking the knowledge of the aspects of the path or the knowledge of all aspects as self or non-self;
whether seeking all-knowledge as pure or impure; whether seeking the knowledge of the aspects of the path or the knowledge of all aspects as pure or impure.
Kauśika, I say that one who practices diligence based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of diligence that is characterized by apprehension.
As previously stated, you should know that all these are descriptions of a semblance of the perfection of diligence characterized by apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kausika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, explain that all dharanī-doors are either permanent or impermanent; explain that all samādhi-doors are either permanent or impermanent;
explain that all dharanī-doors are either pleasant or painful; explain that all samādhi-doors are either pleasant or painful;
explain that all dharanī-doors are either self or non-self; explain that all samādhi-doors are either self or non-self;
He teaches all dharanī-doors, whether pure or impure; he teaches all samādhi-doors, whether pure or impure.
If there is one who is able to practice with diligence based upon such dharmas as these, this is the practice of the perfection of diligence (vīrya-pāramitā).
Furthermore, it is said:
One who practices diligence should seek all dhāraṇī-doors as either permanent or impermanent; one should seek all samādhi-doors as either permanent or impermanent;
one should seek all dhāraṇī-doors as either pleasant or painful; one should seek all samādhi-doors as either pleasant or painful.
One should seek all dharani-doors whether they are with self or without self; one should seek all samadhi-doors whether they are with self or without self.
One should seek all dharani-doors whether they are pure or impure; one should seek all samadhi-doors whether they are pure or impure.
If there are those who are able to seek such dharmas as these and practice with diligence, this is the practice of the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*). "Kauśika!
If sons of good family or daughters of good family seek all dharani-doors, whether they be permanent or impermanent, and seek all samadhi-doors, whether they be permanent or impermanent;..."
They seek all dharani-doors whether as pleasure or as suffering; they seek all samadhi-doors whether as pleasure or as suffering.
They seek all dharani-doors whether as self or as non-self; they seek all samadhi-doors whether as self or as non-self.
They seek all dharani-doors whether as pure or as impure; they seek all samadhi-doors whether as pure or as impure.
Kauśika, I say that one who practices diligence based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of diligence characterized by the apprehension of something to be attained.
As previously stated, you should know that all these describe a semblance of the perfection of diligence characterized by apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons, good daughters, and others who have resolved upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment should be told that the stage of entering the stream and the fruit of stream-entry are either permanent or impermanent; or told that the stage of entering once-returning and the fruit of once-returning, the stage of entering non-returning and the fruit of non-returning, and the stage of entering arhatship and the fruit of arhatship are either permanent or impermanent;

or told that the stage of entering the stream and the fruit of stream-entry are either pleasant or painful; or told that the stage of entering once-returning and the fruit of once-returning, the stage of entering non-returning and the fruit of non-returning, and the stage of entering arhatship and the fruit of arhatship are either pleasant or painful;

or told that the stage of entering the stream and the fruit of stream-entry are either self or non-self; or told that the stage of entering once-returning and the fruit of once-returning, the stage of entering non-returning and the fruit of non-returning, and the stage of entering arhatship and the fruit of arhatship are either self or non-self; [they would fall into error].

He speaks of the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry and the fruit of stream-entry, whether pure or impure; he speaks of the candidate for the fruit of once-returning and the fruit of once-returning, the candidate for the fruit of non-returning and the fruit of non-returning, and the candidate for the fruit of arhatship and the fruit of arhatship, whether pure or impure.
If there are those who are able to practice with diligence in accordance with such dharmas as these, this is the practice of the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*).
Furthermore, it is said:

one who practices diligence should seek the fruit of the candidate for stream-entry (*srotāpatti-pratipannaka*) and the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna-phala*), whether they are permanent or impermanent; one should seek the fruit of the candidate for once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmi-pratipannaka*) up to the fruit of arhatship (*arhat-phala*), whether they are permanent or impermanent.

One should seek the fruit of stream-entry and the path of stream-entry, whether as pleasure or as pain; one should seek the fruits up to arhatship and their respective paths, whether as pleasure or as pain.

One should seek the fruit of stream-entry and the path of stream-entry, whether as self or as non-self; one should seek the fruits up to arhatship and their respective paths, whether as self or as non-self.

One should seek the fruit of stream-entry and the path of stream-entry, whether as pure or as impure; one should seek the fruits up to arhatship and their respective paths, whether as pure or as impure.
If there are those who are able to seek such dharmas as these and practice with diligence, this is the practice of the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*). "Kauśika!

If sons of good family or daughters of good family seek, in this manner, entry into the stream and the fruit of stream-entry, whether as permanent or impermanent; or seek the fruit of once-returning up to the fruit of arhatship, whether as permanent or impermanent; [they are practicing the perfection of diligence]."

Seeking the state of entering the stream and the fruit of stream-entry as either pleasant or painful; seeking the state of entering once-returning up to the fruit of arhatship as either pleasant or painful;

seeking the state of entering the stream and the fruit of stream-entry as either self or non-self; seeking the state of entering once-returning up to the fruit of arhatship as either self or non-self;
seeking the state of entering the stream and the fruit of stream-entry as either pure or impure; seeking the state of entering once-returning up to the fruit of arhatship as either pure or impure.
Kauśika, I say that for one who practices diligence based on such dharmas, it is called a semblance perfection of diligence characterized by the apprehension of something to be attained.
As previously stated, it should be understood that all of these describe a semblance of the perfection of diligence characterized by apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kausika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, were to speak of all pratyekabuddha-bodhi as either permanent or impermanent; speak of all pratyekabuddha-bodhi as either pleasant or painful; speak of all pratyekabuddha-bodhi as either self or non-self; or speak of all pratyekabuddha-bodhi as either pure or impure.
If there are those who are able to practice with diligence in accordance with such teachings as these, this is the practice of the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*).
Furthermore, it is said:

one who practices diligence should seek all pratyekabuddha-enlightenment whether it be permanent or impermanent; one should seek all pratyekabuddha-enlightenment whether it be pleasant or painful; one should seek all pratyekabuddha-enlightenment whether it be self or non-self; and one should seek all pratyekabuddha-enlightenment whether it be pure or impure.
If there are those who are able to seek such dharmas as these and practice with diligence, this is the practice of the perfection of diligence.

"Kauśika! If sons of good family or daughters of good family seek all pratyekabuddha enlightenment in terms of permanence or impermanence; seek all pratyekabuddha enlightenment in terms of pleasure or suffering; seek all pratyekabuddha enlightenment in terms of self or non-self; and seek all pratyekabuddha enlightenment in terms of purity or impurity."
Kauśika, I declare that one who practices diligence based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance perfection of diligence characterized by the apprehension of something to be attained.
As previously stated, you should know that all of these describe a semblance of the perfection of diligence characterized by apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, should speak of all the practices of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas as either permanent or impermanent; speak of all the practices of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas as either pleasant or painful; speak of all the practices of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas as either self or non-self; or speak of all the practices of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas as either pure or impure.
If there is one who is able to practice with diligence in accordance with such dharmas as these, this is the practice of the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*).
Furthermore, it is said:

One who practices diligence should seek all the practices of the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas regarding whether they are permanent or impermanent; one should seek all the practices of the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas regarding whether they are pleasant or painful; one should seek all the practices of the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas regarding whether they have a self or are without a self; and one should seek all the practices of the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas regarding whether they are pure or impure.
If there are those who are able to seek such dharmas as these and practice with diligence, this is the practice of the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*).

"Kauśika! If good sons and good daughters thus seek all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas—whether they are permanent or impermanent; seek all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas—whether they are pleasant or painful; seek all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas—whether they are self or non-self; seek all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas—whether they are pure or impure."
Kauśika, I declare that one who practices diligence based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of diligence characterized by the apprehension of something to be attained.
As previously stated, you should know that all these are descriptions of a semblance of the perfection of diligence characterized by apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kausika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, were to speak of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas as either permanent or impermanent; speak of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas as either pleasant or painful; speak of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas as either self or non-self; or speak of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas as either pure or impure.
If there are those who are able to practice with diligence by relying on such teachings as these, this is the practice of the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*).
Furthermore, it is said:

one who practices diligence should seek the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*) of all Buddhas as either permanent or impermanent; should seek the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas as either blissful or suffering; should seek the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas as either self or non-self; and should seek the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas as either pure or impure.
If there are those who are able to seek such dharmas as these and practice with diligence, this is the practice of the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*). "Kauśika!

If sons of good family or daughters of good family seek the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas as either permanent or impermanent; seek the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas as either pleasant or painful; seek the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas as either self or non-self; seek the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas as either pure or impure."
Kauśika, I declare that one who practices diligence based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of diligence characterized by grasping at attainments.
"As previously explained, one should know that all these are said to be the semblance of the perfection of diligence characterized by apprehension.

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 143, translated by the Dharma Master Xuanzang under Imperial Decree. Part One, Chapter Thirty, Sub-section Three: "Comparing Merits. At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

How is it that those sons and daughters of good family who speak of the perfection of patience with the notion of something to be attained are said to be speaking of a semblance of the perfection of patience?
The Buddha said, “Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved upon unsurpassed bodhicitta, speak of form as either permanent or impermanent, and speak of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as either permanent or impermanent;”
One speaks of form as either pleasant or painful; one speaks of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as either pleasant or painful.
One speaks of form as either self or non-self; one speaks of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as either self or non-self.
One speaks of form as either pure or impure; one speaks of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as either pure or impure.
If there are those who are able to practice patience (*kṣānti*) by relying on such dharmas as these, they are practicing the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*).
Furthermore, it is said:

one who practices patience should investigate whether form (*rūpa*) is permanent or impermanent; one should investigate whether feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are permanent or impermanent.
One should investigate whether form is pleasant or painful; one should investigate whether feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are pleasant or painful.
One should investigate whether form is self or non-self; one should investigate whether feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are self or non-self.
One should investigate whether form is pure or impure; one should investigate whether feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice patience, they are practicing the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*). "Kauśika!

If sons of good family or daughters of good family seek form (*rūpa*) as either permanent or impermanent; if they seek feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) as either permanent or impermanent;..."
One seeks whether form is pleasant or painful; one seeks whether feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are pleasant or painful.
One seeks whether form is self or non-self; one seeks whether feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are self or non-self.
One seeks whether form is pure or impure; one seeks whether feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are pure or impure.
Kauśika, I say that one who practices patience based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance perfection of patience characterized by the apprehension of something to be attained.
As previously stated, you should know that all of these describe a semblance of the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā) characterized by apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, explain whether the eye-base is permanent or impermanent; explain whether the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases are permanent or impermanent;
explain whether the eye-base is pleasant or painful; explain whether the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases are pleasant or painful;
explain whether the eye-base is self or non-self; and explain whether the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases are self or non-self;
To speak of the sense base of the eye as either pure or impure, and to speak of the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind as either pure or impure—
if one is able to practice patience in reliance upon such dharmas as these, this is the practice of the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā).
Furthermore, it is said:

One who practices patience should investigate whether the sense base of the eye is permanent or impermanent; one should investigate whether the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are permanent or impermanent;
one should investigate whether the sense base of the eye is pleasant or painful; one should investigate whether the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are pleasant or painful.
One should investigate whether the sense base of the eye is self or non-self; one should investigate whether the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are self or non-self.
One should investigate whether the sense base of the eye is pure or impure; one should investigate whether the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice patience, they are practicing the perfection of patience. "Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters seek whether the sense-base of the eye is permanent or impermanent, and seek whether the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are permanent or impermanent;
They seek whether the eye-base is pleasant or painful; they seek whether the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases are pleasant or painful.
They seek whether the eye-base is self or non-self; they seek whether the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases are self or non-self.
They seek whether the eye-base is pure or impure; they seek whether the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases are pure or impure.
Kauśika, I declare that one who practices patience based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of patience characterized by the apprehension of something to be attained.
