If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment, explain internal emptiness as either permanent or impermanent; or explain external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersal emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence—whether as permanent or impermanent;

Whether it be pleasant or painful, one speaks of internal emptiness; one speaks of external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature—whether they be pleasant or painful.

He speaks of inner emptiness—whether as self or as non-self—and he speaks of outer emptiness, inner-and-outer emptiness, emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, unchanging emptiness, essential emptiness, emptiness of own-marks, emptiness of common marks, emptiness of all dharmas, emptiness of the unapprehendable, emptiness of non-existence, emptiness of own-nature, and emptiness of the own-nature of non-existence—whether as self or as non-self.

One speaks of internal emptiness as either pure or impure; one speaks of external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersion emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence—each as either pure or impure.
If there is one who is able to practice patience (kṣānti) by relying on such teachings as these, this is the practice of the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā).
Furthermore, it is said:

One who practices patience should seek whether internal emptiness (adhyātma-śūnyatā) is permanent or impermanent; they should seek whether external emptiness (bahirdhā-śūnyatā), up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature (abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā), is permanent or impermanent.

One should seek whether inner emptiness is pleasant or painful; one should seek whether outer emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature, is pleasant or painful.
One should seek whether inner emptiness is self or non-self; one should seek whether outer emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature, is self or non-self.
One should seek whether inner emptiness is pure or impure; one should seek whether outer emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of non-existence of intrinsic nature, is pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice patience, they are practicing the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*). "Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters seek internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*) as either permanent or impermanent, or seek external emptiness (*bahirdhā-śūnyatā*) up to the emptiness of non-existence and self-nature (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*) as either permanent or impermanent; [they are practicing the perfection of patience]."
One seeks whether internal emptiness is pleasant or painful; one seeks whether external emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, is pleasant or painful.
One seeks whether internal emptiness is self or non-self; one seeks whether external emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, is self or non-self.
One seeks whether internal emptiness is pure or impure; one seeks whether external emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, is pure or impure.
Kauśika, I declare that one who practices patience based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of patience characterized by the apprehension of something to be attained.
As previously stated, you should know that all these refer to a semblance of the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) characterized by apprehension (*upalambha*).
"Furthermore, Kauśika!"

If good sons, good daughters, or others who have resolved upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment should speak of whether the Tathatā (Suchness) is permanent or impermanent; or speak of whether the dharmadhātu (Dharma-realm), dharmatā (Dharma-nature), avitathatā (non-falsity), ananyathābhāvatā (unchanging nature), samatā (equality), anutpādadharmatā (nature of non-arising), dharmasthititā (stability of phenomena), dharmaniyāmatā (fixed course of phenomena), bhūtakoṭi (the limit of reality), ākāśadhātu (space-element), and acintyadhātu (inconceivable element) are permanent or impermanent;

or speak of whether the Tathatā is pleasant or painful; or speak of whether the dharmadhātu, dharmatā, avitathatā, ananyathābhāvatā, samatā, anutpādadharmatā, dharmasthititā, dharmaniyāmatā, bhūtakoṭi, ākāśadhātu, and acintyadhātu are pleasant or painful.

Whether one speaks of true thusness as having a self or being without a self, or whether one speaks of the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, non-falsity, non-alteration, equality, the state beyond birth, the fixed nature of dharmas, the stability of dharmas, the limit of reality, the realm of empty space, or the inconceivable realm as having a self or being without a self;

whether one speaks of true thusness as pure or impure, or whether one speaks of the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, non-falsity, non-alteration, equality, the state beyond birth, the fixed nature of dharmas, the stability of dharmas, the limit of reality, the realm of empty space, or the inconceivable realm as pure or impure.
If there are those who are able to practice patience (kṣānti) by relying on such teachings as these, they are practicing the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā).
Furthermore, it is said:

one who practices patience should seek whether true suchness (tathatā) is permanent or impermanent; one should seek whether the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), up to the inconceivable realm (acintyadhātu), is permanent or impermanent.
One should seek whether true thusness is pleasant or painful; one should seek whether the dharma-realm, up to and including the inconceivable realm, is pleasant or painful.
One should seek whether true thusness is self or non-self; one should seek whether the dharma-realm, up to and including the inconceivable realm, is self or non-self.
One should seek whether true thusness is pure or impure; one should seek whether the dharma-realm, up to and including the inconceivable realm, is pure or impure.
If there are those who are able to seek such dharmas as these and practice patience, they are practicing the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*). "Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters, and others like them, thus seek whether true suchness is permanent or impermanent, or seek whether the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) up to the inconceivable realm is permanent or impermanent; [they are practicing the perfection of patience]."
Seeking the reality-limit as either pleasure or suffering; seeking the dharma-realm, up to the inconceivable realm, as either pleasure or suffering;
seeking the reality-limit as either self or non-self; seeking the dharma-realm, up to the inconceivable realm, as either self or non-self;
seeking the reality-limit as either pure or impure; seeking the dharma-realm, up to the inconceivable realm, as either pure or impure.
Kauśika, I say that one who practices patience based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance perfection of patience characterized by apprehension.
As previously stated, you should know that all of these describe a semblance of the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) characterized by apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!..."

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, should speak of the Noble Truth of Suffering as either permanent or impermanent, or speak of the Noble Truths of Origination, Cessation, and the Path as either permanent or impermanent;
should speak of the Noble Truth of Suffering as either pleasant or painful, or speak of the Noble Truths of Origination, Cessation, and the Path as either pleasant or painful;

should speak of the Noble Truth of Suffering as either self or non-self, or speak of the Noble Truths of Origination, Cessation, and the Path as either self or non-self; [they would be speaking erroneously].
Whether one speaks of the Noble Truth of Suffering as pure or impure, or speaks of the Noble Truths of Origination, Cessation, and the Path as pure or impure—
if there is one who is able to practice patience by relying on such dharmas as these, this is the practice of the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā).
Furthermore, it is said:

One who practices the patience of equanimity should seek whether the Noble Truth of Suffering is permanent or impermanent; one should seek whether the Noble Truths of Origination, Cessation, and the Path are permanent or impermanent;
one should seek whether the Noble Truth of Suffering is pleasant or painful; and one should seek whether the Noble Truths of Origination, Cessation, and the Path are pleasant or painful.
One should seek whether the noble truth of suffering is self or non-self; one should seek whether the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path are self or non-self;
one should seek whether the noble truth of suffering is pure or impure; one should seek whether the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path are pure or impure.
If there are those who are able to seek such dharmas as these and practice patience, this is the practice of the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā). "Kauśika!

If sons of good family or daughters of good family seek the Noble Truth of Suffering as either permanent or impermanent, or seek the Noble Truths of Origination, Cessation, and the Path as either permanent or impermanent; [this is the practice of the perfection of patience]."
One seeks whether the noble truth of suffering is pleasant or painful; one seeks whether the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path are pleasant or painful.
One seeks whether the noble truth of suffering is self or non-self; one seeks whether the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path are self or non-self.
One seeks whether the noble truth of suffering is pure or impure; one seeks whether the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path are pure or impure.
Kauśika, I declare that one who practices patience based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of patience characterized by the apprehension of something to be attained.
As previously stated, you should know that all these refer to a semblance of the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) characterized by apprehension (*upalambha*).
"Furthermore, Kauśika!..."

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment, should speak of the four dhyānas as either permanent or impermanent, or speak of the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments as either permanent or impermanent;
if they should speak of the four dhyānas as either pleasant or painful, or speak of the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments as either pleasant or painful;
if they should speak of the four dhyānas as either self or non-self, or speak of the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments as either self or non-self;
To speak of the four dhyānas, whether pure or impure, and to speak of the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments, whether pure or impure—
if one is able to practice patience by relying on such dharmas as these, this is the practice of the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā).
Furthermore, it is said:

One who practices the patience of tranquility should seek whether the four dhyānas are permanent or impermanent; one should seek whether the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments are permanent or impermanent;
one should seek whether the four dhyānas are pleasant or painful; one should seek whether the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments are pleasant or painful.
One should seek the four dhyānas whether they are with self or without self; one should seek the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments whether they are with self or without self;
one should seek the four dhyānas whether they are pure or impure; one should seek the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments whether they are pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice patience, they are practicing the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*). "Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters seek the four dhyānas as either permanent or impermanent, or seek the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments as either permanent or impermanent; [they are practicing the perfection of patience]."
They seek the four dhyānas as either pleasure or pain; they seek the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments as either pleasure or pain.
They seek the four dhyānas as either self or non-self; they seek the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments as either self or non-self.
They seek the four dhyānas as either pure or impure; they seek the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments as either pure or impure.
Kauśika, I say that one who practices patience based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance perfection of patience characterized by the apprehension of something to be attained.
As previously explained, it should be understood that all these refer to a semblance of the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) based on apprehension (*upalambha*).

The Great Perfection of Wisdom Sūtra, Scroll 141, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Part One: Chapter on the Measurement of Merits, Number Thirty, Section Forty. "Furthermore, Kauśika!..."

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, speak of the eight liberations as being either permanent or impermanent; speak of the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten totalities as being either permanent or impermanent;

speak of the eight liberations as being either pleasant or painful; speak of the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten totalities as being either pleasant or painful;

or speak of the eight liberations as being either self or non-self; speak of the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten totalities as being either self or non-self;
To speak of the eight liberations as either pure or impure, and to speak of the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten totalities as either pure or impure—
if one is able to rely upon such dharmas as these to practice patience, this is the practice of the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā).
Furthermore, it is said:

One who practices the patience of equanimity should seek whether the eight liberations are permanent or impermanent; one should seek whether the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities are permanent or impermanent;

one should seek whether the eight liberations are pleasant or painful; one should seek whether the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities are pleasant or painful.

One should seek the eight liberations whether they are self or non-self; one should seek the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities whether they are self or non-self;

one should seek the eight liberations whether they are pure or impure; one should seek the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities whether they are pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice patience, they are practicing the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*). "Kauśika!

If sons of good family or daughters of good family seek the eight liberations (*aṣṭa-vimokṣa*) as either permanent or impermanent; or seek the eight bases of mastery (*abhibhv-āyatana*), the nine successive attainments (*anupūrva-samāpatti*), and the ten totalities (*daśa-kṛtsnāyatana*) as either permanent or impermanent;..."

They seek whether the eight liberations are pleasant or painful; they seek whether the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten totalities are pleasant or painful.
They seek whether the eight liberations are self or non-self; they seek whether the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten totalities are self or non-self.
They seek whether the eight liberations are pure or impure; they seek whether the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten totalities are pure or impure.
Kauśika, I say that one who practices patience based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance perfection of patience characterized by the apprehension of a referent.
As previously stated, you should know that all these refer to a semblance of the perfection of patience characterized by apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, explain whether the four foundations of mindfulness are permanent or impermanent; explain whether the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path are permanent or impermanent;

explain whether the four foundations of mindfulness are pleasant or painful; explain whether the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path are pleasant or painful;

explain whether the four foundations of mindfulness are self or non-self; [they likewise explain] whether the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path are self or non-self.

He speaks of the four foundations of mindfulness as either pure or impure; he speaks of the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path as either pure or impure.
If there is one who is able to practice patience (kṣānti) by relying on such dharmas as these, this is the practice of the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā).
Furthermore, it is said:

One who practices patience should seek whether the four foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) are permanent or impermanent; one should seek whether the four right efforts (samyakprahāṇa), up to and including the eightfold noble path (āryāṣṭāṅgamārga), are permanent or impermanent.

One should seek whether the four foundations of mindfulness are pleasant or painful; one should seek whether the four right efforts, up to and including the eightfold noble path, are pleasant or painful.
One should seek whether the four foundations of mindfulness are self or non-self; one should seek whether the four right efforts, up to and including the eightfold noble path, are self or non-self.
One should seek whether the four foundations of mindfulness are pure or impure; one should seek whether the four right efforts, up to and including the eightfold noble path, are pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice patience, they are practicing the perfection of patience. "Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters seek the four foundations of mindfulness as either permanent or impermanent, or seek the four right efforts up to the eightfold noble path as either permanent or impermanent;

They seek whether the four foundations of mindfulness are pleasant or painful; they seek whether the four right efforts, up to and including the eight factors of the noble path, are pleasant or painful.
They seek whether the four foundations of mindfulness are self or non-self; they seek whether the four right efforts, up to and including the eight factors of the noble path, are self or non-self.
They seek whether the four foundations of mindfulness are pure or impure; they seek whether the four right efforts, up to and including the eight factors of the noble path, are pure or impure.
Kauśika, I say that one who practices patience based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of patience characterized by the apprehension of something to be attained.
As previously stated, one should know that all these refer to a semblance of the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) characterized by apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, should speak of the gate of liberation of emptiness as either permanent or impermanent, or speak of the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness as either permanent or impermanent;
should speak of the gate of liberation of emptiness as either pleasant or painful, or speak of the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness as either pleasant or painful;
should speak of the gate of liberation of emptiness as either self or non-self, or speak of the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness as either self or non-self;
To speak of the gate of liberation of emptiness as either pure or impure, and to speak of the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness as either pure or impure—
if one is able to rely upon such dharmas as these to practice patience, this is the practice of the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).
Furthermore, it is said:

One who practices the patience of equanimity should seek whether the gate of liberation of emptiness is permanent or impermanent; one should seek whether the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness are permanent or impermanent;
one should seek whether the gate of liberation of emptiness is pleasant or painful; one should seek whether the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness are pleasant or painful.
One should seek the gate of liberation of emptiness whether it be self or non-self; one should seek the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness whether they be self or non-self;
one should seek the gate of liberation of emptiness whether it be pure or impure; one should seek the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness whether they be pure or impure.
If there are those who are able to seek such dharmas as these and practice patience, they are practicing the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*). "Kauśika!

If sons of good family or daughters of good family seek the gate of liberation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha*) as either permanent or impermanent, or seek the gates of liberation of signlessness (*animitta*) and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*) as either permanent or impermanent;..."
They seek whether the gate of liberation of emptiness is pleasant or painful; they seek whether the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness are pleasant or painful.
They seek whether the gate of liberation of emptiness is self or non-self; they seek whether the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness are self or non-self.
They seek whether the gate of liberation of emptiness is pure or impure; they seek whether the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness are pure or impure.
Kauśika, I declare that one who practices patience based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of patience characterized by the apprehension of something to be attained.
As previously stated, you should know that all these refer to a semblance of the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) characterized by apprehension (*upalambha*).
"Furthermore, Kauśika!"

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, speak of the five eyes as being either permanent or impermanent, or speak of the six supernormal powers as being either permanent or impermanent;
speak of the five eyes as being either pleasant or painful, or speak of the six supernormal powers as being either pleasant or painful;
speak of the five eyes as being either self or non-self, or speak of the six supernormal powers as being either self or non-self;
To speak of the five eyes as pure or impure, and to speak of the six supernormal powers as pure or impure—
if one is able to practice patience in reliance upon such dharmas as these, this is the practice of the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā).
Furthermore, he spoke thus:
"One who practices the patience of equanimity should seek whether the five eyes are permanent or impermanent; one should seek whether the six supernormal powers are permanent or impermanent;
one should seek whether the five eyes are pleasant or painful; one should seek whether the six supernormal powers are pleasant or painful."
One should seek the five eyes whether they are self or non-self; one should seek the six supernormal powers whether they are self or non-self;
one should seek the five eyes whether they are pure or impure; one should seek the six supernormal powers whether they are pure or impure.
If there are those who are able to seek such dharmas as these and practice patience, this is the practice of the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā). "Kauśika!

If sons of good family or daughters of good family seek in this way the five eyes, whether they are permanent or impermanent, or seek the six supernormal powers (abhijñā), whether they are permanent or impermanent;..."
They seek the five eyes as either pleasant or painful; they seek the six supernormal powers as either pleasant or painful.
They seek the five eyes as either self or non-self; they seek the six supernormal powers as either self or non-self.
They seek the five eyes as either pure or impure; they seek the six supernormal powers as either pure or impure.
Kauśika, I declare that one who practices patience based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of patience characterized by the apprehension of something to be attained.
As previously explained, it should be understood that all of these refer to a semblance of the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) characterized by apprehension (*upalambha*).
"Furthermore, Kauśika!"

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, should speak of the Buddha’s ten powers as being either permanent or impermanent; or speak of the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha as being either permanent or impermanent;

or speak of the Buddha’s ten powers as being either pleasant or painful; or speak of the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha as being either pleasant or painful;

They speak of the ten powers of a Buddha as being either self or non-self; they speak of the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha as being either self or non-self.

They speak of the ten powers of a Buddha as being either pure or impure; they speak of the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha as being either pure or impure.
If there are those who are able to practice patience (kṣānti) by relying on such teachings as these, they are practicing the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā).
Furthermore, it is said:

one who practices patience should investigate whether the ten powers (daśabala) of a Buddha are permanent or impermanent; one should investigate whether the four fearlessnesses (vaiśāradya), up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (āveṇika-buddhadharma), are permanent or impermanent.

One should seek whether the ten powers of a Buddha are pleasant or painful; one should seek whether the four fearlessnesses, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, are pleasant or painful.

One should seek whether the ten powers of a Buddha are self or non-self; one should seek whether the four fearlessnesses, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, are self or non-self.

One should seek whether the ten powers of a Buddha are pure or impure; one should seek whether the four fearlessnesses, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, are pure or impure.
If there are those who are able to seek such dharmas as these and practice patience, this is the practice of the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*). "Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters, and so forth, thus seek whether the ten powers of a Buddha are permanent or impermanent, or seek whether the four fearlessnesses up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are permanent or impermanent; [this is the practice of the perfection of patience]."
Seeking whether the ten powers of a Buddha are pleasant or painful; seeking whether the four fearlessnesses up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are pleasant or painful;
seeking whether the ten powers of a Buddha are self or non-self; seeking whether the four fearlessnesses up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are self or non-self;
seeking whether the ten powers of a Buddha are pure or impure; seeking whether the four fearlessnesses up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are pure or impure.
Kauśika, I say that one who practices patience based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance perfection of patience characterized by the apprehension of something to be attained.
As previously stated, you should know that all these refer to a semblance of the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) based on apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!..."

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment, speak of the quality of non-forgetfulness as either permanent or impermanent, or speak of the nature of constant equanimity as either permanent or impermanent;
speak of the quality of non-forgetfulness as either pleasant or painful, or speak of the nature of constant equanimity as either pleasant or painful;
speak of the quality of non-forgetfulness as either self or non-self, or speak of the nature of constant equanimity as either self or non-self;
To speak of the quality of non-forgetfulness as either pure or impure, and to speak of the nature of constant equanimity as either pure or impure—
if one is able to rely upon such dharmas as these to practice patience, this is the practice of the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā).
Furthermore, it is said:

One who practices the patience of equanimity should seek whether the quality of non-forgetfulness is permanent or impermanent, and should seek whether the nature of constant abiding in equanimity is permanent or impermanent;
one should seek whether the quality of non-forgetfulness is pleasant or painful, and should seek whether the nature of constant abiding in equanimity is pleasant or painful.
One should seek the quality of non-forgetfulness whether it be self or selfless; one should seek the state of constant equanimity whether it be self or selfless;
one should seek the quality of non-forgetfulness whether it be pure or impure; and one should seek the state of constant equanimity whether it be pure or impure.
If there are those who are able to seek such dharmas as these and practice patience, this is the practice of the perfection of patience. "Kauśika!
If good sons and good daughters seek the dharma of non-forgetfulness as either permanent or impermanent, or seek the nature of constant equanimity as either permanent or impermanent;
One seeks the quality of non-forgetfulness whether it be pleasure or pain; one seeks the state of constant equanimity whether it be pleasure or pain.
One seeks the quality of non-forgetfulness whether it be self or non-self; one seeks the state of constant equanimity whether it be self or non-self.
One seeks the quality of non-forgetfulness whether it be pure or impure; one seeks the state of constant equanimity whether it be pure or impure.
Kauśika, I say that one who practices patience based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance perfection of patience characterized by the apprehension of something to be attained.
As previously stated, you should know that all these refer to a semblance of the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) characterized by apprehension (*upalambha*).
"Furthermore, Kauśika!..."

If good sons, good daughters, and others who have generated the mind set upon unsurpassed bodhi should speak of omniscience as either permanent or impermanent, or speak of the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects as either permanent or impermanent;
if they should speak of omniscience as either pleasant or painful, or speak of the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects as either pleasant or painful;
if they should speak of omniscience as either self or non-self, or speak of the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects as either self or non-self;
Whether one speaks of all-knowledge as pure or impure, or of the knowledge of the path and the knowledge of all aspects as pure or impure—
if there is one who is able to practice patience in reliance upon such dharmas as these, this is the practice of the perfection of patience.
Furthermore, it is said:

One who practices the patience of equanimity should seek omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) as either permanent or impermanent, and should seek the knowledge of the paths (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) as either permanent or impermanent;
one should seek omniscience as either pleasant or painful, and should seek the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects as either pleasant or painful.

One should seek omniscience (sarvajñatā) whether it be with self or without self; one should seek the knowledge of the paths (mārgākārajñatā) and the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā) whether they be with self or without self.
One should seek omniscience whether it be pure or impure; one should seek the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects whether they be pure or impure.
If there are those who are able to seek such dharmas as these and practice patience, they are practicing the perfection of patience. “Kauśika!

If good sons or good daughters seek omniscience—whether it be permanent or impermanent—and seek the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects—whether they be permanent or impermanent;”
Seeking omniscience as either pleasure or pain; seeking the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects as either pleasure or pain;
seeking omniscience as either self or non-self; seeking the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects as either self or non-self;
seeking omniscience as either pure or impure; seeking the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects as either pure or impure.
Kauśika, I declare that one who practices patience based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of patience characterized by the apprehension of something to be attained.
As previously stated, you should know that all of these refer to a semblance of the perfection of patience characterized by apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved upon the unsurpassed bodhicitta, explain that all dharanī-doors are either permanent or impermanent; explain that all samādhi-doors are either permanent or impermanent;
explain that all dharanī-doors are either pleasant or painful; explain that all samādhi-doors are either pleasant or painful;
explain that all dharanī-doors are either self or non-self; explain that all samādhi-doors are either self or non-self;
He speaks of all dharanī-doors, whether pure or impure; he speaks of all samādhi-doors, whether pure or impure.
If there is one who is able to practice patience (kṣānti) by relying on such dharmas as these, this is the practice of the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā).
Furthermore, it is said:
One who practices the patience of tranquility should seek all *dhāraṇī* gates as either permanent or impermanent; one should seek all *samādhi* gates as either permanent or impermanent;
one should seek all *dhāraṇī* gates as either pleasant or painful; one should seek all *samādhi* gates as either pleasant or painful.
One should seek all dharani-doors whether they are with self or without self; one should seek all samadhi-doors whether they are with self or without self;
one should seek all dharani-doors whether they are pure or impure; one should seek all samadhi-doors whether they are pure or impure.
If there are those who are able to seek such dharmas as these and practice patience, they are practicing the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*). "Kauśika!
If good sons and good daughters, and so forth, thus seek all dharani-doors, whether they be permanent or impermanent; or seek all samadhi-doors, whether they be permanent or impermanent;..."
They seek all *dhāraṇī* gates as either pleasure or suffering; they seek all *samādhi* gates as either pleasure or suffering.
They seek all *dhāraṇī* gates as either self or non-self; they seek all *samādhi* gates as either self or non-self.
They seek all *dhāraṇī* gates as either pure or impure; they seek all *samādhi* gates as either pure or impure.
Kauśika, I declare that one who practices patience based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of patience characterized by the apprehension of something to be attained.
As previously stated, you should know that all of these describe a semblance of the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā) characterized by apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment, should speak of the stage of entering the stream and the fruit of stream-entry as either permanent or impermanent; or speak of the stage of entering once-returning and the fruit of once-returning, the stage of entering non-returning and the fruit of non-returning, and the stage of entering arhatship and the fruit of arhatship as either permanent or impermanent;

or speak of the stage of entering the stream and the fruit of stream-entry as either pleasure or suffering; or speak of the stage of entering once-returning and the fruit of once-returning, the stage of entering non-returning and the fruit of non-returning, and the stage of entering arhatship and the fruit of arhatship as either pleasure or suffering;

or speak of the stage of entering the stream and the fruit of stream-entry as either self or non-self; or speak of the stage of entering once-returning and the fruit of once-returning, the stage of entering non-returning and the fruit of non-returning, and the stage of entering arhatship and the fruit of arhatship as either self or non-self; [they would be speaking erroneously].

He speaks of the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry and the fruit of stream-entry, whether pure or impure; he speaks of the candidate for the fruit of once-returning and the fruit of once-returning, the candidate for the fruit of non-returning and the fruit of non-returning, and the candidate for the fruit of arhatship and the fruit of arhatship, whether pure or impure.
If there is one who is able to practice patience (*kṣānti*) by relying on such dharmas as these, this is the practice of the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*).
Furthermore, it is said:

One who practices patience should seek the fruit of entering the stream (*srotāpatti-pratipannaka*) and the fruit of the stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), whether they are permanent or impermanent; one should seek the fruit of the once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin-pratipannaka*) up to the fruit of the arhat (*arhattva-phala*), whether they are permanent or impermanent.

One should seek the fruit of stream-entry and the path of stream-entry, whether as pleasure or as pain; one should seek the fruits from the path of once-returning up to arhatship, whether as pleasure or as pain.

One should seek the fruit of stream-entry and the path of stream-entry, whether as self or as non-self; one should seek the fruits from the path of once-returning up to arhatship, whether as self or as non-self.

One should seek the fruit of stream-entry and the path of stream-entry, whether as pure or as impure; one should seek the fruits from the path of once-returning up to arhatship, whether as pure or as impure.
If there are those who are able to seek such dharmas as these and practice patience, this is the practice of the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*). "Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters, and so forth, thus seek the stage of entering the stream (*srotāpatti-pratipannaka*) and the fruit of the stream-enterer (*srotāpanna-phala*), whether they be permanent or impermanent; or seek the stage of the once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmi-pratipannaka*) up to the fruit of the arhat (*arhat-phala*), whether they be permanent or impermanent;..."

To seek the state of entering the stream (*srotāpatti-pratipannaka*) or the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*), whether as pleasure or as pain; to seek the state of entering the once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmi-pratipannaka*) up to the fruit of arhatship (*arhattva-phala*), whether as pleasure or as pain;

to seek the state of entering the stream or the fruit of stream-entry, whether as self or as non-self; to seek the state of entering the once-returner up to the fruit of arhatship, whether as self or as non-self;

to seek the state of entering the stream or the fruit of stream-entry, whether as pure or as impure; to seek the state of entering the once-returner up to the fruit of arhatship, whether as pure or as impure.
Kauśika, I say that one who practices patience based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance perfection of patience characterized by the apprehension of something to be attained.
As previously stated, you should know that all these refer to a semblance of the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) characterized by apprehension (*upalambha*).
"Furthermore, Kauśika!..."

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, were to speak of all pratyekabuddha-enlightenment as either permanent or impermanent; speak of all pratyekabuddha-enlightenment as either pleasant or painful; speak of all pratyekabuddha-enlightenment as either self or non-self; or speak of all pratyekabuddha-enlightenment as either pure or impure.
If there are those who are able to practice patience (*kṣānti*) by relying on such dharmas as these, they are practicing the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*).
Furthermore, it is said:

one who practices patience should seek all pratyekabuddha-enlightenment (*pratyekabodhi*) as either permanent or impermanent; should seek all pratyekabuddha-enlightenment as either pleasant or painful; should seek all pratyekabuddha-enlightenment as either self or non-self; and should seek all pratyekabuddha-enlightenment as either pure or impure.
If there are those who are able to seek such dharmas as these and practice patience, this is the practice of the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*). "Kauśika!

If sons of good family or daughters of good family seek all pratyekabuddha-enlightenment as either permanent or impermanent; seek all pratyekabuddha-enlightenment as either pleasant or painful; seek all pratyekabuddha-enlightenment as either self or non-self; seek all pratyekabuddha-enlightenment as either pure or impure."
Kauśika, I declare that one who practices patience based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of patience characterized by the apprehension of something to be attained.
As previously stated, you should know that all of these describe a semblance of the perfection of patience characterized by apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, were to speak of all the practices of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas as either permanent or impermanent; speak of all the practices of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas as either pleasant or suffering; speak of all the practices of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas as either self or non-self; or speak of all the practices of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas as either pure or impure.
If there is one who is able to practice patience (*kṣānti*) by relying on such dharmas as these, this is the practice of the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*).
Furthermore, it is said:

One who practices patience should seek whether all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are permanent or impermanent; one should seek whether all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are pleasant or painful; one should seek whether all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are self or non-self; and one should seek whether all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are pure or impure.
If there are those who are able to seek such dharmas as these and practice patience, this is the practice of the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*). "Kauśika!

If sons of good family or daughters of good family seek all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as either permanent or impermanent; seek all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as either pleasant or painful; seek all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as either self or non-self; and seek all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as either pure or impure."
Kauśika, I declare that one who practices patience based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance perfection of patience characterized by apprehension.
As previously stated, it should be understood that all these refer to a semblance of the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) characterized by apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!..."

If good sons, good daughters, and others, for the sake of those who have resolved upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment, were to speak of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas as either permanent or impermanent; speak of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas as either pleasant or painful; speak of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas as either self or non-self; or speak of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas as either pure or impure.
If there are those who are able to practice patience (*kṣānti*) by relying on such teachings as these, they are practicing the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).
Furthermore, it is said:

one who practices patience should seek the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*) of the Buddhas as either permanent or impermanent; should seek the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas as either pleasant or painful; should seek the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas as either self or non-self; and should seek the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas as either pure or impure.
If there are those who are able to seek such dharmas as these and practice patience, this is the practice of the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*). "Kauśika!

If sons of good family or daughters of good family seek the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas as either permanent or impermanent; seek the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas as either pleasant or painful; seek the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas as either self or non-self; seek the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas as either pure or impure."
Kauśika, I say that practicing patience based on such dharmas is called the semblance perfection of patience characterized by the apprehension of something to be attained.
"As previously explained, it should be understood that all these refer to a semblance of the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) characterized by apprehension.
Then, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

How is it that those sons and daughters of good family who speak of the perfection of ethical discipline with the notion of something to be attained are said to be speaking of a counterfeit perfection of ethical discipline?
The Buddha said, “Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved upon unsurpassed bodhicitta, speak of form as either permanent or impermanent, or speak of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as either permanent or impermanent;”
One speaks of form as either pleasant or painful; one speaks of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as either pleasant or painful.
One speaks of form as either self or non-self; one speaks of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as either self or non-self.
One speaks of form as either pure or impure; one speaks of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as either pure or impure.
If there is one who is able to practice pure ethical discipline (*śīla*) by relying on such teachings as these, this is the practice of the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*).
Furthermore, it is said:

"One who practices ethical discipline should investigate whether form (*rūpa*) is permanent or impermanent; one should investigate whether feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are permanent or impermanent."
One should seek whether form is pleasant or painful; one should seek whether feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are pleasant or painful.
One should seek whether form is self or non-self; one should seek whether feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are self or non-self.
One should seek whether form is pure or impure; one should seek whether feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice pure ethical discipline, they are practicing the perfection of ethical discipline. "Kauśika!
If good sons and good daughters seek form as either permanent or impermanent, and seek feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as either permanent or impermanent;
They seek whether form is pleasant or painful; they seek whether feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are pleasant or painful.
They seek whether form is self or non-self; they seek whether feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are self or non-self.
They seek whether form is pure or impure; they seek whether feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are pure or impure.
Kauśika, I say that one who practices pure ethical discipline based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of ethical discipline characterized by apprehension.
As previously stated, you should know that all of these describe a semblance of the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) characterized by apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, should speak of the eye-base as either permanent or impermanent; speak of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases as either permanent or impermanent;
speak of the eye-base as either pleasant or painful; speak of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases as either pleasant or painful;
speak of the eye-base as either self or non-self; speak of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases as either self or non-self;
One speaks of the sense base of the eye as either pure or impure, and one speaks of the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind as either pure or impure.
If there is one who is able to practice the pure precepts by relying on such dharmas as these, this is the practice of the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā).
Furthermore, it is said:

One who practices the pure precepts should investigate whether the sense base of the eye is permanent or impermanent; one should investigate whether the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are permanent or impermanent;
one should investigate whether the sense base of the eye is pleasant or painful; one should investigate whether the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are pleasant or painful.
One should investigate whether the eye-base is self or non-self; one should investigate whether the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases are self or non-self.
One should investigate whether the eye-base is pure or impure; one should investigate whether the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases are pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice the pure precepts, they are practicing the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*). "Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters seek the sense base of the eye (*cakṣur-āyatana*) as either permanent or impermanent, and seek the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind (*manas-āyatana*) as either permanent or impermanent;
They seek whether the eye-base is pleasant or painful; they seek whether the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases are pleasant or painful.
They seek whether the eye-base is self or non-self; they seek whether the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases are self or non-self.
They seek whether the eye-base is pure or impure; they seek whether the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases are pure or impure.

Kauśika, I declare that one who practices pure ethical discipline based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of ethical discipline characterized by the apprehension of something to be attained.
As previously stated, you should know that all of these describe a semblance of the perfection of ethical discipline characterized by apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, should speak of the sphere of form as either permanent or impermanent, or speak of the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena as either permanent or impermanent;
if they should speak of the sphere of form as either pleasant or painful, or speak of the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena as either pleasant or painful;
if they should speak of the sphere of form as either self or non-self, or speak of the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena as either self or non-self;
To speak of the sphere of form as either pure or impure, and to speak of the spheres of sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena as either pure or impure—
if one is able to practice the pure precepts based upon such dharmas as these, this is the practice of the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*).
Furthermore, it is said:

One who practices pure ethical discipline should investigate whether the sphere of form is permanent or impermanent; one should investigate whether the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena are permanent or impermanent;

one should investigate whether the sphere of form is pleasant or painful; and one should investigate whether the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena are pleasant or painful.
One should investigate whether the sphere of form is self or non-self; one should investigate whether the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena are self or non-self.
One should investigate whether the sphere of form is pure or impure; one should investigate whether the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena are pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice pure ethical discipline, they are practicing the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*). "Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters seek whether the sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) is permanent or impermanent, and seek whether the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) are permanent or impermanent;..."
They seek whether the sphere of form is pleasant or painful; they seek whether the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena are pleasant or painful.
They seek whether the sphere of form is self or non-self; they seek whether the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena are self or non-self.
They seek whether the sphere of form is pure or impure; they seek whether the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena are pure or impure.
Kauśika, I say that one who practices pure ethical discipline based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of ethical discipline characterized by apprehension.
As previously explained, you should know that all these refer to what is called the semblance perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*) characterized by apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment, explain whether the eye-element is permanent or impermanent; explain whether the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, eye-contact, and all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition are permanent or impermanent;

explain whether the eye-element is pleasant or painful; explain whether the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, eye-contact, and all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition are pleasant or painful;

explain whether the eye-element is self or non-self; [and explain whether] the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, eye-contact, and all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition are self or non-self.

One speaks of the eye-element as either pure or impure; one speaks of the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, and eye-contact, as well as all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, as either pure or impure.
If there are those who are able to practice pure ethical discipline by relying on such teachings as these, they are practicing the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*).
Furthermore, it is said:

one who practices ethical discipline should investigate whether the eye-element is permanent or impermanent; one should investigate whether the form-element, and so forth, up to the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, are permanent or impermanent.
One should seek whether the eye-element is pleasant or painful; one should seek whether the form-element, and so on up to the feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, are pleasant or painful.
One should seek whether the eye-element is self or non-self; one should seek whether the form-element, and so on up to the feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, are self or non-self.
One should seek whether the eye-element is pure or impure; one should seek whether the form-element, and so on up to the feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, are pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice the pure precepts, this is the practice of the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*). "Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters seek the eye-element (*cakṣur-dhātu*) as either permanent or impermanent, and seek the form-element (*rūpa-dhātu*) up to the various feelings (*vedanā*) produced with eye-contact as condition as either permanent or impermanent; [this is their practice]."
They seek whether the eye-element is pleasant or painful; they seek whether the form-element, and so on up to the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, are pleasant or painful.
They seek whether the eye-element is self or non-self; they seek whether the form-element, and so on up to the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, are self or non-self.
They seek whether the eye-element is pure or impure; they seek whether the form-element, and so on up to the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, are pure or impure.
Kauśika, I say that one who practices pure ethical discipline by relying on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of ethical discipline characterized by apprehension.
As previously stated, you should know that all of these describe a semblance of the perfection of ethical discipline characterized by apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment, explain whether the ear-element is permanent or impermanent; explain whether the sound-element, the ear-consciousness-element, ear-contact, and the various sensations produced with ear-contact as condition are permanent or impermanent;

explain whether the ear-element is pleasant or painful; explain whether the sound-element, the ear-consciousness-element, ear-contact, and the various sensations produced with ear-contact as condition are pleasant or painful;

explain whether the ear-element is self or non-self; explain whether the sound-element, the ear-consciousness-element, ear-contact, and the various sensations produced with ear-contact as condition are self or non-self.

One speaks of the ear element as either pure or impure; one speaks of the sound element, the ear-consciousness element, and ear-contact, as well as the various feelings arising with ear-contact as their condition, as either pure or impure.
If there are those who, relying on such teachings as these, practice pure ethical discipline, they are practicing the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*).
Furthermore, it is said:

one who practices pure ethical discipline should investigate whether the sphere of the ear (*śrotra-dhātu*) is permanent or impermanent; one should investigate whether the sphere of sound (*śabda-dhātu*), and so forth, up to the various sensations (*vedanā*) produced with ear-contact as a condition, are permanent or impermanent.

One should seek whether the ear element is pleasant or painful; one should seek whether the sound element, and so on up to the various feelings produced with ear-contact as condition, are pleasant or painful.

One should seek whether the ear element is self or non-self; one should seek whether the sound element, and so on up to the various feelings produced with ear-contact as condition, are self or non-self.
One should seek whether the ear element is pure or impure; one should seek whether the sound element, and so on up to the various feelings produced with ear-contact as condition, are pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice pure ethical discipline, this is the practice of the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*). "Kauśika!

If good sons or good daughters seek the ear-element (*śrotra-dhātu*) as either permanent or impermanent, or seek the sound-element (*śabda-dhātu*) up to the various feelings (*vedanā*) produced with ear-contact as a condition, as either permanent or impermanent;
They seek whether the ear-element is pleasant or painful; they seek whether the sound-element, and so on up to the various feelings produced with ear-contact as condition, are pleasant or painful.
They seek whether the ear-element is self or non-self; they seek whether the sound-element, and so on up to the various feelings produced with ear-contact as condition, are self or non-self.
They seek whether the ear-element is pure or impure; they seek whether the sound-element, and so on up to the various feelings produced with ear-contact as condition, are pure or impure.

were to speak of the Noble Truth of Suffering as either pleasant or painful, or speak of the Noble Truths of Origination, Cessation, and the Path as either pleasant or painful;
were to speak of the Noble Truth of Suffering as either self or non-self, or speak of the Noble Truths of Origination, Cessation, and the Path as either self or non-self;
Whether one speaks of the Noble Truth of Suffering as pure or impure, or speaks of the Noble Truths of Origination, Cessation, and the Path as pure or impure—
if there is anyone who is able to rely upon such dharmas to practice pure ethical discipline, this is the practice of the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*).
Furthermore, he spoke thus:

"One who practices pure ethical discipline should investigate whether the Noble Truth of Suffering is permanent or impermanent; one should investigate whether the Noble Truths of Origination, Cessation, and the Path are permanent or impermanent;

one should investigate whether the Noble Truth of Suffering is pleasant or painful; and one should investigate whether the Noble Truths of Origination, Cessation, and the Path are pleasant or painful."
One should seek whether the Noble Truth of Suffering is self or non-self; one should seek whether the Noble Truths of Origination, Cessation, and the Path are self or non-self;
one should seek whether the Noble Truth of Suffering is pure or impure; one should seek whether the Noble Truths of Origination, Cessation, and the Path are pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice pure ethical discipline, they are practicing the perfection of ethical discipline. “Kauśika!

If sons or daughters of good family seek the noble truth of suffering as either permanent or impermanent, and seek the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path as either permanent or impermanent;”
One seeks whether the noble truth of suffering is pleasant or painful; one seeks whether the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path are pleasant or painful.
One seeks whether the noble truth of suffering is self or non-self; one seeks whether the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path are self or non-self.
One seeks whether the noble truth of suffering is pure or impure; one seeks whether the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path are pure or impure.
Kauśika, I say that one who practices pure ethical discipline based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of ethical discipline characterized by apprehension.
As previously stated, you should know that all these refer to a semblance of the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā) characterized by apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment, speak of the four dhyānas as being either permanent or impermanent, or speak of the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions as being either permanent or impermanent;
if they speak of the four dhyānas as being either pleasant or painful, or speak of the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions as being either pleasant or painful;
if they speak of the four dhyānas as being either self or non-self, or speak of the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions as being either self or non-self;
To speak of the four dhyānas, whether pure or impure, and to speak of the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions, whether pure or impure—
if one is able to rely upon such dharmas as these to practice pure ethical discipline, this is the practice of the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā).
Furthermore, it is said:

One who practices the pure precepts should seek the four dhyānas as either permanent or impermanent; one should seek the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments as either permanent or impermanent;
one should seek the four dhyānas as either pleasant or painful; one should seek the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments as either pleasant or painful.
One should seek the four dhyānas whether they are with self or without self; one should seek the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments whether they are with self or without self;
one should seek the four dhyānas whether they are pure or impure; one should seek the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments whether they are pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice the pure precepts, they are practicing the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*). "Kauśika!
If good sons and good daughters seek the four dhyānas as either permanent or impermanent, or seek the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions as either permanent or impermanent;
They seek the four dhyānas as either pleasant or painful; they seek the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments as either pleasant or painful.
They seek the four dhyānas as either self or non-self; they seek the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments as either self or non-self.
They seek the four dhyānas as either pure or impure; they seek the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments as either pure or impure.

Kauśika, I say that one who practices pure ethical discipline based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of ethical discipline characterized by the apprehension of something to be attained.
As previously stated, you should know that all these refer to what is called the semblance perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā) characterized by apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, speak of the eight liberations as being either permanent or impermanent; speak of the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten totalities as being either permanent or impermanent;

speak of the eight liberations as being either pleasant or painful; speak of the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten totalities as being either pleasant or painful;

or speak of the eight liberations as being either self or non-self; speak of the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten totalities as being either self or non-self;
To speak of the eight liberations as either pure or impure, and to speak of the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten totalities as either pure or impure—
if one is able to rely upon such dharmas as these to practice pure ethical discipline, this is the practice of the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*).
Furthermore, it is said:

One who practices the pure precepts should seek whether the eight liberations are permanent or impermanent; one should seek whether the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten spheres of totality are permanent or impermanent;

one should seek whether the eight liberations are pleasant or painful; one should seek whether the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten spheres of totality are pleasant or painful.

One should seek the eight liberations whether they are self or non-self; one should seek the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities whether they are self or non-self.

One should seek the eight liberations whether they are pure or impure; one should seek the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities whether they are pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice the pure precepts, this is the practice of the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*). "Kauśika!

If sons of good family or daughters of good family seek the eight liberations (*aṣṭa-vimokṣa*) as either permanent or impermanent; if they seek the eight bases of mastery (*abhibhv-āyatana*), the nine successive attainments (*anupūrva-vihāra-samāpatti*), or the ten totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*) as either permanent or impermanent; [they are practicing the perfection of ethical discipline]."
They seek the eight liberations as either pleasant or painful; they seek the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities as either pleasant or painful.
They seek the eight liberations as either self or non-self; they seek the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities as either self or non-self.
They seek the eight liberations as either pure or impure; they seek the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities as either pure or impure.
Kauśika, I declare that one who practices pure ethical discipline based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of ethical discipline characterized by apprehension.
As previously stated, you should know that all of these describe a semblance of the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā) characterized by apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment, explain whether the four foundations of mindfulness are permanent or impermanent; explain whether the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path are permanent or impermanent;

explain whether the four foundations of mindfulness are pleasant or painful; explain whether the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path are pleasant or painful;

explain whether the four foundations of mindfulness are self or non-self; explain whether the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path are self or non-self.

He speaks of the four foundations of mindfulness as either pure or impure; he speaks of the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path as either pure or impure.
If there are those who are able to practice pure ethical discipline by relying on such dharmas as these, they are practicing the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*).
Furthermore, it is said:

One who practices ethical discipline should seek whether the four foundations of mindfulness are permanent or impermanent; one should seek whether the four right endeavors, up to and including the eightfold noble path, are permanent or impermanent.

One should seek whether the four foundations of mindfulness are pleasant or painful; one should seek whether the four right endeavors, up to and including the eightfold noble path, are pleasant or painful.
One should seek whether the four foundations of mindfulness are self or non-self; one should seek whether the four right endeavors, up to and including the eightfold noble path, are self or non-self.
One should seek whether the four foundations of mindfulness are pure or impure; one should seek whether the four right endeavors, up to and including the eightfold noble path, are pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice pure ethical discipline, they are practicing the perfection of ethical discipline. Kausika,

if good sons and good daughters seek the four foundations of mindfulness as either permanent or impermanent, and seek the four right efforts up to the eightfold noble path as either permanent or impermanent;
They seek whether the four foundations of mindfulness are pleasant or painful; they seek whether the four right efforts, up to and including the eightfold noble path, are pleasant or painful.
They seek whether the four foundations of mindfulness are self or non-self; they seek whether the four right efforts, up to and including the eightfold noble path, are self or non-self.
They seek whether the four foundations of mindfulness are pure or impure; they seek whether the four right efforts, up to and including the eightfold noble path, are pure or impure.
Kauśika, I declare that one who practices pure ethical discipline based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of ethical discipline characterized by apprehension.
As previously stated, you should know that all these refer to what are merely semblances of the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā) characterized by apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment, should speak of the gate of liberation of emptiness as either permanent or impermanent, or speak of the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness as either permanent or impermanent;
should speak of the gate of liberation of emptiness as either pleasant or painful, or speak of the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness as either pleasant or painful;
should speak of the gate of liberation of emptiness as either self or non-self, or speak of the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness as either self or non-self;
To speak of the gate of liberation of emptiness as either pure or impure, and to speak of the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness as either pure or impure—
if one is able to rely upon such dharmas as these to practice pure ethical discipline, this is the practice of the perfection of ethical discipline.
Furthermore, it is said:

One who practices pure ethical discipline should seek the gate of liberation of emptiness as either permanent or impermanent; one should seek the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness as either permanent or impermanent;
