one should seek the gate of liberation of emptiness as either pleasant or painful; one should seek the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness as either pleasant or painful.
One should seek the gate of liberation of emptiness whether it be self or non-self; one should seek the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness whether they be self or non-self;
one should seek the gate of liberation of emptiness whether it be pure or impure; one should seek the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness whether they be pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice pure ethical discipline, they are practicing the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*). "Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters seek the gate of liberation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha*)—whether it be permanent or impermanent—and seek the gates of liberation of signlessness (*animitta*) and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*)—whether they be permanent or impermanent;..."
They seek whether the gate of liberation of emptiness is pleasant or painful; they seek whether the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness are pleasant or painful.
They seek whether the gate of liberation of emptiness is self or non-self; they seek whether the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness are self or non-self.
They seek whether the gate of liberation of emptiness is pure or impure; they seek whether the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness are pure or impure.
Kauśika, I declare that one who practices pure ethical discipline based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of ethical discipline characterized by apprehension.
As previously explained, you should know that all of these describe a semblance of the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā) characterized by apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, should speak of the five eyes as being either permanent or impermanent, or speak of the six supernormal powers as being either permanent or impermanent;
should speak of the five eyes as being either pleasant or painful, or speak of the six supernormal powers as being either pleasant or painful;
should speak of the five eyes as being either self or non-self, or speak of the six supernormal powers as being either self or non-self;
One speaks of the five eyes as being either pure or impure, and one speaks of the six superknowledges as being either pure or impure.
If there is one who is able to practice pure ethical discipline by relying on such dharmas as these, this is the practice of the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā).
Furthermore, it is said:
One who practices pure precepts should seek the five eyes as either permanent or impermanent, and should seek the six supernormal powers as either permanent or impermanent;
one should seek the five eyes as either pleasant or painful, and should seek the six supernormal powers as either pleasant or painful.
One should seek the five eyes whether they are self or non-self; one should seek the six supernormal powers whether they are self or non-self;
one should seek the five eyes whether they are pure or impure; one should seek the six supernormal powers whether they are pure or impure.
If there are those who are able to seek such dharmas as these and practice pure ethical discipline, they are practicing the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*). "Kauśika!
If sons of good family or daughters of good family seek the five eyes, whether they are permanent or impermanent, or seek the six supernormal powers, whether they are permanent or impermanent;
One seeks the five eyes as either pleasant or painful; one seeks the six supernormal powers as either pleasant or painful.
One seeks the five eyes as either self or non-self; one seeks the six supernormal powers as either self or non-self.
One seeks the five eyes as either pure or impure; one seeks the six supernormal powers as either pure or impure.
Kauśika, I say that one who practices pure ethical discipline based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of ethical discipline characterized by apprehension.
As previously explained, you should know that all these refer to what is called the semblance of the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*) characterized by apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kausika!..."

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, were to speak of the Buddha’s ten powers as either permanent or impermanent; were to speak of the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha as either permanent or impermanent;

or were to speak of the Buddha’s ten powers as either pleasant or painful, and speak of the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha as either pleasant or painful;

He speaks of the ten powers of a Buddha as being either self or non-self; he speaks of the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha as being either self or non-self.

He speaks of the ten powers of a Buddha as being either pure or impure; he speaks of the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha as being either pure or impure.
If there are those who, relying on such dharmas as these, practice pure ethical discipline, they are practicing the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā).
Furthermore, it is said:

one who practices pure ethical discipline should seek whether the ten powers of a Buddha are permanent or impermanent; one should seek whether the four fearlessnesses, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, are permanent or impermanent.

One should seek whether the ten powers of a Buddha are pleasant or painful; one should seek whether the four fearlessnesses, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, are pleasant or painful.

One should seek whether the ten powers of a Buddha are self or non-self; one should seek whether the four fearlessnesses, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, are self or non-self.

One should seek whether the ten powers of a Buddha are pure or impure; one should seek whether the four fearlessnesses, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, are pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice pure ethical discipline, this is the practice of the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*). "Kauśika!

If sons of good family or daughters of good family seek the ten powers of a Buddha—whether they are permanent or impermanent—and seek the four fearlessnesses, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha—whether they are permanent or impermanent; [this is the practice of the perfection of ethical discipline]."

They seek whether the ten powers of a Buddha are pleasant or painful; they seek whether the four fearlessnesses, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, are pleasant or painful.
They seek whether the ten powers of a Buddha are self or non-self; they seek whether the four fearlessnesses, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, are self or non-self.
They seek whether the ten powers of a Buddha are pure or impure; they seek whether the four fearlessnesses, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, are pure or impure.
Kauśika, I say that one who practices pure ethical discipline based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of ethical discipline characterized by apprehension.
As previously stated, you should know that all of these describe a semblance of the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā) characterized by grasping at attainment.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!"

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment, speak of the quality of non-forgetfulness as either permanent or impermanent, or speak of the nature of constant equanimity as either permanent or impermanent;
speak of the quality of non-forgetfulness as either pleasant or painful, or speak of the nature of constant equanimity as either pleasant or painful;
or speak of the quality of non-forgetfulness as either self or non-self;
He speaks of the nature of constant equanimity as either self or non-self;
he speaks of the quality of non-forgetfulness as either pure or impure, and he speaks of the nature of constant equanimity as either pure or impure.
If there are those who are able to practice pure ethical discipline (*śīla*) by relying on such teachings as these, they are practicing the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*).
Furthermore, it is said:

One who practices pure ethical discipline should seek the quality of non-forgetfulness (*asaṃpramoṣadharma*), whether it be permanent or impermanent; one should seek the nature of constant equanimity (*upekṣā*), whether it be permanent or impermanent.
One should seek the quality of non-forgetfulness whether in pleasure or in pain; one should seek the state of constant equanimity whether in pleasure or in pain.
One should seek the quality of non-forgetfulness whether in self or in non-self; one should seek the state of constant equanimity whether in self or in non-self.
One should seek the quality of non-forgetfulness whether in purity or in impurity; one should seek the state of constant equanimity whether in purity or in impurity.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice pure ethical discipline, this is the practice of the perfection of ethical discipline. "Kauśika!

If sons of good family, daughters of good family, and others seek the quality of non-forgetfulness—whether it be permanent or impermanent—and seek the nature of constant equanimity—whether it be permanent or impermanent;
Whether it be pleasure or pain, they seek the quality of non-forgetfulness; whether it be pleasure or pain, they seek the state of constant abiding in equanimity.
Whether it be self or non-self, they seek the quality of non-forgetfulness; whether it be self or non-self, they seek the state of constant abiding in equanimity.
Whether it be pure or impure, they seek the quality of non-forgetfulness; whether it be pure or impure, they seek the state of constant abiding in equanimity.
Kauśika, I say that one who practices pure ethical discipline based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of ethical discipline characterized by apprehension.
As previously stated, you should know that all these refer to what is called the semblance of the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) characterized by apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, speak of all-knowledge as either permanent or impermanent; speak of the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects as either permanent or impermanent;
speak of all-knowledge as either pleasant or suffering; speak of the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects as either pleasant or suffering;
speak of all-knowledge as either self or non-self; speak of the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects as either self or non-self;
He speaks of all-knowledge as being either pure or impure, and he speaks of the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects as being either pure or impure.
If there is one who is able to practice the pure precepts by relying on such dharmas as these, this is the practice of the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*).
Furthermore, it is said:

One who practices pure ethical discipline should seek omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) as either permanent or impermanent, and should seek the knowledge of the paths (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) as either permanent or impermanent;
one should seek omniscience as either pleasant or painful, and should seek the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects as either pleasant or painful.

One should seek all-knowledge (sarvajñatā) whether it be with self or without self; one should seek the knowledge of the paths (mārgākārajñatā) and the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā) whether they be with self or without self.
One should seek all-knowledge whether it be pure or impure; one should seek the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects whether they be pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice pure ethical discipline, they are practicing the perfection of ethical discipline. "Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters seek omniscience—whether it be permanent or impermanent—and seek the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects, whether they be permanent or impermanent;
Whether it be pleasant or painful, one seeks all-knowledge; whether it be pleasant or painful, one seeks the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects.
Whether it be self or non-self, one seeks all-knowledge; whether it be self or non-self, one seeks the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects.
Whether it be pure or impure, one seeks all-knowledge; whether it be pure or impure, one seeks the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects.
Kauśika, I declare that one who practices pure ethical discipline based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of ethical discipline characterized by apprehension.
As previously explained, you should know that all these refer to a semblance of the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) characterized by apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment, explain whether all dharani-gates are permanent or impermanent; explain whether all samadhi-gates are permanent or impermanent;
explain whether all dharani-gates are pleasant or painful; explain whether all samadhi-gates are pleasant or painful;
explain whether all dharani-gates are self or non-self; explain whether all samadhi-gates are self or non-self;
He speaks of all dharanī-gates, whether pure or impure; he speaks of all samādhi-gates, whether pure or impure.
If there is one who is able to practice the pure precepts by relying on such dharmas as these, this is the practice of the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā).
Furthermore, it is said:
One who practices pure ethical discipline should seek all *dhāraṇī* gates as either permanent or impermanent; one should seek all *samādhi* gates as either permanent or impermanent;
one should seek all *dhāraṇī* gates as either pleasant or painful; one should seek all *samādhi* gates as either pleasant or painful.
One should seek all dharani-doors whether they are with self or without self; one should seek all samadhi-doors whether they are with self or without self;
one should seek all dharani-doors whether they are pure or impure; one should seek all samadhi-doors whether they are pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice pure ethical discipline, they are practicing the perfection of ethical discipline. "Kauśika!
If good sons and good daughters seek all doors of dhāraṇī—whether they be permanent or impermanent—and seek all doors of samādhi—whether they be permanent or impermanent;
They seek all dharani-gates as either pleasure or suffering; they seek all samadhi-gates as either pleasure or suffering.
They seek all dharani-gates as either self or non-self; they seek all samadhi-gates as either self or non-self.
They seek all dharani-gates as either pure or impure; they seek all samadhi-gates as either pure or impure.
Kauśika, I say that one who practices pure ethical discipline based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of ethical discipline characterized by apprehension.
As previously stated, it should be understood that all these refer to a semblance of the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) characterized by apprehension (*upalambha*).
The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Scroll 143, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Part One: Chapter on the Measurement of Merit, Section 30-42. "Furthermore, Kauśika!"

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment, were to speak of the stage of entering the stream and the fruit of stream-entry as either permanent or impermanent; were to speak of the stage of entering once-returning and the fruit of once-returning, the stage of entering non-returning and the fruit of non-returning, and the stage of entering arhatship and the fruit of arhatship as either permanent or impermanent;

were to speak of the stage of entering the stream and the fruit of stream-entry as either pleasant or painful; were to speak of the stage of entering once-returning and the fruit of once-returning, the stage of entering non-returning and the fruit of non-returning, and the stage of entering arhatship and the fruit of arhatship as either pleasant or painful;

were to speak of the stage of entering the stream and the fruit of stream-entry as either self or non-self; were to speak of the stage of entering once-returning and the fruit of once-returning, the stage of entering non-returning and the fruit of non-returning, and the stage of entering arhatship and the fruit of arhatship as either self or non-self; [they would be speaking erroneously].

He speaks of the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry and the fruit of stream-entry, whether pure or impure; he speaks of the candidate for the fruit of once-returning and the fruit of once-returning, the candidate for the fruit of non-returning and the fruit of non-returning, and the candidate for the fruit of arhatship and the fruit of arhatship, whether pure or impure.
If there are those who, relying on such teachings as these, practice the pure precepts, they are practicing the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*).
Furthermore, it is said:

One who practices ethical discipline should seek the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*) and the path to stream-entry (*srotāpatti-mārga*), whether they are permanent or impermanent; one should seek the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmi-phala*) up to the fruit of arhatship (*arhat-phala*) and the paths thereto, whether they are permanent or impermanent.

One should seek the fruit of stream-entry and the path of stream-entry, whether as pleasure or as pain; one should seek the fruits from the path of once-returning up to arhatship, whether as pleasure or as pain.

One should seek the fruit of stream-entry and the path of stream-entry, whether as self or as non-self; one should seek the fruits from the path of once-returning up to arhatship, whether as self or as non-self.

One should seek the fruit of stream-entry and the path of stream-entry, whether as pure or as impure; one should seek the fruits from the path of once-returning up to arhatship, whether as pure or as impure.
If there are those who are able to seek such dharmas as these and practice pure ethical discipline, this is the practice of the perfection of ethical discipline. "Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters, and so forth, thus seek the stage of entering the stream and the fruit of stream-entry—whether as permanent or impermanent—and seek the stage of entering the once-returner up to the fruit of arhatship—whether as permanent or impermanent;
Seeking the fruit of stream-entry or the path of stream-entry as either pleasure or pain; seeking the fruits up to arhatship or their respective paths as either pleasure or pain;
seeking the fruit of stream-entry or the path of stream-entry as either self or non-self; seeking the fruits up to arhatship or their respective paths as either self or non-self;
seeking the fruit of stream-entry or the path of stream-entry as either pure or impure; seeking the fruits up to arhatship or their respective paths as either pure or impure.
Kauśika, I declare that one who practices pure ethical discipline based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of ethical discipline characterized by apprehension.
As previously stated, you should know that all these refer to a semblance of the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*) characterized by apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, were to speak of all pratyekabuddha-enlightenment as either permanent or impermanent; speak of all pratyekabuddha-enlightenment as either pleasant or painful; speak of all pratyekabuddha-enlightenment as either self or non-self; or speak of all pratyekabuddha-enlightenment as either pure or impure.
If there is one who is able to practice pure ethical discipline (*śīla*) by relying on such teachings as these, this is the practice of the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*).
Furthermore, it is said:

One who practices ethical discipline should seek all pratyekabuddha enlightenment whether it be permanent or impermanent; one should seek all pratyekabuddha enlightenment whether it be pleasant or painful; one should seek all pratyekabuddha enlightenment whether it be self or selfless; one should seek all pratyekabuddha enlightenment whether it be pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice pure ethical discipline, this is the practice of the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*). "Kauśika!

If sons of good family or daughters of good family seek all the enlightenment of a solitary realizer (*pratyekabuddha-bodhi*) as either permanent or impermanent; seek all the enlightenment of a solitary realizer as either pleasant or painful; seek all the enlightenment of a solitary realizer as either self or non-self; seek all the enlightenment of a solitary realizer as either pure or impure."
Kauśika, I declare that one who practices pure ethical discipline based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of ethical discipline characterized by apprehension.
As previously explained, you should know that all these refer to what is called the semblance of the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) characterized by apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!..."

If good sons, good daughters, and others who have resolved upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment should explain that all practices of Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are either permanent or impermanent; explain that all practices of Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are either pleasant or painful; explain that all practices of Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are either self or non-self; or explain that all practices of Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are either pure or impure.
If there are those who are able to practice pure ethical discipline (*śīla*) by relying on such teachings as these, they are practicing the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*).
Furthermore, it is said:

One who practices pure ethical discipline should seek all the practices of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas regarding whether they are permanent or impermanent; one should seek all the practices of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas regarding whether they are pleasant or painful; one should seek all the practices of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas regarding whether they have a self or are selfless; and one should seek all the practices of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas regarding whether they are pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice pure ethical discipline, this is the practice of the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*). "Kauśika!

If sons of good family or daughters of good family seek all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as either permanent or impermanent; seek all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as either pleasant or painful; seek all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as either self or non-self; and seek all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as either pure or impure."
Kauśika, I say that one who practices pure ethical discipline based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of ethical discipline characterized by apprehension.
As previously stated, you should know that all of these describe a semblance of the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā) characterized by apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, were to speak of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas as either permanent or impermanent; speak of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas as either pleasant or painful; speak of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas as either self or non-self; or speak of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas as either pure or impure.
If there are those who are able to practice pure ethical discipline (*śīla*) by relying on such teachings as these, they are practicing the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*).
Furthermore, it is said:

one who practices pure ethical discipline should seek the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*) of all Buddhas as either permanent or impermanent; should seek the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas as either pleasant or painful; should seek the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas as either self or non-self; and should seek the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas as either pure or impure.
If there are those who, seeking such dharmas as these, practice the pure precepts, they are practicing the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*). "Kauśika!

If sons of good family or daughters of good family seek the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas as either permanent or impermanent; seek the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas as either pleasure or suffering; seek the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas as either self or non-self; seek the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas as either pure or impure."
Kauśika, I say that one who practices pure ethical discipline based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of ethical discipline characterized by apprehension.
"As previously stated, you should know that all these refer to what is called the semblance of the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā) characterized by apprehension.
Then, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
How is it that those sons and daughters of good family who speak of the perfection of generosity with the notion of attainment are said to be speaking of a counterfeit perfection of generosity?
The Buddha said, "Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment, speak of form as either permanent or impermanent, and speak of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as either permanent or impermanent;
One speaks of form as either pleasant or painful; one speaks of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as either pleasant or painful.
One speaks of form as either self or non-self; one speaks of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as either self or non-self.
One speaks of form as either pure or impure; one speaks of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as either pure or impure.
If there are those who, relying on such dharmas as these, practice giving, this is the practice of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).
Furthermore, it is said:

one who practices giving should seek whether form (*rūpa*) is permanent or impermanent; one should seek whether feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are permanent or impermanent.
One should seek whether form is pleasant or painful; one should seek whether feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are pleasant or painful.
One should seek whether form is self or non-self; one should seek whether feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are self or non-self.
One should seek whether form is pure or impure; one should seek whether feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are pure or impure.
If there are those who, seeking such dharmas as these, practice giving, this is the practice of the perfection of giving. "Kauśika!
If sons of good family or daughters of good family seek form as either permanent or impermanent, or seek feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as either permanent or impermanent;
One seeks whether form is pleasant or painful; one seeks whether feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are pleasant or painful.
One seeks whether form is self or non-self; one seeks whether feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are self or non-self.
One seeks whether form is pure or impure; one seeks whether feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are pure or impure.
Kauśika, I declare that one who practices generosity based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of generosity characterized by the apprehension of a referent.
As previously explained, you should know that all these are merely descriptions of a semblance of the perfection of giving based on apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, explain whether the eye-base is permanent or impermanent; explain whether the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases are permanent or impermanent;
explain whether the eye-base is pleasant or painful; explain whether the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases are pleasant or painful;
explain whether the eye-base is self or non-self; and explain whether the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases are self or non-self.
One speaks of the sense base of the eye as either pure or impure; one speaks of the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind as either pure or impure.
If there is one who is able to practice giving by relying on such dharmas as these, this is the practice of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).
Furthermore, it is said:

One who practices giving should investigate whether the sense-base of the eye is permanent or impermanent; one should investigate whether the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are permanent or impermanent;
one should investigate whether the sense-base of the eye is pleasant or painful; one should investigate whether the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are pleasant or painful.
One should investigate whether the eye-base is self or non-self; one should investigate whether the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases are self or non-self.
One should investigate whether the eye-base is pure or impure; one should investigate whether the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases are pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice generosity, they are practicing the perfection of generosity. "Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters seek the sense-base of the eye as either permanent or impermanent, and seek the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind as either permanent or impermanent;
One seeks whether the sphere of the eye is pleasant or painful; one seeks whether the spheres of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are pleasant or painful.
One seeks whether the sphere of the eye is self or non-self; one seeks whether the spheres of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are self or non-self.
One seeks whether the sphere of the eye is pure or impure; one seeks whether the spheres of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are pure or impure.
Kauśika, I say that one who practices giving based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) characterized by apprehension.
As previously stated, you should know that all of these describe a semblance of the perfection of giving characterized by apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kausika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, explain whether the sphere of form is permanent or impermanent; explain whether the spheres of sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena are permanent or impermanent;
explain whether the sphere of form is pleasant or painful; explain whether the spheres of sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena are pleasant or painful;
explain whether the sphere of form is self or non-self; explain whether the spheres of sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena are self or non-self.
One speaks of the sphere of form as either pure or impure; one speaks of the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena as either pure or impure.
If there is one who is able to practice generosity by relying upon such dharmas, this is the practice of the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*).
Furthermore, it is said:

One who practices giving should investigate whether the sphere of form is permanent or impermanent; one should investigate whether the spheres of sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena are permanent or impermanent;
one should investigate whether the sphere of form is pleasant or painful; one should investigate whether the spheres of sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena are pleasant or painful.
One should investigate whether the sphere of form is self or non-self; one should investigate whether the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena are self or non-self.
One should investigate whether the sphere of form is pure or impure; one should investigate whether the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena are pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice giving, this is the practice of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*). "Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters seek the sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) as either permanent or impermanent, and seek the spheres of sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) as either permanent or impermanent;
They seek whether the sphere of form is pleasant or painful; they seek whether the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena are pleasant or painful.
They seek whether the sphere of form is self or non-self; they seek whether the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena are self or non-self.
They seek whether the sphere of form is pure or impure; they seek whether the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena are pure or impure.

Kauśika, I declare that one who practices giving based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) characterized by the apprehension of something to be attained.
As previously explained, you should know that all these are said to be the semblance of the perfection of giving characterized by apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kausika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, explain whether the eye-element is permanent or impermanent; explain whether the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, eye-contact, and the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition are permanent or impermanent;

explain whether the eye-element is pleasant or painful; explain whether the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, eye-contact, and the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition are pleasant or painful;

explain whether the eye-element is self or non-self; and explain whether the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, eye-contact, and the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition are self or non-self.

One speaks of the eye-element as either pure or impure; one speaks of the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, eye-contact, and all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition as either pure or impure.
If there is one who practices giving by relying on such teachings as these, this is the practice of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).
Furthermore, it is said:

"One who practices giving should investigate whether the eye-element is permanent or impermanent; one should investigate whether the form-element, and so forth, up to the feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, are permanent or impermanent."
One should seek whether the eye-element is pleasant or painful; one should seek whether the form-element, and so on up to the feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, are pleasant or painful.
One should seek whether the eye-element is self or non-self; one should seek whether the form-element, and so on up to the feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, are self or non-self.
One should seek whether the eye-element is pure or impure; one should seek whether the form-element, and so on up to the feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, are pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice giving, this is the practice of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*). "Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters seek the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*) as either permanent or impermanent, and seek the form-element (*rūpadhātu*) up to the various feelings (*vedanā*) produced with eye-contact as condition as either permanent or impermanent; [this is the perfection of wisdom]."
They seek whether the eye-element is pleasant or painful; they seek whether the form-element, and so on up to the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, are pleasant or painful.
They seek whether the eye-element is self or non-self; they seek whether the form-element, and so on up to the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, are self or non-self.
They seek whether the eye-element is pure or impure; they seek whether the form-element, and so on up to the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, are pure or impure.
Kauśika, I declare that one who practices giving based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of giving characterized by the apprehension of something to be attained.
As previously explained, you should know that all these are descriptions of a semblance of the perfection of giving characterized by apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, explain whether the ear-element is permanent or impermanent; explain whether the sound-element, the ear-consciousness-element, ear-contact, and the various feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition are permanent or impermanent;

explain whether the ear-element is pleasant or painful; explain whether the sound-element, the ear-consciousness-element, ear-contact, and the various feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition are pleasant or painful;

explain whether the ear-element is self or non-self; explain whether the sound-element, the ear-consciousness-element, ear-contact, and the various feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition are self or non-self;

One speaks of the ear-element as either pure or impure; one speaks of the sound-element, the ear-consciousness-element, and ear-contact, as well as the various feelings arising conditioned by ear-contact, as either pure or impure.
If one is able to practice giving by relying on such teachings as these, this constitutes the practice of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).
Furthermore, it is said:

"One who practices giving should investigate whether the ear-element is permanent or impermanent; one should investigate whether the sound-element, and even the various sensations produced with ear-contact as a condition, are permanent or impermanent."

One should seek whether the ear element is pleasant or painful; one should seek whether the sound element, and so on up to the various feelings produced with ear-contact as condition, are pleasant or painful.

One should seek whether the ear element is self or non-self; one should seek whether the sound element, and so on up to the various feelings produced with ear-contact as condition, are self or non-self.
One should seek whether the ear element is pure or impure; one should seek whether the sound element, and so on up to the various feelings produced with ear-contact as condition, are pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice giving, this is the practice of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*). "Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters seek the ear-element (*śrotradhātu*) as either permanent or impermanent, or seek the sound-element (*śabdadhātu*) and even the various feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition as either permanent or impermanent;
One seeks whether the ear-element is pleasant or painful; one seeks whether the sound-element, and so on up to the various feelings produced with ear-contact as condition, are pleasant or painful.
One seeks whether the ear-element is self or non-self; one seeks whether the sound-element, and so on up to the various feelings produced with ear-contact as condition, are self or non-self.
One seeks whether the ear-element is pure or impure; one seeks whether the sound-element, and so on up to the various feelings produced with ear-contact as condition, are pure or impure.
Kauśika, I say that one who practices generosity based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of generosity characterized by the apprehension of something attained.
As previously stated, you should know that all these are descriptions of a semblance of the perfection of generosity characterized by apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kausika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment, explain whether the nose-element is permanent or impermanent; explain whether the odor-element, the nose-consciousness-element, nose-contact, and all sensations produced with nose-contact as a condition are permanent or impermanent;

explain whether the nose-element is pleasant or painful; explain whether the odor-element, the nose-consciousness-element, nose-contact, and all sensations produced with nose-contact as a condition are pleasant or painful;

explain whether the nose-element is self or non-self; explain whether the odor-element, the nose-consciousness-element, nose-contact, and all sensations produced with nose-contact as a condition are self or non-self.

One speaks of the nose element as either pure or impure; one speaks of the odor element, the nose-consciousness element, nose-contact, and all feelings arisen with nose-contact as condition as either pure or impure.
If there is one who is able to practice giving by relying on such teachings as these, this is the practice of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).
Furthermore, it is said:

"One who practices giving should investigate whether the nose-element (*ghrāṇadhātu*) is permanent or impermanent; one should investigate whether the odor-element (*gandhadhātu*), and so forth, up to the various sensations (*vedanā*) produced with nose-contact as a condition, are permanent or impermanent."

One should investigate whether the nose element is pleasant or painful; one should investigate whether the odor element, and so forth, up to the various feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition, are pleasant or painful.

One should investigate whether the nose element is self or non-self; one should investigate whether the odor element, and so forth, up to the various feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition, are self or non-self.

One should investigate whether the nose element is pure or impure; one should investigate whether the odor element, and so forth, up to the various feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition, are pure or impure.
If there are those who, seeking such dharmas as these, practice giving, this is the practice of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*). "Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters seek the nose-element (*ghrāṇadhātu*) as either permanent or impermanent, and seek the fragrance-element (*gandhadhātu*) up to the various feelings produced with nose-contact as condition as either permanent or impermanent;

One seeks whether the nose element is pleasant or painful; one seeks whether the fragrance element, and so on up to the various feelings produced with nose-contact as condition, are pleasant or painful.
One seeks whether the nose element is self or non-self; one seeks whether the fragrance element, and so on up to the various feelings produced with nose-contact as condition, are self or non-self.
One seeks whether the nose element is pure or impure; one seeks whether the fragrance element, and so on up to the various feelings produced with nose-contact as condition, are pure or impure.
Kauśika, I say that one who practices giving based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of giving characterized by the apprehension of something attained.
As previously explained, you should know that all these describe a semblance of the perfection of giving characterized by apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kausika!"

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment, explain whether the tongue-element is permanent or impermanent; explain whether the taste-element, the tongue-consciousness-element, tongue-contact, and all sensations produced with tongue-contact as condition are permanent or impermanent;

explain whether the tongue-element is pleasant or painful; explain whether the taste-element, the tongue-consciousness-element, tongue-contact, and all sensations produced with tongue-contact as condition are pleasant or painful;

explain whether the tongue-element is self or non-self; explain whether the taste-element, the tongue-consciousness-element, tongue-contact, and all sensations produced with tongue-contact as condition are self or non-self.

One speaks of the tongue element as either pure or impure; one speaks of the taste element, the tongue-consciousness element, tongue-contact, and the various feelings produced with tongue-contact as their condition, as either pure or impure.
If there are those who practice giving by relying on such teachings as these, they are practicing the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā).
Furthermore, it is said:

one who practices giving should investigate whether the tongue-element (jihvādhātu) is permanent or impermanent; one should investigate whether the taste-element (rasadhātu), and so forth, up to the various feelings (vedanā) produced with tongue-contact (jihvā-saṃsparśa) as a condition, are permanent or impermanent.

One should seek whether the tongue element is pleasant or painful; one should seek whether the taste element, and so on up to the various feelings produced with tongue-contact as condition, are pleasant or painful.

One should seek whether the tongue element is self or non-self; one should seek whether the taste element, and so on up to the various feelings produced with tongue-contact as condition, are self or non-self.

One should seek whether the tongue element is pure or impure; one should seek whether the taste element, and so on up to the various feelings produced with tongue-contact as condition, are pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice generosity, this is the practice of the perfection of generosity. "Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters seek whether the tongue-element is permanent or impermanent, and seek whether the taste-element, and so forth, up to the various feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition, are permanent or impermanent;
They seek whether the tongue element is pleasant or painful; they seek whether the taste element, and even the various feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition, are pleasant or painful.
They seek whether the tongue element is self or non-self; they seek whether the taste element, and even the various feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition, are self or non-self.
They seek whether the tongue element is pure or impure; they seek whether the taste element, and even the various feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition, are pure or impure.
Kauśika, I say that one who practices giving based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of giving characterized by apprehension.
As previously explained, you should know that all these are descriptions of a semblance of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) characterized by apprehension (*upalambha*).
"Furthermore, Kausika!"

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, should explain whether the body-element is permanent or impermanent; explain whether the contact-element, the body-consciousness-element, body-contact, and the various feelings produced with body-contact as condition are permanent or impermanent;

explain whether the body-element is pleasant or painful; explain whether the contact-element, the body-consciousness-element, body-contact, and the various feelings produced with body-contact as condition are pleasant or painful;

explain whether the body-element is self or non-self; explain whether the contact-element, the body-consciousness-element, body-contact, and the various feelings produced with body-contact as condition are self or non-self;

One speaks of the body element as either pure or impure; one speaks of the touch element, the body-consciousness element, and body-contact, as well as the various feelings arising with body-contact as their condition, as either pure or impure.
If one is able to practice giving by relying on such teachings as these, this is the practice of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).
Furthermore, it is said:

"One who practices giving should investigate whether the body-element (*kāyadhātu*) is permanent or impermanent; one should investigate whether the contact-element (*spraṣṭavyadhātu*) and even all sensations produced with body-contact as a condition are permanent or impermanent."

One should investigate whether the body element is pleasant or painful; one should investigate whether the contact element, and even the various feelings produced with body-contact as condition, are pleasant or painful.

One should investigate whether the body element is self or non-self; one should investigate whether the contact element, and even the various feelings produced with body-contact as condition, are self or non-self.

One should investigate whether the body element is pure or impure; one should investigate whether the contact element, and even the various feelings produced with body-contact as condition, are pure or impure.
If there are those who, seeking such dharmas as these, practice the giving of alms, this is the practice of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*). "Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters seek the body-element (*kāyadhātu*) to see whether it is permanent or impermanent, or seek the touch-element (*spraṣṭavyadhātu*) and even the various feelings (*vedanā*) produced with body-contact as a condition to see whether they are permanent or impermanent; [this is the practice of the perfection of wisdom]."

They seek whether the body element is pleasant or painful; they seek whether the contact element, up to and including the various feelings produced with body-contact as a condition, are pleasant or painful.

They seek whether the body element is self or non-self; they seek whether the contact element, up to and including the various feelings produced with body-contact as a condition, are self or non-self.
They seek whether the body element is pure or impure; they seek whether the contact element, up to and including the various feelings produced with body-contact as a condition, are pure or impure.
Kauśika, I say that one who practices giving based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of giving characterized by apprehension.
As previously explained, you should know that all these refer to a semblance of the perfection of giving characterized by apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment, speak of the mental faculty (*manodhātu*) as either permanent or impermanent; speak of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), the mental-consciousness realm (*manovijñānadhātu*), and mental contact (*manaḥsaṃsparśa*), as well as all feelings (*vedanā*) produced with mental contact as their condition, as either permanent or impermanent;

speak of the mental faculty as either pleasant or painful; speak of the dharma-realm, the mental-consciousness realm, and mental contact, as well as all feelings produced with mental contact as their condition, as either pleasant or painful;

speak of the mental faculty as either self or non-self; [they] speak of the dharma-realm, the mental-consciousness realm, and mental contact, as well as all feelings produced with mental contact as their condition, as either self or non-self.

He speaks of the mind-element as either pure or impure; he speaks of the dharma-element, the mental-consciousness-element, and mental contact, as well as the various feelings arising with mental contact as condition, as either pure or impure.
If there is one who is able to practice giving by relying on such teachings as these, this is the practice of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).
Furthermore, it is said:

One who practices giving should investigate whether the mind-element (*manodhātu*) is permanent or impermanent; they should investigate whether the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*), and even the feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition, are permanent or impermanent.

One should seek whether the mind-element (*manodhātu*) is pleasant or painful; one should seek whether the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*), and so on up to the various feelings produced with mind-contact as condition, are pleasant or painful.

One should seek whether the mind-element is self or non-self; one should seek whether the dharma-element, and so on up to the various feelings produced with mind-contact as condition, are self or non-self.

One should seek whether the mind-element is pure or impure; one should seek whether the dharma-element, and so on up to the various feelings produced with mind-contact as condition, are pure or impure.
If there are those who, seeking such dharmas as these, practice generosity, this is the practice of the perfection of generosity. "Kauśika!

If sons of good family or daughters of good family seek in this way whether the mind-element is permanent or impermanent; or seek whether the dharma-element, and so forth up to the various feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition, are permanent or impermanent;

One seeks whether the mind-element (*manodhātu*) is pleasant or painful; one seeks whether the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*), up to and including the various feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition, are pleasant or painful.
One seeks whether the mind-element is self or non-self; one seeks whether the dharma-element, up to and including the various feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition, is self or non-self.
One seeks whether the mind-element is pure or impure; one seeks whether the dharma-element, up to and including the various feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition, is pure or impure.
Kauśika, I say that one who practices giving based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) characterized by apprehension.
As previously explained, you should know that all these are said to be semblances of the perfection of giving characterized by apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kausika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, should speak of the earth element as either permanent or impermanent, or speak of the elements of water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness as either permanent or impermanent;
should speak of the earth element as either pleasant or painful, or speak of the elements of water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness as either pleasant or painful;
should speak of the earth element as either self or non-self, or speak of the elements of water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness as either self or non-self;
One speaks of the earth element as being either pure or impure, and one speaks of the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements as being either pure or impure.
If there is one who is able to practice generosity by relying on such dharmas as these, this is the practice of the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*).
Furthermore, it is said:

One who practices giving should investigate whether the earth element is permanent or impermanent; one should investigate whether the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements are permanent or impermanent;
one should investigate whether the earth element is pleasant or painful; one should investigate whether the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements are pleasant or painful.
One should investigate whether the earth element is self or non-self; one should investigate whether the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements are self or non-self.
One should investigate whether the earth element is pure or impure; one should investigate whether the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements are pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice giving, this is the practice of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*). "Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters seek the earth element as either permanent or impermanent, and seek the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements as either permanent or impermanent; [this is the perfection of wisdom]."
One seeks whether the earth element is pleasant or painful; one seeks whether the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements are pleasant or painful.
One seeks whether the earth element is self or non-self; one seeks whether the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements are self or non-self.
One seeks whether the earth element is pure or impure; one seeks whether the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements are pure or impure.
Kauśika, I say that one who practices giving based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of giving characterized by apprehension.
As previously explained, one should know that all these are said to be semblances of the perfection of giving characterized by apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kausika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, explain whether ignorance is permanent or impermanent; explain whether volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are permanent or impermanent;

and explain whether ignorance is pleasant or painful; explain whether volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are pleasant or painful.

One speaks of ignorance as being either self or non-self; one speaks of volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, and aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair as being either self or non-self.

One speaks of ignorance as being either pure or impure; one speaks of volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, and aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair as being either pure or impure.
If there is one who practices giving by relying on such teachings as these, this is the practice of the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*).
Furthermore, it is said:

One who practices giving should investigate whether ignorance is permanent or impermanent; they should investigate whether the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) up to old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair are permanent or impermanent.

One should investigate whether ignorance is pleasant or painful; one should investigate whether the formative forces (*saṃskāra*), up to and including old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair, are pleasant or painful.

One should investigate whether ignorance is self or non-self; one should investigate whether the formative forces, up to and including old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair, are self or non-self.

One should investigate whether ignorance is pure or impure; one should investigate whether the formative forces, up to and including old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair, are pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice giving, this is the practice of the perfection of giving. "Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters seek whether ignorance is permanent or impermanent, and seek whether formations up to old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair are permanent or impermanent;
One seeks whether ignorance is pleasant or painful; one seeks whether formations, up to and including old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair, are pleasant or painful.
One seeks whether ignorance is self or non-self; one seeks whether formations, up to and including old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair, are self or non-self.
One seeks whether ignorance is pure or impure; one seeks whether formations, up to and including old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair, are pure or impure.
Kauśika, I declare that one who practices giving based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) characterized by the apprehension of objects.
As previously stated, you should know that all these are descriptions of a semblance of the perfection of giving characterized by apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kausika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment, explain whether the perfection of giving is permanent or impermanent; explain whether the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom are permanent or impermanent;

explain whether the perfection of giving is pleasant or painful; explain whether the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom are pleasant or painful;
explain whether the perfection of giving is self or non-self; explain whether the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom are self or non-self.

He speaks of the perfection of generosity as being either pure or impure; he speaks of the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom as being either pure or impure.
If there is one who practices giving by relying on such teachings as these, this is the practice of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).
Furthermore, it is said:

One who practices giving should seek whether the perfection of giving is permanent or impermanent; likewise, they should seek whether the perfections from ethical discipline (*śīla*) up to wisdom (*prajñā*) are permanent or impermanent.
One should seek the perfection of generosity whether it be pleasant or painful; one should seek the perfections from ethical discipline up to wisdom whether they be pleasant or painful.
One should seek the perfection of generosity whether it be self or non-self; one should seek the perfections from ethical discipline up to wisdom whether they be self or non-self.
One should seek the perfection of generosity whether it be pure or impure; one should seek the perfections from ethical discipline up to wisdom whether they be pure or impure.
If there are those who, seeking such dharmas as these, practice giving, they are practicing the perfection of giving. Kausika!
If good sons and good daughters seek the perfection of giving—whether as permanent or impermanent—and seek the perfections from ethical discipline up to wisdom—whether as permanent or impermanent;
One seeks whether the perfection of generosity is pleasant or painful; one seeks whether the perfections from ethical discipline up to wisdom are pleasant or painful.
One seeks whether the perfection of generosity is self or non-self; one seeks whether the perfections from ethical discipline up to wisdom are self or non-self.
One seeks whether the perfection of generosity is pure or impure; one seeks whether the perfections from ethical discipline up to wisdom are pure or impure.
Kauśika, I declare that one who practices giving based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of giving characterized by the apprehension of something attained.
As previously explained, you should know that all these refer to a semblance of the perfection of giving characterized by apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kausika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, were to speak of inner emptiness as either permanent or impermanent; or speak of outer emptiness, inner-and-outer emptiness, emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-altering emptiness, essential emptiness, emptiness of self-characteristics, emptiness of common characteristics, emptiness of all phenomena, emptiness of the unapprehendable, emptiness of non-existence, emptiness of intrinsic nature, and emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence—whether as permanent or impermanent;

Whether it be pleasant or painful, one speaks of internal emptiness; one speaks of external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature—whether they be pleasant or painful.

He speaks of internal emptiness—whether as self or as non-self—and he speaks of external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, unchanging emptiness, essential emptiness, emptiness of specific characteristics, emptiness of common characteristics, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature—whether as self or as non-self.

One speaks of internal emptiness as either pure or impure; one speaks of external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all dharmas, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature—each as either pure or impure.
If there are those who are able to practice giving by relying on such dharmas as these, this is the practice of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).
Furthermore, it is said:

one who practices giving should seek whether internal emptiness is permanent or impermanent; they should seek whether external emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, is permanent or impermanent.
One should seek whether inner emptiness is pleasant or painful; one should seek whether outer emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of non-essential nature, is pleasant or painful.
One should seek whether inner emptiness is self or non-self; one should seek whether outer emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of non-essential nature, is self or non-self.
One should seek whether inner emptiness is pure or impure; one should seek whether outer emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of non-essential nature, is pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice giving, this is the practice of the perfection of giving. "Kauśika!

If sons of good family or daughters of good family seek internal emptiness as either permanent or impermanent, or seek external emptiness, up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, as either permanent or impermanent;
One seeks whether internal emptiness is pleasant or painful; one seeks whether external emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, is pleasant or painful.
One seeks whether internal emptiness is self or non-self; one seeks whether external emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, is self or non-self.
One seeks whether internal emptiness is pure or impure; one seeks whether external emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, is pure or impure.
Kauśika, I say that one who practices giving based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of giving characterized by the apprehension of something attained.
As previously explained, it should be understood that all these refer to the semblance of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) characterized by apprehension (*upalambha*).

*Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Fascicle 144, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. First Division, Chapter on the Measurement of Merit (*Guāngōngdé Pǐn*), Part 30-43. "Furthermore, Kauśika!"

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, were to speak of whether the Tathatā (Suchness) is permanent or impermanent; or speak of whether the dharmadhātu, dharmatā, the nature of non-illusoriness, the nature of immutability, sameness, the nature of being free from birth, the fixedness of dharma, the stability of dharma, the limit of reality, the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm are permanent or impermanent;

or speak of whether the Tathatā is pleasant or painful; or speak of whether the dharmadhātu, dharmatā, the nature of non-illusoriness, the nature of immutability, sameness, the nature of being free from birth, the fixedness of dharma, the stability of dharma, the limit of reality, the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm are pleasant or painful;

Whether one speaks of True Suchness as having a self or being without a self, or speaks of the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, non-illusory nature, unchanging nature, equality, the state beyond birth, the fixedness of dharma, the stability of dharma, the limit of reality, the realm of space, or the inconceivable realm as having a self or being without a self;

whether one speaks of True Suchness as pure or impure, or speaks of the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, non-illusory nature, unchanging nature, equality, the state beyond birth, the fixedness of dharma, the stability of dharma, the limit of reality, the realm of space, or the inconceivable realm as pure or impure.
If there are those who practice giving by relying on such teachings as these, this constitutes the practice of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).
Furthermore, it is said:

one who practices giving should seek whether suchness (*tathatā*) is permanent or impermanent; one should seek whether the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), up to the inconceivable realm (*acintyadhātu*), is permanent or impermanent.
One should seek whether true thusness is pleasant or painful; one should seek whether the dharma-realm, up to and including the inconceivable realm, is pleasant or painful.
One should seek whether true thusness is self or non-self; one should seek whether the dharma-realm, up to and including the inconceivable realm, is self or non-self.
One should seek whether true thusness is pure or impure; one should seek whether the dharma-realm, up to and including the inconceivable realm, is pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice giving, this is the practice of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*). "Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters thus seek whether the Tathatā is permanent or impermanent, or seek whether the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) up to the inconceivable realm (*acintyadhātu*) is permanent or impermanent;
Seeking the reality-limit as either pleasure or suffering; seeking the dharma-realm, up to the inconceivable realm, as either pleasure or suffering;
seeking the reality-limit as either self or non-self; seeking the dharma-realm, up to the inconceivable realm, as either self or non-self;
seeking the reality-limit as either pure or impure; seeking the dharma-realm, up to the inconceivable realm, as either pure or impure.
Kauśika, I say that one who practices giving based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of giving characterized by the apprehension of something attained.
As previously explained, you should know that all these refer to a semblance of the perfection of giving characterized by apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kausika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, were to explain whether the Noble Truth of Suffering is permanent or impermanent, or explain whether the Noble Truths of Origination, Cessation, and the Path are permanent or impermanent;
were to explain whether the Noble Truth of Suffering is pleasant or painful, or explain whether the Noble Truths of Origination, Cessation, and the Path are pleasant or painful;
were to explain whether the Noble Truth of Suffering is self or non-self, or explain whether the Noble Truths of Origination, Cessation, and the Path are self or non-self;
Whether one speaks of the noble truth of suffering as pure or impure, or speaks of the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path as pure or impure—
if one is able to practice generosity by relying on such dharmas as these, this is the practice of the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā).
Furthermore, it is said:

One who practices giving should seek whether the Noble Truth of Suffering is permanent or impermanent; one should seek whether the Noble Truths of Origination, Cessation, and the Path are permanent or impermanent;
one should seek whether the Noble Truth of Suffering is pleasant or painful; one should seek whether the Noble Truths of Origination, Cessation, and the Path are pleasant or painful.
One should seek whether the noble truth of suffering is self or non-self; one should seek whether the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path are self or non-self;
one should seek whether the noble truth of suffering is pure or impure; one should seek whether the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path are pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice giving, this is the practice of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*). "Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters seek the Noble Truth of Suffering as either permanent or impermanent, and seek the Noble Truths of Origination, Cessation, and the Path as either permanent or impermanent;
One seeks whether the noble truth of suffering is pleasant or painful; one seeks whether the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path are pleasant or painful.
One seeks whether the noble truth of suffering is self or non-self; one seeks whether the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path are self or non-self.
One seeks whether the noble truth of suffering is pure or impure; one seeks whether the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path are pure or impure.

Kauśika, I declare that one who practices giving based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) characterized by the apprehension of something to be attained.
As previously stated, you should know that all these are descriptions of a semblance of the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) characterized by apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment, should speak of the four dhyānas as being either permanent or impermanent, or speak of the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions as being either permanent or impermanent;
if they should speak of the four dhyānas as being either pleasant or painful, or speak of the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions as being either pleasant or painful;
if they should speak of the four dhyānas as being either self or non-self, or speak of the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions as being either self or non-self;
One speaks of the four dhyānas as either pure or impure, and one speaks of the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions as either pure or impure.
If there is one who is able to practice giving by relying on such dharmas as these, this is the practice of the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā).
Furthermore, it is said:

One who practices giving should seek whether the four dhyānas are permanent or impermanent; one should seek whether the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments are permanent or impermanent;
one should seek whether the four dhyānas are pleasant or painful; one should seek whether the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments are pleasant or painful.
