One should seek the four dhyānas whether they are with self or without self; one should seek the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments whether they are with self or without self;
one should seek the four dhyānas whether they are pure or impure; one should seek the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments whether they are pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice giving, this is the practice of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*). "Kauśika!
If good sons and good daughters seek the four dhyānas as either permanent or impermanent, or seek the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions as either permanent or impermanent;
They seek the four dhyānas as either pleasant or painful; they seek the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments as either pleasant or painful.
They seek the four dhyānas as either self or non-self; they seek the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments as either self or non-self.
They seek the four dhyānas as either pure or impure; they seek the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments as either pure or impure.
Kauśika, I say that one who practices giving based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of giving characterized by apprehension.
As previously explained, you should know that all these are described as the semblance of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) characterized by apprehension (*upalambha*).
"Furthermore, Kausika!..."

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, were to speak of the eight liberations as either permanent or impermanent; speak of the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative concentrations, and the ten totalities as either permanent or impermanent;
speak of the eight liberations as either pleasant or painful; speak of the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative concentrations, and the ten totalities as either pleasant or painful;

or speak of the eight liberations as either self or non-self, and speak of the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative concentrations, and the ten totalities as either self or non-self;
To speak of the eight liberations as either pure or impure, and to speak of the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten totalities as either pure or impure—
if one is able to practice giving by relying on such dharmas as these, this is the practice of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).
Furthermore, it is said:

One who practices giving should seek whether the eight liberations (aṣṭavimokṣa) are permanent or impermanent; one should seek whether the eight bases of mastery (aṣṭābhibhvāyatana), the nine successive meditative attainments (navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti), and the ten totalities (daśakṛtsnāyatana) are permanent or impermanent;

one should seek whether the eight liberations are pleasant or painful; one should seek whether the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten totalities are pleasant or painful.

One should seek the eight liberations whether they are with self or without self; one should seek the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities whether they are with self or without self.

One should seek the eight liberations whether they are pure or impure; one should seek the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities whether they are pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice giving, this is the practice of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*). "Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters seek the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*) as either permanent or impermanent; if they seek the eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), the nine successive attainments (*anupūrvavihārasamāpatti*), and the ten totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*) as either permanent or impermanent;..."
To seek whether the eight liberations are pleasant or painful; to seek whether the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities are pleasant or painful;
to seek whether the eight liberations are self or non-self; to seek whether the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities are self or non-self;
to seek whether the eight liberations are pure or impure; to seek whether the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities are pure or impure.
Kauśika, I say that one who practices giving based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of giving characterized by the apprehension of something to be attained.
As previously stated, you should know that all these are descriptions of a semblance of the perfection of giving characterized by apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment, speak of the four foundations of mindfulness as either permanent or impermanent; speak of the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path as either permanent or impermanent;

speak of the four foundations of mindfulness as either pleasant or painful; speak of the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path as either pleasant or painful;

speak of the four foundations of mindfulness as either self or non-self; [they] speak of the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path as either self or non-self.

He speaks of the four foundations of mindfulness as either pure or impure; he speaks of the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path as either pure or impure.
If there are those who, relying on such dharmas as these, practice generosity, this is the practice of the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā).
Furthermore, it is said:

one who practices generosity should seek whether the four foundations of mindfulness are permanent or impermanent; one should seek whether the four right efforts, up to and including the eightfold noble path, are permanent or impermanent.

One should seek whether the four foundations of mindfulness are pleasant or painful; one should seek whether the four right endeavors, up to and including the eightfold noble path, are pleasant or painful.
One should seek whether the four foundations of mindfulness are self or non-self; one should seek whether the four right endeavors, up to and including the eightfold noble path, are self or non-self.
One should seek whether the four foundations of mindfulness are pure or impure; one should seek whether the four right endeavors, up to and including the eightfold noble path, are pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice giving, this is the practice of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*). "Kauśika!

If sons of good family or daughters of good family seek the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) as either permanent or impermanent; seek the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), up to the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*), as either permanent or impermanent;
One seeks whether the four foundations of mindfulness are pleasant or painful; one seeks whether the four right endeavors, up to and including the eightfold noble path, are pleasant or painful.
One seeks whether the four foundations of mindfulness are self or non-self; one seeks whether the four right endeavors, up to and including the eightfold noble path, are self or non-self.
One seeks whether the four foundations of mindfulness are pure or impure; one seeks whether the four right endeavors, up to and including the eightfold noble path, are pure or impure.
Kauśika, I say that one who practices giving based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) characterized by apprehension.
As previously stated, you should know that all these are described as the semblance of the perfection of giving characterized by apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kausika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, should speak of the gate of liberation of emptiness as either permanent or impermanent, or speak of the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness as either permanent or impermanent;
should speak of the gate of liberation of emptiness as either pleasant or painful, or speak of the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness as either pleasant or painful;
should speak of the gate of liberation of emptiness as either self or non-self, or speak of the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness as either self or non-self;
To speak of the gate of liberation of emptiness as either pure or impure, and to speak of the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness as either pure or impure—
if one is able to practice giving by relying on such dharmas as these, this is the practice of the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā).
Furthermore, it is said:

One who practices giving should seek whether the gate of liberation of emptiness is permanent or impermanent; one should seek whether the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness are permanent or impermanent;
one should seek whether the gate of liberation of emptiness is pleasant or painful; one should seek whether the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness are pleasant or painful.
One should seek the gate of liberation of emptiness whether it be self or non-self; one should seek the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness whether they be self or non-self;
one should seek the gate of liberation of emptiness whether it be pure or impure; one should seek the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness whether they be pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice giving, they are practicing the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*). "Kauśika!

If good sons and good daughters seek the gate of liberation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha*)—whether as permanent or impermanent—and seek the gates of liberation of signlessness (*animitta*) and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*)—whether as permanent or impermanent;
They seek whether the gate of liberation of emptiness is pleasant or painful; they seek whether the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness are pleasant or painful.
They seek whether the gate of liberation of emptiness is self or non-self; they seek whether the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness are self or non-self.
They seek whether the gate of liberation of emptiness is pure or impure; they seek whether the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness are pure or impure.
Kauśika, I declare that one who practices giving based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of giving characterized by the apprehension of something attained.
As previously stated, you should know that all these are descriptions of a semblance of the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) characterized by apprehension (*upalambha*).
"Furthermore, Kausika!"

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, speak of the five eyes as either permanent or impermanent, or speak of the six supernormal powers as either permanent or impermanent;
speak of the five eyes as either pleasant or painful, or speak of the six supernormal powers as either pleasant or painful;
speak of the five eyes as either self or non-self, or speak of the six supernormal powers as either self or non-self;
One speaks of the five eyes, whether they are pure or impure; one speaks of the six supernormal powers, whether they are pure or impure.
If there is one who, relying on such dharmas as these, practices giving, this is the practice of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).
Furthermore, it is said:
One who practices giving should seek the five eyes as either permanent or impermanent, and should seek the six supernormal powers as either permanent or impermanent;
one should seek the five eyes as either pleasant or painful, and should seek the six supernormal powers as either pleasant or painful.
One should seek the five eyes whether they are self or non-self; one should seek the six supernormal powers whether they are self or non-self;
one should seek the five eyes whether they are pure or impure; one should seek the six supernormal powers whether they are pure or impure.
If there are those who, seeking such dharmas as these, practice giving, this is the practice of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*). "Kauśika!
If sons of good family or daughters of good family seek the five eyes, whether they be permanent or impermanent, or seek the six supernormal powers, whether they be permanent or impermanent;
They seek the five eyes as either pleasant or painful; they seek the six supernormal powers as either pleasant or painful.
They seek the five eyes as either self or non-self; they seek the six supernormal powers as either self or non-self.
They seek the five eyes as either pure or impure; they seek the six supernormal powers as either pure or impure.
“Kauśika, I say that one who practices giving based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of giving characterized by the apprehension of something attained.”
As previously explained, you should know that all these refer to what resembles the perfection of giving characterized by apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kausika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, were to speak of the Buddha’s ten powers as either permanent or impermanent; were to speak of the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha as either permanent or impermanent;

or were to speak of the Buddha’s ten powers as either pleasant or painful, and speak of the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha as either pleasant or painful;

He speaks of the ten powers of a Buddha as being either self or non-self; he speaks of the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha as being either self or non-self.

He speaks of the ten powers of a Buddha as being either pure or impure; he speaks of the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha as being either pure or impure.
If there are those who are able to practice giving by relying on such dharmas as these, they are practicing the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*).
Furthermore, it is said:

one who practices giving should seek whether the ten powers of a Buddha are permanent or impermanent; one should seek whether the four fearlessnesses, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, are permanent or impermanent.

One should seek whether the ten powers of a Buddha are pleasant or painful; one should seek whether the four fearlessnesses, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, are pleasant or painful.

One should seek whether the ten powers of a Buddha are self or non-self; one should seek whether the four fearlessnesses, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, are self or non-self.

One should seek whether the ten powers of a Buddha are pure or impure; one should seek whether the four fearlessnesses, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, are pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice giving, this is the practice of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*). "Kauśika!

If sons of good family or daughters of good family seek the ten powers of a Buddha—whether they are permanent or impermanent—and seek the four fearlessnesses, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha—whether they are permanent or impermanent;
To seek the ten powers of a Buddha as either pleasant or painful; to seek the four fearlessnesses, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, as either pleasant or painful;
to seek the ten powers of a Buddha as either self or non-self; to seek the four fearlessnesses, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, as either self or non-self;
to seek the ten powers of a Buddha as either pure or impure; to seek the four fearlessnesses, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, as either pure or impure.
Kauśika, I say that one who practices generosity based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of generosity characterized by the apprehension of something to be attained.
As previously stated, you should know that all these are descriptions of a semblance of the perfection of giving characterized by apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kausika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment, explain whether the quality of non-forgetfulness is permanent or impermanent, or explain whether the nature of constant equanimity is permanent or impermanent;
explain whether the quality of non-forgetfulness is pleasant or painful, or explain whether the nature of constant equanimity is pleasant or painful;
explain whether the quality of non-forgetfulness is self or non-self, or explain whether the nature of constant equanimity is self or non-self;
Whether the qualities of non-forgetfulness are pure or impure, and whether the state of constant equanimity is pure or impure—
if one is able to rely on such dharmas as these to practice generosity, this is the practice of the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā).
Furthermore, it is said:

One who practices giving should seek whether the quality of non-forgetfulness is permanent or impermanent, and should seek whether the state of constant abiding in equanimity is permanent or impermanent;
one should seek whether the quality of non-forgetfulness is pleasant or painful, and should seek whether the state of constant abiding in equanimity is pleasant or painful.
One should seek the quality of non-forgetfulness whether it be self or selfless; one should seek the state of constant equanimity whether it be self or selfless;
one should seek the quality of non-forgetfulness whether it be pure or impure; one should seek the state of constant equanimity whether it be pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice giving, this is the practice of the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā). "Kauśika!

If sons of good family or daughters of good family seek the quality of non-forgetfulness (asaṃpramoṣadharma) as either permanent or impermanent, or seek the nature of constant equanimity (upekṣā) as either permanent or impermanent;
One seeks the quality of non-forgetfulness whether it be pleasant or painful; one seeks the state of constant equanimity whether it be pleasant or painful.
One seeks the quality of non-forgetfulness whether it be self or non-self; one seeks the state of constant equanimity whether it be self or non-self.
One seeks the quality of non-forgetfulness whether it be pure or impure; one seeks the state of constant equanimity whether it be pure or impure.

Kauśika, I declare that one who practices giving based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) characterized by the apprehension of something to be attained.
As previously stated, one should know that all these are descriptions of a semblance of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) characterized by apprehension (*upalambha*).
"Furthermore, Kausika!"

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, speak of all-knowledge as being either permanent or impermanent; speak of the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects as being either permanent or impermanent;
speak of all-knowledge as being either pleasant or painful; speak of the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects as being either pleasant or painful;
speak of all-knowledge as being either self or non-self; speak of the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects as being either self or non-self;

One speaks of the omniscience (sarvajñatā) as being either pure or impure, and speaks of the knowledge of the paths (mārgajñatā) and the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā) as being either pure or impure.
If one is able to practice generosity by relying on such dharmas as these, this constitutes the practice of the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā).
Furthermore, it is said:

One who practices giving should seek omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) as either permanent or impermanent; one should seek the knowledge of the paths (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) as either permanent or impermanent;
one should seek omniscience as either pleasant or painful; one should seek the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects as either pleasant or painful.

One should seek omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) whether it be with self or without self; one should seek the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) whether they be with self or without self.
One should seek omniscience whether it be pure or impure; one should seek the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects whether they be pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice generosity, this is the practice of the perfection of generosity. Kausika!

If sons of good family or daughters of good family seek omniscience—whether it be permanent or impermanent—and seek the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects—whether they be permanent or impermanent;
Seeking omniscience as either pleasure or pain; seeking the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects as either pleasure or pain;
seeking omniscience as either self or non-self; seeking the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects as either self or non-self;
seeking omniscience as either pure or impure; seeking the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects as either pure or impure.
Kauśika, I say that one who practices giving based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of giving characterized by the apprehension of something attained.
As previously explained, you should know that all these are descriptions of a semblance of the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) characterized by apprehension (*upalambha*).
"Furthermore, Kauśika!"

If good sons, good daughters, and others, for the sake of those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, explain that all dharanī-doors are either permanent or impermanent; explain that all samādhi-doors are either permanent or impermanent;
explain that all dharanī-doors are either pleasant or painful; explain that all samādhi-doors are either pleasant or painful;
explain that all dharanī-doors are either self or non-self; explain that all samādhi-doors are either self or non-self;
He speaks of all dharanī-doors, whether pure or impure; he speaks of all samādhi-doors, whether pure or impure.
If there is one who is able to practice giving by relying on such dharmas as these, this is the practice of the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā).
Furthermore, it is said:
One who practices giving should seek all *dhāraṇī* gates as either permanent or impermanent; one should seek all *samādhi* gates as either permanent or impermanent;
one should seek all *dhāraṇī* gates as either pleasant or painful; one should seek all *samādhi* gates as either pleasant or painful.
One should seek all dharani-doors whether they are with self or without self; one should seek all samadhi-doors whether they are with self or without self;
one should seek all dharani-doors whether they are pure or impure; one should seek all samadhi-doors whether they are pure or impure.
If there are those who, seeking such dharmas as these, practice giving, this is the cultivation of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*). "Kauśika!
If good sons and good daughters seek all *dhāraṇī* gates—whether they be permanent or impermanent—and seek all *samādhi* gates—whether they be permanent or impermanent;
They seek all dharani-gates whether as pleasure or as suffering; they seek all samadhi-gates whether as pleasure or as suffering.
They seek all dharani-gates whether as self or as non-self; they seek all samadhi-gates whether as self or as non-self.
They seek all dharani-gates whether as pure or as impure; they seek all samadhi-gates whether as pure or as impure.
Kauśika, I say that one who practices generosity based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of generosity characterized by the apprehension of something attained.
As previously explained, you should know that all these are descriptions of a semblance of the perfection of giving characterized by apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment, should speak of the stage of entering the stream and the fruit of stream-entry as either permanent or impermanent; or speak of the stage of entering once-returning and the fruit of once-returning, the stage of entering non-returning and the fruit of non-returning, and the stage of entering arhatship and the fruit of arhatship as either permanent or impermanent;

or speak of the stage of entering the stream and the fruit of stream-entry as either pleasant or painful; or speak of the stage of entering once-returning and the fruit of once-returning, the stage of entering non-returning and the fruit of non-returning, and the stage of entering arhatship and the fruit of arhatship as either pleasant or painful;

or speak of the stage of entering the stream and the fruit of stream-entry as either self or non-self; or speak of the stage of entering once-returning and the fruit of once-returning, the stage of entering non-returning and the fruit of non-returning, and the stage of entering arhatship and the fruit of arhatship as either self or non-self; [they would be speaking falsely].

He speaks of the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry and the fruit of stream-entry, whether pure or impure; he speaks of the candidate for the fruit of once-returning and the fruit of once-returning, the candidate for the fruit of non-returning and the fruit of non-returning, and the candidate for the fruit of arhatship and the fruit of arhatship, whether pure or impure.
If there are those who are able to practice giving in reliance upon such dharmas as these, this is the practice of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).
Furthermore, it is said:

one who practices giving should seek the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*) or the state of being a candidate for stream-entry (*srotāpattipratipannaka*), whether they be permanent or impermanent; and one should seek the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmi-phala*) up to the fruit of arhatship (*arhattva-phala*) or the state of being a candidate for arhatship, whether they be permanent or impermanent.

One should seek the fruit of stream-entry and the path of stream-entry, whether as pleasure or as pain; one should seek the fruits from the path of once-returning up to arhatship, whether as pleasure or as pain.

One should seek the fruit of stream-entry and the path of stream-entry, whether as self or as non-self; one should seek the fruits from the path of once-returning up to arhatship, whether as self or as non-self.

One should seek the fruit of stream-entry and the path of stream-entry, whether as pure or as impure; one should seek the fruits from the path of once-returning up to arhatship, whether as pure or as impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice giving, they are practicing the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).

"Kauśika! If good sons and good daughters seek entry into the stream (*srotāpatti-pratipannaka*) and the fruit of the stream-enterer (*srotāpanna-phala*), whether as permanent or impermanent; or seek the fruit of the once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*) up to the fruit of the arhat (*arhat-phala*), whether as permanent or impermanent; [they are practicing the perfection of giving]."
Seeking the fruit of stream-entry or the path to stream-entry as either pleasure or pain; seeking the fruits from the once-returner up to arhatship as either pleasure or pain;
seeking the fruit of stream-entry or the path to stream-entry as either self or non-self; seeking the fruits from the once-returner up to arhatship as either self or non-self;
seeking the fruit of stream-entry or the path to stream-entry as either pure or impure; seeking the fruits from the once-returner up to arhatship as either pure or impure.
Kauśika, I declare that one who practices giving based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of giving characterized by the apprehension of something to be attained.
As previously explained, you should know that all these are said to be the semblance of the perfection of giving characterized by apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kausika!

If good sons, good daughters, and others who have resolved upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment should speak of all pratyekabuddha-enlightenment as either permanent or impermanent; speak of all pratyekabuddha-enlightenment as either pleasant or painful; speak of all pratyekabuddha-enlightenment as either self or non-self; or speak of all pratyekabuddha-enlightenment as either pure or impure.
If there are those who are able to practice giving in reliance upon such dharmas as these, this is the practice of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).
Furthermore, it is said:

one who practices giving should seek all pratyekabuddha-enlightenment whether it be permanent or impermanent; one should seek all pratyekabuddha-enlightenment whether it be pleasant or painful; one should seek all pratyekabuddha-enlightenment whether it be self or non-self; one should seek all pratyekabuddha-enlightenment whether it be pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice giving, this is the practice of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*). "Kauśika!

If sons of good family or daughters of good family seek all the enlightenment of a solitary realizer (*pratyekabuddha*) as either permanent or impermanent; seek all the enlightenment of a solitary realizer as either pleasant or painful; seek all the enlightenment of a solitary realizer as either self or non-self; seek all the enlightenment of a solitary realizer as either pure or impure."
Kauśika, I say that one who practices giving based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of giving characterized by the apprehension of something attained.
As previously stated, you should know that all these refer to a semblance of the perfection of giving characterized by apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment, should speak of all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as either permanent or impermanent; speak of all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as either pleasant or painful; speak of all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as either self or non-self; or speak of all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as either pure or impure.
If there are those who are able to practice giving by relying on such dharmas as these, this is the practice of the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*).
Furthermore, it is said:

One who practices giving should seek whether all the practices of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are permanent or impermanent; one should seek whether all the practices of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are blissful or suffering; one should seek whether all the practices of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas involve a self or are selfless; and one should seek whether all the practices of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are pure or impure.
If there are those who, seeking such dharmas as these, practice generosity, this is the practice of the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*). "Kauśika!

If sons of good family or daughters of good family seek all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as either permanent or impermanent; seek all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as either pleasant or painful; seek all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as either self or non-self; seek all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as either pure or impure."
Kauśika, I say that one who practices giving based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of giving characterized by the apprehension of something attained.
As previously explained, you should know that all these refer to a semblance of the perfection of giving characterized by apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kausika!

If good sons, good daughters, and others, for the sake of those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, were to speak of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas as either permanent or impermanent; speak of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas as either pleasure or suffering; speak of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas as either self or non-self; or speak of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas as either pure or impure.
If there are those who practice giving in reliance upon such dharmas as these, they are practicing the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).
Furthermore, it is said:

one who practices giving should seek the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas as either permanent or impermanent; should seek the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas as either pleasant or painful; should seek the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas as either self or non-self; and should seek the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas as either pure or impure.
If there are those who seek such dharmas as these and practice giving, they are practicing the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*). "Kauśika!

If sons of good family or daughters of good family seek the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas as either permanent or impermanent; seek the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas as either pleasant or painful; seek the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas as either self or non-self; seek the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas as either pure or impure."
Kauśika, I say that one who practices giving based on such dharmas is practicing a semblance of the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) characterized by the apprehension of something attained.
As previously explained, you should know that all these refer to what is called a semblance of the perfection of giving characterized by apprehension.
"Furthermore, Kausika!
If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, proclaim the Prajñāpāramitā, speaking these words:
"Come!..."

"Noble son! I shall instruct you in the practice of the *prajñāpāramitā*. If you practice according to my instructions, you will swiftly abide in the first stage, the Stage of Extreme Joy; the second, the Stage of Purity; the third, the Stage of Radiance; the fourth, the Stage of Blazing Wisdom; the fifth, the Stage of Difficult Victory; the sixth, the Stage of Presence; the seventh, the Stage of Far-Going; the eighth, the Immovable Stage; the ninth, the Stage of Excellent Intelligence; and the tenth, the Stage of the Cloud of Dharma."

"Kauśika! If these sons of good family or daughters of good family, employing the means of signs (*nimitta*) and the means of apprehension (*upalambha*), as well as the notion of time and occasion, teach others to practice the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), this is called a counterfeit perfection of wisdom."

“Kauśika! If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment, proclaim the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā), saying:
‘Come!’”

"Good son! I shall instruct you in the cultivation and study of the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*). If you cultivate and study according to my instructions, you shall swiftly abide in the first stage, the Stage of Supreme Joy; the second, the Stage of Purity; the third, the Stage of Luminosity; the fourth, the Stage of Blazing Wisdom; the fifth, the Stage of Difficult Victory; the sixth, the Stage of Presence; the seventh, the Stage of Far-Going; the eighth, the Immovable Stage; the ninth, the Stage of Excellent Intelligence; and the tenth, the Stage of the Cloud of Dharma."

"Kauśika! If these sons or daughters of good family, by means of the conceptualization of signs (*nimitta*), by means of the apprehension of objects (*upalambha*), and by means of the notion of time and occasion, teach others to practice and study the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*), this is called a counterfeit perfection of meditative concentration."
“Kauśika! If good sons and good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved upon the unsurpassed mind of awakening, proclaim the perfection of diligence and speak these words:
‘Come!’”

“Good son! I shall instruct you in the cultivation and study of the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*). If you cultivate and study according to my instructions, you shall swiftly abide in the first stage, the Stage of Supreme Joy; the second, the Stage of Purity; the third, the Stage of Radiant Light; the fourth, the Stage of Blazing Wisdom; the fifth, the Stage of Difficult to Conquer; the sixth, the Stage of Presence; the seventh, the Stage of Far-Going; the eighth, the Immovable Stage; the ninth, the Stage of Excellent Intelligence; and the tenth, the Stage of the Cloud of Dharma.”

"Kauśika! If these sons or daughters of good family, by means of signs as a skillful method, by means of apprehension as a skillful method, and with the notion of time and occasion, teach others to practice the perfection of vigor, this is called a counterfeit perfection of vigor."
“Kauśika! If good sons and good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, proclaim the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā) and speak thus:
‘Come!’”

"Son of good family! I shall instruct you in the cultivation and study of the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*). If you cultivate and study according to my instruction, you shall swiftly abide in the first stage, the Stage of Extreme Joy; the second, the Stage of Purity; the third, the Stage of Radiance; the fourth, the Stage of Blazing Wisdom; the fifth, the Stage of Difficult Victory; the sixth, the Stage of Manifestation; the seventh, the Stage of Far-Going; the eighth, the Immovable Stage; the ninth, the Stage of Excellent Intelligence; and the tenth, the Stage of the Cloud of Dharma."

“Kauśika! If these sons or daughters of good family, by employing the means of signs, the means of apprehension, and the notion of time and occasion, teach others to practice and study the perfection of patience, this is called a counterfeit perfection of patience.”

“Kauśika! If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment, proclaim the perfection of pure ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*), saying:
‘Come!’”

"Son of good family! I shall instruct you in the practice of the perfection of pure ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*). If you practice according to my instruction, you shall swiftly abide in the first stage, the Stage of Utmost Joy; the second, the Stage of Purity; the third, the Stage of Luminosity; the fourth, the Stage of Blazing Wisdom; the fifth, the Stage of Difficult Victory; the sixth, the Stage of Manifestation; the seventh, the Stage of Far-Going; the eighth, the Immovable Stage; the ninth, the Stage of Excellent Intelligence; and the tenth, the Stage of the Cloud of Dharma."

"Kauśika! If these sons of good family or daughters of good family, employing the means of signs and the means of apprehension, as well as the notion of temporal divisions, teach others to practice the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*), this is called a semblance of the perfection of ethical discipline."
“Kauśika! If good sons and good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment, proclaim the perfection of generosity, speaking thus:
‘Come!’”

"Good son! I shall instruct you in the cultivation and study of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*). If you cultivate and study according to my instruction, you shall swiftly abide in the first stage, the Stage of Utmost Joy; the second, the Stage of Purity; the third, the Stage of Radiant Light; the fourth, the Stage of Blazing Wisdom; the fifth, the Stage of Difficult to Conquer; the sixth, the Stage of Manifestation; the seventh, the Stage of Far-Going; the eighth, the Immovable Stage; the ninth, the Stage of Excellent Intelligence; and the tenth, the Stage of the Dharma Cloud."

"Kauśika! If these sons or daughters of good family, by means of signs as their expedient, by means of apprehension as their expedient, and with the notion of temporal divisions, teach others to practice and study the perfection of generosity, this is called a counterfeit perfection of generosity."
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family should proclaim the *prajñāpāramitā* to those who have resolved upon unsurpassed bodhicitta, or speak of the *dhyānapāramitā*, or the *vīryapāramitā*, or the *kṣāntipāramitā*, or the *śīlapāramitā*, or the *dānapāramitā*, saying:
'Come!'"
"Son of good family!

I shall instruct you in the practice and study of the perfections from prajñāpāramitā down to dānapāramitā. If you practice and study according to my instructions, you will swiftly transcend the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas."

"Kauśika! If these sons and daughters of good family, employing the means of signs (*nimitta*), the means of apprehension (*upalambha*), and the notion of time and occasion, teach others to practice the perfection of wisdom, meditative concentration, diligence, patience, ethical discipline, and generosity, this is called teaching counterfeit perfections of wisdom up to generosity."
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons or good daughters proclaim the *prajñāpāramitā* to those who have resolved upon unsurpassed bodhicitta, or speak of the *dhyānapāramitā*, or the *vīryapāramitā*, or the *kṣāntipāramitā*, or the *śīlapāramitā*, or the *dānapāramitā*, saying to them:
'Come!'"
"Good son!

I shall instruct you in the cultivation and study of the *prajñāpāramitā* and even the *dānapāramitā*. If you cultivate and study according to my instructions, you will swiftly enter the bodhisattva’s state of correctness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
Once you have entered the bodhisattva’s state of correctness and departure from birth, you will then attain the bodhisattva’s endurance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)."
Having attained the Bodhisattva’s patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), one then attains the Bodhisattva’s non-regressive supernormal powers (*abhijñā*);

having attained the Bodhisattva’s non-regressive supernormal powers, one is able to traverse all Buddha-fields throughout the ten directions, going from one Buddha-land to another to make offerings, pay homage, show respect, and offer praise to all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, thereby swiftly realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).

"Kauśika! If these sons or daughters of good family, employing the means of signs (*nimitta*), employing the means of apprehension (*upalambha*), and employing the notion of time and occasion (*kāla-saṃjñā*), teach others to practice the perfection of wisdom, meditative concentration, diligence, patience, ethical discipline, and generosity, this is called teaching counterfeit perfections of wisdom up to generosity."
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to say to those abiding in the lineage of bodhisattvas:

'If you can hear, receive and uphold, read and recite, diligently practice and study, and reflect upon the profound Prajñāpāramitā according to the principle, you will certainly obtain immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless merit.'"

"Kauśika! These sons and daughters of good family, employing the means of signs and the means of apprehension, speak in this way; they speak of a semblance of the perfection of wisdom, meditative concentration, diligence, patience, ethical discipline, and generosity."
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family should say to one who abides in the bodhisattva lineage:

'You should rejoice in all the roots of goodness of all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas—past, future, and present—from their first generation of the mind of awakening until their realization of nirvana without remainder; having gathered them all together, you should dedicate them toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening for the sake of all sentient beings. "

"Kauśika! These sons and daughters of good family employ the means of having signs and the means of apprehending something as they speak in this way; they speak of a semblance of the perfection of wisdom, meditative concentration, diligence, patience, ethical discipline, and generosity."

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Scroll 145. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Part One: Chapter on Measuring Merits, Number Thirty-Four. At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
What is meant by the proclamation of the true and correct perfections of wisdom, meditative concentration, diligence, patience, ethical discipline, and generosity?
The Buddha said, “Kauśika!

If sons and daughters of good family speak of the perfection of wisdom, meditative concentration, diligence, patience, ethical discipline, and generosity as being ‘non-apprehensible,’ this is called proclaiming the true and correct perfections of wisdom, meditative concentration, diligence, patience, ethical discipline, and generosity.”
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Why is it that when sons and daughters of good family speak of the *prajñāpāramitā* of non-attainment, they are said to be speaking of the true and correct *prajñāpāramitā*?"
The Buddha said,
“Kauśika! If good sons or good daughters proclaim the Prajñāpāramitā to those who have resolved upon unsurpassed bodhicitta, speaking as follows:”

“O son of good family, you should cultivate the perfection of wisdom; you should not view form as either permanent or impermanent, nor should you view feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as either permanent or impermanent.”

Why is this? Form is empty of the intrinsic nature of form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty of the intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

This intrinsic nature of form is not an intrinsic nature; this intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is also not an intrinsic nature. That which is not an intrinsic nature is precisely the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
In this Prajñāpāramitā, form is unapprehendable, and its permanence or impermanence is likewise unapprehendable;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are all unapprehendable, and their permanence or impermanence is likewise unapprehendable.
Why is this? Because herein even form and the other aggregates cannot be apprehended, let alone permanence or impermanence!
If you can cultivate such prajñā, that is the cultivation of the prajñāpāramitā.
Furthermore, he said this:

"O son of good family, you should cultivate the perfection of wisdom; you should not regard form as either pleasant or painful, nor should you regard feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as either pleasant or painful."

Why is this? Form is empty of the intrinsic nature of form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty of the intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

This intrinsic nature of form is not an intrinsic nature; this intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is also not an intrinsic nature. That which is not an intrinsic nature is precisely the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
In this Prajñāpāramitā, form is unapprehendable, and its pleasure and pain are likewise unapprehendable;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are all unapprehendable, and their pleasure and pain are likewise unapprehendable.
Why is this? Because herein even form and the other aggregates cannot be apprehended, let alone pleasure and pain!
If you can cultivate such prajñā, this is the cultivation of the prajñāpāramitā.
Furthermore, he spoke these words:

"O son of good family, you should cultivate the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā); you should not view form as either self or non-self, nor should you view feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as either self or non-self."

Why is this? Form is empty of the intrinsic nature of form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty of the intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

This intrinsic nature of form is not an intrinsic nature; this intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is also not an intrinsic nature. That which is not an intrinsic nature is precisely the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
In this Prajñāpāramitā, form (*rūpa*) cannot be apprehended, nor can its self or non-self be apprehended;
feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are all unapprehendable, and their self or non-self likewise cannot be apprehended.
Why is this? Because herein even form and the other aggregates cannot be apprehended, much less that self or non-self!
If you can cultivate such prajñā, this is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Furthermore, he said this:

"O son of good family, you should practice the perfection of wisdom; you should not contemplate form as either pure or impure, nor should you contemplate feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as either pure or impure."

Why is this? Form is empty of the intrinsic nature of form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty of the intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

This intrinsic nature of form is not an intrinsic nature; this intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is also not an intrinsic nature. That which is not an intrinsic nature is precisely the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
In this Prajñāpāramitā, form is unapprehendable, and its purity or impurity is likewise unapprehendable;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are all unapprehendable, and their purity or impurity is likewise unapprehendable.
Why is this? Because herein even form and the other aggregates cannot be apprehended, let alone purity or impurity!
If you can cultivate such prajñā, this is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
“Kauśika! When these sons and daughters of good family speak in this manner, they are proclaiming the true and correct Prajñāpāramitā.”
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family expounds the *prajñāpāramitā* to those who have resolved upon unsurpassed bodhicitta, saying:

'You, son of good family, should cultivate the *prajñāpāramitā*; you should not regard the sense-base of the eye as either permanent or impermanent; you should not regard the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as either permanent or impermanent.'"

Why is this? The sense-base of the eye is empty of the intrinsic nature of the sense-base of the eye; the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are empty of the intrinsic nature of the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.

This intrinsic nature of the sense-base of the eye is non-intrinsic nature; this intrinsic nature of the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind is likewise non-intrinsic nature. That which is non-intrinsic nature is precisely the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
In this Prajñāpāramitā, the sense-base of the eye is not apprehended, nor are its permanence or impermanence apprehended;
the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are all unapprehendable, nor are their permanence or impermanence apprehended.
Why is this? Because within this, even the sense-base of the eye and so forth cannot be found; how much less could there be that which is permanent or impermanent!
If you can cultivate such prajñā, this is the cultivation of the prajñāpāramitā.
Furthermore, he said this:

"O son of good family, you should cultivate the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā); you should not contemplate the sense base of the eye as either pleasant or painful, nor should you contemplate the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as either pleasant or painful."

Why is this? The sense-base of the eye is empty of the intrinsic nature of the sense-base of the eye; the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are empty of the intrinsic nature of the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.

This intrinsic nature of the sense-base of the eye is not an intrinsic nature; this intrinsic nature of the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind is also not an intrinsic nature. That which is not an intrinsic nature is precisely the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
In this Prajñāpāramitā, the sense-base of the eye is not to be found, nor are its pleasure and pain to be found;
the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are all not to be found, nor are their pleasure and pain to be found.
Why is this? Because herein even the sense-base of the eye and so forth cannot be apprehended, much less pleasure or pain!
If you can cultivate such prajñā, this is the cultivation of the prajñāpāramitā.
Furthermore, he spoke these words:

"O son of good family, you should cultivate the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā); you should not contemplate the sense base of the eye as either self or non-self, nor should you contemplate the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as either self or non-self."

Why is this? The sense-base of the eye is empty of the intrinsic nature of the sense-base of the eye; the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are empty of the intrinsic nature of the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.

This intrinsic nature of the sense-base of the eye is not an intrinsic nature; this intrinsic nature of the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind is also not an intrinsic nature. That which is not an intrinsic nature is precisely the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
In this Prajñāpāramitā, the sense-base of the eye is not apprehended, nor are its self or non-self apprehended;
the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are all unapprehendable, nor are their selves or non-selves apprehended.
Why is this? Because herein even the sense-base of the eye and so forth cannot be apprehended, let alone that self and non-self!
If you can cultivate such prajñā, this is the cultivation of the prajñāpāramitā.
Furthermore, he spoke these words:

"O son of good family, you should cultivate the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā); you should not contemplate the sense base of the eye as either pure or impure, nor should you contemplate the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as either pure or impure."

Why is this? The sense-base of the eye is empty of the intrinsic nature of the sense-base of the eye; the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are empty of the intrinsic nature of the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.

This intrinsic nature of the sense-base of the eye is not an intrinsic nature; this intrinsic nature of the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind is also not an intrinsic nature. That which is not an intrinsic nature is precisely the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
In this Prajñāpāramitā, the sense-base of the eye cannot be apprehended, nor can its purity or impurity be apprehended;
the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are all unapprehendable, and their purity or impurity is likewise unapprehendable.
Why is this? Because herein even the sense-base of the eye and so forth cannot be apprehended, let alone that which is pure or impure!
If you can cultivate such prajñā, this is the cultivation of the prajñāpāramitā.
“Kauśika! When these sons and daughters of good family speak in this manner, they are proclaiming the true and correct Prajñāpāramitā.”
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
If good sons or good daughters teach the *prajñāpāramitā* to those who have resolved upon unsurpassed bodhicitta, they should speak as follows: 'O good son, you should practice the *prajñāpāramitā*;

you should not contemplate the sphere of form (*rūpa-āyatana*) as either permanent or impermanent, nor should you contemplate the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental phenomena (*dharma-āyatana*) as either permanent or impermanent.'"

Why is this? The sphere of form is empty of the intrinsic nature of the sphere of form; the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena are empty of the intrinsic nature of the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena.

This intrinsic nature of the sphere of form is not an intrinsic nature; this intrinsic nature of the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena is also not an intrinsic nature. That which is not an intrinsic nature is precisely the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
In this Prajñāpāramitā, the sphere of form (rūpa-āyatana) is not apprehended, nor are its permanence or impermanence apprehended;
the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena (dharma-āyatana) are all unapprehendable, nor are their permanence or impermanence apprehended.
Why is this? Because herein even the sense-bases such as form (*rūpāyatana*) cannot be apprehended, much less that which is permanent or impermanent!
If you can cultivate such prajñā, this is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Furthermore, he spoke these words:

"O son of good family, you should cultivate the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā); you should not regard the sphere of form as either pleasant or painful, nor should you regard the spheres of sound, odor, taste, touch, or mental phenomena as either pleasant or painful."

Why is this? The sphere of form is empty of the intrinsic nature of the sphere of form; the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena are empty of the intrinsic nature of the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena.

This intrinsic nature of the sphere of form is not an intrinsic nature; this intrinsic nature of the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena is also not an intrinsic nature. That which is not an intrinsic nature is precisely the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
In this Prajñāpāramitā, the sphere of form (rūpa-āyatana) cannot be apprehended, nor can its pleasure or pain;
the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena (dharma-āyatana) are all unapprehendable, nor can their pleasure or pain be apprehended.

Furthermore, he spoke these words:

"O son of good family, you should cultivate the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā); you should not contemplate the sphere of form (rūpāyatana) as either self or non-self, nor should you contemplate the spheres of sound, odor, taste, touch, or mental phenomena (dharmāyatana) as either self or non-self."

Why is this? The sense-base of form is empty of the intrinsic nature of the sense-base of form; the sense-bases of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena are empty of the intrinsic nature of the sense-bases of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena.

This intrinsic nature of the sense-base of form is precisely no-intrinsic-nature; this intrinsic nature of the sense-bases of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena is also no-intrinsic-nature. That which is no-intrinsic-nature is precisely the *prajñāpāramitā*.
In this Prajñāpāramitā, the sphere of form (rūpa-āyatana) is unapprehendable; therein, both self and non-self are likewise unapprehendable.
The spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena (dharma-āyatana) are all unapprehendable; therein, both self and non-self are likewise unapprehendable.
Why is this? Because herein even the sense-bases such as form cannot be apprehended, much less that "self" or "non-self"!
If you can cultivate such prajñā, this is the cultivation of the prajñāpāramitā.
Furthermore, he said this:

"O son of good family, you should cultivate the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā); you should not contemplate the sphere of form (rūpāyatana) as either pure or impure, nor should you contemplate the spheres of sound, odor, taste, touch, or mental phenomena (dharmāyatana) as either pure or impure."

Why is this? The sphere of form is empty of the intrinsic nature of the sphere of form; the spheres of sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena are empty of the intrinsic nature of the spheres of sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena.

This intrinsic nature of the sphere of form is not an intrinsic nature; this intrinsic nature of the spheres of sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena is also not an intrinsic nature. That which is not an intrinsic nature is precisely the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
In this Prajñāpāramitā, the sphere of form cannot be apprehended, nor can its purity or impurity be apprehended;
the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena are all unapprehendable, and their purity or impurity likewise cannot be apprehended.
Why is this? Because herein even the sense-bases such as form cannot be apprehended, let alone that which is pure or impure!
If you can cultivate such prajñā, this is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
“Kauśika! When these sons and daughters of good family speak in this manner, they are proclaiming the true and correct Prajñāpāramitā.”
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family explains the *prajñāpāramitā* to those who have resolved upon unsurpassed bodhicitta, saying: 'O son of good family, you should cultivate the *prajñāpāramitā*;

you should not view the eye-element as either permanent or impermanent; you should not view the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, eye-contact, or the various feelings produced with eye-contact as conditions as either permanent or impermanent.'"

Why is this? Because the eye-element is empty of the intrinsic nature of the eye-element; the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, eye-contact, and all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition are empty of the intrinsic nature of the form-element, up to and including all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition.

This intrinsic nature of the eye-element is non-intrinsic nature; this intrinsic nature of the form-element, up to and including all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, is also non-intrinsic nature. That which is non-intrinsic nature is precisely the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
In this Prajñāpāramitā, the eye-element is not apprehended, nor are its permanence or impermanence apprehended;
from the form-element up to all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, none are apprehended, nor are their permanence or impermanence apprehended.
Why is this so? Because herein even the eye-element and so forth cannot be apprehended, let alone that which is permanent or impermanent!
If you can cultivate such prajñā, this is the cultivation of the prajñāpāramitā.
Furthermore, he spoke these words:

"O son of good family, you should cultivate the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā); you should not contemplate the eye-element as either pleasant or painful, nor should you contemplate the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, eye-contact, or the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition as either pleasant or painful."

Because the eye-element is empty of the intrinsic nature of the eye-element; the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, and eye-contact, as well as all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, are empty of the intrinsic nature of the form-element up to the feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition.

from the form-element up to the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, none can be apprehended, nor can their pleasure or pain be apprehended.
Why is this? Because herein even the eye-faculty and so forth cannot be apprehended, let alone pleasure and pain!
If you can cultivate such prajñā, that is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Again, he spoke these words:

Because the eye-element is empty of the intrinsic nature of the eye-element; the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, and eye-contact, as well as all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, are empty of the intrinsic nature of the form-element up to the feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition.

from the form-element up to the feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, all are not apprehended, nor are their purity or impurity apprehended.
Why is this? Because herein even the eye-faculty and so forth cannot be apprehended, much less that which is pure or impure!
If you can cultivate such Prajñā, this is the cultivation of the Prajñāpāramitā.
“Kauśika! When these sons and daughters of good family speak in this manner, they are proclaiming the true and authentic Prajñāpāramitā.”
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved upon unsurpassed bodhicitta, proclaim the Perfection of Wisdom and speak thus:

"Furthermore, Kauśika!

from the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) up to the inconceivable realm (acintyadhātu), none can be apprehended, nor can their permanence or impermanence be apprehended.

This intrinsic nature of the gate of liberation of emptiness is non-intrinsic nature; this intrinsic nature of the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness is also non-intrinsic nature. That which is non-intrinsic nature is precisely the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Within this Prajñāpāramitā, the gate of liberation of emptiness is unapprehendable, and therein neither self nor non-self is apprehendable;
the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness are all unapprehendable, and therein neither self nor non-self is apprehendable.
Why is this? Because within this, even the gate of liberation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha*) cannot be apprehended, let alone that of self or non-self!
If you can cultivate such prajñā, this is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Furthermore, he spoke these words:

you should not regard the stage of entering the stream or the fruit of stream-entry as either permanent or impermanent; you should not regard the stage of entering once-returning or the fruit of once-returning, the stage of entering non-returning or the fruit of non-returning, or the stage of entering arhatship or the fruit of arhatship as either permanent or impermanent.'"
