Because the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry and the fruit of stream-entry are empty of the intrinsic nature of the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry and the fruit of stream-entry; likewise, the candidate for the fruit of once-returning and the fruit of once-returning, the candidate for the fruit of non-returning and the fruit of non-returning, and the candidate for the fruit of arhatship and the fruit of arhatship—from the candidate for the fruit of once-returning up to the fruit of arhatship—are empty of their own intrinsic nature.

This intrinsic nature of the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry and the fruit of stream-entry is itself no intrinsic nature; this intrinsic nature of the candidate for the fruit of once-returning up to the fruit of arhatship is also no intrinsic nature. That which is no intrinsic nature is precisely the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Within this *prajñāpāramitā*, the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry and the fruit of stream-entry itself cannot be apprehended, nor can their permanence or impermanence be apprehended;
likewise, the candidates for the fruit of once-returning up to the fruit of arhatship cannot be apprehended, nor can their permanence or impermanence be apprehended.
Why is this? Because within this state, even the stage of a candidate for the first fruit cannot be apprehended, let alone that which is permanent or impermanent!
If you can cultivate such prajñā, this is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Furthermore, he said this:

"O son of good family, you should cultivate the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā); you should not regard the stage of entering the stream (srotāpattipratipanna) or the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpattiphala) as either pleasant or painful; nor should you regard the stage of entering once-returning (sakṛdāgāmipratipanna) or the fruit of once-returning, the stage of entering non-returning (anāgāmipratipanna) or the fruit of non-returning, or the stage of entering arhatship (arhattvapratipanna) or the fruit of arhatship as either pleasant or painful."

Why is this? Because the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry and the fruit of stream-entry are empty of the intrinsic nature of the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry and the fruit of stream-entry; likewise, the candidate for the fruit of once-returning and the fruit of once-returning, the candidate for the fruit of non-returning and the fruit of non-returning, and the candidate for the fruit of arhatship and the fruit of arhatship—from the candidate for the fruit of once-returning up to the fruit of arhatship—are empty of their own intrinsic nature.

This intrinsic nature of the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry and the fruit of stream-entry is itself no intrinsic nature; this intrinsic nature of the candidate for the fruit of once-returning up to the fruit of arhatship is also no intrinsic nature. That which is no intrinsic nature is precisely the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Within this Prajñāpāramitā, the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry and the fruit of stream-entry itself are unapprehendable; their pleasure and their suffering are likewise unapprehendable.
The candidate for the fruit of once-returning up to the fruit of arhatship are all unapprehendable; their pleasure and their suffering are likewise unapprehendable.
Why is this? Because herein even the stream-enterer candidate and so forth cannot be found; how much less could there be pleasure or pain!
If you can cultivate such prajñā, this is the cultivation of the prajñāpāramitā.
Again, he spoke these words:

"O son of good family, you should cultivate the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). You should not contemplate the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry or the fruit of stream-entry as either self or non-self; you should not contemplate the candidate for the fruit of once-returning or the fruit of once-returning, the candidate for the fruit of non-returning or the fruit of non-returning, or the candidate for the fruit of arhatship or the fruit of arhatship as either self or non-self."

Why is this? Because the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry and the fruit of stream-entry are empty of the intrinsic nature of the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry and the fruit of stream-entry; likewise, the candidate for the fruit of once-returning and the fruit of once-returning, the candidate for the fruit of non-returning and the fruit of non-returning, and the candidate for the fruit of arhatship and the fruit of arhatship—from the candidate for the fruit of once-returning up to the fruit of arhatship—are empty of their own intrinsic nature.

This intrinsic nature of the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry and the fruit of stream-entry is itself no intrinsic nature; the intrinsic nature of the candidate for the fruit of once-returning up to the fruit of arhatship is also no intrinsic nature. That which is no intrinsic nature is precisely the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

Within this Prajñāpāramitā, the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry and the fruit of stream-entry itself are unapprehendable; both "self" and "non-self" regarding them are likewise unapprehendable.
The candidate for the fruit of once-returning up to the fruit of arhatship are all unapprehendable; both "self" and "non-self" regarding them are likewise unapprehendable.
Why is this? Because herein even the stream-enterer candidate and so forth cannot be found; how much less could there be such things as "self" and "non-self"!
If you can cultivate such prajñā, this is the cultivation of the prajñāpāramitā.
Furthermore, he said this:

"O son of good family, you should cultivate the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā); you should not contemplate the stage of entering the stream or the fruit of stream-entry as either pure or impure; you should not contemplate the stage of entering once-returning or the fruit of once-returning, the stage of entering non-returning or the fruit of non-returning, or the stage of entering arhatship or the fruit of arhatship as either pure or impure."

Why is this? Because the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry and the fruit of stream-entry are empty of the intrinsic nature of the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry and the fruit of stream-entry; likewise, the candidate for the fruit of once-returning and the fruit of once-returning, the candidate for the fruit of non-returning and the fruit of non-returning, and the candidate for the fruit of arhatship and the fruit of arhatship—from the candidate for the fruit of once-returning up to the fruit of arhatship—are empty of their own intrinsic nature.

This intrinsic nature of the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry and the fruit of stream-entry is itself no intrinsic nature; this intrinsic nature of the candidate for the fruit of once-returning up to the fruit of arhatship is also no intrinsic nature. That which is no intrinsic nature is precisely the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Within this Prajñāpāramitā, the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry and the fruit of stream-entry itself cannot be apprehended, nor can their purity or impurity be apprehended;
likewise, the candidates for the fruit of once-returning up to the fruit of arhatship cannot be apprehended, nor can their purity or impurity be apprehended.
Why is this? Because herein even the stages such as the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry cannot be found; how much less could there be that which is pure or impure!
If you can cultivate such wisdom, this is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
“Kauśika! When these sons and daughters of good family speak in this manner, they are proclaiming the true and correct Prajñāpāramitā.”

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Scroll 148. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Part One: Chapter on Measuring Merit, Number Thirty, Section Fourteen. "Furthermore, Kauśika!
If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, proclaim the Prajñāpāramitā and speak thus:
"Good son, you should cultivate the Prajñāpāramitā; you should not perceive the awakening of a pratyekabuddha as either permanent or impermanent."

Why is this? Because the awakening of all pratyekabuddhas is empty of the intrinsic nature of the awakening of all pratyekabuddhas; that which is the intrinsic nature of the awakening of all pratyekabuddhas is itself no-intrinsic-nature, and that which is no-intrinsic-nature is precisely the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Within this Prajñāpāramitā, the enlightenment of all Pratyekabuddhas cannot be apprehended, nor can their permanence or impermanence be apprehended. Why is this?
In this, even the enlightenment of a solitary buddha (*pratyekabuddha*) cannot be found, let alone permanence or impermanence!
If you can cultivate such wisdom (*prajñā*), this is the cultivation of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
"Furthermore, he says this:
'O son of good family, you should practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā); you should not regard the awakening of a solitary buddha (pratyekabuddhabodhi) as either pleasant or painful.'"

Why is this? Because the enlightenment of all pratyekabuddhas is empty of the intrinsic nature of the enlightenment of all pratyekabuddhas; that which is the intrinsic nature of the enlightenment of all pratyekabuddhas is non-intrinsic nature, and that which is non-intrinsic nature is precisely the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Within this Prajñāpāramitā, the enlightenment of all Pratyekabuddhas is unattainable, and their pleasure and suffering are likewise unattainable. Why is this so?
Within this, even the enlightenment of a solitary buddha (*pratyekabuddha*) cannot be found; how much less could there be pleasure or suffering!
If you can cultivate such prajñā, this is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Furthermore, he said this:

"O son of good family, you should cultivate the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā); you should not contemplate the awakening of a solitary buddha (pratyekabuddhabodhi) as either 'self' or 'non-self.'"

Why is this? Because the awakening of all pratyekabuddhas is empty of the intrinsic nature of the awakening of all pratyekabuddhas; that which is the intrinsic nature of the awakening of all pratyekabuddhas is itself no-intrinsic-nature, and that which is no-intrinsic-nature is precisely the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Within this Prajñāpāramitā, the enlightenment of all pratyekabuddhas is unattainable, and both self and non-self are likewise unattainable. Why is this so?
Within this, even the enlightenment of a solitary buddha (*pratyekabuddha*) cannot be found; how much less could there be "self" or "non-self"!
If you can cultivate such wisdom (*prajñā*), that is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Furthermore, he spoke these words:
"O son of good family, you should cultivate the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), but you should not regard the awakening of a solitary buddha (pratyekabuddhabodhi) as either pure or impure."

Why is this? Because the enlightenment of all pratyekabuddhas is empty of the intrinsic nature of the enlightenment of all pratyekabuddhas; that which is the intrinsic nature of the enlightenment of all pratyekabuddhas is non-intrinsic nature, and that which is non-intrinsic nature is precisely the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Within this Prajñāpāramitā, the enlightenment of all pratyekabuddhas cannot be apprehended, nor can their purity or impurity be apprehended. Why is this so?
Within this, even the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha cannot be found, let alone that which is pure or impure!
If you can cultivate such wisdom, this is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
“Kauśika! When these sons and daughters of good family speak in this manner, they are proclaiming the true and correct Prajñāpāramitā.”
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved upon unsurpassed bodhicitta, expound the Prajñāpāramitā, speaking thus:
'You, good son, should practice the Prajñāpāramitā; you should not regard the practices of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as either permanent or impermanent.'"

Why is this? Because the practice of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is empty of the intrinsic nature of the practice of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; that which is the intrinsic nature of the practice of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is itself no-intrinsic-nature, and that which is no-intrinsic-nature is precisely the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Within this Prajñāpāramitā, the practice of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot be apprehended, nor can their permanence or impermanence be apprehended.
Why is this? Because herein not even all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas can be apprehended, let alone permanence or impermanence!
If you can cultivate such prajñā, this is the cultivation of the prajñāpāramitā.
Furthermore, he spoke these words:
"O son of good family, you should cultivate the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), and you should not regard the practices of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as either pleasant or painful."

Why is this? Because the practice of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is empty of the intrinsic nature of the practice of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; that which is the intrinsic nature of the practice of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is itself no-intrinsic-nature, and that which is no-intrinsic-nature is precisely the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Within this Prajñāpāramitā, the practices of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot be apprehended, nor can their pleasure or suffering be apprehended.
Why is this? Because herein not even any bodhisattva-mahāsattva practice can be apprehended, let alone pleasure or suffering!
If you can cultivate such prajñā, that is the cultivation of the prajñāpāramitā.
Furthermore, he spoke these words:
"O son of good family, you should cultivate the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), and you should not regard the practices of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as either 'self' or 'non-self.'"

Why is this? Because the practice of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is empty of the intrinsic nature of the practice of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; that which is the intrinsic nature of the practice of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is itself non-intrinsic nature, and that which is non-intrinsic nature is precisely the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Within this Prajñāpāramitā, the practice of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot be apprehended; neither self nor non-self can be apprehended therein.
Why is this? Because herein not even any practice of a bodhisattva mahāsattva can be apprehended, let alone such things as self or non-self!
If you are able to cultivate such prajñā, this is the cultivation of the prajñāpāramitā.
Furthermore, he spoke these words:
"O son of good family, you should practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), but you should not regard the conduct of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as either pure or impure."

Why is this? Because the practice of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is empty of the intrinsic nature of the practice of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; that which is the intrinsic nature of the practice of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is itself no-intrinsic-nature, and that which is no-intrinsic-nature is precisely the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Within this Prajñāpāramitā, the practices of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot be apprehended, nor can their purity or impurity be apprehended.
Why is this? Because herein not even any bodhisattva-mahāsattva practice can be apprehended, let alone that which is pure or impure!
If you can cultivate such prajñā, this is the cultivation of the prajñāpāramitā.
“Kauśika! When these sons and daughters of good family speak in this manner, they are proclaiming the true and correct Prajñāpāramitā.”
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
If good sons or good daughters explain the *prajñāpāramitā* to those who have resolved upon unsurpassed bodhicitta, they should speak as follows:
'O good son, you should cultivate the *prajñāpāramitā*, but you should not regard the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas as either permanent or impermanent.'"

Why is this? The unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas is empty of intrinsic nature; that which is the intrinsic nature of the unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas is itself no intrinsic nature. That which is no intrinsic nature is precisely the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Within this Prajñāpāramitā, the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas cannot be apprehended, nor can its permanence or impermanence be apprehended.
Why is this? Because herein even the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas cannot be apprehended, let alone that which is permanent or impermanent!
If you can cultivate such prajñā, you are cultivating the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Furthermore, he spoke thus:

"O son of good family, you should cultivate the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), and you should not regard the unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment of the Buddhas as either pleasure or suffering."

Why is this? The unexcelled, perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas is empty of intrinsic nature; the intrinsic nature of this unexcelled, perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas is itself no-intrinsic-nature. That which is no-intrinsic-nature is precisely the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Within this Prajñāpāramitā, the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas cannot be apprehended, nor can pleasure and suffering be apprehended.
Why is this? Because herein even the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas cannot be apprehended, let alone that pleasure or pain!
If you can cultivate such prajñā, this is the cultivation of the prajñāpāramitā.
Furthermore, he said this:
"O son of good family, you should cultivate the perfection of wisdom; you should not regard the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas as either self or non-self."

Why is this? The unexcelled, perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas is empty of intrinsic nature; the intrinsic nature of this unexcelled, perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas is itself no-intrinsic-nature, and that which is no-intrinsic-nature is precisely the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Within this *prajñāpāramitā*, the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas cannot be apprehended; neither self nor non-self can be apprehended therein.
Why is this? Because herein even the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas cannot be apprehended, let alone that which is "self" or "non-self"!
If you can cultivate such prajñā, this is the cultivation of the prajñāpāramitā.
Furthermore, he spoke these words:

"O son of good family, you should practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), but you should not regard the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas as either pure or impure."

Why is this? The unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas is empty of intrinsic nature; the intrinsic nature of this unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas is itself no-intrinsic-nature. That which is no-intrinsic-nature is precisely the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Within this Prajñāpāramitā, the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas cannot be apprehended, nor can its purity or impurity be apprehended.
Why is this? Because herein even the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas cannot be apprehended, let alone that which is pure or impure!
If you can cultivate such prajñā, this is the cultivation of the prajñāpāramitā.
“Kauśika! When these sons and daughters of good family speak in this manner, they are proclaiming the true and authentic Prajñāpāramitā.”
Then, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, again addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One,

why is it that when good sons and good daughters speak of the perfection of meditative concentration of non-apprehension, they are said to be speaking of the true and correct perfection of meditative concentration?”
The Buddha said,
“Kauśika! If good sons and good daughters proclaim the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*) to those who have resolved upon unsurpassed bodhicitta, speaking as follows:”

“O son of good family, you should cultivate the perfection of meditative concentration; you should not regard form as either permanent or impermanent, nor should you regard feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness as either permanent or impermanent.”

Why is this? Form is empty of the intrinsic nature of form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty of the intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

This intrinsic nature of form is no intrinsic nature; this intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is also no intrinsic nature. That which is no intrinsic nature is precisely the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*).
In this perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*), form (*rūpa*) is not apprehended, nor are its permanence or impermanence apprehended;
feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are all not apprehended, nor are their permanence or impermanence apprehended.
Why is this? Because herein even form and the other aggregates cannot be apprehended, let alone permanence or impermanence!
If you can cultivate meditative concentration in this manner, this is the cultivation of the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā).
Furthermore, he spoke these words:

"O son of good family, you should cultivate the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*); you should not regard form as either pleasant or painful, nor should you regard feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as either pleasant or painful."

Why is this? Form is empty of the intrinsic nature of form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty of the intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

This intrinsic nature of form is not an intrinsic nature; this intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is also not an intrinsic nature. That which is not an intrinsic nature is precisely the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*).
In this perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*), form (*rūpa*) cannot be apprehended, nor can its pleasure or pain;
feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are all unapprehendable, and their pleasure or pain likewise cannot be apprehended.
Why is this? Because herein even form and so forth cannot be apprehended, let alone pleasure and pain!
If you can cultivate such meditative concentration, this is the cultivation of the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā).
Furthermore, he said this:

"O son of good family, you should cultivate the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā); you should not view form as either self or non-self, nor should you view feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as either self or non-self."

Why is this? Form is empty of the intrinsic nature of form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty of the intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

This intrinsic nature of form is not an intrinsic nature; this intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is also not an intrinsic nature. That which is not an intrinsic nature is the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyāna-pāramitā).
In this perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*), form (*rūpa*) is not apprehended, nor are its self or non-self apprehended;
feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are all not apprehended, nor are their self or non-self apprehended.
Why is this? Because herein even form and the other aggregates cannot be apprehended, let alone that self or non-self!
If you can cultivate such meditative concentration, this is the cultivation of the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā).
"Furthermore, he spoke these words:

'You, son of good family, should cultivate the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā); you should not regard form as either pure or impure, nor should you regard feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as either pure or impure.'"
Why is this? Form is empty of its own intrinsic nature; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty of their own intrinsic natures.

This intrinsic nature of form is not an intrinsic nature; this intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is also not an intrinsic nature. That which is not an intrinsic nature is precisely the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*).
In this perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*), form (*rūpa*) is unapprehendable, and its purity or impurity is likewise unapprehendable;
feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are all unapprehendable, and their purity or impurity is likewise unapprehendable.
Why is this? Because herein even form and so forth cannot be apprehended, much less that which is pure or impure!
If you can cultivate such meditative concentration, this is the cultivation of the perfection of meditative concentration.
“Kauśika! When these sons and daughters of good family speak in this manner, they are proclaiming the true perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā).”
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved upon unsurpassed bodhicitta, proclaim the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā), saying:

'You, good son, should cultivate the perfection of meditative concentration; you should not contemplate the sense base of the eye as either permanent or impermanent, nor should you contemplate the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as either permanent or impermanent.'"

Why is this? The sense base of the eye is empty of the intrinsic nature of the sense base of the eye; the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are empty of the intrinsic nature of the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.

This intrinsic nature of the sense base of the eye is precisely no-intrinsic-nature; the intrinsic nature of the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind is likewise no-intrinsic-nature. That which is no-intrinsic-nature is itself the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyāna-pāramitā).
In this perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*), the sense base of the eye (*cakṣurāyatana*) is not apprehended, and its permanence or impermanence is likewise not apprehended;
the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are all not apprehended, and their permanence or impermanence is likewise not apprehended.
Why is this? Because within this state, even the sense bases such as the eye cannot be apprehended, let alone that which is permanent or impermanent!
If you can cultivate meditative concentration in this manner, this is the cultivation of the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā).
Again, he spoke these words:

"O son of good family, you should cultivate the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā); you should not contemplate the sense base of the eye as either pleasant or painful, nor should you contemplate the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as either pleasant or painful."

Why is this? The sense base of the eye is empty of the intrinsic nature of the sense base of the eye; the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are empty of the intrinsic nature of the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.

This intrinsic nature of the sense base of the eye is itself no intrinsic nature; this intrinsic nature of the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind is likewise no intrinsic nature. That which is no intrinsic nature is precisely the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā).
In this perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*), the sense base of the eye (*cakṣurāyatana*) cannot be apprehended, nor can its pleasure or pain;
the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind (*manasāyatana*) are all unapprehendable, and their pleasure and pain are likewise unapprehendable.
Why is this? Because herein even the sense-base of the eye and so forth cannot be found; how much less could there be that pleasure or pain!
If you can cultivate such meditative concentration, this is the cultivation of the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā).
Furthermore, he spoke these words:

"O son of good family, you should cultivate the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā); you should not regard the sense base of the eye as either self or non-self, nor should you regard the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as either self or non-self."

Why is this? Because the sense-base of the eye is empty of the intrinsic nature of the sense-base of the eye; the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are empty of the intrinsic nature of the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.

This intrinsic nature of the sense-base of the eye is not an intrinsic nature; this intrinsic nature of the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind is also not an intrinsic nature. That which is not an intrinsic nature is precisely the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*).
In this perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*), the sense base of the eye (*cakṣurāyatana*) is not apprehended, nor are its self or non-self apprehended;
the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are all not apprehended, nor are their self or non-self apprehended.
Why is this? Because herein even the sense-base of the eye and so forth cannot be found; how much less could there be such things as "self" and "non-self"!
If you can cultivate meditative concentration in this manner, this is the cultivation of the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyāna-pāramitā).
Again he said:

"Furthermore, Kauśika!

This intrinsic nature of the ten powers of a Buddha is itself no intrinsic nature; this intrinsic nature of the four fearlessnesses up to the eighteen unique qualities is also no intrinsic nature. That which is no intrinsic nature is precisely the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*).
Within this perfection of meditative concentration, the ten powers of a Buddha are unapprehendable, and their pleasure and pain are likewise unapprehendable;
from the four fearlessnesses up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, all are unapprehendable, and their pleasure and pain are likewise unapprehendable.
Why is this? Because herein even the ten powers of a Buddha cannot be found, let alone pleasure or suffering!
If you can cultivate such meditative concentration, this is the cultivation of the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā).
Furthermore, he said this:

"O son of good family, you should cultivate the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*). You should not contemplate whether the ten powers of a Buddha are self or non-self; you should not contemplate whether the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great joy, great equanimity, or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are self or non-self."

Why is this? The ten powers of a Buddha are empty of the intrinsic nature of the ten powers of a Buddha; the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha—from the four fearlessnesses up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha—are empty of the intrinsic nature of those [qualities].

Within this perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*), the ten powers of a Buddha (*daśabala*) are not apprehended, nor are "self" or "non-self" apprehended therein;
the four fearlessnesses (*caturvaiśāradya*) up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*) are all not apprehended, nor are "self" or "non-self" apprehended therein.
Why is this? Because herein even the ten powers of a Buddha cannot be apprehended, let alone that self or non-self!
If you can cultivate such meditative concentration, this is the cultivation of the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā).
Furthermore, he said this:

"O son of good family, you should cultivate the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā). You should not contemplate whether the ten powers of a Buddha are pure or impure; you should not contemplate whether the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are pure or impure."

Why is this? The ten powers of a Buddha are empty of the intrinsic nature of the ten powers of a Buddha; the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha—from the four fearlessnesses up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha—are empty of their own intrinsic nature.

If you can cultivate such meditative concentration, this is the cultivation of the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā).

all doors of samādhi are unapprehendable, and their permanence or impermanence is likewise unapprehendable.
Why is this? Because herein not even any *dhāraṇī* gates can be found, let alone permanence or impermanence!
If you can cultivate such meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), this is the cultivation of the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*).

Why is this? All dharani-doors are empty of the intrinsic nature of all dharani-doors; all samadhi-doors are empty of the intrinsic nature of all samadhi-doors.

all gateways of samādhi are unapprehendable, and their pleasure and pain are likewise unapprehendable.
Why is this? Because herein not even any dharani-doors can be apprehended, much less pleasure or pain!

Why is this? All dharani-doors are empty of the intrinsic nature of all dharani-doors; all samadhi-doors are empty of the intrinsic nature of all samadhi-doors.

“Kauśika! When these sons and daughters of good family speak in this manner, they are proclaiming the true perfection of meditative concentration.”
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons or good daughters explain the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*) to those who have resolved upon unsurpassed bodhicitta, they should speak as follows: 'You, good son, should cultivate the perfection of meditative concentration;

you should not contemplate whether the stage of entering the stream (*srotāpattipratipannaka*) or the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*) are permanent or impermanent. You should not contemplate whether the stage of entering once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmipratipannaka*) or the fruit of once-returning, the stage of entering non-returning (*anāgāmipratipannaka*) or the fruit of non-returning, or the stage of entering arhatship (*arhattvapratipannaka*) or the fruit of arhatship are permanent or impermanent.'"

Why is this? Because the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry and the fruit of stream-entry are empty of the intrinsic nature of the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry and the fruit of stream-entry; the candidate for the fruit of once-returning and the fruit of once-returning, the candidate for the fruit of non-returning and the fruit of non-returning, and the candidate for the fruit of arhatship and the fruit of arhatship—from the candidate for the fruit of once-returning up to the fruit of arhatship—are empty of their own intrinsic nature.

This intrinsic nature of the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry and the fruit of stream-entry is itself no intrinsic nature; this intrinsic nature of the candidate for the fruit of once-returning up to the fruit of arhatship is also no intrinsic nature. That which is no intrinsic nature is precisely the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*).

Within this perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*), the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry and the fruit of stream-entry itself are unapprehendable; their permanence or impermanence is likewise unapprehendable.
The candidate for the fruit of once-returning up to the fruit of arhatship are all unapprehendable; their permanence or impermanence is likewise unapprehendable.
Why is this? Within this state, even the stage of a candidate for the fruit of stream-entry cannot be found, let alone that of permanence or impermanence!
If you can cultivate such meditative concentration, this is the cultivation of the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā).
"Furthermore, he said this:

'O son of good family, you should cultivate the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā). You should not regard the stage of entering the stream (srotāpattipratipannaka) or the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpattiphala) as either pleasure or suffering; nor should you regard the stage of entering once-returning (sakṛdāgāmipratipannaka) or the fruit of once-returning, the stage of entering non-returning (anāgāmipratipannaka) or the fruit of non-returning, or the stage of entering arhatship (arhattvapratipannaka) or the fruit of arhatship as either pleasure or suffering.'"

Why is this? Because the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry and the fruit of stream-entry are empty of the intrinsic nature of the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry and the fruit of stream-entry; likewise, the candidate for the fruit of once-returning and the fruit of once-returning, the candidate for the fruit of non-returning and the fruit of non-returning, and the candidate for the fruit of arhatship and the fruit of arhatship—from the candidate for the fruit of once-returning up to the fruit of arhatship—are empty of their own intrinsic nature.

This intrinsic nature of the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry and the fruit of stream-entry is precisely no intrinsic nature; this intrinsic nature of the candidate for the fruit of once-returning up to the fruit of arhatship is also no intrinsic nature. That which is no intrinsic nature is itself the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyāna-pāramitā).

Within this perfection of meditative concentration, the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry and the fruit of stream-entry itself cannot be apprehended, nor can their pleasure and suffering be apprehended;
likewise, the candidate for the fruit of once-returning up to the fruit of arhatship cannot be apprehended, nor can their pleasure and suffering be apprehended.
Why is this? Because herein even the stream-enterer candidate and so forth cannot be found, much less pleasure or pain!
If you can cultivate such meditative concentration, this is the cultivation of the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā).
He further said: "O son of good family, you should cultivate the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā).

You should not contemplate the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry or the fruit of stream-entry as either self or non-self; nor should you contemplate the candidate for the fruit of once-returning or the fruit of once-returning, the candidate for the fruit of non-returning or the fruit of non-returning, or the candidate for the fruit of arhatship or the fruit of arhatship as either self or non-self."

Why is this? Because the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry and the fruit of stream-entry are empty of the intrinsic nature of the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry and the fruit of stream-entry; likewise, the candidate for the fruit of once-returning and the fruit of once-returning, the candidate for the fruit of non-returning and the fruit of non-returning, and the candidate for the fruit of arhatship and the fruit of arhatship—from the candidate for the fruit of once-returning up to the fruit of arhatship—are empty of their own intrinsic nature.

This intrinsic nature of the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry and the fruit of stream-entry is itself no intrinsic nature; this intrinsic nature of the candidate for the fruit of once-returning up to the fruit of arhatship is also no intrinsic nature. That which is no intrinsic nature is precisely the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*).

Within this perfection of meditative concentration, the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry and the fruit of stream-entry itself are unapprehendable; both "self" and "non-self" therein are likewise unapprehendable.
The candidate for the fruit of once-returning, up to and including the fruit of arhatship, are all unapprehendable; both "self" and "non-self" therein are likewise unapprehendable.
Why is this? Within this state, even the stage of a candidate for the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-pratipannaka*) cannot be found, let alone such things as "self" or "non-self"!
If you can cultivate meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) in this manner, that is the cultivation of the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*).
Furthermore, he said this:

"O son of good family, you should cultivate the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā). You should not contemplate whether the stage of entering the stream (srotāpattipratipannaka) or the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpattiphala) are pure or impure; nor should you contemplate whether the stage of entering once-returning (sakṛdāgāmipratipannaka), the fruit of once-returning, the stage of entering non-returning (anāgāmipratipannaka), the fruit of non-returning, or the stage of entering arhatship (arhattvapratipannaka) or the fruit of arhatship are pure or impure."

Why is this? Because the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry and the fruit of stream-entry are empty of the intrinsic nature of the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry and the fruit of stream-entry; likewise, the candidate for the fruit of once-returning and the fruit of once-returning, the candidate for the fruit of non-returning and the fruit of non-returning, and the candidate for the fruit of arhatship and the fruit of arhatship—from the candidate for the fruit of once-returning up to the fruit of arhatship—are empty of their own intrinsic nature.

This intrinsic nature of the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry and the fruit of stream-entry is itself no intrinsic nature; this intrinsic nature of the candidate for the fruit of once-returning up to the fruit of arhatship is also no intrinsic nature. That which is no intrinsic nature is precisely the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*).

Within this perfection of meditative concentration, the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry and the fruit of stream-entry itself are unapprehendable, and their purity or impurity is likewise unapprehendable;
the candidate for the fruit of once-returning up to the fruit of arhatship are all unapprehendable, and their purity or impurity is likewise unapprehendable.
Why is this? Because herein even the stage of a candidate for the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-pratipannaka*) cannot be found, let alone that which is pure or impure!
If you can cultivate such meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), this is the cultivation of the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*).
“Kauśika! When these sons and daughters of good family speak in this manner, they are proclaiming the true perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā).”
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family should proclaim the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*) to those who have resolved upon unsurpassed bodhicitta, saying:
'You, son of good family, should cultivate the perfection of meditative concentration; you should not contemplate whether the awakening of a pratyekabuddha is permanent or impermanent. Why is that?'"

All pratyekabuddha-enlightenment is empty of the intrinsic nature of all pratyekabuddha-enlightenment; this intrinsic nature of all pratyekabuddha-enlightenment is itself no-intrinsic-nature, and that which is no-intrinsic-nature is the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*).

Within this perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*), the awakening of all pratyekabuddhas is unattainable, and neither permanence nor impermanence is attainable therein. Why is this so?
In this state, even the enlightenment of a solitary buddha (*pratyekabuddha*) cannot be found, let alone permanence or impermanence!
If you can cultivate such meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), this is the cultivation of the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*).
Furthermore, he said this:

"O son of good family, you should cultivate the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā), and you should not regard the enlightenment of all pratyekabuddhas as either pleasant or painful."

Why is this? Because the enlightenment of all pratyekabuddhas is empty of the intrinsic nature of the enlightenment of all pratyekabuddhas; this intrinsic nature of the enlightenment of all pratyekabuddhas is itself no intrinsic nature, and that which is no intrinsic nature is precisely the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*).
Within this perfection of meditative concentration, the awakening of all pratyekabuddhas cannot be apprehended, nor can their pleasure or suffering be apprehended. Why is this?
In this state, even the awakening of a solitary buddha (*pratyekabuddha*) cannot be found, let alone pleasure or suffering!
If you can cultivate such meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), this is the cultivation of the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*).
"Furthermore, he said this:
'You, son of good family, should cultivate the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā); you should not contemplate whether all pratyekabuddha-enlightenment is self or non-self.'"

Why is this? Because the awakening of all pratyekabuddhas is empty of the intrinsic nature of the awakening of all pratyekabuddhas; this intrinsic nature of the awakening of all pratyekabuddhas is itself no-intrinsic-nature, and that which is no-intrinsic-nature is precisely the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā).

Furthermore, he said this:

Why is this? Within this, not even the enlightenment of a solitary buddha can be found, let alone that which is pure or impure!
If you are able to cultivate such meditative concentration, this is the cultivation of the perfection of meditative concentration.
“Kauśika! When these sons and daughters of good family speak in this manner, they are proclaiming the true perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā).”

Then, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, again addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One,
how is it that when good sons and good daughters speak of the perfection of vigor of non-attainment, they are said to be speaking of the true and correct perfection of vigor?”
The Buddha said:
“Kauśika! If good sons or good daughters proclaim the perfection of diligence to those who have resolved upon unsurpassed bodhicitta, speaking as follows:”

"O son of good family, you should cultivate the perfection of diligence; you should not regard form as either permanent or impermanent, nor should you regard feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as either permanent or impermanent."

Why is this? Form is empty of the intrinsic nature of form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty of the intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

This intrinsic nature of form is not an intrinsic nature; this intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is also not an intrinsic nature. That which is not an intrinsic nature is the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*).
In this perfection of diligence, form is unapprehendable, and its permanence or impermanence is likewise unapprehendable;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are all unapprehendable, and their permanence or impermanence is likewise unapprehendable.
Why is this? Because herein even form and so forth cannot be apprehended, let alone permanence or impermanence!
If you can cultivate such diligence, that is the cultivation of the perfection of diligence (vīrya-pāramitā).
Furthermore, he said this:

"O son of good family, you should cultivate the perfection of diligence; you should not regard form as either pleasant or painful, nor should you regard feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as either pleasant or painful."

Why is this? Form is empty of the intrinsic nature of form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty of the intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

This intrinsic nature of form is not an intrinsic nature; this intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is also not an intrinsic nature. That which is not an intrinsic nature is precisely the perfection of vigor (vīryapāramitā).
In this perfection of diligence, form is unapprehendable, and its pleasure and pain are likewise unapprehendable;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are all unapprehendable, and their pleasure and pain are likewise unapprehendable.
Why is this? Because herein even form and the other aggregates cannot be apprehended, much less pleasure or pain!
If you can cultivate such diligence, this is the cultivation of the perfection of diligence (vīrya-pāramitā).
"Furthermore, he said this:

'You, son of good family, should cultivate the perfection of diligence; you should not view form as either self or non-self, nor should you view feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as either self or non-self.'"

Why is this? Form is empty of the intrinsic nature of form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty of the intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

Why is this? Because herein even the sense-base of the eye and so forth cannot be found; how much less could there be such things as permanence or impermanence!

Furthermore, he spoke these words:

"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons or good daughters explain the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*) to those who have generated the mind set on unsurpassed enlightenment, they should say: 'You, good son, should cultivate the perfection of diligence;

If you can cultivate such diligence, this is the cultivation of the perfection of diligence (vīrya-pāramitā).
"Kauśika! When these sons and daughters of good family speak in this manner, they are proclaiming the truly authentic perfection of diligence."
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved upon unexcelled bodhicitta, proclaim the perfection of diligence (vīryapāramitā), they should speak thus:

'You, good son, should cultivate the perfection of diligence; you should not contemplate the eye-element as either permanent or impermanent, nor should you contemplate the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, eye-contact, or the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition as either permanent or impermanent.'"

Why is this? Because the eye-element is empty of the intrinsic nature of the eye-element; the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, and eye-contact, as well as all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, are empty of the intrinsic nature of the form-element up to the feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition.

This intrinsic nature of the eye-element is itself no intrinsic nature; this intrinsic nature of the form-element up to the feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition is also no intrinsic nature. That which is no intrinsic nature is the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā).
In this perfection of vigor, the eye-element is not apprehended, nor are its permanence or impermanence apprehended;
from the form-element up to all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, none are apprehended, nor are their permanence or impermanence apprehended.
Why is this? Because herein even the eye-element and so forth cannot be apprehended, let alone that which is permanent or impermanent!
If you can cultivate such diligence, this is the cultivation of the perfection of diligence (vīrya-pāramitā).

you should not regard the eye-element as either pleasant or painful, nor should you regard the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, eye-contact, or the various feelings produced with eye-contact as conditions as either pleasant or painful."

Why is this? Because the eye-element is empty of the intrinsic nature of the eye-element; the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, and eye-contact, as well as all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, up to the feeling produced with eye-contact as a condition, are empty of the intrinsic nature of those [form-elements] up to the feeling produced with eye-contact as a condition.

This intrinsic nature of the eye-element is itself no intrinsic nature; this intrinsic nature of the form-element up to the feeling produced with eye-contact as a condition is also no intrinsic nature. That which is no intrinsic nature is precisely the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*).

from the form-element up to all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, none are to be apprehended, nor are their pleasure and pain to be apprehended.

"Furthermore, he says this:

Why is this? Because the mind-element (*manodhātu*) is empty of the intrinsic nature of the mind-element; the dharma-element, the mind-consciousness-element, mental contact (*manaḥsaṃsparśa*), and all feelings produced with mental contact as a condition are empty of the intrinsic nature of the dharma-element up to the feelings produced with mental contact as a condition.

This intrinsic nature of the mind-element is itself no intrinsic nature; this intrinsic nature of the dharma-element up to the feelings produced with mental contact as a condition is also no intrinsic nature. That which is no intrinsic nature is precisely the perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*).

from the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*) up to the various feelings produced with mental contact as a condition, all are unapprehendable, and both self and non-self therein are likewise unapprehendable.

"Furthermore, Kauśika!

Why is this? The earth element is empty of the intrinsic nature of the earth element; the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements are empty of the intrinsic nature of the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements.

This intrinsic nature of the earth element is non-intrinsic nature; the intrinsic nature of the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements is likewise non-intrinsic nature. That which is non-intrinsic nature is itself the perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*).

the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements are all unapprehendable, and their permanence or impermanence is likewise unapprehendable.
Why is this? Because within this, even the earth element and so forth cannot be apprehended, let alone that which is permanent or impermanent!

"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons or good daughters proclaim the perfection of diligence (*vīryapāramitā*) to those who have resolved upon unsurpassed bodhicitta, they should say: 'You, good son, should cultivate the perfection of diligence;

you should not contemplate ignorance as either permanent or impermanent, nor should you contemplate volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), feeling (*vedanā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), becoming (*bhava*), birth (*jāti*), or old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair as either permanent or impermanent.'"

Why is this? Ignorance is empty of the intrinsic nature of ignorance; volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and old age, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are likewise empty of the intrinsic nature of old age, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.

Why is this so? Because herein even ignorance and the like are not to be found; how much less could there be such things as permanence or impermanence!
If you can cultivate such diligence, this is the cultivation of the perfection of diligence (vīrya-pāramitā).

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Scroll 153. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Part One: Chapter on Measuring Merit, Number Thirty, Section Five-Twelve. "Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment, proclaim the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*), they should speak thus: "O good son, you should cultivate the perfection of diligence;

you should not contemplate whether suchness (*tathatā*) is permanent or impermanent. You should not contemplate whether the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the non-falsity of phenomena (*avitathatā*), the unchanging nature of phenomena (*ananyathābhāvatā*), equality (*samatā*), the state beyond birth (*anirodhatā*), the fixed nature of phenomena (*dharmasthititā*), the stability of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the realm of space (*ākāśadhātu*), or the inconceivable realm (*acintyadhātu*) is permanent or impermanent."

Why is this? Because True Suchness (tathatā) is empty of the intrinsic nature of True Suchness; the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), the Dharma-nature (dharmatā), the non-erroneous nature, the unchanging nature, the nature of equality, the nature of freedom from birth, the fixed nature of phenomena (dharmaniyāmatā), the stability of phenomena (dharmaniyamatā), the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), the realm of space (ākāśadhātu), and the inconceivable realm—these, from the Dharma-realm up to the inconceivable realm, are empty of their own intrinsic nature.

This intrinsic nature of True Suchness is itself no intrinsic nature; the intrinsic nature of these [realms], from the Dharma-realm up to the inconceivable realm, is likewise no intrinsic nature. That which is no intrinsic nature is precisely the perfection of vigor (vīryapāramitā).
Within this perfection of vigor, suchness is unapprehendable, and both permanence and impermanence are likewise unapprehendable;

Furthermore, he spoke these words:

the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness are all unapprehendable, nor can their purity or impurity be apprehended.
Why is this? Because herein even the gate of liberation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha*) cannot be apprehended, let alone purity or impurity!

“Kauśika! When these sons and daughters of good family speak in this manner, they are proclaiming the true perfection of diligence (vīryapāramitā).”

the six supernormal powers are unapprehendable, and their permanence or impermanence is likewise unapprehendable.
Why is this? Because within this state, even the five eyes cannot be apprehended, let alone permanence or impermanence!

the six supernormal powers are unapprehendable, and both self and non-self therein are likewise unapprehendable.
Why is this? Because within this state, even the five eyes cannot be found, let alone such things as self and non-self!

"Furthermore, he spoke these words:

Why is this? Because the ten powers of a Buddha are empty of the intrinsic nature of the ten powers of a Buddha; the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha—from the four fearlessnesses up to the eighteen unique qualities—are empty of the intrinsic nature of those eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.

the four fearlessnesses up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are all unattainable, and their pleasure and suffering are likewise unattainable.
Why is this? Because within this state, even the ten powers of a Buddha cannot be found, let alone pleasure or suffering!

Furthermore, he spoke these words:

"O son of good family, you should cultivate the perfection of diligence; you should not contemplate whether the ten powers of a Buddha are self or non-self, nor should you contemplate whether the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are self or non-self."

"Furthermore, he said this:

"Furthermore, Kauśika!

you should not contemplate the fruit of stream-entry or the path of the stream-enterer as either permanent or impermanent. You should not contemplate the fruit of once-returning or the path of the once-returner, nor the fruit of non-returning or the path of the non-returner, nor the fruit of arhatship or the path of the arhat as either permanent or impermanent.'"

Why is this? Because the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry and the fruit of stream-entry are empty of the intrinsic nature of the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry and the fruit of stream-entry; likewise, the candidate for the fruit of once-returning and the fruit of once-returning, the candidate for the fruit of non-returning and the fruit of non-returning, and the candidate for the fruit of arhatship and the fruit of arhatship—from the candidate for the fruit of once-returning up to the fruit of arhatship—are empty of their own intrinsic nature.

This intrinsic nature of the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry and the fruit of stream-entry is itself no intrinsic nature; this intrinsic nature of the candidate for the fruit of once-returning up to the fruit of arhatship is also no intrinsic nature. That which is no intrinsic nature is precisely the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*).
Within this perfection of vigor, the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry and the fruit of stream-entry itself are unapprehendable; their permanence or impermanence is likewise unapprehendable.
The candidate for the fruit of once-returning, up to and including the fruit of arhatship, are all unapprehendable; their permanence or impermanence is likewise unapprehendable.
Why is this? Because herein even the state of one "entering the stream" (srotāpanna-pratipannaka) and so forth cannot be found; how much less could there be such things as permanence or impermanence!
If you can cultivate such diligence, this is the cultivation of the perfection of diligence (vīrya-pāramitā).

"O son of good family, you should cultivate the perfection of diligence; you should not regard the stage of entering the stream or the fruit of stream-entry as either pleasant or painful; you should not regard the stage of entering once-returning or the fruit of once-returning, the stage of entering non-returning or the fruit of non-returning, or the stage of entering arhatship or the fruit of arhatship as either pleasant or painful."

“Kauśika! When these sons and daughters of good family speak in this manner, they are proclaiming the true and correct perfection of diligence.”
Then, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
In what way do those sons and daughters of good family speak of the perfection of patience that is non-apprehension as being the true and correct perfection of patience?”
The Buddha said:
“Kauśika! If good sons and good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, proclaim the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā), speaking as follows:”

"O son of good family, you should cultivate the perfection of patience; you should not regard form as either permanent or impermanent, nor should you regard feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as either permanent or impermanent."

Why is this? Form is empty of the intrinsic nature of form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty of the intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

This intrinsic nature of form is not an intrinsic nature; this intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is also not an intrinsic nature. That which is not an intrinsic nature is precisely the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).
In this perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*), form (*rūpa*) cannot be apprehended, nor can its permanence or impermanence be apprehended;
feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are all unapprehendable, and their permanence or impermanence likewise cannot be apprehended.
Why is this? Because herein even form and the other aggregates cannot be apprehended, let alone permanence or impermanence!
If you can cultivate such patience, this is the cultivation of the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā).

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Scroll 155. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Part One: Chapter on Measuring Merits, Number Thirty, Section Five-Four. "Furthermore, Kauśika!
If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved upon unexcelled bodhicitta, proclaim the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), they should speak thus:

"O good son, you should cultivate the perfection of patience; you should not contemplate the eye-element as either permanent or impermanent, nor should you contemplate the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, eye-contact, or the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition as either permanent or impermanent."

Why is this? Because the eye-element is empty of the intrinsic nature of the eye-element; the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, and eye-contact, as well as all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, are empty of the intrinsic nature of the form-element up to the feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition.

This intrinsic nature of the eye-element is itself no intrinsic nature; this intrinsic nature of the form-element up to the feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition is also no intrinsic nature. That which is no intrinsic nature is precisely the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).
Within this perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), the eye-element (*cakṣur-dhātu*) is not apprehended, nor are its permanence or impermanence apprehended;
from the form-element (*rūpa-dhātu*) up to all feelings (*vedanā*) produced with eye-contact as a condition, none are apprehended, nor are their permanence or impermanence apprehended.
Why is this so? Because herein even the eye-faculty and its objects cannot be apprehended, let alone that which is permanent or impermanent!
If you can cultivate such patience, this is the cultivation of the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā).
Again, he spoke these words:

"O son of good family, you should cultivate the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā); you should not regard the eye-element as either pleasant or painful, nor should you regard the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, eye-contact, or the various feelings produced with eye-contact as conditions as either pleasant or painful."

Why is this? Because the eye-element is empty of the intrinsic nature of the eye-element; the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, and eye-contact, as well as all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, are empty of the intrinsic nature of those [form-elements] up to and including all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition.

This intrinsic nature of the eye-element is non-intrinsic nature; this intrinsic nature of the form-element up to and including all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition is also non-intrinsic nature. That which is non-intrinsic nature is precisely the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).
In this perfection of patience, the eye-element is unapprehendable, and its pleasure and pain are likewise unapprehendable;
from the form-element up to all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, these are all unapprehendable, and their pleasure and pain are likewise unapprehendable.
Why is this? Because herein even the eye-element and so forth cannot be apprehended, let alone pleasure or pain!
If you can cultivate such patience, this is the cultivation of the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā).

In this perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), the eye-element (*cakṣur-dhātu*) is not apprehended, nor are its self or non-self apprehended;

Why is this? The ten powers of a Buddha are empty of the intrinsic nature of the ten powers of a Buddha; the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha—from the four fearlessnesses up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha—are empty of the intrinsic nature of those eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.

“World-Honored One!”

How is it that those sons and daughters of good family who speak of the perfection of pure ethical discipline as being without attainment are said to be speaking of the true and correct perfection of pure ethical discipline?
The Buddha said,
“Kauśika! If good sons and good daughters proclaim the perfection of pure ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) to those who have resolved upon unsurpassed bodhicitta, speaking as follows:”

“O son of good family, you should cultivate the perfection of pure ethical discipline; you should not regard form as either permanent or impermanent, nor should you regard feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as either permanent or impermanent.”

Why is this? Form is empty of the intrinsic nature of form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty of the intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

This intrinsic nature of form is not an intrinsic nature; this intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is also not an intrinsic nature. That which is not an intrinsic nature is precisely the perfection of pure ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*).
Within this perfection of pure ethical discipline, form cannot be apprehended, nor can its permanence or impermanence be apprehended;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are all unapprehendable, and their permanence or impermanence likewise cannot be apprehended.
Why is this? Within this state, even form and the other aggregates cannot be apprehended, let alone permanence or impermanence!
If you can cultivate such pure ethical discipline, this is the cultivation of the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*).
He further said:

"O son of good family, you should cultivate the perfection of pure ethical discipline; you should not regard form as either pleasant or painful, nor should you regard feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as either pleasant or painful."

Why is this? Form is empty of the intrinsic nature of form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty of the intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

This intrinsic nature of form is not an intrinsic nature; this intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is also not an intrinsic nature. That which is not an intrinsic nature is the perfection of pure ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*).
Within this perfection of pure ethical discipline, form is unapprehendable, and its pleasure and pain are likewise unapprehendable;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are all unapprehendable, and their pleasure and pain are likewise unapprehendable.
Why is this? Because herein even form and the other aggregates cannot be apprehended, much less pleasure and pain!
If you can cultivate such pure ethical discipline, this is the cultivation of the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā).
"Furthermore, he spoke these words:

'O son of good family, you should cultivate the perfection of pure ethical discipline; you should not view form as either self or non-self, nor should you view feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as either self or non-self.'"

Why is this? Form is empty of its own intrinsic nature; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty of their own intrinsic natures. If you can cultivate such pure ethical discipline, this is the cultivation of the perfection of pure ethical discipline.

The body-element (*kāyadhātu*) is empty of the intrinsic nature of the body-element; the touch-element (*spraṣṭavyadhātu*), the body-consciousness-element (*kāyavijñānadhātu*), as well as body-contact (*kāyasparśa*) and all feelings produced with body-contact as a condition—from the touch-element up to all feelings produced with body-contact as a condition—are empty of their own intrinsic nature.

This intrinsic nature of the body-element is itself no intrinsic nature; the intrinsic nature of the touch-element up to all feelings produced with body-contact as a condition is likewise no intrinsic nature. That which is no intrinsic nature is precisely the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*).
Within this perfection of pure ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*), the body element (*kāyadhātu*) cannot be apprehended, nor can its purity or impurity be apprehended;
the tactile element (*spraṣṭavyadhātu*) and all feelings (*vedanā*) arising with body-contact as a condition cannot be apprehended, nor can their purity or impurity be apprehended.
Why is this? Because herein even the body-element and so forth cannot be found, much less that which is pure or impure!
If you can cultivate such pure morality, this is the cultivation of the perfection of morality (śīla-pāramitā).
“Kauśika! When these sons and daughters of good family speak in this manner, they are proclaiming the true and perfect perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā).”
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family explains the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) to those who have resolved upon unsurpassed bodhicitta, they should say: 'You, son of good family, should cultivate the perfection of ethical discipline;

Why is this? The mental faculty realm (*manodhātu*) is empty of the intrinsic nature of the mental faculty realm; the phenomena realm (*dharmadhātu*), the mental consciousness realm (*manovijñānadhātu*), and mental contact (*manaḥsaṃsparśa*), as well as all feelings produced with mental contact as a condition, up to the intrinsic nature of those feelings, are empty of intrinsic nature.

That which is no intrinsic nature is the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*).
Within this perfection of pure ethical discipline, the mental faculty (*manodhātu*) is not apprehended, nor are its permanence or impermanence apprehended;

Why is this so? Because within this state, even the mental faculty (*manodhātu*) and its objects cannot be apprehended, let alone such things as permanence or impermanence!
If you can cultivate pure ethical discipline (*śīla*) in this manner, that is the cultivation of the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*).
Furthermore, he said this:

This intrinsic nature of the quality of non-forgetfulness is no intrinsic nature, and this intrinsic nature of the state of constant equanimity is also no intrinsic nature. That which is no intrinsic nature is the perfection of pure ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*).
Within this perfection of pure ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*), the quality of non-forgetfulness (*asaṃpramoṣadharma*) is unapprehendable, and its purity or impurity is likewise unapprehendable;

Why is this? The candidate for the fruit of once-returning, up to and including the fruit of arhatship, are all unapprehendable; their permanence or impermanence is likewise unapprehendable.
Why is this? Because herein even the stream-enterer candidate and others cannot be found; how much less could there be such things as permanence or impermanence!
