from the odor element up to the various feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition, all are unapprehendable, and their permanence or impermanence is likewise unapprehendable.
Why is this? Because herein even the nose-element and so forth cannot be apprehended, let alone permanence or impermanence!
If you can practice giving in this manner, that is the cultivation of the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā).
Furthermore, he said this:

"O son of good family, you should practice the perfection of generosity; you should not regard the nose element as either pleasant or painful, nor should you regard the odor element, the nose-consciousness element, nose-contact, or the various sensations arising with nose-contact as conditions as either pleasant or painful."

Why is this? The nose element is empty of the intrinsic nature of the nose element; the odor element, the nose-consciousness element, nose-contact, and the various feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition—all these, from the odor element up to the various feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition, are empty of intrinsic nature.

This intrinsic nature of the nose element is itself no intrinsic nature; this intrinsic nature of the odor element up to the various feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition is also no intrinsic nature. That which is no intrinsic nature is the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*).
In this perfection of giving, the nose-element (*ghrāṇadhātu*) is unapprehendable, and its pleasure and pain are likewise unapprehendable;
from the odor-element (*gandhadhātu*) up to the various feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition, all are unapprehendable, and their pleasure and pain are likewise unapprehendable.
Why is this? Because herein even the nose-element (*ghrāṇadhātu*) and so forth cannot be apprehended, much less pleasure or pain!

If you can cultivate such non-self, you should not regard the nose-object element (*gandhadhātu*), the nose-consciousness element (*ghrāṇavijñānadhātu*), nose-contact (*ghrāṇasparśa*), or the various feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition as either self or non-self.

Why is this? The nose element is empty of the intrinsic nature of the nose element; the fragrance element, the nose-consciousness element, nose-contact, and the various sensations produced with nose-contact as a condition are empty of the intrinsic nature of the fragrance element up to the various sensations produced with nose-contact as a condition.

from the odor element up to the various feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition, all are unapprehendable, and both self and non-self therein are likewise unapprehendable.
Why is this? Because herein even the nose-element and so forth cannot be found; how much less could there be such things as "self" or "non-self"!
If you can practice giving in this manner, that is the cultivation of the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā).
Again, he spoke thus:

"O son of good family, you should cultivate the perfection of generosity; you should not contemplate the nose element as either pure or impure, nor should you contemplate the odor element, the nose-consciousness element, nose-contact, or the various feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition as either pure or impure."

from the odor element up to the various feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition, all are unapprehendable, and their purity or impurity is likewise unapprehendable.
Why is this? Because herein even the nose-element and so forth cannot be apprehended, let alone that which is pure or impure!

the taste element, and even all feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition, are unapprehendable, and their pleasure and pain are likewise unapprehendable.
Why is this? Because herein even the tongue-element and so forth cannot be apprehended, let alone pleasure and pain!

Why is this? Because the tongue-element is empty of the intrinsic nature of the tongue-element; the taste-element, the tongue-consciousness-element, as well as tongue-contact and the various feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition are empty of the intrinsic nature of the taste-element up to the various feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition.

the taste element, and even all sensations produced with tongue-contact as a condition, are unapprehendable, and both self and non-self therein are likewise unapprehendable.

If you can practice such giving as this, you are practicing the perfection of generosity (dāna-pāramitā).
Again, he spoke these words:

"O son of good family, you should cultivate the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā), but you should not contemplate whether the tongue-element (jihvādhātu) is pure or impure; nor should you contemplate whether the taste-element (rasadhātu), the tongue-consciousness-element (jihvāvijñānadhātu), tongue-contact (jihvāsamsparśa), or the various feelings (vedanā) produced with tongue-contact as a condition are pure or impure."

Why is this? Because the tongue-element is empty of the intrinsic nature of the tongue-element; the taste-element, the tongue-consciousness-element, tongue-contact, and all sensations produced with tongue-contact as a condition are empty of the intrinsic nature of the taste-element up to the sensations produced with tongue-contact as a condition.

This intrinsic nature of the tongue-element is itself no intrinsic nature; this intrinsic nature of the taste-element up to the sensations produced with tongue-contact as a condition is likewise no intrinsic nature. That which is no intrinsic nature is the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā).
In this perfection of giving, the tongue element is not apprehended, nor are its purity or impurity apprehended;
the taste element, and even all feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition, are not apprehended, nor are their purity or impurity apprehended.
Why is this? Because herein even the tongue-element and so forth cannot be apprehended, much less that which is pure or impure!
If you can practice giving in this manner, this is the cultivation of the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā).

from the contact element up to the various feelings produced with body-contact as a condition, all are unapprehendable, and both self and non-self therein are likewise unapprehendable.

"Furthermore, he says this:

'O son of good family, you should cultivate the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā), but you should not contemplate the body-element as either pure or impure; nor should you contemplate the touch-element, the body-consciousness-element, body-contact, or the various feelings arising with body-contact as a condition as either pure or impure.'"

"Kauśika! When these sons and daughters of good family speak in this manner, they are proclaiming the true perfection of generosity."
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons or good daughters explain the perfection of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*) to those who have resolved upon unsurpassed bodhicitta, they should speak as follows: 'You, good son, should cultivate the perfection of generosity;

you should not contemplate the mental faculty (*manas-dhātu*) as either permanent or impermanent, nor should you contemplate the dharma-faculty (*dharma-dhātu*), the mental-consciousness faculty (*mano-vijñāna-dhātu*), mental contact (*manaḥ-saṃsparśa*), or the various sensations (*vedanā*) arising with mental contact as condition, as either permanent or impermanent.'"

Why is this? Because the mind-element (*manodhātu*) is empty of the intrinsic nature of the mind-element; the dharma-element, the mind-consciousness-element, and mental contact (*manaḥsaṃsparśa*), as well as all feelings produced with mental contact as a condition, up to the intrinsic nature of those very feelings, are empty of intrinsic nature.

This intrinsic nature of the mind-element is itself no intrinsic nature; this intrinsic nature of the dharma-element, up to the intrinsic nature of all feelings produced with mental contact as a condition, is likewise no intrinsic nature. That which is no intrinsic nature is precisely the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).
In this perfection of giving, the mind-element (*manodhātu*) cannot be apprehended, nor can its permanence or impermanence be apprehended;
from the dharma-element up to all feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition, none can be apprehended, nor can their permanence or impermanence be apprehended.
Why is this so? Because within this, even the mental faculty (*manodhātu*) and its objects cannot be apprehended, let alone that which is permanent or impermanent!
If you can practice giving in such a manner, this is the cultivation of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).
Furthermore, he said this:

"O son of good family, you should cultivate the perfection of generosity; you should not regard the mental faculty as either pleasant or painful, nor should you regard the dharma-realm, the mental-consciousness realm, mental contact, or the various feelings arising with mental contact as conditions as either pleasant or painful."

Why is this? Because the mind-element (*manodhātu*) is empty of the intrinsic nature of the mind-element; the dharma-element, the mental-consciousness-element, and mental contact (*manaḥsaṃsparśa*), as well as all feelings produced with mental contact as a condition, up to the feeling produced with mental contact as a condition, are empty of their own intrinsic nature.

This intrinsic nature of the mind-element is itself no intrinsic nature; this intrinsic nature of the dharma-element, up to the feeling produced with mental contact as a condition, is likewise no intrinsic nature. from the dharma-element up to all feelings produced with mind-contact as condition, they are all unapprehendable, and their pleasure and pain are likewise unapprehendable.
Why is this? Within this state, even the mental faculty (*manodhātu*) and so forth cannot be found; how much less could there be pleasure or pain!

Furthermore, he said this:

"O son of good family, you should practice the perfection of generosity; you should not view the mind-element as either self or non-self, nor should you view the dharma-element, the mind-consciousness-element, or mental contact, nor the various feelings produced with mental contact as conditions, as either self or non-self."

This intrinsic nature of the mind-element is itself no intrinsic nature; this intrinsic nature of the dharma-element up to the intrinsic nature of all feelings produced with mental contact as a condition is also no intrinsic nature. In this perfection of giving, the mind-element (*manodhātu*) is not apprehended, nor are its self or non-self apprehended;
from the dharma-element up to all feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition, none are apprehended, nor are their self or non-self apprehended.
Why is this? Because within this state, even the sphere of mind (*manodhātu*) and so forth cannot be apprehended, let alone that self or non-self!
If you can practice giving in such a manner, this is the cultivation of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).
Furthermore, he said this:

"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, for the sake of those who have resolved upon unsurpassed bodhicitta, expounds the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*), saying: 'O son of good family, you should practice the perfection of generosity;

you should not view ignorance as either permanent or impermanent; you should not view volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), feeling (*vedanā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), becoming (*bhava*), birth (*jāti*), or old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair as either permanent or impermanent.'"

Why is this? Ignorance is empty of the intrinsic nature of ignorance; volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and old age, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are likewise empty of the intrinsic nature of old age, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.

That which is no intrinsic nature is precisely the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*).
Within this perfection of giving, the ten powers of a Buddha cannot be apprehended, nor can their permanence or impermanence be apprehended;
likewise, from the four fearlessnesses up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, none can be apprehended, nor can their permanence or impermanence be apprehended.
Why is this? Because herein even the ten powers of a Buddha cannot be found, let alone that which is permanent or impermanent!
If you can practice such giving as this, you are practicing the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā).
"Furthermore, he says this:

'O son of good family, you should practice the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā); you should not view the ten powers of a Buddha as either pleasant or painful, nor should you view the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great joy, great equanimity, or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha as either pleasant or painful.'"

Why is this? The ten powers of a Buddha are empty of the intrinsic nature of the ten powers of a Buddha; the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha—from the four fearlessnesses up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha—are empty of the intrinsic nature of those qualities.

from the four fearlessnesses up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, none can be apprehended, nor can that self or non-self be apprehended.

"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons or good daughters explain the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) to those who have resolved upon unsurpassed bodhicitta, they should speak as follows: 'You, good son, should cultivate the perfection of giving;

This intrinsic nature of the quality of non-forgetfulness is not an intrinsic nature, and this intrinsic nature of the state of constant equanimity is also not an intrinsic nature. That which is not an intrinsic nature is the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*).
Within this perfection of giving, the quality of non-forgetfulness is unapprehendable, and its permanence or impermanence is likewise unapprehendable;
the nature of constant equanimity is unapprehendable, and its permanence or impermanence is likewise unapprehendable.

If you can practice giving in this manner, that is practicing the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā).

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 164. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Part One: Chapter on Measuring Merits, Number Thirty-Six. "Furthermore, Kauśika!

If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, proclaim the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), they should speak thus: "Good son, you should practice the perfection of giving;

you should not contemplate the stage of entering the stream (*srotāpattipratipannaka*) or the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*) as either permanent or impermanent. You should not contemplate the stage of entering once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmipratipannaka*) or the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmiphala*), the stage of entering non-returning (*anāgāmipratipannaka*) or the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*), or the stage of entering arhatship (*arhattvapratipannaka*) or the fruit of arhatship (*arhattvaphala*) as either permanent or impermanent."

Why is this? Because the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry and the fruit of stream-entry are empty of the intrinsic nature of the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry and the fruit of stream-entry; the candidate for the fruit of once-returning and the fruit of once-returning, the candidate for the fruit of non-returning and the fruit of non-returning, and the candidate for the fruit of arhatship and the fruit of arhatship—from the candidate for the fruit of once-returning up to the fruit of arhatship—are empty of their own intrinsic nature.

This intrinsic nature of the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry and the fruit of stream-entry is itself no intrinsic nature; this intrinsic nature of the candidate for the fruit of once-returning up to the fruit of arhatship is also no intrinsic nature. That which is no intrinsic nature is precisely the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*).
Within this perfection of giving, the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry and the fruit of stream-entry itself are unapprehendable; their permanence or impermanence is also unapprehendable.
The candidate for the fruit of once-returning up to the fruit of arhatship are all unapprehendable; their permanence or impermanence is also unapprehendable.
Why is this? Because herein even the stream-enterer candidate and so forth cannot be found; how much less could there be that which is permanent or impermanent!
If you can practice such giving as this, you are practicing the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā).
He further said:

"O son of good family, you should practice the perfection of generosity, but you should not regard the stage of entering the stream or the fruit of stream-entry as either pleasant or painful; nor should you regard the stage of entering once-returning or the fruit of once-returning, the stage of entering non-returning or the fruit of non-returning, or the stage of entering arhatship or the fruit of arhatship as either pleasant or painful."

Why is this? Because the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry and the fruit of stream-entry are empty of the intrinsic nature of the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry and the fruit of stream-entry; likewise, the candidate for the fruit of once-returning and the fruit of once-returning, the candidate for the fruit of non-returning and the fruit of non-returning, and the candidate for the fruit of arhatship and the fruit of arhatship—from the candidate for the fruit of once-returning up to the fruit of arhatship—are empty of their own intrinsic nature.

This intrinsic nature of the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry and the fruit of stream-entry is itself no intrinsic nature; this intrinsic nature of the candidate for the fruit of once-returning up to the fruit of arhatship is also no intrinsic nature. That which is no intrinsic nature is precisely the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*).

Within this perfection of giving, the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry and the fruit of stream-entry itself are unapprehendable; their pleasure and their suffering are likewise unapprehendable.
The candidate for the fruit of once-returning up to the fruit of arhatship are all unapprehendable; their pleasure and their suffering are likewise unapprehendable.
Why is this? Within this state, even the stage of a candidate for the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-pratipannaka*) cannot be found, let alone pleasure or suffering!
If you can practice such generosity, this is the cultivation of the perfection of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*).
Furthermore, he spoke these words:

"O son of good family, you should cultivate the perfection of generosity, but you should not contemplate whether the state of one entering the stream or the fruit of stream-entry is self or non-self; you should not contemplate whether the state of one entering the once-returning stage or the fruit of once-returning, the state of one entering the non-returning stage or the fruit of non-returning, or the state of one entering arhatship or the fruit of arhatship is self or non-self."

Why is this? Because the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry and the fruit of stream-entry are empty of the intrinsic nature of the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry and the fruit of stream-entry; the candidate for the fruit of once-returning and the fruit of once-returning, the candidate for the fruit of non-returning and the fruit of non-returning, and the candidate for the fruit of arhatship and the fruit of arhatship—from the candidate for the fruit of once-returning up to the fruit of arhatship—are empty of their own intrinsic nature.

This intrinsic nature of the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry and the fruit of stream-entry is itself no intrinsic nature; this intrinsic nature of the candidate for the fruit of once-returning up to the fruit of arhatship is also no intrinsic nature. That which is no intrinsic nature is precisely the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).
Within this perfection of giving, the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry and the fruit of stream-entry itself cannot be apprehended; neither "self" nor "non-self" can be apprehended therein.
Likewise, the candidates for the fruit of once-returner up to the fruit of arhatship cannot be apprehended; neither "self" nor "non-self" can be apprehended therein.
Why is this? Because herein even the stream-enterer candidate and so forth cannot be found; how much less could there be "self" or "non-self"!
If you can practice such giving as this, that is the cultivation of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).
Furthermore, he said this:

"O son of good family, you should practice the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā), but you should not contemplate whether the stage of entering the stream (srotāpattipratipannaka) or the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpattiphala) are pure or impure; nor should you contemplate whether the stage of entering once-returning (sakṛdāgāmipratipannaka) or the fruit of once-returning, the stage of entering non-returning (anāgāmipratipannaka) or the fruit of non-returning, or the stage of entering arhatship (arhattvapratipannaka) or the fruit of arhatship are pure or impure."

Why is this? Because the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry and the fruit of stream-entry are empty of the intrinsic nature of the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry and the fruit of stream-entry; likewise, the candidate for the fruit of once-returning and the fruit of once-returning, the candidate for the fruit of non-returning and the fruit of non-returning, and the candidate for the fruit of arhatship and the fruit of arhatship—from the candidate for the fruit of once-returning up to the fruit of arhatship—are empty of their own intrinsic nature.

This intrinsic nature of the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry and the fruit of stream-entry is itself no intrinsic nature; this intrinsic nature of the candidate for the fruit of once-returning up to the fruit of arhatship is also no intrinsic nature. That which is no intrinsic nature is precisely the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).
Within this perfection of generosity, the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry and the fruit of stream-entry itself are unapprehendable, and their purity or impurity is likewise unapprehendable;
the candidate for the fruit of once-returning up to the fruit of arhatship are all unapprehendable, and their purity or impurity is likewise unapprehendable.
Why is this? Because herein even the stream-enterer candidate and so forth cannot be found; how much less could there be that which is pure or impure!
If you can practice such giving, this is the cultivation of the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā).
“Kauśika! When these sons and daughters of good family speak in this manner, they are proclaiming the true perfection of generosity.”
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
If good sons or good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, proclaim the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*), saying:
'O good son, you should practice the perfection of generosity; you should not contemplate the awakening of a solitary buddha (*pratyekabuddhabodhi*) as either permanent or impermanent.'"

Why is this? Because the enlightenment of all pratyekabuddhas is empty of the intrinsic nature of the enlightenment of all pratyekabuddhas; that which is the intrinsic nature of the enlightenment of all pratyekabuddhas is itself no-intrinsic-nature, and that which is no-intrinsic-nature is the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā).
Within this perfection of generosity, the awakening of all pratyekabuddhas cannot be apprehended, nor can their permanence or impermanence be apprehended. Why is this?
Within this, even the enlightenment of a solitary buddha (*pratyekabuddha*) cannot be found, let alone that which is permanent or impermanent!
If you can practice such generosity, this is the cultivation of the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*).
Furthermore, he said this:
"O son of good family, you should cultivate the perfection of generosity; you should not regard the enlightenment of a solitary buddha as either pleasant or painful."

Why is this? Because the enlightenment of all pratyekabuddhas is empty of the intrinsic nature of the enlightenment of all pratyekabuddhas; that which is the intrinsic nature of the enlightenment of all pratyekabuddhas is itself no-intrinsic-nature, and that which is no-intrinsic-nature is precisely the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā).
Within this perfection of giving, the enlightenment of all pratyekabuddhas cannot be apprehended, nor can their pleasure or suffering be apprehended. Why is this?
In this state, not even the enlightenment of a solitary buddha can be found, let alone pleasure or pain!
If you can practice such generosity, that is the cultivation of the perfection of generosity.
He further said:
"O son of good family, you should practice the perfection of generosity; you should not contemplate solitary-buddha enlightenment as either self or non-self."

Why is this? Because the awakening of all pratyekabuddhas is empty of the intrinsic nature of the awakening of all pratyekabuddhas; this intrinsic nature of the awakening of all pratyekabuddhas is itself no intrinsic nature, and that which is no intrinsic nature is the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā).
Within this perfection of giving, the enlightenment of all pratyekabuddhas is unattainable, and both self and non-self are likewise unattainable. Why is this so?
Within this, even the enlightenment of a solitary realizer (pratyekabuddha) cannot be found, let alone such things as "self" and "non-self"!
If you can practice giving in this manner, that is the cultivation of the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā).
Furthermore, he said this:
"O son of good family, you should practice the perfection of generosity; you should not observe whether the awakening of a pratyekabuddha is pure or impure."

Why is this? Because the awakening of all pratyekabuddhas is empty of the intrinsic nature of the awakening of all pratyekabuddhas; that which is the intrinsic nature of the awakening of all pratyekabuddhas is itself no intrinsic nature, and that which is no intrinsic nature is precisely the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā).
Within this perfection of giving, the enlightenment of all pratyekabuddhas cannot be apprehended, nor can its purity or impurity be apprehended. Why is this?
In this state, even the enlightenment of a solitary buddha (pratyekabuddha) cannot be found, let alone purity or impurity!
If you can practice such generosity, this is the cultivation of the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā).
“Kauśika! When these sons and daughters of good family speak in this manner, they are proclaiming the true perfection of generosity.”
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
If good sons or good daughters explain the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) to those who have resolved upon unsurpassed bodhicitta, saying:
'You, good son, should practice the perfection of giving; you should not regard the conduct of all bodhisattva mahāsattvas as either permanent or impermanent.'"

Why is this? Because the practice of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is empty of the intrinsic nature of the practice of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; that which is the intrinsic nature of the practice of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is itself no-intrinsic-nature, and that which is no-intrinsic-nature is precisely the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā).
Within this perfection of giving, the practice of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot be apprehended, nor can their permanence or impermanence be apprehended.
Why is this? Because herein not even any practice of a bodhisattva mahāsattva can be apprehended, much less that which is permanent or impermanent!
If you can cultivate such giving as this, you are cultivating the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā).
"Furthermore, he says this:
'O son of good family, you should practice the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā), but you should not regard the conduct of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as either pleasant or painful.'"

Why is this? Because the practice of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is empty of intrinsic nature; that which is the intrinsic nature of the practice of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is itself no intrinsic nature, and that which is no intrinsic nature is the perfection of generosity (dāna-pāramitā).
Within this perfection of generosity, the practices of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot be apprehended, nor can their pleasure or suffering be apprehended.
Why is this? Because herein not even any practice of a bodhisattva mahāsattva can be apprehended, let alone pleasure or suffering!
If you can cultivate such generosity as this, that is the cultivation of the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā).

Why is this? Because herein not even the practice of a bodhisattva mahāsattva can be apprehended, let alone such things as self and non-self!
If you can cultivate giving in this manner, that is the cultivation of the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā).

Why is this? Because the practice of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is empty of the intrinsic nature of the practice of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; that which is the intrinsic nature of these practices of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is itself no-intrinsic-nature, and that which is no-intrinsic-nature is precisely the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā).
Within this perfection of giving, the practices of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cannot be apprehended, nor can their purity or impurity be apprehended.
Why is this? Because herein not even any bodhisattva-mahāsattva practice can be apprehended, let alone purity or impurity!
If you can cultivate such generosity, this is the cultivation of the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā).
“Kauśika! When these sons and daughters of good family speak in this manner, they are proclaiming the true and correct perfection of giving.”
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
If good sons and good daughters, for the sake of those who have resolved upon unsurpassed bodhicitta, proclaim the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*), saying:

Why is this? The unexcelled, perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas is empty of intrinsic nature; the intrinsic nature of this unexcelled, perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas is itself no intrinsic nature. That which is no intrinsic nature is precisely the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*).
Within this perfection of giving, the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas cannot be apprehended, nor can its permanence or impermanence be apprehended.
Why is this? Because herein even the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas is not to be found, let alone that which is permanent or impermanent!
If you can practice giving in such a manner, this is the cultivation of the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā).
"Furthermore, he says this:
'O son of good family, you should cultivate the perfection of generosity; you should not regard the unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment of the Buddhas as either pleasure or suffering.'"

Why is this? The unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas is empty of intrinsic nature; this intrinsic nature of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas is itself no intrinsic nature, and that which is no intrinsic nature is precisely the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā).
Within this perfection of generosity, the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas cannot be apprehended, nor can pleasure and suffering be apprehended.
Why is this? Because herein even the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas cannot be apprehended, let alone that pleasure or pain!
If you can practice such giving as this, you are practicing the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā).
Furthermore, he spoke these words:

Why is this? Why is this? Because herein even the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas cannot be apprehended, let alone that [distinction between] self and non-self!
If you can practice giving in this manner, you are practicing the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā).

'Come!'"
"Noble son!
I shall instruct you in the practice and study of the *pāramitās*, from *prajñā* down to *dāna*.

When you practice and study, do not observe any dharma whatsoever as something that can be dwelled in, transcended, entered, attained, realized, or received and maintained—nor any merit obtained therein that could be rejoiced in and dedicated toward enlightenment."

Why is this? Within this *prajñāpāramitā* and even up to the *dānapāramitā*, there is ultimately not the slightest dharma that can be dwelled upon, transcended, entered, attained, realized, or upheld—nor any merit obtained therein that can be rejoiced in and dedicated toward enlightenment.

Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty and utterly non-existent; that which is non-existent is precisely the perfection of wisdom, and so on, up to the perfection of generosity.

Within this Prajñāpāramitā, up to and including the Dānapāramitā, there is ultimately not even the slightest dharma that can be apprehended as entering or exiting, arising or ceasing, being annihilated or eternal, being identical or different, or coming or going.

“Kauśika! When these sons and daughters of good family speak in this manner, they are speaking of the true perfection of wisdom, meditative concentration, diligence, patience, ethical discipline, and generosity.”

For this reason, Kauśika, sons and daughters of good family should, with the method of non-apprehension, receive, uphold, recite, and contemplate according to the principle the Prajñāpāramitā; they should extensively explain it to others through various skillful words and meanings, proclaiming, expounding, clarifying, interpreting, analyzing its significance, and making it easy to understand.

“Kauśika! For this reason, I say that if a son of good family or a daughter of good family, regarding this Prajñāpāramitā, by means of the method of non-apprehension, receives, maintains, recites, and reflects upon it according to the principle; and furthermore, for even a brief moment, uses various skillful words and meanings to explain, proclaim, expound, reveal, interpret, analyze the purport, and make it easy to understand for others, the mass of merit they obtain will be far greater than the former.”
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to instruct all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa, causing them all to abide in the fruit of a stream-enterer—what do you think?"
"Would these sons and daughters of good family, by reason of this cause and condition, acquire much merit?
Śakra, Lord of Devas, replied:
"Very much!"
“World-Honored One!
It is very much so! Sugata!”

listen to, receive and uphold, read and recite this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, master it thoroughly, contemplate it according to the principle, and diligently practice and study in accordance with this Dharma-gate."

Kauśika! The merit obtained by good men and good women in the future will be far greater than that of the former. Why is this?

Kauśika! Because Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas dwelling on the stage of non-retrogression do not rely excessively upon the teachings they have heard, because they are certain to advance toward unsurpassed awakening, and because they do not regress from great enlightenment.

Because the bodhisattva mahāsattva who swiftly proceeds toward great enlightenment must rely extensively upon the teachings that are expounded; because he seeks to proceed swiftly toward unsurpassed awakening; and because he contemplates the suffering of birth and death for all sentient beings and gives rise to a heart of great compassion that is most poignant.

Setting aside the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa and Pūrvavideha, suppose a son or daughter of good family were to instruct all the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa, Pūrvavideha, and Avaragodānīya so that they all attain non-retrogression from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; and furthermore, were to extensively explain to them the immeasurable Dharma-gates of the Prajñāpāramitā with skillful words and meanings, proclaiming, expounding, clarifying, and interpreting them, analyzing their significance and purport to make them easy to understand; [would they generate much merit?]"

If there are sons or daughters of good family who, among them, exhort even one person to swiftly proceed toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, causing them to preach the three vehicles to save all beings; and furthermore, for their sake, extensively explain the immeasurable Dharma-gates of the *prajñāpāramitā* with skillful phrasing and meaning, proclaiming, expounding, revealing, clarifying, and interpreting it, analyzing its significance so that it may be easily understood.
Kauśika! The merit obtained by good men and good women in the future will be far greater than that of the former. Why is this?

Kauśika! Because Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas dwelling on the stage of non-retrogression do not rely heavily upon the teachings they proclaim, because they are certain to advance toward unsurpassed awakening, and because they do not regress from great bodhi.

Because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who swiftly proceeds toward great enlightenment must rely upon the Dharma that is taught, because he seeks to swiftly proceed toward unsurpassed awakening, and because he contemplates the suffering of birth and death and directs a heart of great compassion toward all sentient beings with the utmost intensity.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

Setting aside the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa, Pūrvavideha, and Aparagoyānī, suppose a son or daughter of good family were to instruct all the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa, Pūrvavideha, Aparagoyānī, and Uttarakuru so that they all attain non-retrogression from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; and furthermore, were to extensively explain for them the immeasurable Dharma-gates of the Prajñāpāramitā with skillful phrasing and meaning, proclaiming, expounding, clarifying, interpreting, analyzing the significance, and making it easy for them to understand; [would they generate much merit?]"

If there are sons or daughters of good family who, among them, exhort even one person to swiftly proceed toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, causing them to preach the three vehicles to save all beings; and if they further extensively expound for that person the immeasurable Dharma-gates of the Prajñāpāramitā with skillful phrasing and meaning—proclaiming, revealing, elucidating, explaining, analyzing the significance, and making it easy to understand.
Kauśika! The merit obtained by good men and good women in the future will be far greater than that of the former. Why is this?

Kauśika! A bodhisattva mahāsattva who dwells on the stage of non-retrogression does not rely heavily upon the teachings being expounded, because they are certain to advance toward unsurpassed awakening and do not regress from great bodhi.

Because the bodhisattva mahāsattva who swiftly proceeds toward great enlightenment must rely extensively upon the Dharma that is taught, because he seeks to swiftly proceed toward unsurpassed awakening, and because he contemplates the suffering of birth and death of all sentient beings with a heart of great compassion that is most intensely poignant.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

Setting aside the sentient beings of the four great continents, suppose a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to teach all the sentient beings of a small thousandfold world system so that they all attain non-retrogression from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment; and furthermore, were to extensively explain for them the immeasurable dharma-gates of the *prajñāpāramitā* with skillful phrasing and meaning, proclaiming, expounding, clarifying, interpreting, analyzing the significance, and making it easy for them to understand; [would they generate much merit?]"

If there are sons or daughters of good family who, among them, exhort even one person to swiftly proceed toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, causing them to preach the three vehicles to deliver all beings; and furthermore, for their sake, extensively expound the immeasurable dharma-gates of the *prajñāpāramitā* with skillful words and meanings, proclaiming, revealing, elucidating, explaining, and analyzing the significance and intent so that they may easily understand it.
Kauśika! The merit obtained by good men and good women in the future will be far greater than that of the former. Why is this?

Kauśika! Because Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas dwelling on the stage of non-retrogression do not rely heavily upon the teachings they proclaim, because they are certain to advance toward unsurpassed awakening, and because they do not regress from great bodhi.

Because a bodhisattva mahāsattva who seeks to swiftly proceed toward great enlightenment must rely extensively upon the teachings that have been expounded; because they seek to swiftly attain unsurpassed awakening; and because, observing the suffering of birth and death, they arouse a heart of great compassion for all sentient beings with the utmost intensity.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

Setting aside the sentient beings of a small thousandfold world system, suppose a son or daughter of good family were to teach all the sentient beings of a medium thousandfold world system so that they all attain non-retrogression from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; and furthermore, were to extensively explain for them the immeasurable Dharma-gates of the *prajñāpāramitā* through skillful words and meanings, proclaiming, expounding, clarifying, interpreting, analyzing the significance, and making it easy to understand; [would their merit be great?]"

If there are sons or daughters of good family who, among them, exhort one person to swiftly proceed toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, causing them to preach the three vehicles to deliver all beings; and furthermore, for that person’s sake, extensively explain the immeasurable dharma-gates of the *prajñāpāramitā* with skillful phrasing and meaning, proclaiming, revealing, expounding, clarifying, and interpreting them, analyzing their significance so as to make them easy to understand.
Kauśika! The merit obtained by good men and good women in the future will be far greater than that of the former. Why is this?

Kauśika! Because bodhisattva-mahāsattvas dwelling on the stage of non-retrogression do not rely excessively upon the teachings they expound, because they are certain to advance toward unsurpassed awakening, and because they do not regress from great enlightenment.

Because a bodhisattva mahāsattva who seeks to swiftly proceed toward great enlightenment must rely extensively upon the teachings that have been expounded, because they seek to swiftly attain unsurpassed awakening, and because they observe the suffering of birth and death of all sentient beings and give rise to a heart of great compassion with the utmost intensity.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

Setting aside the sentient beings of the intermediate thousandfold world system, suppose a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to teach and transform all the sentient beings of a trichiliocosm so that they all attain non-retrogression from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; and furthermore, were to extensively explain for them the immeasurable dharma-gates of the *prajñāpāramitā* with skillful words and meanings, proclaiming, expounding, revealing, clarifying, and interpreting them, analyzing their significance and purport to make them easy to understand; [would they generate much merit?]"

If there are sons or daughters of good family who, within that assembly, exhort even one person to swiftly proceed toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, causing them to preach the three vehicles to save all beings; and furthermore, if they extensively explain for them the immeasurable Dharma-gates of the *prajñāpāramitā* with skillful phrasing and meaning, proclaiming, expounding, clarifying, interpreting, analyzing the significance, and making it easy to understand—[this merit is far greater].
Kauśika! The merit obtained by good men and good women in the future will be far greater than that of the former. Why is this?

Kauśika! Because Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas dwelling on the stage of non-retrogression do not rely extensively upon the teachings they proclaim, because they are certain to advance toward unsurpassed awakening, and because they do not regress from great bodhi.

Because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who seeks to swiftly attain great enlightenment must rely extensively upon the teachings he expounds; because he seeks to swiftly attain unsurpassed awakening; and because, observing the suffering of birth and death, he gives rise to a heart of great compassion for all sentient beings that is most intensely poignant.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

Setting aside these sentient beings of this trichiliocosm, suppose a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to teach and transform all sentient beings in as many worlds in each of the ten directions as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, causing them all to attain non-retrogression from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; and furthermore, were to extensively explain for them the immeasurable Dharma gates of the Prajñāpāramitā with skillful phrasing and meaning, proclaiming, expounding, clarifying, explaining, and analyzing their significance so that they may easily understand them; [would such a person generate much merit?]"

If there are sons or daughters of good family who, among them, exhort even one person to swiftly proceed toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, causing them to teach the three vehicles to save all beings; and furthermore, for their sake, extensively expound the immeasurable dharma-gates of the *prajñāpāramitā* with skillful words and meanings, proclaiming, revealing, elucidating, explaining, analyzing the significance, and making it easy to understand—[this merit is far greater].
Kauśika! The merit obtained by sons and daughters of good family in the future will be far greater than that of the former. Why is this?

Kauśika! Because bodhisattva-mahāsattvas dwelling on the stage of non-retrogression do not rely excessively upon the teachings they expound, because they are certain to advance toward unsurpassed awakening, and because they do not regress from great enlightenment.

Because the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who seeks to swiftly proceed toward Great Enlightenment must rely extensively upon the teachings he expounds; because he seeks to swiftly attain unsurpassed awakening; and because, observing the suffering of birth and death, he gives rise to a heart of great compassion for all sentient beings with the utmost intensity.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
Setting aside these sentient beings in each of the worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;

suppose that sons and daughters of good family were to teach and transform all sentient beings in all the worlds of the ten directions, causing them all to attain non-retrogression from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and further extensively expound for them the immeasurable dharma-gates of the *prajñāpāramitā* with skillful words and meanings, proclaiming, revealing, elucidating, explaining, analyzing their significance, and making them easy to understand."

If there are sons or daughters of good family who, among them, exhort even one person to swiftly proceed toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, causing them to preach the three vehicles to rescue and deliver all beings; and furthermore, who extensively explain for them the immeasurable dharma-gates of the *prajñāpāramitā* with skillful phrasing and meaning—proclaiming, expounding, clarifying, interpreting, analyzing the significance, and making it easy to understand.
Kauśika! The merit obtained by good men and good women in the future will be far greater than that of the former. Why is this?

Kauśika! Because Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas dwelling on the stage of non-retrogression do not rely excessively upon the teachings they proclaim, because they are certain to advance toward unsurpassed awakening, and because they do not regress from great bodhi.

Because the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who swiftly proceeds toward Great Enlightenment must rely extensively upon the Dharma that is taught, because he seeks to swiftly proceed toward unsurpassed awakening, and because he contemplates the suffering of birth and death and gives rise to a most poignant heart of great compassion for all sentient beings.
At that time, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

To the extent that a bodhisattva mahāsattva draws closer to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, to that same extent one should swiftly instruct and admonish that bodhisattva mahāsattva by means of the perfection of giving."

To the extent that a bodhisattva mahāsattva draws closer to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, to that same extent one should swiftly instruct and admonish that bodhisattva mahāsattva with the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.

“Bhagavān, as a bodhisattva mahāsattva draws closer and closer to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, so too should that bodhisattva mahāsattva be swiftly instructed and exhorted by means of internal emptiness (adhyātma-śūnyatā).”

To the extent that a bodhisattva mahāsattva draws closer to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, to that same extent one should swiftly provide them with instruction and counsel regarding outer emptiness, inner-and-outer emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersal emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common-characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.
“World-Honored One!

To the extent that a bodhisattva mahāsattva draws closer to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, to that same extent one should swiftly instruct and admonish that bodhisattva mahāsattva by means of *tathatā* (suchness).

To the extent that a bodhisattva mahāsattva draws closer to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, to that same extent one should swiftly instruct and admonish that bodhisattva mahāsattva by means of the *dharmadhātu* (dharma-realm), *dharmatā* (dharma-nature), non-falsity, non-alteration, equality, the nature of being free from birth, the fixedness of dharma, the stability of dharma, the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*), the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm.”
“World-Honored One!

To the extent that a bodhisattva mahāsattva draws closer to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, to that same extent one should swiftly instruct and advise that bodhisattva mahāsattva with the noble truth of suffering;

to the extent that a bodhisattva mahāsattva draws closer to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, to that same extent one should swiftly instruct and advise that bodhisattva mahāsattva with the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path.”
“World-Honored One!

To the extent that a bodhisattva mahāsattva draws closer to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, to that same extent one should swiftly instruct and exhort that bodhisattva mahāsattva by means of the four dhyānas;

to the extent that a bodhisattva mahāsattva draws closer to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, to that same extent one should swiftly instruct and exhort that bodhisattva mahāsattva by means of the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments.”
“World-Honored One!

To the extent that a bodhisattva mahāsattva draws closer to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, to that same extent one should swiftly instruct and admonish that bodhisattva mahāsattva with the eight liberations;

to the extent that a bodhisattva mahāsattva draws closer to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, to that same extent one should swiftly instruct and admonish that bodhisattva mahāsattva with the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities.”

“Bhagavān! To the extent that a bodhisattva mahāsattva draws closer to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, to that same extent one should swiftly instruct and admonish that bodhisattva mahāsattva by means of the four applications of mindfulness;

to the extent that a bodhisattva mahāsattva draws closer to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, to that same extent one should swiftly instruct and admonish that bodhisattva mahāsattva by means of the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold noble path.”
“World-Honored One!

To the extent that a bodhisattva mahāsattva draws closer to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, to that same extent one should swiftly instruct and admonish that bodhisattva mahāsattva by means of the gate of liberation of emptiness;

to the extent that a bodhisattva mahāsattva draws closer to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, to that same extent one should swiftly instruct and admonish that bodhisattva mahāsattva by means of the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness.”
“World-Honored One!

To the extent that a bodhisattva mahāsattva draws closer to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, to that same extent one should swiftly instruct and admonish that bodhisattva mahāsattva by means of the five eyes;

to the extent that a bodhisattva mahāsattva draws closer to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, to that same extent one should swiftly instruct and admonish that bodhisattva mahāsattva by means of the six supernormal powers.”
“World-Honored One!

To the extent that a bodhisattva mahāsattva draws closer to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, to that same extent one should swiftly instruct and admonish that bodhisattva mahāsattva by means of the ten powers of a Buddha;

to the extent that a bodhisattva mahāsattva draws closer to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, to that same extent one should swiftly instruct and admonish that bodhisattva mahāsattva by means of the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.”
“World-Honored One!

To the extent that a bodhisattva mahāsattva draws closer to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, to that same extent one should swiftly instruct and exhort that bodhisattva mahāsattva with the quality of non-forgetfulness;

to the extent that a bodhisattva mahāsattva draws closer to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, to that same extent one should swiftly instruct and exhort that bodhisattva mahāsattva with the quality of constant equanimity.”

“Bhagavān, to the extent that a bodhisattva mahāsattva draws closer to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, to that same extent one should swiftly instruct and admonish that bodhisattva mahāsattva with the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñatā*);

to the extent that a bodhisattva mahāsattva draws closer to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, to that same extent one should swiftly instruct and admonish that bodhisattva mahāsattva with the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).”
“World-Honored One!

To the extent that a bodhisattva mahāsattva draws closer to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, to that same extent one should swiftly instruct and admonish that bodhisattva mahāsattva by means of all the doors of dhāraṇī;

to the extent that a bodhisattva mahāsattva draws closer to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, to that same extent one should swiftly instruct and admonish that bodhisattva mahāsattva by means of all the doors of samādhi.”
“World-Honored One!

To the extent that a bodhisattva mahāsattva draws closer to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, to that same extent one should provide offerings and support for that bodhisattva mahāsattva with excellent robes, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and various requisites as they may require.”
“World-Honored One!

If good sons and good daughters are able to provide offerings and support for those Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas through such gifts of Dharma and gifts of material wealth, the merit obtained by these good sons and good daughters will be far greater than the former.”
Why is this? "World-Honored One!

It is because those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are sustained by the instructions and exhortations of these perfections of giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom that they swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

“Bhagavān! It is precisely because those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are sustained by these instructions and exhortations—namely, inner emptiness, outer emptiness, inner-and-outer emptiness, emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, emptiness of dispersion, unchanging emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, emptiness of all phenomena, non-apprehendable emptiness, emptiness of non-existence, emptiness of intrinsic nature, and emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence—that they swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.”
“World-Honored One!

It is precisely because those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are sustained by the instruction and guidance of this suchness, the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, the non-falsity, the non-alteration, the equality, the state beyond birth, the fixedness of dharma, the stability of dharma, the limit of reality, the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm, that they swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”
“World-Honored One!

It is precisely because those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are sustained by these instructions and exhortations regarding the noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin, the noble truth of cessation, and the noble truth of the path that they swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”
“World-Honored One!

It is precisely because those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are sustained by the instruction and admonition of these four dhyānas, four immeasurables, and four formless attainments that they swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”
“World-Honored One!

It is precisely because those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are sustained by the instruction and guidance of these eight liberations, eight bases of mastery, nine successive attainments, and ten totalities that they swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”
“World-Honored One!

It is precisely because those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are sustained by the instruction and exhortation of these four foundations of mindfulness, four right efforts, four bases of power, five faculties, five powers, seven factors of enlightenment, and eightfold noble path that they swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”
“World-Honored One!

It is precisely because those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are sustained by these instructions and exhortations regarding the gate of liberation of emptiness, the gate of liberation of signlessness, and the gate of liberation of wishlessness that they swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”
“World-Honored One!

It is precisely because those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are sustained by these instructions and exhortations regarding the five eyes and the six supernormal powers that they swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”
“World-Honored One!

It is precisely because those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are sustained by the instruction and guidance of these ten powers of a buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, that they swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”
“World-Honored One!

It is precisely because those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are sustained by the instruction and admonition of this quality of non-forgetfulness and the constant abiding in equanimity that they swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”
“Blessed One!

It is precisely because those bodhisattva mahāsattvas are sustained by the instructions and exhortations of this knowledge of all things, the knowledge of the aspects of the path, and the knowledge of all aspects that they swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”

“Bhagavān! It is precisely because those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are sustained by these instructions and exhortations regarding all the gates of dhāraṇī and all the gates of samādhi that they swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”
“World-Honored One!

Furthermore, because those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are sustained by these various requisites—namely, robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicine, according to their needs—they will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed Śakra, the Lord of the Devas, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"

Kauśika! That you are able to exhort those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, further able to sustain those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and also able to protect and assist those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas—now you have performed that which a holy disciple of the Buddha ought to do.

All Tathāgatas and their noble disciples, desiring to bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings, employ skillful means to exhort and encourage those Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, causing them to swiftly advance toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; they sustain, protect, and assist those Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas through the gift of Dharma and the gift of material wealth, so that they may swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Why is this? "Kauśika!
All Tathāgatas, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and the supreme matters of the world are born from those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas."
Why is this? If there were no bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who resolve to attain unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi),
then there would be none capable of practicing and training in generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration.
Furthermore, in the Prajñāpāramitā, there is likewise no one who can abide in internal emptiness,
external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness,
conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, unchanging emptiness, or essential nature [emptiness].
Emptiness, the emptiness of self-characteristics, the emptiness of common characteristics, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable,
the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence—
there is likewise no one who can abide in suchness, the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, non-falsity, immutability, or equanimity.
Sameness, the nature of being free from birth, the fixed nature of phenomena, the stability of phenomena, the limit of reality, the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm—
there is likewise no one who can abide in the noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin, the noble truth of cessation, or the noble truth of the path;
nor is there anyone who can practice and train in the four dhyānas or the four immeasurables.
...the four formless absorptions; nor is there anyone able to train in the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, or the ten totalities;

nor is there anyone able to train in the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the eightfold noble path.
Among those factors of the path, there is likewise no one who can train in the gate of liberation of emptiness, the gate of liberation of signlessness, or the gate of liberation of wishlessness;
nor is there anyone who can train in the five eyes or the six supernormal powers;
nor is there anyone who can train in the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, or the great...

There is likewise no one who can train in the four immeasurables—loving-kindness, great compassion, great joy, and great equanimity—the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, nor the quality of non-forgetfulness, nor the state of constant abiding in equanimity;

nor is there anyone who can train in all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), or the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*); nor is there anyone who can train in even one...
All dhāraṇī-doors and all samādhi-doors.
If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas did not train in and abide in such matters, then none would be able to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

If bodhisattva mahāsattvas did not realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, then there would be no one capable of establishing the bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or the supreme worldly matters.
“Kauśika! Because there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have resolved their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi,
they are then able to practice and train in generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration.”
Furthermore, the Prajñāpāramitā is also able to cause one to dwell securely in internal emptiness,
external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate truth, the emptiness of conditioned phenomena,
the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, the emptiness of dispersion, the emptiness of non-alteration, and the emptiness of intrinsic nature.
Emptiness, the emptiness of self-characteristics, the emptiness of common characteristics, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable,
the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence; furthermore, there are those who are able to abide in suchness,
the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, non-falsity, non-alteration, and equanimity.
The nature of equality, the nature of freedom from birth, the fixedness of phenomena, the stability of phenomena, the limit of reality, the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm;
furthermore, there are those who are able to abide in the noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin, the noble truth of cessation, and the noble truth of the path;
and furthermore, there are those who are able to cultivate and train in the four dhyānas and the four immeasurables.
...the four formless absorptions; furthermore, there are those capable of training in the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities;

and furthermore, there are those capable of training in the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path.

Regarding the factors of the path, there are those who can cultivate and train in the gate of liberation of emptiness, the gate of liberation of signlessness, and the gate of liberation of wishlessness;
there are also those who can cultivate and train in the five eyes and the six supernormal powers;
and there are also those who can cultivate and train in the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the great...
There are those who can cultivate and study the four immeasurables—loving-kindness, great compassion, great joy, and great equanimity—and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
there are also those who can cultivate and study the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant abiding in equanimity;

there are also those who can cultivate and study all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*); and there are also those who can cultivate and study the single...
All dhāraṇī-doors and all samādhi-doors.
Because bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice, study, and abide in such matters, they are then able to realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Because there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they sever all the realms of hell, the animal realm, and the hungry ghost realm in the world, and they are also able to diminish the hosts of asuras while increasing the assembly of devas.
“Kauśika! Because there are bodhisattva mahāsattvas who realize unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment,
there come into being great clans of kṣatriyas, great clans of brahmins, and great clans of householders.”

When noble clans appear in the world, by this means there further arise the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, the Heaven of the Thirty-three, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven;
and by this means there further arise the Brahmakāyika, the Brahmapurohita, and the Brahma... Heaven.
The Ābhāsvara, Mahābrahmā, Parīttābha, Apramāṇābha, Ābhāsvara, Śubha,
Parīttaśubha, Apramāṇaśubha, Śubhakṛtsna, Bṛhatphala, Parīttabṛhatphala, Apramāṇabṛhatphala, and Bṛhatphala devas appeared in the world.
From this, there further appear in the world the Avṛha Heaven, the Atapa Heaven, the Sudṛśa Heaven, the Sudarśana Heaven,
and the Akaniṣṭha Heaven; from this, there further appear the Ākāśānantyāyatana Heaven,
the Vijñānānantyāyatana Heaven, the Ākiṃcanyāyatana Heaven, and the Naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana Heaven.
In this world, by means of this, there further appear in the world the perfection of generosity, the perfection of ethical discipline,
the perfection of patience, the perfection of diligence, the perfection of meditative concentration,
and the perfection of wisdom; by means of this, there further appears inner emptiness.
External emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate truth, the emptiness of conditioned phenomena,
the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, absolute emptiness, the emptiness of the limitless, the emptiness of dispersion, the emptiness of non-alteration,
the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the emptiness of self-characteristics, the emptiness of common characteristics, the emptiness of all phenomena, and the unapprehendable...
When emptiness, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence appear in the world,
there further arise from this suchness, the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, non-falsity,
immutability, equality, the state beyond birth, the fixed nature of dharmas, the stability of dharmas, and the limit of reality.
The realm of space and the inconceivable realm appear in the world;
from this, furthermore, the Noble Truth of Suffering, the Noble Truth of the Origin, the Noble Truth of Cessation, and the Noble Truth of the Path appear in the world;
from this, furthermore, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments appear in the world. By means of these...
Furthermore, there appear in the world the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities; and by means of these,
there further appear in the world the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power,
the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eight branches of the noble path.
From this, furthermore, the gate of liberation of emptiness, the gate of liberation of signlessness, and the gate of liberation of wishlessness appear in the world;
from this, furthermore, the five eyes and the six supernormal powers appear in the world;
and from this, furthermore, the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and great compassion [appear].
Great compassion, great joy, and great equanimity, as well as the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, appear in the world;
from these, furthermore, the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant abiding in equanimity appear in the world;
and from these, furthermore, all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) appear in the world.
From this, furthermore, all dhāraṇī-doors and all samādhi-doors appear in the world;
from this, furthermore, all Śrāvaka-vehicles, all Pratyekabuddha-vehicles,
and all Mahāyānas appear in the world.
Chapter 31: Dedication through Rejoicing, Part One. At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya addressed the Elder Subhūti, saying:
“Venerable One!”

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, regarding all the merits and virtuous deeds associated with sympathetic joy belonging to all sentient beings, were to dedicate these virtuous deeds together with all sentient beings toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, by means of the expedient of non-apprehension; [this would be the perfection of the perfection of giving].
If other sentient beings rejoice in and dedicate various meritorious deeds— whether they be the meritorious deeds of ordinary worldlings, śrāvakas, or pratyekabuddhas,
namely the three types of meritorious deeds consisting of giving, ethical discipline, and cultivation; or the four foundations of mindfulness,
the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five...
The powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eight branches of the noble path,
the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the four noble truths, the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery,
the nine successive attainments, the ten totalities, the gates of liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, and the four analytical knowledges.
The merit derived from the various bases of meritorious action, such as the [five] superknowledges and the six supernormal powers,
as well as all the merit of a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s rejoicing and dedication,

is the most supreme, the most excellent, the most honored, the most exalted, the most sublime, the most exquisite, and the highest among the various bases of meritorious action belonging to ordinary beings, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas.
It is unsurpassed, peerless, and equal to the unequaled. Why is this so,
O Virtuous One?

While ordinary beings cultivate meritorious deeds merely for their own mastery, peace, and happiness; and while Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas cultivate meritorious deeds for their own subduing, their own tranquility, and their own nirvāṇa; the merit of all rejoicings and dedications belonging to Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas is universally for the sake of the subduing, the tranquilizing, and the parinirvāṇa of all sentient beings.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya, saying: "Great Being!

This bodhisattva mahāsattva’s mind of sympathetic joy and dedication universally takes as its object the countless, immeasurable, and boundless worlds of the ten directions. Within each and every world, regarding all the Buddhas who have already entered *parinirvāṇa*—from their first generation of the mind of awakening until they attained unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and continuing thus through their successive stages until their entry into *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* and even until the extinction of the Dharma—all the roots of virtue associated with the six *pāramitās* during that interval, as well as all other roots of virtue associated with the countless, immeasurable, and boundless qualities of a Buddha."
Whatever meritorious deeds consisting of giving, morality, and cultivation belong to those ordinary disciples;
and whatever untainted roots of goodness belonging to the stages of training and beyond training belong to those śrāvaka disciples;

If one diligently practices and trains in accordance with all the aggregates of morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation belonging to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas; and all the countless, immeasurable, and boundless Buddha-dharmas of great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity for the sake of benefiting and gladdening all sentient beings; and the True Dharma taught by those Buddhas—then by such practice, one may attain the fruit of a Stream-enterer, the fruit of a Once-returner, the fruit of a Non-returner, the fruit of an Arhat, the enlightenment of a Pratyekabuddha, or enter the Bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth.

Thus, all these roots of goodness, as well as the roots of goodness planted by other sentient beings toward the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and their assemblies of Śrāvakas and Bodhisattva disciples—whether they currently abide in the world or have entered parinirvāṇa—I now rejoice in them all collectively, manifesting my sympathetic joy.
Having thus rejoiced, he further dedicates all these meritorious deeds accompanied by such rejoicing, together with all sentient beings, toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment:
"May I, by means of these roots of goodness, together with all sentient beings, jointly realize unsurpassed bodhi."
