By virtue of these causes and conditions, that bodhisattva mahāsattva’s rejoicing and dedication is free from the perversion of conceptualization, free from the perversion of mind, and free from the perversion of view.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya asked the Venerable Subhūti: "Virtuous One, how is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva,

while not apprehending any signs regarding the meritorious roots and the bases of meritorious action associated with rejoicing in the qualities of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and their assemblies of disciples, is nevertheless able to rejoice and dedicate [that merit] toward unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment?"
The Venerable Subhūti replied: "Great Being!

You should know that within the perfection of wisdom in which bodhisattva mahāsattvas train, there are such skillful means that, although they do not apprehend signs, their activities are accomplished. It is not apart from the perfection of wisdom that one can initiate meritorious deeds accompanied by sympathetic joy and dedicate them toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
Maitreya Bodhisattva Mahāsattva said:
"Virtuous Subhūti!
Do not speak in this way."

Why is this? Because within the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, the merits and roots of goodness of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and their assemblies of disciples are non-existent and unapprehendable; because the various meritorious deeds performed with sympathetic joy are also non-existent and unapprehendable; and because the resolve to dedicate [merit] toward unsurpassed enlightenment is likewise non-existent and unapprehendable.
In this regard, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they should contemplate in this way:

"The nature of the roots of virtue and merit of the past Buddhas and their assemblies of disciples has already ceased; the nature of the meritorious deeds performed with sympathetic joy and the resolve for dedication toward unsurpassed enlightenment is entirely quiescent. If I were to grasp at signs and engage in conceptual discrimination regarding those roots of virtue and merit of all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas and their disciples, or if I were to grasp at signs and engage in conceptual discrimination regarding the meritorious deeds performed with sympathetic joy and the resolve for dedication toward unsurpassed enlightenment, then by employing such skillful means of grasping at signs and conceptualizing, to initiate sympathetic joy and dedication toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment—this is not permitted by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones."

Why is this? Because to take signs and make conceptual distinctions regarding the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, and their disciples who have already entered parinirvāṇa, and then to rejoice and dedicate [the merit] toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, constitutes a great grasping at acquisitions.

"Therefore, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to correctly generate sympathetic joy and dedicate toward unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment the roots of virtue and merit of all Buddhas and their assemblies of disciples, they should not generate sympathetic joy and dedication through the conceptualization of grasping at signs or the apprehension of anything obtainable therein. If one were to generate sympathetic joy and dedication therein through the conceptualization of grasping at signs or the apprehension of anything obtainable, the Buddha would not say that such a person possesses great benefit."
Why is this? Because such a mind of sympathetic joy and dedication is mixed with the poisonous medicine of deluded conceptualization.

It is like food that, though endowed with excellent color, fragrance, and flavor, is mixed with poison. A foolish person of shallow understanding greedily takes it up and eats it; although it is pleasing at first and brings joy and happiness, once the food is digested, one undergoes manifold sufferings, or even dies, losing one's life.
In this way, a certain class of individuals, who have not properly upheld, investigated, or recited [the teachings], and do not understand their meaning, says to those of the Mahāyāna lineage:
"Come!..."
"Noble son!

Regarding all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past, future, and present—from their first generation of the mind of awakening until they attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; from their turning of the sublime wheel of Dharma and delivering immeasurable multitudes, through their entry into parinirvāṇa without remainder and until the extinction of the Dharma—in the interval between these times, whatever roots of virtue have been accumulated, will be accumulated, or are being accumulated by practicing the perfection of wisdom; or whatever roots of virtue have been accumulated, will be accumulated, or are being accumulated by practicing the perfections of meditative concentration, diligence, patience, ethical discipline, and generosity; [all such roots of virtue...]"

If one dwells in inner emptiness, having accumulated, will accumulate, or is currently accumulating roots of goodness; or if one dwells in outer emptiness, inner-and-outer emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-altering emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, having accumulated, will accumulate, or is currently accumulating roots of goodness;

If one abides in *tathatā* (suchness), the roots of goodness already accumulated, those to be accumulated, and those currently being accumulated; or if one abides in the *dharmadhātu* (dharma-realm), *dharmatā* (dharma-nature), non-illusory nature, unchanging nature, equality, the state beyond birth, the fixed nature of dharmas, the stability of dharmas, the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm, the roots of goodness already accumulated, those to be accumulated, and those currently being accumulated;

or if one abides in the Noble Truth of Suffering, the roots of goodness already accumulated, those to be accumulated, and those currently being accumulated; or if one abides in the Noble Truths of Origination, Cessation, and the Path, the roots of goodness already accumulated, those to be accumulated, and those currently being accumulated;

or if one cultivates the four *dhyānas* (meditative concentrations), the roots of goodness already accumulated, those to be accumulated, and those currently being accumulated; [these are all dedicated to supreme perfect enlightenment].
If one has cultivated, will cultivate, or is currently cultivating the roots of goodness of the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments;

if one has cultivated, will cultivate, or is currently cultivating the roots of goodness of the eight liberations; if one has cultivated, will cultivate, or is currently cultivating the roots of goodness of the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative absorptions, and the ten totalities;

if one has cultivated, will cultivate, or is currently cultivating the roots of goodness of the four foundations of mindfulness; and if one has cultivated, will cultivate, or is currently cultivating the roots of goodness of the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path—[all these are dedicated to unexcelled, perfect enlightenment].
If one has cultivated, will cultivate, or is currently cultivating the roots of goodness of the gate of liberation of emptiness;
if one has cultivated, will cultivate, or is currently cultivating the roots of goodness of the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness;
or if one has cultivated, will cultivate, or is currently cultivating the roots of goodness of the five eyes;
If they have cultivated, will cultivate, or are currently cultivating the roots of goodness of the six supernormal powers;

if they have cultivated, will cultivate, or are currently cultivating the roots of goodness of the ten powers of a Buddha; if they have cultivated, will cultivate, or are currently cultivating the roots of goodness of the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;

if they have cultivated, will cultivate, or are currently cultivating the roots of goodness of the quality of non-forgetfulness; if they have cultivated, will cultivate, or are currently cultivating the roots of goodness of the nature of constant dwelling in equanimity;

If one has cultivated, will cultivate, or is currently cultivating the roots of goodness for the sake of all-knowledge; if one has cultivated, will cultivate, or is currently cultivating the roots of goodness for the sake of the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects;

if one has cultivated, will cultivate, or is currently cultivating the roots of goodness for the sake of all dharani-doors; if one has cultivated, will cultivate, or is currently cultivating the roots of goodness for the sake of all samadhi-doors;

if one has cultivated, will cultivate, or is currently cultivating the roots of goodness for the sake of purifying buddha-fields; or if one has cultivated, will cultivate, or is currently cultivating the roots of goodness for the sake of maturing sentient beings;

Whatever aggregates of morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation possessed by all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, as well as all other countless, immeasurable, and boundless qualities;

If a disciple of the Buddha takes all roots of virtue—whether with outflows or without outflows—and all the merits of the various *tathāgatas*, *arhats*, and *samyak-saṃbuddhas* regarding the *pratyekabuddha-bodhi* of gods, humans, and others, both past, future, and present; and if he takes all the roots of virtue already accumulated, yet to be accumulated, or currently being accumulated by gods, *nāgas*, *yakṣas*, *gandharvas*, *asuras*, *garuḍas*, *kiṃnaras*, *mahoragas*, humans, non-humans, and so forth; and if that son or daughter of good family initiates roots of virtue through sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) toward these merits and dedicates them; and if he thus gathers, weighs, and brings before him all such things with sympathetic joy, and together with all sentient beings, collectively dedicates them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

"Such rejoicing and dedication as described above, employing the skillful means of conceptualizing through the grasping of signs and the apprehension of attainments, is like food mixed with poison: it benefits at first but harms later; therefore, this is not a wholesome rejoicing and dedication."

Why is this? Because if one gives rise to a mind of sympathetic joy and dedication that apprehends objects, grasps at signs, and engages in conceptual discrimination, there will be causes, conditions, mental engagements, and conceptual proliferation; such a mind is not in accord with the perfection of wisdom.

Because it is mixed with poison, it constitutes a slander against the Buddha; it does not follow the Buddha’s teaching nor accord with the Dharma-discourse. A person belonging to the bodhisattva lineage should not practice or train according to what that person says.
"Therefore, Venerable One!

You should explain how sons and daughters of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle should, with respect to all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and their disciples throughout the worlds of the ten directions in the past, future, and present, rejoice in and dedicate their roots of merit and virtue."

That is to say, from the time those Buddhas first resolved their minds until they attained unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; from when they turned the sublime wheel of Dharma and delivered immeasurable multitudes, until they entered parinirvāṇa without remainder and even until the extinction of the Dharma—in the interval between these times, whether they were cultivating the perfection of wisdom and accumulating various roots of goodness, or cultivating the perfections of meditative concentration, diligence, patience, ethical discipline, and generosity and accumulating various roots of goodness;

If one dwells in internal emptiness and accumulates all roots of goodness; or if one dwells in external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all dharmas, unapprehendable emptiness, non-existence emptiness, intrinsic nature emptiness, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, and accumulates all roots of goodness;

or if one dwells in suchness and accumulates all roots of goodness; or if one dwells in the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, non-falsity, non-alteration, equality, the nature of being free from birth, the fixedness of dharmas, the stability of dharmas, the limit of reality, the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm, and accumulates all roots of goodness.
If one abides in the noble truth of suffering and accumulates all roots of goodness; if one abides in the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path and accumulates all roots of goodness;
if one cultivates the four dhyānas and accumulates all roots of goodness; if one cultivates the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and accumulates all roots of goodness;

if one cultivates the eight liberations and accumulates all roots of goodness; or if one cultivates the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities and accumulates all roots of goodness.

If one cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness and accumulates all roots of goodness; if one cultivates the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path and accumulates all roots of goodness;

if one cultivates the gate of liberation of emptiness and accumulates all roots of goodness; if one cultivates the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness and accumulates all roots of goodness;
if one cultivates the five eyes and accumulates all roots of goodness; or if one cultivates the six supernormal powers and accumulates all roots of goodness;

If they cultivate the ten powers of a Buddha and accumulate all roots of goodness; if they cultivate the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha and accumulate all roots of goodness;
if they cultivate the quality of non-forgetfulness and accumulate all roots of goodness; if they cultivate the nature of constant dwelling in equanimity and accumulate all roots of goodness;
if they cultivate all-knowledge and accumulate all roots of goodness; or if they cultivate the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects and accumulate all roots of goodness.
Whether it be cultivating all the gateways of dhāraṇī to gather all roots of goodness; or cultivating all the gateways of samādhi to gather all roots of goodness;
or adorning and purifying buddha-fields to gather all roots of goodness; or bringing sentient beings to maturity to gather all roots of goodness;

or the aggregates of morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation belonging to all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, as well as all other countless, immeasurable, and boundless merits;

If there are all the contaminated and uncontaminated roots of goodness of the Buddha’s disciples; or the merits of the various Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas—past, future, and present—who have bestowed predictions upon gods, humans, and others regarding their attainment of Pratyekabuddha-bodhi;

or the roots of goodness accumulated by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and so forth—if a son of good family or a daughter of good family initiates roots of goodness through rejoicing in and dedicating these merits, how should those sons and daughters of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva-yāna initiate rejoicing in and dedicate those merits and roots of goodness toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
The Venerable Subhūti said:
"O Great Being!

If sons and daughters of good family who abide in the vehicle of the bodhisattvas wish to practice the perfection of wisdom and, without slandering the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy and dedication, they should form this thought:"

"Just as all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, through their unsurpassed Buddha-wisdom, have fully realized and comprehended that these various types, natures, characteristics, and dharmas of meritorious roots are such that they may be rejoiced in, so too shall I now rejoice in them."

Furthermore, just as all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, through their unsurpassed Buddha-wisdom, have fully realized and thoroughly understood that these various meritorious deeds should be dedicated toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, so too shall I now dedicate them in this same way.

“Sons and daughters of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle should perform such rejoicing and dedication toward the roots of virtue and merits of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and their disciples. If they perform such rejoicing and dedication, they do not slander the Buddha; they follow the Buddha’s instructions and speak in accordance with the Dharma.”
The mind of this bodhisattva-mahāsattva, which thus rejoices and dedicates, is forever free from all poisons and will ultimately reach the nectar of unsurpassed bodhi.
"Furthermore, Great Being!"

Those sons and daughters of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle and practice the perfection of wisdom should, regarding the roots of virtue and merits of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and their disciples, perform such rejoicing and dedication.

Just as form does not fall within the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm, and since it does not fall within the three realms, it is neither past, future, nor present; so too should rejoicing and dedication be understood.

Just as feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness do not fall within the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm, and since they do not fall within the three realms, they are neither past, future, nor present; so too should rejoicing and dedication be understood.

"Just as the sense base of the eye does not fall within the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm—and since it does not fall within the three realms, it is neither past, future, nor present—so too should one's sympathetic joy and dedication be understood.

Just as the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind do not fall within the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm—and since they do not fall within the three realms, they are neither past, future, nor present—so too should one's sympathetic joy and dedication be understood."

"Just as the sense base of form does not fall within the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm—and since it does not fall within the three realms, it is neither past, future, nor present—so too should rejoicing and dedication be understood.

Just as the sense bases of sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena do not fall within the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm—and since they do not fall within the three realms, they are neither past, future, nor present—so too should rejoicing and dedication be understood."

"Just as the eye-element does not fall within the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm, and since it does not fall within the three realms, it is neither past, future, nor present; so too should one's sympathetic joy and dedication be understood.

Just as the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, eye-contact, and the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition do not fall within the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm, and since they do not fall within the three realms, they are neither past, future, nor present; so too should one's sympathetic joy and dedication be understood."

"Just as the ear-element does not fall within the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm, and since it does not fall within the three realms, it is neither past, future, nor present; so too should one's sympathetic joy and dedication be understood.

Just as the sound-element, the ear-consciousness-element, ear-contact, and the various feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition do not fall within the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm, and since they do not fall within the three realms, they are neither past, future, nor present; so too should one's sympathetic joy and dedication be understood."

"Just as the nose-element does not fall within the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm—and since it does not fall within the three realms, it is neither past, future, nor present—so too should rejoicing and dedication be understood.

Just as the odor-element, the nose-consciousness-element, nose-contact, and the various feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition do not fall within the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm—and since they do not fall within the three realms, they are neither past, future, nor present—so too should rejoicing and dedication be understood."

"Just as the tongue-element does not fall within the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm—and since it does not fall within the three realms, it is neither past, future, nor present—so too should one's sympathetic joy and dedication be understood.

Just as the taste-element, the tongue-consciousness-element, tongue-contact, and all sensations produced with tongue-contact as a condition do not fall within the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm—and since they do not fall within the three realms, they are neither past, future, nor present—so too should one's sympathetic joy and dedication be understood."

"Just as the body-element does not fall within the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm, and since it does not fall within the three realms, it is neither past, future, nor present; so too should one's sympathetic joy and dedication be understood.

Just as the touch-element, the body-consciousness-element, body-contact, and all feelings produced with body-contact as a condition do not fall within the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm, and since they do not fall within the three realms, they are neither past, future, nor present; so too should one's sympathetic joy and dedication be understood."

"The realm of mental volition does not fall within the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm; since it does not fall within the three realms, it is neither past, future, nor present. In the same way, one's sympathetic joy and dedication should also be thus.

Just as the dharma-realm, the consciousness-realm, mental contact, and the various feelings produced with mental contact as a condition do not fall within the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm; since they do not fall within the three realms, they are neither past, future, nor present. In the same way, one's sympathetic joy and dedication should also be thus."

"Just as the earth element does not fall into the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm—and since it does not fall into the three realms, it is neither past, future, nor present—so too should rejoicing and dedication be understood.

Just as the elements of water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness do not fall into the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm—and since they do not fall into the three realms, they are neither past, future, nor present—so too should rejoicing and dedication be understood."

"Just as ignorance does not fall within the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm—and since it does not fall within the three realms, it is neither past, future, nor present—so too should rejoicing and dedication be understood.

Just as volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and old age, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair do not fall within the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm—and since they do not fall within the three realms, they are neither past, future, nor present—so too should rejoicing and dedication be understood."

"Just as the perfection of generosity does not fall into the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm—and since it does not fall into the three realms, it is neither past, future, nor present—so too should rejoicing and dedication be performed.

Just as the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom do not fall into the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm—and since they do not fall into the three realms, they are neither past, future, nor present—so too should rejoicing and dedication be performed."

"Just as internal emptiness does not fall into the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm, and since it does not fall into the three realms, it is neither past, future, nor present; so too should rejoicing and dedication be understood."

Just as external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence do not fall within the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm—and since they do not fall within the three realms, they are neither past, future, nor present—so too should one’s sympathetic joy and dedication be understood.

"Just as suchness does not fall into the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm—and since it does not fall into the three realms, it is neither past, future, nor present—so too should rejoicing and dedication be understood.

Just as the dharma-realm, the nature of phenomena, non-falsity, immutability, equality, the state beyond birth, the fixed nature of phenomena, the stability of phenomena, the reality-limit, the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm do not fall into the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm—and since they do not fall into the three realms, they are neither past, future, nor present—so too should rejoicing and dedication be understood."

"Just as the Noble Truth of Suffering does not fall within the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm, and since it does not fall within the three realms, it is neither past, future, nor present; so too should rejoicing and dedication be understood.

Just as the Noble Truths of Origination, Cessation, and the Path do not fall within the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm, and since they do not fall within the three realms, they are neither past, future, nor present; so too should rejoicing and dedication be understood."

"Just as the four dhyānas do not fall within the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm, and since they do not fall within the three realms, they are neither past, future, nor present; so too should rejoicing and dedication be understood.

Just as the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments do not fall within the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm, and since they do not fall within the three realms, they are neither past, future, nor present; so too should rejoicing and dedication be understood."

"Just as the eight liberations do not fall within the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm—and since they do not fall within the three realms, they are neither past, future, nor present—so too should rejoicing and dedication be understood.

Just as the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities do not fall within the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm—and since they do not fall within the three realms, they are neither past, future, nor present—so too should rejoicing and dedication be understood."

"Just as the four foundations of mindfulness do not fall within the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm—and since they do not fall within the three realms, they are neither past, future, nor present—so too should rejoicing and dedication be understood.

Just as the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path do not fall within the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm—and since they do not fall within the three realms, they are neither past, future, nor present—so too should rejoicing and dedication be understood."

"Just as the liberation door of emptiness does not fall into the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm—and since it does not fall into the three realms, it is neither past, future, nor present—so too should rejoicing and dedication be understood.

Just as the liberation doors of signlessness and wishlessness do not fall into the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm—and since they do not fall into the three realms, they are neither past, future, nor present—so too should rejoicing and dedication be understood."

"Just as the five eyes do not fall within the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm, and since they do not fall within the three realms, they are neither past, future, nor present; so too should rejoicing and dedication be understood.

Just as the six supernormal powers do not fall within the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm, and since they do not fall within the three realms, they are neither past, future, nor present; so too should rejoicing and dedication be understood."

"Just as the ten powers of a Buddha do not fall within the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm—and since they do not fall within the three realms, they are neither past, future, nor present—so too should one's sympathetic joy and dedication be likewise.

Just as the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha do not fall within the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm—and since they do not fall within the three realms, they are neither past, future, nor present—so too should one's sympathetic joy and dedication be likewise."

"Just as the quality of non-forgetfulness does not fall into the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm—and since it does not fall into the three realms, it is neither past, future, nor present—so too should rejoicing and dedication be understood.

Just as the nature of constant equanimity does not fall into the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm—and since it does not fall into the three realms, it is neither past, future, nor present—so too should rejoicing and dedication be understood."

"Just as all-knowledge (sarvajñatā) does not fall within the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm, and since it does not fall within the three realms, it is neither past, future, nor present; so too should rejoicing and dedication be understood.

Just as the knowledge of the aspects of the path (mārgākārajñatā) and all-aspect knowledge (sarvākārajñatā) do not fall within the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm, and since they do not fall within the three realms, they are neither past, future, nor present; so too should rejoicing and dedication be understood."

"Just as all *dhāraṇī* gateways do not fall within the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm—and since they do not fall within the three realms, they are neither past, future, nor present—so too should rejoicing and dedication be understood.

Just as all *samādhi* gateways do not fall within the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm—and since they do not fall within the three realms, they are neither past, future, nor present—so too should rejoicing and dedication be understood."

"Just as the aggregate of ethical discipline does not fall within the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm—and since it does not fall within the three realms, it is neither past, future, nor present—so too should rejoicing and dedication be understood.

Just as the aggregates of concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation do not fall within the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm—and since they do not fall within the three realms, they are neither past, future, nor present—so too should rejoicing and dedication be understood."

"Just as the fruit of stream-entry does not fall into the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm—and since it does not fall into the three realms, it is neither past, future, nor present—so too should sympathetic joy and dedication be understood.

Just as the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and the fruit of arhatship do not fall into the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm—and since they do not fall into the three realms, they are neither past, future, nor present—so too should sympathetic joy and dedication be understood."

"Just as the enlightenment of a Pratyekabuddha does not fall within the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm—and since it does not fall within the three realms, it is neither past, future, nor present—so too should rejoicing and dedication be understood."

"Just as the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice without falling into the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm—since they do not fall into the three realms, they are neither of the past, the future, nor the present; likewise, rejoicing and dedication should also be performed in this manner."

"Just as the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas does not fall within the realm of desire, the realm of form, or the formless realm—and since it does not fall within the three realms, it is neither past, future, nor present—so too should rejoicing and dedication be performed."

"Why is this? Because those dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature, they do not fall within the three realms and are not subsumed by the three periods of time; rejoicing and dedicating [merit] are likewise so."
This means that because the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are empty of intrinsic nature, they do not fall within the three realms and are not subsumed by the three periods of time.
Because the merits of the Buddhas are empty of intrinsic nature, they do not fall within the three realms and are not subsumed by the three periods of time.
Because the self-nature of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, humans, devas, and so forth is empty, they do not fall into the three realms and are not subsumed within the three periods of time.
Because the self-nature of those roots of goodness is empty, they do not fall into the three realms and are not subsumed within the three periods of time.
Because the nature of that sympathetic joy is empty, it does not fall within the three realms and is not subsumed by the three times.
Because the nature of the phenomena toward which one dedicates is empty, they do not fall within the three realms and are not subsumed by the three times.
Because that which can dedicate is empty of intrinsic nature, it does not fall into the three realms and is not subsumed within the three times.

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom knows form as it truly is, such that it does not fall into the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm; and knows feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness as they truly are, such that they do not fall into the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm—if both [the object and the subject] do not fall into the three realms, then they are neither past, future, nor present. If they are not of the three times, then one cannot take their having marks as a means, nor taking anything obtainable as a means, to generate sympathetic joy and dedicate it toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

Why is this? Because dharmas such as form (*rūpa*) are unarisen by their very nature (*svabhāva*); if a dharma is unarisen, it is non-existent. Since that which is non-existent cannot be rejoiced in or dedicated as something non-existent.

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know as it truly is that the sense base of the eye does not fall within the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm; they know as it truly is that the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind do not fall within the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm. If they do not fall within the three realms, they are neither past, future, nor present. If they are not of the three times, one cannot, by means of their having marks or by means of apprehension, generate sympathetic joy and dedicate it toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”

Why is this? Because the dharmas such as the sense-base of the eye are by their very nature unarisen; if a dharma is unarisen, it is non-existent, and one cannot rejoice in or dedicate that which is non-existent toward that which is non-existent.

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know the sphere of form as it truly is, such that they do not fall into the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm; they know the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena as they truly are, such that they do not fall into the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm. If one does not fall into any of the three realms, then one is neither past, future, nor present. If one is not of the three times, then one cannot take the characteristic of existence as a means, nor take the apprehension of something as a means, to generate sympathetic joy and dedicate it toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

Why is this? Because the dharmas such as the sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*) are by their very nature unarisen; if a dharma is unarisen, it is non-existent. One cannot rejoice in that which is non-existent and dedicate it toward that which is non-existent.

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know the eye-element as it truly is, not falling into the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm; they know the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, eye-contact, and the various feelings produced with eye-contact as conditions as they truly are, not falling into the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm. If these do not fall into the three realms, they are neither past, future, nor present. If they are not of the three times, one cannot, by means of their marks or by means of apprehension, generate rejoicing and dedicate [merit] toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”

Why is this? Because when the eye-faculty and other dharmas practice the *prajñāpāramitā* themselves, one knows the ear-faculty as it truly is: it does not fall within the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm. One knows the sound-faculty, the ear-consciousness-faculty, ear-contact, and all sensations produced with ear-contact as conditions as they truly are: they do not fall within the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm. If these are all non-falling within the three realms, they are neither past, future, nor present. If they are not of the three times, then one cannot, by means of their marks or by means of apprehension, generate sympathetic joy and dedicate it toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.

Why is this? Because the dharmas such as the ear-element (*śrotra-dhātu*) are by their own nature unarisen; if a dharma is unarisen, it is non-existent. Since that which is non-existent cannot be rejoiced in or dedicated as something non-existent.

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know the nose-element (*ghrāṇadhātu*) as it truly is, not falling into the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm; they know the odor-element (*gandhadhātu*), the nose-consciousness element (*ghrāṇavijñānadhātu*), nose-contact (*ghrāṇasamsparśa*), and the various feelings (*vedanā*) produced with nose-contact as condition, as they truly are, not falling into the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm. If these do not fall into the three realms, they are neither past, future, nor present. If they are not of the three times, one cannot, by means of their marks or by means of apprehension, generate sympathetic joy and dedicate it toward unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment."

Why is this? Because the dharmas such as the nose-element (*ghrāṇadhātu*) are by their very nature unarisen; if a dharma is unarisen, it is non-existent. Since that which is non-existent cannot be rejoiced in and dedicated as something non-existent.

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know the tongue element as it truly is, not falling into the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm; they know the taste element, the tongue-consciousness element, tongue-contact, and all feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition as they truly are, not falling into the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm. If these do not fall into the three realms, they are not of the past, future, or present. If they are not of the three times, one cannot, by means of their marks or by means of apprehension, generate sympathetic joy and dedicate it toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”

Why is this? Because the dharmas such as the tongue-element (*jihvā-dhātu*) are by their very nature unarisen; if a dharma is unarisen, it is non-existent. Since that which is non-existent cannot be rejoiced in and dedicated as something non-existent.

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know the body-element (*kāyadhātu*) as it truly is, not falling into the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm; they know the touch-element (*spraṣṭavyadhātu*), the body-consciousness element (*kāyavijñānadhātu*), as well as body-contact (*kāyasparśa*) and the various feelings (*vedanā*) produced with body-contact as a condition, as they truly are, not falling into the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm. If these do not fall into the three realms, they are neither past, future, nor present. If they are not of the three times, one cannot, by means of their marks of existence or by means of apprehension, generate sympathetic joy and dedicate [merit] toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”

Why is this? Because the dharmas such as the body-element (*kāyadhātu*) are by their very nature unarisen; if a dharma is unarisen, it is non-existent. Since that which is non-existent cannot be rejoiced in or dedicated as something non-existent.

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom knows, as it truly is, that the mind-element does not fall into the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm; and knows, as it truly is, that the dharma-element, the mind-consciousness-element, mental contact, and the various feelings produced with mental contact as condition do not fall into the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm—if they all do not fall into the three realms, then they are neither past, future, nor present. If they are not of the three times, then one cannot, by means of their marks of existence or by means of apprehension, generate sympathetic joy and dedicate it toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”

Why is this? Because the dharmas such as the mental faculty (*manodhātu*) do not arise by their own nature; if a dharma does not arise, it is non-existent. Since that which is non-existent cannot be rejoiced in or dedicated as a non-existent dharma, [it is so].

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 173. Translated by the Dharma Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Part One: Chapter Thirty-One on Rejoicing and Dedication, Section Four. "If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know the earth element as it truly is, such that it does not fall into the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm. They know the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements as they truly are, such that they do not fall into the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm. If they do not fall into any of the three realms, they are neither past, future, nor present. If they are not of the three times, one cannot use their having marks (*nimitta*) as a means, nor use the apprehension of something as a means, to generate rejoicing and dedication toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of dharmas such as the earth element is non-arising; if a dharma does not arise, it is non-existent, and one cannot rejoice in or dedicate that non-existent dharma toward a non-existent [result].

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know as it truly is that ignorance does not fall within the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm; they know as it truly is that volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and old age, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair do not fall within the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm. If these are all non-falling within the three realms, they are neither past, future, nor present. If they are not of the three times, then one cannot, by means of their marks or by means of apprehension, generate sympathetic joy and dedicate [merit] toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

Why is this? Because dharmas such as ignorance are by their very nature unarisen; if a dharma is unarisen, it is non-existent. Since that which is non-existent cannot be rejoiced in or dedicated by means of a non-existent dharma.

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom knows, as it truly is, that the perfection of generosity does not fall into the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm; and knows, as it truly is, that the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom do not fall into the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm—if they do not fall into the three realms, they are not of the past, future, or present. If they are not of the three times, one cannot, by means of their having signs or by means of apprehending them, generate rejoicing and dedicate toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

Why is this? Because the dharmas such as the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) are by nature unarisen; if a dharma is unarisen, it is non-existent, and one cannot rejoice in or dedicate that which is non-existent toward that which is non-existent.
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom,
they know internal emptiness as it truly is and do not fall into the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm; they know external emptiness,
internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, and unconditioned emptiness as they truly are.”
Ultimate emptiness, boundless emptiness, emptiness of dispersion, emptiness of non-alteration, emptiness of intrinsic nature, emptiness of self-characteristic,
emptiness of common characteristic, emptiness of all phenomena, emptiness of the unapprehendable, emptiness of non-existence, emptiness of intrinsic nature,
and emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence do not fall into the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm.
The formless realm— if both are not included within the three realms, they are neither past, future, nor present;
and if they do not belong to the three times, one cannot, by means of their characteristics or by means of apprehension,
generate sympathetic joy and dedicate it toward unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.

Why is this? Because the dharmas such as internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*) are by their very nature unarisen; if a dharma is unarisen, it is non-existent, and one cannot rejoice in or dedicate that which is non-existent toward that which is non-existent.

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom knows reality (*tathatā*) as it truly is, they do not fall into the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm; they know the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), non-falsity (*avitathatā*), non-alteration (*ananyathātā*), equality (*samatā*), the nature of freedom from birth (*aniṣyandadharmatā*), the fixedness of phenomena (*dharmasthititā*), the stability of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the realm of space (*ākāśadhātu*), and the inconceivable realm (*acintyadhātu*) as they truly are, and do not fall into the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm. If one does not fall into any of the three realms, then one is neither past, future, nor present. If one is not of the three times, then one cannot, by means of signs or by means of apprehension, give rise to rejoicing and dedicate [merit] toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”

Why is this? Because dharmas such as *tathatā* (suchness) are by their very nature unarisen; if a dharma is unarisen, it is non-existent. Since that which is non-existent cannot be rejoiced in or dedicated as something non-existent, [it is not possible].

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom knows the noble truth of suffering as it truly is, they do not fall into the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm; if they know the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path as they truly are, they do not fall into the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm. If one does not fall into the three realms, then one is neither of the past, future, nor present. If one is not of the three times, then one cannot, by means of signs or by means of apprehension, give rise to sympathetic joy and dedicate it toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”

Why is this? Because the dharmas such as the Noble Truth of Suffering are by their very nature unarisen; if a dharma is unarisen, it is non-existent, and one cannot rejoice in or dedicate that which is non-existent toward that which is non-existent.

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know the four dhyānas as they truly are, such that they do not fall into the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm; they know the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments as they truly are, such that they do not fall into the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm. Since they do not fall into the three realms, they are neither past, future, nor present. If they are not of the three times, one cannot use their marks as a means or use the apprehension of something as a means to generate sympathetic joy and dedicate it toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”

Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of the dharmas such as the four dhyānas does not arise; if a dharma does not arise, it is non-existent, and one cannot rejoice in or dedicate that non-existent dharma toward that which is non-existent.

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom knows, as it truly is, that the eight liberations do not fall within the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm; and knows, as it truly is, that the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities do not fall within the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm—if they do not fall within the three realms, they are neither past, future, nor present. If they are not of the three times, one cannot take their marks as a means or take them as objects of attainment to generate rejoicing and dedicate toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”

Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of the dharmas such as the eight liberations is non-arising; if a dharma does not arise, it is non-existent. Since that which is non-existent cannot be rejoiced in or dedicated by means of a non-existent dharma.

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom knows, as it truly is, that the four applications of mindfulness do not fall into the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm; and knows, as it truly is, that the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold noble path do not fall into the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm—if they do not fall into the three realms, they are neither past, future, nor present. If they are not of the three times, one cannot take their marks as a means, nor take them as objects of attainment, to generate sympathetic joy and dedicate [the merit] toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.”

Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of dharmas such as the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) is non-arising; if a dharma does not arise, it is non-existent, and one cannot rejoice in or dedicate that which is non-existent by means of a dharma that is itself non-existent.

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know the liberation door of emptiness as it truly is and do not fall into the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm; they know the liberation doors of signlessness and wishlessness as they truly are and do not fall into the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm. If one does not fall into the three realms, then one is neither past, future, nor present. If one is not of the three times, then one cannot, by means of signs or by means of apprehension, generate sympathetic joy and dedicate [merit] toward unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment."

Why is this? Because the dharmas such as the gate of liberation of emptiness are by their very nature unarisen; if a dharma is unarisen, it is non-existent, and one cannot rejoice in or dedicate that which is non-existent toward that which is non-existent.

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom knows, as it truly is, that the five eyes do not fall into the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm; and knows, as it truly is, that the six superknowledges do not fall into the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm—if they do not fall into the three realms, they are neither past, future, nor present. If they are not of the three times, one cannot take their having marks as a means, nor taking them as something obtainable as a means, to generate sympathetic joy and dedicate it toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”

Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of the dharmas such as the five eyes is non-arising; if a dharma does not arise, it is non-existent, and one cannot rejoice in or dedicate that which is a non-existent dharma toward that which is non-existent.

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom knows, as it truly is, that the ten powers of a buddha do not fall within the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm; and knows, as it truly is, that the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha do not fall within the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm—if they do not fall within the three realms, they are not of the past, future, or present. If they are not of the three times, one cannot, by means of their having signs or by means of apprehension, generate sympathetic joy and dedicate it toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”

Why is this? Because the dharmas such as the ten powers of a Buddha are by their very nature unarisen; if a dharma is unarisen, it is non-existent, and one cannot rejoice in or dedicate that non-existent dharma toward that which is non-existent.

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom knows, as it truly is, that the quality of non-forgetfulness does not fall into the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm; and knows, as it truly is, that the nature of constant equanimity does not fall into the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm—if both do not fall into the three realms, they are neither past, future, nor present. If they are not of the three times, one cannot, by means of their marks or by means of apprehension, generate sympathetic joy and dedicate it toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.”

Why is this? Because dharmas such as the quality of non-forgetfulness are by nature unarisen; if a dharma is unarisen, it is non-existent, and one cannot rejoice in or dedicate that non-existent dharma toward that which is non-existent.

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) as it truly is, not falling into the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm; they know the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) as they truly are, not falling into the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm. If these do not fall into the three realms, they are neither past, future, nor present. If they are not of the three times, one cannot take their having marks as a means, nor taking anything obtainable as a means, to generate rejoicing and dedicate [merit] toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”

Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all dharmas such as omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) is non-arising; if a dharma does not arise, it is non-existent, and one cannot rejoice in or dedicate that which is non-existent by means of a dharma that is itself non-existent.

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know as it truly is that all doors of dhāraṇī do not fall into the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm; they know as it truly is that all doors of samādhi do not fall into the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm. If they do not fall into any of the three realms, then they are neither past, future, nor present. If they are not of the three times, then one cannot use their marks as a means, nor use anything obtainable as a means, to generate sympathetic joy and dedicate it toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of all dharmas, such as the gateways of dhāraṇī, is non-arising; if a dharma does not arise, it is non-existent. Since that which is non-existent cannot be rejoiced in or dedicated by means of a non-existent dharma.

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know the aggregate of ethical discipline as it truly is—not falling into the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm; they know the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation as they truly are—not falling into the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm. If these do not fall into the three realms, they are neither past, future, nor present. If they are not of the three times, one cannot, by means of their having signs or by means of apprehending them, generate sympathetic joy and dedicate it toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.”

Why is this? Because the dharmas of the aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*) and so forth are by their very nature unarisen; if a dharma is unarisen, it is non-existent, and one cannot rejoice in or dedicate that non-existent dharma toward that which is non-existent.

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know as it truly is that the fruit of stream-entry does not fall within the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm; they know as it truly is that the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and the fruit of arhatship do not fall within the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm. If these are all non-falling within the three realms, then they are neither past, future, nor present. If they are not of the three times, then one cannot, by means of their having marks or by means of apprehension, generate rejoicing and dedicate [the merit] toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

Why is this? Because the dharmas such as the fruit of stream-entry are by nature unarisen; if a dharma is unarisen, it is non-existent, and one cannot rejoice in that non-existent dharma and dedicate it toward that which is non-existent.

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know truly that the enlightenment of the pratyekabuddhas does not fall within the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm. If it does not fall within the three realms, then it is not of the past, future, or present. If it is not of the three times, then one cannot, by means of its having signs or by means of apprehending it as an object, generate sympathetic joy and dedicate it toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

Why is this? Because the dharmas of the enlightenment of the pratyekabuddhas are by nature unarisen; if a dharma is unarisen, it is non-existent, and one cannot rejoice in that non-existent dharma and dedicate it toward that which is non-existent.

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know as it truly is that the practice of bodhisattva mahāsattvas does not fall into the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm. If one does not fall into the three realms, then one is not of the past, future, or present. If one is not of the three times, then one cannot, by means of signs or by means of apprehension, generate sympathetic joy and dedicate it toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of the dharmas practiced by bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is non-arising; if a dharma does not arise, it is non-existent, and one cannot rejoice in that non-existent dharma and dedicate it toward that which is non-existent.

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they know as it truly is that the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas does not fall within the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm. If it does not fall within the three realms, then it is not of the past, future, or present. If it is not of the three times, then one cannot, by means of signs or by means of apprehension, generate sympathetic joy and dedicate it toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

Why is this? Because the nature of the dharmas of the unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas is non-arising; if a dharma does not arise, it is non-existent. Since that which is non-existent cannot be rejoiced in or dedicated as a non-existent dharma.
"When this bodhisattva-mahāsattva thus rejoices and dedicates, it is unmixed with any poisons and will ultimately lead to the nectar-like, unsurpassed enlightenment.
Furthermore, Great Being!"

If sons or daughters of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle, using the sign as a means or using the attainment of something as a means, generate sympathetic joy toward the roots of virtue and merit of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and their disciples, and dedicate them toward unexcelled perfect enlightenment—such is a perverted dedication of sympathetic joy.
This mind of wrong sympathetic joy and dedication is not praised by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.

Because such a mind of sympathetic joy and dedication is not praised by the Buddha, the World-Honored One, it cannot bring to fulfillment the perfections of giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; nor can it bring to fulfillment the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, or the four formless attainments; nor can it bring to fulfillment the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, or the ten totalities; nor can it bring to fulfillment the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the eightfold noble path; nor can it bring to fulfillment the gate of liberation of emptiness, the gate of liberation of signlessness, or the gate of liberation of wishlessness.
Because they cannot fulfill the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom;
because they cannot fulfill the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments;
and because they cannot fulfill the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, and the nine successive...
Furthermore, because they lack the eight liberations, the nine successive attainments, the ten totalities, and because they cannot fulfill the four foundations of mindfulness,
the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path,
they cannot fulfill the gate of liberation of emptiness, the gate of liberation of signlessness, or the gate of liberation of wishlessness.
Because of this gateway, one cannot fulfill internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness,
the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness,
absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential nature emptiness, and self-characteristic emptiness.
They cannot also fulfill the emptiness of common characteristics, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unobtainable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature,
and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence; nor can they fulfill suchness, the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature,
non-illusoriness, immutability, equality, and the nature of being free from birth.
The fixed dharma, the abiding of dharma, the limit of reality, the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm likewise cannot fulfill the noble truth of suffering,
the noble truth of the origin, the noble truth of cessation, and the noble truth of the path.
Because they are unable to fulfill internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness,
the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness,
absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-altering emptiness, essential emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, and common-characteristic emptiness.
Because all phenomena are empty— being empty of the unattainable, empty of non-existence, empty of intrinsic nature,
and empty of the intrinsic nature of non-existence— one cannot fulfill suchness, the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, non-falsity,
immutability, equality, the state beyond birth, and the fixed nature of dharmas.
Because of the stability of phenomena (*dharmasthiti*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the realm of space (*ākāśadhātu*),

and the inconceivable realm (*acintyadhātu*), one cannot fulfill the Noble Truth of Suffering, the Noble Truth of the Origin, the Noble Truth of Cessation, and the Noble Truth of the Path; consequently,
one cannot fulfill the five eyes, the six supernormal powers, nor the ten powers of a Buddha or the four [fearlessnesses].

They cannot fulfill the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
nor can they fulfill the quality of non-forgetfulness or the state of constant abiding in equanimity;
nor can they fulfill all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, or the knowledge of all aspects.
Furthermore, they will not be able to fulfill all the gates of dhāraṇī or all the gates of samādhi.

Because they cannot fulfill the five eyes and the six superknowledges, they cannot fulfill the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. Because they cannot fulfill the quality of non-forgetfulness and the nature of constant equanimity, because they cannot fulfill all-knowledge, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects, and because they cannot fulfill all the gates of dhāraṇī and all the gates of samādhi, they will be unable to fulfill the purification of a Buddha-field, nor will they be able to fulfill the maturation of sentient beings.

Because one cannot fully perfect and purify the Buddha-field, and because one cannot fully bring sentient beings to maturity, one will be unable to realize unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Why is this? Because that which has arisen from their sympathetic joy and dedication is mixed with various poisons.
"Furthermore, Great Being!..."
When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they should form this thought:

"Just as all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas throughout the worlds of the ten directions truly perceive and realize the roots of virtue and their meritorious qualities through such dharmas, and can, by relying on these dharmas, give rise to unerring sympathetic joy and dedication; so too should I now, relying on such dharmas, give rise to sympathetic joy and dedicate it toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment—this is what constitutes correctly giving rise to sympathetic joy and dedication."
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the Venerable Subhūti, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"Subhūti!

You have now performed the work of a Buddha, namely, by skillfully and unerringly teaching the sympathetic rejoicing and dedication for the sake of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and others. This teaching of sympathetic rejoicing and dedication is done by means of the signless (*animitta*), by means of non-apprehensibility (*anupalambha*), by means of non-arising (*anutpāda*), by means of non-cessation (*anirodha*), by means of non-defilement (*asaṃkleśa*), by means of non-purity (*avyavadāna*), by means of the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*), by means of the emptiness of self-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*), by means of the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*), by means of suchness (*tathatā*), by means of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), by means of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), by means of the non-falsity (*avitathatā*), and by means of the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*)."
"Subhūti!

Suppose all sentient beings in the trichiliocosm were to achieve the ten paths of wholesome action, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless absorptions, and the five supernormal powers. What do you think?"
"Would the merit of these sentient beings be great?
Subhūti replied,
"It would be very great!"
"O Bhagavān,
it is very much so!
O Sugata!"
The Buddha said, “Subhūti!

If sons or daughters of good family give rise to non-attached sympathetic joy and dedicate the roots of goodness of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, as well as their disciples, the merit they obtain is far greater than the former.”
"Subhūti!

This kind of rejoicing and dedication generated by these sons and daughters of good family is the most excellent, the most supreme, the most honored, the most sublime, the most wondrous, the most exquisite, the highest, and the unsurpassed; it is peerless and equal to the unequaled."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Suppose all sentient beings in a trichiliocosm were to attain the fruit of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, and arhatship. If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to provide for those stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, and arhats throughout their entire lives—honoring, revering, respecting, and praising them, and offering them immeasurable kinds of clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and other necessities—what do you think?"
"By this causal condition, would these sons and daughters of good family acquire much merit?
Subhūti replied, "Very much!"
"O Bhagavān,
it is very much so!
O Sugata!"
The Buddha said, “Subhūti!

If good sons and good daughters give rise to unattached sympathetic joy and dedicate the roots of goodness of the merits of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and their disciples, the mass of merit they obtain will be far greater than the former.”

Subhūti! This rejoicing and dedication generated by these sons and daughters of good family is the most supreme, the most excellent, the most honored, the most exalted, the most wondrous, the most subtle, the highest, the unsurpassed, the peerless, and the equal to the unequaled.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Suppose all sentient beings in the trichiliocosm were to become pratyekabuddhas. If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to provide for those pratyekabuddhas throughout their entire lives—honoring, revering, respecting, and praising them, and offering them immeasurable kinds of clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and other necessities—what do you think?"
"By this cause and condition, would those sons or daughters of good family acquire much merit?
Subhūti replied, "Very much!"
"World-Honored One!
It is very much so! Sugata!"
The Buddha said:

“Subhūti! If sons or daughters of good family give rise to an unattached sympathetic joy toward the roots of virtue and meritorious qualities of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and their disciples, and dedicate them [toward enlightenment], the mass of merit they obtain is far greater than the former.”
"Subhūti!

This rejoicing and dedication generated by these sons and daughters of good family is the most supreme, the most excellent, the most honored, the most lofty, the most wondrous, the most subtle, the highest, the unsurpassed, the peerless, and the equal to the unequaled."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Suppose all sentient beings in the trichiliocosm were to set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; and suppose further that all sentient beings in as many worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River in each of the ten directions were to approach each of those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and provide them with offerings, honor, respect, and praise, presenting them with immeasurable kinds of clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and other superior, exquisite, and pleasant requisites for life, for as many great eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River—what do you think?"
“By this cause and condition, would those sentient beings acquire much merit?
Subhūti replied, “Very much!”
“O Bhagavat,
it is very much so! O Sugata, it is very much so!”
Such a mass of merit is incalculable, immeasurable, boundless, and limitless; it is difficult to fathom through calculation or analogy.
World-Honored One!
If this mass of merit were to possess form and color, the worlds of the ten directions, each as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, would not be sufficient to contain it.
The Buddha said:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
"Subhūti! The measure of that mass of merit is as you have described.

However, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to give rise to a non-attached sympathetic joy toward the roots of virtue and merits of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and their disciples, and dedicate them [toward enlightenment], the mass of merit they would obtain would be far greater than the former."

Subhūti! This rejoicing and dedication generated by these sons and daughters of good family is the most excellent, the most superior, the most honored, the most sublime, the most wondrous, the most exquisite, the highest, and the unsurpassed; it is peerless and equal to the unequaled.
"Subhūti!

If one were to compare the former merit with this mass of merit, the former would not equal even a hundredth part of it; it would not equal a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth part, nor a koṭi-th part, nor a hundred-koṭi-th part, nor a thousand-koṭi-th part, nor a hundred-thousand-koṭi-th part, nor a hundred-thousand-koṭi-nayuta-th part. It would not equal even a numerical fraction, a calculable fraction, a reckoned fraction, a metaphorical fraction, or even a fraction of the infinitesimal (upaniṣad)."
Why is this? Subhūti!

Those sentient beings have accomplished the ten paths of wholesome action, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and the five supernormal powers, all by means of having signs and having something to be attained.

When those sons and daughters of good family honor, revere, respect, and praise the stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arhats, and pratyekabuddhas by offering them immeasurable kinds of clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and other requisites, the mass of merit they obtain is all due to employing the expedient means of having signs and being characterized by apprehension.

Those sentient beings who offer worship, respect, honor, and praise, and who present various kinds of clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and other superior and exquisite articles of life to those bodhisattvas who have set out for unsurpassed enlightenment, acquire a mass of merit that is based upon signs and the apprehension of objects.
