At that time, the Four Great Heavenly Kings, together with their retinues of twenty thousand devaputras, leaped for joy and, rising with palms joined, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and said:
“World-Honored One!

In this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to initiate such vast sympathetic joy and dedication (*pariṇāmanā*). That is to say, through skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), employing the means of signlessness (*animitta*), the means of non-apprehensibility (*anupalambha*), the means of non-attachment (*asaṅga*), and the means of non-conceptualization (*anabhisamskāra*), that bodhisattva mahāsattva generates sympathetic joy toward the roots of virtue and merit of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksambuddhas, and their disciples, and dedicates them toward unexcelled perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*). Such sympathetic joy and dedication as thus initiated does not fall into either duality (*dvaya-dharma*) or non-duality (*advaya-dharma*).

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, together with his retinue of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of devaputras, each holding various celestial and exquisite flower garlands, incense for burning, unguents, powdered incense, robes, necklaces, jeweled banners, pennants, canopies, and many other wonderful and rare treasures, played celestial music as an offering to the Buddha, and addressed him, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."

In this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to initiate such vast rejoicing and dedication; that is to say, through skillful means, employing the method of signlessness, the method of non-apprehension, the method of non-attachment, and the method of non-conditioning, they generate rejoicing and dedicate toward unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment the roots of virtue and merits of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and their disciples. Such rejoicing and dedication as thus initiated does not fall into either dualistic dharmas or non-dualistic dharmas.

At that time, Suyāma, the King of the Suyāma Heaven, together with his retinue of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of devaputras, each holding various celestial and exquisite flower garlands, incense for burning, unguents, powdered incense, robes, necklaces, jeweled banners, pennants, canopies, and many other wonderful and rare treasures, played celestial music as an offering to the Buddha, and addressed him, saying:
"World-Honored One!

In this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to initiate such vast sympathetic joy and dedication; that is to say, through the skillful means of those bodhisattva mahāsattvas—employing the means of signlessness, the means of non-apprehension, the means of non-attachment, and the means of non-conceptual activity—they generate sympathetic joy toward the roots of virtue and merit of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and their disciples, and dedicate them toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. This sympathetic joy and dedication thus initiated does not fall into either dualistic dharmas or non-dualistic dharmas.

At that time, the Deva King Śāntuṣita, together with his retinue of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of devaputras, each holding various celestial and exquisite flower garlands, incense for burning, unguents, powdered incense, robes, necklaces, jeweled banners, flags, parasols, and many other wonderful and rare treasures, played celestial music as an offering to the Buddha, and addressed him, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."

In this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to initiate such vast sympathetic rejoicing and dedication; that is to say, by means of skillful means, employing the method of signlessness, the method of non-apprehensibility, the method of non-attachment, and the method of non-conditioning, that bodhisattva mahāsattva generates sympathetic rejoicing toward the roots of virtue and merit of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and their disciples, dedicating them toward unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. Such sympathetic rejoicing and dedication as thus initiated does not fall into either dualistic dharmas or non-dualistic dharmas.

At that time, the Deva King Sunirmita, together with his retinue of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of devaputras, each holding various celestial flower garlands, incense, ointments, powdered perfumes, robes, necklaces, jeweled banners, flags, canopies, and many other exquisite and rare treasures, played celestial music as an offering to the Buddha, and addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!

In this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to initiate such vast sympathetic joy and dedication (*pariṇāmanā*). That is to say, through skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), employing the means of signlessness (*animitta*), the means of non-apprehensibility (*anupalambha*), the means of non-attachment (*asaṅga*), and the means of non-conditioning (*anabhisaṃskāra*), that bodhisattva mahāsattva generates sympathetic joy toward the roots of virtue and merit of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksambuddhas, and their disciples, and dedicates them toward unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*). Such sympathetic joy and dedication as thus initiated does not fall into either dualistic dharmas or non-dualistic dharmas.

At that time, the Celestial King Vaśavartin, together with his retinue of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of devaputras, each holding various celestial and exquisite flower garlands, incense for burning, unguents, powdered incense, robes, necklaces, precious banners, pennants, canopies, and many wonderful and rare treasures, played various celestial music as an offering to the Buddha, and addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!

In this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to initiate such vast sympathetic joy and dedication—that is, that bodhisattva mahāsattva, through skillful means, employing the method of signlessness, the method of non-apprehension, the method of non-attachment, and the method of non-conditioning, generates sympathetic joy toward the roots of virtue and merits of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and their disciples, and dedicates them toward unexcelled perfect enlightenment. This sympathetic joy and dedication thus initiated does not fall into either dualistic dharmas or non-dualistic dharmas.

At that time, the Great Brahmā King, together with an assembly of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of Brahmās, approached the place where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and together raised their voices, saying:
"How rare! How extraordinary!"
“World-Honored One!

Because such bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are sustained by the perfection of wisdom and skillful means, they surpass the roots of goodness cultivated by those sons and daughters of good family who lack skillful means, who dwell on signs, and who grasp at attainments.”

At that time, the Ābhāsvara devas, together with an immeasurable multitude of hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of light-bearing devas, approached the Buddha, prostrated at his feet, and in unison cried out:
“How marvelous! How rare!”
"Bhagavān!

Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are embraced by the perfection of wisdom and skillful means, they surpass the roots of goodness cultivated by those sons and daughters of good family who previously lacked skillful means and who possessed signs and apprehension."

At that time, the Śubhakṛtsna devas, together with an immeasurable multitude of hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of Śuddhāvāsa devas, approached the Buddha, prostrated at his feet, and cried out in unison:
"How marvelous! How extraordinary!"
"Bhagavān!

Because such bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are sustained by the perfection of wisdom and skillful means, they surpass the roots of goodness cultivated by those sons and daughters of good family who lack skillful means, who possess signs, and who apprehend objects."

At that time, the deva of the Vast Fruit Heaven (Bṛhatphala), together with an assembly of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of Vast Devas, approached the place where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and in unison cried out:
"How marvelous! How rare!"
“World-Honored One!

Because such bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are sustained by the perfection of wisdom and skillful means, they surpass the roots of goodness cultivated by those sons and daughters of good family who lack skillful means and who dwell upon signs and objective apprehension.”

At that time, the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, together with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of Śuddhāvāsa devas, approached the Buddha’s presence, prostrated at his feet, and cried out in unison:
“How marvelous! How rare!”
“World-Honored One!

Because such bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are embraced by the perfection of wisdom and skillful means, they surpass the roots of goodness cultivated by those sons and daughters of good family who lack skillful means, who possess signs, and who grasp at attainments.”

At that time, the Buddha addressed the gods of the Realm of the Four Great Kings, the Heaven of the Thirty-three, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, the Brahmakāyika Heaven, the Brahmapurohita Heaven, the Brahmakāyika-sabhā Heaven, the Mahābrahmā Heaven, the Ābhāsvara Heaven, the Parīttābha Heaven, the Apramāṇābha Heaven, the Ābhāsvara-śuddha Heaven, the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven, the Parīttaśubha Heaven, the Apramāṇaśubha Heaven, the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven, the Bṛhatphala Heaven, the Avṛha Heaven, the Atapa Heaven, the Sudṛśa Heaven, the Sudarśana Heaven, and the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, saying:
"Suppose all sentient beings in the trichiliocosm were to each resolve toward Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi..."
Regarding the mind of unsurpassed complete enlightenment, throughout the past, future, and present, in all worlds of the ten directions,
for all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas— from their first generation of the mind until they attain unsurpassed complete enlightenment,
turn the sublime wheel of Dharma, and enter parinirvāṇa without remainder, and even until the extinction of the Dharma— within this [interval]:
All the roots of virtue associated with the cultivation of the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence,
meditative concentration, and wisdom therein; or if one abides in internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness,
the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate, the emptiness of conditioned phenomena, and so forth—
The roots of goodness associated with the emptiness of the unconditioned, ultimate emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersion emptiness, non-alteration emptiness,
essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable,
the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.
If one abides in roots of goodness associated with suchness, the dharma-realm, the nature of phenomena, non-falsity, immutability, equality,
the state beyond birth, the fixed nature of phenomena, the stability of phenomena, the limit of reality, the realm of space,
and the inconceivable realm; or if one abides in the noble truth of suffering, the [noble truth of] origination...
the wholesome roots associated with the Noble Truths, the Noble Truth of Cessation, and the Noble Truth of the Path;
or the wholesome roots associated with the cultivation of the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments;
or the wholesome roots associated with the cultivation of the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities; or...

One cultivates the roots of goodness associated with the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path;
or one cultivates the roots of goodness associated with the gate of liberation of emptiness, the gate of liberation of signlessness, and the gate of liberation of wishlessness. If one cultivates...
They cultivate roots of goodness associated with the five eyes and the six supernormal powers;

they cultivate roots of goodness associated with the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; and they cultivate the quality of non-forgetfulness.

The roots of goodness associated with the state of constant equanimity; the roots of goodness associated with the cultivation of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*);
the roots of goodness associated with the cultivation of all doors of dhāraṇī and all doors of samādhi; and the cultivation of the practices of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
Corresponding roots of goodness—whether they be the roots of goodness corresponding to the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas;

or whatever roots of goodness belong to the disciples; or the aggregates of ethical discipline, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, as well as others.
The immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas; whether it be the true Dharma taught by the Tathāgatas,
or the three types of meritorious actions— those of giving, morality, and cultivation— practiced in reliance upon that Dharma,
or the diligent training in reliance upon that Dharma which results in attaining the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, or the attainment of Arhatship...
The fruit of arhatship, the attainment of pratyekabuddha enlightenment, the entry of bodhisattvas into the state of right determination (samyaktva-niyāma),
and whatever roots of virtue are produced by sentient beings through the practice of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence,
meditative concentration, and wisdom— all these taken together and weighed, [if one were to] take them as having signs...
Using skillful means— employing the means of apprehending something, the means of attachment, the means of volitional activity,
and the means of duality and non-duality— they manifest sympathetic joy; having thus rejoiced,
they dedicate [the merit] toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
“Suppose there are sons or daughters of good family who have set out for unsurpassed,
perfect, and complete enlightenment, and who, throughout the past, future, and present, in all the worlds of the ten directions, [make offerings] to all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas—
from their first generation of the mind of enlightenment, until they attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, turn the sublime wheel of Dharma, and enter [parinirvāṇa]...”
From the time of parinirvāṇa without remainder until the extinction of the Dharma,
all the roots of goodness associated with the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration,
and wisdom practiced during that interval— whether one abides in internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, or emptiness...
Emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness,
emptiness of dispersion, emptiness of non-alteration, emptiness of intrinsic nature, emptiness of self-characteristics,
emptiness of common characteristics, emptiness of all phenomena, emptiness of the unapprehendable, emptiness of non-existence, and emptiness of self...
Roots of goodness associated with the emptiness of nature and the emptiness of the self-nature of non-existence;
if one abides in suchness, the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, the non-erroneous nature, the unchanging nature, equality,
the state beyond birth, the fixedness of dharmas, the stability of dharmas, the limit of reality, the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm.

Wholesome roots associated with [the truths], namely wholesome roots associated with abiding in the noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin, the noble truth of cessation, and the noble truth of the path;
or wholesome roots associated with cultivating the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments;
or wholesome roots associated with cultivating the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, and the nine...
The wholesome roots associated with the successive meditative absorptions (anupūrvavihārasamāpatti) and the ten totalities (daśakṛtsnāyatana);

or the wholesome roots associated with the cultivation of the four foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna), the four right efforts (samyakprahāṇa), the four bases of power (ṛddhipāda), the five faculties (indriya), the five powers (bala), the seven factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga), and the eightfold noble path (āryāṣṭāṅgamārga);
or the cultivation of the gateway of liberation of emptiness (śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha) and the gateway of liberation of signlessness (animitta-vimokṣamukha).
...the roots of goodness associated with the door of liberation of wishlessness; or if one cultivates the roots of goodness associated with the five eyes and the six supernormal powers;

or if one cultivates the Buddha’s ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
The roots of goodness associated with it—namely, the roots of goodness associated with the cultivation of the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant equanimity;
the roots of goodness associated with the cultivation of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*);
and the roots of goodness associated with the cultivation of all doors of dhāraṇī and all doors of samādhi.
Roots of goodness— whether they are roots of goodness associated with the practices of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas,
or roots of goodness associated with the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of the Buddhas,
or whatever roots of goodness belong to the disciples, or the aggregates of ethical discipline, concentration, and wisdom of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas...
The aggregates, the aggregate of liberation, the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation, and all other immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas;

the true Dharma taught by the Tathāgatas; the three types of meritorious action consisting of the nature of giving, the nature of morality, and the nature of cultivation practiced in reliance upon that Dharma;
and the fruit of stream-entry attained through diligent training in reliance upon that Dharma.
...attaining the fruit of once-returning, attaining the fruit of non-returning, attaining the fruit of arhatship,
attaining pratyekabuddha-enlightenment, or entering the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and departure from birth;
as well as whatever roots of virtue are produced by sentient beings practicing generosity, pure ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
Having thus gathered and weighed all these together, one manifests sympathetic joy by means of signlessness,
by means of non-apprehension, by means of non-attachment, by means of non-action, and by means of non-duality and non-non-duality;
having thus rejoiced, one dedicates [the merit] toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Bodhi. This rejoicing and dedication by these sons and daughters of good family is the most excellent, the most supreme, the most honored, the highest, the most sublime, the most subtle, the superior, the unsurpassed, the peerless, and the equal to the unequaled; it is a hundred times more excellent than the rejoicing and dedication of the aforementioned sentient beings, a thousand times more excellent, a hundred-thousand times more excellent, a koṭi times more excellent, a hundred-koṭi times more excellent, a thousand-koṭi times more excellent, a hundred-thousand-koṭi times more excellent, a hundred-thousand-koṭi-nayuta times more excellent, and even many times, calculated times, reckoned times, compared times, and even up to *upaniṣad* times more excellent.

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Scroll 171. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Part One: Chapter Thirty-one, "Rejoicing and Dedication," Section Five. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
As the Blessed One has said:

"The rejoicing and dedication of these sons and daughters of good family is the most excellent, the most supreme, the most honored, the most sublime, the most wondrous, the most subtle, the highest, the unsurpassed, the peerless, and the equal to the unequaled."

“World-Honored One, to what extent is this rejoicing and dedication said to be the most excellent, the most superior, the most honorable, the most sublime, the most wondrous, the most exquisite, the highest, the unsurpassed, the peerless, and the equal to the unequaled?”
The Buddha said, “Subhūti!

These sons of good family and daughters of good family universally regard all the roots of goodness of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and all other sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions in the past, future, and present. They neither grasp nor reject them; they neither boast of nor despise them. They do not perceive anything as being attained, nor do they perceive anything as being unattained. Furthermore, they know that all phenomena are without arising and without cessation, without defilement and without purity, without increase and without decrease, without going and without coming, without accumulation and without dispersal, and without entering and without exiting. They form this thought:”

"Just as the suchness, the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, the non-falsity, the non-alteration, the equality, the state beyond birth, the fixedness of dharma, the stability of dharma, the limit of reality, the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm of all dharmas of the past, future, and present, so too do I rejoice and dedicate [this merit]."

"Subhūti! To this extent, the rejoicing and dedication undertaken by a bodhisattva mahāsattva—I declare it to be the most excellent, the most superior, the most noble, the most lofty, the most sublime, the most exquisite, the highest, the unsurpassed, the peerless, and the equal to the unequaled."
"Subhūti!

Such rejoicing and dedication surpasses other forms of rejoicing and dedication by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, a hundred-thousandfold, a koṭi-fold, a hundred-koṭi-fold, a thousand-koṭi-fold, a hundred-thousand-koṭi-fold, a hundred-thousand-koṭi-nayuta-fold, and by multiples of number, calculation, reckoning, analogy, and even up to the *upaniṣad* (infinitesimal) multiple. Therefore, I declare that such rejoicing and dedication as thus generated is the most excellent, the most supreme, the most honored, the most lofty, the most wondrous, the most subtle, the highest, the unsurpassed, the unequaled, and the equal to the unequaled."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
Those sons of good family and daughters of good family who abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle and wish, regarding all Tathāgatas, Arhats,
and Samyaksaṃbuddhas in the worlds of the ten directions throughout the past, future, and present, from their first generation of the mind..."
All the roots of virtue associated with the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom—
from the attainment of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, through the turning of the sublime wheel of Dharma,
until the entry into nirvana without remainder and the subsequent disappearance of the Dharma— in the interval between these points.

Whether it be the aggregate of ethical discipline, the aggregate of meditative concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, or the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation;
whether it be the other immeasurable and boundless qualities of a Buddha; whether it be the roots of virtue and merit belonging to all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas;
or whatever belongs to other sentient beings by way of the three types of merit—those consisting of giving, those consisting of ethical discipline, and those consisting of cultivation—
Regarding the bases of meritorious action and other wholesome dharmas, one who gathers them together, weighs them,
and gives rise before them to a mind of unerring sympathetic joy and dedication should form this thought:
"As is liberation, so too is form."
As it is with liberation, so it is with feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
As it is with liberation, so it is with the sense base of the eye;
as it is with liberation, so it is with the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
As with liberation, so it is with the sense-base of form;
as with liberation, so it is with the sense-bases of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena.
As with liberation, so it is with the eye-element.

As with liberation, so it is with the form element (*rūpadhātu*), the eye-consciousness element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*), eye-contact (*cakṣuḥsaṃsparśa*), and all feelings (*vedanā*) produced with eye-contact as a condition.
As with liberation, so it is with the ear element (*śrotradhātu*);

as with liberation, so it is with the sound element (*śabdadhātu*), the ear-consciousness element (*śrotravijñānadhātu*), ear-contact (*śrotrasaṃsparśa*), and all feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition.
As with liberation, so it is with the nose element;
as with liberation, so it is with the odor element, the nose-consciousness element, nose-contact, and all feelings produced with nose-contact as their condition.
As with liberation, so it is with the tongue element;
as with liberation, so it is with the taste element, the tongue-consciousness element, tongue-contact, and all sensations produced with tongue-contact as a condition.
As with liberation, so it is with the body element;
as with liberation, so it is with the tangible object element, the body-consciousness element, body-contact, and all feelings produced with body-contact as their condition.
As it is with liberation, so it is with the mind element;
as it is with liberation, so it is with the mental-object element, the mind-consciousness element, and all feelings arisen with mind-contact as condition.
As with liberation, so it is with the earth element;
as with liberation, so it is with the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements.
As with liberation, so it is with ignorance.

As it is with liberation, so it is with volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, and old age, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
As it is with liberation, so it is with the perfection of generosity;
as it is with liberation, so it is with the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
As with liberation, so it is with internal emptiness;

as with liberation, so it is with external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate truth, the emptiness of conditioned phenomena, the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersion emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature.
As is liberation, so too is suchness;

as is liberation, so too are the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, the non-falsity, the non-alteration, the equality, the state beyond birth, the fixedness of dharma, the stability of dharma, the reality-limit, the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm.
As with liberation, so it is with the noble truth of suffering;
as with liberation, so it is with the noble truths of its origin, its cessation, and the path.
As with liberation, so it is with the four dhyānas.
As it is with liberation, so it is with the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments.
As it is with liberation, so it is with the eight liberations;
as it is with liberation, so it is with the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities.
As it is with liberation, so it is with the four foundations of mindfulness;
as it is with liberation, so it is with the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path.
As it is with liberation, so it is with the gate of liberation of emptiness;
as it is with liberation, so it is with the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness.
As it is with liberation, so it is with the five eyes.
As it is with liberation, so it is with the six supernormal powers.
As it is with liberation, so it is with the ten powers of a Buddha.

As it is with liberation, so it is with the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
As with liberation, so it is with the quality of non-forgetfulness;
as with liberation, so it is with the state of constant equanimity.
As with liberation, so it is with omniscience.
As it is with liberation, so it is with the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects.
As it is with liberation, so it is with all doors of dhāraṇī;
as it is with liberation, so it is with all doors of samādhi.
As it is with liberation, so it is with the aggregate of ethical discipline;
as it is with liberation, so it is with the aggregates of concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.
As is liberation, so too are all phenomena of the past, future, and present;
as is liberation, so too are all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the ten directions throughout the past, future, and present worlds.
As is liberation, so too are the bodhi and nirvāṇa of all Buddhas;
as is liberation, so too are the countless, immeasurable, and boundless Buddha-dharmas.
As is liberation, so too are all the disciples of the Buddha;
as is liberation, so too is the maturation of the faculties of all the disciples of the Buddha;
as is liberation, so too is the parinirvāṇa of all the disciples of the Buddha.
As is liberation, so too are all dharmas of the Buddha's disciples;
as is liberation, so too are all pratyekabuddhas;
as is liberation, so too is the maturation of the faculties of all pratyekabuddhas.
As it is with liberation, so it is with the parinirvāṇa of all pratyekabuddhas;
as it is with liberation, so it is with all the dharmas of the pratyekabuddhas.
As it is with liberation, so it is with the dharma-nature of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and the pratyekabuddha-dharmas of the disciples of the Buddha.
As is liberation, so too are all sentient beings;
as is liberation, so too is the nature of all phenomena;
as is liberation, so too are all acts of sympathetic joy and dedication.

Just as the nature of all phenomena is neither bound nor liberated, neither defiled nor pure, neither arising nor ceasing, neither born nor extinguished, and neither grasped nor relinquished, I rejoice in these roots of goodness and merit with manifest presence and dedicate them toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
In this way, rejoicing is not that which rejoices, because there is nothing to rejoice in.
In this way, dedication is not that which dedicates, because there is nothing to dedicate.
"Such rejoicing and dedication as thus arisen neither turn nor cease, because they are without arising or ceasing. "Subhūti!

This rejoicing and dedication of the bodhisattva mahāsattva is the most supreme, the most excellent, the most honored, the most sublime, the most wondrous, the most exquisite, the highest, and the unsurpassed; it is peerless and equal to the unequaled."
"Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes such rejoicing and dedication, they will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Furthermore, Subhūti!"

If sons or daughters of good family who have set out upon the Mahāyāna were to, for as long as their lives last, provide offerings, honor, respect, and praise to all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and their assemblies of disciples throughout as many worlds in the ten directions as there are sands in the Ganges—using the conceptualization of signs as a means and the apprehension of objects as a means—and furthermore, were to present them with various garments, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and other excellent articles of life and enjoyment;

After those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, along with their assemblies of disciples, have entered parinirvāṇa, one takes their śarīras and constructs high and vast stūpas made of the seven precious jewels. Day and night, one diligently pays homage, prostrates, and circumambulates them to the right. Furthermore, with various kinds of exquisite flower garlands, powdered and incense perfumes for smearing and scattering, robes, necklaces, precious banners, flags, canopies, and all manner of wonderful, rare, musical instruments, and lamps, one offers worship, respect, reverence, and praise with everything one possesses.

Furthermore, taking the perception of signs as a means and the apprehension of objects as a means, they cultivate the roots of virtue associated with the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.

Furthermore, by employing the method of having signs and the method of apprehending something as real, they generate sympathetic joy toward the roots of virtue and merits of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and their disciples, and dedicate them toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.

“There are sons and daughters of good family who have set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and who, employing the method of signlessness and the method of non-apprehension, cultivate the roots of virtue associated with the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.”

Furthermore, employing the method of signlessness and the method of non-apprehension, they generate sympathetic joy toward the roots of virtue and merit of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and their disciples, and dedicate them toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.

Because these sons and daughters of good family, by relying on the skillful means of the *prajñāpāramitā*, perform this rejoicing and dedication, it surpasses the previously mentioned rejoicing and dedication by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, a hundred-thousandfold, a *koṭī*-fold, a hundred-*koṭī*-fold, a thousand-*koṭī*-fold, a hundred-thousand-*koṭī*-fold, a hundred-thousand-*koṭī*-nayuta-fold, and even by multiples of number, calculation, reckoning, analogy, and up to the *upaniṣad* multiple. Therefore, such rejoicing and dedication is said to be the most supreme, the most excellent, the most honored, the most exalted, the most wondrous, the most subtle, the highest, the unsurpassed, the unequaled, and the equal to the unequaled.

"Therefore, Subhūti, all bodhisattva mahāsattvas who have set out in the Great Vehicle should, by means of the signless and by means of non-apprehension, cultivate and train in the roots of virtue associated with the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; and, relying on the skillful means of the perfection of wisdom, they should generate sympathetic joy toward the roots of virtue and merits of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and their disciples, and dedicate them toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
32. Praising Prajñā, Part One: Chapter Thirty-Two, Praising Prajñā, Section One. At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"Is what has been thus explained not indeed the Prajñāpāramitā?
The Buddha said,
"Śāriputra!..."
"What has been thus explained is itself the Prajñāpāramitā.
At that time, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"In this way, the Perfection of Wisdom is able to provide illumination because it is ultimately pure.
'World-Honored One!
This Perfection of Wisdom should be honored and revered by all, for it is that which we gods and humans hold in high esteem.'"
“World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā is without attachment, for it cannot be defiled by any worldly dharmas.
World-Honored One!”
"In this way, the Perfection of Wisdom is free from all cataracts of the triple world, for it can eliminate the darkness of afflictions and all [wrong] views.
World-Honored One!"
"In this way, the perfection of wisdom is the foremost, for it is most supreme among all factors of enlightenment in every respect.
World-Honored One!"
"In this way, the Perfection of Wisdom can provide security by forever severing all causes of alarm, fear, affliction, and calamity.
World-Honored One!"
"In this way, the Perfection of Wisdom can bestow radiance, for it gathers in all sentient beings and enables them to attain the five eyes.
'World-Honored One!
In this way, the Perfection of Wisdom can demonstrate the Middle Way, for it causes those who have lost their way to leave behind the two extremes.'"
“World-Honored One!
This prajñāpāramitā is thus well able to give rise to the knowledge of all modes, because it forever severs all continuous afflictions along with their habitual tendencies.”
“World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā is the mother of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, for all the Buddha-dharmas cultivated by bodhisattvas arise from it.”
“World-Honored One!
This prajñāpāramitā is neither born nor extinguished, because its own-characteristic is empty.
World-Honored One!”
In this way, the perfection of wisdom is remote from birth and death, because it is neither permanent nor subject to destruction.
"World-Honored One!
This perfection of wisdom can act as a refuge, for it bestows the jewels of all dharmas."
“World-Honored One!
This prajñāpāramitā can bring about the ten powers of a Buddha, because it cannot be overcome.
World-Honored One!”

In this way, the perfection of wisdom is able to turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma with its three revolutions and twelve aspects, because it realizes that all phenomena are without turning or returning.
“World-Honored One!
This prajñāpāramitā is able to demonstrate the non-perverted nature of all dharmas, because it reveals the emptiness of the self-nature of non-existence.”

“Bhagavān! How should those sentient beings who abide in the vehicle of the bodhisattvas, or the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, or the vehicle of the śrāvakas dwell with respect to this perfection of wisdom?”
The Buddha said:

"Śāriputra! These sentient beings should abide toward this *prajñāpāramitā* as they would toward a Buddha; they should make offerings to, pay homage to, and contemplate the *prajñāpāramitā* as they would make offerings to, pay homage to, and contemplate the Blessed One, the Buddha."

Why is this? The Prajñāpāramitā is not different from the Buddha, the Bhagavān; the Buddha, the Bhagavān, is not different from the Prajñāpāramitā. The Prajñāpāramitā is itself the Buddha, the Bhagavān; the Buddha, the Bhagavān, is himself the Prajñāpāramitā.
Why is this? "Śāriputra!
It is because all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas appear by means of the perfection of wisdom."

“Śāriputra! It is because all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, pratyekabuddhas, arhats, non-returners, once-returners, and stream-enterers, as well as others, all appear by means of the perfection of wisdom.”

“Śāriputra! All the ten paths of wholesome action in the world, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and the five supernormal powers all appear by virtue of the perfection of wisdom.”
“Śāriputra! All perfections of giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom arise from the perfection of wisdom.”

“Śāriputra! All internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, emptiness of the ultimate truth, emptiness of conditioned phenomena, emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, absolute emptiness, emptiness of the limitless, emptiness of dispersion, emptiness of non-alteration, emptiness of intrinsic nature, emptiness of specific characteristics, emptiness of common characteristics, emptiness of all phenomena, emptiness of the unapprehendable, emptiness of non-existence, emptiness of intrinsic nature, and emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence—all these arise by virtue of the perfection of wisdom.”

“Śāriputra! All suchness, the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, the non-illusory nature, the unchanging nature, equality, the state beyond birth, the fixedness of dharmas, the stability of dharmas, the limit of reality, the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm all appear by virtue of the perfection of wisdom.”
“Śāriputra! All the noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin, the noble truth of cessation, and the noble truth of the path all appear by virtue of the perfection of wisdom.”
“Śāriputra! All four dhyānas, four immeasurables, and four formless absorptions appear by virtue of the perfection of wisdom.”
“Śāriputra! All eight liberations, eight bases of mastery, nine successive attainments, and ten totalities arise because they are brought forth by the perfection of wisdom.”

“Śāriputra! All the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold noble path all appear by virtue of the perfection of wisdom.”
“Śāriputra! All the doors of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—arise because they are brought forth by the perfection of wisdom.”
“Śāriputra! All five eyes and six supernormal powers appear by virtue of the perfection of wisdom. Śāriputra!”

Because all the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha all appear by means of the perfection of wisdom.
“Śāriputra! All qualities of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant abiding in equanimity appear by virtue of the perfection of wisdom. Śāriputra!”
All-knowledge, the knowledge of the aspects of the path, and the knowledge of all aspects all arise from the perfection of wisdom.
"Śāriputra!..."
"Because all dharani-doors and all samadhi-doors arise from the perfection of wisdom.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, secretly had this thought:
"For what reason and by what cause does Śāriputra now ask about this matter?"
At that time, Śāriputra, knowing his thoughts, addressed him, saying: “Kauśika!

Because they are sustained by the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) and skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), bodhisattva mahāsattvas are able to take all the roots of merit and virtue—from the initial generation of the mind of awakening until the attainment of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, the turning of the sublime wheel of Dharma, and even the extinction of the Dharma—of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas throughout the ten directions in the past, future, and present; as well as the roots of merit and virtue of all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and other sentient beings. Having gathered and weighed them together, they manifest sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) and dedicate them toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. It is for this reason that you ask about this matter.”
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

The perfection of wisdom studied by bodhisattva mahāsattvas surpasses the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration by immeasurable multiples. It is like a multitude of hundreds of thousands of those born blind who, lacking one with pure vision to skillfully guide them, cannot even approach the right path, much less reach the great city of abundant prosperity in the distance!"

In this way, these groups of those born blind—consisting of the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration—if they lack the guidance of the pure eye of the perfection of wisdom, are unable even to set out upon the correct path of a bodhisattva, let alone be able to enter the city of omniscience!
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
These perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration are called 'possessing eyes' because they are embraced by this perfection of wisdom."
"Furthermore, because they are embraced by the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), all [virtues] such as generosity (*dāna*) attain the name 'reaching the other shore' (*pāramitā*).
At that time, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, addressed the Venerable Śāriputra, saying:
"As the Great Virtuous One has said, 'The five perfections, such as generosity, must be embraced by the perfection of wisdom before they can be called "reaching the other shore. "

In that case, would it not be impossible to say that the other five [perfections] only attain the name "perfection" (pāramitā) because they are embraced by the perfection of generosity (dāna-pāramitā),
and that the other five only attain the name "perfection" because they are embraced by the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā)?
Is it because they are embraced by the perfection of patience that the other five attain the name "perfections"?
Or is it because they are embraced by the perfection of diligence that the other five attain the name "perfections"?
If it is because they are embraced by the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*) that the other five [perfections] attain the name "perfection" (*pāramitā*),
then for what reason is only wisdom (*prajñā*) praised as being superior to the other five perfections?
Śāriputra said: "No, indeed!
No, indeed!"
Why is this? Kauśika!
It is not because they are embraced by the perfection of generosity that the other five [perfections] receive the name "reaching the further shore."
It is not because they are embraced by the perfection of ethical discipline that the other five are designated as "perfections";
it is not because they are embraced by the perfection of patience that the other five are designated as "perfections";
it is not because they are embraced by the perfection of diligence that the other five are designated as "perfections."
It is not because they are embraced by the perfection of meditative concentration that the other five are designated as "perfections" (pāramitā);
rather, it is solely because they are embraced by the perfection of wisdom that the other five are designated as "perfections."

Why is this? Because it is only by abiding in the perfection of wisdom that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to fulfill the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; they cannot accomplish these matters by abiding in the other five [perfections].

Therefore, among these five, the perfection of wisdom is the most supreme, the most excellent, the most honored, the most exalted, the most sublime, the most exquisite, the highest, the unsurpassed, the unequaled, and the equal to the unequaled.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how should bodhisattva-mahāsattvas bring forth the perfection of wisdom?”
The Buddha said:
“Śāriputra! A bodhisattva mahāsattva should bring forth the perfection of wisdom not for the sake of bringing forth form;”
"One should bring forth the perfection of wisdom not for the sake of bringing forth feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
"World-Honored One,
how is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva should bring forth the perfection of wisdom not for the sake of bringing forth form?"
“Is it for the sake of bringing forth feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness that one should bring forth the perfection of wisdom?
“Śāriputra, because form is without activity,

without cessation, without arising, without ceasing, without formation, without disintegration, without acquisition, without relinquishment, and because it lacks intrinsic nature, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should bring forth the perfection of wisdom not for the sake of bringing forth form.”

Because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are without activity and without cessation, without arising and without ceasing, without formation and without destruction, without acquisition and without relinquishment, and because they lack intrinsic nature, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice the perfection of wisdom not for the sake of producing feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not cultivate the perfection of wisdom for the sake of producing the sense base of the eye;
nor should they cultivate the perfection of wisdom for the sake of producing the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind."
“World-Honored One!
How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva bring forth the perfection of wisdom so as not to bring forth the sense-sphere of the eye?”
“Is it for the sake of bringing about the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind that one should bring about the perfection of wisdom?
“Śāriputra! [It is not.]”

Because the sense base of the eye is without activity, without cessation, without arising, without ceasing, without formation, without destruction, without acquisition, without relinquishment, and because it lacks intrinsic nature, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice the perfection of wisdom not for the sake of producing the sense base of the eye.

Because the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are without activity, without cessation, without arising, without ceasing, without formation, without destruction, without acquisition, without relinquishment, and because they lack intrinsic nature, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice the perfection of wisdom not for the sake of producing the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not cultivate the perfection of wisdom for the sake of producing the sphere of form;
he should not cultivate the perfection of wisdom for the sake of producing the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental phenomena."
“World-Honored One!
How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva bring forth the perfection of wisdom without bringing forth the sphere of form?”
“Is it for the sake of bringing forth the spheres of sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena that one should bring forth the perfection of wisdom?
“Śāriputra! [The Buddha replied.]

Because the sphere of form is without activity, without cessation, without arising, without ceasing, without formation, without destruction, without attainment, without relinquishment, and because it lacks intrinsic nature, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice the perfection of wisdom not for the sake of producing the sphere of form;

because the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena are without activity, without cessation, without arising, without ceasing, without formation, without destruction, without attainment, without relinquishment, and because they lack intrinsic nature, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice the perfection of wisdom not for the sake of producing the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva should bring forth the perfection of wisdom not for the sake of bringing forth the eye-element;

he should bring forth the perfection of wisdom not for the sake of bringing forth the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, eye-contact, or the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition."
“World-Honored One!
How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva bring forth the perfection of wisdom without bringing forth the eye-element?”

Is it for the sake of not producing the form realm, the eye-consciousness element, eye-contact, and the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition that one should practice the perfection of wisdom?

“Śāriputra! Because the eye-element is without activity, without cessation, without arising, without ceasing, without formation, without destruction, without attainment, without relinquishment, and because it lacks intrinsic nature, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice the perfection of wisdom not for the sake of producing the eye-element.

Because the form-element, up to and including the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, are without activity, without cessation, without arising, without ceasing, without formation, without destruction, without attainment, without relinquishment, and lack intrinsic nature, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice the perfection of wisdom not for the sake of producing the form-element, up to and including the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition.”
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva should cultivate the perfection of wisdom not for the sake of producing the ear element,

nor for the sake of producing the sound element, the ear-consciousness element, ear-contact, or the various feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition. He should cultivate the perfection of wisdom [for the sake of realizing emptiness]."
“World-Honored One!
How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva bring forth the perfection of wisdom so as not to bring forth the sphere of the ear?”

Is it for the sake of not producing the sphere of sound, the sphere of auditory consciousness, ear-contact, and the various feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition that one should produce the perfection of wisdom?

“Śāriputra! Because the ear element is without activity and without cessation, without arising and without ceasing, without formation and without destruction, without acquisition and without relinquishment, and because it lacks intrinsic nature, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice the perfection of wisdom not for the sake of producing the ear element.

Because the sound element, and even the various feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition, are without activity and without cessation, without arising and without ceasing, without formation and without destruction, without acquisition and without relinquishment, and because they lack intrinsic nature, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice the perfection of wisdom not for the sake of producing the sound element, and even the various feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition.”
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva should bring forth the perfection of wisdom not for the sake of bringing forth the nose element;

they should bring forth the perfection of wisdom not for the sake of bringing forth the odor element, the nose-consciousness element, nose-contact, or the various feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition."
“World-Honored One!
How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva bring forth the perfection of wisdom without bringing forth the olfactory element?”

Is it for the sake of not giving rise to the fragrance element, the nose-consciousness element, nose-contact, and the various feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition that one should give rise to the perfection of wisdom?

“Śāriputra! Because the nose element (*ghrāṇadhātu*) is without activity, without cessation, without arising, without ceasing, without formation, without disintegration, without acquisition, without relinquishment, and because it lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), a bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) not for the sake of bringing forth the nose element.

Because the odor element (*gandhadhātu*) and even the various sensations produced with nose-contact as a condition are without activity, without cessation, without arising, without ceasing, without formation, without disintegration, without acquisition, without relinquishment, and because they lack intrinsic nature, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice the perfection of wisdom not for the sake of bringing forth the odor element and even the various sensations produced with nose-contact as a condition.”
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva should cultivate the perfection of wisdom not for the sake of producing the tongue element,

nor for the sake of producing the taste element, the tongue-consciousness element, tongue-contact, or the various feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition. One should cultivate the perfection of wisdom [for these reasons]."
“World-Honored One!
How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva bring forth the perfection of wisdom without bringing forth the tongue-element?”

Is it for the sake of producing the taste element, the tongue-consciousness element, tongue-contact, and the various feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition that one should produce the perfection of wisdom?

“Śāriputra! Because the tongue element is without activity, without cessation, without arising, without ceasing, without formation, without destruction, without attainment, without relinquishment, and because it lacks intrinsic nature, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, for the sake of not bringing forth the tongue element, should bring forth the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

Because the taste element, and even the various feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition, are without activity, without cessation, without arising, without ceasing, without formation, without destruction, without attainment, without relinquishment, and because they lack intrinsic nature, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, for the sake of not bringing forth the taste element and even the various feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition, should bring forth the perfection of wisdom.”
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva should bring forth the perfection of wisdom not for the sake of bringing forth the body element;

they should bring forth the perfection of wisdom not for the sake of bringing forth the touch element, the body-consciousness element, body-contact, or the various feelings produced with body-contact as a condition."
“World-Honored One!
How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva bring forth the perfection of wisdom so as not to bring forth the body-element?”

Is it for the sake of not giving rise to the sphere of tangibles, the sphere of body-consciousness, body-contact, and the various feelings produced with body-contact as a condition that one should give rise to the perfection of wisdom?

“Śāriputra! Because the body-element (*kāyadhātu*) is without activity, without cessation, without arising, without ceasing, without formation, without destruction, without acquisition, without relinquishment, and because it lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), a bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) not for the sake of producing the body-element.

Because the element of tangibility (*spraṣṭavyadhātu*) and even the various feelings produced with body-contact as a condition are without activity, without cessation, without arising, without ceasing, without formation, without destruction, without acquisition, without relinquishment, and because they lack intrinsic nature, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice the perfection of wisdom not for the sake of producing the element of tangibility and even the various feelings produced with body-contact as a condition.”
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva should bring forth the perfection of wisdom not for the sake of bringing forth the mind-element (manodhātu),

nor for the sake of bringing forth the dharma-element, the mind-consciousness-element (manovijñānadhātu), as well as mind-contact (manaḥsaṃsparśa) and the various feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition; rather, they should bring forth the perfection of wisdom."
“World-Honored One!
How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the perfection of wisdom so as not to bring about the manifestation of the mental faculty?”

Is it for the sake of not giving rise to the dharma-element, the consciousness-element, mental contact, and the various feelings produced with mental contact as a condition that one should give rise to the perfection of wisdom?

“Śāriputra! Because the mind-element (manodhātu) is without activity, without cessation, without arising, without ceasing, without formation, without destruction, without acquisition, without relinquishment, and because it lacks intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva), a bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) not for the sake of producing the mind-element.

Because the dharma-element (dharmadhātu) and even the various feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition are without activity, without cessation, without arising, without ceasing, without formation, without destruction, without acquisition, without relinquishment, and because they lack intrinsic nature, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice the perfection of wisdom not for the sake of producing the dharma-element and even the various feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition.”
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not cultivate the perfection of wisdom for the sake of producing the earth element;
he should not cultivate the perfection of wisdom for the sake of producing the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements."
“World-Honored One!
How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the perfection of wisdom so as not to bring about the production of the earth element?”
"Is it for the sake of bringing forth the elements of water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness that one should bring forth the perfection of wisdom?
"Śāriputra! [The Buddha replied:]

Because the earth element is without activity, without cessation, without arising, without ceasing, without formation, without destruction, without acquisition, without relinquishment, and without intrinsic nature, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice the perfection of wisdom not for the sake of producing the earth element;

because the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements are without activity, without cessation, without arising, without ceasing, without formation, without destruction, without acquisition, without relinquishment, and without intrinsic nature, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice the perfection of wisdom not for the sake of producing the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva should bring forth the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) not for the sake of bringing forth ignorance;

he should bring forth the perfection of wisdom not for the sake of bringing forth volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, existence, birth, or old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair."
“World-Honored One!
How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivate the perfection of wisdom so as not to bring about the production of ignorance?”

Is it for the sake of not producing volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair that one should produce the perfection of wisdom?

“Śāriputra! Because ignorance is without activity, without cessation, without arising, without ceasing, without formation, without destruction, without acquisition, without relinquishment, and because it lacks intrinsic nature, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, for the sake of not producing ignorance, should practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

Because volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) up to old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are without activity, without cessation, without arising, without ceasing, without formation, without destruction, without acquisition, without relinquishment, and because they lack intrinsic nature, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, for the sake of not producing volitional formations up to old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair, should practice the perfection of wisdom.”
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not cultivate the perfection of wisdom for the sake of inducing the perfection of giving;
nor should they cultivate the perfection of wisdom for the sake of inducing the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, or wisdom."
“World-Honored One!
How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva bring forth the perfection of wisdom without doing so for the sake of bringing forth the perfection of generosity?”
Should one bring forth the perfection of wisdom for the sake of bringing forth the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom?

“Śāriputra! Because the perfection of giving is without activity and without cessation, without arising and without ceasing, without formation and without disintegration, without attainment and without relinquishment, and because it lacks intrinsic nature, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, for the sake of bringing forth the perfection of giving, should bring forth the perfection of wisdom.

Because the perfections from ethical discipline up to wisdom are without activity and without cessation, without arising and without ceasing, without formation and without disintegration, without attainment and without relinquishment, and because they lack intrinsic nature, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, for the sake of bringing forth the perfections from ethical discipline up to wisdom, should bring forth the perfection of wisdom.”

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not cultivate the perfection of wisdom for the sake of bringing forth internal emptiness; nor should they cultivate the perfection of wisdom for the sake of bringing forth external emptiness,

internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, endless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential nature emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, or the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature."
“World-Honored One!
How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva bring forth the perfection of wisdom without bringing forth internal emptiness?”

Is it for the sake of not giving rise to the emptiness of the external, the emptiness of the internal and external, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate truth, the emptiness of the conditioned, the emptiness of the unconditioned, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, the emptiness of dispersion, the emptiness of non-alteration, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the emptiness of specific characteristics, the emptiness of common characteristics, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence that one should give rise to the perfection of wisdom?

“Śāriputra! Because internal emptiness is without activity, without cessation, without arising, without ceasing, without formation, without destruction, without attainment, without relinquishment, and because it lacks intrinsic nature, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of producing internal emptiness;

because external emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, is without activity, without cessation, without arising, without ceasing, without formation, without destruction, without attainment, without relinquishment, and because they lack intrinsic nature, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of producing external emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature.”
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva should bring forth the perfection of wisdom not for the sake of bringing forth suchness; nor for the sake of bringing forth the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu),

the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), non-falsity, immutability, equality, the state beyond birth, the fixed nature of phenomena, the stability of phenomena, the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), the realm of space, or the inconceivable realm, should they bring forth the perfection of wisdom."
“World-Honored One!
How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva bring forth the perfection of wisdom without bringing forth true suchness?”

Is it for the sake of bringing forth the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), non-falsity, immutability, equality, the state beyond birth, the fixed nature of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*), the stability of phenomena (*dharmasthititā*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the realm of space (*ākāśadhātu*), and the inconceivable realm (*acintyadhātu*) that one should bring forth the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*)?

“Śāriputra! Because true thusness (tathatā) is without activity, without cessation, without arising, without ceasing, without formation, without destruction, without attainment, without relinquishment, and because it lacks intrinsic nature, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of bringing forth true thusness; rather, they should practice the perfection of wisdom.

Because the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), up to the inconceivable realm, are without activity, without cessation, without arising, without ceasing, without formation, without destruction, without attainment, without relinquishment, and because they lack intrinsic nature, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of bringing forth the realm of phenomena, up to the inconceivable realm; rather, they should practice the perfection of wisdom.”
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not cultivate the perfection of wisdom for the sake of bringing forth the noble truth of suffering;
he should not cultivate the perfection of wisdom for the sake of bringing forth the noble truths of origin, cessation, or the path."
“World-Honored One!
How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva bring forth the perfection of wisdom without bringing forth the noble truth of suffering?”
“Is it for the sake of bringing forth the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path that one should bring forth the perfection of wisdom? “Śāriputra,

because the noble truth of suffering is without activity and without cessation, without arising and without ceasing, without formation and without destruction, without acquisition and without relinquishment, and because it lacks intrinsic nature, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should bring forth the perfection of wisdom not for the sake of bringing forth the noble truth of suffering.”

Because the noble truths of origination, cessation, and the path are without activity or stillness, without arising or ceasing, without formation or disintegration, without acquisition or relinquishment, and because they lack intrinsic nature, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice the perfection of wisdom not for the sake of bringing about the noble truths of origination, cessation, and the path.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva should bring forth the perfection of wisdom not for the sake of bringing forth the four dhyānas,
and should bring forth the perfection of wisdom not for the sake of bringing forth the four immeasurables or the four formless attainments."
“World-Honored One!
How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva bring forth the perfection of wisdom without bringing forth the four dhyānas?”
“Is it for the sake of bringing forth the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions that one should bring forth the perfection of wisdom? “Śāriputra!

Because the four dhyānas are without activity and without cessation, without arising and without ceasing, without formation and without destruction, without attainment and without relinquishment, and because they lack intrinsic nature, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of producing the four dhyānas;

because the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions are without activity and without cessation, without arising and without ceasing, without formation and without destruction, without attainment and without relinquishment, and because they lack intrinsic nature, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of producing the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions.
The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 172. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Part One: Praise of Prajñā, Chapter Thirty-Two, Part Two. "Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
A bodhisattva mahāsattva should bring forth the perfection of wisdom not for the sake of bringing forth the eight liberations,
nor for the sake of bringing forth the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, or the ten totalities.
“World-Honored One!
How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva bring forth the perfection of wisdom without bringing forth the eight liberations?”
"Is it not for the sake of bringing forth the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten universal bases that one should bring forth the perfection of wisdom? "Śāriputra!"

Because the eight liberations are without activity, without cessation, without arising, without ceasing, without formation, without destruction, without attainment, without relinquishment, and because they lack intrinsic nature, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should cultivate the perfection of wisdom not for the sake of producing the eight liberations.

Because the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten totalities are without activity, without cessation, without arising, without ceasing, without formation, without destruction, without attainment, without relinquishment, and because they lack intrinsic nature, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should cultivate the perfection of wisdom not for the sake of producing the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, or the ten totalities.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not cultivate the perfection of wisdom for the sake of bringing forth the four applications of mindfulness;

nor should he cultivate the perfection of wisdom for the sake of bringing forth the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the eightfold noble path."
“World-Honored One!
How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva bring forth the perfection of wisdom without bringing forth the four foundations of mindfulness?”

Is it for the sake of bringing forth the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path that one should bring forth the perfection of wisdom?

“Śāriputra! Because the four foundations of mindfulness are without activity and without cessation, without arising and without ceasing, without formation and without disintegration, without attainment and without relinquishment, and because they lack intrinsic nature, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, for the sake of not bringing forth the four foundations of mindfulness, should bring forth the perfection of wisdom.

Because the four right endeavors, up to and including the eight branches of the noble path, are without activity and without cessation, without arising and without ceasing, without formation and without disintegration, without attainment and without relinquishment, and because they lack intrinsic nature, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, for the sake of not bringing forth the four right endeavors up to and including the eight branches of the noble path, should bring forth the perfection of wisdom.”
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva should bring forth the perfection of wisdom not for the sake of bringing forth the gate of liberation that is emptiness,
nor for the sake of bringing forth the gates of liberation that are signlessness and wishlessness."
“World-Honored One!

How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva bring forth the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) without doing so for the sake of bringing forth the gate of liberation that is emptiness (śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha)?”
"Is it for the sake of not bringing forth the gateways to liberation of signlessness and wishlessness that one should bring forth the perfection of wisdom?
"Śāriputra! [The Buddha replied:]

Because the gate of liberation of emptiness is without activity and without cessation, without arising and without ceasing, without formation and without destruction, without attainment and without relinquishment, and because it lacks intrinsic nature, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not cultivate the perfection of wisdom for the sake of eliciting the gate of liberation of emptiness;

because the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness are without activity and without cessation, without arising and without ceasing, without formation and without destruction, without attainment and without relinquishment, and because they lack intrinsic nature, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not cultivate the perfection of wisdom for the sake of eliciting the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva should bring forth the perfection of wisdom not for the sake of bringing forth the five eyes,
nor for the sake of bringing forth the six supernormal powers."
“World-Honored One!
How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva bring forth the perfection of wisdom without bringing forth the five eyes?”
"Is it not for the sake of manifesting the six supernormal powers that one should manifest the perfection of wisdom?
