"This perfection of wisdom performs great and small deeds for the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and likewise performs great and small deeds for the unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment of the Buddhas;
it gathers and disperses the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and likewise gathers and disperses the unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment of the Buddhas."
They conceive of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas as finite or infinite, and likewise conceive of the Buddha’s unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment as finite or infinite;
they conceive of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas as vast or narrow, and likewise conceive of the Buddha’s unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment as vast or narrow;
they conceive of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas as powerful or powerless, and likewise conceive of the Buddha’s unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment as powerful or powerless.
“World-Honored One!
Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to such a notion, they are not practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, World-Honored One!”

If a newly trained bodhisattva mahāsattva, not relying on the perfections of wisdom, meditative concentration, diligence, patience, ethical discipline, and generosity, gives rise to such a thought as this:
"This perfection of wisdom makes all phenomena large or small, gathered or dispersed, finite or infinite, broad or narrow, powerful or powerless."
"World-Honored One!
Because this bodhisattva-mahāsattva gives rise to such a notion, they are not practicing the perfection of wisdom. Why is this?"
“World-Honored One!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to such a thought as this:

‘This prajñāpāramitā, with respect to form, whether it makes it large or small, or does not make it large or small; with respect to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, whether it makes them large or small, or does not make them large or small;’”

Whether one conceives of form as being gathered or dispersed, or does not conceive of it as being gathered or dispersed; whether one conceives of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as being gathered or dispersed, or does not conceive of them as being gathered or dispersed;

whether one conceives of form as being finite or infinite, or does not conceive of it as being finite or infinite; whether one conceives of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as being finite or infinite, or does not conceive of them as being finite or infinite;

whether one conceives of form as being broad or narrow, or does not conceive of it as being broad or narrow; whether one conceives of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as being broad or narrow, or does not conceive of them as being broad or narrow.

Whether one regards form as having power or lacking power, or does not regard it as having power or lacking power; whether one regards feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness as having power or lacking power, or does not regard them as having power or lacking power.
“World-Honored One!
All such things as these are not the outflow-results (*niṣyanda-phala*) of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Furthermore, World-Honored One!”
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to such a thought:

"This prajñāpāramitā, with respect to the sense base of the eye, whether it be made large or not made large; with respect to the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, whether they be made large or not made large;

with respect to the sense base of the eye, whether it be made to accumulate or disperse, or not made to accumulate or disperse; with respect to the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, whether they be made to accumulate or disperse, or not made to accumulate or disperse;"

Regarding the sense base of the eye, whether one conceives of it as finite or infinite, or does not conceive of it as finite or infinite; regarding the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, whether one conceives of them as finite or infinite, or does not conceive of them as finite or infinite;

regarding the sense base of the eye, whether one conceives of it as broad or narrow, or does not conceive of it as broad or narrow; regarding the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, whether one conceives of them as broad or narrow, or does not conceive of them as broad or narrow;

regarding the sense base of the eye, whether one conceives of it as powerful or powerless, or does not conceive of it as powerful or powerless; regarding the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, whether one conceives of them as powerful or powerless, or does not conceive of them as powerful or powerless.
"World-Honored One!
All such things as these are not the outflow fruits of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Furthermore, World-Honored One!"
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to such a thought as this:

"This prajñāpāramitā, regarding the sphere of form, whether it makes it large or small, or does not make it large or small; regarding the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena, whether it makes them large or small, or does not make them large or small;

regarding the sphere of form, whether it makes it accumulate or disperse, or does not make it accumulate or disperse; regarding the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena, whether it makes them accumulate or disperse, or does not make them accumulate or disperse;"

Regarding the sphere of visible forms (*rūpāyatana*), whether one conceives of them as finite or infinite, or does not conceive of them as finite or infinite; regarding the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibles, and mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*), whether one conceives of them as finite or infinite, or does not conceive of them as finite or infinite;

regarding the sphere of visible forms, whether one conceives of them as broad or narrow, or does not conceive of them as broad or narrow; regarding the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibles, and mental phenomena, whether one conceives of them as broad or narrow, or does not conceive of them as broad or narrow;

regarding the sphere of visible forms, whether one conceives of them as powerful or powerless, or does not conceive of them as powerful or powerless; regarding the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibles, and mental phenomena, whether one conceives of them as powerful or powerless, or does not conceive of them as powerful or powerless.
"World-Honored One!
All such things as these are not the outflow fruits (*niṣyanda-phala*) of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Furthermore, World-Honored One!"
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to such a notion as this:

"This *prajñāpāramitā* either makes the eye-element large or small, or does not make it large or small; [likewise] regarding the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, and eye-contact, as well as the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, it either makes them large or small, or does not make them large or small;

regarding the eye-element, it either makes it accumulated or dispersed, or does not make it accumulated or dispersed; [likewise] regarding the form-element up to the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, it either makes them accumulated or dispersed, or does not make them accumulated or dispersed."

Regarding the eye-element, whether one conceives it as finite or infinite, or does not conceive it as finite or infinite; regarding the form-element, up to and including the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, whether one conceives them as finite or infinite, or does not conceive them as finite or infinite;

regarding the eye-element, whether one conceives it as broad or narrow, or does not conceive it as broad or narrow; regarding the form-element, up to and including the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, whether one conceives them as broad or narrow, or does not conceive them as broad or narrow;

regarding the eye-element, whether one conceives it as powerful or powerless, or does not conceive it as powerful or powerless; regarding the form-element, up to and including the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, whether one conceives them as powerful or powerless, or does not conceive them as powerful or powerless.
"World-Honored One!
All such things as these are not the outflow-fruits (*niṣyanda-phala*) of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Furthermore, World-Honored One!"
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to such a conception as this:

"This *prajñāpāramitā* either makes the ear-element large or small, or does not make it large or small; it either makes the sound-element, the ear-consciousness-element, and ear-contact, as well as the various feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition, large or small, or does not make them large or small;

it either makes the ear-element accumulate or disperse, or does not make it accumulate or disperse; it likewise either makes the sound-element, up to the various feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition, accumulate or disperse, or does not make them accumulate or disperse."

Regarding the ear-element (*śrotra-dhātu*), whether one conceives it as finite or infinite, or does not conceive it as finite or infinite; regarding the sound-element (*śabda-dhātu*) and even the various feelings produced with ear-contact (*śrotra-saṃsparśa-pratyaya-utpanna-vedanā*) as conditions, whether one conceives them as finite or infinite, or does not conceive them as finite or infinite;

regarding the ear-element, whether one conceives it as broad or narrow, or does not conceive it as broad or narrow; regarding the sound-element and even the various feelings produced with ear-contact as conditions, whether one conceives them as broad or narrow, or does not conceive them as broad or narrow;

regarding the ear-element, whether one conceives it as powerful or powerless, or does not conceive it as powerful or powerless; regarding the sound-element and even the various feelings produced with ear-contact as conditions, whether one conceives them as powerful or powerless, or does not conceive them as powerful or powerless.
“World-Honored One!
All such things as these are not the outflow-results (*niṣyanda-phala*) of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Furthermore, World-Honored One!”
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to such a conception as this:

"This prajñāpāramitā, regarding the nose element (*ghrāṇadhātu*), whether it makes it large or small, or does not make it large or small; regarding the odor element (*gandhadhātu*), the nose-consciousness element (*ghrāṇavijñānadhātu*), nose-contact (*ghrāṇasparśa*), and the various feelings (*vedanā*) produced with nose-contact as condition, whether they make them large or small, or do not make them large or small;

regarding the nose element, whether it makes it a collection or a dispersion, or does not make it a collection or a dispersion; regarding the odor element, up to the various feelings produced with nose-contact as condition, whether they make them a collection or a dispersion, or do not make them a collection or a dispersion;"

Regarding the nose element (*ghrāṇadhātu*), whether one conceives it as finite or infinite, or does not conceive it as finite or infinite; regarding the odor element (*gandhadhātu*) up to the various feelings produced with nose-contact as condition (*ghrāṇasparśapratyayaja-vedanā*), whether one conceives them as finite or infinite, or does not conceive them as finite or infinite;

regarding the nose element, whether one conceives it as broad or narrow, or does not conceive it as broad or narrow; regarding the odor element up to the various feelings produced with nose-contact as condition, whether one conceives them as broad or narrow, or does not conceive them as broad or narrow;

regarding the nose element, whether one conceives it as powerful or powerless, or does not conceive it as powerful or powerless; regarding the odor element up to the various feelings produced with nose-contact as condition, whether one conceives them as powerful or powerless, or does not conceive them as powerful or powerless.
"World-Honored One!
All such things as these are not the outflow-fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*) of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Furthermore, World-Honored One!"
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to such a thought:

"This prajñāpāramitā, with respect to the tongue-element, whether it makes it large or small, or does not make it large or small; with respect to the taste-element, the tongue-consciousness-element, tongue-contact, and the various feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition, whether it makes them large or small, or does not make them large or small;

with respect to the tongue-element, whether it makes it accumulate or disperse, or does not make it accumulate or disperse; and with respect to the taste-element up to the various feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition, whether it makes them accumulate or disperse, or does not make them accumulate or disperse;"

Regarding the tongue element (*jihvā-dhātu*), whether one conceives it as finite or infinite, or does not conceive it as finite or infinite; regarding the taste element (*rasa-dhātu*) up to the various feelings (*vedanā*) produced with tongue-contact (*jihvā-saṃsparśa*) as a condition, whether one conceives them as finite or infinite, or does not conceive them as finite or infinite;

regarding the tongue element, whether one conceives it as broad or narrow, or does not conceive it as broad or narrow; regarding the taste element up to the various feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition, whether one conceives them as broad or narrow, or does not conceive them as broad or narrow;

regarding the tongue element, whether one conceives it as powerful or powerless, or does not conceive it as powerful or powerless; regarding the taste element up to the various feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition, whether one conceives them as powerful or powerless, or does not conceive them as powerful or powerless.
"World-Honored One!
All such things as these are not the outflow-fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*) of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Furthermore, World-Honored One!"
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to such a thought:

"This prajñāpāramitā, regarding the body-element (*kāyadhātu*), whether it be made large or not made large; regarding the touch-element (*spraṣṭavyadhātu*), the body-consciousness-element (*kāyavijñānadhātu*), and body-contact (*kāyasparśa*), as well as all feelings (*vedanā*) produced with body-contact as a condition, whether they be made large or not made large;

regarding the body-element, whether it be made to gather or disperse, or not made to gather or disperse; regarding the touch-element up to all feelings produced with body-contact as a condition, whether they be made to gather or disperse, or not made to gather or disperse;"

Regarding the body element (*kāyadhātu*), whether one conceives it as finite or infinite, or does not conceive it as finite or infinite; regarding the contact element (*spraṣṭavyadhātu*) up to the various sensations produced with body-contact as a condition, whether one conceives them as finite or infinite, or does not conceive them as finite or infinite;

regarding the body element, whether one conceives it as broad or narrow, or does not conceive it as broad or narrow; regarding the contact element up to the various sensations produced with body-contact as a condition, whether one conceives them as broad or narrow, or does not conceive them as broad or narrow;

regarding the body element, whether one conceives it as powerful or powerless, or does not conceive it as powerful or powerless; regarding the contact element up to the various sensations produced with body-contact as a condition, whether one conceives them as powerful or powerless, or does not conceive them as powerful or powerless.
"World-Honored One!
All such things as these are not the outflow-fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*) of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Furthermore, World-Honored One!"
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to such a thought as this:

"Regarding this *prajñāpāramitā*, whether one conceives of the mind-element (*manodhātu*) as large or not large; whether one conceives of the dharma-element, the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*), and mental contact (*manaḥsaṃsparśa*), as well as the various feelings produced with mental contact as their condition, as large or not large;

whether one conceives of the mind-element as accumulating or dispersing, or does not conceive of it as accumulating or dispersing; and whether one conceives of the dharma-element, up to the various feelings produced with mental contact as their condition, as accumulating or dispersing, or does not conceive of them as accumulating or dispersing;"

Regarding the mind-element (*manodhātu*), whether one conceives it as finite or infinite, or does not conceive it as finite or infinite; regarding the mental-object-element (*dharmadhātu*) and even the various feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition (*manasparśapratyayaja-vedanā*), whether one conceives them as finite or infinite, or does not conceive them as finite or infinite;

regarding the mind-element, whether one conceives it as broad or narrow, or does not conceive it as broad or narrow; regarding the mental-object-element and even the various feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition, whether one conceives them as broad or narrow, or does not conceive them as broad or narrow;

regarding the mind-element, whether one conceives it as powerful or powerless, or does not conceive it as powerful or powerless; regarding the mental-object-element and even the various feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition, whether one conceives them as powerful or powerless, or does not conceive them as powerful or powerless.
"World-Honored One!
All such things as these are not the outflow fruits (*niṣyanda-phala*) of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Furthermore, World-Honored One!"
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to such a conception as this:

"This *prajñāpāramitā* either makes the earth element large or small, or does not make it large or small; it either makes the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements large or small, or does not make them large or small;

it either causes the earth element to gather or disperse, or does not cause it to gather or disperse; it either causes the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements to gather or disperse, or does not cause them to gather or disperse."

Regarding the earth element, whether one conceives of it as finite or infinite, or does not conceive of it as finite or infinite; regarding the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements, whether one conceives of them as finite or infinite, or does not conceive of them as finite or infinite;

regarding the earth element, whether one conceives of it as broad or narrow, or does not conceive of it as broad or narrow; regarding the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements, whether one conceives of them as broad or narrow, or does not conceive of them as broad or narrow;

regarding the earth element, whether one conceives of it as powerful or powerless, or does not conceive of it as powerful or powerless; regarding the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements, whether one conceives of them as powerful or powerless, or does not conceive of them as powerful or powerless.
"World-Honored One!
All such things as these are not the outflow-fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*) of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Furthermore, World-Honored One!"
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to such a conception as this:

"This *prajñāpāramitā* either makes ignorance large or small, or does not make it large or small; [it likewise] either makes volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), feeling (*vedanā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), becoming (*bhava*), birth (*jāti*), and old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair large or small, or does not make them large or small;

[it likewise] either causes ignorance to gather or disperse, or does not cause it to gather or disperse; [and so on] up to causing old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair to gather or disperse, or not causing them to gather or disperse."

Regarding ignorance, whether one conceives it as finite or infinite, or does not conceive it as finite or infinite; regarding formations up to old age, death, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair, whether one conceives them as finite or infinite, or does not conceive them as finite or infinite;

regarding ignorance, whether one conceives it as broad or narrow, or does not conceive it as broad or narrow; regarding formations up to old age, death, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair, whether one conceives them as broad or narrow, or does not conceive them as broad or narrow;

regarding ignorance, whether one conceives it as powerful or powerless, or does not conceive it as powerful or powerless; regarding formations up to old age, death, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair, whether one conceives them as powerful or powerless, or does not conceive them as powerful or powerless.
"World-Honored One!
All such things as these are not the outflow-fruits (*niṣyanda-phala*) of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Furthermore, World-Honored One!"
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to such a thought:

"This perfection of wisdom, whether it makes the perfection of giving large or small, or does not make it large or small; whether it makes the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom large or small, or does not make them large or small;

whether it makes the perfection of giving accumulate or disperse, or does not make it accumulate or disperse; and whether it makes the perfections from ethical discipline up to wisdom accumulate or disperse, or does not make them accumulate or disperse;"

Regarding the perfection of generosity, whether one conceives of it as finite or infinite, or does not conceive of it as finite or infinite; regarding the perfections from ethical discipline up to wisdom, whether one conceives of them as finite or infinite, or does not conceive of them as finite or infinite;

regarding the perfection of generosity, whether one conceives of it as broad or narrow, or does not conceive of it as broad or narrow; regarding the perfections from ethical discipline up to wisdom, whether one conceives of them as broad or narrow, or does not conceive of them as broad or narrow;

regarding the perfection of generosity, whether one conceives of it as powerful or powerless, or does not conceive of it as powerful or powerless; regarding the perfections from ethical discipline up to wisdom, whether one conceives of them as powerful or powerless, or does not conceive of them as powerful or powerless.
"World-Honored One!
All such things as these are not the outflow fruits (*niṣyanda-phala*) of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Furthermore, World-Honored One!"
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to such a thought as this:

"This prajñāpāramitā, regarding internal emptiness, whether it be made large or not made large; regarding external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-altering emptiness, essential emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common-characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all dharmas, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature—whether these be made large or not made large;"

Whether one conceives of inner emptiness as having accumulation or dispersion, or does not conceive of it as having accumulation or dispersion; whether one conceives of outer emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, as having accumulation or dispersion, or does not conceive of it as having accumulation or dispersion;

whether one conceives of inner emptiness as being finite or infinite, or does not conceive of it as being finite or infinite; whether one conceives of outer emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, as being finite or infinite, or does not conceive of it as being finite or infinite;

whether one conceives of inner emptiness as being broad or narrow, or does not conceive of it as being broad or narrow; whether one conceives of outer emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, as being broad or narrow, or does not conceive of it as being broad or narrow; [in all these cases, there is no difference].

Whether one considers inner emptiness as having power or lacking power, or whether one does not consider it as having power or lacking power; and whether one considers outer emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence, as having power or lacking power, or whether one does not consider them as having power or lacking power.
“World-Honored One!
This is because all such things are not the outflow-fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*) of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
[The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Scroll 177, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree; First Division, Chapter 32 on Praising Prajñā, Part 7] ‘Furthermore, World-Honored One!’”
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to such a thought:

"This *prajñāpāramitā* either makes the *tathatā* large or small, or does not make it large or small; [likewise] regarding the *dharmadhātu*, *dharmatā*, non-erroneous nature, unchanging nature, equality, nature free from birth, fixedness of dharma, stability of dharma, the limit of reality, the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm, it either makes them large or small, or does not make them large or small;

[likewise] regarding the *tathatā* it either makes it accumulated or dispersed, or does not make it accumulated or dispersed; [likewise] regarding the *dharmadhātu* up to the inconceivable realm, it either makes them accumulated or dispersed, or does not make them accumulated or dispersed."

Regarding the *tathatā*, whether one conceives it as finite or infinite, or does not conceive it as finite or infinite; regarding the *dharmadhātu* up to the inconceivable realm (*acintyadhātu*), whether one conceives them as finite or infinite, or does not conceive them as finite or infinite;

regarding the *tathatā*, whether one conceives it as broad or narrow, or does not conceive it as broad or narrow; regarding the *dharmadhātu* up to the inconceivable realm, whether one conceives them as broad or narrow, or does not conceive them as broad or narrow;

regarding the *tathatā*, whether one conceives it as having power or lacking power, or does not conceive it as having power or lacking power; regarding the *dharmadhātu* up to the inconceivable realm, whether one conceives them as having power or lacking power, or does not conceive them as having power or lacking power.
“World-Honored One!
All such things as these are not the outflow fruits (*niṣyanda-phala*) of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Furthermore, World-Honored One!”
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to such a thought as this:

"This prajñāpāramitā, regarding the noble truth of suffering, whether it be made large or small, or not made large or small; regarding the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path, whether they be made large or small, or not made large or small;

regarding the noble truth of suffering, whether it be made accumulated or dispersed, or not made accumulated or dispersed; regarding the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path, whether they be made accumulated or dispersed, or not made accumulated or dispersed;"

Regarding the noble truth of suffering, whether one conceives of it as finite or infinite, or does not conceive of it as finite or infinite; regarding the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path, whether one conceives of them as finite or infinite, or does not conceive of them as finite or infinite;

regarding the noble truth of suffering, whether one conceives of it as broad or narrow, or does not conceive of it as broad or narrow; regarding the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path, whether one conceives of them as broad or narrow, or does not conceive of them as broad or narrow;

regarding the noble truth of suffering, whether one conceives of it as powerful or powerless, or does not conceive of it as powerful or powerless; regarding the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path, whether one conceives of them as powerful or powerless, or does not conceive of them as powerful or powerless.
"World-Honored One!
All such things as these are not the outflow-fruits (*niṣyanda-phala*) of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Furthermore, World-Honored One!"
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to such a thought:

"This prajñāpāramitā, regarding the four dhyānas, whether it makes them large or small, or does not make them large or small; regarding the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments, whether it makes them large or small, or does not make them large or small;

regarding the four dhyānas, whether it makes them accumulate or disperse, or does not make them accumulate or disperse; regarding the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments, whether it makes them accumulate or disperse, or does not make them accumulate or disperse..."

Regarding the four dhyānas, whether they are made finite or infinite, or not made finite or infinite; regarding the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments, whether they are made finite or infinite, or not made finite or infinite;

regarding the four dhyānas, whether they are made broad or narrow, or not made broad or narrow; regarding the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments, whether they are made broad or narrow, or not made broad or narrow;

regarding the four dhyānas, whether they are made powerful or powerless, or not made powerful or powerless; regarding the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments, whether they are made powerful or powerless, or not made powerful or powerless.
"World-Honored One!
All such things as these are not the outflow fruits of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Furthermore, World-Honored One!"
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to such a thought:

"This prajñāpāramitā, regarding the eight liberations, whether it conceives of them as large or small, or does not conceive of them as large or small; regarding the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten universal bases, whether it conceives of them as large or small, or does not conceive of them as large or small;

regarding the eight liberations, whether it conceives of them as gathering or dispersing, or does not conceive of them as gathering or dispersing; regarding the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten universal bases, whether it conceives of them as gathering or dispersing, or does not conceive of them as gathering or dispersing..."

Regarding the eight liberations, whether one conceives of them as finite or infinite, or does not conceive of them as finite or infinite; regarding the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities, whether one conceives of them as finite or infinite, or does not conceive of them as finite or infinite;

regarding the eight liberations, whether one conceives of them as broad or narrow, or does not conceive of them as broad or narrow; regarding the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities, whether one conceives of them as broad or narrow, or does not conceive of them as broad or narrow;

regarding the eight liberations, whether one conceives of them as powerful or powerless, or does not conceive of them as powerful or powerless; regarding the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities, whether one conceives of them as powerful or powerless, or does not conceive of them as powerful or powerless.
"World-Honored One!
All such things as these are not the outflow-fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*) of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Furthermore, World-Honored One!"
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to such a thought as this:

"This prajñāpāramitā, regarding the four foundations of mindfulness, whether it makes them large or small, or does not make them large or small; regarding the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path, whether it makes them large or small, or does not make them large or small;

regarding the four foundations of mindfulness, whether it causes their accumulation or dispersal, or does not cause their accumulation or dispersal; regarding the four right efforts up to the eightfold noble path, whether it causes their accumulation or dispersal, or does not cause their accumulation or dispersal;"

Regarding the four foundations of mindfulness, whether one conceives of them as limited or unlimited, or does not conceive of them as limited or unlimited; regarding the four right efforts up to the eight factors of the noble path, whether one conceives of them as limited or unlimited, or does not conceive of them as limited or unlimited;

regarding the four foundations of mindfulness, whether one conceives of them as narrow or broad, or does not conceive of them as narrow or broad; regarding the four right efforts up to the eight factors of the noble path, whether one conceives of them as narrow or broad, or does not conceive of them as narrow or broad;

regarding the four foundations of mindfulness, whether one conceives of them as powerful or powerless, or does not conceive of them as powerful or powerless; regarding the four right efforts up to the eight factors of the noble path, whether one conceives of them as powerful or powerless, or does not conceive of them as powerful or powerless.
"World-Honored One!
All such things as these are not the outflow fruits (*niṣyanda-phala*) of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Furthermore, World-Honored One!"
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to such a thought as this:

"This prajñāpāramitā, regarding the gate of liberation of emptiness, whether it be made large or small, or not made large or small; regarding the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness, whether they be made large or small, or not made large or small;

regarding the gate of liberation of emptiness, whether it be made to accumulate or disperse, or not made to accumulate or disperse; regarding the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness, whether they be made to accumulate or disperse, or not made to accumulate or disperse;"

Regarding the gate of liberation of emptiness, whether one conceives of it as finite or infinite, or does not conceive of it as finite or infinite; regarding the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness, whether one conceives of them as finite or infinite, or does not conceive of them as finite or infinite;

regarding the gate of liberation of emptiness, whether one conceives of it as broad or narrow, or does not conceive of it as broad or narrow; regarding the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness, whether one conceives of them as broad or narrow, or does not conceive of them as broad or narrow;

regarding the gate of liberation of emptiness, whether one conceives of it as powerful or powerless, or does not conceive of it as powerful or powerless; regarding the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness, whether one conceives of them as powerful or powerless, or does not conceive of them as powerful or powerless.
"World-Honored One!
All such things as these are not the outflow-fruits (*niṣyanda-phala*) of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Furthermore, World-Honored One!"
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to such a thought as this:

"This prajñāpāramitā, regarding the five eyes, whether it makes them large or small, or does not make them large or small; regarding the six supernormal powers, whether it makes them large or small, or does not make them large or small;

regarding the five eyes, whether it makes them gather or disperse, or does not make them gather or disperse; regarding the six supernormal powers, whether it makes them gather or disperse, or does not make them gather or disperse;"

Regarding the five eyes, whether one conceives of them as finite or infinite, or does not conceive of them as finite or infinite; regarding the six supernormal powers, whether one conceives of them as finite or infinite, or does not conceive of them as finite or infinite;

regarding the five eyes, whether one conceives of them as broad or narrow, or does not conceive of them as broad or narrow; regarding the six supernormal powers, whether one conceives of them as broad or narrow, or does not conceive of them as broad or narrow;

regarding the five eyes, whether one conceives of them as powerful or powerless, or does not conceive of them as powerful or powerless; regarding the six supernormal powers, whether one conceives of them as powerful or powerless, or does not conceive of them as powerful or powerless.
“World-Honored One!
All such things as these are not the outflow-results (*niṣyanda-phala*) of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Furthermore, World-Honored One!”
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to such a thought as this:

"This *prajñāpāramitā* either makes the ten powers of a Buddha large or small, or does not make them large or small; it either makes the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha large or small, or does not make them large or small;

it either causes the ten powers of a Buddha to gather or disperse, or does not cause them to gather or disperse; it likewise either causes the four fearlessnesses up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha to gather or disperse, or does not cause them to gather or disperse."

Whether one conceives of the ten powers of a Buddha as finite or infinite, or does not conceive of them as finite or infinite; whether one conceives of the four fearlessnesses up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha as finite or infinite, or does not conceive of them as finite or infinite;

whether one conceives of the ten powers of a Buddha as broad or narrow, or does not conceive of them as broad or narrow; whether one conceives of the four fearlessnesses up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha as broad or narrow, or does not conceive of them as broad or narrow;
whether one conceives of the ten powers of a Buddha as powerful or powerless, or does not conceive of them as powerful or powerless; [it is likewise for the other qualities].
"World-Honored One!
All such things as these are not the outflow fruits (*niṣyanda-phala*) of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Furthermore, World-Honored One!"
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to such a thought as this:

"This prajñāpāramitā, regarding the quality of non-forgetfulness, whether it be made large or small, or not made large or small; regarding the state of constant equanimity, whether it be made large or small, or not made large or small;

regarding the quality of non-forgetfulness, whether it be made to accumulate or disperse, or not made to accumulate or disperse; regarding the state of constant equanimity, whether it be made to accumulate or disperse, or not made to accumulate or disperse;"

Regarding the quality of non-forgetfulness (*asaṃpramoṣadharma*), whether one conceives of it as finite or infinite, or does not conceive of it as finite or infinite; regarding the state of constant equanimity (*upekṣā*), whether one conceives of it as finite or infinite, or does not conceive of it as finite or infinite;

regarding the quality of non-forgetfulness, whether one conceives of it as broad or narrow, or does not conceive of it as broad or narrow; regarding the state of constant equanimity, whether one conceives of it as broad or narrow, or does not conceive of it as broad or narrow;

regarding the quality of non-forgetfulness, whether one conceives of it as powerful or powerless, or does not conceive of it as powerful or powerless; regarding the state of constant equanimity, whether one conceives of it as powerful or powerless, or does not conceive of it as powerful or powerless.
“World-Honored One!
All such things as these are not the outflow-fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*) of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Furthermore, World-Honored One!”
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to such a thought as this:

"This prajñāpāramitā, whether it makes all-knowledge large or small, or does not make it large or small; whether it makes the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects large or small, or does not make them large or small;

whether it makes all-knowledge accumulate or disperse, or does not make it accumulate or disperse; whether it makes the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects accumulate or disperse, or does not make them accumulate or disperse;"

Regarding all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), whether one conceives of it as finite or infinite, or does not conceive of it as finite or infinite; regarding the knowledge of the paths (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), whether one conceives of them as finite or infinite, or does not conceive of them as finite or infinite;

regarding all-knowledge, whether one conceives of it as broad or narrow, or does not conceive of it as broad or narrow; regarding the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects, whether one conceives of them as broad or narrow, or does not conceive of them as broad or narrow;

regarding all-knowledge, whether one conceives of it as powerful or powerless, or does not conceive of it as powerful or powerless; regarding the knowledge of the paths and the knowledge of all aspects, whether one conceives of them as powerful or powerless, or does not conceive of them as powerful or powerless.
"World-Honored One!
All such things as these are not the outflow-fruits (*niṣyanda-phala*) of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Furthermore, World-Honored One!"
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to such a thought as this:

"This prajñāpāramitā, regarding all dhāraṇī-doors, whether it makes them large or small, or does not make them large or small; regarding all samādhi-doors, whether it makes them large or small, or does not make them large or small;

regarding all dhāraṇī-doors, whether it makes them accumulate or disperse, or does not make them accumulate or disperse; regarding all samādhi-doors, whether it makes them accumulate or disperse, or does not make them accumulate or disperse;"

Regarding all *dhāraṇī* gates, whether they are made finite or infinite, or not made finite or infinite; regarding all *samādhi* gates, whether they are made finite or infinite, or not made finite or infinite;
regarding all *dhāraṇī* gates, whether they are made broad or narrow, or not made broad or narrow; regarding all *samādhi* gates, whether they are made broad or narrow, or not made broad or narrow;

regarding all *dhāraṇī* gates, whether they are made powerful or powerless, or not made powerful or powerless; regarding all *samādhi* gates, whether they are made powerful or powerless, or not made powerful or powerless.
"World-Honored One!
All such things as these are not the outflow-fruits (niṣyanda-phala) of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Furthermore, World-Honored One!"
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to such a perception as this:

"This prajñāpāramitā, regarding a stream-enterer, whether it makes them large or small, or does not make them large or small; regarding a once-returner, a non-returner, or an arhat, whether it makes them large or small, or does not make them large or small;

regarding a stream-enterer, whether it causes their gathering or dispersal, or does not cause their gathering or dispersal; regarding a once-returner, a non-returner, or an arhat, whether it causes their gathering or dispersal, or does not cause their gathering or dispersal;"

Regarding the stream-enterer, whether one conceives of them as finite or infinite, or does not conceive of them as finite or infinite; regarding the once-returner, the non-returner, and the arhat, whether one conceives of them as finite or infinite, or does not conceive of them as finite or infinite;

regarding the stream-enterer, whether one conceives of them as broad or narrow, or does not conceive of them as broad or narrow; regarding the once-returner, the non-returner, and the arhat, whether one conceives of them as broad or narrow, or does not conceive of them as broad or narrow;

regarding the stream-enterer, whether one conceives of them as powerful or powerless, or does not conceive of them as powerful or powerless; regarding the once-returner, the non-returner, and the arhat, whether one conceives of them as powerful or powerless, or does not conceive of them as powerful or powerless.
"World-Honored One!
All such things as these are not the outflow-fruits of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Furthermore, World-Honored One!"
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to such a conception as this:

"This *prajñāpāramitā* either makes the stage of entering the stream (*srotāpatti-pratipannaka*) and the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*) large or small, or does not make them large or small; it either makes the stage of entering once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmi-pratipannaka*) and the fruit of once-returning, the stage of entering non-returning (*anāgāmi-pratipannaka*) and the fruit of non-returning, and the stage of entering arhatship (*arhattva-pratipannaka*) and the fruit of arhatship large or small, or does not make them large or small;

it either causes the stage of entering the stream and the fruit of stream-entry to accumulate or disperse, or does not cause them to accumulate or disperse; and it either causes the stage of entering once-returning up to the fruit of arhatship to accumulate or disperse, or does not cause them to accumulate or disperse."

Regarding the stage of entering the stream and the fruit of stream-entry, whether one conceives them as finite or infinite, or does not conceive them as finite or infinite; regarding the stage of entering once-returning up to the fruit of arhatship, whether one conceives them as finite or infinite, or does not conceive them as finite or infinite;

regarding the stage of entering the stream and the fruit of stream-entry, whether one conceives them as broad or narrow, or does not conceive them as broad or narrow; regarding the stage of entering once-returning up to the fruit of arhatship, whether one conceives them as broad or narrow, or does not conceive them as broad or narrow;

regarding the stage of entering the stream and the fruit of stream-entry, whether one conceives them as powerful or powerless, or does not conceive them as powerful or powerless; regarding the stage of entering once-returning up to the fruit of arhatship, whether one conceives them as powerful or powerless, or does not conceive them as powerful or powerless.
“World-Honored One!
All such things as these are not the outflow-results (*niṣyanda-phala*) of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Furthermore, World-Honored One!”
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to such a thought as this:

"This prajñāpāramitā, whether it conceives of a solitary realizer as large or small, or does not conceive of them as large or small; whether it conceives of the enlightenment of a solitary realizer as large or small, or does not conceive of it as large or small;

whether it conceives of a solitary realizer as gathering or dispersing, or does not conceive of them as gathering or dispersing; whether it conceives of the enlightenment of a solitary realizer as gathering or dispersing, or does not conceive of it as gathering or dispersing;"

Whether one conceives of the pratyekabuddha as finite or infinite, or does not conceive of him as finite or infinite; whether one conceives of the awakening of a pratyekabuddha as finite or infinite, or does not conceive of it as finite or infinite;

whether one conceives of the pratyekabuddha as broad or narrow, or does not conceive of him as broad or narrow; whether one conceives of the awakening of a pratyekabuddha as broad or narrow, or does not conceive of it as broad or narrow;

whether one conceives of the pratyekabuddha as powerful or powerless, or does not conceive of him as powerful or powerless; whether one conceives of the awakening of a pratyekabuddha as powerful or powerless, or does not conceive of it as powerful or powerless.
"World-Honored One!
All such things as these are not the outflow-fruits (*niṣyanda-phala*) of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Furthermore, World-Honored One!"
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva gives rise to such a conception as this:

"This *prajñāpāramitā* either makes the bodhisattva-mahāsattva great or small, or does not make the bodhisattva-mahāsattva great or small; it either makes the practice of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva great or small, or does not make the practice of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva great or small;

it either makes the bodhisattva-mahāsattva accumulate or disperse, or does not make the bodhisattva-mahāsattva accumulate or disperse; it either makes the practice of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva accumulate or disperse, or does not make the practice of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva accumulate or disperse."

Whether one conceives of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva as finite or infinite, or does not conceive of him as finite or infinite; whether one conceives of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s practice as finite or infinite, or does not conceive of it as finite or infinite;

whether one conceives of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva as broad or narrow, or does not conceive of him as broad or narrow; whether one conceives of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s practice as broad or narrow, or does not conceive of it as broad or narrow;

whether one conceives of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva as powerful or powerless, or does not conceive of him as powerful or powerless; whether one conceives of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s practice as powerful or powerless, or does not conceive of it as powerful or powerless.
“World-Honored One!
All such things as these are not the outflow-fruits (*niṣyanda-phala*) of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Furthermore, World-Honored One!”
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to such a thought as this:

"This prajñāpāramitā, whether it makes the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas large or small, or does not make them large or small; whether it makes the Buddha’s unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment large or small, or does not make it large or small;

whether it makes the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas accumulate or disperse, or does not make them accumulate or disperse; whether it makes the Buddha’s unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment accumulate or disperse, or does not make it accumulate or disperse..."

Whether one conceives of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas as finite or infinite, or does not conceive of them as finite or infinite; whether one conceives of the Buddha’s unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment as finite or infinite, or does not conceive of it as finite or infinite;

whether one conceives of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas as broad or narrow, or does not conceive of them as broad or narrow; whether one conceives of the Buddha’s unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment as broad or narrow, or does not conceive of it as broad or narrow;

whether one conceives of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas as possessing power or lacking power, or does not conceive of them as possessing power or lacking power; [the same applies to the Buddha’s unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment].
"World-Honored One!
All such things as these are not the outflow-results (*niṣyanda-phala*) of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Furthermore, World-Honored One!"
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to such a conception as this:

"This prajñāpāramitā, regarding all phenomena, whether it treats them as large or small, or does not treat them as large or small; whether it treats them as accumulating or dispersing, or does not treat them as accumulating or dispersing; whether it treats them as finite or infinite, or does not treat them as finite or infinite; whether it treats them as broad or narrow, or does not treat them as broad or narrow; whether it treats them as powerful or powerless, or does not treat them as powerful or powerless."
“World-Honored One!
All such things as these are not the outflow fruits of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
World-Honored One!”
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to such a thought as this:

"This prajñāpāramitā, with respect to form, whether it makes it large or small, or does not make it large or small; with respect to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, whether it makes them large or small, or does not make them large or small;

with respect to form, whether it makes it accumulate or disperse, or does not make it accumulate or disperse; with respect to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, whether it makes them accumulate or disperse, or does not make them accumulate or disperse;"

Regarding form, whether one conceives of it as finite or infinite, or does not conceive of it as finite or infinite; regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, whether one conceives of them as finite or infinite, or does not conceive of them as finite or infinite;

regarding form, whether one conceives of it as broad or narrow, or does not conceive of it as broad or narrow; regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, whether one conceives of them as broad or narrow, or does not conceive of them as broad or narrow;

regarding form, whether one conceives of it as powerful or powerless, or does not conceive of it as powerful or powerless; regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, whether one conceives of them as powerful or powerless, or does not conceive of them as powerful or powerless.
"World-Honored One!
This bodhisattva-mahāsattva is said to have great attainment; he is not practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). Why is this?"
It is because one cannot realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment through the notion of something to be attained.
"Furthermore, Blessed One,
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to such a notion as this:"

"In this way, regarding the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), whether one conceives of the sense base of the eye as large or not large, or whether one does not conceive of it as large or not large; whether one conceives of the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind as large or not large, or whether one does not conceive of them as large or not large;

whether one conceives of the sense base of the eye as gathering or dispersing, or whether one does not conceive of it as gathering or dispersing; whether one conceives of the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind as gathering or dispersing, or whether one does not conceive of them as gathering or dispersing;

whether one conceives of the sense base of the eye as finite or infinite, or whether one does not conceive of it as finite or infinite; whether one conceives of the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind as finite or infinite, or whether one does not conceive of them as finite or infinite—"

Whether one conceives of the eye-base as extensive or limited, or does not conceive of it as extensive or limited; whether one conceives of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-base as extensive or limited, or does not conceive of them as extensive or limited;

whether one conceives of the eye-base as powerful or powerless, or does not conceive of it as powerful or powerless; whether one conceives of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind-base as powerful or powerless, or does not conceive of them as powerful or powerless.
"World-Honored One!
This bodhisattva-mahāsattva is said to have a great attainment; he is not practicing the perfection of wisdom. Why is this?"
"It is not because of a perception of something to be attained that one can realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Furthermore, World-Honored One,
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to such a perception as this:"

"In this way, regarding the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), whether one conceives of the sphere of form (rūpa-āyatana) as large or not large, or whether one does not conceive of it as large or not large; whether one conceives of the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental objects (śabda-gandha-rasa-spraṣṭavya-dharma-āyatana) as large or not large, or whether one does not conceive of them as large or not large;

whether one conceives of the sphere of form as accumulation or dispersal, or whether one does not conceive of it as accumulation or dispersal; whether one conceives of the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental objects as accumulation or dispersal, or whether one does not conceive of them as accumulation or dispersal;

whether one conceives of the sphere of form as finite or infinite, or whether one does not conceive of it as finite or infinite; whether one conceives of the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental objects as finite or infinite, or whether one does not conceive of them as finite or infinite—"

Whether one conceives of the sphere of form as extensive or limited, or does not conceive of it as extensive or limited; whether one conceives of the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibles, and mental phenomena as extensive or limited, or does not conceive of them as extensive or limited;

whether one conceives of the sphere of form as powerful or powerless, or does not conceive of it as powerful or powerless; whether one conceives of the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibles, and mental phenomena as powerful or powerless, or does not conceive of them as powerful or powerless.
"World-Honored One!
This bodhisattva-mahāsattva is said to have great attainment; he is not practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). Why is this?"
Because one cannot realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment through the notion of something to be attained.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One,
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to such a notion as this:"

"In this way, regarding the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*), whether one conceives it as large or not large; regarding the form-element (*rūpadhātu*), the eye-consciousness-element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*), eye-contact (*cakṣuḥsaṃsparśa*), and the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition (*cakṣuḥsaṃsparśapratyayajātā vedanā*), whether one conceives them as large or not large;

regarding the eye-element, whether one conceives it as accumulating or dispersing, or not accumulating or dispersing; regarding the form-element up to the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, whether one conceives them as accumulating or dispersing, or not accumulating or dispersing;

regarding the eye-element, whether one conceives it as finite or infinite, or not finite or infinite; regarding the form-element up to the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, whether one conceives them as finite or infinite, or not finite or infinite;"

Whether one conceives of the eye-element as extensive or limited, or does not conceive of it as extensive or limited; whether one conceives of the form-element, and so on up to the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, as extensive or limited, or does not conceive of them as extensive or limited;

whether one conceives of the eye-element as powerful or powerless, or does not conceive of it as powerful or powerless; whether one conceives of the form-element, and so on up to the various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, as powerful or powerless, or does not conceive of them as powerful or powerless.
"World-Honored One!
This bodhisattva mahāsattva is said to have great attainment; he is not practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). Why is this?"
It is because one cannot realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment through the notion that there is something to be attained.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One,
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to such a thought as this:"

"In this way, regarding the sphere of the ear (*śrotra-dhātu*), whether one conceives it as large or not large; regarding the sphere of sound (*śabda-dhātu*), the sphere of auditory consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna-dhātu*), auditory contact (*śrotra-saṃsparśa*), and all feelings (*vedanā*) produced with auditory contact as a condition, whether one conceives them as large or not large;

regarding the sphere of the ear, whether one conceives it as accumulating or dispersing, or not accumulating or dispersing; regarding the sphere of sound, up to the feelings produced with auditory contact as a condition, whether one conceives them as accumulating or dispersing, or not accumulating or dispersing;

regarding the sphere of the ear, whether one conceives it as finite or infinite, or not finite or infinite; regarding the sphere of sound, up to the feelings produced with auditory contact as a condition, whether one conceives them as finite or infinite, or not finite or infinite."

Regarding the ear element, whether one conceives it as extensive or limited, or does not conceive it as extensive or limited; regarding the sound element, and even the various feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition, whether one conceives them as extensive or limited, or does not conceive them as extensive or limited;

regarding the ear element, whether one conceives it as powerful or powerless, or does not conceive it as powerful or powerless; regarding the sound element, and even the various feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition, whether one conceives them as powerful or powerless, or does not conceive them as powerful or powerless.
"World-Honored One!
This bodhisattva-mahāsattva is said to have a great attainment; he is not practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). Why is this?"
It is because one cannot realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment through the notion of something to be attained.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One,
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to such a notion as this:"

"In this way, regarding the sphere of the nose (*ghrāṇadhātu*), whether one conceives of it as large or not large; regarding the sphere of odors (*gandhadhātu*), the sphere of nose-consciousness (*ghrāṇavijñānadhātu*), nose-contact (*ghrāṇasparśa*), and all feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition, whether one conceives of them as large or not large;

regarding the sphere of the nose, whether one conceives of it as accumulating or dispersing, or not accumulating or dispersing; regarding the sphere of odors, up to all feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition, whether one conceives of them as accumulating or dispersing, or not accumulating or dispersing;

regarding the sphere of the nose, whether one conceives of it as finite or infinite, or not finite or infinite; regarding the sphere of odors, up to all feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition, whether one conceives of them as finite or infinite, or not finite or infinite."

Regarding the nose element (*ghrāṇadhātu*), whether one conceives of it as expansive or narrow, or does not conceive of it as expansive or narrow; regarding the odor element (*gandhadhātu*) and even the various feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition (*ghrāṇasparśapratyayaja-vedanā*), whether one conceives of them as expansive or narrow, or does not conceive of them as expansive or narrow;

regarding the nose element, whether one conceives of it as powerful or powerless, or does not conceive of it as powerful or powerless; regarding the odor element and even the various feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition, whether one conceives of them as powerful or powerless, or does not conceive of them as powerful or powerless.
"World-Honored One!
This bodhisattva-mahāsattva is said to have great attainment; he is not practicing the perfection of wisdom. Why is this?"
It is not by means of the notion of something to be attained that one can realize unsurpassed, perfect,
and complete enlightenment. "Furthermore, Blessed One,
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to such a notion as this:"

"In this way, regarding the tongue-element (*jihvā-dhātu*), whether one conceives it as large or not large; regarding the taste-element (*rasa-dhātu*), the tongue-consciousness-element (*jihvā-vijñāna-dhātu*), tongue-contact (*jihvā-saṃsparśa*), and the various feelings (*vedanā*) produced with tongue-contact as condition, whether one conceives them as large or not large;

regarding the tongue-element, whether one conceives it as accumulating or dispersing, or not accumulating or dispersing; regarding the taste-element up to the various feelings produced with tongue-contact as condition, whether one conceives them as accumulating or dispersing, or not accumulating or dispersing;

regarding the tongue-element, whether one conceives it as finite or infinite, or not finite or infinite; regarding the taste-element up to the various feelings produced with tongue-contact as condition, whether one conceives them as finite or infinite, or not finite or infinite;"

Regarding the tongue element, whether one conceives of it as expansive or narrow, or does not conceive of it as expansive or narrow; regarding the taste element, up to the various feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition, whether one conceives of them as expansive or narrow, or does not conceive of them as expansive or narrow;

regarding the tongue element, whether one conceives of it as powerful or powerless, or does not conceive of it as powerful or powerless; regarding the taste element, up to the various feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition, whether one conceives of them as powerful or powerless, or does not conceive of them as powerful or powerless.
“World-Honored One!
This bodhisattva-mahāsattva is said to have great attainment; he is not practicing the perfection of wisdom. Why is this? Because—”
"It is not because of a perception of something to be attained that one can realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Furthermore, World-Honored One,
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to such a perception as this:"

"In this way, regarding the body-element (*kāyadhātu*), whether one conceives of it as large or small, or does not conceive of it as large or small; regarding the touch-element (*spraṣṭavyadhātu*), the body-consciousness-element (*kāyavijñānadhātu*), and body-contact (*kāyasparśa*), as well as the various feelings (*vedanā*) produced with body-contact as a condition, whether one conceives of them as large or small, or does not conceive of them as large or small;

regarding the body-element, whether one conceives of it as accumulating or dispersing, or does not conceive of it as accumulating or dispersing; regarding the touch-element up to the various feelings produced with body-contact as a condition, whether one conceives of them as accumulating or dispersing, or does not conceive of them as accumulating or dispersing;

regarding the body-element, whether one conceives of it as finite or infinite, or does not conceive of it as finite or infinite; regarding the touch-element up to the various feelings produced with body-contact as a condition, whether one conceives of them as finite or infinite, or does not conceive of them as finite or infinite;"

Whether one conceives of the body element as extensive or limited, or does not conceive of it as extensive or limited; whether one conceives of the tangible object element, up to the various feelings produced with body-contact as condition, as extensive or limited, or does not conceive of them as extensive or limited;

whether one conceives of the body element as powerful or powerless, or does not conceive of it as powerful or powerless; whether one conceives of the tangible object element, up to the various feelings produced with body-contact as condition, as powerful or powerless, or does not conceive of them as powerful or powerless.
"World-Honored One!
This bodhisattva-mahāsattva is said to have great attainment; he is not practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). Why is this?"
It is because one cannot realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment through the notion of something to be attained.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One,
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to such a notion as this:"

"In this manner, regarding the element of mind (*manodhātu*), whether one conceives of it as large or small, or does not conceive of it as large or small; regarding the element of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), the element of mental consciousness (*manovijñānadhātu*), and mental contact (*manaḥsaṃsparśa*)—as well as the various feelings (*vedanā*) produced with mental contact as a condition—whether one conceives of them as large or small, or does not conceive of them as large or small;

regarding the element of mind, whether one conceives of it as accumulating or dispersing, or does not conceive of it as accumulating or dispersing; regarding the element of phenomena, up to the various feelings produced with mental contact as a condition, whether one conceives of them as accumulating or dispersing, or does not conceive of them as accumulating or dispersing;

regarding the element of mind, whether one conceives of it as finite or infinite, or does not conceive of it as finite or infinite; regarding the element of phenomena, up to the various feelings produced with mental contact as a condition, whether one conceives of them as finite or infinite, or does not conceive of them as finite or infinite."

Whether one conceives of the mind-element as extensive or limited, or does not conceive of it as extensive or limited; whether one conceives of the phenomena-element, up to and including the various feelings produced with mind-contact as condition, as extensive or limited, or does not conceive of them as extensive or limited;

whether one conceives of the mind-element as powerful or powerless, or does not conceive of it as powerful or powerless; whether one conceives of the phenomena-element, up to and including the various feelings produced with mind-contact as condition, as powerful or powerless, or does not conceive of them as powerful or powerless.
“World-Honored One!
This bodhisattva-mahāsattva is said to have great attainment; he is not practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Why is this? Because...”
It is because one cannot realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment through the perception of something to be attained.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One,
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to such a perception as this:"

"In this way, regarding the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), whether one conceives of the earth element as large or not large, or whether one does not conceive of it as large or not large; whether one conceives of the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements as large or not large, or whether one does not conceive of them as large or not large;

whether one conceives of the earth element as accumulating or dispersing, or whether one does not conceive of it as accumulating or dispersing; whether one conceives of the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements as accumulating or dispersing, or whether one does not conceive of them as accumulating or dispersing;

whether one conceives of the earth element as finite or infinite, or whether one does not conceive of it as finite or infinite; whether one conceives of the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements as finite or infinite, or whether one does not conceive of them as finite or infinite—"

Regarding the earth element, whether one conceives of it as extensive or limited, or does not conceive of it as extensive or limited; regarding the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements, whether one conceives of them as extensive or limited, or does not conceive of them as extensive or limited;

regarding the earth element, whether one conceives of it as having power or lacking power, or does not conceive of it as having power or lacking power; regarding the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements, whether one conceives of them as having power or lacking power, or does not conceive of them as having power or lacking power.
"World-Honored One!
This bodhisattva-mahāsattva is said to have great attainment; he is not practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). Why is this?"
"It is not because of the notion of something to be attained that one can realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Furthermore, World-Honored One,
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to such a notion as this:"

"In this way, regarding this *prajñāpāramitā*, whether one conceives of ignorance as large or small, or does not conceive of it as large or small; whether one conceives of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), feeling (*vedanā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), becoming (*bhava*), birth (*jāti*), and old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair as large or small, or does not conceive of them as large or small;

whether one conceives of ignorance as accumulating or dispersing, or does not conceive of it as accumulating or dispersing; whether one conceives of [volitional formations] up to old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair as accumulating or dispersing, or does not conceive of them as accumulating or dispersing;

whether one conceives of ignorance as finite or infinite, or does not conceive of it as finite or infinite; whether one conceives of [volitional formations] up to old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair as finite or infinite, or does not conceive of them as finite or infinite..."

Whether one considers ignorance to be extensive or limited, or does not consider it to be extensive or limited; whether one considers the formative forces up to old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair to be extensive or limited, or does not consider them to be extensive or limited;

whether one considers ignorance to be powerful or powerless, or does not consider it to be powerful or powerless; whether one considers the formative forces up to old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair to be powerful or powerless, or does not consider them to be powerful or powerless.

Furthermore, World-Honored One,
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to such a perception as this:"

"In this way, regarding the perfection of wisdom, whether one conceives of the perfection of generosity as large or small, or does not conceive of it as large or small; whether one conceives of the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom as large or small, or does not conceive of them as large or small;

whether one conceives of the perfection of generosity as accumulating or dispersing, or does not conceive of it as accumulating or dispersing; whether one conceives of the perfections from ethical discipline up to wisdom as accumulating or dispersing, or does not conceive of them as accumulating or dispersing;

whether one conceives of the perfection of generosity as finite or infinite, or does not conceive of it as finite or infinite; whether one conceives of the perfections from ethical discipline up to wisdom as finite or infinite, or does not conceive of them as finite or infinite—"

Whether one conceives of the perfection of generosity as extensive or limited, or does not conceive of it as extensive or limited; whether one conceives of the perfections from ethical discipline up to wisdom as extensive or limited, or does not conceive of them as extensive or limited;

whether one conceives of the perfection of generosity as powerful or powerless, or does not conceive of it as powerful or powerless; whether one conceives of the perfections from ethical discipline up to wisdom as powerful or powerless, or does not conceive of them as powerful or powerless.
"World-Honored One!
