Furthermore, World-Honored One,
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to such a perception as this:"

"Thus, regarding this Prajñāpāramitā, whether one conceives of internal emptiness as large or small, or does not conceive of it as large or small; whether one conceives of external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-altering emptiness, essential emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common-characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, or the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature as being large or small, or does not conceive of them as large or small;

whether one conceives of internal emptiness as accumulating or dispersing, or does not conceive of it as accumulating or dispersing; and whether one conceives of external emptiness, up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, as accumulating or dispersing, or does not conceive of them as accumulating or dispersing;"

Regarding inner emptiness, whether one conceives of it as finite or infinite, or does not conceive of it as finite or infinite; regarding outer emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of non-essential nature and essential nature, whether one conceives of them as finite or infinite, or does not conceive of them as finite or infinite;

regarding inner emptiness, whether one conceives of it as broad or narrow, or does not conceive of it as broad or narrow; regarding outer emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of non-essential nature and essential nature, whether one conceives of them as broad or narrow, or does not conceive of them as broad or narrow;

regarding inner emptiness, whether one conceives of it as powerful or powerless, or does not conceive of it as powerful or powerless; regarding outer emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of non-essential nature and essential nature, whether one conceives of them as powerful or powerless, or does not conceive of them as powerful or powerless.
"World-Honored One!
This bodhisattva-mahāsattva is said to have great attainment; he is not practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). Why is this?"
"It is not because of the perception of something to be attained that one can realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Furthermore, World-Honored One,
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to such a perception as this:"

"In this way, regarding this *prajñāpāramitā*, whether one conceives of the *tathatā* as large or small, or does not conceive of it as large or small; whether one conceives of the *dharmadhātu*, *dharmatā*, *avitathatā*, *ananyathātā*, *samatā*, *niḥsaraṇatā*, *dharmatā*, *dharmasthititā*, *bhūtakoṭi*, *ākāśadhātu*, or *acintyadhātu* as large or small, or does not conceive of them as large or small;

whether one conceives of the *tathatā* as accumulating or dispersing, or does not conceive of it as accumulating or dispersing; whether one conceives of the *dharmadhātu* up to the *acintyadhātu* as accumulating or dispersing, or does not conceive of them as accumulating or dispersing;

whether one conceives of the *tathatā* as finite or infinite, or does not conceive of it as finite or infinite; whether one conceives of the *dharmadhātu* up to the *acintyadhātu* as finite or infinite, or does not conceive of them as finite or infinite..."

Whether one conceives of the *tathatā* as expansive or limited, or does not conceive of it as expansive or limited; whether one conceives of the *dharmadhātu*, up to and including the inconceivable realm (*acintyadhātu*), as expansive or limited, or does not conceive of them as expansive or limited;

whether one conceives of the *tathatā* as possessing power or lacking power, or does not conceive of it as possessing power or lacking power; whether one conceives of the *dharmadhātu*, up to and including the inconceivable realm, as possessing power or lacking power, or does not conceive of them as possessing power or lacking power.
"World-Honored One!

This is because one cannot realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment through the notion of something to be attained.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One,
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to such a notion as this:"

"In this Prajñāpāramitā, regarding the Noble Truth of Suffering, whether one conceives of it as large or small, or does not conceive of it as large or small; regarding the Noble Truths of Origination, Cessation, and the Path, whether one conceives of them as large or small, or does not conceive of them as large or small;

regarding the Noble Truth of Suffering, whether one conceives of it as accumulating or dispersing, or does not conceive of it as accumulating or dispersing; regarding the Noble Truths of Origination, Cessation, and the Path, whether one conceives of them as accumulating or dispersing, or does not conceive of them as accumulating or dispersing;

regarding the Noble Truth of Suffering, whether one conceives of it as finite or infinite, or does not conceive of it as finite or infinite; regarding the Noble Truths of Origination, Cessation, and the Path, whether one conceives of them as finite or infinite, or does not conceive of them as finite or infinite;"

Whether one conceives of the noble truth of suffering as broad or narrow, or does not conceive of it as broad or narrow; whether one conceives of the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path as broad or narrow, or does not conceive of them as broad or narrow;

whether one conceives of the noble truth of suffering as having power or lacking power, or does not conceive of it as having power or lacking power; whether one conceives of the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path as having power or lacking power, or does not conceive of them as having power or lacking power.
"World-Honored One!
This bodhisattva-mahāsattva is said to have a great attainment of something; he is not practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). Why is this?"
"It is not because of a perception of something to be attained that one can realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Furthermore, World-Honored One,
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to such a perception as this:"

"In this way, regarding the four dhyānas, whether one treats them as small or not small, or whether one does not treat them as small or not small; regarding the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments, whether one treats them as small or not small, or whether one does not treat them as small or not small;

regarding the four dhyānas, whether one treats them as accumulated or dispersed, or whether one does not treat them as accumulated or dispersed; regarding the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments, whether one treats them as accumulated or dispersed, or whether one does not treat them as accumulated or dispersed;

regarding the four dhyānas, whether one treats them as limited or unlimited, or whether one does not treat them as limited or unlimited; regarding the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments, whether one treats them as limited or unlimited, or whether one does not treat them as limited or unlimited—"

Regarding the four dhyānas, whether one treats them as extensive or limited, or does not treat them as extensive or limited; regarding the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments, whether one treats them as extensive or limited, or does not treat them as extensive or limited;

regarding the four dhyānas, whether one treats them as powerful or powerless, or does not treat them as powerful or powerless; regarding the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments, whether one treats them as powerful or powerless, or does not treat them as powerful or powerless.
"World-Honored One!

if a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to such a perception as this:"

whether one conceives of the eight liberations as accumulating or dispersing, or does not conceive of them as accumulating or dispersing;
whether one conceives of the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities as finite or infinite, or does not conceive of them as finite or infinite—"

Whether one conceives of the eight liberations as broad or narrow, or does not conceive of them as broad or narrow; whether one conceives of the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities as broad or narrow, or does not conceive of them as broad or narrow;

whether one conceives of the eight liberations as powerful or powerless, or does not conceive of them as powerful or powerless; whether one conceives of the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities as powerful or powerless, or does not conceive of them as powerful or powerless.

if a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to such a perception as this:"

"In this way, regarding the perfection of wisdom, whether one treats the four foundations of mindfulness as great or small, or does not treat them as great or small; whether one treats the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the eightfold noble path as great or small, or does not treat them as great or small;

whether one treats the four foundations of mindfulness as gathering or dispersing, or does not treat them as gathering or dispersing; whether one treats the four right efforts up to the eightfold noble path as gathering or dispersing, or does not treat them as gathering or dispersing;

whether one treats the four foundations of mindfulness as finite or infinite, or does not treat them as finite or infinite; whether one treats the four right efforts up to the eightfold noble path as finite or infinite, or does not treat them as finite or infinite..."

whether one treats the four foundations of mindfulness as powerful or powerless, or does not treat them as powerful or powerless; whether one treats the four right endeavors up to the eight factors of the noble path as powerful or powerless, or does not treat them as powerful or powerless.

if a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to such a perception as this:"

whether one conceives of the gate of emptiness as a collection or a dispersal, or does not conceive of it as a collection or a dispersal; whether one conceives of the gates of signlessness and wishlessness as a collection or a dispersal, or does not conceive of them as a collection or a dispersal;

whether one conceives of the gate of emptiness as finite or infinite, or does not conceive of it as finite or infinite; whether one conceives of the gates of signlessness and wishlessness as finite or infinite, or does not conceive of them as finite or infinite—"

Regarding the gate of liberation of emptiness, whether one conceives of it as expansive or limited, or does not conceive of it as expansive or limited; regarding the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness, whether one conceives of them as expansive or limited, or does not conceive of them as expansive or limited;

regarding the gate of liberation of emptiness, whether one conceives of it as possessing power or lacking power, or does not conceive of it as possessing power or lacking power; regarding the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness, whether one conceives of them as possessing power or lacking power, or does not conceive of them as possessing power or lacking power.

"Furthermore, World-Honored One,
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to such a thought as this:"

"In this way, the *prajñāpāramitā* neither conceives of nor does not conceive of the five eyes as being large or small; it neither conceives of nor does not conceive of the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) as being large or small.

It neither conceives of nor does not conceive of the five eyes as being accumulated or dispersed; it neither conceives of nor does not conceive of the six supernormal powers as being accumulated or dispersed.
It neither conceives of nor does not conceive of the five eyes as being finite or infinite; it neither conceives of nor does not conceive of the six supernormal powers as being finite or infinite."

Regarding the five eyes, whether one conceives of them as broad or narrow, or does not conceive of them as broad or narrow; regarding the six supernormal powers, whether one conceives of them as broad or narrow, or does not conceive of them as broad or narrow;

regarding the five eyes, whether one conceives of them as having power or lacking power, or does not conceive of them as having power or lacking power; regarding the six supernormal powers, whether one conceives of them as having power or lacking power, or does not conceive of them as having power or lacking power.
"World-Honored One!

Chapter 33: Slandering the Perfection of Wisdom. Part One: Slandering the Perfection of Wisdom, Chapter Thirty-Three. At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to have faith and understanding in this profound prajñāpāramitā, from where did they pass away to come and be born here?
"Bhagavān!
For how long has this bodhisattva mahāsattva set out toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening?
Bhagavān!"
"How many Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas has this bodhisattva mahāsattva previously approached, served, and made offerings to? Bhagavān,
for how long has this bodhisattva mahāsattva practiced the pāramitās of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom?"
“World-Honored One!
How does this bodhisattva mahāsattva believe in and understand the profound meaning and intent of such a perfection of wisdom?
The Buddha said:

“Śāriputra! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to have faith and understanding in this profound prajñāpāramitā, they have passed away from the assemblies of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas—countless, immeasurable, and boundless—in the worlds of the ten directions, and have come to be born here.”

Śāriputra! These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment after already passing through countless, immeasurable, and boundless hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of kalpas.

Śāriputra! These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have already personally attended upon, served, and made offerings to countless, immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, and incalculable Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.

Śāriputra! From the first generation of the mind of awakening, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have constantly and diligently practiced the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom for countless, immeasurable, and boundless hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of kalpas.
Śāriputra! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva sees this Prajñāpāramitā, they should form this thought:
"I am seeing the Buddha."
Upon hearing this Prajñāpāramitā, they will think:
"I have heard the Buddha's teaching. Śāriputra!

By means of the skillful methods of signlessness, non-duality, and non-apprehension, this bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to correctly believe in and understand the profound meaning and intent of this prajñāpāramitā.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
is there anyone who can hear or see this profound perfection of wisdom?”
The Buddha said, “Subhūti!
Thus, this prajñāpāramitā truly has no one who can hear it or see it; likewise, this prajñāpāramitā is neither that which is heard nor that which is seen.”
Why is this? "Subhūti!
Form is neither heard nor seen, because all dharmas are insentient."
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither heard nor seen, because all phenomena are insentient.
"Subhūti! The eye-base is neither heard nor seen, because all phenomena are insentient."
The sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are neither heard nor seen, because all phenomena are insentient.
The sense base of form is neither heard nor seen, because all phenomena are insentient;
the sense bases of sound, odor, taste, tangibles, and mental objects are neither heard nor seen, because all phenomena are insentient.
“Subhūti! The eye-element is neither heard nor seen, because all phenomena are insentient;
the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element, eye-contact, and the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition are neither heard nor seen, because all phenomena are insentient.”
The ear-element has neither hearing nor seeing, because all phenomena are insentient;
the sound-element, the ear-consciousness-element, ear-contact, and the various feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition have neither hearing nor seeing, because all phenomena are insentient.
The nose element is neither heard nor seen, because all phenomena are insentient;
the odor element, the nose-consciousness element, nose-contact, and the various feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition are neither heard nor seen, because all phenomena are insentient.
The tongue element is neither heard nor seen, because all phenomena are insentient;

the taste element, the tongue-consciousness element, tongue-contact, and the various sensations produced with tongue-contact as a condition are neither heard nor seen, because all phenomena are insentient.
The body element is neither heard nor seen, because all phenomena are insentient;

the tangible element, the body-consciousness element, body-contact, and the various feelings produced with body-contact as a condition are neither heard nor seen, because all phenomena are insentient.
The mind-element is neither heard nor seen, because all phenomena are insentient;

the dharma-element, the mind-consciousness-element, and the mental contact, as well as the various feelings produced with mental contact as a condition, are neither heard nor seen, because all phenomena are insentient.
“Subhūti! The earth element is neither heard nor seen, because all phenomena are insentient;
the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements are neither heard nor seen, because all phenomena are insentient.”
“Subhūti! Ignorance is neither heard nor seen, because all phenomena are insentient;

volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, and old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair are neither heard nor seen, because all phenomena are insentient.”
“Subhūti! The perfection of generosity is neither heard nor seen, because all phenomena are insentient;
the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom are neither heard nor seen, because all phenomena are insentient.”
"Subhūti! Internal emptiness is neither heard nor seen, because all phenomena are insentient.

External emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-alteration emptiness, essential emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common-characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature are neither heard nor seen, because all phenomena are insentient."
"Subhūti! Suchness is neither heard nor seen, because all phenomena are insentient.

The realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the non-erroneous nature, the unchanging nature, equality, the nature free from birth, the fixed nature of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*), the stability of phenomena (*dharmasthititā*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the realm of space (*ākāśadhātu*), and the inconceivable realm are neither heard nor seen, because all phenomena are insentient."
“Subhūti! The noble truth of suffering is neither heard nor seen, because all phenomena are insentient;
the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path are neither heard nor seen, because all phenomena are insentient.”
"Subhūti! The four dhyānas are neither heard nor seen, because all dharmas are insentient;
the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments are neither heard nor seen, because all dharmas are insentient."
“Subhūti! The eight liberations are neither heard nor seen, because all phenomena are insentient;
the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten totalities are neither heard nor seen, because all phenomena are insentient.”
"Subhūti! The four foundations of mindfulness are neither heard nor seen, because all phenomena are insentient;

the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path are neither heard nor seen, because all phenomena are insentient."
“Subhūti! The gate of liberation that is emptiness is neither heard nor seen, because all phenomena are insentient;
the gates of liberation that are signlessness and wishlessness are neither heard nor seen, because all phenomena are insentient.”
"Subhūti! The five eyes neither hear nor see, because all dharmas are insentient;
the six supernormal powers neither hear nor see, because all dharmas are insentient."
“Subhūti! The ten powers of a Buddha are neither heard nor seen, because all phenomena are insentient;

the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are neither heard nor seen, because all phenomena are insentient.”
"Subhūti! The quality of non-forgetfulness is neither heard nor seen, because all phenomena are insentient;
the state of constant abiding in equanimity is neither heard nor seen, because all phenomena are insentient."
"Subhūti! All-knowledge (sarvajñatā) is neither heard nor seen, because all phenomena are insentient;
the knowledge of the paths (mārgajñatā) and the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā) are neither heard nor seen, because all phenomena are insentient."
“Subhūti! All dhāraṇī-doors are neither heard nor seen, because all phenomena are insentient;
all samādhi-doors are neither heard nor seen, because all phenomena are insentient.”
“Subhūti! The stream-enterer has neither hearing nor seeing, because all dharmas are insentient;
the once-returner, the non-returner, and the arhat have neither hearing nor seeing, because all dharmas are insentient.”
“Subhūti! The stage of entering the stream and the fruit of stream-entry are neither heard nor seen, because all phenomena are insentient;

the stage of entering once-returning and the fruit of once-returning, the stage of entering non-returning and the fruit of non-returning, and the stage of entering arhatship and the fruit of arhatship are neither heard nor seen, because all phenomena are insentient.”
“Subhūti! Pratyekabuddhas neither hear nor see, because all dharmas are insentient;
the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha neither hears nor sees, because all dharmas are insentient.”
“Subhūti! Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas neither hear nor see, because all dharmas are insentient;
bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice without hearing or seeing, because all dharmas are insentient.”
“Subhūti! The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha neither hears nor sees, because all dharmas are insentient;
unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment neither hears nor sees, because all dharmas are insentient.”
“Subhūti, all dharmas are neither heard nor seen, because all dharmas are insentient.
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
For how long must Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas accumulate their practices before they are able to study and cultivate the profound Prajñāpāramitā?
The Buddha said:
“Subhūti! Regarding this matter, one should explain it through differentiation.
Subhūti!”

There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, from the very first moment they resolve their minds [on enlightenment], are able to practice and study the profound perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), as well as the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā), the perfection of diligence (vīryapāramitā), the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā), the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), and the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā).
Subhūti! Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva possesses skillful means, he does not slander any dharmas, and regarding all dharmas, he neither increases nor decreases them.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva is never apart from practices associated with the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; nor is he ever separated from the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and the assembly of bodhisattva mahāsattvas.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva travels from one buddha-field to another, desiring to provide offerings, pay homage, show respect, and offer praise to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, as well as to the bodhisattva mahāsattvas, using rare and wondrous articles of offering; he accomplishes these according to his wishes and is likewise able to plant various roots of goodness under those Tathāgatas.
Wherever this bodhisattva-mahāsattva receives a body, he does not fall into birth from within a mother’s womb or a placenta.
This bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s mind never dwells in association with afflictions, nor has he ever given rise to the mind of the two vehicles.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva never remains apart from superior supernormal powers, proceeding from one buddha-field to another buddha-field to mature sentient beings and adorn and purify buddha-fields.
"Subhūti!
This bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to correctly train in the profound perfection of wisdom. Subhūti!"
There are sons and daughters of good family belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle who, although they have seen many Buddhas—
whether many hundreds of Buddhas, many thousands of Buddhas, many hundreds of thousands of Buddhas,
many koṭis of Buddhas, many hundreds of koṭis of Buddhas, many thousands of koṭis of Buddhas, or many hundreds of thousands of koṭis of Buddhas— ...

Even if one has practiced generosity, pure ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom for many hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of buddhas under those various buddhas,
if one does so by means of the expedient of "attainment," one will be unable to study the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
Furthermore, they will also be unable to cultivate and study the perfection of meditative concentration,
the perfection of diligence, the perfection of patience, the perfection of ethical discipline, and the perfection of generosity.
Subhūti! When these sons and daughters of good family hear this profound perfection of wisdom being taught, they rise from their seats and depart from the assembly.

“Subhūti! These sons and daughters of good family do not revere this profound perfection of wisdom, nor do they revere the Buddha; having abandoned this profound perfection of wisdom, they have also abandoned all Buddhas.”
Now, there are also those of such a kind within this assembly who, upon hearing me teach this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, do not find it pleasing and depart from the assembly.

Why is this? Because these sons and daughters of good family, having previously heard the teaching of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and yet departed, now hear this *prajñāpāramitā* being taught and, due to the power of their past habits, once again depart.

"These sons and daughters of good family, regarding this profound *prajñāpāramitā* as it has been taught, have failed to bring their body, speech, and mind into accord with it; by means of this, they create and increase the karmic offenses of delusion and impaired wisdom."

Due to having committed and accumulated the karmic offenses of delusion and impaired wisdom, upon hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā* being taught, they immediately slander, obstruct, and abandon it.
Since they thus slander, obstruct, and abandon this perfection of wisdom, they thereby slander, obstruct, and abandon the knowledge of all aspects of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.

By slandering, obstructing, and abandoning the omniscience of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present, they thereby create and increase the karma that leads to the deprivation of the true Dharma.

Because they have committed and accumulated karma that leads to the deprivation of the true Dharma, they fall into the great hells and remain there for many years—whether for many hundreds of years, many thousands of years, many hundreds of thousands of years, many koṭis of years, many hundreds of koṭis of years, many thousands of koṭis of years, many hundreds of thousands of koṭis of years, or even many hundreds of thousands of koṭi-nayutas of years—experiencing various agonizing and intense sufferings within those great hells.

"Because his offenses are grave, he shall pass from one great hell to another great hell within this world until the kalpas of fire, water, and wind have not yet arisen, during which time he will undergo various forms of agonizing and intensely sharp suffering."

If the fire, water, or wind kalpas arise in this world, because their karma of obstructing the Dharma is not yet exhausted, they die and are reborn in a similar great hell in another world. There, for many years—whether many hundreds of years, many thousands of years, many hundreds of thousands of years, many koṭis of years, many hundreds of koṭis of years, many thousands of koṭis of years, many hundreds of thousands of koṭis of years, or many hundreds of thousands of koṭi-nayutas of years—they undergo various agonizing and intense sufferings within that great hell.

"Because his transgression is so grave, he shall pass from one great hell to another in other worlds, undergoing various forms of agonizing and intense suffering until the kalpas of fire, water, and wind have yet to arise."

If the fire, water, or wind kalpas arise in other worlds, because the karma of their deprivation of the Dharma is not yet exhausted, after they die they are reborn in a similar great hell in another direction, where they experience various agonizing and fierce sufferings for many years—whether many hundreds of years, many thousands of years, many hundreds of thousands of years, many koṭis of years, many hundreds of koṭis of years, many thousands of koṭis of years, many hundreds of thousands of koṭis of years, or even many hundreds of thousands of koṭi-nayutas of years—within that great hell.

"Because their offenses are so grave, they shall pass from one great hell to another great hell in other worlds, undergoing all manner of agonizing and intense suffering until the kalpas of fire, water, and wind have yet to arise."
In this manner, they successively traverse all other worlds in the eastern direction, undergoing various agonizing and intense great sufferings within the great hells.
In this manner, they successively traverse all other worlds in the southern direction, undergoing various agonizing and intense great sufferings within the great hells.
In this manner, they successively traverse all other worlds in the western direction, undergoing various agonizing and intense great sufferings within the great hells.
In this manner, they successively traverse all other worlds in the northern direction, undergoing various agonizing and intense great sufferings within the great hells.
In this manner, they successively traverse all other worlds in the northeast, undergoing various forms of agonizing and intense great suffering within their great hells.
In this manner, they successively traverse all other worlds in the southeast, undergoing various forms of agonizing and intense great suffering within their great hells.
In this manner, they successively traverse all other worlds in the southwestern direction, undergoing various agonizing and intense sufferings within the great hells.
In this manner, they successively traverse all other worlds in the northwestern direction, undergoing various agonizing and intense sufferings within the great hells.
In this manner, they successively traverse all other worlds below, undergoing various agonizing and intense great sufferings within the great hells;
likewise, they successively traverse all other worlds above, undergoing various agonizing and intense great sufferings within the great hells.

"If, when the fire, water, and wind kalpas arise in those other worlds of the ten directions, because their karma of obstructing the Dharma is not yet exhausted, they die and are reborn here in this world within the great hells; passing from one great hell to another great hell, they undergo various agonizing and fierce sufferings until the fire, water, and wind kalpas have arisen."

If the fire, water, or wind kalpas arise in this world, because their karma of depriving others of the Dharma is not yet exhausted, they die here and are reborn in other worlds throughout the ten directions, where they undergo all manner of agonizing and fierce sufferings within the great hells.

Thus they wander in saṃsāra for incalculable kalpas; when the force of their karmic offenses from the sin of depriving others of the Dharma has somewhat diminished, they emerge from hell and fall into the realm of animals, where for many years—whether many hundreds of years, many thousands of years, many hundreds of thousands of years, many koṭis of years, many hundreds of koṭis of years, many thousands of koṭis of years, many hundreds of thousands of koṭis of years, or even many hundreds of thousands of koṭi-nayutas of years—they assume the bodies of animals and undergo all manner of suffering, including being slaughtered, harmed, and terrified.

Because their offenses are not yet exhausted, they shall wander from one perilous and evil place to another within this world; until the kalpas of fire, water, and wind have arisen, they will fully experience the sufferings of being mangled, harmed, terrified, and oppressed.

"When this world is destroyed by the three calamities, those whose karma of deprivation of the Dharma has not yet exhausted its residual force die and are reborn in other worlds within the animal realm (*tiryagyoni*) of a similar nature. There they pass many years—whether many hundreds of years, or even many hundreds of thousands of *koṭi-nayuta* years—experiencing the bodies of animals and undergoing various sufferings such as being slaughtered and threatened."

Because their offenses are not yet exhausted, they wander from one perilous and evil place to another in other worlds, undergoing all manner of suffering such as being slaughtered and threatened, until the kalpas of fire, water, and wind have not yet arisen.

If, at the time when the three calamities destroy another world-system, the residual force of their karma of deprivation of the Dharma has not yet been exhausted, they die and are reborn in another world-system among animals of a similar kind. There they spend many years—whether many hundreds of years, or even many hundreds of thousands of *koṭi-nayuta* years—experiencing animal bodies and undergoing all manner of suffering, such as being slaughtered and threatened.

Because their offenses have not yet been exhausted, they pass from one perilous and evil place to another within other worlds, undergoing all manner of suffering—including slaughter, injury, and intimidation—until the fire, water, and wind kalpas have arisen.

"In this manner, they travel successively through all other worlds in the ten directions, taking birth in the form of animals and undergoing various sufferings such as being slaughtered, harmed, threatened, and oppressed.

When those other worlds in the ten directions are destroyed by the three calamities, because the residual force of their karma of depleting the Dharma has not yet been exhausted, after death they are reborn here in this world among the animal realm (tiryagyoni). From one perilous and evil place to another perilous and evil place, until the fire, water, and wind kalpas have arisen, they undergo all manner of sufferings such as being slaughtered, harmed, threatened, and oppressed."

If this world is destroyed by the three calamities, those whose karma of deprivation of the Dharma has not yet exhausted its residual force will, after death, be reborn in other worlds throughout the ten directions, undergoing manifold sufferings within the realm of animals.

Thus they circulate through countless eons until the force of their karmic offenses from depriving others of the Dharma gradually thins. They escape the animal realm and fall instead into the realm of hungry ghosts, where they pass many years—whether hundreds, thousands, hundreds of thousands, many koṭis, many hundreds of koṭis, many thousands of koṭis, many hundreds of thousands of koṭis, or even many hundreds of thousands of koṭi-nayutas of years—suffering all manner of afflictions such as emaciation, hunger, and thirst within that ghost realm.

Because their offenses have not yet been exhausted, they wander from one realm of hungry ghosts to another within this world; until the kalpas of fire, water, and wind have arisen, they undergo all manner of sufferings such as emaciation, weakness, hunger, and thirst.

"When this world is destroyed by the three calamities, those whose karma of deprivation regarding the Dharma has not yet exhausted its residual force die and are reborn in another world system among the class of hungry ghosts similar to those here. There they undergo for many years—whether for many hundreds of years, or even for many hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of years—the various sufferings of emaciation, hunger, thirst, and so forth within the realm of ghosts."

Because their offenses are not yet exhausted, they travel from one realm of hungry ghosts to another in other worlds; until the kalpas of fire, water, and wind have arisen, they undergo all manner of suffering, such as emaciation, weakness, hunger, and thirst.

If, at the time when the three calamities destroy other worlds, the residual force of their karma of deprivation of the Dharma has not yet been exhausted, they die and are reborn in another world in a similar realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*). There, for many years—whether many hundreds of years, or even many hundreds of thousands of *koṭi-nayuta* years—they undergo all manner of sufferings within the ghost realm, such as emaciation, hunger, and thirst.

Because their offenses are not yet exhausted, they travel from one realm of hungry ghosts to another in other worlds; until the kalpas of fire, water, and wind have arisen, they undergo all manner of sufferings such as emaciation, weakness, hunger, and thirst.

"In this manner, they travel successively throughout all other worlds in the ten directions, undergoing the sufferings of emaciation, hunger, thirst, and the like within the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*).

When those other worlds in the ten directions are destroyed by the three calamities, because the residual force of their karma of obstructing the Dharma has not yet been exhausted, after death they return to be born here in this world among the realm of hungry ghosts. From one ghostly land to another ghostly land, until the kalpas of fire, water, and wind have arisen, they continue to undergo the sufferings of emaciation, hunger, thirst, and the like."

If, when this world is destroyed by the three calamities, the residual force of their karma of depriving others of the Dharma has not yet been exhausted, they die and are reborn in other worlds throughout the ten directions, undergoing manifold sufferings extensively within the realm of hungry ghosts.
"Thus they wander through countless kalpas until the residual force of that karma of depriving others of the Dharma is nearly exhausted;
though they may obtain human birth, they dwell in lowly and base conditions— namely, being born into the family of those born blind,
or into the families of caṇḍālas, or pukkāsas, or butchers, or fishermen and hunters, or..."
Whether born into the families of artisans, musicians, those with wrong views, or other base and miscellaneous families of improper discipline;
or whether the body they have received is devoid of eyes, ears, nose, tongue, hands, or feet;
or afflicted by abscesses, scabies, leprosy, insanity, epilepsy, or physical deformities.
Hunchbacked, short and deformed, with crippled limbs and impaired faculties, impoverished, emaciated, dull-witted, and ignorant—whenever they appear among people, all treat them with contempt;

or else, in the places where they are born, they do not hear the name of the Buddha, the name of the Dharma, the name of the Saṅgha, the name of Bodhisattvas, or the name of Pratyekabuddhas; or furthermore, [they may be born]...
Born into a world of profound darkness, they are forever without day or night and do not behold light.
Because they have committed and increased karmic actions that deprive them of the Dharma to such an extreme degree, they experience such undesirable and complete fruits of suffering.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Can the karma created and accumulated by those who cause the true Dharma to be impoverished be said to be similar to the five deeds of immediate retribution?”
The Buddha said:
"Śāriputra! That karma of depriving others of the Dharma is most extremely coarse and heavy; it cannot be compared even to the five deeds of immediate retribution."
That is to say, upon hearing the teaching of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they immediately lack faith and slander it, disparaging it by saying:

"Such a teaching was not expounded by the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas; it is not the Dharma, not the Vinaya, and not the instruction of the Great Teacher; we should not train ourselves in this."
Those who slander the Dharma thus slander the Prajñāpāramitā themselves, and they also teach immeasurable sentient beings to engage in such slander;
they destroy their own bodies and cause others to destroy theirs as well;
they drink poisonous medicine themselves and cause others to drink it too.
They themselves lose the fruit of rebirth in heaven and liberation, and cause others to lose them as well;
they themselves cast their own bodies into the fires of hell, and cause others to cast theirs into the fires of hell;
they themselves lack faith and understanding in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and likewise teach others not to have faith or understanding in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
They cause themselves to fall into and drown in the ocean of suffering, and they likewise cause others to fall into and drown in the ocean of suffering. Śāriputra,
regarding such profound *prajñāpāramitā*, I do not even allow those who slander the true Dharma to hear its name, much less explain it to them!

Śāriputra! As for those who slander the Dharma, I do not even permit sons or daughters of good family who have set out in the Bodhisattva vehicle to hear their names, let alone allow them to see them with their own eyes!
How could one permit them to dwell together?
Why is this so, Śāriputra?

Those who revile the profound *prajñāpāramitā* should be known as destroyers of the true Dharma; they fall into the category of darkness like foul snails, defiling themselves and others like a mass of putrid excrement.
If one places trust in those who destroy the Dharma, they too shall undergo the great suffering as previously described. Śāriputra!
You should know that all those who destroy the profound *prajñāpāramitā* are, in effect, hell-beings, animals, or hungry ghosts; therefore, the wise should not revile the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
Then, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

For what reason do you speak only of how those who destroy the True Dharma fall into the great hells, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts to suffer for a long time, yet do not describe their physical appearance or bodily dimensions?”
The Buddha said, “Śāriputra, stop!
One should not speak of the dimensions of the miserable realms to which those who destroy the True Dharma will be reborn in the future. Why is this?

If I were to fully describe the dimensions of the miserable realms to which those who destroy the True Dharma will be reborn, they would be so terrified upon hearing it that they would vomit hot blood, leading to their death or the agony of near-death; their minds would be suddenly stricken with grief as if pierced by a poisoned arrow, and their bodies would gradually wither away like cut-down grain stalks.

Fearing that upon hearing it described, those who slander the True Dharma might become terrified and lose their lives by assuming such a body of great ugliness and suffering, I have compassion for them and therefore do not describe to you the appearance or dimensions of the body resulting from the sin of destroying the True Dharma.
Śāriputra said:

"I pray that the Buddha will describe the dimensions of the miserable realms to be experienced in the future by those who destroy the True Dharma; may he provide a clear warning for the sake of the future, so that they may know that destroying the Dharma results in great suffering as retribution and refrain from committing such a sin."
The Buddha said, “Śāriputra!

What I have previously stated is sufficient as a clear admonition: that those sons and daughters of good family in future ages who hear my teaching on the karma of destroying the True Dharma and who create and increase it to the point of full completion, shall fall into the great hells, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts—into each of these destinies—to suffer for a long time. This alone is sufficient to cause them to maintain themselves with vigilance and not destroy the True Dharma.”
Then, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying: “So be it,
World-Honored One!”
"So be it! Sugata!

In the future, those sons and daughters of good family who possess pure faith, having heard the Buddha’s prior teaching on how the karma of destroying the True Dharma brings about suffering for a long duration as a sufficient warning, would rather sacrifice their own bodies and lives than ever slander the Dharma, lest they themselves suffer such misery in the future."
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If there are intelligent sons or daughters of good family who, having heard what the Buddha has taught regarding those who slander the True Dharma and will undergo great suffering for a long time in future ages, should well protect and maintain their actions of body, speech, and mind; they must not revile or destroy the True Dharma, lest they fall into the three evil realms and suffer for a long duration, failing to see the Buddhas, hear the True Dharma, or encounter the Saṃgha for a vast period of time; nor shall they be born in a land where a Buddha resides, but even if born among humans, they will be lowly, impoverished, ugly, dull-witted, deficient in limbs, and whatever they say will not be believed or accepted by others.”
The Venerable Subhūti spoke again:
“World-Honored One,
is it not by practicing unwholesome verbal karma that one creates and increases the karma that leads to the deprivation of the Dharma?”
The Buddha said,
“So it is, Subhūti! It is just so.”
It is so! Indeed, because of the habitual practice of the karma of harsh speech, they have created and increased the karma that results in the deprivation of the Dharma.
Within my true Dharma and Vinaya, there will be certain foolish renunciants who, although they call me their Great Teacher, will slander and destroy the profound *prajñāpāramitā* that I have taught.
“Subhūti, you should know this:
whoever slanders and reviles the profound *prajñāpāramitā* thereby slanders and reviles the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*) of all Buddhas.”
If one slanders or disparages the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all Buddhas, one thereby slanders the knowledge of all aspects of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
If one slanders or disparages the knowledge of all aspects, one slanders the Buddha.
If one slanders the Buddha, one slanders the Dharma.
If one slanders the Dharma, one slanders the Saṅgha.
If one slanders the Sangha, then one must slander right view in the world.
If one slanders right view in the world, then one must slander the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence,
meditative concentration, and wisdom, and one must also slander the internal [realities].
Emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate truth, the emptiness of conditioned phenomena,
the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, absolute emptiness, the emptiness of the limitless, the emptiness of dispersion, the emptiness of non-alteration,
the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the emptiness of specific characteristics, the emptiness of common characteristics, and the emptiness of all phenomena.
The emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence—
these would likewise slander and revile suchness, the dharma-realm, the dharma-nature, the non-falsity,
the immutability, the equality, the state beyond birth, the fixed nature of dharmas, the stability of dharmas, the limit of reality, and the void.
They will also slander the element of space and the inconceivable element;

they will also slander the noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin, the noble truth of cessation, and the noble truth of the path; they will also slander the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments;
and they will also slander the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, and the nine successive stages.

They will also slander the meditative concentrations and the ten totalities; they will likewise slander the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path;
and they will also slander the gate of liberation of emptiness, the gate of liberation of signlessness, and the gate of liberation of wishlessness.
They will also slander and revile the five eyes and the six supernormal powers;

they will likewise slander and revile the Buddha’s ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
they will also slander and revile the quality of non-forgetfulness and the state of constant abiding in equanimity.
They will also slander all-knowledge, the knowledge of the aspects of the path, and the knowledge of all aspects;
they will also slander all doors of dhāraṇī and all doors of samādhi.
By slandering and disparaging the mass of all virtues, they thereby take upon themselves a mass of countless, immeasurable, and boundless sins.

Because they have taken upon themselves this mass of countless, immeasurable, and boundless sins, they thereby take upon themselves the mass of countless, immeasurable, and boundless sufferings within the great hells, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, and among human beings.
Then, the Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
by how many causes and conditions do foolish people slander and revile such profound *prajñāpāramitā*?”
The Buddha said,
“Subhūti, it is by way of four causes and conditions.”
What are the four?
First, because they are instigated and deluded by various māras and evil spirits, they cause the ignorant and foolish to slander and revile such profound prajñāpāramitā.
Second, because they lack faith and understanding in the profound Dharma, they cause ignorant persons to revile and disparage this profound *prajñāpāramitā*.

Third, because they do not apply themselves with diligence, are firmly attached to the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), and are influenced by evil associates (*pāpamitra*), they cause ignorant persons to revile and disparage this profound *prajñāpāramitā*.

Fourth, because they harbor much malice, delight in practicing unwholesome dharmas, take pleasure in self-exaltation, and disparage others, they cause the ignorant to slander and revile this profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
"Subhūti! It is because they possess these four causes and conditions that foolish people slander and revile this profound *prajñāpāramitā*.

*The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Fascicle 181, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Chapter 34: Difficult to Believe and Understand, Part One. Chapter 34, Section One: Difficult to Believe and Understand. The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“Bhagavān, those who do not exert diligent effort, who have not planted roots of goodness, who possess unwholesome roots, and who are taken under the influence of evil associates, will find it truly difficult to believe and understand this profound Prajñāpāramitā spoken by the Buddha.”
The Buddha said,
“So it is, Subhūti!”
"So it is! It is just as you have said.

Those who do not apply themselves with diligent effort, who have not planted roots of virtue, who possess unwholesome roots, and who are under the influence of evil associates, will find this profound *prajñāpāramitā* truly difficult to believe and understand."
The Venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In what way is this perfection of wisdom so profound that it is difficult to believe and difficult to understand?
The Buddha said:
“Subhūti! Form is neither bound nor liberated. Why is this?
Because form has the nature of non-existence as its own intrinsic nature.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither bound nor liberated. Why is this?
Because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness have the nature of non-existence, they constitute the intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
"The eye-base is neither bound nor liberated."
Why is this? Because the eye-base has non-existence as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Thus, the bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are neither bound nor liberated.
Why is this? Because the non-existence of the spheres of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind constitutes the intrinsic nature of the spheres of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
“The sphere of form is neither bound nor liberated.
Why? Because the nature of the sphere of form is the very absence of intrinsic existence; such is the self-nature of the sphere of form.”
The spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena are neither bound nor liberated. Why is this?

Because the nature of the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena is their very lack of intrinsic existence; this constitutes the self-nature of the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena.
“The eye-element is neither bound nor liberated.
Why? Because the nature of the eye-element is the very absence of intrinsic existence (anupalabdhi-svabhāva).”
The form realm, the eye-consciousness realm, eye-contact, and all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition are neither bound nor liberated.

Why is this? Because the form realm, up to and including all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, have the nature of non-existence, which constitutes the intrinsic nature of the form realm, up to and including all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition.
“The ear-element is neither bound nor liberated.
Why is this? Because the nature of the ear-element is the very absence of intrinsic existence; such is the self-nature of the ear-element.”
The sphere of sound, the sphere of ear-consciousness, ear-contact, and all feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition are neither bound nor liberated.

Why is this? Because the sphere of sound up to the feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition have the nature of non-existence, which is the very intrinsic nature of the sphere of sound up to the feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition.
“The nose element is neither bound nor liberated.
Why is this? Because the nature of the nose element is the very absence of inherent existence, which constitutes its own intrinsic nature.”
The fragrance element, the nose-consciousness element, nose-contact, and all sensations produced with nose-contact as a condition are neither bound nor liberated.

Why is this? Because the fragrance element, up to and including the sensations produced with nose-contact as a condition, have the nature of non-existence, which is the very intrinsic nature of the fragrance element, up to and including the sensations produced with nose-contact as a condition.
"The tongue-element is neither bound nor liberated.
Why is this? Because the tongue-element has the nature of non-existence as its own intrinsic nature."
The taste element, the tongue-consciousness element, and tongue-contact, as well as all sensations produced with tongue-contact as a condition, are neither bound nor liberated.

Why is this? Because the taste element, up to and including all sensations produced with tongue-contact as a condition, have the nature of non-existence, which constitutes the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of the taste element, up to and including all sensations produced with tongue-contact as a condition.
"The body-element is neither bound nor liberated.
Why is this? Because the nature of the body-element is the very absence of any intrinsic existence of the body-element."
The sphere of tangibles, the sphere of body-consciousness, body-contact, and all feelings produced with body-contact as a condition are neither bound nor liberated.

Why is this? Because the non-existence of the sphere of tangibles up to the feelings produced with body-contact as a condition constitutes the intrinsic nature of the sphere of tangibles up to the feelings produced with body-contact as a condition.
"The mind-element is neither bound nor liberated.
Why is this? Because the nature of the mind-element is its lack of intrinsic existence; such is the self-nature of the mind-element."
The dharma-element, the mind-consciousness-element, and mental contact, as well as the various feelings produced with mental contact as a condition, are neither bound nor liberated.

Why is this? Because the dharma-element, up to and including the various feelings produced with mental contact as a condition, have the nature of non-existence, which constitutes the intrinsic nature of the dharma-element, up to and including the various feelings produced with mental contact as a condition.
"The earth element is neither bound nor liberated.
Why is this? Because the earth element has the nature of non-existence as its own intrinsic nature."
The elements of water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness are neither bound nor liberated.
Why is this? Because the nature of the elements of water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness is the very absence of intrinsic existence, which constitutes their own-being.
“Ignorance is neither bondage nor liberation.
Why is this? Because the nature of ignorance is the absence of any intrinsic existence; such is the very self-nature of ignorance.”

Volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, and old age, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are neither bound nor liberated.

Why is this? Because the nature of non-existence of the formative forces up to old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair constitutes the intrinsic nature of the formative forces up to old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair.
"The perfection of generosity is neither bound nor liberated.
Why is this? Because the perfection of generosity has the nature of non-existence as its own intrinsic nature."
The perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom are neither bound nor liberated.
Why is this? Because the nature of ethical discipline up to and including wisdom is the very self-nature of ethical discipline up to and including wisdom, being devoid of any intrinsic existence.
“Inner emptiness is neither bound nor liberated.
Why is this? Because the nature of inner emptiness is the very absence of anything therein; such is the intrinsic nature of inner emptiness.”

Outer emptiness, inner-and-outer emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate truth, the emptiness of conditioned phenomena, the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, the emptiness of dispersion, the emptiness of non-alteration, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the emptiness of specific characteristics, the emptiness of common characteristics, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of non-apprehensibility, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence are neither bound nor liberated.

Why is this? Because the non-existence of external emptiness up to the non-existence of the emptiness of the nature of non-nature constitutes the intrinsic nature of external emptiness up to the emptiness of the nature of non-nature.
“Suchness is neither bound nor liberated.
Why? Because the nature of suchness is the very absence of anything [inherently existent], which constitutes the self-nature of suchness.”

The dharma-realm, the nature of phenomena, non-falsity, immutability, equality, the state beyond birth, the fixedness of phenomena, the stability of phenomena, the limit of reality, the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm are neither bound nor liberated.

Why is this? Because the non-existent nature of the dharma-realm, up to and including the inconceivable realm, constitutes the intrinsic nature of the dharma-realm, up to and including the inconceivable realm.
"The Noble Truth of Suffering is neither bound nor liberated. Why is this?
Because the Noble Truth of Suffering has non-existence as its intrinsic nature."
The noble truths of suffering, origination, cessation, and the path are neither bound nor liberated. Why is this?
Because the noble truths of suffering, origination, cessation, and the path have the nature of non-existence as their own-being (svabhāva).
"The four dhyānas are neither bound nor liberated.
Why is this? Because the nature of non-existence is the intrinsic nature of the four dhyānas."
The four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions are neither bound nor liberated. Why is this?
Because the nature of non-existence constitutes the intrinsic nature of the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions.
“The eight liberations are neither bound nor liberated.
Why? Because the non-existence of the eight liberations constitutes their very intrinsic nature.”
The eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities are neither bound nor liberated. Why?
Because the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities have the nature of non-existence as their own intrinsic nature.
"The four foundations of mindfulness are neither bound nor liberated. Why is this?
Because the nature of non-existence constitutes the intrinsic nature of the four foundations of mindfulness."
The four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path are neither bound nor liberated. Why is this?
Because the self-nature of the four right efforts, up to and including the eightfold noble path, is the non-existence of those very things;
therefore, the gate of liberation of emptiness is neither bound nor liberated.
Why is this? Because the emptiness liberation door has the nature of non-existence as its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
The signless and wishless liberation doors are neither bound nor liberated.
Why is this? Because the signless and wishless gates of liberation, being of the nature of non-existence, constitute the intrinsic nature of the signless and wishless gates of liberation.
The ten stages of a bodhisattva are neither bound nor liberated. Why is this?
Because the non-existent nature of the ten stages of a bodhisattva constitutes their very self-nature.
“The five eyes are neither bound nor liberated.
Why is this? Because the non-existence of the five eyes constitutes their own intrinsic nature.”
The six supernormal powers are neither bound nor liberated.
Why is this? Because the six supernormal powers have the nature of non-existence as their own intrinsic nature.
“The ten powers of a Buddha are neither bound nor liberated.
Why is this? Because the nature of the ten powers of a Buddha is the absence of intrinsic existence, which constitutes the self-nature of the ten powers of a Buddha.”

The four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are neither bound nor liberated.

Why is this? Because the non-existent nature of the four fearlessnesses, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, constitutes the intrinsic nature of the four fearlessnesses, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
“The quality of non-forgetfulness is neither bound nor liberated. Why?
Because the quality of non-forgetfulness has the nature of non-existence as its own intrinsic nature.”
The state of constant abiding in equanimity is neither bound nor liberated. Why is this?
Because the state of constant abiding in equanimity has the nature of non-existence as its own intrinsic nature.
"All-knowledge is neither bound nor liberated. Why is this?
Because the nature of all-knowledge is the absence of any intrinsic existence; such is the self-nature of all-knowledge."
The knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects are neither bound nor liberated. Why is this?

Because the non-existence of the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects constitutes the intrinsic nature of the knowledge of the aspects of the path and the knowledge of all aspects.
"All dharani gates are neither bound nor liberated. Why is this?
Because the nature of non-existence is the intrinsic nature of all dharani gates."
All gateways of samādhi are neither bound nor liberated. Why is this?
Because the non-existent nature of all gateways of samādhi constitutes their very intrinsic nature.
"The fruit of stream-entry is neither bound nor liberated.
Why is this? Because the fruit of stream-entry has the nature of non-existence as its own intrinsic nature."
The fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and the fruit of arhatship are neither bound nor liberated. Why is this?
Because the non-existent nature of the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and the fruit of arhatship constitutes their own intrinsic nature.
“Pratyekabuddha-enlightenment is neither bound nor liberated.
Why is this? Because the nature of non-existence is the intrinsic nature of pratyekabuddha-enlightenment.”
"All the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are neither bound nor liberated.
Why is this? Because the non-existence of all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas constitutes the intrinsic nature of all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas."
“The unexcelled, perfect enlightenment of the Buddhas is neither bound nor liberated.
Why is this? Because the nature of non-existence constitutes the intrinsic nature of the unexcelled, perfect enlightenment of the Buddhas.”
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
The prior limit of form is neither bound nor liberated. Why is this?
The prior limit of form is the state of non-existence, because it is the intrinsic nature of the prior limit of form.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither bound nor liberated at their prior limit.

Why is this? Because the prior limit of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is the state of non-existence, which constitutes the intrinsic nature of the prior limit of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
“The prior limit of the eye-base is neither bound nor liberated.
Why? Because the prior limit of the eye-base has the nature of non-existence, which is the very self-nature of the prior limit of the eye-base.”
The ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind bases are neither bound nor liberated at their prior limit. Why is this?

Because the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind bases have no existent nature at their prior limit, for that is the very intrinsic nature of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind bases at their prior limit.
“The prior limit of the sphere of form is neither bound nor liberated.
Why? Because the prior limit of the sphere of form has the nature of non-existence, which is the very self-nature of the prior limit of the sphere of form.”
The prior limit of the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena is neither bound nor liberated.

Why is this? Because the prior limit of the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena has the nature of non-existence, which is the very intrinsic nature of the prior limit of those spheres.
“The prior limit of the eye-element is neither bound nor liberated.
Why? Because the prior limit of the eye-element has the nature of non-existence, for such is the intrinsic nature of the prior limit of the eye-element.”
The form realm, the eye-consciousness realm, eye-contact, and all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition are neither bound nor liberated at their prior limit.

Why is this? Because the prior limit of the form realm, up to and including all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, has the nature of non-existence; for such is the intrinsic nature of the prior limit of the form realm, up to and including all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition.
“The prior limit of the ear-element is neither bound nor liberated.
Why is this? Because the prior limit of the ear-element has the nature of non-existence, for it is the very self-nature of the prior limit of the ear-element.”
The sound element, the ear-consciousness element, ear-contact, and all feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition are neither bound nor liberated at their prior limit.

Why is this? Because the sound element, up to and including all feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition, have no existence at their prior limit; for that is the very nature of the sound element, up to and including all feelings produced with ear-contact as a condition, at their prior limit.
“The prior limit of the nose-element is neither bound nor liberated.
Why? Because the prior limit of the nose-element has the nature of non-existence, being the very self-nature of the prior limit of the nose-element.”
The fragrance element, the nose-consciousness element, nose-contact, and all feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition are neither bound nor liberated at their prior limit.

Why is this? Because the fragrance element, up to and including all feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition, have no existent nature at their prior limit; this is because the prior limit of the fragrance element, up to and including all feelings produced with nose-contact as a condition, is their very intrinsic nature.
"The prior limit of the tongue-element is neither bound nor liberated.
Why is this? Because the prior limit of the tongue-element has the nature of non-existence, for that is the intrinsic nature of the prior limit of the tongue-element."
The taste element, the tongue-consciousness element, tongue-contact, and all feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition were neither bound nor liberated at their prior limit.

Why is this? Because the taste element up to the feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition have no existence at their prior limit; such non-existence constitutes the very intrinsic nature of the taste element up to the feelings produced with tongue-contact as a condition at their prior limit.
"The prior limit of the body-element is neither bound nor liberated.
Why? Because the prior limit of the body-element has the nature of non-existence, being the very self-nature of the prior limit of the body-element."
The sphere of tangibles, the sphere of body-consciousness, body-contact, and the various feelings produced with body-contact as a condition were neither bound nor liberated at their prior limit.

Why is this? Because the sphere of tangibles up to the various feelings produced with body-contact as a condition have no existence at their prior limit; this is because the prior limit of the sphere of tangibles up to the various feelings produced with body-contact as a condition is their very intrinsic nature.
“The mind-element (*manodhātu*) at its prior limit is neither bound nor liberated. Why is this?
Because the mind-element at its prior limit has the nature of non-existence, which is the very intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the mind-element at its prior limit.”
The dharma-element, the mental-consciousness-element, and mental contact, as well as all feelings produced with mental contact as a condition, were neither bound nor liberated at their prior limit.

Why is this? Because the dharma-element, up to and including all feelings produced with mental contact as a condition, have the nature of non-existence at their prior limit; this is because the dharma-element, up to and including all feelings produced with mental contact as a condition, have that very [non-existent] nature as their own-being at their prior limit.
“The prior limit of the earth element is neither bound nor liberated.
Why? Because the prior limit of the earth element has the nature of non-existence, for that is the intrinsic nature of the prior limit of the earth element.”
The prior limit of the elements of water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness is neither bound nor liberated.

Why is this? Because the prior limit of the elements of water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness has the nature of non-existence, which is the very self-nature of the prior limit of the elements of water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness.
“The prior limit of ignorance is neither bound nor liberated.
Why? Because the prior limit of ignorance has the nature of non-existence, as it is the very self-nature of the prior limit of ignorance.”

Volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, becoming, birth, and old age, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are neither bound nor liberated at the prior limit.

Why is this? It is because the prior limit of volitional formations, up to old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair, has the nature of non-existence, as that is the very intrinsic nature of the prior limit of volitional formations, up to old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair.
“The prior limit of the perfection of generosity is neither bound nor liberated.
Why? Because the prior limit of the perfection of generosity has the nature of non-existence, which is the very self-nature of the prior limit of the perfection of generosity.”
The perfection of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom are neither bound nor liberated at their prior limit.

Why is this? Because the prior limit of the perfections from ethical discipline through wisdom is the non-existence of a self-nature; such is the very nature of the prior limit of the perfections from ethical discipline through wisdom.
"The prior limit of the internal emptiness is neither bound nor liberated.
Why is this? Because the prior limit of the internal emptiness has the nature of non-existence, as it is the very self-nature of the prior limit of the internal emptiness."

Outer emptiness, inner-and-outer emptiness, emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, emptiness of the ultimate truth, emptiness of the conditioned, emptiness of the unconditioned, absolute emptiness, emptiness of the limitless, emptiness of dispersion, emptiness of non-alteration, emptiness of intrinsic nature, emptiness of specific characteristics, emptiness of common characteristics, emptiness of all phenomena, emptiness of the unapprehendable, emptiness of non-existence, emptiness of intrinsic nature, and emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence—their prior limit is neither bound nor liberated.

Why is this? Because the prior limit of the emptiness of the external, up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, has as its intrinsic nature the non-existence of the prior limit of the emptiness of the external, up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature.
“Suchness is neither bound nor liberated at its prior limit. Why?
Because the non-existence of a prior limit is the very intrinsic nature of suchness.”

The dharma-realm, the nature of phenomena, non-illusory nature, non-alteration, equality, the state beyond birth, the fixedness of phenomena, the stability of phenomena, the limit of reality, the realm of space, and the inconceivable realm—these were neither bound nor liberated at the prior limit.

Why is this? Because the non-existence of a prior limit for the dharma-realm, up to and including the inconceivable realm, constitutes the intrinsic nature of the prior limit of the dharma-realm, up to and including the inconceivable realm.
"The Noble Truth of Suffering is neither bound nor liberated at its prior limit.
Why is this? Because the prior limit of the Noble Truth of Suffering has the nature of non-existence, which is the very self-nature of the prior limit of the Noble Truth of Suffering."
The noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path are neither bound nor liberated at their prior limit. Why is this?

Because the prior limit of the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path has the nature of non-existence, being the very self-nature of the prior limit of the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path.
“The prior limit of the four dhyānas is neither bound nor liberated.
Why? Because the prior limit of the four dhyānas has the nature of non-existence, which is the very self-nature of the prior limit of the four dhyānas.”
The four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions are neither bound nor liberated at their prior limit. Why is this?

Because the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions have the nature of non-existence at their prior limit; such is the intrinsic nature of the prior limit of the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions.
"The prior limit of the eight liberations is neither bound nor liberated.
